articles.text: Community members are invited to Piedmont Community Church’s Snow Day this Friday, December 22 from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. It’s a first for the church and the city. The free event is hosted by NextGen, PCC’s youth ministry, which launched last August. “No matter anyone’s faith or age, we want to spread Christmas and general holiday cheer this time of year to build relationships and goodwill in our community and have fun with our neighbors,” said Kerry Persichitte, the church’s NextGen director. With 20 tons of imported snow, the church will create two sledding hills in its parking lot behind the church, with sleds provided for both children and adults. (Bring your own if you have one ready for some winter fun.) Two bounce houses will be on-site – one gingerbread-themed and one snowman themed. Throughout the event, there will be visits with Santa, elves with free hot cocoa for children, a face painter, a balloon artist, opportunities to sing Christmas carol, a snow playground safe for toddlers to make snow angels and build snowmen, plus a Red Sauce Meatball food truck in the courtyard. There will also be donation bins throughout the church grounds for donated hats, coats, mittens and socks for adults and children. All donations will go to CityTeam Oakland. “We expect that it’ll get quite chilly, and recommend that everyone bring cold weather gear, like mittens and boots,” said Persichitte. “As it’s our first year holding this event,” she explained, “we don’t know how many people will come. But, when I held a similar one for a church in Burlingame, 1,000 people came the first year, and by year four we had 3,000.” “People love getting to know their neighbors, and we’re excited to make them feel welcome to have fun,” she added. articles.text: Luke 1:26 In the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a town in Galilee called Nazareth. Of Gabriel, the Oxford Companion To The Bible writes, “Gabriel is one of the most prominent angels in postexilic Jewish literature and in Christian texts… He is portrayed as one of seven archangels close to God’s throne. This proximity to God results in his distinctive functions. Gabriel intercedes with God for those oppressed by evil, he brings Enoch into God’s very presence, he explains mysteries about future political events and he delivers special revelations from God.” It is this latter role that he fulfills when he visits Mary and announces to her that she will be the mother of Jesus. We don’t know all that much about Mary. In all likelihood she was young. She is engaged to Joseph, whom we also don’t know much about. We also don’t know if she looked forward to this marriage with joy or with dread. Likely, she didn’t have much say in the matter. We don’t know what Gabriel thought about this assignment. The late Frederick Buechner thinks that he worried about God entrusting the Savior of the World to one who was not much more than a child herself. Was God mistaken? Was this very young woman up to the task? Was the world truly going to be healed by the faith of a frightened teenager and the child she would raise? articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) met last week to consider the type of tree that will replace an historic sequoia tree previously located at the intersection of Mountain & Bellevue Avenues. Discussion was described as “lively and knowledgeable,” by attendees of the meeting. In September, the City of Piedmont removed a prominent sequoia tree at the intersection of Bellevue and Mountain Avenues on the recommendation of multiple arborists due to a “significant lean” that posed a danger to nearby homes. The sequoia tree had been in Piedmont since 1890, making it 133 years old at the time of removal. It was also used as the city’s official Christmas tree throughout the 1930s up until the beginning of World War II. Discussion about the tree’s replacement took place at a regularly scheduled PBF meeting on December 12. “There is general recognition that the replacement tree must be special, but the conditions at the site are still quite adverse,” said Cameron Wolfe, a member of the PBF. “The traffic circle in which the tree must be planted is very small, and it has no source of water.” These restrictions have severely limited the kind of trees the foundation can consider for this site. Despite these difficult requirements, a popular frontrunner has emerged from the PBF’s spirited discussions – quercus tomontella, the Island Oak. “It is an evergreen oak that is extremely hardy and trouble-free and has very little need for water,” said Wolfe. “It is a California native, nowadays mainly found on the Channel Islands and Santa Catalina.” As a replacement option, the Island Oak has received considerable praise from members and trustees of the PBF, including Nancy Kent, Parks & Projects Manager for the City of Piedmont. Although the PBF does not have the final decision over what the tree will be, they do provide a significant amount of funding and support for beautification projects like this one, which is why their opinion is valued by city officials. At the meeting, Park Commission Chair Tom Smegal indicated the decision most likely will be made at the commission’s meeting in March. Once the Park Commission has made its selection, the PBF plans to mount a campaign to cover the cost of a choice specimen, prepare the site for planting, and care for the plant during its first two years while it gets situated. Citizens interested in the future replacement of the Sequoia tree are invited to submit their thoughts and recommendations to the Park Commission, c/o City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, or by contacting Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager, at email nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at (510) 420-3064. Staff photo A young Island Oak stands on St. James Dr. Although not fully grown at just two years old, this is the kind of tree the PBF and Parks Commission are considering as a replacement for a Sequoia tree that had to be removed due to significant deterioration. Despite these difficult requirements, a popular frontrunner has emerged from the PBF’s spirited discussions – quercus tomontella, the Island Oak. “It is an evergreen oak that is extremely hardy and trouble-free and has very little need for water,” said Wolfe. “It is a California native, nowadays mainly found on the Channel Islands and Santa Catalina.” As a replacement option, the Island Oak has received considerable praise from members and trustees of the PBF, including Nancy Kent, Parks & Projects Manager for the City of Piedmont. Although the PBF does not have the final decision over what the tree will be, they do provide a significant amount of funding and support for beautification projects like this one, which is why their opinion is valued by city officials. At the meeting, Park Commission Chair Tom Smegal indicated the decision most likely will be made at the commission’s meeting in March. Once the Park Commission has made its selection, the PBF plans to mount a campaign to cover the cost of a choice specimen, prepare the site for planting, and care for the plant during its first two years while it gets situated. Citizens interested in the future replacement of the Sequoia tree are invited to submit their thoughts and recommendations to the Park Commission, c/o City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, or by contacting Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager, at email nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at (510) 420-3064. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is sponsoring a blood drive through the American Red Cross on Saturday, December 30, from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. at the Veterans Memorial Hall, 401 Highland Avenue. Donating blood products is important to community health, according to the Red Cross. Every two seconds someone in the U.S. needs blood and or platelets, but only about 3% of age-eligible people donate each year. Blood donations through the Red Cross are used for patients in need of surgery, cancer treatment, and transfusions for blood loss from traumatic injuries. In addition to traditional blood donation, the Red Cross will also be soliciting “Power Red” donations, a new process where a specialized machine allows donors to safely donate two units of red blood cells during one donation while also returning any plasma and platelets to the donor’s body. This way, donors can give nearly twice the amount of red cells at one time and help more patients. For busy donors looking to maximize their impact on the community, Power Red donations are an effective method. Power red cell donation takes about 20-30 minutes longer than a whole blood donation and you can donate approximately every four months. Donors may select either blood donation or Power Red donation at the time of registration. To register for your appointment, visit http://RedCrossBlood. org and enter sponsor code PIEDMONT, or call 1-800-REDCROSS.

articles.text: A menorah stands in front of Community Hall as audiences prepares to sing. Scores of families from Piedmont’s Jewish community and beyond convened outside of Community Hall on Sunday morning, December 10, for the Recreation Department’s Donuts and Dreidels annual Hannukah event. Scheduled this year on the third day of Hannukah, nearly 250 people gathered to celebrate the holiday by making menorahs, playing dreidel, singing Hanukkah songs, and enjoying refreshments like sufganiyot, the traditional fried jelly donut eaten at Hannukah celebrations around the world. Bagels and cream cheese were donated by Berkeley Auto Care. For one member of the Jewish community, events like this are a wonderful way to share Hannukah with the community. “The commandment is actually to publicize the miracle,” said Rabbi Mark Bloom, Senior Rabbi at Temple Beth Abraham. “It involves bringing Hanukkah to the broader community.” At Donuts & Dreidels, Rabbi Photo by Jesse Rosenberg Bloom introduced Beth Abraham’s singing group, “Glee BA,” and led them in seven Hanukkah songs, including a favorite from recent years, “Puppy for Hanukkah” written by Oakland native and Tony-award-winning actor Daveed Diggs. “Considering the increase in anti-Semitism in the Bay Area the event means extra this year to have a community that welcomes the Jewish community and celebrates with us, and that we can do so publicly and while feeling safe,” he said.
articles.title: Donuts & Dreidels has big turnout

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is in its final week of accepting donations for the annual Toys for Tots drive through December 23. Piedmont residents are encouraged to place new unwrapped toys in donation bins at the Piedmont Fire Station. “Our annual toy drive is one of the favorite times of the year for Piedmont’s firefighters. We enjoy every time a community member brings in donations of new toys,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Working with Toys for Tots and Three Wise Men toy giveaway ensures the community’s generosity reaches as many children as possible.” Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County. Toys donated before December 8 were distributed through the US Marine Corps Reserve Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Bins will remain at City Hall for donations through December 23. New Piedmont fireman Kevin Sauder stands with a Baby Alive princess doll and a barn for toy animals, both donations to this year’s Toys for Tots drive. Photos by Echa Schneider New Piedmont fireman Christopher Kruger stands with a doll, one of many donations to this year’s toy drive.
articles.title: Toys for Tots donation bins will remain out until December 23

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District will open enrollment for the 2024-25 school year on Tuesday, January 9. articles.text: The Standards and Criteria Committee, a joint venture between Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) leaders, teachers’ union representatives and a School Board member presented to the board at its Wednesday, December 13, meeting a report on how Piedmont teachers’ pay compares to nearby districts. The report – the first comprehensive overview of pay (which includes salary and health benefits) since 2006 – found that the city ranks eighth in compensation compared to 18 other districts, paying an average of $745 per day for teachers with at least 25 years of experience. Dublin School District ranked highest for those metrics, paying an average of $806 for 185 days, while Castro Valley Unified ranked lowest, paying an average of $638 for those days. Piedmont teachers were compared with others according to highest salary and experience levels because, said representatives of the committee at the board meeting, 23% of Piedmont teachers have 25 years of experience. These representatives included Ruth Alahydoian, PUSD’s Chief Business Officer; Ariel Dolowich, PUSD’s Assistant Superintendent of Educational Services; Shoshana Beary, Wildwood Elementary School teacher; GabriMuch of the trouble in raising teacher pay owes to the fact that over half of PUSD funding depends on student enrollment, which has declined for nearly a decade. elle Kashani, Piedmont High School teacher; Linsey Sandrew, a speech and language pathologist at Havens and PUSD Preschool; and Cory Smegal, School Board member. The Standards and Criteria Committee was created last August to establish common information that the district and the teacher’s union, the Piedmont Association of Teachers, could use in labor negotiations with the shared goals of “being in the top position among unified, non-basic aid districts” and “attract[ing] and retain[ing] the highest qualified teachers,” said Smegal. “Basic aid districts” are those funded fully by property taxes rather than partly by the state. Because PUSD is not such a district, however, over half of its funding depends upon student enrollment and daily attendance, and thus its compensation goals have been hindered by a decline in enrollment and attendance numbers stretching back nearly a decade, well before the pandemic, explained Dolowich. From a peak of 2,708 students in 2015, 2,305 students were enrolled in 2023, a 15% decline. Given that Piedmont currently ranks eighth in teacher compensation, the Standards and Criteria Committee presentation before the school board concluded that “Piedmont is not currently achieving its goal of being in the top position,” as labor negotiations between the district and its teachers continue on. The committee’s full report and a presentation summarizing this report are available at bit. ly/3ve4bQY.
articles.title: First full report of Piedmont teacher pay since 2006 presented to School Board

articles.text: At its meeting on Wednesday, December 13, the Piedmont School Board re-elected Veronica Thigpen-Anderson in her current role as president which she has served since 2020, and elected new board member Lindsay Thomasson to replace current vice president Hillary Cooper. Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn continues to serve as secretary, per school district bylaws. Although not present at the meeting, Ruchi Medhekar, a new board member, was the only board member to offer extended remarks. Reading Medhekar’s written comments, Superintendent Hawn said, “Under Veronica and Hillary’s leadership this year, we have voted on a mission, vision and core values that incorporate and reflect the values of the community. We have hired a truly talented, gifted and experienced individual as our new superintendent. We have put together and passed a set of strategic priorities that will guide the board and district’s work and serve as the guidepost for the new LCAP For the next three years.” The LCAP Medhekar referred to was the Local Control and Accountability Plan, an annually updated three-year funding plan required for local school districts by the California Department of Education. “Veronica has led us through all of these hugely important processes,” Hawn continued, reading Medhekar’s remarks, “and has done so with grace, determination, and a tremendous amount of skill, doing her best to ensure that all of our voices are represented. At a time when we’re inundated with articles about how challenging it is to accomplish anything in government, I am so moved by how functional the democratic process has been in our school board.” “I would happily wax poetic about how smart, thoughtful and committed to students, staff, and administrators each of my fellow board members are and how they encourage and push me and each other to see things from different perspectives,” Hawn added, “but because someone else is graciously reading my comments, instead I will thank Hillary for her time as VP. I offer my best wishes to Veronica as she continues in her role as president, and Lindsay as she steps into the VP role. I am so grateful that I get to be a part of this board with all of you. Onward.” The Piedmont School Board re-elected Veronica Thigpen Anderson as president. The school board elected new member Lindsay Thomasson as vice president. The school board also elected Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn to serve as its secretary, per district bylaws
articles.title: School Board elects Thomasson as VP; Thigpen-Anderson remains Pres.

pages.text: 10 Wednesday, December 20, 2023 By Jay Russell The Havens Parents Club transformed Ellen Driscoll Playhouse into a Winter Fest Market on Friday, December 15 for the enjoyment of over a hundred kids, parents and siblings. The event featured the wares of local artisans for unique holiday gifts, culinary treats, and carnival games to create an inclusive holiday spirit that was fun for all. Havens Winter Fest Market a rousing success The market brought together community members and utilized the Havens main breezeway, off Highland for a social event spanning generations. The event raised funds for noble causes, and for three hours at the end of the week, time sprawled to a cheerful winter’s pace. “We are so proud of the Havens Parents Club family engagement team, led by Raquel Navarro, for a beautiful event A big crowd circled through the booths inside the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse which was decorated with student artwork overhead and on the walls. Will Kennedy (right) on bass, Alden Meil on sax and Ryan St. John on drums played provided just the right vibe at Havens WinterFest. Piedmonters Jordan and Joel DiGiorgio own Arthur Mac’s pizza place at MLK and 40th in Oakland. 4th grader Logan Piotrowski (left) with Sarah Eisemon, the TriSchool SERVES Coordinator. Anne Wheeler with daughter Izzy at the Salty Sisters Bakeshop booth. Raquel Navarro (left) sells tamales while June Groboske sells latkes. Erin Burrise’s botanically infused preserves has turned into a full-time business called Berry and Thyme. Kathie-Louise Clarke of Persephone Prints [Friday] afternoon,” said Parent Club President Brook Meakins. “It was incredibly successful in bringing together our community, helping raise funds, and celebrating winter.” Shortly after the vendors opened their stalls inside, the three-piece jazz combo of Ryan St. John, Alden Meil and Will Kennedy broke into tune outside. The band of PHS seniors played provided a classy and energetic soundtrack for the family affair. Arthur Mac’s pizza restaurant owned by a Piedmont High grad brought its cooked pizza inside the auditorium. Food options included cookies, muffins, jams, latkes and tamales. Havens Parent Club member June Groboske acquired the latkes from Saul’s Restaurant and Deli in Berkeley, with proceeds being given to support Piedmont teachers’ salaries. Havens mom Sarah Eisemon had a booth at Winter Fest for SERVES, the service group for elementary school students. Eisemon and her Havens’ 4th and 5th grade enrichment group were selling elephant greeting cards. Vendors at Winter Fest included Piedmont mom Anne Wheeler who sold cookies and baked goods with daughter Izzy. She went to culinary school before becoming the mother of three children and has started up Salty Sisters Bakeshop. Whether there for the food, carnival games, raffle or to pick up a holiday present, Havens Winter Fest Market pleased a large crowd and celebrated the holiday spirit.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Staff Photos The Highlanders look to regroup after a tough loss to University. Piedmont took a tough onesided 93-61 loss against University on Tuesday, December 12. The Red Devils, currently 7-2, entered the season as among the top teams in the Division 3 North Coast Section. Piedmont has one game left in December, against Novato on Friday, December 22. Once the Highlanders return from winter break, they look ahead to the start of the Western Alameda County Conference schedule with games against Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, January 4 and defending league champion, Berkeley, two days later on January 6. Despite the loss to University, sophomore Dillon Casey had a productive game with 21 points. The Red Devils won last year’s Div. 4 NCS title and reached the second round of the CIF State tournament. Game Recap Piedmont trailed 22-13 by the end of the first quarter and 49-24 at halftime. The Highlanders allowed 24 points to the Red Devils in the third quarter while they put up 17 points of their own to trail 73-41 going into the fourth, closing out with 20 more points in the final going while also allowing 20 for the 93-61 final. In the first quarter, Piedmont actually opened productively and briefly held an 8-6 lead, but it marked the only time the Highlanders held the advantage. The closest it got was University holding a 14-13 in the early minutes with help of three 3-pointers by Casey—who scored 11 of PHS’ 13 points. The Red Devils closed the quarter on a nine-point scoring run. In the second, Piedmont opened with a 3-pointer to make the deficit 22-16, but University then went on a 14-1 scoring run to lead handily 36-17. Most of Piedmont’s production came in the second half with 37 points, Senior Brit Burden put up seven points in the third while Casey had six, including a pair of 3-pointers by Burden and one by the sophomore guard. Final stats: Casey scored 21 points, Burden scored 14, Ravi Silverberg had 12, Cash Panico and Arjun Bornstein scored four. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-5) hosts Novato in Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, December 22 at 7:00 p.m. Ravi Silverberg scored 12 points against the Red Devils. Arjun Bornstein looks to make a play.
articles.title: Piedmont loses by 30 to University

articles.text: Louisa Symkowick had a goal and assist versus the Pirates, while she also had an assist against Mt. Eden. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team continues to pile up the goals through the first four games of the season, winning 4-0 over Mt. Eden on the road in Hayward on Wednesday, December 13, and posting a 3-0 shutout of San Leandro at Burrell Field two days later. The pair of matches brings the Highlanders’ record to 4-0-0 to start the year with a goal-differential of +17 with just one goal allowed. It was productive games for Julianna Thornborrow and Louisa Symkowick. Thornborrow had a goal and assist against San Leandro, and Symkowick scored a goal and had an assist against both the Pirates and Monarchs. Lola Biehn led the attack against Mt. Eden, with two goals and an assist. Piedmont has one match before the end of the year, with Arroyo this week on Thursday. When they return from Winter Break, the Highlanders travel to Castro Valley for their first Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division match. 3-0 over San Leandro San Leandro attempted to start the game early with a high defensive line to stifle Piedmont’s aggressive attack, but it left their back line vulnerable for counter attacks. It didn’t take the Highlanders long to get on the board with a pair of early goals by Julianna Thornborrow and Louisa Symkowick on plays in transition. On Thornborrow’s goal, winger Ryo Woltag played a pass to Sykowick, who sent a forward pass to Thornborrow unmarked, wheeling the ball into the penalty area before unloading a right footed shot. Symkowick’s goal came unconventionally, wheeling down the right side before sending a low cross into the box. Her pass took a deflection off a defender’s foot, redirecting the ball into the net for an own goal. Staff Photos Lola Biehn scored twice and had an assist against Mt. Eden. In the second half, Thornborrow and wingback Elle Ruegg connected on a nice goal, when Thornborrow sent a low-cross toward Ruegg charging into the penalty area, slotting away her shot into net. 4-0 over Mt. Eden After an onslaught of shots in the early minutes, Lola Biehn broke the deadlock after receiving a through-ball from Symkowick to put her team on the board, 1-0, with a shot on the first touch. For the second goal, Symkowick played a sharp pass to Hannah Sullivan, who redirected the pass on her first touch to Biehn, allowing her to make an incisive run through the defense. Biehn scored on a right-footed shot on her first touch with a defender draped on her. Piedmont’s third goal came on a play where the Biehn played a poor header off of Mt. Eden’s center back, playing her own header over the Monarch’s back line toward Sullivan, who took one touch to score on a low shot past the keeper. The Highlanders’ final goal came in the second half on an own-goal by the Monarch’s defense. Thornborrow sent a pass towards Biehn, but the defender played the ball off the mark towards her keeper. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-0-0) host Arroyo at Estuary Park in Alameda tomorrow, December 21, for their final game before winter break at 7:00 p.m. Elle Ruegg scored against Mt. Eden.
articles.title: Highlanders record shutouts against Mt. Eden, San Leandro

articles.text: When mention current athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can get easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers in college. In this week’s edition, we take a look at Izzy Epstein at Chapman University, Parker Terrill at the University of California, and Claire Dean at Stanford. with a 1.36 ERA, 123 innings pitched, and 187 strikeouts. She finished the season with 15 complete games, threw a perfect game against Hayward, and recorded an astonishing 19 strikeouts in Piedmont’s 10-1 win over Arcata in the first round of the D4 NCS Playoffs. She led the team to an 18-7 overall record and a perfect 10-0 against Shoreline teams on their way to a league title where they defeated Encinal 8-5.With the bat in her hands, Epstein hit .368 with 25 hits and four home runs – the first four of her high school career. Epstein was also the Post’s honorable mention for Freshman of the Year in 2019 and Sophomore of the Year in 2020. Parker Terrill Track & Field, UC Berkeley Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, finished his freshman track and field season at the University of California. Terrill was a record-setting Pole Vaulter at Piedmont High and continues his focus as a decathlete in college. He’s clocked a 100 meter dash time of 11.44, a 400 meter time of 52.41, clocked a 5:07.31 in the 1500, 1.75 meters in the high jump, 6.55 meters in the long jump, 38 meters in the discus, 37.02 meters in the javelin, 10.98 meters for the shot put, and 16 feet, 5.25 inches in the pole vault. Terrill competed in the 2023 Pac-12 Championship in the Pole Vault, finishing 10th with a height of 16 feet, 3.5 inches. He departed from Piedmont High as the school’s all-time record holder in the pole vault with a height of 16 feet, 1 inch, 2 feet, 1 inch higher than Marshall Wentworth’s record set in 2011. In the 4x400, Terrill made more history with a time of 3:21.77 as the anchor leg on a team with Alban, Cooper Downing, and Long. They broke a 33-year old record pf a team anchored by. Photo courtesy of Chapman University Softball pitcher Izzy Epstein, PHS Class of 2022, finished her freshman season at Chapman University with a sterling 1.77 ERA. As a freshman pitcher on the softball team, she helped lead her school to a 26-15 record, including a SCIAC Tournament Championship appearance, where they lost 2-1 in 10 innings to Redlands. In 2023, Epstein made 12 appearances and totaled 23.2 innings, carrying a sterling 1.77 ERA with 15 strikeouts and just six earned runs allowed. She was the Post’s 2022 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year after being the WACC Shoreline’s Pitcher of the Year, going 12-1 regular as a senior Photo courtesy of Cal Athletics Decathlete Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is entering her sophomore year on Cal’s track and field team. Piedmont Hall of Fame runner Gordon Johnson. Terrill was named our Co-Athlete of the Year in 2022 by the Post. As a freshman, she earned a 9.775 on the high bar at the Super 14 Invitational in her first collegiate routine, and was 10th of 24 athletes. She also earned a 9.625 on the beam, and was 11th of 24 on her floor routine, scoring a 9.825. [From January 2021] It marks for a perfect location to watch the giant +15-foot waves The Tule Elk State Natural forecasted for Christmas weekReserve can be found north of end. Tomales Bay State Park and the small town of Inverness in the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Sunday’s High Surf Advisory along the California coast made for terrific wave-watching. Taking the five mile hike to Tomales Point Taking the 9.7 out-and-back Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay which overlooks remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific coast to your left and Tomales Bay and Dillon Beach to your right. The hike starts at Pierce Point Ranch, a historic farmstead of the Pt. Reyes Peninsula that has informative markers to describe the early dairy farming culture of the area. The five mile walk to Tomales Point is adjacent to the Tule Elk Reserve, where tou will see herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves. The ending is a bluff overlooking tidepools and an array of pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while redtailed hawks and turkey vultures. The main attraction, the Tule Elk, are native to Central California and regarded as the smallest subspecies of elk. They were a big part of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore’s induction in 1976. At that time, the species faced local extinction due to hunting in the 1850s. In the fall of 1978, the National Park Service released 17 elk into the area after converting decommissioned farmland into a reserve. Now an estimated 400 elk graze in the area. On the popular destination due to the elk, we passed 133 people on Sunday late morning, and counted another 68 on the way back to the car. The area is located along the wind-swept region of Bodega Bay on the ridgeline of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Without any tree coverage, visitors should wear proper attire given the likelihood of high winds, fog, and the possibility of rain.. The trip was a total of 10-1/2 miles and an elevation gain of 1,336 feet. To locate this hike, punch in “Tomales Point Trailhead” or “Pierce Point Ranch” to your GPS device. articles.text: Emmy and Tony Award winner Billy Crudup will reprise his award-winning role in David Cale’s Harry Clarke at Berkeley Repertory Theatre now through Saturday, December 23. This wickedly funny thriller by Obie Award-winning writer David Cale features the exploits of Philip, an awkward Midwestern man, who leads an outrageous double life as the smug Londoner Harry Clarke. He moves to New York City and, posing as the alluring Harry, charms his way into a wealthy family. Soon, his impetuous and dangerous behavior threatens to unravel more than his persona. Crudup (Coast of Utopia, No Man’s Land, The Morning Show, Almost Famous) returns to Berkeley Rep in a tour-de-force solo performance helmed by Obie Award-winning director Leigh Silverman (Suffs, Violet, Soft Power, In the Wake). Reprising his acclaimed performance, Crudup plays 19 different characters in the play. Harry Clarke had its world premiere at Off-Broadway New York venue Vineyard Theatre in 2017. For his performance, Crudup won an Outer Critics Circle Award, Off-Broadway Alliance Award, Lucille Lortel Award, Drama Desk Award and Obie Award, and was nominated for a Drama League Award. “In addition to his justifiably lauded performances in film and television, in projects from Almost Famous to Spotlight to The Morning Show, Billy Crudup is one of the greatest stage actors of his generation,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Emmy and Tony Award winner Billy Crudup stars in David Cale’s Harry Clarke at Berkeley Repertory Theatre now through December 30. Pfaelzer. “I have been lucky enough to watch his work over the last 30 years, and he just gets better and better,” she added. “His performance as Harry Clarke is definitive, filled with charm and wit and skill. What Billy, Leigh and David have made together is a true theatrical delight, and I can’t wait to welcome them back to Berkeley Rep.” Tickets ($110 - $314) for the performance at Berkeley Rep’s Roda Theater (2015 Addison St.) are available at berkeleyrep.org, or through the box office at 647- 2949. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker returns to the War Memorial Opera House with performances through Saturday, December 30. Experience the magical winter wonderland of toy soldiers, King of the Mice, Sugar Plum Fairy, and much more. This dazzling production is a kaleidoscope of over 150 dancers accompanied by the SF Ballet Orchestra performing Tchaikovsky’s beloved score. As the first American company to present a full-length production of Nutcracker in 1944, SF Ballet paved the way for the work to become an American holiday classic. The current version is set in San Francisco in 1915 during the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, with choreography by previous SF Ballet Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson, scenic design by Tony Award winner Michael Yeargan, costume design by Tony Award winner Martin Pakledinaz, lighting design by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. The Principal Dancers are Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, and Aaron Robison; and soloist Jasmine Jimison and Corps de Ballet member Mingxuan Wang in the iconic roles of the Sugar Plum Fairy, Grand Pas de Deux, and Queen and King of the Snow. Nutcracker transforms San Francisco into an early twentieth century realm of dreams and fantasy; audience members can even spot an ode to the city’s iconic Painted Ladies in Act 1. Since its founding in 1933 as the oldest professional ballet company in the United States, the SF Ballet has been an innovator and an originator of beloved cultural traditions, from staging the first American performance of Swan Lake to bringing this annual holiday production of Nutcracker to audiences across the U.S. Tickets for matinee and evening performances ($25-$398) for Nutcracker at the War Memorial Opera House, 301 Van Ness Avenue, are available online at sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker or through the SF Ballet box office at 415-865-2000. 12-MONTHS FINANCING 0% INTEREST WE PAY TAX SALE* *on all installed jobs CL#788850

The concert invites audiences to experience the diversity and vibrancy of French music, traversing from the Impressionist era to contemporary times. French Reverie is the second of four Symphonic Series performances by Berkeley Symphony, and will feature the acclaimed Dr. Robert Young on saxophone. The concert will feature the evocative beauty of Claude Debussy’s Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, a symphonic poem that vividly translates words into sound. A Kind of Trane by Guillaume Connesson pays tribute to jazz legend John Coltrane, blending classical elements with jazz influences. In a testament to her pioneering creworks to life, from poetry, jazz, and even other composers,” said Joseph Young, Music Director of Berkeley Symphony. “I also have the joy of introducing Berkeley to someone I’ve known and loved for a very long time,” he added. “My brother, saxophonist Dr. Robert Young, will make his Berkeley Symphony debut in Connesson’s A Kind of Trane.” Ticketholders can arrive early for a free pre-concert chat at 3 p.m., one hour before the show. This engaging pre-concert talk will provide fascinating insights into the music of French Reverie. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony presents two festive movies with live performances this week with the film Home Alone played with a live score on Friday, December 22 and December 23 and A Charlie Brown Christmas played with a live score tonight through December 23. First, see the beloved holiday movie Home Alone on the big screen as never before. Directed by Chris Columbus and with a music score by John Williams, the San Francisco Symphony will be conducted bv Joshua Gersen. Pacific Boychoir and Ragazzi Boys Chorus will perform with the Symphony. The highest-grossing holiday film of all time, and starring an adorable Macaulay Culkin, this hilarious and heartwarming comedy is holiday fun for the entire family. A Charlie Brown Christmas returns to Davies Symphony Hall with conductor Lawrence Loh leading the San Francisco Symphony and Chorus in four performances that bring the classic Christmas animated TV special to life. The presentation features Vince Guaraldi’s iconic score, an animated backdrop of the film, as well as on-stage singers, actors and dancers that embody Charles Schulz’s beloved Peanuts characters. The Charlie Brown program opens with a selection of holiday favorites performed by Loh, the San Francisco Symphony, and the San Francisco Symphony Chorus, including Edward Pola and George Wyle’s It’s the Most Wonderful Time of the Year, Irving Berlin’s White Christmas, John Debney’s Elf Suite, ‘Twas the Night Before Christmas with dancers and narrator Michael Covert. Tickets for Home Alone ($112.50 - $375) and A Charlie Brown Christmas ($24.50 - $300) are available at sfsymphony.org, or through the box office at 415- 864-6000. A Charlie Brown Christmas returns to the SF Symphony this week, along with live scored performances of Home Alone. articles.text: From December 28 through December 31, Colombian Jazz-fusion group Monsieur Periné will perform for four nights at SF Jazz. The group specializes in a signature blend of 1920s-era guitar-driven jazz, Latin American pop, and Afro-Colombian cumbia. Audiences may also watch the December 29 & 30 performances from home through the venue’s streaming service, “SF Jazz at Home,” for $5/month. The band’s performance on New Year’s Eve will also include audience party favors, specially-created visuals projected on stage, and a countdown to 2024. All performances will include dance floor tickets as well as balcony and main floor seating. Since its formation in 2008, the seven-piece band has cultivated a fervent following by blending the spirit of 1930s jazz music with the joyous and sophisticated sounds of contemporary Latin American pop – a boundary-blurring approach that prompted the LA Weekly to hail them as “one of the most exciting emerging artists in Latin music.” Since their entry onto the world stage, the band has earned a Latin Grammy Award for “Best New Artist,” played one of the most popular performances in NPR’s Tiny Desk Concert series, and released a hit single, “Nuestra Canción,” which went viral online in 2021. SF Jazz is located at 201 Franklin St in San Francisco. Tickets may be purchased online at www. sfjazz.org, over the phone at (866) 920-5299, or in-person at the SF Jazz box office. Ticket prices will vary based on seat location. Balcony seats will be between $30- $50, main floor and terrace seats will be between $30-$70, and all dance floor tickets will be $50. The Bogotá-based jazz-fusion ensemble Monsieur Periné performs on their latest tour.

articles.text: The first-ever exhibition dedicated to the drawings of Renaissance painter Sandro Botticelli will be on view at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor through February 11, 2024. The exhibition, simply titled Botticelli Drawings traces the painter’s artistic journey through rough sketches and studies dating from his apprenticeship under Fra Filippo to the operation of his own workshop in Florence. Notably, Botticelli Drawings features rarely seen and newly attributed works from the artist in its display. Although Botticelli was an expert draftsman, his surviving drawings are surprisingly scarce, with fewer than thirty securely attributed sheets in existence today. In a unique reunion of his art pieces, Botticelli’s Adoration of the Magi (c.1475) will be displayed side-by-side with one of his preparatory drawings of the famous painting, allowing audiences a deeper glimpse into the artist’s creative process for the first time in 500 years. Known for some of the world’s greatest paintings, including Birth of Venus (c. 1486), Botticelli (c. 1445-1510) has had an enduring influence on contemporary culture, from art and design to dance, music, fashion, and film. His art has inspired artists including Andy Warhol, Jean Onlookers (c. 1500) is a fragment of a preparatory drawing for Botticelli’s Adoration of the Magi, reunited with its final work for the first time in more than 500 years. Paul Gaultier, Cindy Sherman, and Salvador Dalí. The Legion of Honor is located at 100 34th Ave in San Francisco. Tickets can be purchased online

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum is displaying The Heart of Zen through December 31, an exhibition featuring two traditional ink paintings on display in the United States for the first time. The featured art works, Six Persimmons and Chestnuts, are attributed to the 13th-century monk Muqi. These historic compositions were painted in China but have been in Japan where they have been designated as important cultural properties and displayed at Daitokuji Ryokoin Zen temple in Kyoto. The exhibit now in San Francisco explores the history and significance of these paintings, their place in temple life, and their eventual elevation as classic examples of Zen art in the United States. The museum is displaying each painting individually, one at a time, for three weeks only. Chestnuts will be displayed through December 31, but Six Persimmons is no longer being shown. Space for the exhibit is limited, and entry into this special exhibition is on a first-come, firstserve basis. The Asian Art Museum is located at 200 Larkin St. in San Francisco and is open to the public Thursday – Monday from 10 a.m. – 5 p.m. The museum is closed on Tuesday and Wednesday. Tickets may be purchased online at www.asianart.org. For questions about admissions to the museum, contact (415) 581- 3500. The museum encourages attendees to purchase tickets in advance. Photo by Asian Art Museum SF Chestnuts (left), sits side-by-side with Six Persimmons, both works of the 13th-century monk, Muqi. Chestnuts will remain on display through December 31.

articles.text: Trio Solano, an award-winning ensemble consisting of wellknown Bay Area musicians, will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, January 13 at 7 p.m. Trio Solano founders Dan Flanagan (violin), Paul Ehrlich (viola), and Vicky Ehrlich (cello) will be joined by guest artist Michael Seth Orland on piano. While these long-time friends have performed countless times together in the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, their first performance as Trio Solano was a live-stream for Music on the Hill in October 2020. They have since performed throughout the Bay Area. Trio Solano received a grant in 2021 from InterMusic SF to record a video of Dan Flanagan’s composition “Ehrlichia,” Rhapsody in Discomfort #6 for Youtube, which has received thousands of views and brought catharsis to hundreds of Lyme Disease victims. In 2022, they received a Silver Medal for that performance from Global Music Awards. In 2023, Trio Solano received a second grant from InterMusic SF to commission Cindy Cox to compose a trio inspired by the art and poetry of John Campion, and record it for the album, The Bow and the Brush Volume II, which will be released by MSR Classics. Dan Flanagan has built a multifaceted career as a soloist, composer and orchestral musician, performing concertos with orchestras in California and recitals throughout the United States and Europe. Flanagan currently serves as Concertmaster of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera, Concertmaster of West Edge Opera, and Instructor of Violin at University of California, Berkeley. The 2023-24 season includes solo recitals at the Center for New Music in SF, Boston University, Carnegie Hall, University of Rome, and The American Library in Paris. His program, The Bow and the Brush, includes 23 newly composed solo violin pieces inspired by paintings and sculptures. Already performed in New York City, San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, Sacramento, Riverside, San Diego, Eugene, Denton, Houston, Chicago, Rome, Perugia, London, Bordeaux, and Paris, sixteen of these pieces can be heard on his album, The Bow and the Brush, released by MSR Classics. Flanagan has performed as Concertmaster with the Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, California Symphony, California Musical Theater, Festival Opera of Walnut Creek, Symphony San Jose, Modesto Symphony, Opera Paralelle, and Symphony Napa Valley. He performs regularly with the San Francisco Opera and Ballet and records film, video game, and television soundtracks with the Skywalker Symphony Orchestra. In addition to performing with Trio Solano, he’s a member of the Eco Ensemble and was a founding member of the Farallon Quintet. Paul Ehrlich is a member of The San Francisco Ballet Orchestra; he also performs frequently with The San Francisco Opera Orchestra and San Francisco Symphony. His previous positions have included The Saint Paul Chamber Orchestra and Phoenix Symphony. A frequent chamber music performer, he is a member of The Sacramento Chamber Music Society and collaborates with several other Bay Area chamber groups. Dr. Ehrlich was educated at The Royal College of Music, London, Cambridge University, and Yale School of Music, where he completed the Doctor of Musical

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers last week included Noemi Alvarado, Adrienne Hamlin, Kathy Rolfson, Lisa Euphrat, Elizabeth Richter, Kat Lang, Phil Witte, Chuck Oraftik, Sherry Jacobs, Charlene Louie, Martin Levy, Bill Ahern, Rob Smith, Joyce Ahern, Brenda Ferrero, Meghan Bennett, Nancy Henn, Helene Farber, Jim Kellogg, Sharona Fischrup, Mark Davis, Pat Keller, Jim Kuo, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Joanne Larson, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Carole Lyons, Sarah Johnson, Ken Young, Alissa Quan, Christine Calliste, Dottie Hutch, Claudine Bach, FangFang Lei, and Dick Carter. The walkers were pleased Carole Lyons brought Christina Miller, and that daughter and mother, Stefanie Chung and Irmhild Liang, were with the group for the first time. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group had another great, late fall morning for their walk on December 13. It was cool, but sunny, perfect for walking. There was a strong turnout of 42 walkers, but no K-9 best friends. It had been over a year since Charlene Louie had taken the group on a tour of the streets that were on the Key System’s 10 Line streetcar route firm the early 20th century. Charlene shared that in the 1890s the area that would become Piedmont was largely dairy farms and open space. As the East Bay’s population grew, land developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate.” In 1895, it acquired 13,000 acres of undeveloped land in the East Bay from North Berkeley to San Leandro. To sell this land, transportation had to be provided within the communities and to San Francisco. Smith and Havens’ transportation system was a consolidation of several streetcar lines that they assembled in the late 1890s and early 1900s. In 1897, they acquired a cable car line in Piedmont and East Bay, which had been electrified. The Key System was founded and incorporated in 1902 as the San Francisco, Oakland, and San Jose Railway. It was marketed as “the Key System” because its East Bay routes looked like circles on the top of a key. Its first service was from downtown Berkeley to the ferry pier in 1903, and their Piedmont service started in 1904. The system connected the East Bay to San Francisco with a pier on the Bay where passengers boarded a ferry to San Francisco. After the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, Key System trains ran on the lower deck of the bridge, with the upper deck for cars going both east and west. Piedmont had three streetcar lines, the Numbers 10, 11, and 12. The 10 line went from downtown Oakland along Broadway to the Piedmont Avenue station at 41st along Pleasant Valley and Grand Avenues through central Piedmont and what is now the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton. The Key System streetcars were discontinued and replaced by buses in 1948, and the trains to San Francisco were stopped in 1958. The system provided mass transit in the cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Emeryville, Piedmont, San Leandro, Richmond, Albany, and El Cerrito from 1903 until 1960, when it was sold to a newly formed public agency, AC Transit. Charlene led the walkers down Highland Avenue to Park Way to explore the lower Piedmont portion of the 10 route. Along this section of Highland there are four lanes because it had to accommodate streetcars, horses and buggies, and later cars. However, at Park, Highland narrows to two lanes because the 10 turned down Park. Charlene had a 1943 photo of a 10 car with a Highland Avenue home in the background. The walkers thought this same home’s steps were a fun spot for a group photo. The trains went down Park Way’s hill, and over to what is now Ramona and Arroyo Avenues. The group walked down Park, recognizing the designs of the older homes on the left side and the newer mid-century homes on the right. These infill homes were built after the trains stopped running and the system’s right-of-way land was sold for home construction. The walkers took a 107-foot path from Park up to Ramona and followed Ramona to Monticello Avenue. They noted a hidden pathway that goes up to the Lorita Avenue cul-de-sac, The group passed Charlene’s home on Arroyo, and went on York Drive to a 272-foot path at Holly Place that took them up to Ricardo Avenue. From there, it was up El Cerrito Avenue to Magnolia and back to the Exedra. The group agreed the walk had been a perfect 10. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
articles.title: Wed. Walkers explore former No. 10 Line

articles.text: Ah, the French Riviera! The sun, the sea, the art! What could possibly go wrong? Wait. Wasn’t the Riviera the setting for Alfred Hitchcock’s To Catch a Thief, in which a very great deal went wrong for its star, Cary Grant? Let’s think again: there’s money on the Riviera, so there must be guys with itchy fingers who long to get their mitts on it. Earning it is for suckers, and stealing it is dicey. Why not trick its owners out of it instead? That’s exactly what con men, Lawrence Jamieson (Michael Caine) and Freddy Benson (Steve Martin) collaborate to do in the 1988 comedy, Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, directed by Frank Oz. The film is a reworking of 1964’s Bedtime Story, which starred Marlon Brando and David Niven, and Piedmont moviegoers got to take a look at the remake at last week’s Second Thursday Film Fest. Jamieson and Benson’s association is a prickly one. The deft and classy Jamieson doesn’t take to Benson’s brash style, but after attempting to get rid of him, he decides to work with him for a while. That doesn’t pan out, so they agree on a bet: the first to con $50,000 out of a selected sucker wins, and the other has to pack up and leave town. They target new arrival Janet Colgate (Glenn Headley), the seemingly naïve “United States Soap Queen.” The climax of the movie arrives when Colgate turns out, to be, just like Jamieson and Benson, not what she seems. Dirty Rotten Scoundrels is alternately sophisticated and slapsticky, and the Thursday audience enjoyed watching actors Caine and Martin play off one another. Mike Gallant introduced the movie by describing how the pair competed on set to see which could make the other laugh during filming. Walkers explore former No. 10 Line Scoundrels spark smiles First Thursday Film Fest screens classic crime comedy By Bob Hall Ah, the French Riviera! The sun, the sea, the art! What could possibly go wrong? Wait. Wasn’t the Riviera the setting for Alfred Hitchcock’s To Catch a Thief, in which a very great deal went wrong for its star, Cary Grant? Let’s think again: there’s money on the Riviera, so there must be guys with itchy fingers who long to get their mitts on it. Earning it is for suckers, and stealing it is dicey. Why not trick its owners out of it instead? That’s exactly what con men, Lawrence Jamieson (Michael Caine) and Freddy Benson (Steve Martin) collaborate to do in the 1988 comedy, Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, directed by Frank Oz. The film is a reworking of 1964’s Bedtime Story, which starred Marlon Brando and David Niven, and Piedmont moviegoers got to take a look at the remake at last week’s Second Thursday Film Fest. Jamieson and Benson’s association is a prickly one. The deft and classy Jamieson doesn’t take to Benson’s brash style, but after attempting to get rid of him, he decides to work with him for a while. That doesn’t pan out, so they agree on a bet: the first to con $50,000 out of a selected sucker wins, and the other has to pack up and leave town. They target new arrival Janet Colgate (Glenn Headley), the seemingly naïve “United States Soap Queen.” The climax of the movie arrives when Colgate turns out, to be, just like Jamieson and Benson, not what she seems. Dirty Rotten Scoundrels is alternately sophisticated and slapsticky, and the Thursday audience enjoyed watching actors Caine and Martin play off one another. Mike Gallant introduced the movie by describing how the pair competed on set to see which could make the other laugh during filming. The walkers were pleased Carole Lyons brought Christina Miller, and that daughter and mother, Stefanie Chung and Irmhild Liang, were with the group for the first time. By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group had another great, late fall morning for their walk on December 13. It was cool, but sunny, perfect for walking. There was a strong turnout of 42 walkers, but no K-9 best friends. It had been over a year since Charlene Louie had taken the group on a tour of the streets that were on the Key System’s 10 Line streetcar route firm the early 20th century. Charlene shared that in the 1890s the area that would become Piedmont was largely dairy farms and open space. As the East Bay’s population grew, land developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate.” In 1895, it acquired 13,000 acres of undeveloped land in the East Bay from North Berkeley to San Leandro. To sell this land, transportation had to be provided within the communities and to San Francisco. Smith and Havens’ transportation system was a consolidation of several streetcar lines that they assembled in the late 1890s and early 1900s. In 1897, they acquired a cable car line in Piedmont and East Bay, which had been electrified. The Key System was founded and incorporated in 1902 as the San Francisco, Oakland, and San Jose Railway. It was marketed as “the Key System” because its East Bay routes looked like circles on the top of a key. Its first service was from downtown Berkeley to the ferry pier in 1903, and their Piedmont service started in 1904. The system connected the East Bay to San Francisco with a pier on the Bay where passengers boarded a ferry to San Francisco. After the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, Key System trains ran on the lower deck of the bridge, with the upper deck for cars going both east and west. Piedmont had three streetcar lines, the Numbers 10, 11, and 12. The 10 line went from downtown Oakland along Broadway to the Piedmont Avenue station at 41st along Pleasant Valley and Grand Avenues through central Piedmont and what is now the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton. The Key System streetcars were discontinued and replaced by buses in 1948, and the trains to San Francisco were stopped in 1958. The system provided mass transit in the cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Emeryville, Piedmont, San Leandro, Richmond, Albany, and El Cerrito from 1903 until 1960, when it was sold to a newly formed public agency, AC Transit. Charlene led the walkers down Highland Avenue to Park Way to explore the lower Piedmont portion of the 10 route. Along this section of Highland there are four lanes because it had to accommodate streetcars, horses and buggies, and later cars. However, at Park, Highland narrows to two lanes because the 10 turned down Park. Charlene had a 1943 photo of a 10 car with a Highland Avenue home in the background. The walkers thought this same home’s steps were a fun spot for a group photo. The trains went down Park Way’s hill, and over to what is now Ramona and Arroyo Avenues. The group walked down Park, recognizing the designs of the older homes on the left side and the newer mid-century homes on the right. These infill homes were built after the trains stopped running and the system’s right-of-way land was sold for home construction. The walkers took a 107-foot path from Park up to Ramona and followed Ramona to Monticello Avenue. They noted a hidden pathway that goes up to the Lorita Avenue cul-de-sac, The group passed Charlene’s home on Arroyo, and went on York Drive to a 272-foot path at Holly Place that took them up to Ricardo Avenue. From there, it was up El Cerrito Avenue to Magnolia and back to the Exedra. The group agreed the walk had been a perfect 10. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Piedmont Seniors gather at Golden Gate Fields: (front) Carol Warren (left), Sue Getreuer, Mona Jamieson, Madeline Moore, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer; (back) Jim Ayotte, Fred Pemberton, Gregory Jurin, and Carole Jones. Not pictured: Larry and Patti Singer, Carla Betts, and Elizabeth Sussman. Fifteen members of the Piedmont Seniors attended a “Day at the Races” on Saturday, November 18 at picturesque Golden Gate Fields in Albany. The group was anxious to get a last opportunity to try their luck before the venerable racetrack closes. The track was originally scheduled to close in 2023, but there has been an extension into mid-2024. After that time, the horses will head to Southern California leaving Northern California without a racetrack. It was a relaxing day for the Seniors as they sat in the Turf Club atop the track. Along with having a wonderful view of the track, the restaurant also offers breathtaking views of the East Bay Hills. Even though the food and admission has increased over time, the bets remain at a reasonable $2.00. No one from the group came out a big winner (nor a big loser), but everyone had a great time. The Turf Club still offers an occasional buffet luncheon, but it has become rather expensive at $99/person. Golden Gate Fields is a great place to take out-of-town visitors or to host a special event, such as a birthday or an anniversary party, as it is close to Piedmont. Competitive horse racing in this part of the East Bay originated in 1871 with the Oakland Trotting Track. It was forced to close in 1911 when the state banned horse racing. However, in 1933 the state repealed the ban on horse racing. Then, just before World War II, Golden Gate Fields built a new grandstand and held its inaugural race on February 1, 1941. In the period just before the war, the track was used as the scene of the crime in the movie Shadow of the Thin Man. With the onset of World War II, the U.S. Navy took over the property as the Naval Landing Force Equipment Depot, storing hundreds of landing craft destined for use in the Pacific theater. After the war, Golden Gate Fields resumed horse racing. Golden Gate Fields made history in 2016 when it hired 29-year-old Angela Hermann as its track announcer, succeeding Michael Wrona. Hermann was the first full-time female race caller in the United States since Ann Elliott in the 1960s at Jefferson Downs near New Orleans. Golden Gate Fields, a one-mile synthetic track course, currently has stalls for 1,420 horses, has a main grandstand with seating for about 8,000 patrons, a clubhouse with seating for about 5,200 customers, and a Turf Club with seating for about 1,500 people. Historical highlights Golden Gate Fields also has had plenty of highlights. In 1957, the horse Silky Sullivan came to the track and with him came the excitement that followed throughout his life. In 2008, jockey Russell Baze got his 10,000th career win, winning over half of his races at Golden Gate Fields. Currently. the last day of thoroughbred racing at Golden Gate Fields is scheduled in June 2024. About Piedmont Seniors If you would like to join in the fun with the Piedmont Seniors, they meet monthly, usually on the 4th Wednesday of the month from 10 am to 12 noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. They also go on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. For questions contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov. The group welcomes new members, and Piedmont residency is not required. Piedmont Seniors enjoy the views and lunch at Golden Gate Fields Turf Club. articles.text: Whether your loved one has been recently diagnosed with a form of dementia or is in an advanced stage of the disease, the hustle and bustle of the holidays can be extra challenging for them and their family caregivers. When it comes to enjoying this festive time together, there are tips to follow that will benefit the caregiver and other things to be done for the good of the person living with dementia. Normal-ish The holidays must go on! And they still can, with a few specific considerations: • Avoid using blinking lights as these can be confusing or scary to a person living with dementia • Avoid putting out any decorations that look like food as they could be mistaken for being edible. • Say yes to gifts, but do suggest useful items like recordings of favorite music and comfortable clothing. • Build in rests and breaks for yourself and the person living with dementia. Take a step back Between the shopping, the cards, the decorating, the baking, the traveling, and more, the holidays can feel overwhelming for even the healthiest person. Consider: • reducing the amount of stimulation in the home of a loved one living with dementia • keeping your feelings of being overwhelmed to yourself instead of sharing with your care receiver (do consider sharing with your support system) • be selective about which parties or visitors are appropriate When someone living with dementia is over-stimulated, they may exhibit difficult behaviors and increase stress for everyone involved. Instead, adjust your expectations and activity plans: • Choose activities your loved one can still participate in rather than trying to get them to do something that is currently beyond their ability. • Use an approach of engagement so that you join your loved in an activity rather than just leaving them to figure it out or remember how to do a task, whether it is cooking or putting together a puzzle. It is important to keep in mind that changes in behavior and memory are caused by the disease and not the person. Take care of you too When you are caring for another person, whether during the holidays or another time of year, it helps if you can be your own caregiver too. The holidays can be an emotionally draining time for some people and the best defense against this is preparation: • Visiting family members may arrive full of opinions on how care should be administered for the person living with dementia. Rather than take offense, try to let this be accepted as merely a different perspective. • Use the additional help from visitors as a chance to take a break for yourself. You might even ask for respite care, either from another family member or professional in-home care agency, as a gift. • Scale back your own task list and delegate holiday chores. Maybe a holiday dinner can be a brunch, or a friend can go to the post office for you. Just because someone in your family is living with dementia does not mean that you and your loved one cannot enjoy the spirit of the holiday season this year. If you gave the scammers your credit card number, immediately call your bank and cancel that credit card. articles.text: Dear MacMama: I got a call from Apple and the technician told me there was some suspicious activity on my Apple ID. He said that he would charge $55 to diagnose the issue, and then there would be an hourly rate. He said that in the case of my issue, it would probably end up being less than $500. He said that if I pay him, he could guarantee that my Apple ID would be secure, but if I didn’t, Apple could not guarantee my identity safety. I felt funny about the call, so I hung up. But now I am terrified that my Apple ID is compromised. Should I have paid Apple to make sure my ID is safe? –Goeffrey D., Oakland Dear Goeffrey: Just so you know, AppleCare will never call you unless you set up an appointment with them. They don’t watch your Apple ID account and call you to tell you there is a problem. This call that you received was a “phishing” attempt. Phishing refers to fraudulent attempts to get personal information from you, usually by email, but also by phone and text message. What some of the scammers have been doing is “spoofing” legitimate numbers from tech companies, including Apple. So, if you see 1-800-275-2273, which is AppleCare’s number on your caller ID, your immediate thought might be, that it’s legit. By using fake caller ID devices, they can spoof many legitimate numbers. And of course, we all worry about identity theft, when we see a legitimate number, and speak with a technician, who seems very concerned for our safety, it’s very easy for even the most savvy of computer users to get taken. Phishing comes in many forms, including fraudulent emails or text messages, scam phone calls or voicemail, pop-up ads that says your device has a security problem, fake promotions that offer money or free products, and even unwanted calendar invitations. If you receive any of these, and they seem suspicious, it’s safer to presume that it’s a scam. If you’re worried about your Apple ID, the best idea is for you to call Apple at the number above. If you have recently bought a machine and used your phone number as a contact method, Apple should be able to tell it’s you just by your phone number. As a matter of fact, when I call Apple for some reason, the robot on the phone says, “hi Cookie”. What can you do to prevent yourself from becoming victim to these scammers? The advice below is straight from Apple’s website: • Never share personal information like credit card numbers, unless you can verify the recipient is who they claim to be. • Protect your Apple ID. French levels 1A, 1B, 2 and 3 start the week of January 8. The in-person classes are taught by Jean Monnier, who has been teaching at the Adult School since 2007. Previously, Monnier taught at UC Berkeley, Head Royce and Campolindo High Schools. In addition, he has written multiple papers and books on French involvement in the California Gold Rush and other topics. Spanish Intermediate 1, 2 and 3 classes also start in person the week of January 8. Instructor Afsaneh Olinga has been with the Adult School for nine years. Spanish Beginning 1 and 2 classes will start the week of February 26 and will be taught by Helmi Waits. She has been teaching at the Adult School since 2012. Phishing refers to fraudulent attempts to get personal information from you, usually by email, but also by phone and text message. What some of the scammers have been doing is “spoofing” legitimate numbers from tech companies, including Apple. So, if you see 1-800-275-2273, which is AppleCare’s number on your caller ID, your immediate thought might be, that it’s legit. By using fake caller ID devices, they can spoof many legitimate numbers. And of course, we all worry about identity theft, when we see a legitimate number, and speak with a technician, who seems very concerned for our safety, it’s very easy for even the most savvy of computer users to get taken. Phishing comes in many forms, including fraudulent emails or text messages, scam phone calls or voicemail, pop-up ads that says your device has a security problem, fake promotions that offer money or free products, and even unwanted calendar invitations. If you receive any of these, and they seem suspicious, it’s safer to presume that it’s a scam. If you’re worried about your Apple ID, the best idea is for you to call Apple at the number above. If you have recently bought a machine and used your phone number as a contact method, Apple should be able to tell it’s you just by your phone number. As a matter of fact, when I call Apple for some reason, the robot on the phone says, “hi Cookie”. What can you do to prevent yourself from becoming victim to these scammers? The advice below is straight from Apple’s website: • Never share personal information like credit card numbers, unless you can verify the recipient is who they claim to be. • Protect your Apple ID. Use two-factor authentication, always keep your contact information secure and up to date, and never share your Apple ID password or verification codes with anyone. Apple never asks for this information to provide support. • Never use Apple Gift Cards to make other kinds of payments. • Learn how to identify legitimate Apple emails about your App Store or iTunes Store purchases. If you send or receive money with Apple Pay (U.S. only), treat it like any other private transaction. • Learn how to keep your Apple devices and data secure. • Download software only from sources you can trust. • Don’t follow links or open or save attachments in suspicious or unsolicited messages. If you gave the scammers your credit card number, immediately call your bank and cancel that credit card. If you inadvertently gave a scammer any information, like passwords, change those passwords right away. You can also report suspicious phone calls to reportfraud.ftc.gov. If you receive a suspicious FaceTime call from what seems to be a bank or credit card company, send a screenshot of the call info to reportfacetimefraud@apple. com. To report spam or other suspicious emails that you receive in your iCloud.com, me.com, or mac.com inbox, send them to abuse@icloud.com. Now more than ever good passwords and good security etiquette with your devices is important. The more we figure out how to lock our devices down, the more the scammers try to find ways to break through. articles.text: With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!”

articles.text: Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers in 1818, the answer was an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ had broken with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices – equally straightforward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later, the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, eventually attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years, it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades, uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a courtroom trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818, they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we can still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We can create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth.
