articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. The Twelve Days OF Christmas – the Song On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me: A partridge in a pear tree. On the second day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Two turtle doves, and a partridge in a pear tree. On the third day of Christmas my true love gave to me Three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fourth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fifth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the sixth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the seventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eighth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the ninth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the tenth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eleventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eleven pipers piping, ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the twelfth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Twelve drummers drumming, eleven pipers piping, ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. They can be viewed via our website at: www.zionlutheran.net L a k e o r e s h A v u e e n B a i s t p t C h u r c h Sunday, December 24 10:00 am – Morning Service – Service of Carols “What Might An Angel Say To You?” Pastor Jim Hopkins preaching � Sunday, December 24 6:00 pm – Evening Service “The Music of the Season”� Music by Voices of Lakeshore, LABC Handbell Ensemble, LABC and Guest Musicians Reflection by Pastor Jim – “A Change of Heart” � Sunday, December 31 10:00 am – Morning Service “Watch Night Service” Reverend Sydney Webster preaching Services are In-person and available on Zoom and YouTube 3534 Lakeshore Avenue (Lakeshore & Mandana) • 893-2484 • www.labcoakland.org The 12 Days of Christmas Background OF the Song The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. The Twelve Days OF Christmas – the Song On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me: A partridge in a pear tree. On the second day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Two turtle doves, and a partridge in a pear tree. On the third day of Christmas my true love gave to me Three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fourth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fifth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the sixth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the seventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eighth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the ninth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the tenth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eleventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eleven pipers piping, ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the twelfth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Twelve drummers drumming, eleven pipers piping, ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. articles.text: On Saturday, December 2, at Triangle Park on Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues, the city of Piedmont hosted an event to describe plans for the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial. It will memorialize Piedmont’s first black homeowners who were driven out of town approximately 100 years ago. Invitations went out to 200 residents living nearby. The event was intended to let community members voice their input on the memorial’s development, including what they like about the park, how they use the space, and how the memorial could be best integrated into the park. The event was organized by City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Bayon Moore provided the project’s history, followed by an hour-long session where city officials heard neighbors’ questions, comments, and concerns about the space. “We looked to learn more about how residents use the park today and asked them to share any neighborhood-specific needs we should consider while developing design concepts,” she said. “Many of the neighbors in the immediate vicinity really cherish the existing space,” said Gonzales. “Children in the community use it frequently, and it is a lovely, wooded area that feels almost secluded. And everyone seems to appreciate the existing redwood trees that are there”. The Sidney and Irene Dearing memorial is the city’s response to a dark chapter in Piedmont’s history. Sidney and Irene Dearing purchased a home in 1924 and were Piedmont’s first black homeowners. A mob of white residents, abetted by the city council and police, forced the couple to sell their house and move. A memorial for Sidney & Irene Dearing was officially announced by the city on October 24, 2023. Hood Design Studio was chosen to create a memorial. The future site of the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial, beloved by the community for its seclusion and proximity to nature.
articles.title: Residents near Triangle Park meet with city about memorial

articles.text: The following letter was sent to Kevin Jackson, City Planner for the City of Piedmont. Dear Mr. Jackson: I attended the November 30 community workshop about the proposed Moraga Canyon housing project. You and I spoke about several issues, and you welcomed me to send you follow-up observations. I am concerned about the project’s isolation, the low-income residents’ separation, and the willingness of the project’s managers to incorporate community feedback into the plans. No opportunity was given for workshop attendees to question the project planners as a group. General questions about the overall nature of the project would not be answered by staff personnel who were designated to discuss specific options at individual poster-board stations. This gave me and several other people the feeling that the City isn’t really interested in hearing and addressing our concerns. I am concerned about the isolation of the 132 new units planned for the Moraga area. There is no “urban fabric” connecting that location with the rest of Piedmont, except for the heavily-trafficked Moraga Ave. Walkers or bike riders would not see other Piedmont houses for over a quarter mile. Isolation may be a more severe problem for residents of the 60 subsidized units who may not have cars available for both going to work and for shopping or going to school. This problem could be mitigated if the City were to operate a shuttle bus, similar to the shuttles that Emeryville operates to and from BART. The City could operate the shuttle for the first five years, and then evaluate whether the amount of ridership justifies continuing. A more serious problem is the planned separation of the below-market units from the market-rate units. This is a terrible idea that will have dangerous consequences. It would create a low-income “ghetto” in the midst of high-income housing. While you agreed that integration was a good idea, Mr. Jackson, you contended that separation was necessary because the subsidized housing had to be built as a separate project. This was not my experience when I developed housing for low and moderate income people, financed by both Federal and State programs ago. Section 8 below-market rental housing units were part of a larger market-rate project financed through HUD (the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development). There was no physical difference between the rental units. Some of the 132 units could be sold to individuals (72 at market rate, 60 at below-market rate), with unsold units being sold to a non-profit agency which would rent the market-rate units and the subsidized units together, with no physical distinction among the units. articles.text: Last month, the Shell station at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenues was sold back to the Shell corporation after nearly 17 years of private operation and ownership by Jeff Hansen under the name Piedmont Auto Care. On Thursday, November 16, Shell announced they would replace the existing structure with a new, 14-bay electric vehicle (EV) charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. An open house for neighbors was held at Kehilla Community Synagogue on Tuesday, November 28, where Shell representatives answered residents’ questions about the new EV Hub. Until recently, the project has lacked a central figure that community members could recognize and direct their questions toward. Questions may now be directed to Jeremy Randolph, the new program manager of the Shell Recharge EV Hub. This week, the company announced that Randolph would be the “focal contact” for the company, “overseeing all activities regarding this project.” Originally from Miami, Florida, Randolph has lived in Oakland since 2021. He attended college at Florida State University where he studied Mechanical Engineering. In the past, he has worked on projects in both charging infrastructure and electric vehicle design. He became involved with Shell in 2022 and has been with the company for a little over a year. He currently lives in downtown Oakland, only 10 minutes away from the site of the new Shell Recharge Hub. Randolph said that Shell chose Piedmont as the EV Hub’s new location based on several criteria, including “a lack of nearby charging facilities – specifically, fast chargers.” If approved by the City of Piedmont, Randolph believes the new Shell Recharge hub will help address this need and allow drivers to refuel between trips. Pricing at the new station will be on a pay-as-you-go basis. Just as at home, charging prices will vary based on the time of day. Drivers will be able to find the real-time cost of their charge via the Shell app. The app will also allow drivers to locate the nearest charger, check the station’s charging status and make payments. In contrast with the previous gas station, Randolph confirmed there will be no employees on-site regularly at the new EV Staff Photo Jeremy Randolph answers questions from community members at Shell’s open house on Tuesday, November 28.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont announced on Tuesday, December 12 the launch of a new online permitting system for Planning, Building, and Public Works permits. The new system, called “eTRAKiT,” is designed to serve as a “one-stop shop” for all permit-related activities. It will allow community members to apply for and check the status of their applications in real-time. As a result, the City will no longer accept paper or email applications for most planning, building, and public works permit types. These applications now must be handled through eTRAKiT. City officials hope that these changes will make the overall permit process simpler, increase accountability in city staff, and ultimately decrease wait times for residents seeking permits. According to Paki Muthig, Building Official with the Planning & Building Department, this update has been a long time coming. Piedmont is facing a mandate from the State of California to introduce these changes by January 2024, but a public portal for city permits has been planned since Muthig was hired by the City in 2018. Muthig was excited about the efficiency the new process promises. “Now, as a user, you will be able to look at the status of your permit at any time. You don’t have to call and say, ‘Hey, where’s my permit?’ You’ll know. And it won’t just sit on someone’s desk for 16 weeks,” said Muthig. Muthig insisted that the adoption of eTRAKiT would not affect the in-person staffing of his department and that eTRAKiT is not intended to replace the department’s workers. The Planning & Building Department will still assist with permitting through eTRAKiT on the phone and in-person at one of their two kiosk stations, now present at City Hall. The average time to process building permits in Piedmont is currently 2-4 weeks for small projects and 5-8 weeks for permits for larger jobs. During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, applicants faced wait times nearing 16 weeks because of backed-up department workloads. With their new system, the city hopes to decrease these times. The eTRAKiT system is used by 60 cities and counties in California. For questions about eTRAKiT, please call (510) 420-3050 or email buildingpermits@piedmont.ca.gov. Staff photo Piedmont Building Official Paki Muthig shows off the new eTRAKiT system at a kiosk in City Hall. Members of the public are invited to use these stations to apply for permits.
articles.title: Permit system being overhauled at City Hall

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department has received an abundance of donations for the annual Toys for Tots drive. The Piedmont Fire Department is currently accepting donations for the annual Toys for Tots drive through December 23. Piedmont residents are encouraged to donate new unwrapped toys and place them in donation bins at the Piedmont Fire Station, “Our annual toy drive is one of the favorite times of the year for Piedmont’s firefighters. We enjoy every time a community member brings in donations of new toys,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Working with Toys for Tots and Three Wise Men toy giveaway ensures the community’s generosity reaches as many children as possible.” Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County, and any toys donated before December 8 will be distributed through the US Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Bins will remain at City Hall for donations through December 23. Firefighter Brandon Clupny with a toy doll and a Piedmont firefighter Brittany Borges with a basketball and toy doll, part of the Toys for Tots drive in December Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Cancer League’s 50th Anniversary Holly Ball, The Golden Gala, was held Friday, December 1, at Claremont Country Club. The event, chaired by Melissa Partovi, was attended by 220 generous supporters who came together to raise over $350,000. Proceeds from the event will fund numerous seedstage grants focused on breakthrough cancer research and treatments. Extravagant sights of gold welcomed partygoers; women in glamorous gold evening gowns were escorted by dapper men dressed in black tie to celebrate 50 years of seeding the cure. Delicious food and excellent wine triggered a battle of the bidding paddles. The evening concluded with joyous dancing among oldand new-found friends. “We couldn’t have done it without our amazing donors. I am so grateful to everyone that supported Holly Ball. Thank you for your incredible generosity towards our cause,” said Holly Ball Chair Melissa Partovi. Holly Ball is The Cancer League’s largest fundraiser of the year, providing significant support for accredited non-profit organizations dedicated to the fight against cancer. The organization offers seed-level funding for researchers working on new cutting-edge cancer research and treatments. articles.text: Negotiations over the contracts of Piedmont teachers will take a new step on Thursday, December 14, when both sides will meet the assigned Mediator Ken Glenn at 1:30 p.m. Once mediation has begun the two sides will be prohibited from talking about points of discussion. Glenn was appointed by the Public Employment Relations Board last month and will soon be called on to end the impasse between teachers and school district. The Association of Piedmont Teachers union (APT) will retain the same negotiation team consisting of APT President Elise Marks, Mercedes Foster, Ben Spencer, Craig Best, and Katie Terhar along with California Teachers Association Representative Gray Harris. The district’s current offer allots for 2% raises for this school year, 4% next year and 3% the year after that. APT is asking for 8.22% this year which is the Cost of Living Adjustment amount determined by inflation in the state. “No matter how tight the budget is, more money must somehow be found.” said Marks to the Post. “Educators are stretched too tight financially as it is, and cannot sacrifice even more to balance the district budget.” Thursday’s mediation will signal a pause on updates given to the public, and even to members of the teachers union not on the negotiating team. Before the mandated public silence around negotiations APT members will rally for support outside City Hall at 5:30 p.m. on Wednesday, December 13. Marks and APT will make a brief statement before the closed session. They have called on members of the community to participate in the open session of the school board which starts at 7:00 p.m. tonight.

articles.text: Kids who stutter have a lot to say, and friends can show them how in Stuttering: For Kids By Kids, a DVD in English and Spanish, starring kids who stutter. It is available at most public libraries and through inter-library loans. Many children who stutter have never met others who struggle with the same disability. In this DVD from the Stuttering Foundation, they meet kids who recount how they handle challenges such as teasing, speaking out in class, and teaching others about stuttering. Swish, a lively and engaging animated basketball character designed by students at Purdue University, narrates the DVD. The children, who range in age from first grade to high school, offer frank and sometimes differing views of stuttering. For example, Matthew, age 10, says “It’s no big deal,” but Kate, age 9, worries about talking, what is going to happen next and whether or not she’ll stutter. Arianne, age 14, says, “The hardest part about stuttering is to get through it and to stay in there when you’re stuck.” Umang, age 12, agrees: “Sometimes it gets kind of annoying when you want to say something and you can’t. I also get worried what other people might think if I stutter and wonder if I’ll be able to get out of my blocks.” “All those interested in helping kids learn more about stuttering will want to see this tape,” said speech-language pathologist Bill Murphy of Purdue University. “The children featured are a perfect example of how to openly and honestly handle stuttering.” “This is an important tool for families and teachers of kids who stutter,” added Jane Fraser, president of the nonprofit Stuttering Foundation. Other professionals and specialists in stuttering in this production include Kristin Chmela of Northwestern University, Joe Donaher of Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Lisa Scott of Florida State University, and Lee Caggiano of Friends. Since 1947, the nonprofit Stuttering Foundation has provided free materials to public libraries nationwide. A library that will shelve them can download a request form at stutteringhelp.org/libraries-information or email info@stutteringhelp.org.
articles.title: Help for kids who stutter is as close as your library

articles.text: Piedmont Makers will grant a record $21,000 to Piedmont Unified School District to support and inspire teachers in developing 21st Century curriculum and hands-on classroom experiences. Piedmont Makers recognizes and supports the extraordinary STEAM (science, technology, engineering, art and mathematics) work in Piedmont schools through its annual grant program. In addition, Piedmont Makers is giving $4,000 to further outfit the engineering lab patio with a much-needed storage container. Piedmont Makers funded grants at each school and grade level. Example grants include: Elementary schools: • $1,500 – STEAM books for each elementary school library Piedmont Middle School: • $5,150 – Laser Cutter for PMS Makerspace • $3,100 – SolRun Car Kits for 8th Grade Science Piedmont & Millennium High School: • $3,620 – Gel electrophoresis machines for AP Biology and Biology • $3,306 – Buy materials to make mini bluetooth speakers for Guitar Engineering, College Prep Physics and Honors Physics students. A full list of grants can be found at www.piedmontmakers.org/community. Educators and faculty in the Piedmont Unified School District were asked to dream – and dream they did. Thirty-three applications were submitted requesting over $120,000 in funding, which shows a need in our community. Unfortunately, due to the incredible response, not all of the proposed projects could be funded. This year’s amazing grant award-winning educators will be encouraged to participate and present their projects along with their students at the Piedmont School Maker Faire on May 19th, helping highlight how the Maker attitude shines brightly in the Piedmont community.
articles.title: Piedmont Makers provides $25,000 to schools

articles.text: As we enter the heart of the giving season, our community faces a critical challenge: securing the remaining funds for the Piedmont School Giving Campaign. With just weeks to go, we stand $800,000 short of our ambitious yet essential $3.5 million goal. Reaching this goal is vital to ensuring a vibrant and enriching education for every child in the Piedmont Unified School District. Every dollar raised through the Giving Campaign directly impacts our students. These funds bridge the gap between state funding and the true cost of providing a high-quality education. They support vital programs like: • Small class sizes: Allowing for individualized attention and fostering a nurturing learning environment. • Dedicated teachers and aides: Ensuring our students have access to the best educators and support staff possible. • Arts and music programs: Cultivating creativity and fostering a lifelong appreciation for the arts. • Honors and AP courses: Providing opportunities for academic challenge and preparing students for college and beyond. • Wellness and mental health resources: Supporting the emotional and mental well-being of our students. This is not just about numbers; it’s about the future of our children and our community. A strong public education system is the foundation of any thriving society. It fosters critical thinking, cultivates creativity, and prepares our youth for successful lives and engaged citizenship. But we can’t do it alone. Reaching our $3.5 million goal requires the full participation of our community. Every single contribution, regardless of size, makes a difference. Consider donating online, sending a check, or transferring stock. And please spread the word. Together, let’s make this holiday season truly special by investing in our future. Every student deserves the opportunity to thrive, and we have the power to make that happen. Let’s make a strong finish for the Giving Campaign and ensure a bright future for generations to come. There are just a few weeks left to make your contribution. Visit Piedmontedfoundation.org/ donate. Together, we can make a difference.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team returned to the pitch last week with two victories to open its 2023 season. They traveled to Hayward for a 2-1 victory on Wednesday, December 6, and also defeated Tennyson in Hayward 2-0 two days later. Both teams are non-league opponents in the Shoreline Division; Piedmont plays in the upper Foothill Division. Piedmont continued its usual stifling system under coach Todd Sullivan, where the Highlanders press high to quickly regain possession and force teams to beat them with long balls in counterattack situations. “We’ve worked in practice on our high press, in particular on goal kicks. I was pleased the way we executed. We had to play a wet and slick field, so it was a case of playing more risk averse soccer,” said Sullivan. Hayward’s lone goal came on a penalty kick in the final minute of the game. Other than that, the Farmers struggled to create opportunities with just one threatening look on a counterattack in the 10th minute. Bosco Lorin and Aiden Woolwine scored goals against Hayward, and the Highlander offense unleashed 13 shot attempts with six on target, rarely allowing Hayward out of its own half. Bernales and Woolwine scored one goal each in the 2-0 shutout of Tennyson. The two games marked the first varsity starts for wingers Lorin and Gianluca Bini, who link up well with Woolwine and Bernales. The two are tall, rangy forwards who allow Piedmont to play vertically. “I thought we played with good energy,” said Bernales. “Eight of our players are new to varsity, but most of us have been playing together since we were about seven years old. Photo by Scott Stratman Enzo Bernales celebrates after his goal against Tennyson with Gianluca Bini joining him. Staff Photos Bosco Lorin charges towards the Hayward net on the way to scoring a goal.
articles.title: Piedmont soccer team opens season with pair of wins

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team won its annual tournament, the Paris Twins Classic, with a thrilling 81-68 double overtime victory over Vanden on Friday, December 8 at Binks Rawlings Gym. They followed up with a onesided 62-32 romp over Berwick College, a high school outside of Melbourne, Australia. This year’s tournament did not have traditional brackets for a three-day event because only seven teams participated, Friday’s game against Vanden marked Piedmont’s first real challenge of the season. The Lady Vikings went 25-8 last season and won the Division 3 title in the San Joaquin Section. Senior Natalia Martinez continued her illustrious scoring run, recording 40 points against Vanden without any 3-pointers. It marked the third game in which she has scored at least 40 points. The Highlanders are now 5-0 to start the season. “I can’t do it without my teammates, just finding a way to get me the ball and attacking. I know I didn’t have a 3-pointer today, but they were still finding ways to get me the ball on the perimeter. The trust we have is incredible,” said Martinez. Aside from Martinez’s prowess on the court, Friday’s victory couldn’t have been achieved without senior Sam Smith. She finished with 15 points, including the game-winning 3-pointer with 1:10 left. Smith was a reserve forward on last year’s NCS and WACC championship team. During the offseason, she was one of the hardest working players on Bryan Staff Photos Natalia Martinez scored 40 points against Vanden, her third 40-point performance in five games. Gardere’s squad, often putting every spare minute of time on the court. “I knew I was going to be open and called to Shakila [Zuberi] for the ball. She got it to me right on time. I’ve shot that shot a million times… I try to get in the gym as much as possible during my free period and after school during the offseason. To see it pay off feels really incredible,” said Smith. “Sam has put in extra, extra work. When no one is here in the gym, she’s getting in extra free throws and shots. We share the shooting machine all the time,” said Martinez. 71-68 win in double OT Piedmont led 11-7 by the end of the first quarter but the two sides went into halftime deadlocked at 19-19. After a high-scoring third quarter, the Lady Vikings led by six points, 41-35, going into the fourth. In the last quarter, Piedmont went on a 12-2 scoring run to Sam Smith scored the eventual game-winning 3-pointer in Piedmont’s 71-68 double overtime win over Vanden to win the Paris Twins Classic. Shakila Zuberi drives for a layup against Vanden. gain a 47-43 lead with four minutes left. After back-and-forth scoring, Vanden tied the game at 54-54 with a 3-pointer with 47 seconds left. Vanden had a final possession with 26 seconds left, but Smith made a late steal to send the game into overtime. Both teams scored six points in the first four-minute overtime, but Vanden held a three-point 60-57 lead in the late seconds. However, Martinez hit a freethrow, then turned a steal into a layup to tie it at 60-60 with around 30 seconds left sending the game into a second overtime period. After more back-and-forth scoring, Vanden held a 66-65 lead with 2:05 left. After a Martinez free throw, the Vikings’ center missed a pair of free throws. Zuberi passed the ball to Smith beyond the arc, and she scored for a go-ahead 3-pointer to make it 69-66 with 1:10 left in the game. With strong defense, PHS kept Vanden off the boards until they converted a pair of free throws in the waning seconds 69-68 Piedmont. With 7.9 seconds left, and Piedmont leading by a thread at 69-68, Piedmont made two free throws for the final, 71-68. Final stats: Martinez scored 40 points, six rebounds, three assists, three steals, and hit 18 of 25 free throws. Smith scored 15 points, seven rebounds. Lindsey Wirgler scored 10 points, two rebounds, one assist, one steal. Zuberi scored three points, seven rebounds, one assist, one steal. Kat Melian had 16 rebounds, one steal. Shay Johnson had two points and a rebound. 62-32 win vs. Berwick Piedmont allowed just four points in the first quarter to lead 22-4 going into the second. They led 32-11 at halftime and put up 23 more points in the third, leading 55-19 to start the final quarter. Final stats: Martinez scored 25 points, 10 rebounds, eight assists, and three steals. Wirgler scored 21 points, eight rebounds, one assist. Zuberi scored 11 points, six rebounds, two assists. Smith had five points, four rebounds, one steal. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-0) host Berkeley tonight, December 13, at 5:00 p.m. for their first league game.

articles.text: Can you host a Ukrainian mother and daughter, a senior at PHS, from February 1, 2024 until the daughter goes to college in the fall of 2024? They need 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom, preferably an in-law/ ADU, but a shared home would be welcome. They are wonderful people who were forced to flee their country and are missing their husband and father in Ukraine. The mother drives and could shop and run errands. For more information and references, call Piedmont resident Lauren Tate at 510-333-3877.

During the offseason, she was one of the hardest working players on Bryan Staff Photos Natalia Martinez scored 40 points against Vanden, her third 40-point performance in five games. Gardere’s squad, often putting every spare minute of time on the court. “I knew I was going to be open and called to Shakila [Zuberi] for the ball. She got it to me right on time. I’ve shot that shot a million times… I try to get in the gym as much as possible during my free period and after school during the offseason. To see it pay off feels really incredible,” said Smith. “Sam has put in extra, extra work. When no one is here in the gym, she’s getting in extra free throws and shots. We share the shooting machine all the time,” said Martinez. 71-68 win in double OT Piedmont led 11-7 by the end of the first quarter but the two sides went into halftime deadlocked at 19-19. After a high-scoring third quarter, the Lady Vikings led by six points, 41-35, going into the fourth. In the last quarter, Piedmont went on a 12-2 scoring run to Sam Smith scored the eventual game-winning 3-pointer in Piedmont’s 71-68 double overtime win over Vanden to win the Paris Twins Classic. Shakila Zuberi drives for a layup against Vanden. gain a 47-43 lead with four minutes left. After back-and-forth scoring, Vanden tied the game at 54-54 with a 3-pointer with 47 seconds left. Vanden had a final possession with 26 seconds left, but Smith made a late steal to send the game into overtime. Both teams scored six points in the first four-minute overtime, but Vanden held a three-point 60-57 lead in the late seconds. However, Martinez hit a freethrow, then turned a steal into a layup to tie it at 60-60 with around 30 seconds left sending the game into a second overtime period. After more back-and-forth scoring, Vanden held a 66-65 lead with 2:05 left. After a Martinez free throw, the Vikings’ center missed a pair of free throws. Zuberi passed the ball to Smith beyond the arc, and she scored for a go-ahead 3-pointer to make it 69-66 with 1:10 left in the game. With strong defense, PHS kept Vanden off the boards until they converted a pair of free throws in the waning seconds 69-68 Piedmont. With 7.9 seconds left, and Piedmont leading by a thread at 69-68, Piedmont made two free throws for the final, 71-68. articles.text: Staff Photos Brit Burden was elected to the Chris Huber Classic All-Tournament team. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up a strong performance in the 9th annual Chris Huber Classic at Acalanes in Lafayette from Thursday through Saturday, December 7-9, winning two of its three games. They opened with a narrow 52-48 loss to Monte Vista, then defeated De Anza 62-37 and beating St. Joseph 58-49 on the final day. The loss to Monte Vista comes against a Division 1 North Coast Section team that is undefeated thus far at 7-0. The Mustangs went 19-10 last year and received the No. 4 seed in the Div. 1 NCS postseason playoffs. “It was a great game against Monte Vista and we almost pulled off the win,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. Brit Burden was selected for the All-Tournament team, Dillon Casey received an Honorable Mention, and Thorin Holmes was awarded the Chris Huber Inspirational Award. 58-49 over St. Joseph Piedmont led 18-15 at the end of the first quarter and took a commanding 36-23 advantage through the second quarter. But in the third, St. Joe outscored Piedmont 17-9 to cut the Highlanders’ lead to 45-40. Piedmont’s defense rallied in the fourth quarter to limit the Pilots to nine points, while scoring 13 to win 58-49. In the fourth quarter, the Pilots hit a 3-pointer to cut Piedmont’s lead to 48-43, but Dillon Casey and Ravi Silverberg quickly responded with 3-pointers to put the Highlanders up 54-43. Final stats: Casey led the way with 19 points, Burden scored 17, Silverberg had 15 points, Declan Linnane had five. Thorin Holmes had eight rebounds. Dillon Casey scored 19 points against St. Joseph and had double-doubles against De Anza and Monte Vista.

articles.text: Staff Photos Hannah Sullivan scored four goals and one assist against Tennyson. She also scored against Skyline. Two games with a +11 goal differential is an impressive way to start your soccer season. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team recently shut out Tennyson 5-0 on Thursday, December 7 after opening the season with a 6-1 victory at Skyline in Oakland on Tuesday, “We have a lot of new players and I’m happy with how we’re playing,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “We’re linking up quite well. As the games get tougher, we’re going to have to improve and our defense is going to get tested more. But I’m happy with how it’s looking. Even though we lost a big group of seniors from last year, we’ve kept the same style of play.” Junior Hannah Sullivan was especially impressive with four goals and an assist in Piedmont’s 5-0 shutout of Tennyson. She also scored her first varsity goal against Skyline. “It’s all very new in these first few games, but I think we have great chemistry in the final third. It’s been really fun working together and improving that side of our game,” said Sullivan. Piedmont’s attack was dominant in both games, with frequently shots on goal, Against Tennyson, the Highlanders had 39 shot attempts with 21 on target. “We have a lot of good chemistry, especially in the midfield,” said midfielder Louisa Symkowick. “Juliana [Thornborrow] and I have played together for a long time, and Elsa [Wallway] is fitting in perfectly. The connections we make benefit in every aspect, not just building out from the back, but getting the ball to the front – like how Hannah got her goals.” 5-0 win over Tennyson It didn’t take long for Piedmont to get on the board. Sullivan scored in the second minute of action. From there, PHS recorded eight shot attempts before their next goal in the 16th when Sullivan cleaned up a shot on target from Juliana Thornborrow. The Highlanders went into halftime holding a 2-0 lead and recorded 12 shot attempts in the remaining time. In the second half, Sullivan required just seconds to land her third goal for a hat trick right out of the gate in the 41st minute. Lola Biehn then assisted Sullivan on her fourth goal two minutes later for a 4-0 lead. Sullivan assisted Biehn for the game’s final goal in the 63rd minute. PHS still pressed on for more goals and h ad nine more shots in the remaining 17 minutes of action. 6-1 over Skyline Piedmont opened its season with a convincing 6-1 win over Skyline. Ava Sauer scored first for Piedmont after cleaning up a blocked shot by Darcy McKee. Later in the first half, McKee jumped on a sloppy pass back to the center back, wheeling it into the penalty area for a goal. Thornborrow then scored the third after a receiving a throughball into the area by McKee. In the second half, Thornborrow made it 4-0 after receiving a pass from a corner kick. Thornborrow then assisted Sullivan for her first varsity goal, 5-0. After a Skyline goal, Ryo Woltag put them game away with a nice shot from a couple of feet above the penalty area. pages.text: Wednesday, December 13, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Donner Pass: a mystifying winter adventure By Jonathan Comeaux This treasure of California is among the best winter-time hikes in the Sierra Nevada Mountains. Donner Pass is home to an abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. The trek takes you through mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass above Donner Lake. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party tragically met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846 – becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train Snow piles on sections of the Donner Pass trail. A frozen wall of ice creates a surreal winter sight. A view of Donner Lake and the Donner Pass snow sheds covered in snow. tunnels is brief at just 2.1 miles to the last snow shed, but it gives you the magic of a Tahoe winter without getting knee deep into snow. It’s a great place for children, families, or beginning snowshoers. During warmer weather you can walk past the last snow shed and up to Donner Peak. From the Post’s starting point, we take the same route as our 2018 summer visit from McGlashan Point past a Native American petroglyph site that you can see in the warmer months. It’s now a popular sledding site with the fresh snow. The Central Pacific Railroad created its route through Donner Pass in the spring of 1868 after three years of construction. It was accomplished largely through the efforts of Chinese workers. The Donner Pass trail starts at The China Wall, a handmade construction that was the platform for the railroad leading into the first snow tunnel. Inside the 1,659-foot Tunnel #6, hikers can spot a second Chinese Wall with boulders piled neatly up to the roof. Through the Staff Photos The starting point for the trail from McGlashan Point up a popular sledding hill to the China Wall and first tunnel. The China Wall is a platform created by Chinese Labor Camp workers while building the transcontinental railroad in 1868. hollowed out mountains, large icicles glisten through the tiny peaks of light along the roof and walls. Some large frozen sections of water created massive blocks of ice that are clear as a piece of glass. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, December 13, 2023 Lights Up Continued from page 1 Scouts served hot cider donated by Piedmont Grocery and hot cocoa courtesy of Heafy-Baum Group. Meanwhile members of the Piedmont Recreation Department served latkes donated by the Chabad Jewish Center. Inside Community Hall, a line formed to see Santa Claus as children waited their turn to tell Santa what they wanted for Christmas. Parents waited patiently for an opportunity to take photos. A station for writing letters to Santa was crowded with young writers whose messages were destined for the North Pole. The range of requests were diverse. “I’m asking for the newest Babysitter’s Club novel,” said Addy Feldman, eight. Her friend, Maya Sweeney, added, “I want a hundred-mile walkie-talkie so I can play with my friend.” Others were harder to predict. “I want a remote-control drone!” exclaimed Nico Simon-Hsu, five. At 7:10 p.m., Karen Sullivan, President of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, welcomed the large gathering from the steps opposite Community Hall. “Good evening to all you intrepid citizens who won’t let a little bit of rain disturb their night!” joked Sullivan. She thanked the attendees of the event for coming out despite the high chance of rain and gave a brief history of the event which the PBF has organized since 1969. articles.text: American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco ushers in the holiday season with its celebrated production of the Charles Dickens classic, A Christmas Carol, at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theater now through Sunday, December 24. This will be the final chance to see this version of A Christmas Carol, one that has enchanted hundreds of thousands of audience members since 2005. In 2024, A.C.T. will present a brand-new production of this classic. Under the direction of A.C.T. Conservatory Director Peter J. Kuo, this version of A Christmas Carol – adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and based on the original direction by Perloff – stays true to the heart of Dickens’s timeless story of redemption and brings a playful sensibility to his rich language. It features a lively cast, delightful music, gorgeous costumes, and those deliciously spooky ghosts. The show is a cornerstone of the A.C.T. repertory and has become a holiday tradition for families throughout the Bay Area. Showtime information and tickets ($25–$130) are available at the A.C.T. Box Office at 415- 749-2228 or online at act-sf.org/ carol23. Groups of 10 or more save up to 20% and enjoy free tickets for group leaders. For group sales, call 415-439-2306. articles.text: Oakland Ballet will present The Nutcracker at the Paramount Theater on Saturday and Sunday, Dec. 16-17, with music by Oakland Symphony and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. With live music by Oakland Symphony alongside the voices of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker will bring the spirit of the holidays to life this weekend with performances on Saturday and Sunday, Dec. 16 and 17. This elegant production at Oakland’s Paramount Theater features art nouveau set design and costumes, and a cast of two dozen professional dancers as well as over 40 youth dancers, ages seven to seventeen, in the roles of snowballs, mice, soldiers and candies. Cheer on Marie and her soldiers as she rescues the Nutcracker Prince from the evil Rat King and then soar with our dancing snowflakes to the Land of Sweets where luscious treats await. Join the cast after the matinee performance on each day for a Sweet Treats Party with cookies, refreshments, and an opportunity to take photos with cast members. Tickets range from $21 - $115, with an extra $20 for the Sweet Treats Party. The Paramount Theater is located at 2025 Broadway in downtown Oakland. Tickets are now on sale at oaklandballet. org/performances-events/graham-lustigs-the-nutcracker.
articles.title: Performances at Paramount Theater on Sat. & Sun, Dec. 16-17

articles.text: Offering a snappy spin for the holiday season, San Francisco Playhouse is staging a new look at the Broadway hit Guys and Dolls with performances through Saturday, January 13. Helmed by San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English with music direction by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer, the new production reexamines the classic musical, bringing alive writer Damon Runyon’s gritty world of New York’s Lower East Side and Harlem during the 1930s. Filled to the brim with beloved Broadway standards including “Luck Be a Lady,” “Sit Down, You’re Rocking the Boat,” and “I’ve Never Been in Love Before,” the production premiered on Broadway in 1950, winning the Tony Award for Best Musical. It has since received five Broadway revivals and has been performed around the world. The Washington Post lauded “Frank Loesser’s priceless score” and called the show a “magnitude of delight.” In 2015, The New York Times said, “There are many students of the form who proclaim ‘Guys and Dolls’ the best musical comedy ever, and they may well be right.” Inspired by Runyon’s stories about post-Prohibition New York, Frank Loesser, Abe Burrows, and Jo Swerling’s beloved musical tale of gamblers, gangsters, and betting on love follows two unlikely pairs: a high-roller wooing a cautious missionary to win a bet, and a burlesque dancer whose slippery long-time fiancé won’t commit. An uplifting story of redemption perfect for the holiday season, the San Francisco Playhouse (450 Post Street) is performing matinee and evening performances through January 13. Tickets ($15-$125) and more details are available at sfplayhouse.org, or through the box office at 415-677-9596. Photo by Jessica Palopoli The Tony Award-winning Broadway musical Guys and Dolls is in production at San Francisco Playhouse through January 13.
articles.title: Guys and Dolls at SF Playhouse through Jan. 13

articles.text: Photo by Stefan Cohen The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus will perform their Holiday Spectacular this Sunday December 17 at Zellerbach Hall. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus will perform its annual Holiday Spectacular this Sunday, December 17 at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Audiences can watch as the 100-member-strong, critically acclaimed chorus performs beloved holiday classics like “Jingle Bells” and “I’ll Be Home for Christmas” alongside timely, funny sketches in an event that has become a much-anticipated highlight of their performance season. Now celebrating its 45th year, the Chorus sparked a nationwide LGBTQ+ choral movement after its first public performance at a vigil on the steps of San Francisco’s City Hall following the assassinations of Supervisor Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone in 1978. Since then, the chorus has received critical recognition, organized national tours, and released several albums of original music. The show will be performed without intermission and last approximately 90 minutes. Tickets may be purchased at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in-person at the Zellerbach Hall box, open Tuesday – Friday from 12:00 – 5:30 p.m. and Saturday – Sunday, 1 p.m.–5 p.m. Tickets are halfprice for UC Berkeley Students. Additional information can be found online at www.calperformances.org/2023-24-season.
articles.title: San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus Holiday concert at Zellerbach on Sunday

articles.text: With Claire’s grandson, Charlie Vanessa Redgrave, an actress Love is in the air, but not Letters to Juliet. Directed by Frances McDormand in Nomadland Review by Chris Honoré If you love movies, if you find extraordinary their ability to tell stories that encompass a wide spectrum of the human condition, then Nomadland is a film not to be missed. It won two Academy Awards in 2021, for Best Picture and for Chloé Zhao as Best Director. The narrative focuses on Fern, a 61-year-old woman, a character inhabited flawlessly by the remarkable, endlessly courageous, Oscar-winning actor Francis McDormand (Fargo; Three Billboards Outside Ebbin, Missouri). The film opens with Fern preparing to leave Empire, Nevada. She has recently lost her husband, and now, after years working in a gypsum plant, she has lost her job when the factory closes its doors. So Fern begins packing up her aging van, and, having found no work in the area, decides to leave Empire for warmer climes in the Southwest. Nomadland soon reveals itself to be a quirky, quietly profound, and a deeply human road story. She gradually discovers that while she is decidedly alone, she is not isolated, and soon comes across people at rest stops, most her age or older, living by choice in similarly converted vans. They view themselves as nomads, befriend one another, barter, give advice and share lessons of the road. They drift, and all seem to agree it’s not the destination but the journey. When leaving a camp they simply wave and say, “See you down the road.” Absent a traditional plot, Nomadland is a collection of compelling, interesting encounters with fellow nomads who embrace the beautiful desert vistas and distant horizons. Fern stops at a camp, perhaps takes a job, shares roadie vignettes, gleans a road less traveled wisdom from old-timer Bob Wells (playing himself), or the stoic Swankie (also portraying herself). And then moves on. McDormand is so wonderfully talented, she seems to be one of the drifters the filmmakers happen to meet as they assemble nomads where they find them, all seemingly content to inhabit society’s remote fringe. Surprisingly there is not a moment of bitterness in Fern’s encounters. Instead, we see a kind of resilient optimism. As an aside, there are only two actors in Nomadland: McDormand and David Strathairn as Dave. While they consider a relationship, Fern is unable to commit to anything more than the road. Finally, this tapestry of drifters (“not homeless but houseless”), captured in this film, can easily be characterized as an ethnographic revelation of a people who are otherwise all but invisible. Nomadland. Directed by Chloé Zhao. Starring Francis McDormand, David Strathairn, and Linda May. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated R. Released 2021. Now streaming on VUDU/hulu/Prime/ Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIE FOR ADULTS Award-winning Nomadland is an exceptional film

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, December 13, 2023 MOVIE FOR ADULTS Letters to Juliet Review by Chris Honoré Letters to Juliet is a nice surprise. There have been so many mediocre if not downright awful romantic comedies of late, the assumption was that this film would take its place next to the detritus that has come before. It doesn’t. Of course, the movie is all about love, that most human and elusive and fragile emotion. And then there is Verona and the Veneto region of Italy, awash in a haze of golden glow. The film shimmers with optimism. Brief ly, Sophie (Amanda Seyfried), a young fact-checker for The New Yorker, arrives in Verona as part of a pre-honeymoon trip with her fiancé, Victor (Gael Garcia Bernal), an obsessed chef and restaurateur. While he is off on a wine buying trip in the south of Italy, Amanda, left alone for the day in Verona, serendipitously finds a letter left behind in a sandstone wall near the assumptive home of Juliet, a place possessing a magnetic draw for heartbroken women who write their emotional missives and leave them behind. Amanda takes the letter, written in 1967, carefully from its weathered envelope. Fascinated, she reads the words of Claire (Vanessa Redgrave), a teenage schoolgirl, who fled back to England rather than follow her heart and embrace her summer love, Lorenzo Bertilini (Franco Nero). She has lived with the regret ever since. Amanda answers the letter, prompting Claire, now a widow living in England, to come to Verona and try and find Lorenzo, having no idea if he is still alive, or if he will even remember her after so much life has happened. With Claire’s grandson, Charlie (Christopher Egan), a thirty-something English businessman, the three drive through the gorgeous Italian landscape – sun-kissed vineyards covering gently rolling hills; quaint cobblestone towns, the roofs covered in red tile, all beneath cobalt blue skies; the three of them sharing long afternoons, drinking enticing red and white wines, studying a map filled with dots and possible locations of a man named Lorenzo Bertilini. Vanessa Redgrave, an actress of enormous talent, is luminescent as Claire. Her lovely face is made only lovelier by the lines of age and experience. Amanda Seyfried is perfect as the vulnerable yet feisty Sophie who encourages Claire to pursue her quest and risk the possible heartache that may be the result of not finding Lorenzo. Charlie bridles at the idea from the beginning, and, naturally, he and Sophie are oil and water. Love is in the air, but not between Victor and Sophie. Destiny has now taken charge, leading to an ending that is sweet and completely expected – how could it end any other way? Letters to Juliet. Directed by Gary Winick. Starring Amanda Seyfried, Vanessa Redgrave, Christopher Egan. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. articles.text: Sunny Pawar and Abhishek Bharate in Lion The challenge inherent in reviewing a splendid film such as Lion is how to offer the reader a sense of the film and yet give nothing away. Perhaps the only aspects of the story that should be disclosed are those shown in the trailer, three minutes that give just enough information to frame what will be a life changing event in a small boy’s life. Saroo (newcomer Sunny Pawar in a spectacular performance) is 5-years-old. His mother is a laborer in a rock quarry in Khandwa, India. He and his older brother, Guddu (Abhishek Bharate), scramble each day to supplement the family’s small income, often stealing coal from passing trains. Poverty defines the family, but the boys are resilient and deeply close. One night, Guddu ventures out to find anything he can sell or trade and tells Saroo he must stay at home. Saroo begs to go along and finally Guddu relents. At a local train station, Saroo is sleepy, exhausted, and Guddu leaves him on a bench, telling him not to wait for him. Saroo promises and immediately falls asleep. When he wakes, some hours later, the station is empty and all is quiet. He calls out for Guddu but hears only silence. He wanders over to an empty train waiting trackside and makes the fateful decision to go on board. Finding a softer seat than the station bench, he again falls asleep. When he awakens it is daylight and the train is moving, the countryside flashing by. He runs up and down the vacant aisles, calling out for Guddu… for anyone. The train does not stop until it reaches a station in Kolkata (Calcutta) and massive numbers of people, waiting on the platform, begin to board. Saroo pushes his way off the train, looking around for anything familiar. What he is unaware of is that he is 1,000 miles away from home and at a complete loss as how to get back. He doesn’t know where back is. He is suddenly alone. Lost. Endless crowds of people move around him, ignoring him, like a small rock in a rushing stream. This long first act is gripping, breathtaking, filled with heartfelt tension. How will small Saroo ever survive on the urban streets where predatory adults victimize abandoned children? And so begins a brief act two, which leads into act three and we meet a grown Saroo (Dev Patel) whose life has been completely transformed. But for his older Saroo, what was once lost now must be found. Be prepared to be captured by this wonderful film. It will touch you as you absorb not only little Saroo’s circumstances, but as you later engage with him as a young man. Both Dev Patel and Nicole Kidman were nominated for Golden Globe Awards for their very fine performances in Lion. Lion. Directed by Garth Davis. Starring Dev Patel, Nicole Kidman, Rooney Mara. 2 hrs. articles.text: Holidays at Filoli Gardens is open through January 7. Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside to see the 16-acre estate brightly illuminated for the holidays. The nonprofit historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through Sunday, January 7. Take photos with Santa Claus on December 16, 17, 21, 22 and 23 from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Afterwards, view a dozen festooned Christmas trees inside the estate. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing decorations inside and outside the mansion, and miles upon miles of string lights that drape the interior. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Evening admission from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. promises a world of wonder where the garden transforms into a mesmerizing display. With sell-out nights expected, securing preferred dates early is encouraged. Returning favorites like the spectacular 200-foot light tunnel come to life under the stars, while a fresh palette of rich pinks, mystical blues, and warm whites embrace the magic of the night Garden. Every Wednesday at 11am, visitors are welcome to join the Gilded Guide tour led by Filoli’s curators. This exclusive experience unveils the stories that breathe life into the House, revealing the meticulous preparations and behind-the-scenes magic that transform Filoli into a holiday wonderland. The festivities extend into the Woodland Court, open daily from 11 a.m.to 9 p.m. with holiday libations, sweet treats, and warm gatherings by the fire pits. The Quail Café serves seasonal menus with hearty soups, stews, and delightful treats, while the Clock Tower Shop provides a chance to shop locally and discover unique gifts. On January 1, 2024, from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m., the Hair of the Dog Hike also invites participants to rejuvenate and embrace fresh beginnings with this invigorating outdoor experience, plus the infamous “hair of the dog” cure for all post-New Year’s Eve ailments. Last year, the Filoli team installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. Filoli Gardens is considered one of the finest remaining country estates of the twentieth century, featuring a 54,000+ squarefoot Georgian revival-style mansion, 16 acres of exquisite English Renaissance gardens, a 6.8-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, and hundreds of acres of Natural Lands with five distinct ecosystems and a 1-mile Estate Trail. The two-story historic Filoli mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. To purchase tickets and learn more about Holidays at Filoli events, visit filoli.org/events/holidays.
articles.title: Holidays at Filoli Gardens open through Jan. 7

The choreography and direction were also extraordinarily good, and the sets were good. Do yourselves a favor and attend the Nutcracker this year. San Francisco’s connection The history of The Nutcracker follows the success and psychoses of composer Tchaikovsky. His music always has a ballet quality. The interesting thing is that Tchaikovsky composed only three ballets. His Nutcracker was the second. The story is by E.T.A. Hoffmann. Tchaikovsky and his backer made some minor changes. The story is certainly more pleasant in Tchaikovsky’s version than the original one by Hoffmann. Tchaikovsky began to compose the ballet in Moscow and then took a three-week trip to America to open Carnegie Hall in New York. He returned to Europe and finished the score while vacationing in France. The world premiere was not a success. Critics found many ways to denigrate the ballet. Fortunately, the musical score was an immediate success, and it continued as The Nutcracker Suite until the San Francisco Ballet produced it to great appreciation and acclaim in 1944. Worldwide adulation followed soon after. Almost everyone got into the act after this. There were pop versions and swing versions and jazz versions and cartoon versions. Just about every musical version works. There is even a moral to the story – the triumph of imagination proving that the mind is limitless. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers last week included Cheryl Coleman Jones, Wenny Young, Angela Tom, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Noemi Alvarado, Elane Rehr, Martin Levy, Elizabeth Richter, Chuck Oraftik, Nancy Henn, Will Adams, Alicia Rivera, Irene Thompson, Lori Austin, Tina Shum, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Ken Young, Helen Dong, Charlene Louie, Kathy Rolfson, Ian Morgan, Lisa Euphrat, Joanne Larson, John Engemann, Matt Gerhardt, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Christine Calliste, Mark Davis, Quincy Dong, Jim Kuo, Alissa Quan, Harriette Louie, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. For months, the walkers have been monitoring the construction progress of a garage being built for a Crocker Avenue home owned by Jeremy Bo Droga and his wife, Marie-Elise. The group had talked with Jeremy during the construction, and he had offered the walkers a tour when the project was done. The walkers headed to Wildwood Avenue to Crocker Avenues, where the Drogas’ house is located. Jeremy is a charming Australian and a noted sculptor. According to his website, https:// www.bodroga.com/, his artwork evolves with the type of materials and spaces he encounters. He has exhibited all over Europe, America, and Australia. Marie-Elise is French and Jeremy said there is sometimes a conflict over which flag – the Australian or French – should be on the flagpole in front of their house. The property was named “Strawberry Hills” by the original owners, the granddaughter of Hiram Tubbs who founded the Tubbs Cordage Company and built the famous Tubbs Hotel near Lake Merritt. The house was designed by Albert Farr, and construction was finished in February 1906, two months before the earthquake in San Francisco. The house was Farr’s first major commission in Piedmont. Although it is large, this house suggests an English cottage with rolled eaves on the left front gable. It offers grand views of Oakland, San Francisco, and the Bay. The home withstood the earthquake and must have had a dramatic view of the destruction. The house originally had a garage on what is now the site of the home next door, but that land was sold, and a house was built there in 1957. Jeremy and Marie-Elise bought “Strawberry Hills” in 2020, when they began a threeyear project to create a garage at street level below the raised property of the house. They spent a year and a half working with the Piedmont Planning Commission and three months excavating the hill in front of the house. The Drogas were especially sensitive to respecting Albert Farr’s design in the creation of the garage. They hired Greg Kline, a local architect who incorporated the homeowners’ practical needs with classic, historical design references of Strawberry Hills Estate. The garage is two stories and complements the height of the house. There are columns, arches, and a set of windows on the exterior that echo Farr’s design of the main house. The garage interior is open with 16-foot ceilings that offer light, flexibility, and versatility for future needs. A spiral staircase goes to a rooftop garden and an elevator exists. Landscaping will complete this beautiful project. Jeremy put together a large box of fruits from his pineapple guava trees and invited walkers to take as many as they liked home. In return the group gave Jeremy an appreciative round of applause. After the visit, the walkers headed to Sea View Avenue, and then loop back to the city center. Along the way the Grinch was stealing some Christmas tree lights from a front yard, and Santa and his sleigh were making a visit to another front yard. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: We are heartbroken to announce the passing of our daughter and sister, Lorinda Harris, on November 29, 2023. Shortly before her passing, she was thoughtfully selecting gifts for her nephews in preparation for Thanksgiving. Two weeks later, she was unexpectedly gone as a result of an accident outside her home in Sebec, Maine, leaving the many who loved her devastated. Born on September 21, 1968, she was the daughter of Ted Harris and Karen Oleson, the oldest of five siblings. As a young girl, Lorinda loved the living room dance parties she and her siblings improvised to the tunes of Donna Summer and ABBA. One of her siblings remembers their dad, newly single, taking all five kids up to the family cabin and forgetting to bring sunblock along. After a day at the lake and the sunburns that followed, Lorinda spent the night slathering her four siblings head to toe in Noxzema. She was a concerned helper and a consummate older sister, and whether it was with over-thecounter skin cream or another emblem or demonstration of love, she was always quick to extend herself, especially for her family. This made a real difference when before finishing high school, the family gained three stepsisters from her father’s second marriage to Heidi Clawson. Following a predictable pattern, these new sisters quickly came to look up to and adore her as well. Lorinda was a Piedmont High School Varsity Cheerleader and was often seen driving around town in the family’s wood paneled station wagon, frequently with Lou Gramm blasting on the radio. In a family full of Spanish and Portuguese speakers, Lorinda chose to study German. And while she always insisted that she greatly admired the members of her own family, they couldn’t help but notice that German was the home language of her best friend Michelle Mueller’s family, whose house became a second home to Lorinda during her teenage years. Lorinda was always grateful for the influence of the many loyal friends she enjoyed both in Piedmont and her later homes elsewhere. Upon graduating from high school, Lorinda attended UC Irvine, where she quickly fell in with a wonderful group of friends and sorority sisters in the Tri Delta Sorority. She even went on to serve as the Sorority President. These friendships and relationships brought her immense joy during formative years. They could also be the source of some mischief from time to time. Europe and Asia where in many locations she reconnected with friends who themselves had gone abroad. Following her return to the U.S., Lorinda was accepted into the National Security Studies program at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore and received her certificate with Honors. She started a new career in government and law, working for Senator Susan Collins of Maine as a legal advisor, which included working for the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Lorinda eventually returned to Northern California, this time to Sacramento, where she worked for the law firm DLA Piper in their labor law practice group. Lorinda eventually left her career and moved to a beautiful lakeside house in Maine — a dream she had harbored for some time. She focused her energies into making her house a home that was beautiful and thoughtful. She loved to host friends and family for lobster boils, boating on the lake, and cozy fireside visits. She bravely hosted a Harris Family reunion there. Being the oldest sibling in a family of eight kids gave Lorinda the ability to act as a mother to many. All agreed that her generosity towards friends and family knew no bounds. Her nephews were frequent objects of thoughtful videos, visits, gifts and drawing sessions she did with them. Lorinda departs this life with a legacy of loyalty, kindness, and unwavering love for family and friends, and leaves an indelible mark of these notable attributes on all who were fortunate enough to know her. We will greatly miss her. Lorinda leaves behind her father and stepmother Ted and Heidi Harris; brother Ted Harris, Jr.; six sisters: Rebecca Harris, Anne Harris, Amelia Clawson (Chad Carter), Abby Low (Brian), Jennifer Harris, and Greta Clawson; her five nephews: Thomas, Matthew, Andrew, Alec, and Nico; and a wide circle of adoring aunts, uncles, and cousins, all of whom held a special place in her heart. She was preceded in death by her mother Karen Oleson. The family is grateful for the outpouring of love and support following this sudden loss. Memorial service on Dec. 16 A memorial service will be held on Saturday, December 16, at 4:00 p.m. at the Sequoyah Country Club, 4550 Heafey Road, Oakland, California. The memorial service will also be livestreamed via Zoom at the following link: https://shorturl.at/sRU25 Lorinda Beth Harris died on November 29, 2023. She was 55. Her siblings remember one spring break when the family drove to Southern California to see the amusement parks and visit Lorinda during her freshman year. While in town, Lorinda had all seven siblings stay in the dorms with her for the night while many students were away on vacation. Rumor has it that she took her siblings to a dorm party that evening. Rumor also has it that none of the underaged partygoers ever told their parents or ever complained! After graduating, she followed in her father’s footsteps and pursued a degree in law. While at law school she was able to put her German to use, spending part of a semester in Germany on a study abroad program. She graduated from the University of San Diego School of Law and spent the following years practicing in law firms in San Diego and Orange County. Despite her advanced academic degree and professional success, Lorinda remained down to earth and able to laugh at herself. Eventually, Lorinda returned to the Bay Area to work at the law firm Thelen, Reid & Priest, where her father practiced law. When her dad found out about Lorinda’s offer of employment at the firm, he was worried that they were hiring her because of her connection to him, a senior partner. He was relieved and pleased to discover that she was hired on the strength of her own merit. During this time, Lorinda also developed a love of cooking and became quite accomplished, Her siblings remember Lorinda cooking, hosting, and serving a delicious and beautifully planned Christmas dinner for the entire family. Lorinda poured over issues of “Food & Wine” and “Bon Appétit” magazines, drawn to the more complicated recipes. After many years working in law, Lorinda decided to take time off to travel and see the world. Her travels took her throughout
