articles.text: A turnout of 15 readers gathered at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on December 4 for the First Mondays Reading Group’s discussion of The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman. The book was written in 2009 and made into a movie in 2016. Gerry Gragg reported that the action film took some Hollywood license with some departures from fact. The Finest Hours is the true story of two heroic U.S. Coast Guard rescues in the winter of 1952 when New England was battered by the most brutal nor’easter in many years. While the storm raged, two oil tankers, the Pendleton and the Fort Mercer which were built during World War II and not for this kind of sea, both split in two. On shore four young Coast Guardsmen were given what was almost a suicide mission of trying to save the dozens of men huddling inside the broken halves of the two ships. They would have to do it in a 36-foot lifeboat with 70-foot waves crashing around them. It was one of the most daring events in the history of the U.S. Coast Guard. Gerry and Darby Gragg had visited the story’s Coast Guard Motor Lifeboat CG-36500 where it is berthed at Rock Harbor in Orleans, Massachusetts. Gerry also volunteers for the Coast Guard. His and Darby’s experience with the Coast Guard, and their knowledge of sailing, made The Finest Hours especially meaningful. The Coast Guardsmen were simple, modest, young people who had made a commitment of service and were unflinchingly meeting it. The book’s narrative was fast and exciting, and it was a quick, enjoyable read for some of the group. Other readers found the book’s back and forth storytelling between the different ships’ situations didn’t keep them involved. It was sometimes hard to tell which ship was being written about. For others the book seemed like news reporting, and the prose didn’t suit them. This led to the question of how two authors write a book together and produce a common style for it. Other readers said the book didn’t provide an understanding of the main characters, and extraneous people were included who were distractions. Additionally, some readers didn’t get a full sense of the waves and storm’s magnitude, but they did feel the cold the men experienced. The Finest Hours also made clear that different types of books perform different functions. Some make readers appreciate history, others writing styles and word craft, while others are inspirational. Group members said that reading different types of books, fiction for some and non-fiction for others, had made them broader readers, and especially appreciative of The First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected Station Eleven by Canadian writer Emily St. John Mandel for their January read and The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson for February. A committee led by Lois Price and Laura Goldman had built on Priscilla Wanerus’ book list to develop a new book selection process and candidates file. After Bob Hall presented three of the candidates, Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis was selected for March. The group’s next discussion will be on January 8th at 1:30 p.m. If the weather is cold or rainy, it will be held inside the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. The First Monday Reading group in December included Hilary Honore, Darby Gragg, Adrienne Hamlin, Bella Almanzan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Ken Young, Gerry Gragg, Phil Witte, Lois Price, Laura Goldman, Mike Henn, Sarah Johnson, Bob Hall, Laura Goldman, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, December 13, 2023 Hiking with Jon Continued from page 15 As the tunnel opens, we begin a walk through some fresh powder. Above is the view of Donner Peak. graffiti covering each wall of the sheds, some pieces more magnificent in detail than other common tag-names. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals that are awe-striking. Proper hiking gear is required at some ice-covered area to prevent slipping and accidental falls. With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park off the road along Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook parking lot. In our five miles of hiking, The Post passed just 27 hikers during our time in the tunnels, but another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the China Wall. A second China Wall is inside the long tunnel in the mountainside. Watch for massive ice blocks and icicles during this winter walk. The entire walk has graffiti on the tunnel walls. Some pieces are magnificent and well-detailed, like the mural on the right. To enter this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook to their GPS device for common starting areas. Return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and walk up to Donner Peak. Reprinted from January 2021 Piedmont Post. Piedmont Real Estate Update December 2023 A Year in Review and the Outlook for 2024 To say the 2023 real estate market was a roller coaster is an understatement! The year began with bomb cyclones, bank failures, and tech layoffs. The uncertainty continued with unprecedented interest rate increases and an inventory shortage due to many sellers waiting out the market. Let’s take a moment to reflect on the year behind us and consider the forecast for 2024. Home Retention Reached a Record High New listings have been declining year-overyear for 15 months. * In 2023, homeowners had little motivation to sell. Holding tight to their low interest rates and avoiding capital gains taxes were two top reasons for staying in place, with the added dilemma of where to go next. These concerns resulted in the highest homeownership tenure in decades, with a retention of 12 years. Years Owned Home Before Selling Rent vs. Buy In 2005, David Leonhardt of the New York Times wrote an article entitled “Is It Better to Buy or Rent?” in which he encouraged homeowners to “take another look at renting. ” (We remember when this article came out – yes, we have been around that long!) In our market, if that person sold their one-million dollar home in 2005, they would have missed out on the concerns of the Great Recession. However, they would have also missed out on an average annual appreciation of approximately 6% per year, which compounds and would make that home worth roughly $2.8M today. Recently, Leonhardt published another article entitled “Rent Now, Buy Later, ” and the Economist published a study showing that renting may make sense in many parts of the United States. In 2014, the NY Times developed a fantastic Rent vs. Buy Calculator, which is one of the best we have seen (simply Google NYTimes “Rent vs. Buy Calculator”). Our advice? There can be several reasons, financial and otherwise, that affect a decision about whether now is the right time to buy, sell, or rent. The answer to this question can be very personal and impacted by geography and housing types. If you are contemplating a real estate decision and would like a market expert to help you consider options, feel free to reach out. We would be happy to have a candid conversation and walk you through a personal net sheet. Cost Comparison for a Renter and a Homeowner *Source: California Association of Realtors Buyer Challenges Low inventory presented a double-whammy for first-time homebuyers who were already grappling with far less buying power due to rising interest rates. If you add economic uncertainty resulting from layoffs, difficulty in obtaining insurance, inflation, and unsettling geopolitical events, it’s easy to understand how single-family home sales were down 22.2% *Source: California Association of Realtors The chart above shows a cost comparison for a renter and a homeowner over a seven-year period. The renter starts out paying $800 per month with annual increases of 5%. The homeowner purchases a home for $110,000 and pays a monthly mortgage of $1,000. After six years, the homeowner’s payment is lower than the renter’s monthly payment. With the tax savings of homeownership, the homeowner’s payment is less than the rental payment after three years. Piedmont Real Estate Update December 2023 Outlook 2024 Despite the challenges faced in 2023, the forecast for 2024 is cautiously optimistic. Expect rates to remain elevated for the near future, affecting borrowing costs. However, a slow decline is forecasted for 2024, offering some relief to prospective buyers and potentially stimulating market activity. articles.text: Editor: I’m writing out of great concern that the woefully under-managed Witter Field project is reaching a breaking point. It has been painfully clear since the start of this project that the District’s contractor has been leading the District around by the nose. When the Contractor says “jump” the District asks “how high?” This lack of leadership has come at great cost to the residents of Piedmont. The project’s completion date has been repeatedly pushed back through a lack of disciplined oversight, harming the District’s students, which is inexcusable. In addition, the double standard shown by the District and the City regarding parking restrictions in place for this project shows enormous disrespect to the community. Every weekday before 8:00 a.m., Palm Drive residents dutifully move their cars off of the even-numbered side of the street and scramble to find alternate parking spaces, in accordance with the agreed-upon rules for the Witter project. More times than I can count (at least a dozen), the District’s contractor has violated those same rules, with giant dump trucks rumbling down Palm Drive before the agreed start time of 8:00 a.m. These trucks often idle, engines belching noxious fumes, in front of our houses. Time and time again we have complained to the School District about these worksite violations. Time and time again we have been assured it will be addressed with the contractor. But nothing changes. The residents follow the rules, but the District does not. If a resident repeatedly violated Piedmont’s rules by having a contractor work on their house with loud power tools every day before 8:00 a.m., the City would step in with an enforcement action. In this case, the City looks away, allowing the District to break the rules. To add insult to injury to these serial violations of respect and rules, Palm Drive residents were awakened today – Saturday – by the sound of trucks grinding down Palm Drive at 7:45 a.m. to work on the Witter project. Yet again the District violated the City rules, but this time the indifference to residents was compounded because we were never informed that work would be happening on a weekend. Informing residents and taking our needs into account seems to be a very low priority for the District.
articles.title: Witter Field project remains out of control

articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Tree Lot will be open until Saturday, December 16, or “whenever we sell out,” according to Tom Smegal, head of the tree lot’s volunteer committee. Since its opening on Saturday, November 25, the tree lot has sold 1300 trees of its total stock of 1800, and they are quickly running out of fan-favorite items. “We are selling our largest and smallest trees as the season goes on. If you’re a customer who wants a six- to eight-foot tree, we still have a very nice selection of those trees. However, if you want a very large or very small tree, you’ve got to be quick,” said Smegal. Despite early sales approaching a record pace, the Scouts still have more trees to sell than last year. “The Silvertips came through this year,” proclaimed Smegal. Last year the truck couldn’t arrive on time due to heavy snow. “We’ve been able to sell quite a few of those this year. We definitely do have trees, and we definitely will have trees this weekend. I’d encourage people to get to the tree lot before then, because after that it will be a limited selection.” The Scout tree lot is still taking orders at this time. Located in the parking lot of Coaches Field, community members and business owners looking to celebrate the holidays, can still buy trees, wreaths, garlands, tree stands, The Piedmont Scout Tree Lot also has a selection of fresh wreaths, garlands, and mistletoe for the holidays.

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department welcomed four new recruits in a formal swearing-in ceremony at the December 4 city council meeting. The recruits’ families were in attendance. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan briefly introduced each new member of the department. “This group comes to us after a long and thorough selection process which included interviews, EMS assessments, group dynamic assessments, and extensive background checks,” explained Brannigan. “All four are experienced firefighters who made the choice to bring their experience and skills to the city of Piedmont.” The first to receive her pin was Firefighter-EMT Brittany Borges, originally from the Humboldt Bay Fire Department where she served for four years. Borges is an outdoor enthusiast who enjoys hunting, fishing, and backpacking. She was pinned by Piedmont Fire Captain Justin McNulty. Firefighter-EMT Brandon Clupny, formerly of North Shore Fire Protection District in Lake County, comes from a family of musicians. articles.text: Over a period of three years I wrote essays titled The Pandemic Diaries. Those vignettes attempted to capture in snapshot form what now already seems a distant memory. Yet for those of us who lived through those endless days and months, trailing into years, can seem surreal. I realize now I was often searching for an analog – a fragile comparison. What follows below is but one example. For millennia artists – writers, painters, sculptors, photographers, and filmmakers – have been driven to capture their meditations on periods of extreme dislocation, suffering and uncertainty. We carry with us still those images of the pandemic, of eerily empty streets and masked denizens of gowned and shielded health care workers, their exhaustion written in their vacant stares; the haunting whisper of ventilators connected to the desperately ill; stretching lines of cars waiting at food banks; school halls and classrooms eerily silent, waiting; stores, both large and small, shuttered; refrigerator trucks idling near hospitals, shrouded in a fearful finality. We lived with all of it, the arc of history bending toward the unknown. I recall coming across a photograph taken by Dorothea Lange in 1936 at the height of the Great Depression, a period in our history often used as an analog to profound social disconnection, sustained uncertainty, and economic ruination experienced by so many during the pandemic. The stark image by Lange was of a migrant mother and her three children, huddled together under a canvas lean-to tent. She is sitting, cradling a sleeping infant in her arms. A young boy stands next to her, leaning in, shielding himself, his back to the camera, as does his small sister, her face hidden behind her mother’s shoulder. They are refugees of the heartland, their lives seemingly unbearable, all that was left behind layered with a patina For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Mark’s audience knew harassment, disparagement and persecution. Nero blamed them for a 64 CE fire that nearly destroyed the city. One of the messages Mark wanted to share with them was. “Jesus too knew what it was to be misunderstood and persecuted. But hold on. God is with you as God was with Jesus. The best is yet to come.” The beginning verses of Mark’s gospel are representative of the message that the best is yet to come. In them he tells of John the Baptist, whom the followers of Jesus in Rome likely had heard of, maybe even remembered, as popular, courageous, charismatic and odd, saying that though he, John, had important work to do, it was really work that was primarily to prepare the way for Jesus. Again, the message: the best is yet to come. Children, especially as Christmas approaches, generally do not need any convincing that the best is yet to come. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, December 6, 2023 Opinion VIEWPOINT The Pandemic Diaries – Sometimes, Always, Remembered By Chris Honoré Over a period of three years I wrote essays titled The Pandemic Diaries. Those vignettes attempted to capture in snapshot form what now already seems a distant memory. Yet for those of us who lived through those endless days and months, trailing into years, can seem surreal. I realize now I was often searching for an analog – a fragile comparison. What follows below is but one example. For millennia artists – writers, painters, sculptors, photographers, and filmmakers – have been driven to capture their meditations on periods of extreme dislocation, suffering and uncertainty. We carry with us still those images of the pandemic, of eerily empty streets and masked denizens of gowned and shielded health care workers, their exhaustion written in their vacant stares; the haunting whisper of ventilators connected to the desperately ill; stretching lines of cars waiting at food banks; school halls and classrooms eerily silent, waiting; stores, both large and small, shuttered; refrigerator trucks idling near hospitals, shrouded in a fearful finality. We lived with all of it, the arc of history bending toward the unknown. I recall coming across a photograph taken by Dorothea Lange in 1936 at the height of the Great Depression, a period in our history often used as an analog to profound social disconnection, sustained uncertainty, and economic ruination experienced by so many during the pandemic. The stark image by Lange was of a migrant mother and her three children, huddled together under a canvas lean-to tent. She is sitting, cradling a sleeping infant in her arms. A young boy stands next to her, leaning in, shielding himself, his back to the camera, as does his small sister, her face hidden behind her mother’s shoulder. They are refugees of the heartland, their lives seemingly unbearable, all that was left behind layered with a patina See Viewpoint on page 31 Collecting photos for Where in the World For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. We adults are likely to be much more skeptical. We have heard it all before. We are worn down by the onslaught of glimmering promises from advertisers, politicians and preachers that if we would just buy the right product, vote the right way, or believe the right things, heaven on earth will be ours. We are on guard against getting fooled again. Mark gets it. His people knew all about false promises. The promise of Pax Romana. The promise of an emperor who was sent by the gods. Promises that threatened now to destroy them. Thus, his invitation is guarded. Listen to the story of this man named Jesus. See his compassion. Perceive his heart. Hear his teaching. Take note of the way he lived. Take note of the way he died. Then decide, decide for yourself, if there is anything to this promise, the promise that the best is yet to come. articles.text: On Thursday, November 30, the City of Piedmont held a public workshop regarding the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan and the city’s effort to create 132 units of new housing in the area near the Corporation Yard and Coaches Field. 60 units would be designated low-income housing. City officials said that resident input from these workshops and surveys will help City Council members prioritize features for the preferred site plan. More than 80 members of the community attended the event. City officials and consultants began the night with a presentation on the project, followed by an open house and light refreshments. Stations were set up inside the Veterans Hall, each with one of four proposed project options that differed based on their building layout. Community members were encouraged to write down their feedback for each plan on sticky notes and place them on each board. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore and Planning Director Kevin Jackson began the event with a few words before introducing Drew Watkins, a consultant with JZMK Partners, who led the bulk of the night’s presentation. During his presentation, Watkins revealed the results of a city survey about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, detailing how coumminity members spend their time at Moraga Canyon and what improvements they would like to see. The survey received more than 1100 responses. Watkins also revealed that in all four proposed housing plans the low-income housing developments would be separate buildings from market-rate developments. When asked if the move could isolate members of low-income housing from the rest of the Piedmont community, Jackson replied that although a mixed-income housing development “would be beneficial,” financial constraints would make it difficult to find developers for it. Staff Photos Planning Director Kevin Jackson talks to community members at a workshop on November 30. Veterans Hall bustled with discussion about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan at a public meeting on Thursday, November 30. “The market doesn’t provide for developers who would do a mix of 50/50 low-income and market-rate housing in a single development. If we wanted to see housing constructed in Moraga Canyon, it was most likely that the affordable housing project would need to be separate from the market rate housing project,” said Jackson. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is part of a larger initiative by the City of Piedmont to add new housing units to the community. A mandate by the state of California requires cities to plan additional housing units in their communities to help meet housing needs across the state. The City of Piedmont was charged with creating plans to accommodate 587 units of new housing, including 257 affordable units by 2031. articles.text: A free Christmas Concert, a gift to the community, will be held on Sunday, December 17, at 2:30 p.m. at First Church of Christ, Scientist, 1880 Mountain Blvd. in Montclair. Featured local artists will be organist/pianist Michael Moran, sopranos Katy Stephan and Kate Offer, tenor Darron Flagg, baritone Steve Rogino, cellist Joseph Hébert, violinist Shauna Revelli, and Justice Freeman on saxophone and clarinet. articles.text: On Thursday, November 30, members of Piedmont’s Public Safety Committee met with an agenda that included how to get more residents involved with the Neighborhood Watch program. The meeting began with a presentation by Echa Schneider, the city’s Communications Manager, on the results of a recent survey which indicates that Piedmont residents are interested in learning more about Neighborhood Watch. “As far as topics that people asked to hear about that they’d like information about, by far, the top request was Neighborhood Watch,” said Schneider. This survey received 540 responses and was promoted through the city’s newsletter, which reaches more than 4,700 people. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers reported that the police department (PPD) has put together a preliminary guidebook written by Police Captain Chris Monahan on how to get involved with the neighborhood watch program, including starting your own group. Although Committee Chair Marilyn Weber recognized the guieline’s importance, she said that whatever material is produced should be limited to one page to make it more accessible. Cory Smegal advocated for the importance of a guidebook Staff Photos Police Chief Jeremy Bowers reports on the department’s guidebook on Neighborhood Watch currently in development. but expressed concern that a lack of the right training and resources for neighborhood watch members could lead to racial profiling incidents. Smegal recommended that creating a guide on “when not to call” the police could be an equally useful resource for the community. Other agenda items included a recap of Police Chief Bowers’ quarterly crime report and eightpoint response plan presented at the November 20 City Council meeting and a discussion of the Piedmont Fire Department’s emergency plans by Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. According to Chief Bowers, crime has increased in nearly every category compared with the same time last year, including robbery, assault, burglary, larceny theft, and vehicle theft. However, police have made significant progress toward reducing crime in the last quarter by deploying extra officers, crime suppression cars and increasing the amount of surveillance cameras and Automatic License Plate Readers in the community. To become involved with a Neighborhood Watch group, contact Police Sgt. Nicole Casalnuovo at (510) 420-3000 (ncasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov). The Police Department will put residents in contact with the Neighborhood Watch group in their neighborhood, or if there is not currently an active group in your neighborhood, the PPD will help you organize one. Public Safety Committee members: Jeanne Solnordal (left), Cory Smegal, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Committee Chair Marilyn Weber, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Jeffery Horner, Marie Retherford, and Liz O’Neil in the City Council Chambers
articles.title: Public Safety Committee looks to increase Neighborhood Watch

articles.text: On Wednesday, November 29, representatives from Shell Corporation hosted an open house at Kehilla Community Synagogue on Grand Avenue to announce their plans to replace the Shell Gas Station at Wildwood and Grand Avenues with an electric vehicle charging hub. The new station will be branded under the company Shell Recharge. “Pending permitting and regulatory approvals, Shell hopes to construct a new, 14-bay electric vehicle (EV) charging hub at the site under the Shell Recharge brand. Shell envisions this site to be a part of our growing state and national network of fast charging for electric vehicles,” the company stated in a letter that invited community members to the meeting. During the open house, seven members of the Shell Recharge team were available to answer questions about the project. 3D renderings of the future EV charging hub were displayed on posters in the hall in Kehilla. Light refreshments were also provided. Jeremy Randolph, a Program Manager and team lead of the local Shell Recharge team, led the open house. He will be responsible for interfacing with city Jeremy Randolph, Program Manager and lead member of the local Shell Recharge team. government about the projects, including permits for building and construction. The proposed EV hub will have 14 charging ports available for vehicles 24 hours a day. Customers will be able to view charging availability at the station and pay for charging through the Shell Recharge App. No workers will be on-site regularly. Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2024. For details and more information contact the Shell Recharge Team at 1-888-GO-SHELL (888-467-4355). To ensure your feedback is properly received, please refer to the location at 29 Wildwood Ave. in Piedmont, CA during your phone call.
articles.title: Shell Recharge holds open house for new electric vehicle Hub in Piedmont

articles.text: I’ve been reading Michelle Obama’s new book, “The Light We Carry,” which starts out with a chapter on how knitting helped get her through the worst of the pandemic. How, in the moments when she couldn’t do anything else, she taught herself to knit, and it brought her a moment of ease and a sense of accomplishment that then helped her tackle the bigger challenges. She talks about how knitting gave her a break from her brain doing all the thinking and instead, let her hands just take over for a little while. I see this description as an absolutely perfect explanation of why creative play is so critical for all of us at all times of our lives, not just during a complete shutdown due to a worldwide pandemic. So much of our stress comes from over saturation of the stories and questions that our Knitting and other similar activities relax the mind. minds fixate on–Will my kindergartner learn how to read? Will my toddler ever potty train? How can I ensure that my kids have a good relationship with their grandparents? What does work/life balance look like when I go back to work after my maternity leave and I’m still expected to work 60 hours per week? In her November 28 Piedmont Pulse newsletter to the school community Hawn stated, “Parents, please remember that if your child needs to be out of school, you can submit payment for the lost revenue. Each day that a student is out of school (for any reason, including illness) means a loss of revenue in the following amounts per day.” TK-3rd Grade - $61.32 4th-6th Grade - $56.39 7th-8th Grade - $58.06 9th-12th Grade - $61.20 B2db.edulnk.com/e/d03tu/ aJCyf6?__$u__ Hawn said this is an invitational way to donate. Finance Director Ruth Alahydoian and school principals brought the idea to Hawn’s attention, as it was done in the past before COVID. During COVID average daily attendance was suspended from impacting districts. Since schools reopened, funding calculations use an average of previous years so funding would not suddenly decline. Alahydoian stated during the October 11 board meeting that attendance in Piedmont schools is consistently around 97%, but that has dropped to 94%-95%. “We are losing about $1,000,000, and recouping any of this loss would be great,” said Hawn. over driving the train of life for just a few minutes? articles.text: Bright and early in the morning on Thanksgiving, each year the residents of Piedmont come together to be part of the annual Turkey Trot, 3.1 miles around the neighborhoods with well-wishers practically on every corner. As the participants walk, jog, or run, they are surrounded by the red and orange leaves falling from the trees, the sound of cowbells ringing in support, and crisp autumn air. Ever since I can remember, I have participated in the Turkey Trot. I remember pretending that I was asleep on the morning of the race in hopes I would be left behind and could stay in the warmth of my bed. But that never happened. I would don my shirt, racing bib, and running shoes and begrudgingly walk up Magnolia Avenue to the starting line. As the race started and people were making their way through the starting arch, I would put on my headphones and mentally prepare myself. Despite the fact that I was formerly on a cross-country team, running long distances is not my forte. But with the aid of my headphones, the trot became more bearable. I would run/walk the entire distance. Nothing beats the feeling of finally crossing the finish line and being done with the race. This year, as someone who hates running, I escaped the rigors of running by being a member of the press corps. And even though I wasn’t running, I still had to rise out of my bed at the crack of dawn to get ready. As my family and I were walking up Magnolia to the starring line, I noticed for the first time how truly quiet the streets are at that time. It wasn’t the type of quiet when everyone is asleep, but the type of quiet when there’s absolutely nobody around. As we walked closer to Highland Ave., I could hear the sound of music and someone’s voice on the microphone getting progressively louder. And soon as we walk past the high school, we see the masses of people standing at the start ready to fulfill the race motto: “Move your feet before you eat”. I took a step back, leaned against an arch at the Exedra and looked around. From my vantage point I could see all the families hyping each other up, old high school friends reuniting after being away at college, even friends from high school milling about with each other observing the race just like I was. As the race began, the announcer would call out friends that she saw. But what was important was that morale was being raised. At the start, people were smiling and in high spirits ready for the run. When the final participant crossed the start line, volunteers began to move the barriers towards the finish arch to create space for the runners when they arrived. I realized that the Turkey Trot wasn’t just a Thanksgiving race, but a real community event. In different cities and towns, I doubt that they have a similar loyal fan base, cheering on the runners at every turn of the course, and with volunteers that make the race an enjoyable experience. In Piedmont the race isn’t just an opportunity to show off one’s running skills, but an opportunity to reconnect with friends, to engage in friendly familial competition and to come together as a community to create a race that’s entertaining. As the runners started trickling to the finish line, every runner was cheered on as they came up the final hill, giving them that last bit of a boost to get across the finish line. Sometimes all you need is for one person to encourage you and your feet start moving a bit faster and you pump your arms more for that final push. Next year on Thanksgiving morning, when the sun shines and the runners get ready for the Turkey Trot, I will be with them – ready to run before the madness of last- minute meal preparations begin. Piedmont resident Larissa Edel is a junior at Bentley School.
articles.title: The Turkey Trot dilemma – do I run this year or not?

pages.text: 10 Wednesday, December 6, 2023 New Firefighters Continued from page 1 Colter. Firefighter-EMT Kevin Sauder is an experienced firefighter from the Cloverdale Fire Department, where he served for 15 years. Besides playing disc golf with his two children, Sauder enjoys riding motorcycles and dirt bikes in his spare time. He was pinned by his wife, Laura. Firefighter-Paramedic Christopher Kruger comes from the Lake County Fire District where he served for two years. Kruger is married and the father of three daughters. He was pinned by Captain McNulty. Following the ceremonial badge pinning, the four took an oath of office with City Clerk Anna Brown. Three additional recruits will be added in January for a total of seven. This hiring will increase the Fire Department’s staffing from 21 to 28, an increase of 33%. Of the seven recruits, two are women, a fact Borges sees as an opportunity. “I’m super proud to be a female firefighter. That’s far and few between. It’s a hard job, and it’s a cool opportunity to be one of the first female hires here in almost 18 years,” said Borges. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys basketball team came up two points shy of winning its own tournament, the 33rd annual Winter Classic in a 57-56 loss to Redwood High of Larkspur on Saturday, December 2. PHS opened the three-day tournament with a 60-47 win over Hayward, and remained successful with a 54-50 victory over Acalanes in Friday’s semifinals. Redwood was ranked No. 11 in the North Coast Section last year by MaxPrep.com, compared to Piedmont (No. 27) and Acalanes (No. 31). Redwood and Acalanes both play in Division 2 and Hayward plays in Piedmont’s Div. 3. Impressively Piedmont is without starting forward Alex Anderson. Sophomore guard Dillon Casey stepped up with a 25-point performance against Redwood. Some hoops fans compare him to PHS Class of 2022 standout JoJo Murphy. “We battled back and took a brief lead that was brutal,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “Dillon is a steady player; he never gets too high or too low. Alex is such a great player; he’s long and we can put him as our primary on-ball defender. Hopefully we can get him back,” said coach Ben Spencer. This year’s tournament was sponsored by WestCoastPreps. com, a local prep-sports site. “It was a great tournament, with five games decided by seven or fewer points,” said Spencer. “I’ve had a good relationship with Chris Jackson since he started West Coast Preps. He reached out Staff Photos Brit Burden had 14 points and eight rebounds in Piedmont’s 57-56 loss to Redwood pf Larkspur. Senior point guard Arjun Bornstein looks to make a play. Sophomore Dillon Casey scored 25 points against Redwood. and asked about hosting a tournament and I said ‘absolutely.” 57-56 loss to Redwood Piedmont trailed 17-8 at the end of the first quarter and 37-23 by halftime, but slowly worked its way back to a potential win. They cut the deficit in the third period to 46-40 and took a 55-54 lead in the final minutes. A 3-pointer ultimately did the Highlanders in. Redwood also dominated the offensive boards, recording 14 offensive rebounds, which led to eight points for the Giants. It was a magnificent second-half for sophomore Dillon Casey, who scores 19 of his 25 points in the final two quarters. Starting the third quarter in a 14-point deficit, Piedmont went on a 12-4 scoring run to end the quarter. In the fourth, PHS opened with a 6-2 run, and later on Brit Burden hit Declan Linnane for a quick lay-in before Burden turned a rebound into a fast break score too make it a two-point game at 52-50. After trading possessions, Casey hit a 3-pointer behind a Burden screen to give Piedmont’s its first lead of the game at 53-52 with a minute left. PHS had a chance to extend the lead, but missed. Redwood then grabbed an offensive rebound to score and regain the lead at 54-53. Burden then hit a 3-pointer from the top of the key, making it 56-54 with the clock ticking away. On Redwood’s next possession, Brennan Woodley hit a 3-pointer for the 57-56 game winner. On Piedmont’s final possession, Burden handed off to Casey, who fit a pass into Linnane in the corner for a 3-pointer attempt but his shot skipped off the rim. Final stats: Casey led the way with 25 points, five rebounds, and a steal. Burden had 14 points, eight rebounds, three assists and three steals. Silverberg scored 13 points, two rebounds, and a steal. Cash Panico scored two points, two rebounds, and three assists. Linnane had two points, three rebounds, one assist and three steals. 54-50 win over Acalanes Piedmont led 14-9 through the first quarter and 27-21 by halftime. Acalanes outscored PHS 20-12 in the third quarter to pull within 41-39 to start the fourth. The Highlander defense shined to limit the Dons’ to just nine points in the final going, winning 54-50. 60-47 victory over Hayward Piedmont opened with a 13-8 lead to end the first quarter, but Hayward stormed back to a 24-22 lead by halftime. The Highlanders battled back to a 35-33 lead through the third quarter, and then exploded in the fourth quarter with 25 points to win 60-47. Tuesday vs. Campolindo Piedmont traveled to Campolindo in Moraga on Tuesday, December 5. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-2) faces Monte Vista in the first round of the Chris Huber Classic hosted by Acalanes HS in Lafayette on Thursday, December 7 at 8:30 p.m.
articles.title: Piedmont falls 57-56 to Redwood in Winter Classic Final

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team opened the season by winning the Bryan Ayer Classic at Lompoc High School on Saturday, December 2. In the threeday tournament, PHS dominated with a 75-5 romp over Fresno Christian on Thursday, 62-44 over Dos Pueblos of Goleta in the semifinals, and 63-37 against Orcutt Academy for the championship. Senior team captain Natalia Martinez scored 116 points in three games, including a careerhigh 43 points in Piedmont’s semifinals win over Dos Pueblos. She was named the tournament’s Most Valuable Player. Piedmont won the tournament in 2021 and did not compete in it last year. “It’s great to take these road trips; they really build the team closer together. It’s a great high school experience. Defensively, Sam Smith did a great job against some tough players; she made every shot difficult. Shalika Zuberi guarded their top shooter with pressure and toughness,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Piedmont now hosts the 2023 Paris Twins Classic from Thursday through Saturday, December 7-9. 63-37 over Orcutt Academy Piedmont led 15-7 by the end of the first quarter and jumped out to a 31-18 advantage by halftime. Piedmont limited Orcutt to just nine points in the third and put in 26 points, including 16 points from Martinez, who scored seven points from the free throw line. PHS closed out with six points in the fourth for the 63-37 win. Final stats: Martinez scored 40 points, 11 rebounds, three assists, and three steals. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, December 6, 2023 Sports Piedmont falls 57-56 to Redwood in Winter Classic Final By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys basketball team came up two points shy of winning its own tournament, the 33rd annual Winter Classic in a 57-56 loss to Redwood High of Larkspur on Saturday, December 2. Redwood was ranked No. 11 in the North Coast Section last year by MaxPrep.com, compared to Piedmont (No. 27) and Acalanes (No. 31). Redwood and Acalanes both play in Division 2 and Hayward plays in Piedmont’s Div. 3. Impressively Piedmont is without starting forward Alex Anderson. Sophomore guard Dillon Casey stepped up with a 25-point performance against Redwood. Some hoops fans compare him to PHS Class of 2022 standout JoJo Murphy. “We battled back and took a brief lead that was brutal,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “Dillon is a steady player; he never gets too high or too low. Alex is such a great player; he’s long and we can put him as our primary on-ball defender. Hopefully we can get him back,” said coach Ben Spencer. This year’s tournament was sponsored by WestCoastPreps. com, a local prep-sports site. “It was a great tournament, with five games decided by seven or fewer points,” said Spencer. “I’ve had a good relationship with Chris Jackson since he started West Coast Preps. He reached out Staff Photos Brit Burden had 14 points and eight rebounds in Piedmont’s 57-56 loss to Redwood pf Larkspur. Senior point guard Arjun Bornstein looks to make a play. Sophomore Dillon Casey scored 25 points against Redwood. and asked about hosting a tournament and I said ‘absolutely.” 57-56 loss to Redwood Piedmont trailed 17-8 at the end of the first quarter and 37-23 by halftime, but slowly worked its way back to a potential win. They cut the deficit in the third period to 46-40 and took a 55-54 lead in the final minutes. A 3-pointer ultimately did the Highlanders in. Redwood also dominated the offensive boards, recording 14 offensive rebounds, which led to eight points for the Giants. It was a magnificent second-half for sophomore Dillon Casey, who scores 19 of his 25 points in the final two quarters. Starting the third quarter in a 14-point deficit, Piedmont went on a 12-4 scoring run to end the quarter. In the fourth, PHS opened with a 6-2 run, and later on Brit Burden hit Declan Linnane for a quick lay-in before Burden turned a rebound into a fast break score too make it a two-point game at 52-50. The defending North Coast Section champion girls’ and boys’ teams have no home field this winter. With the season starting this week, the teams are still searching for a field for the season. “There’s a lot of organizations, schools, and clubs competing for a limited amount of field space,” said PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “As we get updates on our own field it’s made things a bit difficult. There’s been multiple reasons for the completion date of Witter Field moving from November 1, when initially planned, to February, so we’ve had to adjust.” Both teams were slated to play home games at Wilder Fields in Orinda, but the City of Orinda indicated their schedules didn’t align with Piedmont’s. “I had spoken with the City of Orinda and tried to work out field availability. Both PHS teams have been practicing at Laney College, but the field is unable to host games because it lacks lines for soccer. articles.text: Photo courtesy of SF State Perseas Gioukaris, PHS Class of 2023, is a freshman at San Francisco State. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team got underway by winning the 2023 Bryan Ayer Classic at Lompoc High School last weekend. We pause to take a look at three former basketball stars currently active at the collegiate level: Perseas Gioukaris of San Francisco State, Maddy Meadows of William Jessup, and Maddie Hill of Rocky Mountain University. Perseas Gioukaris San Francisco State Perseas Gioukaris, PHS Class of 2023, is a freshman at San Francisco State. She is a former starter on Piedmont’s 2023 Division 4 North Coast Section and Western Alameda County Conference championship team. San Francisco State is currently 2-4 to start its season with Gioukaris earning a role as a newcomer. So far this season, she has appeared in all six games, totaling 103 minutes with 27 points, converting 43 percent of her field goals. She’s also recorded nine rebounds, four assists, six steals, and one block. At Piedmont she earned firstteam All-League honors after being forced to miss her junior year due to CIF transfer rules. She had 12 points and two steals in Piedmont’s 75-49 win over Branson for the NCS title. Gioukaris also knocked down a critical 3-pointer in a 69-62 win over Bishop O’Dowd, Maddy Meadows William Jessup Maddy Meadows, PHS Class of 2020, is a senior at William Jessup University in Rocklin after transferring from Biola University following her sophomore year. Her team is currently 6-1 to start its season. Meadows has appeared in 84 minutes through six games, recording 31 points by converting 40 percent of her field goals, to go along with 28 rebounds, 12 assists, and four steals. In 2023, Meadows appeared in 18 games, 237 minutes and has scored 81 total points, to go along with 37 rebounds, eight assists, and 11 steals. Meadows only played her senior year at Piedmont, and helped them to a 21-7 overall record. She was named to the All-League second team. In 2019/2020, Piedmont reached the quarterfinals of the D4 NCS playoffs with the No. 5 seed. Photo courtesy of William Jessup Maddy Meadows, PHS Class of 2020, is a senior at William Jessup. Photo courtesy of Rocky Mountain University Maddie Hill, PHS Class of 2023, is a freshman at Rocky Mountain University. Maddie Hill Rocky Mountain University Maddie Hill, PHS Class of 2023, is a freshman at Rocky Mountain University in Provo, Utah, and another member of Piedmont’s NCS and WACC Championship winning teams. Her Rocky Mountain team is currently 7-0 to start its season. As a college freshman, Hill has appeared in four games for 29 minutes, scoring 13 points on 45 percent shooting from the field, while she’s also hit three of six 3-point attempts. At Piedmont, Maddie was a four-year starter and a key player. She earned second-team AllLeague honors as a senior. She was named by the Post Honorable Mention for Freshman of the Year in 2020.

articles.text: With winter sports ramping up the soccer and basketball season, here is a look at four key athletes to watch this season. ENZO BERNALES Soccer Enzo Bernales, Class of 2025, was named the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2023 after helping lead the Highlanders to their second consecutive North Coast Section championship. He burst onto the scene as a first-year starter, and finished the year as the team’s top scorer. He’ll be one of the premier attacking players in Todd Sullivan’s system as a forward who can run centrally and rotate out to the wing, while also dropping back as a midfielder at times. He scored a penalty kick against No. 5 Kimball in Piedmont’s 2-0 win in the Div. 3 NorCal opening round of the State championships. Bernales also sent the game-winning Staff Photo Enzo Bernales, a junior, was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year. assist on Mile Corcoran’s goal in the D4 NCS Quarterfinals to upset No. 1 Cardinal Newman, He also picked up a goal and assist in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over No. 9 St. Helena in the opening round. Bernales was named to the All-League Honorable Mention team. AMY DERR Soccer Amy Derr, Class of 2024, is a defender on Piedmont’s Division 4 North Coast Section championship team. The strength of Piedmont’s back line shined last winter, helping the team go 13-1-6 including 10 shutout victories. During Piedmont’s run to the NCS title, the Highlanders limited their opponents to two goals in four games, including an 11-2 goal differential. Though playing as a defender, Derr made her presence felt on offense. She scored in a 5-0 win over Castro Valley and scored a 35-yard goal on a free kick in a 1-1 tie against Alameda. SAMANTHA SMITH Basketball Staff Photo Amy Derr is a senior leader on the defending NCS champion girls’ soccer team. Sam Smith, Class of 2024, is a second year varsity player and is entering a starting role on Bryan Gardere’s roster. She’s emerged as a forward, recording 18 points and 10 rebounds in their win over Fresno Academy in the Bryan Ayer Classic, where she recorded 29 points and 22 rebounds over three games. Last year, Smith was a reserve forward in Piedmont’s Western Alameda County Conference and Division 4 North Coast Section championship team which finished the year with a 27-1 overall record after reaching the second round of the CIF Open Division tournament, reserved for the best teams in the state. She transferred to Piedmont from Dublin HS last year, where she was a member of their varsity team as a sophomore. articles.text: Photos courtesy of Rodger Sherman All of the Pac-12 mascots gather for one last photo together at the 2023 Pac-12 Championship Game, which marked the end of the storied West Coast conference. As the minutes ticked by in Saturday’s Pac-12 Championship football game between the Oregon Ducks and Washington Huskies (the Huskies won 34-31), it began to sink in. Video clips went viral of every Pac-12 mascot dancing together on the sidelines while waving goodbye to fans. It put an emphasis to the fact that December 2’s game marked the end of a 108-year-old tradition. The conference has been shattered and has left fans disillusioned. Following this weekend, California and Stanford will join the Atlantic Coastal Conference with games 3000 miles away. Heading to the Big 10 Conference are Washington, Oregon, USC, and UCLA, and joining the Big 12 Conference will be Arizona, Arizona State, Colorado, and Utah. Washington State and Oregon State, meanwhile, are still looking for a home. Something about TV revenue it seems. A lot can be made of the Pac- 12’s dissolution and finger-pointing on the cause. ad. Were USC and UCLA at fault for starting the trend in June? Can you spell G-RE-E-D? Does the blame completely rest on Pac-12 commissioner, Larry Scott, who balked at Texas joining the conference in 2010 and recently failed to get the Pac-12 Network coverage on major TV providers? What is done is done, and a new future starts. As a season ticket holder for the California Golden Bears’ football team for nearly two decades, learned about the traditions in the Pac-12 from my uncle and that is what drove my curiosity of the college game. Cal and Stanford’s Big Game, one of the best and famous rivalries in college sports, is now in an East Coast-based conference. Why would any Duke or North Carolina fan care about the Big Game, or that Cal have hoisted the Axe for three consecutive years? My fondest memories of Pac- 12 games include when DeSean Jackson had one of his legendary punt returns against Oregon in 2006 and when Marshawn Lynch hijacked a an injury cart to go joyriding on the field after defeating Washington. Jahvid Best provided some of the most electrifying moments on a football field against Oregon, UCLA, and Stanford, and lighting up this year’s Pac-12 champions, Washington, for a school-record 311 yards and four touchdowns. Many will forget that Washington was once the cupcakes of the Pac-12 conference, only for them now to spurn its historic rival in Washington State for the greener pastures of a Big 10 super conference. Time will tell what happens with the continued conference re-alignment happening in college football. But one thing is clear; the almighty dollar means school tradition plays second-fiddle to the big-business of football. – Lord Acton, English historian, politician, writer Here lies the Pac-12 Conference.
articles.title: Reflecting on the Pac-12 Conference’s tragic end

Washington State and Oregon State, meanwhile, are still looking for a home. Something about TV revenue it seems. A lot can be made of the Pac- 12’s dissolution and finger-pointing on the cause. ad. Were USC and UCLA at fault for starting the trend in June? Can you spell G-RE-E-D? Does the blame completely rest on Pac-12 commissioner, Larry Scott, who balked at Texas joining the conference in 2010 and recently failed to get the Pac-12 Network coverage on major TV providers? What is done is done, and a new future starts. As a season ticket holder for the California Golden Bears’ football team for nearly two decades, learned about the traditions in the Pac-12 from my uncle and that is what drove my curiosity of the college game. Cal and Stanford’s Big Game, one of the best and famous rivalries in college sports, is now in an East Coast-based conference. Why would any Duke or North Carolina fan care about the Big Game, or that Cal have hoisted the Axe for three consecutive years? My fondest memories of Pac- 12 games include when DeSean Jackson had one of his legendary punt returns against Oregon in 2006 and when Marshawn Lynch hijacked a an injury cart to go joyriding on the field after defeating Washington. Jahvid Best provided some of the most electrifying moments on a football field against Oregon, UCLA, and Stanford, and lighting up this year’s Pac-12 champions, Washington, for a school-record 311 yards and four touchdowns. Many will forget that Washington was once the cupcakes of the Pac-12 conference, only for them now to spurn its historic rival in Washington State for the greener pastures of a Big 10 super conference. Time will tell what happens with the continued conference re-alignment happening in college football. But one thing is clear; the almighty dollar means school tradition plays second-fiddle to the big-business of football. “Power tends to corrupt; absolute power corrupts absolutely.” – Lord Acton, English historian, politician, writer Here lies the Pac-12 Conference.

articles.text: Mission Peak Summit is among the most popular trails of East Bay Regional Park District and considered the most frequented attraction in the City of Fremont. On a Sunday morning and early afternoon, the location can become a highway of foot traffic, with families, dog walkers and bikers making their way to the Mission Peak Summit Pole for a photo opportunity. Arriving at the Mission Peak Trailhead by 3 p.m. will enable you to have a more secluded trek, and offering a striking view of a burning orange sunset as the sun dips below the mountains surrounding the Peninsula. Standing at the Summit Pole the view includes the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge with the Dumbarton Bridge and Fremont in the distance. You can watch the lights flicker on through Union City and Hayward, with a glimpse of the San Mateo Bridge and San Francisco off in the distance. To the South are Milpitas and the cityscape feeding toward San Jose and the remaining Mission Peak Regional Preserve. articles.text: Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe’s show on November 25 at the Sound Room in Oakland was a tribute to Jeff Beck performed by Jules’ band, “the Family Jules Band”. My own love of Jeff Beck goes back to 1965 when I heard the song “Heart Full Of Soul” on AM top 40 radio. I probably heard it in the car with my mom at the wheel. Beck was 21 at the time and has a very tasty guitar solo in the middle of this 2-minute,19-second song. The next song that blew my mind was also from the year 1965 – The Yardbirds doing “I’m A Man”. Both of these recordings can be heard on YouTube. The first time I heard Jeff Beck play live was at the ARMS Benefit Concert for Ronnie Lane who had multiple-sclerosis at the Cow Palace in Brisbane. The Cow Palace is where the Beatles played during their first world tour in 1964. The Rolling Stones played there the following year. The benefit concert that I saw in 1985 featured Eric Clapton doing a set followed by Jeff Beck which was followed by Jimmy Page of Led Zeppelin fame. Joe Cocker was also in the mix. I must say that Jeff Beck blew the roof off of the place with his partner Jan Hammer on keyboards. That concert can be watched on YouTube as well. Fast forward to the year 2002 to a concert Jeff Beck gave at the Warfield Theater on Market Street in San Francisco. The four of us – Mom, Dad, Sis and Bro – had been to the Great American Music Theater to hear Doc Watson on a Sunday night. Jules was about 12 years old at that time. When we were driving down Market Street with my wife at the wheel, I saw the marquee at the Warfield, which said “Jeff Beck eight and ten o’clock”. Emphatically I said, “stop the car!“ My wife, Laura, knew that I am mischievous and was about to take her 12-year-old son to a rock ‘n’ roll concert on a school night at 10 o’clock. I ran across Market Street and got two tickets in the balcony and said, “Come on Jules. We’re going to go see Jeff Beck”. And that was the night that Jules decided he was going to get serious about playing an electric guitar. He saved all his paper route and babysitting money and went down to Guitar Center to purchase a Fender Stratocaster. About one year later, I was making the bed when the phone rang. It was Jules, who said, “Dad/ Jeff Beck died!” “Oh no”, I responded. We were both crying. We were lucky to see Jeff’s third-to-last show a little over a year ago in San Jose. The next night, he played Sacramento. His last show ever was the following night in Reno. A month or two later he was gone. He died of bacterial meningitis at age 78. The Sound Room tribute show on November 25 featured Jules’ take on Jeff Beck compositions. The Family Jules Band consists of Jules Leyhe on guitar, Ian Mcardle, on keyboards, Isaac Schwartz on drums, and Matt Rhodes on bass. Ian studied at Juilliard and there is a jazz influence in his playing. Isaac is also very talented with his percussion. Isaac’s work for the Jeff Beck tribute featured both quiet, playing with brushes and mallets, as well as full tilt rock ‘n’ roll. Matt Rhodes skillfully held down the bottom with his bass guitar. The last song of the evening was a medley of the new Beatles song “Now And Then”, which Jules merged into “Beck’s Bolero” to finish the show. Everybody left The Sound Room with a smile on their face. Photo by Bob Hakins Lead guitarist Jules Leyhe and the Family Jules Band performed a tribute concert at the Sound Room on November 25 honoring the work of guitarist Jeff Beck.
articles.title: Family Jules Band pays tribute to Jeff Beck with Sound Room concert

articles.text: The San Francisco Opera will present its acclaimed San Francisco Opera Chorus to conclude the fall season this Friday, December 8. Chorus Director John Keene will conduct the Opera Chorus and Associate Chorus Master Fabrizio Corona will accompany on keyboard for an evening of a cappella and accompanying choral works. The program features selections from opera repertoires, with music by Clara Schumann, Fanny Mendelssohn Hensel, Lili Boulanger and Florence Price as well as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Gabriel Fauré and Stephen Paulus. Seating is general admission. For tickets, visit sfopera.com, the San Francisco Opera Box Office at 301 Van Ness Avenue or call (415) 864-3330. Additional information can be found at sfopera. com/chorusinconcert. San Francisco Opera will be accompanied by its chorus this Friday.
articles.title: Evening performance features SF Opera Chorus

articles.text: Photos by Erik Tomassan Wona Park and Wei Wang, Elizabeth Powell and Lonnie Weeks, and Nikishi Fogo in San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker. San Francisco Ballet announced principal casting for Nutcracker, its classic holiday production, which begins December 13. Principal Dancers Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, and Aaron Robison; as well as Soloist Jasmine Jimison and Corps de Ballet member Mingxuan Wang will dance the roles of the Sugar Plum Fairy, Grand Pas de Deux, and Queen and King of the Snow. Nutcracker is choreographed by former artistic director Helgi Tomasson, and features designs by Tony Award–winners Michael Yeargan and Martin Pakledinaz, lighting designs by James Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall Harrington. San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo leads the principal dancers and the company performed to Tchaikovsky’s iconic score. “I am both humbled and exhilarated by the boundless creativity and passion of our dancers,” said Rojo. “The enchantment of Nutcracker can already be felt throughout the city.” Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. It features the production every year with “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers. A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani. The production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks. Nutcracker is appropriate for children age five and older. No children under the age of three will be permitted. Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. The ballet will be shown onstage at the War Memorial Opera House through December 30. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling Ticket Services at 415- 865-2000, open Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
articles.title: SF Ballet prepares for month of Nutcracker

articles.text: Veteran Bay Area actor James Carpenter’s powerful portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge leads American Conservatory Theater’s production of A Christmas Carol, an annual highlight of the holiday season in the Bay Area. The production opens tonight, December 6, on Geary Street. The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dickens’ novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly 100 years. ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo, with music scored by Karl Lundenberg and choreography by Val Caniparoli. A Christmas Carol has been included in ACT’s repertory for decades, and Carpenter has resided in the role of Scrooge for 15 consecutive seasons. Performances will take place at the Toni Rembe Theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. The production uses theatrical haze and lighting that may not be appropriate for photosensitive groups. The holiday classic will play onstage through December 24. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets, or call the box office at 415-749-2228. Photo by Kevin Berne James Carpenter as Ebenezer Scrooge in ACT’s A Christmas Carol.
articles.title: San Francisco’s favorite holiday classic opens today

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) opened its newest exhibition, Por el Pueblo: The Legacy and Influence of Malaquías Montoya, last month in the museum’s Great Hall. Montoyo, now 85, is originally from Albuquerque, New Mexico. He was raised by a single mother in a family of migrant farm workers in California’s Central Valley, a location that heavily inf luences his work. Montoya often uses political imagery in his work and has produced substantial art centered around the issue of immigration. His posters, graphic prints, and murals often highlighted political and social justice issues, and helped define the Chicano identity and culture for nearly 50 years. Artists from multiple generations cite Montoya as an influence, including Julio Salgado, Elyse Doyle-Martinez, Leslie Lopez, Israel Campos, and Arely Hernández. Por el Pueblo will be on view at Oakland Museum through June 30, 2024. To learn more, visit https://museumca.org/on-view/ por-el-pueblo/.
articles.title: Malaquías Montoya exhibit at OMCA now on view

articles.text: Isaiah Stone, Jennifer Lawrence, and Ashlee Thompson in Winter’s Bone The first stark images of Winter’s Bone are of two children playing in a yard, surrounded by trees winter bare, the sunlight diffuse, without warmth. The house is more a shack than not, wood frame and hard used. Dead cars and appliances sit deep in weeds. The setting is a hamlet in the southern Missouri Ozarks, a place apart, where people – hard scrabble, insular – live on the frayed edges of society. Many exist off the grid, suspicious, even paranoid, a source of income the cooking and sale of methamphetamine. The children in the yard, a brother and sister, are the siblings of Ree Dooly (Jennifer Lawrence), 17, who carries the full weight of the family. Her mother is paralyzed by a deep depression and her father, Jessup, recently arrested for cooking meth, has just made bond and been released from jail. What Ree soon learns from the local sheriff is that in order to post bond, Jessup has put up the house and the surrounding acreage, some of it rich with timber, as collateral. If he fails to make his court date all will be forfeited. She and her family will be homeless. Ree sets out to find her father, a journey that takes her to the center of the Dolly clan where she discovers that family ties will only protect her to a certain point and no further. She’s told to leave it alone by men and women who look at her with cold eyes and grimly set mouths, their secrets impenetrable, while standing in front of houses as closed and damaged as they are. For Ree, the stakes are high, finding her father crucial, and she’s prepared to risk all. Winter’s Bone is remarkable. The performance by Lawrence is astonishing as she captures with a steely grittiness the intractable place in which Ree finds herself. As a character, Ree is the anchor of her family and alone faces a reality she barely understands. Lawrence demonstrates an uncanny subtlety and power in her portrayal, considering that the dialogue is laconic, stripped of all excess language. So authentic is this film that it borders on cinema-verite’. As the story unfolds, it’s easy to forget the actors are not locals but are delivering, like Lawrence, exceptional performances. Winter’s Bone is, at its core, a woman’s film. For all of their truculence and need to control, leavened with a subtext of violence, the men are almost peripheral. It’s the women, and, of course, Ree, who are central to the events as they slowly and ominously develop and it is the women who place Ree in harm’s way. This fact gives the story an interesting and compelling dimension. If you love movies that illuminate, that are an unsettling and penetrating window into the human condition, Winter’s Bone is not to be missed. Winter’s Bone. Directed by Debra Granik. Starring Jennifer Lawrence, John Hawkes, Dale Dickey and Garret Dillahunt. Released 2010. 1hr 39min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/peacock/ Prime//MAX/Apple tv
articles.title: MOVIE FOR ADULTS Winter’s Bone a stunning, realistic film

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Who would’ve thought? Angelina Jolie, consummate actress, regarded as a porcelain beauty, has fashioned herself into a premier action hero, equal to any of the men doing similar genre films today. It’s been a remarkable transformation for the award-winning Jolie – Oscar for Best Supporting Actress, Golden Globe Award, Screen Actors Guild Award, all for her incomparable performance in Girl Interrupted. She also established her Indiana Jones bona fides with the Lara Croft: Tomb Raider films, followed by The Bone Collector and Gone in 60 Seconds. And not to forget Mr.& Mrs. Smith, the movie that sent the tabloids into fits of ecstasy, the icing on the celluloid cake. With the release of Salt, a let’er rip action thriller where Jolie demonstrates not only her wellhoned acting ability, but a fearless ability to leap from moving semirigs, destroy massive amounts of public property, and keep the audiences breathlessly engaged as she makes a harrowing dash from pillar to post (word is she did many of her own stunts). No matter that the plot is skinny as a swivel stick, this movie is a barn-burner with plenty of tight shots of Jolie, pursing her signature lips, contemplating her next getaway. It would be pointless to recap the convoluted plot. Sure, it’s improbably outrageous. But Salt is a flat-out gestalt of ferocious action that entertains from the first to last frame. The opening setup has her being brutally tortured by North Koreans who think she’s a spy, and the nicely done final scene which suggests its might be an introduction to a sequel. Salt. Directed by Phillip Noyce, Starring Angelina Jolie, Live Schreiber, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Andre Braugher and Daniel Olbrychski. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, December 6, 2023 MOVIE FOR ADULTS Winter’s Bone a stunning, realistic film Salt an action flick with Angelina Jolie Review by Chris Honoré Who would’ve thought? Angelina Jolie, consummate actress, regarded as a porcelain beauty, has fashioned herself into a premier action hero, equal to any of the men doing similar genre films today. It’s been a remarkable transformation for the award-winning Jolie – Oscar for Best Supporting Actress, Golden Globe Award, Screen Actors Guild Award, all for her incomparable performance in Girl Interrupted. She also established her Indiana Jones bona fides with the Lara Croft: Tomb Raider films, followed by The Bone Collector and Gone in 60 Seconds. And not to forget Mr.& Mrs. Smith, the movie that sent the tabloids into fits of ecstasy, the icing on the celluloid cake. With the release of Salt, a let’er rip action thriller where Jolie demonstrates not only her wellhoned acting ability, but a fearless ability to leap from moving semirigs, destroy massive amounts of public property, and keep the audiences breathlessly engaged as she makes a harrowing dash from pillar to post (word is she did many of her own stunts). No matter that the plot is skinny as a swivel stick, this movie is a barn-burner with plenty of tight shots of Jolie, pursing her signature lips, contemplating her next getaway. It would be pointless to recap the convoluted plot. Sure, it’s improbably outrageous. But Salt is a flat-out gestalt of ferocious action that entertains from the first to last frame. The opening setup has her being brutally tortured by North Koreans who think she’s a spy, and the nicely done final scene which suggests its might be an introduction to a sequel. Salt. Directed by Phillip Noyce, Starring Angelina Jolie, Live Schreiber, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Andre Braugher and Daniel Olbrychski. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on VUDU/peacock/ Prime/Apple tv. Isaiah Stone, Jennifer Lawrence, and Ashlee Thompson in Winter’s Bone By Chris Honoré The first stark images of Winter’s Bone are of two children playing in a yard, surrounded by trees winter bare, the sunlight diffuse, without warmth. The house is more a shack than not, wood frame and hard used. Dead cars and appliances sit deep in weeds. The setting is a hamlet in the southern Missouri Ozarks, a place apart, where people – hard scrabble, insular – live on the frayed edges of society. Many exist off the grid, suspicious, even paranoid, a source of income the cooking and sale of methamphetamine. The children in the yard, a brother and sister, are the siblings of Ree Dooly (Jennifer Lawrence), 17, who carries the full weight of the family. Her mother is paralyzed by a deep depression and her father, Jessup, recently arrested for cooking meth, has just made bond and been released from jail. What Ree soon learns from the local sheriff is that in order to post bond, Jessup has put up the house and the surrounding acreage, some of it rich with timber, as collateral. If he fails to make his court date all will be forfeited. She and her family will be homeless. Ree sets out to find her father, a journey that takes her to the center of the Dolly clan where she discovers that family ties will only protect her to a certain point and no further. She’s told to leave it alone by men and women who look at her with cold eyes and grimly set mouths, their secrets impenetrable, while standing in front of houses as closed and damaged as they are. For Ree, the stakes are high, finding her father crucial, and she’s prepared to risk all. Winter’s Bone is remarkable. The performance by Lawrence is astonishing as she captures with a steely grittiness the intractable place in which Ree finds herself. As a character, Ree is the anchor of her family and alone faces a reality she barely understands. Lawrence demonstrates an uncanny subtlety and power in her portrayal, considering that the dialogue is laconic, stripped of all excess language. So authentic is this film that it borders on cinema-verite’. As the story unfolds, it’s easy to forget the actors are not locals but are delivering, like Lawrence, exceptional performances. Winter’s Bone is, at its core, a woman’s film. For all of their truculence and need to control, leavened with a subtext of violence, the men are almost peripheral. It’s the women, and, of course, Ree, who are central to the events as they slowly and ominously develop and it is the women who place Ree in harm’s way. This fact gives the story an interesting and compelling dimension. If you love movies that illuminate, that are an unsettling and penetrating window into the human condition, Winter’s Bone is not to be missed. Winter’s Bone. Directed by Debra Granik. Starring Jennifer Lawrence, John Hawkes, Dale Dickey and Garret Dillahunt. Released 2010. 1hr 39min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/peacock/ Prime//MAX/Apple tv Angelina Jolie in Salt

articles.text: Miley Cyrus and Liam Hemsworth in The Last Song No matter what the critics may say, Nicholas Sparks is a master at what he does, though there are those who will argue that he’s a shameless manipulator of the easily accessible emotions of tweenteen girls who embrace his movies and may even read his novels. Or not. Hard to dispute that Sparks has nailed this adolescent demographic by developing a winning formula that he can superimpose on just about any love story. Recall the Dear John movie; same difference. Granted, sometimes his characters grow up, meaning they’ve grown taller. Examples would be The Notebook, Message in a Bottle and Night in Rodanthe. So, judging The Last Song from the point of view of 16-yearold girls it’s impossible to say anything other than they will love this movie and will sniffle and sigh and feel their eyes welling with tears as Sparks and director Julie Ann Robinson take them through the formulaic, rollercoaster paces. In a nutshell: Ronnie Miller (Miley Cyrus) and her brother Jonah (Bobby Coleman) are driven by their mom, Kim (Kelly Preston), to spend the summer with their dad, Steve, who lives in a spacious and chic-worn beach house on Tybee Island, off the coast of Georgia. Mom and dad are divorced. Ronnie, feeling hurt and abandoned by her dad, is perpetually angry and hostile and not happy to be spending a weekend let alone a summer on the island. These are emotions that she shares at every opportunity. She pouts and snarls and stalks off in all directions. Until she meets Will (Liam Hensworth), an island resident, beach volleyball player, summer mechanic, who, like Ronnie, has just graduated from high school and is waiting to go to Vanderbilt University in the fall. Ronnie, a piano prodigy, has been accepted to Julliard for a full ride but refuses to go and, for good measure, refuses to play. She’s too angry and believes she will hurt her father, a composer, by walking away from her scholarship and her talent. Sparks is a master of girl meets boy girl on the beach, followed by boy pursues girl hoping to ignite a nascent spark. In this case, Ronnie practices complete indifference to Will’s attention (you can almost hear that quintessentially terrible teen word, “whatever,” trailing Ronnie from house to beach and back), while keeping her nose buried in Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina. When Ronnie discovers endangered sea turtle eggs in front of the beach house, she sets about trying to protect them from raccoons. Will, volunteering for a marine sanctuary, shows up to stand vigil with her. Romance takes hold and angry, indifferent Ronnie gets less angry and way less indifferent with everyone, her dad included. And so Sparks sets the hook, and, just to be sure, includes engaging montages of Will and Ronnie swimming, playing tag, getting in a mud fight, talking intensely, meeting his parents (he’s hugely wealthy) and, indeed, kissing. Lots of kissing. All chaste and lovely and very emotive. Of course, Sparks loves to pump up the volume regarding unfinished issues, pre-fab subplots and misunderstandings, willing to throw in, predictably, a terminal illness or an unsettling speed bump just to keep things interesting. And just when you thought it was safe to put away the tissue. Now remember who’s sitting in the audience, all those teen girls identifying with Ronnie and loving every moment. By that measure, The Last Song succeeds and then some, making Nicholas Sparks happy and rich and very good at what he does: gently and not so gently squeezing the hearts of tween-teen girls who love every minute. One last thing: The Last Song is a transition film for Miley who has paid her dues as Hannah Montana, a long-running tween-teen television show of the same name, one that became a cultural event for young girls. She’s been a phenom who has grown up on television. She can sing. But can she act and so carry a feature film? Perhaps a better question is: Is she credible to young people in the role of a girl with issues who finds herself on the cusp of becoming a woman? Answer: indeed. The Last Song. Directed by Julie Ann Robinson. Starring Miley Cyrus, Liam Hensworth, Greg Kinnear, Bobby Coleman and Kelly Preston. Released in 2010. Rated PG. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv.
