articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Star Wars: The Force Awakens is the seventh in what is one of the most successful franchises in film history. Over the decades, starting in May 1977, the generic Star Wars has morphed into a cultural phenom, one that has captured the imaginations of moviegoers globally. They remain popular even when the sequels and prequels didn’t quite reach the bar established with the initial trilogy, Star Wars IV: A New Hope, The Empire Strikes Back, and Return of the Jedi. Woven through all the Star Wars films is the question: what is there about these stories, these characters, that is so compelling and has consistently resonated with wide-ranging audiences? Perhaps the genius of George Lucas was in crafting a blend of high tech/low tech medieval lore (Princesses, Jedi Knights, mystical swords and dark Lords), combined with storytelling similar to mid-20th century Republic serials that kids flocked to movie theaters every Saturday to watch cliff-hanging installments of action movies like Don Winslow of the Navy and Flash Gordon. And hands down, there’s never been a better example of a character from the dark side than Darth Vader (aka Lord Vader), surrounded by armed storm troopers, his menacing black mask covering a visage we can only imagine, every breath a wheezing sound. His persona – voice and stature – was inspired and breathtaking. This was sci-fi fantasy unlike anything we had seen before. And so began a narrative that would span three movies and would introduce a galaxy far, far away that was both myth and entertainment, proving to be irresistible. Ultimately, these films, and now The Force Awakens. are wonderfully constructed morality plays, primal fantasies that reduce our complex world to good vs. evil. The loosely structured band of Rebels – never ominously militaristic – also represents the best impulses of men and women who yearn for Democracy. And they still possess those familiar X-Wing fighters, while remaining ready to confront Fascism’s jackbooted soldiers and their deadly armaments, to include a Death Star equipped with a planet-destroying ray. The Force Awakens is the first installment of a fresh trilogy that introduces a new generation of characters such as Rey (Daisy Ridley), a space junk scavenger; and Finn (John Boyega), a reluctant storm trooper; as well as Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), a hotshot Resistance pilot sent in search of Luke Skywalker. And not to forget Darth Vader’s masked acolyte, Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), who kneels at the feet of the supreme leader, Snoke (Andy Serkis), one very large dude. The story manages to skirt a precipice of nostalgia while avoiding being maudlin as it builds a bridge between the original trilogy, featuring Han Solo (Harrison Ford), Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) who is now a general in the Resistance, and Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill). Clearly, the coming films will focus on what will be the ongoing battle in all its permutations between The Resistance and The Front. So, if The Force Awakens is considered in great part prologue, then some of the best is yet to come. In essence it is the first reboot of the initial Star Wars and pays homage to those first three films that so completely solidified the brand. For those proto-fans who sat down for the first time back in 1977 and watched the yellow block script scroll slowly into the dark distance, words that framed the battles ahead, even today that moment remains unforgettable. But that was then and this is now. Kids having the same experience with The Force Awakens won’t be disappointed. The force is beginning to awaken. Wait for it. Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Directed by J.J. Abrams. Starring Harrison Ford, Daisy Ridley and John Boyega. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2015. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. articles.text: Margaret Mead once told my father: “success is measured on the yardstick of dollars and cents.” She and my father had many conversations because my father was her hairdresser in New York in the 1930s. Dr. Mead’s statement made me think about success in music – orchestra conductors in particular. Classic cartoons captured the persona of the symphony orchestra conductor to perfection. It is worth seeing the one featuring Leopold Stokowski. You will remember his music from Walt Disney’s Fantasia. Speaking of Walt Disney, he featured Mickey Mouse as an orchestra conductor. Whether Mickey was Walt’s alter ego or not, the cartoon was priceless…Instructive, also. In classical music, the conductor is the superstar. All eyes are riveted to the podium. Not so long ago rank-and-file musicians of the San Francisco Symphony made about $100,000. The conductor was paid about $1 million just for his local duties. If he conducted elsewhere, he got additional fees. We’re talking big money. Is the conductor really worth the adulation, not to mention the fortune? There is a classic book which instructs conductors on the best way to direct an orchestra. Most conductors don’t read it, and most of them never even heard of it. It is the “grammar of conducting.” As a music critic, I go to many concerts. Most of the time the conductor tries to get the orchestra to play faster than they can. If the orchestra can play at a ridiculously fast tempo, the conductor tries to go even faster. Pay attention to this the next time you go to a concert. Another thing that conductors frequently do is mug for the audience. The fact is, these faces and crocodile tears do nothing to make the music better. The musicians need a clear beat and intelligent direction – and that is all. Sacha Grippando Gemologist M Ma ag gn no ol li

articles.text: Friday, December 8, 6 p.m. Sacha Grippando Retro Jewelry Lectures Piedmont resident and gemologist Sacha Grippando continues her lecture series focused on the development of the jewelry arts, with a pair of illustrated lectures exploring the spectacular jewelry collections of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor. This lecture will be the first of two, with a focus on the Duchess of Windsor’s amazing collection. Part 2, scheduled for February 1, will focus on Elizabeth Taylor’s collection and mid- century jewelry, 1950-1970. Come learn more about this fabulous period and its jewelry. Doors open at 5:30 pm. Donations will be gratefully accepted at the door and refreshments will be provided following the talk. Sunday, December 10, 4:30 p.m. PCA Jazz Club: In the Tradition Piano Trio Please join us for some late afternoon relaxation enlivened by the In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Anthony Pegram – performing Music of the Holidays, The event is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing its magnificent Steinway grand piano. Come spend a couple of hours in an intimate club-like environment with snacks and complimentary wine. Bring a friend and plan to meet some new ones. Tickets $25 at the door, or $23 at https://bpt. me/5691334. Seating is limited to the first 50 patrons. The result is a book that is riveting and darkly funny and, in all senses of the word, unclassifiable. Fire Weather by John Vaillant In 2016, raging wildfires consumed Fort McMurray in the Canadian province of Alberta. In the all-too-timely Fire Weather, Vaillant details how the blaze started, how it grew, the damage it wrought – and the perfect storm of factors that led to the catastrophe. We are introduced to firefighters, oil workers, meteorologists and insurance assessors. But the real protagonist here is the fire itself: an unruly and terrifying force with insatiable appetites. This book is both a real-life thriller and a momentby-moment account of what happened — and why, as the climate changes and humans don’t, it will continue to happen again and again. Master Slave Husband Wife by Ilyon Woo In 1848, Ellen and William Craft, an enslaved couple in Georgia, made a daring escape north disguised as a sickly young white planter and his male slave — Ellen as the wealthy scion in a stovepipe hat, dark green glasses and a sling over her right arm to conceal her illiteracy. Improbably, despite close calls and determined slave catchers, the Crafts succeeded in their flight, going on to tour the abolitionist speaker circuit in England and to write a popular account of their journey. Their story, which a leading American abolitionist called “one of the most thrilling in the nation’s annals,” is remarkable enough. Some People Need Killing by Patricia Evangelista This powerful book mostly covers the years between 2016 and 2022, when Rodrigo Duterte was president of the Philippines and pursued a murderous campaign of extrajudicial killings — EJKs for short. Such killings became so frequent that journalists like Evangelista, then a reporter for the independent news site Rappler, kept folders on their computers that were organized not by date but by hour of death. Offering the intimate disclosures of memoir and the larger context of Philippine history, Evangelista also pays close attention to language, and not only because she is a writer. Language can be used to communicate, to deny, to threaten, to cajole. It can propagate lies, but it also allows one to speak the truth.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, December 6, 2023 Features Walking on Wednesday A trip to the stairways of Trestle Glen By Dick Carter It had rained the night before, but on Wednesday morning last week, it was cloudy and cool, with 38 walkers and two K-9 best friends on hand to enjoy a weekly walk together. After walking the streets of Piedmont for over five years, identifying a new Piedmont walkway seemed unimaginable, but that’s what Mike Henn did. He saw there are stairs between St. James Place (not St. James Drive) and Trestle Glen Road and realized the group had never gone there. The walkers hadn’t gone to Trestle Glen or St. James Place very often. It was decided they could walk there, go down the stairs, and then do a loop up Trestle Glen to another set of stairs that goes back to St. James Drive. It was recalled that in the early 20th century Piedmont real estate and transportation development were closely linked. People needed to be able to get from their homes to work. Paths and stairs to Key System streetcars were often the solution. The walkers had heard of the Key System’s Transbay C Line that ran through Piedmont to Oakland and San Francisco in the first half of the century. There was also the Trestle Glen B Line. The Trestle Glen neighborhood was developed around the B Line in the early 1900s. Access to the trains was possible via paths from Trestle Glen Road, Underhills Road (which runs parallel to Trestle Glen), and other nearby streets. The B-line went down 22nd Street (now Grand Avenue) past Lake Merritt, turned on Lake Park Avenue, passed the Grand Lake Theater, and then turned up Lakeshore Avenue onto a private right-ofway, now the location of Bank of the West. The B Line train began service to San Francisco from the Underhills station on April 20, 1958. Just like Piedmont after the rails were removed, new homes were built on portions of the right of way. Some homeowners extended their back yards on to the former B-train route. Off they went down Highland Avenue. up Sheridan, Wildwood, Crocker, and Hampton to the top of St. James Drive, continuing to St. James Place, where they took a group photo. They went down the hill to the 120-foot set of stairs to Trestle Glen. The stairs had the familiar inlay tiles that marked all of the 1920’s St. James Wood real estate development. The stairs were steep and the walkers were glad there was a hand rail. The group emerged on Trestle Glen where Mike Henn led them uphill past the Cavanaugh Court cul de sac to the second set of stairs. There was only a low concrete railing beside the 151-foot set of stairs, but the walkers took their time and climbed back to St. James Drive. The group retraced their steps back to town center with appreciation for Mike identifying a great walk for them. On the way back the skies fully cleared and it was a beautiful morning, just as it always is for the Wednesday walkers. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Dept. is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Piedmonters Lorna and Cris Strotz at their home away from home, Pickberry Vineyard, near Glen Ellen in Sonoma County. Many a wine lover enjoying a fine glass of wine has contemplated what it would be like to plant your own vineyard and grow your own wine grapes. This is the story of how Chris and Lorna Strotz achieved that very thing. The Piedmont residents were happily pursuing their careers in medicine and art when in 1975 they decided to take the plunge and bought land on the northeast side of Sonoma Mountain. The land was open pasture mixed with an old plum orchard and loads of blackberry patches. The area was home to some historic vineyards including the Jack London Vineyard and Laurel Glen Winery. The Strotz family began spending weekends there, camping at first and then living in an old trailer without indoor plumbing. One of their favorite activities on the land was picking fresh wild blackberries, and their daughter Kirsten started referring to it as the Pickberry Place. When it came time to plant the vineyard. the name stuck. The family decided to focus on Bordeaux grape varieties, so in 1982 they planted Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petite Verdot – the five grape varieties used in classic Bordeaux blends. They chose a 30-acre rolling hillside site of volcanic soil on the northeast slope of Sonoma Mountain near the town of Glen Ellen. articles.text: Carolyn Nell Crocket was born February 6, 1937, in Oakland, California, and passed in the same city on October 29, 2023. She was 86. Carolyn was a lifelong resident of Piedmont and a graduate of Piedmont High School in 1955. After high school Carolyn worked to help people plan trips, which she loved. She later accepted a secretarial position at Standard Oil of California (now Chevron) and rose through the ranks to become the Executive Assistant of the CEO, a position she held until she retired after many years with the company. Carolyn was a third-generation member of P.E.O., a philanthropic organization dedicated to furthering the education of women. She was a member of St. Stephens Episcopal Church in Orinda and was involved with the Masons as part of a long family history. Carolyn was preceded in death by her parents, Will Gray (Bill) Crocket in 1981 and Bernice Estelle (Bernie) Austin Crocket Hansen in 1999. She is survived by her longtime partner of 20 years William Kelly Hope, her brother Will Gray Crocket II (Sandra), nieces Alexandra Crocket (Andrew Stephens), Catherine Crocket (Brandon Barela), and Kylie Crocket (Sotaro Yamaguchi). Services will be held 1 p.m. Carolyn Crocket, who lived her entire life in Piedmont, passed away on October 29. on Saturday, December 9, 2023 at Chapel of the Chimes, 4499 Piedmont Ave., Oakland, CA 94611.
articles.title: Piedmont native Carolyn Crocket dies on October 29

articles.text: Leonore Steiner Foorman passed away peacefully on November 28, 2023, at St. Paul’s Towers in Oakland at the age of 94. Leonore, known by many as Lindy, was born in Vancouver, British Columbia to parents Ann and Bill Steiner and was the younger sister of Irene Fink. She attended the University of British Columbia where she majored in English, Years later she earned her Masters Degree in Health Education from San Francisco State University. Lindy was always adventurous and independent. She traveled to remote areas as a flight attendant on DC-3s for Canadian Pacific Airlines. She subsequently moved to San Francisco, worked for American Airlines, and met Carl, a widower with three children. They were married in August 1961, and Lindy instantly became a mom of three. She gave birth to Gail one year later. Lindy and Carl had a wonderfully vibrant life together with many, many friends and traveled the world. In addition to her work in the airline industry and in the field of health education, Lindy was also the originator of The Riders Guide, an auto tape tour company that guided visitors to several sites in Northern and Central California. She loved the outdoors, was an avid hiker, skier and beachcomber and was a lifelong member of Hadassah and the Sierra Club. Her generosity of spirit as mother, grandmother, friend and matriarch will be sorely missed. Lindy is predeceased by her beloved husband of 53 years, Longtime Piedmont resident Leonora (Lindy) Foorman died on November 28. She was 94. Carl T. Foorman, Jr., and her great-granddaughter, Zoe Foorman. She leaves behind sons David (Robin) Foorman and Bill (Jackie) Foorman, and daughters, Ann Foorman and Gail Foorman (Craig Tovey). She is also survived by grandchildren Rachel (Omer) Ayfer, Max Foorman, Steve (Janine) Nutche, Nathan Foorman, Sean (Tessa) Foorman, Ben Foorman and William Tovey; great grandchildren, Zeki and Reza Ayfer, Levi and Evie Foorman, Janelle and Sydney Nutche, and Isla Foorman; niece, Leslie Fink; nephew, Peter (Shelly) Fink, and many dear cousins and friends. articles.text: Anne Elizabeth Hendrick Gaston MD died peacefully on November 24, 2023, in Atlanta, Georgia. She was a loving wife of sixty-seven years, and an honorable, dedicated, and talented, physician, who was beloved by her many patients, family, and friends. She was a most caring mother, grandmother, and a new great-grandmother. Dr. Gaston was 93 years old. Born Anne Elizabeth Hendrick on November 10, 1930, in Columbus, Georgia, she attended her local schools in Hurtsboro, Alabama in a class of 12 students. She received her undergraduate degree from the University of Alabama in only three years in 1951, and then her medical degree at Emory University in 1955 as one of only two women in her class. At Emory she met and married classmate Harper Gaston, who also became a doctor. She was a Board Certified Neonatologist and Board Certified Pediatrician. In 1961, Drs. Anne and Harper Gaston moved from Atlanta to Piedmont, California, where they joined the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group in the KPMG’s first medical office in San Leandro, California. Their decision to move to California was based primarily upon the fact that the KPMG was one of the only medical groups in the country which would allow both a husband and wife to work at the same time, and to be paid equally for their work. She joyfully loved Lindy Foorman dies November 28 Leonore Steiner Foorman passed away peacefully on November 28, 2023, at St. Paul’s Towers in Oakland at the age of 94. Leonore, known by many as Lindy, was born in Vancouver, British Columbia to parents Ann and Bill Steiner and was the younger sister of Irene Fink. She attended the University of British Columbia where she majored in English, Years later she earned her Masters Degree in Health Education from San Francisco State University. Lindy was always adventurous and independent. She traveled to remote areas as a flight attendant on DC-3s for Canadian Pacific Airlines. She subsequently moved to San Francisco, worked for American Airlines, and met Carl, a widower with three children. They were married in August 1961, and Lindy instantly became a mom of three. She gave birth to Gail one year later. Lindy and Carl had a wonderfully vibrant life together with many, many friends and traveled the world. In addition to her work in the airline industry and in the field of health education, Lindy was also the originator of The Riders Guide, an auto tape tour company that guided visitors to several sites in Northern and Central California. She loved the outdoors, was an avid hiker, skier and beachcomber and was a lifelong member of Hadassah and the Sierra Club. Her generosity of spirit as mother, grandmother, friend and matriarch will be sorely missed. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Oatmeal persimmon cookies are a great winter treat with abundance of persimmons in town. Four generations in my family look forward to these cookies when persimmons are at their peak season. That’s now, and it conveniently coincides with cookie season. The recipe is from the late- 70’s or early-80’s judging from a handwritten recipe card I pulled from my mom’s recipe collection. I’d given it to her years ago, and this season she’s already baked three batches to share with family, including my grandchildren. If you’re fortunate, you have a persimmon tree or neighbors who’ll share their bumper crop. Otherwise, persimmons are plentiful at markets this time of year, too. This recipe uses the Hachiya variety (with a pointy tip), which ripens to a soft, squishy jam-like consistency. When you scoop out the pulp for this recipe, it will be like a mashed, ripe banana. These are soft, chewy cookies with a nice texture from the oats, nuts, and fruit. I added dried cranberries as a nod to the holidays, but we typically do not include them. They may not be the fanciest looking cookies, but they will be among the most flavorful. Oatmeal Persimmon Cookies Makes about 60 2” cookies INGREDIENTS • 3/4 cup unsalted butter, room temperature soft • 3/4 cup brown sugar • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp from squishy-ripe Hachiya variety • 1 teaspoon baking soda • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1 teaspoon cinnamon, ground • 1/2 teaspoon nutmeg, ground

articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on December 9, 2020. Paris, the City of Lights, is magical at Christmas, but while different, this year has many similar traditions. The lights turned up last week inside department stores and neighborhood shops. The store openings were widely heralded after Parisians endured the entire month of November on lockdown. Retailers were chomping at the bit for Christmastime shopping to begin as they try to climb out of the disastrous sales in 2020. Street trees and store windows are dressed up in their best holiday goldware, twinkling seductively for shoppers to hurry in. The temperature is chilly with misty showers and sidewalks full of people and shopping bags, so it feels just like a normal Christmas. Starting December 4th Black Friday sales were everywhere, with featured goods up to 50% off as a way to bring in the hordes. We’re not sure people know what Black Friday is, but the concept, not unlike the United States, starts after Thanksgiving when merchants start to hope that the winding-down selling days for the year begin to move from red ink deficient to black ink and create prosperity. A Parisian symbol of the City of Lights and an oasis for shopping is Galleries Lafayette, which occupies the entire block of Boulevard Haussmann on the Right Bank. After a metro ride, we exited at Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin, where we climbed out of the cavernous underground to the reveal of flashing, vividly hued window displays. Galleries was a luxury bazaar by design, and this is the 1912 Flagship store. It’s on everybody’s must-see list for its spectacular steel and glass dome, a department store inspired for the theater world and Paris Opera. The founders pioneered production of store-brand merchandise: high-fashion styles that were well-made and sold at budget prices. Still very much their marketing edge, this successful enterprise has expanded to 62 Galleries Lafayette locations worldwide. Each Christmas the largest tree imaginable is suspended from the dome. The holiday-decked main floor is wall-to-wall boutiques for cosmetics, perfumes, and accessories, amid hanging displays of color-rich cheer covering every wall and ceiling – or so it seems. It’s a good browse riding the escalators from floor to floor and strolling through beautifully designed displays in its departments. At the main store’s third floor, a glass footbridge allows visitors to cross Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin to Galleries pour Hommes. Across Boulevard Haussmann is Galleries Epicure. We left the Galleries before fulfilling our shoppers’ duty to buy and resisted the pastry kiosk craftily placed at the exit door. We will ourselves to leave and go home for dinner. Christmas Markets The much-loved Christmas Markets have arrived, and although several (Notre Dame Cathedral, Swedish, Alsace at Gare de L’Est) canceled their season due to Covid-19, the markets are spread throughout the Paris districts and located in Saint-Germain des Prés, Les Halles, Place Vendôme (The Ritz), and Hôtel de Ville. Many market shoppers are delighted with the rows of traditional wooden chalet booths with a variety of items for sale: ornaments, handmade craft items, arts and unique objects, holiday foods and produce; ideas for gifts, greenery, and so on. The Christmas Markets originating in Alsace and Germany have more recently been popularized as essential to the holiday season. https://www.parisdiscoveryguide. com/paris-events-december.html Concerts and other venues Standing concerts are scheduled tentatively for the Christmas season, but the exact regulations for capacity are yet being worked out. The same is true for clubs and nightclubs, which don’t yet have a resumption date. Movie theaters, museums, and theaters may be open again starting December 15; however the seating capacity is yet to be announced. Further, the curfew in Paris will remain from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m., which presents questions about event attendees out past curfew and the necessary retention of ticket stubs to avoid a curfew violation with a penalty of €135. That ticket is plenty lofty to ruin an otherwise pleasant evening out for a movie. Here’s a guide to the Paris Church concerts for the holiday season: https://www.parisdiscoveryguide.com/paris-church-concerts.html Shoppers wait to cross at a stoplight outside Galleries Lafayette main store. French News Restaurants and bars will be permitted to reopen in France but not until January 20. It’s been a long slog stuck on idle when typically the City hosts the biggest parties of the season. The Covid- 19 consequences are heartbreaking and breaking the bank of many businesses. As many as 30% of Paris bars and restaurants are expected to close for good. Covid-19 has infected 68 million people worldwide and the tally of deaths is approaching 1.6 million. Mask-wearing continues to be compulsory in France, and people are asked to maintain social distancing. France and U.S. share commonality in the Covid-19 epidemic, which is still not under control. France, too, has rebel merchants and individuals taking a stand against lockdown; but the French do not arm themselves or refuse to wear masks. Covid cases and deaths are rising at a fearful rate, and ICU beds in hospitals are nearing capacity. Her eyes are narrowed against a harsh light as she grimly stares, unseeing, into the distance. Her sweater, covering a checkered shirt, is worn, one frayed sleeve revealing wispy threads hanging loose, unraveling. What she has endured can only be imagined. How did she come to be in this place? What wave of harshness brought her to this moment? And if her gaze is lost in another place – perhaps filled with memories of where she began, or of thoughts about where this journey might end – then her emotions are clearly defined by an unrelenting uncertainty. pages.text: Wednesday, December 6, 2023 31 VIEWPOINT Continued from page 2 of dust and despair. Their only choice was to drive west in hardused cars and trucks, laden with what was salvageable. Lange’s image captures the woman’s face, all angles and creases, her brow furrowed, her lips pressed together in a tight line, as if she had not felt any emotion that could beseech a smile or a shred of hope. Her eyes are narrowed against a harsh light as she grimly stares, unseeing, into the distance. Her sweater, covering a checkered shirt, is worn, one frayed sleeve revealing wispy threads hanging loose, unraveling. What she has endured can only be imagined. How did she come to be in this place? What has her journey been like? The photograph’s caption reads Nipomo, Calif. And what is just outside that tent? A camp of sorts? A rest stop, if only for a night? What wave of harshness brought her to this moment? And if her gaze is lost in another place – perhaps filled with memories of where she began, or of thoughts about where this journey might end – then her emotions are clearly defined by an unrelenting uncertainty. Her moment is the Great Depression, an economic meltdown that swept millions of Americans away, a time made manifest by breadlines, shanty towns, desperate men and women lost, their experiences to be etched forever in their memories. The images from the Depression are vastly different from ours today, yet in many ways they are the same. Our neighborhoods were silent, doors closed, drapes tightly drawn, families, friends, perhaps strangers waiting inside. Unspeaking masked shoppers walking apart, stood in hushed lines in grocery stores and pharmacies, waiting to pay, taking creased bills in change, wondering whose hands they had passed through. Everywhere the floors were marked with small red admonishments to keep a 6-foot distance. Even the hint of a greeting smile was lost behind cloth. Is this the new normal we grimly wondered? A visit to the 2,520-foot summit is on a wide gravel trail with plenty of space for the 100 or more hikers you are likely to see on the way up. A dozen night owls were still trekking their way to the summit on our way back down. We saw roughly 30 hikers per mile in the 6.5-mile day. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way. With a flashlight in hand, there was never a point when we would get too far ahead or too far behind other hikers – giving an assured feeling of safety under the night sky. Be sure to pack a good-sized water bottle to stay hydrated, some granola or source of energy, and a charged battery for videos of an unforgettable sunset. articles.text: Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers presented his quarterly crime report at the city council meeting on Monday, November 20, noting that despite higher than usual crime items, significant progress is being made toward decreasing crime rates and pursuing criminals. Chief Bowers began with a recap of this year’s crime statistics through the 3rd quarter. Compared with the same time period last year, he noted that crime in Piedmont has increased in nearly every category, including robbery, assault, burglary, theft, and vehicle thefts. “This is no surprise to the council,” said Bowers. “This was the trend that we were seeing during my report in September, where we saw increases in everything from robberies to burglaries, and most notably in larceny theft and vehicle burglary or vehicle theft.” “Unfortunately that trend is continuing,” he said. Additionally, vehicle thefts are up “quite a bit,” according to Bowers. Sixty-two vehicle thefts have taken place in Piedmont this year, a fact Bowers attributes to the vulnerabilities of cars by manufacturers like as Kia and Audi. These cars lack a useful anti-theft device called an immobilizer, which prevents a vehicle from starting when the driver attempts to use a key or key fob that doesn’t match the car. Bowers also admitted that there are dimensions of danger not captured by the raw numbers of his statistics. Speaking about failure to yield incidents specifically, Bowers said, “I have anecdotally seen the behavior of individuals involved in this criminal activity [...] becoming more and more dangerous. They’re literally crashing their vehicles into our vehicles without any regard for our officers’ safety.” Bowers was referring to an incident on November 15, 2023, when the driver of a Kia intentionally struck two police cars on Somerset Road before becoming lodged on the roadway. There was some good news, however. Catalytic converter thefts were significantly down. “In July, we had one catalytic converter theft in the city. In August, we had four. In September, we had none,” said Bowers. For reference, Piedmont has experienced 59 catalytic converter thefts in total this year. Recent Piedmont graduate Jack Stein raced to first place in this year’s Turkey Trot and set a course record with a time of 15-minutes, 30 seconds on the 5-kilometer course. A member of the Pomona-Pitzer cross country team that just won the national championship, Stein seemed to glide across the streets of Piedmont. The 22nd running of the Piedmont Turkey Trot attracted runners from near and far and started off the holiday of giving thanks with family fun. Two-thousand four-hundred Turkey Trotters were at the start line at 8:30 a.m. at Highland and Magnolia. Minutes before the race began, a 19-year-old runner with a blue baseball cap approached the starting line from Wells Fargo at a fast pace with graceful strides. The runner, Jack Stein, eventually broke the course record with a pace of roughly five minutes per mile. “It’s a special course,” said Stein. “We ran it in high school, and I was trained on that course. I’ve run up those hills hundreds of times.” Stein’s record time was 17 seconds faster than 2nd place Michael Danielczuk from Albany. articles.text: How can we call America a representative democracy when, at every census, state lawmakers scheme to make peoples’ votes irrelevant? Redistricting, a task which long ago was fair and practical, has been manipulated into a vicious opportunity to cast the opposing party (and its voters) into political irrelevancy. State officials jump at any chance to increase their party’s influence and disadvantage the other at the expense of voters. Reversely, some states have done away with partisan redistricting, and moved to entrusting independent commissions with the task. These commissions are theoretically unbiased, allowing them to draw compact, logical districts, untainted from politics. But these maps draw outcry from state bureaucrats, who will nitpick in an attempt to de-legitimize them. The truth is, drawing a district which pleases everyone is an impossible task. Most Americans live in political clusters which are either incredibly Republican or Democratic. Firstly, this makes it easy for officials to exploit these clusters to their advantage. Secondly, anyone who tries drawing a fair district is in for a tough time. Equal numbers of opposing voters often results in a snakeshaped district in an attempt to include both parties, but which diminishes geographical representation. Drawing a compact district typically results in it being onesided, leaving dissenting voters unheard. If one doesn’t factor race into districting, minorities may be unrepresented entirely. On the other hand, if one tries to make districts fully diverse, minority voices might get diluted. There are few, yet notable guidelines for redistricting. Firstly, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed discriminatory districts. The VRA is effective in protecting minorities, yet there is little legislation for political interference. Constitutional law itself implies that districts should be compact, competitive, and maintain historical political boundaries. Our Founding Fathers’ original vision for redistricting has been dumbed down into an ugly skirmish for political traction. Nate Woodley is a senior at Piedmont High School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 15. articles.text: In November the U.S. will celebrate Native American Heritage Month. This month presents a special opportunity to honor Indigenous cultures and contributions. As with the rest of North America – also known as Turtle Island to some tribes – Piedmont itself sits on Indigenous peoples’ ancestral homes. More specifically, Piedmont occupies the traditional homelands of Ohlone peoples, including the Muwékma Ohlone Tribe and Confederated Villages of Lisjan. Before the arrival of European settlers, these tribes were stewards of this land for thousands of years. Indigenous people have been leaders in reintroducing buffalo in Montana, restoring salmon populations in the Columbia River, and protecting sacred land at Standing Rock in the Dakotas. In California, prescribed burning is a long-standing Indigenous practice that diminishes wildfire risk. The state government opposed this practice in the past, but today prescribed burns are once again a key element of the State’s approach to forest management and wildfire risk reduction. Many Indigenous activists lead the climate movement. At age 21, Xiya Bastida, co-founder of the Re-Earth Initiative, earned a spot in Time Magazine’s Next list for her climate justice activism. Other prominent Indigenous activists include Tara Houska, Quannah Chasinghorse, Winona LaDuke, Siqiñiq Maupin, and Dallas Goldtooth. Here in the East Bay, Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, works with Native and non-native communities to revitalize lost cultural knowledge and caretaking practices on land across the East Bay. Indigenous people in the U.S. have the highest poverty rate among all minority groups (25.4%), and the highest mortality rates for many preventable illnesses, resulting in a life expectancy that is 5.5 years lower than the national average. It indicates that Indigenous people are disproportionately impacted by climate change. In his proclamation of National Native American Heritage Month, President Biden called on all Americans to celebrate November 24 as “Native American Heritage Day.” I encourage all Piedmonters to spend some time on Friday reading or listening to Indigenous voices by visiting the official websites for the Muwékma Ohlone Tribe (www.muwekma.org) and Confederated Villages of Lisjan (www.villagesoflisjan.org) or viewing the following podcasts: Indigenous Earth Community Podcast, Good Fire, and Indigenous Climate Action Pod. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, November 29, 2023 Opinion OPINION Gerrymandering: America’s Dilemma By Nate Woodley How can we call America a representative democracy when, at every census, state lawmakers scheme to make peoples’ votes irrelevant? Redistricting, a task which long ago was fair and practical, has been manipulated into a vicious opportunity to cast the opposing party (and its voters) into political irrelevancy. State officials jump at any chance to increase their party’s influence and disadvantage the other at the expense of voters. Reversely, some states have done away with partisan redistricting, and moved to entrusting independent commissions with the task. These commissions are theoretically unbiased, allowing them to draw compact, logical districts, untainted from politics. But these maps draw outcry from state bureaucrats, who will nitpick in an attempt to de-legitimize them. The truth is, drawing a district which pleases everyone is an impossible task. Most Americans live in political clusters which are either incredibly Republican or Democratic. Firstly, this makes it easy for officials to exploit these clusters to their advantage. Secondly, anyone who tries drawing a fair district is in for a tough time. Equal numbers of opposing voters often results in a snakeshaped district in an attempt to include both parties, but which diminishes geographical representation. Drawing a compact district typically results in it being onesided, leaving dissenting voters unheard. If one doesn’t factor race into districting, minorities may be unrepresented entirely. On the other hand, if one tries to make districts fully diverse, minority voices might get diluted. There are few, yet notable guidelines for redistricting. Firstly, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed discriminatory districts. The VRA is effective in protecting minorities, yet there is little legislation for political interference. Constitutional law itself implies that districts should be compact, competitive, and maintain historical political boundaries. Our Founding Fathers’ original vision for redistricting has been dumbed down into an ugly skirmish for political traction. Nate Woodley is a senior at Piedmont High School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 15. Piedmont to honor Indigenous climate leadership during Native American Heritage Month By Alyssa Romea In November the U.S. will celebrate Native American Heritage Month. This month presents a special opportunity to honor Indigenous cultures and contributions. As with the rest of North America – also known as Turtle Island to some tribes – Piedmont itself sits on Indigenous peoples’ ancestral homes. More specifically, Piedmont occupies the traditional homelands of Ohlone peoples, including the Muwékma Ohlone Tribe and Confederated Villages of Lisjan. Before the arrival of European settlers, these tribes were stewards of this land for thousands of years. Indigenous people have been leaders in reintroducing buffalo in Montana, restoring salmon populations in the Columbia River, and protecting sacred land at Standing Rock in the Dakotas. In California, prescribed burning is a long-standing Indigenous practice that diminishes wildfire risk. The state government opposed this practice in the past, but today prescribed burns are once again a key element of the State’s approach to forest management and wildfire risk reduction. Many Indigenous activists lead the climate movement. At age 21, Xiya Bastida, co-founder of the Re-Earth Initiative, earned a spot in Time Magazine’s Next list for her climate justice activism. Other prominent Indigenous activists include Tara Houska, Quannah Chasinghorse, Winona LaDuke, Siqiñiq Maupin, and Dallas Goldtooth. Here in the East Bay, Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, works with Native and non-native communities to revitalize lost cultural knowledge and caretaking practices on land across the East Bay. Indigenous people in the U.S. have the highest poverty rate among all minority groups (25.4%), and the highest mortality rates for many preventable illnesses, resulting in a life expectancy that is 5.5 years lower than the national average. It indicates that Indigenous people are disproportionately impacted by climate change. In his proclamation of National Native American Heritage Month, President Biden called on all Americans to celebrate November 24 as “Native American Heritage Day.” I encourage all Piedmonters to spend some time on Friday reading or listening to Indigenous voices by visiting the official websites for the Muwékma Ohlone Tribe (www.muwekma.org) and Confederated Villages of Lisjan (www.villagesoflisjan.org) or viewing the following podcasts: Indigenous Earth Community Podcast, Good Fire, and Indigenous Climate Action Pod. Oakland Zoo welcomes 2 mountain lion cubs By Jay Russell Oakland Zoo has two new star attractions – a pair of young, orphaned mountain lion siblings. They were rescued and transported to Oakland Zoo on November 14 by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife following a search for the kittens. Given the names Maple and Willow by the zoo’s staff, they mark the 25th and 26th mountain lion rescues at the zoo since the program started in 2017. Both kittens are female, approximately six to ten weeks old, and each weighed roughly five pounds upon arrival. An adult female mountain lion, who CDFW believes is their mother, was struck by a car and killed on Saturday, November 11, along Highway 280, near the Hillsboro-Burlingame area. Over the weekend, residents reported seeing two cubs alone near the area, and they were found safe in the backyard of one of reporting residents. When the cubs arrived at Oakland Zoo, the Veterinary Hospital staff conducted a thorough health examination of both cubs. The exam included virus testing, parasite treatment, and bloodwork testing. Additionally, vital fluids were administered to the visibly dehydrated kittens. Although underweight and dehydrated, they showed no signs of extreme illness. “Our team will be caring for the cubs daily to restore them to full health and for their overall animal well-being,” said Dr. Alex Herman, Oakland Zoo’s Vice President of Veterinary Services. Orphaned kittens remain on average for eight days in the Zoo’s ICU. Once cleared, they are moved to a holding area at Vet Hospital for weeks until CDFW identifies a proper permanent home for the cubs. On Thanksgiving, Willow and Maple were skewer-fed by keepers to help them get used to people. According to the zoo, Maple has had no trouble with skewer feeding and has been eating like a champ, while Willow is still adjusting to her new diet and how to eat it. In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother to learn survival skills. Because the cubs are so young, they lack those skills and cannot return to the wild. “These cubs became orphans when their mother was struck by a car on a busy highway, a tragedy suffered by wildlife when safe passage across their natural territories isn’t possible. We support and advocate for more wildlife crossings, such as the one opened in Santa Cruz earlier this year on Highway 17,” said Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia. In 2012, the Oakland Zoo participated in a training session focused on resolving conflicts between humans and wildlife. This training led to forming BACAT (Bay Area Cougar Action Team). The alliance brings together various agencies, nonprofit organizations, local parks, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, and mountain lion researchers. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church will host its first Snow Day event on Friday, December 22, from 4-7 p.m. Twenty tons of snow from San Jose Ice Company will be used to make two sledding hills and a snow playground for younger children in the church driveway. Two big rigs will bring the winter wonderland to life with their snow delivery. To conceptualize 40,000 pounds of snow, picture enough fresh snow to cover an entire football field with more than two inches of snow. The church will have two bounce houses, a gingerbread and snowman, outdoor games, face painting, hot cocoa, and the Red Sauce Meatball food truck. This is a free community event, with the exception of the items from the food truck which can be purchased separately. Taking the lead on providing some winter fun in town is Kerry Persichitte, Director of NextGen and Community Engagement at the church. “We want to spread some Christmas cheer in the community, get to know our neighbors, and have some old-fashioned family fun,” she said. Friday, December 22, is the first day of school vacation, so the church is ready for big crowds. It is expecting more than 1,000 people throughout the three-hour event. articles.text: During a closed session of the city council meeting on Monday, November 20, Piedmont City Council met with legal counsel to discuss a recent lawsuit by neighbors of the Linda Beach Pickleball courts. City officials and council members are not at liberty to discuss the contents of litigation or pending litigation. Asking the City Attorney for advice is often an indication of how seriously the city is responding to a suit. And when it comes to this lawsuit filed on behalf of these neighbors by Attorney Richard Drury it appears that the city is quite serious. Earlier this month, a group of seven Piedmont residents filed a lawsuit against the City of Piedmont over what they claim to be faulty procedures by the Piedmont Recreation Commission and the City Council regarding a decision to dedicate a tennis court adjacent to Beach School for exclusive pickleball use. Drury claims that the city has unlawfully violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), explaining that the noise caused by the courts has a significant impact on residents in the surrounding area. His clients are seeking an injunction to stop the development of the courts as full-time pickleball courts. The last formal action taken by City Council was City Council Resolution No. 57-2023, adopted on September 5, approving the dedication and restriping of Linda Beach Tennis Courts exclusively for pickleball use. CEQA has a mandatory early settlement provision to encourage parties to handle things outside of trial. The first mandatory settlement meeting between the group of residents and the City took place on Monday, November 27.

articles.text: Piedmont’s bus riders may need to rethink their commuting plans in the near future. AC Transit met with Piedmont City Council on November 20 to discuss proposed changes to bus routes 18, 33, and 88. AC Transit proposes to eliminate Line 33 and split its services between Lines 18 and 88. Under this new plan, Line 18 would travel down Park Boulevard, across Lake Merritt, and then on Broadway to 20th Street in downtown Oakland, before continuing along the current Line 18 to Berkeley and Albany via Martin Luther King Jr. Way. Line 88 would replace the current line 33 service along Oakland Avenue and Harrison Street, with rides between Piedmont, downtown Oakland, and downtown Berkeley. In addition, AC Transit is also seeking riders’ input on the bus network’s larger goals, asking riders if they prefer a bus system that focuses on a more far-reaching service and more bus stops, or one that has lower wait times and more frequent service. Members of the public may voice their opinion on the proposed changes at AC Transit’s online open house event on December 7. Residents can also visit any Oakland Public Library branch for more information or to submit feedback on the decision. “It’s important now to share this information with your colleagues, your neighbors, your family and friends, and your constituents to ensure that their voices are heard,” said Maria Henderson, External Affairs Representative with AC Transit. AC Transit intends to vote on proposed changes to its bus network in April 2024. For more information visit www.actransit. org/realign. Line 18 is extended to Montclair along Park Blvd. This would replace existing service on Line 33. AC Transit’s proposed changes to Line 18. articles.text: It’s the time of year when gift giving is top of mind, especially for parents searching for toy ideas for their tots. Since play provides the foundation for robust learning, many parents are looking for toys that will be fun as well as infused with learning potential. How do we evaluate the quality of a toy in terms of a beneficial learning edge as well as the fun factor? What do we look for in a toy? We can look to the research for a few guiding principles. Regarding quantity, research shows that a bit less is best. For some children, the overload of all the play items can be overwhelming and distracting, causing the child to pick up one toy, drop it and move on. Regarding quality, research would have us remember the value of the simple “open-ended” toy which can be used in multiple ways. For example, hardwood blocks can be for building, or a make-believe car, or pretend food. Conversely, “closed-ended” toys (which consumers tend to gravitate toward when gift giving) tend to have a “right way” to play, and include such toys as a cash register, Mr. Potato Head, or Legos. Beyond these general principles of quantity and quality, what should be our toy buying guide? To foster problem solving, look to toys such as blocks, instruments or simple board games (or consider keys and containers with lids which you do not have to purchase). To tap into the child’s experimental tendencies, Kids having fun at home consider toys such as a sand or water table (or look to flashlights, colanders, or a whisk to use in the bath which you do not have to purchase). To encourage communication, doll houses and books are excellent choices. You can introduce dress up or rhyming games for similar effects without a price tag. Cognitive development can be fun with toy items such as matching/memory and sorting picture cards, but can also be enjoyed with sorting of silverware, clothing or small household items using a muffin tin for a non-retail option. Creative kids will enjoy gifts of silly putty, paint or other art supplies, and tape, paper towel rolls, paper plates and cotton balls can also be creative fun without additional purchases. Motor development can be enhanced with gifts such as puzzles, balls and shape sorters. And don’t forget that the same fun and developmental stimulation can be had with common kitchen items such as measuring cups, mixing bowls, plastic cups, etc. Regarding social/emotional-based toys, dolls and puppets can’t be beat, and a mirror can do the trick for no purchase. Collaborative toys are always a good idea, such as a construction set or play kitchen. If you want to get the same effect without the specific toy purchase, the laundry basket, sheets and pillows can become a wonderful collaborative fort building experience. Have a wonderful gift-giving season. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School’s Dance Class will present its Winter Dance Concert on Friday and Saturday, December 1 and 2. Performances are at 7:00 p.m. and will be at the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. With original choreography inspired by various aspects of the cinema, the concert is appropriate for the whole family. Featured pieces include dances evoking Hollywood iconic films of the 80s, as well as films that deal with perceptions of time. Tickets, available at the door only, are Adults $12, Seniors $11, students in grades 6-12 $6; students in K-5th grades are admitted free. articles.text: The busy Piedmont High School and Middle School Winter Concert season is just around the corner. Piedmont’s secondary instrumental music program will present three exciting concerts at the Alan Harvey Theater on the PHS campus the week of December 5. Tuesday, December 5, 7:00 p.m. The Piedmont High School Jazz Band and Symphonic Band, directed by new band teacher Trevor Meseroll, will present a Winter Concert showcasing music from the musical Miss Saigon, the rock group Earth, Wind, and Fire, and the video game Cuphead. PHS junior Clare Weiss, a member of the All-State Jazz Choir, will be a soloist on the jazz standard “Misty” by Errol Garner. Wednesday, December 6, 7:00 p.m. The Piedmont Middle School bands, directed by Meseroll (7th grade and 8th grade) and Cathy DeVos (6th grade) will perform a combined concert. The music will include “Amazing Grace”, music from Star Wars with Annalisa Gudiksen as soloist on alto saxophone, and several jazz pieces with improvised saxophone solos by Penelope Welch and Emre Guvendik Maples. Thursday, December 7, 7:00 p.m. The PMS & PHS Orchestra, directed by Sam Wilde, take their turn on the Alan Harvey Theater stage. Music selections on this concert include the beautiful folk song “Danny Boy,” a piece about the legend of King Arthur, “Waltz of the Flowers” from The Nutcracker Suite, folk and fiddle tunes, and the beloved holiday standard, “Jingle Bells.” A special addition to this performance is pre concert background casual chamber music performed in the front lobby by a select group of high school orchestra students. Music Notes Trevor Meseroll is a jazz and classical pianist, and a 2021 Jazz graduate of Berklee School of Music in Boston. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Music Education and a minor in Music Theory. He joined the Piedmont music faculty in July 2023, replacing longtime band director Andria Mullan. Though his music training was centered on piano performance, from a young age he knew he wanted to be a music teacher. In addition to teaching high school Symphonic Band and Jazz Band, he also teaches AP (Advanced Placement) Music Theory, a strength of the school’s music program made popular by former vocal music teacher Joe Piazza. Meseroll also teaches 7th and 8th grade band at the middle school. Retired music teacher Cathy DeVos agreed to come out of retirement to teach the 6th grade Band program this year. To help offset concert expenses at all concerts, a $5 suggested donation for adults will be requested at the door. All students are free.

articles.text: In the FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) league, fall is referred to as the “off season” to contrast the intensity of the build-and-competition season from January through April. But, Highlander Robotics is not off; in fact, this is the busiest time for our outreach projects. We learn a lot when we build our robot each year and through outreach, we leverage our technical skills to teach others and to do service projects. I’d like to share information about the outreach partnerships we have with Oakland Unified District’s Special Education Department (OUSD SPED). We are working with Piedmonter Chantal Guite of Oakland School District to design and fabricate assistive devices for students with a variety of mobility and special needs. My name is Ilana. I’m a mechanical lead of 8033 and a sophomore at Lick Wilmerding High School in San Francisco. I was able to make this project an independent study at my school. This means that I have been getting school credit for this important work and I am able to commit more time to what I am passionate about. Being on the robotics team and working in the Mary G. Ross engineering lab at PHS, I have learned a lot of engineering skills that apply to this project. To start, I use my ability to visualize and prototype before I get to final solutions. This is helpful because the students have very individualized needs – one size doesn’t fit Oakland Unified School District’s 3D printer From CAD to real life all. I have to do a lot of testing to see what will work for each student. Then, I design a 3D model in CAD so we can fabricate using our laser cutter and 3D printers, depending on the project. My teammates started working by making over 20 custom iPad communication guides and clips for kids who are non-verbal and have mobility challenges. The plastic sheets clip onto the devices and guide the student’s fingers to the correct screen button, allowing them to communicate with their teachers and each other. This year, we have expanded the project by making six more key guides, but we have also branched out to help with many other projects. We created a case for what is called a Blue2, essentially a highly intelligent bluetooth button that can be used for many things such as accessing a computer. We designed and fabricated over 25 Blue2 cases. Beyond that, I helped teach several occupational therapists how to use their 3D printer so they can fabricate devices themselves. So far, they have made a toy hearing aid so students that have a hearing aid can use one for their toy. Blue2 Case with student name inscribed Adapting toys for Special Ed students We are excited to be working on a new project with Oakland School District, creating a toy library of adapted toys. Highland Robotics team members are able to modify toys for families with special needs at a much lower price than publicly available. For many of these kids, the only way to interact with toys is via a button, which they click in various ways such as tapping it with their head or knee. Although it is a relatively simple process, adapted toys can be anywhere from 5 to 10 times the price of their unadapted counterparts, making it difficult for lower income families to provide their kids with these modified toys. So far, Highlander Robotics has adapted over 25 toys with hopes of making more. A GoFundMe has been created for this project so that we can buy more materials and toys to adapt. We will also be collecting gently used electronic toys in a bin outside the engineering lab at PHS. To qualify as electric, the toys should be powered by batteries or plug in to a wall outlet. More information is available at (tinyurl.com/p4r5tuy8). All adapted toys will be donated to families through the Oakland School District’s Special Education Dept If you have questions, contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.com. As a community-based team, we do not receive any funding from school which makes sponsorships essential for our success. We appreciate any form of support, whether it is monetary, food, or materials. This money will support us in building a financially sustainable engineering program. Donations may be made at https://www.piedmontmakers.org/. All donations are tax deductible. To learn more, see www.frc8033.com for the sponsorship packet. For sponsorship inquiries, contact Larraine Seiden at lms@larraineseiden. com. articles.text: Located at Coaches Field next to the city Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue, Piedmont’s annual Scout Tree Lot opened to a busy weekend on Saturday and Sunday, November 25 and 26. Residents and business owners got an early start with purchases of trees, wreaths, garlands and mistletoe for the holiday season. The tree lot is also accepting online orders at www.scouttreelot.org. Delivery service will be available throughout Piedmont and select neighborhoods in Oakland. The Scout Tree Lot has been a mainstay of the Piedmont Scout Council for more than 50 years, during which time it has developed a dedicated base of repeat customers. “I think the customers who come here just like to see the volunteers working,” said Isabelle Meyers, a member of Troop 11. “I think that’s why people love coming here.” And at the Scout Tree Lot, other than a Tree Lot Manager, it’s volunteers from top to bottom. At the entrance, customers are greeted by a mixture of Scouts, parents, and volunteers from Monday-Friday Saturday Sunday load trees on customer’s cars. Leo Shrago, a Webelos with Pack 5, describes the difference between Douglas Firs and Silvertips to customers Elena and Thomas McCormick. top of a customer’s car. A row of 8-foot and 9-foot noble firs stands ready for purchase at the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot.
articles.title: Piedmont Scout Tree Lot has big opening weekend

Inside the lot, volunteers help them pick out Christmas trees and answer questions they have about their specific needs for this year’s tree. The trees selected are brought by Scouts on a two-wheel dolly designed just for trees. After buyers pay at the checkout counter, staffed by parent volunteers, their trees are tied to their car roofs by a pair of young adult volunteers. pages.text: Wednesday, November 29, 2023 9 By Matt Simons Located at Coaches Field next to the city Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue, Piedmont’s annual Scout Tree Lot opened to a busy weekend on Saturday and Sunday, November 25 and 26. Residents and business owners got an early start with purchases of trees, wreaths, garlands and mistletoe for the holiday season. Piedmont Scout Tree Lot has big opening weekend The tree lot is also accepting online orders at www.scouttreelot.org. Delivery service will be available throughout Piedmont and select neighborhoods in Oakland. The Scout Tree Lot has been a mainstay of the Piedmont Scout Council for more than 50 years, during which time it has developed a dedicated base of repeat customers. “I think the customers who come here just like to see the volunteers working,” said Isabelle Meyers, a member of Troop 11. “I think that’s why people love coming here.” And at the Scout Tree Lot, other than a Tree Lot Manager, it’s volunteers from top to bottom. At the entrance, customers are greeted by a mixture of Scouts, parents, and volunteers from SCOUT TREE LOT Moraga Avenue at Coaches Field 898 Red Rock Road Monday-Friday Saturday Sunday 4:00 PM - 8:00 PM 9:00 AM - 7:00 PM 9:00 AM - 7:00 PM For information, call the Scout office: 844-4751 Volunteers Nuala Price (left) and Isabelle Meyers stand ready to help load trees on customer’s cars. Leo Shrago, a Webelos with Pack 5, describes the difference between Douglas Firs and Silvertips to customers Elena and Thomas McCormick. Jeff Kobal, a college student and Troop 11 Eagle Scout, ties a tree to the top of a customer’s car. the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC). Inside the lot, volunteers help them pick out Christmas trees and answer questions they have about their specific needs for this year’s tree. The trees selected are brought by Scouts on a two-wheel dolly designed just for trees. After buyers pay at the checkout counter, staffed by parent volunteers, their trees are tied to their car roofs by a pair of young adult volunteers. See Scout Tree Lot on page 31 A row of 8-foot and 9-foot noble firs stands ready for purchase at the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot. Gina Lambright, a parent volunteer with the Piedmont Community Service Crew, runs the check-out counter as a cashier. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Freshman Sebastien Swain with coach Steve Zirkelbach at the State Cross-Country meet in Fresno. Freshman Sebastien Swain represented Piedmont High at the 2023 State Championship Cross-Country meet at Woodward Park in Fresno on Saturday, November 25, He finished 67th of 201 runners with a time of 16:41.3 in the Division 4 meet. Piedmont has had at least one runner qualify for the State meet for the past 35 years. Swain said he wasn’t expecting to get to State when the season began. “It means a lot to me. I’m really excited that I was just able to get there. It’s something I thought wasn’t even on the table before NCS when I qualified. It was fun to have that experience as a freshman at State,” Swain said. Swain was able to successfully conserve some energy for his final kick, resulting in being able to pass 30 runners in the last mile. “Sebastien has an impressive amount of poise and concentration when he is racing. We see it Sebastien Swain passed 30 runners in the final portion of the race at the State meet.

articles.text: In a rematch of last year’s Div. 3 North Coast Section quarterfinals, Piedmont got the job done in similar fashion with a 64-51 win over the Analy Tigers of Sebastopol in the season-opening game at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, November 25. PHS dominated the first quarter and jumped out to a 21-8 lead. The score was 36-22 at halftime and increased to 49-33 in the third quarter before Analy put up 18 points in the fourth quarter. The game provided a suggestion of what Piedmont may look like once it’s clicking on all cylinders; a team that can use its size to grab rebounds, move the ball quickly up court, and utilize its athleticism to make quick cuts to the basket. “We’re young but also old in a sense we have seven seniors. But we’re inexperienced. You can see the flashes of brilliance, but you can also see the mistakes we make. We got the lead up to 20 points, but started committing some turnovers, and the lead was quickly back down to 13. We can score quickly and score in bunches, it’s just a matter of whether we can take care of the basketball,” said coach Ben Spencer. “We’ve been working since the loss to Branson last March. I think we’ll have a different look this year with multiple guys scoring Staff Photos Brit Burden had a double-double with 14 points, 12 rebounds, and six assists against Analy. over 10-15 points a game. It will be a more well-rounded attack which will help us deeper into the season. We have guys who can come off the bench as well,” added senior leader Brit Burden. It proved to be a big game for Ravi Silverberg, who scored 22 points including four 3-pointers, a career high for the junior guard. “It’s good to get the win,” acknowledged Silverberg. “It wasn’t perfect, but it’s the first game of the season, so it’s about getting on track. I got some shots up before the game and was feeling good. The threes started falling in the first quarter and after that, the rest of the game felt easy.” Coach Spencer made the deciGuard Ravi Silverberg knocked down 22 points with four 3-pointers. Sophomore Dillon Casey made a big impact with 14 points against Analy. sion to switch Silverberg to the shooting guard role after appearing as a point guard last year. It’s a switch Spencer feels matched Silverberg’s skill set and is making a difference in practice. In Saturday’s game, Silverberg showcased some of those skills in his new spot. “I think I can play any position coach wants me to play. I feel comfortable as shooting guard or point guard, I felt comfortable today, so it was good,” Silverberg added. The game also marked sophomore guard Dillon Casey’s varsity debut, and it was a big one. He finished with 12 points and eight rebounds. “He gets to practice and hour before everyone and is getting up shots. He’s always working and playing club basketball. He’s ready for the moment and will play a big role for us,” said Burden. Piedmont now looks ahead to hosting its West Coast Preps Winter Classic tournament this weekend from Thursday through Saturday, November 30 to December 2. Game Recap After conceding the game’s opening basketball, Piedmont dominated the first quarter to lead 21-8. The Highlanders converted five 3-pointers, including three by Silverberg, one by Alex Anderson, and one by Casey. In the second quarter, PHS put up 15 points with four different scorers, including Linnane, Burden and Silverberg each scoring four points while Casey hit a 3-pointer. It was another back-and-forth third quarter with PHS scoring 13 points and allowing 11.. Analy outscored Piedmont 18-15 in the fourth quarter, with 3-pointers by Cash Panico and Casey. Final stats: Burden scored 14 points, 12 rebounds, and six assists. Silverberg scored 22 points and two assists. Casey scored 14 points and grabbed eight rebounds. Linnane had eight points, seven boards. Panico and Anderson scored three, Anderson also had an assist. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0) hosts Hayward in the first round of the West Coast Preps Winter Classic on Thursday, November 30 at 8:30 p.m.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team returns after winning last year’s League and North Coast Section titles. Piedmont’s defending Western Alameda County Conference and Division 4 North Coast Section championship team is back in action for the 2023-24 season. The Highlanders return to the court with a significantly different roster. Natalia Martinez, the Post’s 2023 Athlete of the Year, is the only returning starter from last year’s championship team. “Obviously, it’s going to be different. I feel like we’re up for that challenge,” said coach Bryan Gardere, now in his __ season. Gardere has the task of rebuilding a team without four of its five starters. Trinity Zamora, Eva Levingston, Maddie Hill, and Perseas Gioukaris graduated in May. Zamora and Hill played alongside Martinez for the past three years. “It’s definitely different than the last three years, but the girls we have are amazing,” said Martinez. “People have been stepping up into their roles.” Martinez recently committed to San Diego State and has continued to fine-tune her game well ahead of entering college next fall. “Nat has taken her game to another level,” said Gardere. “She’s finishing with contact, has put more time in the weight room, and is looking at the bigger picture. She knows she wants to have a big senior year but also wants to be ready for the next level in college,” said Gardere. Returning to the team roster is three-year varsity players Kat Melian and Shakila Zuberi. Melian is a tall forward, who is a two-sport athlete with water polo. Zuberi is a guard who has shown good defensive skills and can knock down 3-pointers. “Kat scored a ton of goals in water polo and is coming to basketball with a great mindset. She’s one of the toughest kids I’ve coached in all my years. She puts on a smile and works. You need players like her on your team,” said Gardere. “Kat Melian has been incredible,” added Martinez. “She’s stepped up tremendously to help out this team.” Samantha Smith enters her second year on the team and is Natalia Martinez, the Post’s 2023 Athlete of the Year, returns for her senior season on the basketball team. She recently committed to San Diego State for next year. Kat Melian, a two-sport athlete with water polo, is in her third year on the basketball team.

articles.text: It’s been an epic month for Piedmont 2022 graduate Jack Stein. The Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2022, now a sophomore at Pomona-Pitzer, just helped his college reach the highest achievement in its sport by winning the Division 3 NCAA Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 18 in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Stein helped the Sagehens defeat Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159, as Pomona’s fifth-best runner. His time of 25:49.3 was the difference in scoring to give his team another national title. “This year I had the pleasure of joining the travel team with the top-10 guys on the team. The Nationals course was in Pennsylvania and we weren’t ranked really high going into it. It was a crazy race and super hilly, but with our veteran experience, we had a good shot of scoring high. We beat University of Wisconsin-La Crosse by one point. Every point really mattered. It’s such an honor to be Division 3 National Champions. We worked hard for it,” said Stein. Coming into Pomona-Pitzer, Stein had to earn his stripes around an older group which won the national title in 2021 before his arrival. “Our seniors were a part of that 2021 team when they were sophomores. It’s good to have senior leadership and people to look up to, especially in running. Just having mentors and a veteran class completely changed the game in terms of improving,” said Stein. But there was more excitement to come for Stein. He returned home for Thanksgiving and not only won the Turkey Trot, he set a new course record of 15:30 on the 5K course on city streets. “It’s a special course. We ran it in high school and I was trained on that course. There’s a couple of hills that the cross country team does hill-reps on, I’ve ran up those hills hundreds of times. It’s special to me… It’s always nice to come home and be surrounded by friends and family,” said Stein. Setting records is nothing new for him. Upon graduation, he left Piedmont High as the school’s all-time record holder in the 3200 meters with a time of 9:12.62, and also set a new school record in the 1600 meters with a time of 4:14.77. He came back to the Turkey Trot surrounded by an all-star cast of Piedmont alums, including Class of 2023 graduates Christian Taylor and Parker Long, and 2018 grad Walter Teitelbaum. “It was good to be back and see a lot of my teammates from high school who are running in college now. It was great to see Christian Taylor (UC Davis) and Parker Long (Cal Poly), and race with them again. I talked to Walter Teitelbaum, who graduated from UC Santa Cruz. He’s someone I’ve been in contact with. “I was excited to come back and race with them. Of course, you want to win the hometown race, especially after winning the National Championship. I was just feeling really confident. It puts a cap on a terrific month of November for the Stein household with younger brother George Stein, a senior at PHS, leading the water polo team to its first North Coast Section championship. Photo by Gary Zalewski Jack Stein returned to Piedmont on Thanksgiving day to set a course record in the Piedmont Turkey Trot
articles.title: 2021 PHS grad also wins Turkey Trot with record time

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ newest Tony Award-winning production, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, is onstage at the Ashby Theatre in Berkeley now through December 17. Written by John Cameron Mitchell and directed by Richard A. Mosqueda, the play is adapted from the off-Broadway theater hit of the same name, later made into a movie in 2001. Hedwig and the Angry Inch follows German emigrant Hedwig, who is the victim of a botched sex-change operation. This version takes place in a seedy dive bar in Berkeley. Hedwig is an internationally ignored song stylist and East German rock ‘n’ roll goddess. This outrageous play is performed by Pangaea Colter as a member of a rock band with a stand-up comedy routine backed by the band. Mosqueda said the inspiration came from the first viewing of the film in a high school English class. “It was a crudely drawn animation played on the screen detailing a story about the origin of humans, originally three genders, who were once attached and then separated, now looking for the other half. An androgynous blonde bombshell appeared on the screen wailing to the heavens. I was glued to the television. And as a deeply closeted queer kid, I felt seen, if only for a moment,” Mosqueda said. Lyrics and music are by Stephen Trask. To view showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/Online/default.asp. Pangaea Colter as Hedwig and Elizabeth Curtis as Yitzhak on Shotgun Players’ current production of Hedwig and the Angry Inch.
