articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s Cinderella Enchanted, based on the 1997 movie, is playing onstage now through December 22. The classic tale of Cinderella is reborn in this play with a Bay Area twist. Cinderella, played by Kennedy Joy Fullard, is a free-spirited Berkeley artist and Prince Christopher, played by Vinh G. Nguyen, is a wealthy Silicon Valley romantic. Prince Christopher hosts an extravagant ball where he meets Cinderella, only for her to leave the festivities before he can express his true feelings for her. Cinderella leaves behind nothing but a glass slipper which prompts the prince to embark on a mission to find the dainty shoe’s owner. Cinderella Enchanted is directed and choreographed by Khalia Davis with music conducted by Jessica Igarashi. The director explained the significance of the mid-90’s film, and how it influenced Cinderella on stage. “[The 1997 movie] was really iconic and it set the bar for what is possible when you do musicals that are magical in that way,” said Davis. The Berkeley Playhouse production offers some more unique twists, she added. “I’m really excited about the fact that we get to honor and celebrate being able to see Prince Christopher’s life as well as Cinderella’s and the parallel life they are living. Cinderella is this aspiring writer who is fascinated by the world and Christopher is equally fascinated by the world but wants to know what he can do to make a positive impact outside of being married or born into royalty,” Davis said. The cast members include Jennifer Marie Frazier as Fairy Godmother, Erika Coyne as Stepmother, Stephen Kanaski as Lionel, the Steward, Nicole Stanley as Queen Constantini and Kyle Herrera as King Maximillian. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse’s Cinderella Enchanted playing to Dec. 22

articles.text: SF Jazz will present the Spanish Harlem Orchestra at San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium on Friday, December 15. The three-time Grammy winning Latin jazz band makes its debut at SF Jazz, bringing a repertoire of holiday favorites with a touch of salsa picante. Spanish Harlem Orchestra was founded by producer Aaron Levinson and Puerto Rican pianist and musician Oscar Hernandez. Its debut album was released in 2022. The New York-style band has toured worldwide with jazz greats Chick Corea and Joe Lovano. Their most recent release, Anniversary, featuring trumpeter Randy Brecker, was a winner at this year’s 61st Annual Grammy Awards. The orchestra includes Mitch Frohman on saxophone and flute, Manuel Ruiz and Alex Norris on trumpet, Doug Beavers and Juanga Lakunza on trombone, Gerardo Madera on bass, George Delgado on congas, Luisito Quintero on timbales, Jorge Gonzalez on percussion, and vocalists Jeremy Bosch Marco Bermudez and Carlos Cascante. The performance at SF Jazz begins at 7:30 p.m. Tickets are available at https:// www.sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/23-24/spanish-harlem-orchestra/. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, November 29, 2023 Arts & Entertainment The cast of Cinderella Enchanted at Berkeley Playhouse Photo by Ben Krantz Berkeley Playhouse’s Cinderella Enchanted playing to Dec. 22 By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Playhouse’s Cinderella Enchanted, based on the 1997 movie, is playing onstage now through December 22. The classic tale of Cinderella is reborn in this play with a Bay Area twist. Cinderella, played by Kennedy Joy Fullard, is a free-spirited Berkeley artist and Prince Christopher, played by Vinh G. Nguyen, is a wealthy Silicon Valley romantic. Prince Christopher hosts an extravagant ball where he meets Cinderella, only for her to leave the festivities before he can express his true feelings for her. Cinderella leaves behind nothing but a glass slipper which prompts the prince to embark on a mission to find the dainty shoe’s owner. Cinderella Enchanted is directed and choreographed by Khalia Davis with music conducted by Jessica Igarashi. The director explained the significance of the mid-90’s film, and how it influenced Cinderella on stage. “[The 1997 movie] was really iconic and it set the bar for what is possible when you do musicals that are magical in that way,” said Davis. The Berkeley Playhouse production offers some more unique twists, she added. “I’m really excited about the fact that we get to honor and celebrate being able to see Prince Christopher’s life as well as Cinderella’s and the parallel life they are living. Cinderella is this aspiring writer who is fascinated by the world and Christopher is equally fascinated by the world but wants to know what he can do to make a positive impact outside of being married or born into royalty,” Davis said. The cast members include Jennifer Marie Frazier as Fairy Godmother, Erika Coyne as Stepmother, Stephen Kanaski as Lionel, the Steward, Nicole Stanley as Queen Constantini and Kyle Herrera as King Maximillian. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets. Shotgun Players’ Hedwig and the Angry Inch on stage through Dec. 17 By Allyson Aleksey Shotgun Players’ newest Tony Award-winning production, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, is onstage at the Ashby Theatre in Berkeley now through December 17. Written by John Cameron Mitchell and directed by Richard A. Mosqueda, the play is adapted from the off-Broadway theater hit of the same name, later made into a movie in 2001. Hedwig and the Angry Inch follows German emigrant Hedwig, who is the victim of a botched sex-change operation. This version takes place in a seedy dive bar in Berkeley. Hedwig is an internationally ignored song stylist and East German rock ‘n’ roll goddess. This outrageous play is performed by Pangaea Colter as a member of a rock band with a stand-up comedy routine backed by the band. Mosqueda said the inspiration came from the first viewing of the film in a high school English class. “It was a crudely drawn animation played on the screen detailing a story about the origin of humans, originally three genders, who were once attached and then separated, now looking for the other half. An androgynous blonde bombshell appeared on the screen wailing to the heavens. I was glued to the television. And as a deeply closeted queer kid, I felt seen, if only for a moment,” Mosqueda said. Lyrics and music are by Stephen Trask. To view showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/Online/default.asp. Spanish Harlem Orchestra comes to SF Jazz By Allyson Aleksey SF Jazz will present the Spanish Harlem Orchestra at San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium on Friday, December 15. The three-time Grammy winning Latin jazz band makes its debut at SF Jazz, bringing a repertoire of holiday favorites with a touch of salsa picante. Spanish Harlem Orchestra was founded by producer Aaron Levinson and Puerto Rican pianist and musician Oscar Hernandez. Its debut album was released in 2022. The New York-style band has toured worldwide with jazz greats Chick Corea and Joe Lovano. Their most recent release, Anniversary, featuring trumpeter Randy Brecker, was a winner at this year’s 61st Annual Grammy Awards. The orchestra includes Mitch Frohman on saxophone and flute, Manuel Ruiz and Alex Norris on trumpet, Doug Beavers and Juanga Lakunza on trombone, Gerardo Madera on bass, George Delgado on congas, Luisito Quintero on timbales, Jorge Gonzalez on percussion, and vocalists Jeremy Bosch Marco Bermudez and Carlos Cascante. Titled a Legacy of Love, the first talk will take place on Friday, December 8 at 6 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Art, 801 The two lectures will be a survey of retro and mid-century jewelry with a focus on the jewelry collection of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor from the years 1935-1960. Jewelry from that era is bold, Photos by Cecil Beaton Wallace Simpson, the Duchess of Windsor, was always elegantly Photos by Cecil Beaton The Duke and Duchess of Windsor. Gemologist Sacha Grippando colorful and extravagant. The Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor each amassed what are considered today to be the best collections of jewelry from the 20th century. They both had amazing taste and a passion for important gemstones as well as innovative and avant-garde design. As the majority of their collections were acquired as gifts from their husbands, these collections are truly legacies of love. Both women led extraordinary lives that were very public. They were often vilified, criticized and at certain points in their lives portrayed as “the most hated women in the world” by the press. articles.text: Part Six in a series Because movies are so deeply embedded in our culture, we have included their titles and stories as familiar referents. Some are animated, others are portrayals of real life, both filled with a kind of magic. More than a few have become iconic. However, we are likely not as familiar with the countless individuals who write the narratives, create the characters, and oversee the productions. Watch the credits at the end of any film and you get a sense of the extraordinary number of people involved. Animation clearly relies on the engine of imagination while creating characters and worlds and narratives that are extraordinary and involve a kind of… magic. To successfully capture and hold the attention of young audiences is no small thing. Piedmont-based animator Patty Kihm has a career doing exactly that, and her award-winning filmography is remarkable. pursuing a graduate degree, she had the opportunity to join the art department of Pixar Animation Studios. The year was 1997. Pixar has proven to be a perfect fit for her. Over the years she has worked as an animator, starting with the film A Bug’s Life (1998). She has contributed her talent and skill to virtually all of Pixar’s animated features, including Onward, Monster University, Cars 2 and 3, Finding Dory, Incredibles 2, and Toy Story. Patty was the directing animator of the Oscar-winning Disney/ Pixar Toy Story 4, and recently served as Supervising Animator on the feature Turning Red. She has also contributed to short films such as Lifted, Birds and Bao, both Oscar winners. Adding to her remarkable tenure at Pixar, Patty has shared her extensive experience with students in Denmark and at the Pixar studios teaching summer interns while mentoring promising artists. She currently lives in Piedmont with her husband, Ross Stevenson, also an animator at Pixar, and her two children. Piedmont filmmaker Patty Kihm Patty spent her early years in Youngstown, Ohio, followed by moves to New York, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. She enrolled at Boston University, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree with emphases in advertising, graphic design and communication. After graduation, she moved to the San Francisco Bay Area, where she attended San Francisco’s Academy of Art University in its School of Art & Design to focus on graphic design and animation. articles.text: Patricia Clarkson and Alexander Siddig in Cairo Time Review by Chris Honoré Patricia Clarkson, too often relegated to supporting roles in past films, finally takes stage center from the first frame in Cairo Time to the last; the camera never leaves her side. She is a remarkable actress with an enormous range, possessing a soft, yet steely voice that always has a hint of magnolia. Her performance as Juliette, wife of a U.N. official newly arrived in Cairo to vacation with her husband, is filled with extraordinary moments. Upon arriving in Cairo, she is met at the airport by her husband’s colleague and former bodyguard, Tareq, played elegantly by Alexander Siddig. He informs her that her husband, Mark (Tom McCamus), will be delayed in Gaza, and for how long he’s not sure. He offers to be her tour guide while she waits for his return. And so, the couple set out to see Cairo and writer-director Ruba Nadda and cinematographer Luc Montpellier set about creating a love letter to Cairo – an exotic, teeming metropolis of great contrasts and beauty with the pyramids ever in the distance. And while Juliette begins to find Cairo irresistible, she also finds Tareq equally magnetic. Their chemistry is palpable as they sit in coffee houses, walk through marketplaces and warren-like streets. There is no doubt that Juliette loves her husband. In one initial phone conversation, their bond is evident and her worry for his welfare evident. And yet, here she is, 50, an accomplished journalist and magazine editor, two children grown and gone, feeling melancholy and a bit taken aback by her attraction to Mark. Her performance captures her emotions with subtlety and grace and. above all, with restraint. Actually. restraint is an essential aspect to this film as Tareq and Juliette walk toward a precipice from which there will be no turning back. In effect, Juliette is on a journey, not unlike that of Elizabeth Gilbert in Eat Pray Love. But the two films couldn’t be more different. Both are about women at a turning point in their lives; and yet there is something far more honest about Clarkson’s performance and character than that of Julia Roberts’ portrayal in Eat Pray Love. For Juliette, all is resolved and yet nothing is resolved; the ambiguity and ultimate compromise inherent in so much of life is evident right up until the final scene. Cairo Time. Starring Patricia Clarkson, Alexander Siddig, Elena Anaya, Amina Annabi. Directed by Ruba Nadda. 1 hr., 28 min. Rated PG. Released in 2010. Now streaming on Apple tv. articles.text: The golden age of comic books – the 1940s – was launched well before television appeared in living rooms, when that now familiar, almost eerie luminescent glow fills living room windows on any given evening. Growing up, I loved comics, as did my friends. We all had stacks in our rooms, most read until the staples gave way, the pulpy paper dog-eared, their thin spines taped. I kept a china dish in my dresser drawer filled with dimes and nickels saved from my paper route. They were next to my skate key and a dusty, well-oiled Spaulding outfielder’s glove. The comics we coveted were, in the main, wonderfully drawn stories about superheroes: Superman, Batman, Spider Man, and, one of my favorites, Straight Arrow. I recall for a time that I treasured any comic featuring Captain Marvel, published at the time (between 1940 and 1953) by Fawcett comics. They featured a young radio reporter, Billy Batson, who, when he said Shazam! morphed into Captain Marvel, outfitted in latex, a lightning bolt on his chest, an orange cape with a bolt down the back. Like most heroes, he had super powers, could fly faster than anything and shoot lightning bolts from his hands. Fawcett lost its Captain Marvel copyright to DC comics who, in the 1960s, revived the hero, calling him Captain Marvel…but that’s another story. The film Shazam!, released in 2019 is based on the Fawcett version I knew and loved. The film is an origin story, always interesting, and in my opinion best when lots of screen time is devoted to the kids/young teens instead of the adults. Billy Batson (Asher Angel), 14-years old, is in search of his mother. He has been bouncing from foster home to the streets and then back for most of his young life and, not surprisingly, has abandonment issues. He longs for a family and feels intensely and rebelliously alone. When, through a series of circumstances, he is given Shazam! powers, his superhero alter ego, played by Zachary Levi, seems jarringly out of synch with young street-smart Billy, who has knocked around for most of his life. I was disappointed every time Billy said Shazam!. Act three is filled with CGI explosions, all focused on the story’s villain, Dr. Thaddeus Sivana (Mark Strong), who has extraordinary super powers. As a character, he seems a bit silly and tedious and the blow-out battles between Billy/Shazam and Sivana go on way too long, They end with all the kids living in the foster home abruptly transformed into superheroes, none as interesting as the foster kids themselves. By then, I lost interest. Shazam! Directed by David F. Sandberg. Starring Zachery Levi, Mark Strong, Asher Angel. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2019. Zachary Levi as Captain Marvel in Shazam!
articles.title: Shazam! a failed chance for a good movie

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Flipped is set in white suburbia and spans those now iconic years of the late 50s and early 60s. For filmmakers doing a period re-creation, the cars have fins, millions are moving to the suburbs, and the music is a cresting wave of rock and roll, featuring memorable signature songs that filled countless gyms during Friday night sock hops. If you grew up during that time, it’s tempting to believe that no generation before or since experienced anything quite like it. It was a gestalt of culture and change. The soundtrack to that period was Elvis and Buddy, Bill Haley and the Comets, Chubby Checker and the Big Bopper, all leading the way followed by a long line of groups and stand alone singers. Politically, it was the Cold War, the ever-present scimitar of nuclear weapons, and it’s not a stretch to say that if there was a moment when it all ended, it would be in early November 1963 with the assassination of John F, Kennedy. One of the best films that capture this time period George Lucas’ American Graffiti, followed by Rob Reiner’s Stand by Me. Both films are remarkable in that they tell compelling teen stories filled with magic. Because Reiner demonstrated such a deft touch with Stand by Me, seeming to understand reflexively that universal transition called “coming of age,” the expectation was that he would bring the same authentic insight to Flipped. The story is adapted from a contemporary teen novel by Wendelin Van Draanen and hugely popular in 2001. Flipped begins with Juli (Madeline Carroll) and Bryce (Callan McAuliffe), both second graders, who meet when Bryce moves into the neighborhood. Juli is immediately smitten. Bryce is repelled, her being a girl and all. The story soon focuses on how they navigate middle school and Bryce drolly points out that he has spent half a decade avoiding Juli, intimidated by her expressions of affection. She has spent that time resolutely reaching out and being rebuffed. But all of that is about to be upended, meaning flipped. Though there is a nice contrast between the families – Bryce’s is upwardly mobile and somewhat affluent, and Julie’s is working class and outwardly poor – not much is made of these differences and how they impact the two budding adolescents. There’s joy and pain in this story, but Reiner holds back on both counts. He seems content to settle for “nice.” That isn’t the adjective that comes to mind when thinking of Stand by Me. There are truths in this movie, though Reiner, who co-wrote the screenplay, doesn’t explore them. One nugget in Flipped is John Mahoney, a superb character actor, who portrays Bryce’s grandfather in a role that demonstrates the breadth and depth of Mahoney’s talent. He has appeared in supporting roles over the years, and his presence in Flipped is worth the price of admission. If you have a tween sitting on the sofa, already worried that since school is fully underway and all the really cool movies of summer past are long gone, suggest that said grumpy gremlin consider Flipped. It is a sweet movie. Flipped. Directed By Rob Reiner. Starring Calan McAuliffe, Madeline Carroll, and Rebecca DeMournay. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Flipped a coming-of-age gem by Rob Reiner

They featured a young radio reporter, Billy Batson, who, when he said Shazam! morphed into Captain Marvel, outfitted in latex, a lightning bolt on his chest, an orange cape with a bolt down the back. Like most heroes, he had super powers, could fly faster than anything and shoot lightning bolts from his hands. Fawcett lost its Captain Marvel copyright to DC comics who, in the 1960s, revived the hero, calling him Captain Marvel…but that’s another story. The film Shazam!, released in 2019 is based on the Fawcett version I knew and loved. The film is an origin story, always interesting, and in my opinion best when lots of screen time is devoted to the kids/young teens instead of the adults. Billy Batson (Asher Angel), 14-years old, is in search of his mother. He has been bouncing from foster home to the streets and then back for most of his young life and, not surprisingly, has abandonment issues. He longs for a family and feels intensely and rebelliously alone. When, through a series of circumstances, he is given Shazam! powers, his superhero alter ego, played by Zachary Levi, seems jarringly out of synch with young street-smart Billy, who has knocked around for most of his life. I was disappointed every time Billy said Shazam!. Act three is filled with CGI explosions, all focused on the story’s villain, Dr. Thaddeus Sivana (Mark Strong), who has extraordinary super powers. As a character, he seems a bit silly and tedious and the blow-out battles between Billy/Shazam and Sivana go on way too long, They end with all the kids living in the foster home abruptly transformed into superheroes, none as interesting as the foster kids themselves. By then, I lost interest. Shazam! Directed by David F. Sandberg. Starring Zachery Levi, Mark Strong, Asher Angel. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2019. Zachary Levi as Captain Marvel in Shazam! Callan McAuliffe and Madeline Carroll in Flipped Flipped a coming-of-age gem by Rob Reiner Review by Chris Honoré Flipped is set in white suburbia and spans those now iconic years of the late 50s and early 60s. For filmmakers doing a period re-creation, the cars have fins, millions are moving to the suburbs, and the music is a cresting wave of rock and roll, featuring memorable signature songs that filled countless gyms during Friday night sock hops. If you grew up during that time, it’s tempting to believe that no generation before or since experienced anything quite like it. It was a gestalt of culture and change. The soundtrack to that period was Elvis and Buddy, Bill Haley and the Comets, Chubby Checker and the Big Bopper, all leading the way followed by a long line of groups and stand alone singers. Politically, it was the Cold War, the ever-present scimitar of nuclear weapons, and it’s not a stretch to say that if there was a moment when it all ended, it would be in early November 1963 with the assassination of John F, Kennedy. One of the best films that capture this time period George Lucas’ American Graffiti, followed by Rob Reiner’s Stand by Me. Both films are remarkable in that they tell compelling teen stories filled with magic. Because Reiner demonstrated such a deft touch with Stand by Me, seeming to understand reflexively that universal transition called “coming of age,” the expectation was that he would bring the same authentic insight to Flipped. The story is adapted from a contemporary teen novel by Wendelin Van Draanen and hugely popular in 2001. Flipped begins with Juli (Madeline Carroll) and Bryce (Callan McAuliffe), both second graders, who meet when Bryce moves into the neighborhood. Juli is immediately smitten. Bryce is repelled, her being a girl and all. The story soon focuses on how they navigate middle school and Bryce drolly points out that he has spent half a decade avoiding Juli, intimidated by her expressions of affection. She has spent that time resolutely reaching out and being rebuffed. But all of that is about to be upended, meaning flipped. Though there is a nice contrast between the families – Bryce’s is upwardly mobile and somewhat affluent, and Julie’s is working class and outwardly poor – not much is made of these differences and how they impact the two budding adolescents. There’s joy and pain in this story, but Reiner holds back on both counts. He seems content to settle for “nice.” That isn’t the adjective that comes to mind when thinking of Stand by Me. There are truths in this movie, though Reiner, who co-wrote the screenplay, doesn’t explore them. One nugget in Flipped is John Mahoney, a superb character actor, who portrays Bryce’s grandfather in a role that demonstrates the breadth and depth of Mahoney’s talent. He has appeared in supporting roles over the years, and his presence in Flipped is worth the price of admission. If you have a tween sitting on the sofa, already worried that since school is fully underway and all the really cool movies of summer past are long gone, suggest that said grumpy gremlin consider Flipped. It is a sweet movie. Flipped. Directed By Rob Reiner. Starring Calan McAuliffe, Madeline Carroll, and Rebecca DeMournay. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: The important quality-of-life characteristic that planners call “walkability” now seems to be recognized and highly valued everywhere. It is considered an amenity to any neighborhood, and property values are positively affected by a good walkability rating. Simply stated, walkability is how user-friendly an area is for pedestrians; how easy, convenient and safe it is to walk from one place to the next. I am fond of this relatively recent term because as readers of this column know, I value and enjoy walking for many reasons. While in much of today’s world we have designed and built our communities to accommodate the car at the expense of pedestrians, travel on foot will always be the most basic and socially valuable form of getting around. Walking is a community enhancer. When people are on foot, the pace is slow enough to really observe immediate surroundings and the opportunity to meet and talk to other people exists, something that is pretty much impossible when we are isolated from one another in our cars. Like many planning concepts, walkability is strongly linked to other issues and considerations, and chief among them is density. If things are too spread out (low density), walking any distance doesn’t make sense much of the time. But, if destinations are close enough (higher density), walking to school, church, stores or the park is feasible – and they’re healthy and fun. Some may be surprised to learn that Piedmont is a relatively dense city: twice that of The walkability rating of Piedmont, like any city, varies based on the conditions in any local area. Unfortunately, published walkability scores have become inflated due to the economic value of high ratings. The only way to truly know is to judge for yourself. This map of the city shows an approximation of some walking times to the center. Variables include the steepness of the walk in addition to distance. It suggests that while we certainly can’t conveniently walk everywhere we need to go, many of us can easily walk to some of our destinations. Camino de Santiago sketches: The most remarkable example of a place with true walkability this writer has seen is in northern Spain, along the famous Camino de Santiago. People make treks of hundreds of miles solely on foot along routes that support and cater in every way to….walking! I think that much of the rest of the world can learn from this place.

It suggests that while we certainly can’t conveniently walk everywhere we need to go, many of us can easily walk to some of our destinations. There are many different reasons to walk and many of the benefits overlap. It’s possible to cover all the examples shown above in a single walk. But, maybe the most important requirement for true walkability is a positive response to the question, “Is this a nice place to walk?” Piedmont certainly is. Walnut Creek or Hayward, and five times greater than Orinda. Here, the higher density makes the city automatically more walkable. Terrain however, is also a factor. The steeper hilly areas in town have the opposite effect, making walking more strenuous and less convenient. Proximity of destinations is also important in determining how convenient it is to walk. Piedmont’s central core area is full of parks and civic uses but has very limited commercial and business uses. If, for example, you want something from a pharmacy, it is necessary to go out of town. But, like “open space” that we discussed in the last column, because of proximity, we are the beneficiaries of various walkable retail districts in Oakland just outside Piedmont. If we are able to walk more, we mitigate many obvious problems endemic to our culture, including traffic jams and auto pollution. Just a small reduction in auto trips replaced by walking can make a significant difference. But perhaps most important of all, is the health benefit of walking. Researchers tell us that everything from cardiovascular strength, to healthy blood pressure, to energy boosts are improved by even a minimum amount of walking on a regular basis. articles.text: Born Paul Bernard Lahaderne on December 5, 1947 in San Francisco, Paul was the son of Bernard Lahaderne and Mary Traynor. He, his sister, Denise, and his brother, Bob, grew up in a loving multigenerational home on Ashbury Street in the City. Paul often spoke of his childhood, and with great affection and appreciation for his parents whose hard work and sense of family would shape and guide his life. Paul attended St. Agnes School and Saint Ignatius High School. As with his childhood, there were many stories of his high school days. Paul took great pride in his football years at S.I. under Coach Vince Tringali. Paul graduated from University of San Francisco. While attending school, he worked nights and summers to finance his education. He then went on to Hastings College of the Law. Before beginning his legal career, Paul served in the U.S. Army on active duty at Fort Benning, Georgia, followed by the Army Reserve. He retired with the rank of Captain. He went on to have a distinguished career as an attorney. After starting his career at CalTrans, Paul moved to Sedgwick, Detert, Moran and Arnold. For 20 years he was a member of the American Board of Trial Advocates. In 1986, Paul met Teresa Craigie and they married in 1989. They have two sons, Peter and Jack Lahaderne. Paul was a devoted husband and a loving and supportive father. Whether it was driving all over northern California for Peter’s baseball games or building an easel for Jack’s paintings, Paul was a consistent and positive presence in their lives. Paul was also active in the Piedmont community and many knew him from his involvement in youth sports. From coaching the Bruisers soccer team, to serving as President of Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation, to assisting with the Piedmont High School baseball team, he always enjoyed contributing his time. Although it must be admitted that Piedmont resident Paul Lahaderne died on October 28. as a soccer coach he was far more gifted at being a role model and keeping the team in line than with his knowledge of soccer. Paul was beloved by his family, who will dearly miss him and his oft-told stories. He is survived by his wife, Teresa, and sons, Peter and Jack Lahaderne; sister DeeDee Dagemjian; sisters-inlaw Mary Craigie, Ellen Craigie, and Jennifer Craigie; brother-inlaw Peter Craigie (Conna McCarthy); nieces and nephews Kieran Craigie, Cormac Craigie (Lauren Craigie) Kathlyn Craigie, Matthew Bonini (Chelsea Bonini), Vincent Bonini, Robert Lahaderne (Michele Lahaderne), Jonathan Lahaderne (Rebekka Lahaderne), and Martha Lahaderne. Paul also leaves behind a large extended family, as well as many friends, neighbors and colleagues; all knowing Paul’s best story was not the one he told, but the one he lived. A Catholic memorial service will be held on December 8 at 5:00 p.m. at Corpus Christi Catholic Church, 322 St. James Drive in Piedmont. A memorial reception will be at 6:15 p.m. at the Claremont Hotel, 41 Tunnel Road in Berkeley. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial contributions be made to The Tringali Scholarship at St Ignatius College Prep, 2001 37th Avenue, San Francisco CA 94116, or a charity of choice.

articles.text: A group of 36 walkers and one K9 best friend participated in last week’s Walk on Wednesday, November 15. The group included Christine Calliste, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, Dottie Hutch, Priscilla Wanerus, Karin Fetherston, Lisa Euphrat, Judy Love, Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kuo, Joanne Larson, Mimi Engle, Kathy Rolfson, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Sharona Fischrup, Chuck Oraftik, Marj Blackman, Nava Shahan, Melba Yee, Carol Lyons, Stella Houston, Russ Nelson, Kat Lang, Edith Lee, Martin Levy, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, Irene Thompson, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Claudine Bach was walking with them for the first time, and that Melba Yee’s sister, Pansy Yee, was there for a Thanksgiving visit. It was Thanksgiving Eve and members of the Walking on Wednesdays group were where they always are at 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday mornings – in front of the Exedra. It was a lovely morning and 36 walkers and one K-9 best friend were there to enjoy the weather, being together, and work on their Thanksgiving dinner appetites. They knew 2,400 runners and walkers were going to be on this very spot the next morning for the annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. The Wednesday walkers were there to get a head start on them and one day before Thanksgiving, be the first across the finish line. Thanks were shared for the friendships that have come from this walking group, and some Thanksgiving race information was shared. According to “Run Signup,” over 750,000 Americans participated in a turkey trot last Thanksgiving in one of over 730 races across the U.S. The Piedmont Turkey Trot is conducted by an independent non-profit that supports the high school cross-country and track and field teams and the PHS Boosters. This was the 22nd year for the Piedmont Turkey Trot which started in 2001 with 300 runners. Participation has been as high as 3,100 one year. The number of runners was capped at 2,400 this year. Awards are given for the top three male and female finishers in 10 separate age categories, from 13 and under to age 80 and over. Last year’s overall winner was Walter Teitelbaum, a PHS grad, who completed the 5-kilometer course in 16 minutes and two seconds. The walkers did not think they would challenge Walter’s time, but they looked forward to walking the entire Turkey Trot route of 3.1 miles. It was agreed that the walker who finished the course first would be declared the Wednesday Walkers’ winner. Even though the Turkey Trot banner was not yet up at the start & finish line on Magnolia Avenue, the walkers got a fast start anyway, going on Highland Avenue to Wildwood. A homeowner must have thought the walkers needed to be cooled off because their sprinkler was showering the sidewalk. The group stepped around the water, took a left on Wildwood Avenue, then a right on Crocker and Lafayette Avenues, and onto La Salle Avenue. At the corner of Lafayette and La Salle the walkers stopped to catch their breaths and take a group photo with a view of San Francisco in the background. Further down La Salle, at the course’s one-mile spot, homeowner Scott Stratman rang a onemile bell for them, similar to the Boston Marathon. The walkers continued to St. James Drive and Hampton Road and then a long, gradual incline on Sea View Avenue, a part of the race course known as Heartbreak Hill. At the top of Sea View, the group floated down Mountain Avenue to Craig and Highland. The final part of the course includes Vista Avenue to Hillside and on Magnolia past the middle school for the final push to the finish line at the Exedra. It was a contested finish, but Russ Nelson pulled away in the home stretch to be the first walker across the imagined finish line. Russ had an unofficial time of 1:13.45, however all the walkers were winners. They had fun, some exercise, and good conservations with friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Dept. is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors celebrated their 27th Anniversary on September 27th with a special luncheon at the Piedmont Community Hall. The organization was founded in 1996 by Lois Dawers and with the encouragement of Mark Delventhal, the long-time Director of Recreation, the Piedmont Seniors was established. Fifty people were in attendance for the anniversary festivities, Guests included members of the Police and Fire Departments, as well as Recreation staff members. The lunch was catered by Ann’s Catering of Berkeley. Police Chief Bowers, Fire Chief Brannigan and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen offered remarks about current events in Piedmont and their support by the Piedmont Seniors. Before the luncheon the group was fortunate to have Gail Lombardi, President of the Piedmont Historical Society, provide a special presentation about Piedmont’s history, with a slideshow of what early Piedmont looked like. She mentioned the Piedmont Hotel, which is now part of Piedmont Park, and the therapeutic springs which attracted many people to the Piedmont hills at the beginning of the twentieth century. In the 1860s, the discovery of sulphur springs began to attract visitors to Piedmont. Mineral springs were believed to possess great curative powers, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel, built by Walter Blair, opened in 1871 to provide accommodations for those who came to “take the waters.” Built on the site of today’s Exedra, this grand hotel had a wide veranda, 20 bedrooms and 2 suites, 5 dining rooms, and a Grand Saloon with an elegant mahogany bar, billiard table, and pot-bellied stove (for men only). The hotel thrived until 1892 when, at 9:15 a.m. on November 17, the hotel came to a sudden end when a fire in the chimney expanded to the roof. It was not until 11:30 a.m. that Chemical Engine #1 arrived from Oakland to contain the fire. Newspapers reported that “the absence of any water supply left the occupants of the doomed building no other recourse than to sit down in the shade and watch the building burn.” Piedmont became an official city in California in 1907, for two main reasons: people wanted to escape the ravages of the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco, and they wanted to become an entity separate from Oakland. The Piedmont Seniors group meets monthly on the fourth Wednesday at the Piedmont Community Hall at 10 a.m. They also go on monthly excursions to a variety of locations throughout the Greater Bay Area. To learn more about this active group, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Piedmont historian Gail Lombardi gave a special presentation at the Piedmont Seniors 27th anniversary luncheon on September 27. She described details and showed a photo of the former Piedmont Springs Hotel in Piedmont Park.

articles.text: Staying healthy during the holidays can be challenging, especially when there are lots of activities to participate in and meals filled with sweet treats. Even though the excursions and dietary changes during the holidays bring joy, they could also potentially be disruptive for seniors. Here are five ways to help ensure that seniors enjoy a happy and healthy holiday season. 1. Provide healthy snack options The holidays can often be a time to indulge in food. To offset the decadent foods and goodies people eat during this time of year, be sure to offer healthy snack options too. This can be anything from almonds or walnuts covered with cinnamon or holiday spices, to bowls of seasonal fruit such as fresh cranberries. You can also serve lighter meals (such as soup or chili made with ground turkey) throughout the day when you know a big dinner is planned for the evening. You still want your loved ones to be able to enjoy their favorite foods at this time of year, so the key is trying to provide balance in the meals surrounding those big holiday feasts. 2. Drink Lots of Water It can be easy to forget to drink water amid the hustle and bustle of the holidays. However, staying hydrated is essential to remaining healthy. You can help protect the seniors in your life by making sure water is easily accessible for them. If an elderly adult is coming to stay with you for the holidays, make sure you keep their room stocked with water bottles. Additionally, make sure you have water bottles available in the car and your purse while running those holiday errands or going to family gatherings. 3. Exercise The cold weather can make us want to stay cozy inside and may make the thought of exercise seem daunting. Exercise doesn’t need to involve an intense routine though – even just a simple walk around the block can provide mental and physical benefits for seniors. Walking around the neighborhood can also allow you and your loved one to have some quality time together, enjoying Christmas lights or other sights of the season. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, November 29, 2023 Seniors Piedmont Seniors group celebrates 27th anniversary By Janet Epstein The Piedmont Seniors celebrated their 27th Anniversary on September 27th with a special luncheon at the Piedmont Community Hall. The organization was founded in 1996 by Lois Dawers and with the encouragement of Mark Delventhal, the long-time Director of Recreation, the Piedmont Seniors was established. Fifty people were in attendance for the anniversary festivities, Guests included members of the Police and Fire Departments, as well as Recreation staff members. The lunch was catered by Ann’s Catering of Berkeley. Police Chief Bowers, Fire Chief Brannigan and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen offered remarks about current events in Piedmont and their support by the Piedmont Seniors. Before the luncheon the group was fortunate to have Gail Lombardi, President of the Piedmont Historical Society, provide a special presentation about Piedmont’s history, with a slideshow of what early Piedmont looked like. She mentioned the Piedmont Hotel, which is now part of Piedmont Park, and the therapeutic springs which attracted many people to the Piedmont hills at the beginning of the twentieth century. In the 1860s, the discovery of sulphur springs began to attract visitors to Piedmont. Mineral springs were believed to possess great curative powers, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel, built by Walter Blair, opened in 1871 to provide accommodations for those who came to “take the waters.” Built on the site of today’s Exedra, this grand hotel had a wide veranda, 20 bedrooms and 2 suites, 5 dining rooms, and a Grand Saloon with an elegant mahogany bar, billiard table, and pot-bellied stove (for men only). The hotel thrived until 1892 when, at 9:15 a.m. on November 17, the hotel came to a sudden end when a fire in the chimney expanded to the roof. It was not until 11:30 a.m. that Chemical Engine #1 arrived from Oakland to contain the fire. Newspapers reported that “the absence of any water supply left the occupants of the doomed building no other recourse than to sit down in the shade and watch the building burn.” Piedmont became an official city in California in 1907, for two main reasons: people wanted to escape the ravages of the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco, and they wanted to become an entity separate from Oakland. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors pay tribute to Bosco the dog, Sunol’s former mayor, by visiting a statue erected in his honor. Pictured are Edith Hereso (left), Sue Getreuer, Gregory Jurin, Nancy Hinsch, Janet Epstein, Jim Ayotte, Mona Jamieson, Fred Pemberton, Larry Hu, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Tanya Hu. Not pictured: Larry and Patti Singer. Fourteen members of the Piedmont Seniors group went on a round-trip scenic train ride through Niles Canyon to the historic town of Sunol. Their first stop was in front of the old Post Office to see the statue of Sunol’s former mayor, Bosco, a black Labrador Retriever and Rottweiler. Bosco defeated two humans to win the honorary mayoral election in 1981 and served until his death in 1994. A statue was later erected in his honor in 2008. Bosco even appeared as a contestant on the game show “3rd Degree” where the panelists failed to guess Bosco’s occupation. The Seniors then embarked on an 80-minute diesel train ride on the Niles Canyon Railway. This train is a living museum preserving an era of California’s railroad history as the last segment of the original Transcontinental Railroad to San Francisco. The Niles Canyon Railway is operated solely by volunteer members of the Pacific Locomotive Association, whose mission is “to develop and operate a working railroad museum for the benefit of the general public.” The Niles Canyon Railway also has an informative museum on the grounds depicting the important role of Chinese laborers in the construction of the Transcontinental Railroad. The station was built in 1996 and the oldest rail car dates from 1915. In 1988 The Pacific Locomotive Association brought railroad passenger operation back to life in Niles Canyon. The Association wanted to preserve the atmosphere of railroads in small-town America before the 1960s by connecting the historic communities of Sunol, the Niles District of Fremont and eventually Pleasanton. The Association’s goal is to educate the public in railroad history, tradition, and the evolution of all transportation technology. Since the Niles Canyon Railway heavily relies on donations, it has an annual fundraiser at the holiday time, called “The Tree of Lights.” This is an enchanting holiday excursion filled with music, cheer, refreshments, and features holiday lights, decorations, and even a visit by Santa Claus. This has been an annual destination for many Bay Area families for more than 10 years, with steam and diesel trains departing from both Niles and Sunol stations, however this popular trip is currently sold out for 2023. After a relaxing trip between Sunol and Niles, the group worked up an appetite. Returning to Dublin, they enjoyed a delicious Italian lunch at the Dublin restaurant, Frankie, Johnnie & Luigi Too. This restaurant has quite an extensive menu, and no one left hungry as ample portions were available for all. For more information about meetings and excursions of the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov. Meetings are usually held on the fourth Wednesday of each month from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall in Piedmont Park. Piedmont Seniors enjoy a sumptuous lunch at Frankie, Johnnie & Luigi Too restaurant in Dublin.

articles.text: Dear MacMama: I want to buy a new laptop for travel. I have a 2021 iMac that is my main computer. I have thought about an iPad, but have decided on a laptop, since I often have to work when I am away. My main work is spreadsheets and documents. There are so many options, I can’t make heads or tails of the different laptops. What would you suggest? —Marjorie, Oakland Dear Marjorie: I’m glad you told me what tasks you mainly do on your computer. One thing I don’t know is how much space you need, so I’m going to make some suggestions with some variations. I’m assuming that you keep most of your files on your main computer, your 2021 iMac. In a perfect world, these files would be in sync with your travel computer also. So, I’m going to suggest that you make sure that you are syncing your files with iCloud. Very likely, your photos are already synced through iCloud, meaning when you take a picture on your iPhone, it automatically shows up on your computer. And you should be doing the same in your position with your desktop and document files. If you do this on both machines, they will both stay in sync for the work that you must do. Note that iCloud has a setting called “optimize Mac storage” which will store local copies (on your Mac) of files that have been accessed recently if your Mac has enough space. If you’re running out of space on your Mac, it will automatically move files as needed to iCloud. One of the downsides of this is if you haven’t opened a file for a while, and it has been stored in iCloud, and you are in a place with your new laptop that doesn’t have a good internet connection, you will not have access to this file. This can be turned on and off in your System Settings/Apple ID/iCloud. Note that turning this off will start to download all files you have stored in iCloud onto your Mac that are not already there. I often turn this setting off before I travel, so I have access to everything. It’s a good idea to make sure that you have iCloud set to sync your documents before you set up a new machine. As you noticed, there are two types of laptops for sale each with many possibilities of customization, MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. For your purposes, I would suggest a 13” or 15” MacBook Air with an M2 processor, 8 or 16GB RAM, with at least the same size hard drive that your iMac has. Likely a 512 GB Solid State Drive (SSD) is fine, but it might be safer to get a 1 TB SSD. You don’t need a lot of processing power for spreadsheets and documents. But you can no longer upgrade your hard drive or RAM, so it’s best to think ahead and get a machine that you will not outgrow. If you bought a 13 inch MacBook Air with 8 GB RAM and a 1 TB SSD, it would cost $1399 before tax and not including any sales or promotions. A 15-inch Air with the same specs is, $1699. If you told me that you were going to be editing pictures, music or movies, my answer would be very different. In that case you need as much RAM and processing power that you can afford. To give you an example, I would steer you either to get the same machine with 24 GB Ram, $1799 for the 13 inch and $2099 for the 15 inch. Or even better, a MacBook Pro with one of the M3 processors. There are three to choose from. For most folks, the M3 is fine, the M3 Pro is even better, and the M3 Max is overkill. As I said, if you’re doing things that take a lot of processing power, using Final Cut Pro or Adobe After Effects, then the M3 max processor is something you will greatly appreciate. Let’s just look at a couple of those models to see the price difference. A 14 inch MacBook Pro with the basic M3 Pro processor, 18 GB unified memory and a 1 TB SSD will run $2199 before tax. Choose the better M3 Pro processor, bring the memory up to 36GB, and it jumps to $2799. For most content creators, photo and music editors this is plenty. For people who really need (or just like to have the best), the 14 inch MacBook Pro with the most loaded M3 Max processor, 48 GB unified memory, and 1 TB SSD, you are at $3699. And I haven’t even said a thing about the 16 inch MacBook Pro. So, you see it’s really easy to go down the rabbit hole with all of the specifics. But if you’re only working on documents, sending some emails doing light photo editing, the MacBook Air is a great choice. Apple has not provided the MacBook Air with the M3 processor yet, but they probably will. There won’t be enough of a difference between the M2 and the M3 to have you wait. As example, I have a 13 inch MacBook Air with the M2 processor, 16 gigs of RAM, and a 2 TB SSD. This is the machine I travel with, even on my photo trips. I use Adobe Lightroom, and I have no trouble with the specs on this machine. If you have enough time, then you can order a laptop with the exact specifics that makes sense to you. If you are traveling very soon, you may be limited to what Apple has in stock. Make sure to check out other retailers like Best Buy, and even B&H Photo or Amazon. pages.text: Wednesday, November 29, 2023 31 Scout Tree Lot Continued from page 9 “It’s fun to be here,” said Abe Shrago, a Tiger Scout from Pack 5, in his first year volunteering at the tree lot. Despite being one of the youngest Scouts on shift last weekend, he had one of the most important jobs – transporting trees to the checkout counter using a tree dolly larger than he was tall. “I’m just so grateful. People loved me for picking their trees out this weekend. It makes me feel happy,” said Shrago. Equally happy were the many customers that the Scouts helped. Customer Elena McCormick had many of her questions answered by a helpful Webelos Scout. Leo Shrago, Abe’s brother, helped her decide which tree would be best for her home. “After talking to Leo, we decided to get a Douglas fir tree this year,” said McCormick. “Hopefully the needles won’t fall too much, because we have a cat at home who will be enjoying his first Christmas.” After buying a Christmas tree at the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot, Sankalp Sharma watches as Nuala Price helps him lash it to the top of his car. Mike Beuselinck, the parent of a Cub Scout in Pack 5, carries shears to cut the twine around trees to open them up before being put on customers’ cars. “This is a fantastic event in a beautiful city,” said Thomas McCormick, Elena’s brother who was visiting for the holidays. “It’s super nice to explore the city and find this today.” Proceeds from the lot benefit the nearly 1000 Cub Scouts, Scouts, Venturers, Explorers, and members of the Piedmont Language School, who are all part of the Piedmont Scout Council. For more information, visit: www.scouttreelot.org. articles.text: On November 16, Shell Oil issued a press release inviting Piedmont residents to a community meeting to be held on November 16 to inform community members of the conversion of the former Piedmont Auto Care to Shell Recharge, a recharging station for electric vehicles. Equilon Enterprises LLC d/b/a Shell Oil Products U.S. (Shell), a subsidiary of Shell plc, is excited to announce it has acquired a piece of property at 29 Wildwood Ave., in Piedmont, California. This is currently the site of a former gas station previously owned by Piedmont Auto Care. Pending permitting and regulatory approvals, Shell hopes to construct a new, 14-bay electric vehicle (EV) charging hub at the site under the Shell Recharge brand. Shell envisions this site to be part of our growing state and national network of fast charging for electric vehicles. A robust electric vehicle charging network can play a role in California’s plans to achieve 100% of new zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035, and to achieve 25% reduction in smog causing pollution by 2037. Once constructed, the proposed electric vehicle hub at this site in Piedmont would provide fast charging for electric vehicles with power up to 360kW, allowing drivers to recharge most vehicles more quickly, getting them back on the road faster. This location will be owned and operated by Shell. Construction is expected to commence in the first half of 2024. During demolition of the existing infrastructure, and installation of new equipment, you may notice additional traffic, workers on site, and normal construction noise. Shell is committed to being a good neighbor and has a process in place to receive feedback as we build the hub. You can reach us with concerns or feedback by calling 1-888-GO-SHELL (888- 467-4355). Please be sure to refer to the location at 29 Wildwood in Piedmont, California. Also, to learn more about this Piedmont location and Shell e-Mobility, please join us at our open house at Kehilla Community Synagogue, 1300 Grand Avenue, Piedmont on Tuesday, November 28, 2023, from 4:00- 6:00 p.m. We look forward to hosting you and supporting Piedmont’s charging needs. If you have any questions, please contact us at 1-888-GO-SHELL (888-467-4355). Sincerely, Shell Recharge Team Customers of Piedmont Auto Care owned by Jeff Hansen for the past 17 years learned in a news story in the Piedmont Post on November 8 that the station had been sold to Shell Oil and that the gas station had closed. The Piedmont Shell Station has closed after 95 years in business.

Police Captain Chris Monahan said that the only thing left preventing the cameras from being active has been their physical installation and setting up the software needed to use them. Monahan also addressed privacy concerns citizens may have over the installation of surveillance cameras in their community. “We are not attempting to invade anyone’s personal privacy. They are only to prevent crime and provide more information to solve crime in our community,” said Monahan. “We are currently working through the final networking and configuration and expect the cameras to be online in December. This project has not been without its challenges, but we are excited to bring this technology into our toolbelt of investigative resources,” added Police Commander Lisa Douglas. The Piedmont Police Department’s public safety cameras have a history in the community. The intersection at Grand and Oakland Avenue has had a public safety camera in use since 2017 as part of a pilot program. The city pays $8,580 a year for this camera and $1,200 a year for cellular connection at the site. Data from this pilot camera were presented to City Council in 2020, which allowed the police to pursue a request for proposals to bid on the project. On August 2, 2021, City Council approved $121,794 to Applied Video Solutions for the cameras, plus $48,104 for five years of system support. The council also approved a payment of $41,000 annually to Comcast for fiber and internet technology. Some delays in the project have been caused by the City’s requirement to use fiber technology instead of wireless technology. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council’s annual Tree Lot will open this Saturday, November 25, at 9 a.m. The lot is located at Coaches Field, next to the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. Community members looking to add a festive touch to their homes this holiday season will be able to buy trees, wreaths, garlands, tree stands, and mistletoe from the lot for pickup or delivery. The Tree Lot is also currently accepting online pre-orders at www.scouttreelot.org. Delivery of trees will be available throughout Piedmont and select neighborhoods in Oakland. Proceeds from the lot benefit local Cub Scouts, Scouts, Venturers, Explorers, and the Piedmont Language School. “It’s fun because you get to interact with everyone from Piedmont,” said Kevin McKillop, a Troop 6 Scout. “It’s especially fun when we deliver because people are always super happy to receive their trees.” In recent years, the tree lot has become something of a family affair for Kevin. For the last six years, Kevin has volunteered at the tree lot with his father, Sean McKillop, the Scoutmaster for Sunday Photos by Tom Smegal Volunteer Scouts and parents plan for opening day of the Piedmont Scout Tree Lott, scheduled for this Saturday, November 25. Troop 6. “Mostly we try to volunteer together,” explained Kevin. “But, if one of us has something going on at school or at work, we’ll still go separately.” This year, the father-son duo is assisting with set-up, breakdown, and deliveries for the tree lot. Kevin said that even as a teenager, volunteering at the tree lot still holds its appeal. “As a teenager, you’re kind of hesitant to say yes at first because you have other stuff you want to do during the holiday season. But, once you get there, you have more fun. It’s just a good time.” As with everything related to the tree lot, family remains central to the volunteer staff as well. Sean McKillop said that volunteering with the tree lot was a great way to spend time with his son. “To be honest with you, Kevin is going away to college next year, so any opportunity I get to spend time with him is a bonus,” he said. The Scout Tree Lot has been highly successful in previous years. In 2022, sales were high with up to $50,000 generated on its opening weekend, and an additional $30,000 in online sales. The Christmas tree lot will be open until the third weekend in December or until the lot sells out its stock. Kobal. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Beautification Foundation invite community members to the “Lights Up” ceremony on Wednesday night, December 6, at 7:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. Lights Up Piedmont! is the successor to Piedmont’s holiday tree lighting ceremony, which dates back to 1969. This will be the event’s second year under this name, which was changed to “create a more inclusive and welcoming event that celebrates the diversity of our community,” according to the City’s press release. The illumination of the 80-foot redwood tree at the Community Hall will include songs by Piedmont High School’s Troubadours. The event also will include the lighting of a menorah. As with previous years, Santa Claus will be available for photos inside Community Hall. Children are invited to write letters to Santa and deposit them in a special mailbox addressed to the North Pole during the event. For questions, contact Barbara Love at (510) 282-5618 or blovegustke@gmail.com.

It features a German tradition of having booths with gifts and crafts for the Christmas holidays. doors during the month of December and includes German food and the famous “Gluehwein” (spiced hot wine) and a non-alcoholic version called “Kinderpunsch”. Part of the market will be indoors in the Altenheim’s Prior Hall. Live music will be provided and all are welcome. People may enter at the main gate (1720 MacArthur Boulevard) and the back gate at 1699 Excelsior Avenue. Street parking is available. The market is jointly organized by the Excelsior German Center located at the Altenheim Home on MacArthur, the fulltime East Bay German International School in Emeryville, and the Bay Area Kinderstube in Albany. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is currently accepting donations for its annual toy drive through December 23. To ensure that kids everywhere have a present to open for Christmas, Piedmont residents are encouraged to donate new, unwrapped toys to the Fire Department’s annual Toys for Tots Drive. Donation bins are located at the Fire Station and City Hall on Vista Avenue. . You’re never too old to donate, nor too young, as the fire department found out. This week, children from Havens Elementary School’s Minimates walked across the street to the fire station for a photograph in the Post, each holding a donation to the toy drive. The toy drive brings back some fond memories to Piedmont firefighters, “I grew up in a very large family,” said Fire Engineer Anthony Renteria. “I have a lot of younger brothers and sisters. So being able to help out kids in the area really hits home for me.” Firefighter Nadder Shehadeh echoed the sentiment. “Like, certain toys that you see go in these bins, you’re like, ‘Wow, I remember playing with this as a kid.’ Hopefully, these toys bring joy to someone’s day and bring light to their nights this holiday season.” “Seeing some of these toys come in just brings back old memories,” added Shehadeh, smiling. In particular, he said someone’s donated etch-a-sketch reminded him of his own memories of playing with it as a child. “I didn’t know they still made them.” Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County, and any toys donated before December 8 will be distributed through the US Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated on or after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Bins will remain at the F ire Department and City Hall for donations through December 23. A child donates the classic board game Jenga to the toy drive. Minimates students with donations for the Fire Department’s toy drive

articles.text: Are you looking for something to do with that beautiful pumpkin that doesn’t involve a jack-o-lantern? There are plenty of options to get more enjoyment out of the pumpkin, starting with trying to figure out what this strange gourd really is. Did you know pumpkins float and are considered fruits by botanists? Although notoriously heavy, a pumpkin will happily bob to the top of a pool and can be used as a makeshift kickboard. Just make sure there are no weak spots on your pumpkin before adding it to the pool. The defining factor for “fruit or vegetable” status is how the produce grows. Webster defines a fruit as a “usually edible reproductive body of a seed plant, especially one having a sweet pulp associated with the seed.” Anyone who has grown a pumpkin knows it is flowers that turn into pumpkins, making pumpkin a fruit. While commonly miscategorized as a vegetable, it may make more sense as a fruit after learning that most pumpkin varieties, other than the Pumpkin Pie is a staple on many Thanksgiving tables carving pumpkins seen on Halloween, are actually sweet. Although people in the U.S. may not view pumpkins as a common food source, pumpkins are an orange fruit that are a common source of subsistence in other parts of the world. People in China eat nine million tons of pumpkins per year, and in India six million tons. You may want to consider growing a gourd to see if it can be used in the kitchen. articles.text: The Piedmont Junior Running Club held its inaugural race in Dracena Park on November 15. Conditions were ideal as the rain forecasted for that day never materialized. A total of 64 runners from 4th and 5th grades in all three Piedmont elementary schools participated in the 0.9- mile event. The runners navigated the paved path that winds through the park, including uphill and downhill segments and challenging curves. The event was staged in three heats, each comprising about 20 participants. Every runner received a medal for finishing, and individual trophies were awarded to the top three boys and three girls in each heat. The heat winners were: Heat 1: Will Brumfiel (Wildwood), Cate Brasfield (Havens) Heat 2: Timmy Edit (Havens), Lanea Patty (Beach) Heat 3: Max Centeno (Wildwood), Harper Maing (Beach) Max Centeno posted the fastest overall time for the day, finishing the course in 6 minutes, 18 seconds, and Harper Maing was the fastest girl in 6 minutes and 46 seconds. In addition, a perpetual trophy was awarded to the school with the fastest combined top five times regardless of heat or gender. Havens won this year’s trophy, just edging out Wildwood and Beach. The Dracena race represented the culmination of Piedmont Junior Running Club’s 10-week Fall season in which students from the three schools practiced twice weekly to build speed and endurance. The temporary closure of Witter Field meant that runners did not have the benefit of a track, so they trained with long runs in neighborhoods. The coaching staff extends its thanks to the community for sharing Dracena Park on race day and to the Public Works Department and Recreation Department for their assistance. Photos by Minori Tsuge and Andrew Herrgott

articles.text: Caroline Woods’ class took great care in creating impressive props for the 6th grade Festival of the Nile in the middle school’s multi-purpose room. Piedmont Middle School’s sixth graders concluded their studies of the ancient Egyptians with a Festival of the Nile on Thursday, November 16. Each 6th grade class performed a skit to show the mastery of ancient Egyptian social structures, religious beliefs and culture. Stories detailing the beliefs and practices were transformed into contemporary song and dance on stage. Performances described the social hierarchy of the civilization and the 4400-year-old pyramids of Giza. PMS students even learned the ways of mummification in recent Photos by Jay Russell and Anne Smith Ava Ubaka is dressed as a pharaoh. Felix Kansal with a headdress and “gold” around his neck played a dead pharaoh. Mireille Psathas is costumed as Isis, the Ancient Egyptian Goddess of healing and magic. Students in Michael Bracamonte’s 6th grade core class fly through the air in dramatic choreography Posters made by each sixth grade class depict mythological stories from Ancient Egypt. The comic item shows how Seth betrayed his brother, Osiris. weeks. The high priests removed and jarred a dead Pharoah’s organs except for the heart, which was to be weighed against a feather by Anubis before entering the afterworld. Hillary Voigt’s class did a fun version of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.” Class performances had different strengths. Caroline Woods’ class, as example, made fantastic stage props that required hours of work to create a makeshift sarcophagus from paper and cardboard. Lea Lotia’s afternoon core class was light on dress up, but big on the recitation of a song and a choreographed story. Michael Bracamonte’s class staged an elaborate skit portraying the beliefs of the Egyptian afterlife. “Where am I, who are you?” asked a student portraying a dead Pharaoh. “I’m Anubis and you are dead. Remember you’re in the land of the dead now; you have no power here,” said the student wearing the head of a jackal. In its second year as an annual event for sixth graders, the Festival of the Nile has quickly become an enjoyable way for students to showcase their history lessons.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team’s illustrious season came to an end in the first round of the Division 3 CIF NorCal Championship Tournament, in a close 10-8 loss to No. 4 Ponderosa in Elk Grove. The Highlanders finished with a 19-10 record and won the school’s first North Coast Section championship. The team will lose the bulk of its roster to graduation at the end of the school year. Seniors include Peter Krumins. Declan Linnane, George Stein, Quincy Scherman, Finn Burke, Daniel Banin, Spencer Barlow, and Evan Dickason. Next year ‘s team will have returners that include goalie Luke McAuliffe, starters Elles Krieckhaus and Leo Hurwitz, in addition to Charlie Wright, Yotam Kariv, and Ori Aloush. Coach Rik Krumins is also keeping a watchful eye on some of next year’s freshmen arrivals. “We’re hoping this championship season helps build the next 10 years of this program. That’s the excitement we have. There’s a really good class coming in next year, and I’m really excited to be a part of it,” said Krumins. Game Recap Piedmont trailed 3-2 by the end of the first quarter and faced a 6-3 deficit by halftime. Piedmont closed the score to 7-6 at the start of the fourth quarter, but conceded three goals while being held to Staff Photos George Stein scored three goals in his final appearance in a Piedmont cap. Piedmont’s Elles Kreickhaus will likely be among the headline returners in 2024. Declan Linnane scored once against Ponderosa.
articles.title: Piedmont loses 10-8 to Ponderosa in CIF NorCal playoffs

articles.text: Sebastien Swain (1061) stands with cross country runners who qualified for the State meet. Piedmont High’s cross-country team competed in the North Coast Section Championship at Hayward High on Saturday, November 18. The girls’ team finished sixth of 16 schools, and the boys’ team was eighth of 19. It was a wet and stormy day for the event with scattered downpours soaking the course. The big news was freshman Sebastien Swain qualifying for the CIF State Meet by placing 13th of 140 runners with a time of 16:29.5. Individual runners could qualify by finishing among the five fastest runners not on a topthree team. It has been a breakout season for Swain, who helped pace his team late in the season. “By Mile 2, Sebastien in 20th and continued to work his way up, passing other runners to finish in 13th place. The boys’ team was hampered by senior leader Xander Schulte-Sasse dealing with a lingering injury. Following Schulte-Sasse was senior Julien Lee in 27th, clocking a 16:57.2. Sophomore Noah Sohn was 60th in 18:05.5, and freshman Thomas Ero rounded out Piedmont’s top five in 72nd, 18:33.6. articles.text: Staff Photos Tanya Kononova wrapped up her Piedmont High tennis career with a third-place finish in singles at the North Coast Section Individual Tournament. Tanya Kononova completed her Piedmont High tennis career on Monday and Tuesday, November 13-14 at the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament. She finished 3rd in the singles bracket, defeating Noelle Chen of Head-Royce in straight sets, 7-5, 6-1. In the first round, Kononova defeated Iris Bremer of Arcata 6-3, 6-3 and followed up with a 6-2, 6-3 win over Marin Academy’s Eloise Sent. She then ran into the No.1 seed and eventual-champion Vivian Gallaway of Berean Christian in the semifinals, losing 6-1, 6-3. “After playing Vivian, I was really down. Jim [Landes] reminded me it’s my last match. I started playing my game and it felt really good. I just had to get myself all together,” said Kononova. After a narrow first-set win over Chen, Kononova powered her way to the finish in the second set. She showed her usual array of forehands, but also used approaches to net to keep Chen off balance. It marked the second time Kononova faced Chen this season. The Jayhawks’ starter won the first meeting in a narrow 7-5, 7-6 (7-5) straight sets victory. In the NCS post-season championships, it was a different story. “I was going for every shot. I was hitting it like I knew it would be a winner and I was coming up to net a lot. I was playing really risky, but it all worked out. I was playing aggressive and I was making the shots,” said Kononova. Kononova concludes her tennis career at Piedmont High as a two-year starter. She won the 2022 Western Alameda County Conference singles title, placed fourth in last year’s NCS singles tournament, was this year’s WACC runner up, and now takes third in NCS. Her arrival to Piedmont came in the most unconventional circumstances, leaving her home country of Ukraine as a refugee due to the ongoing war. The tennis team represented a return to normalcy and a way for her to enjoy her high school years after she had to leave her home country, with her father still there, and mother in Piedmont. “It taught me a lot. It taught me how things don’t always work out how you expect, but the main thing is to have fun and enjoy it. I really enjoyed being on the team and meeting these girls, who are really amazing. The coaches are also amazing here. Being here gave me people I could talk to around school and friends to hang out with. It’s been a great time,” she added.
articles.title: Tanya Kononova finishes 3rd in NCS Individual Tournament

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team opens its season this Saturday afternoon, November 25, with a 2 p.m. game with Analy at Binks Rawlings Gym. After reaching the semifinals of the North Coast Section post-season playoffs, the Highlanders are hungry for more success. “In the years before, we talked about defense being the thing we needed to improve on, like not being able to stop Branson’s guards. That’s been the big push this offseason. We’ve had more offseason workouts than ever,” said coach Ben Spencer. The Highlanders will have to operate without last year’s leading scorer, A.J. Harris, now playing at Emory University. Leading the team group will be a tall, versatile center, Brit Burden, who Spencer compared to Luke Barrett in 2020. “He looks great. He’s a bit similar to Luke in the sense that he has really good skills with the ball and can push the fast break. He can also play away from the basket, stretch the floor, but also play with his back to the basket,” said Spencer. Tall and lanky is a good way to describe this year’s roster. Declan Linnane is fresh off a highly successful water polo season and will provide a big body to grab boards and play tough defense. Center Scott Cooley, listed at 6 feet, 6 inches, is still working on clearance from section officials. From top to bottom, it’s a tall team. “This is the biggest team we’ve had,” said Spencer. “This year, Brit is 6’6”. Scott Cooley is a new transfer student and he’s 6’6”. Declan is 6’4”, Alex Anderson is 6’3”,” he said. Alongside Burden will be returning guards junior Ravi Silverberg and senior point guard Arjun Bornstein. Sophomore Dillon Casey is another player Spencer who has impressed Spencer. “Ravi had some big games as a sophomore guard, and being a sophomore guard in our league is difficult. We moved him off the ball and he’s a completely different player; his confidence has skyrocketed. Arjun is a senior and I’ve told everyone he’s the heart-and-soul of our team. You add his toughness to our size, length, and grit, and we’ll be good,” added Spencer. Spencer will look for big contributions from players earning their largest roles at the varsity level. Players like Lucas Malecki, Cash Panico, Emmet Asulin, and Finn Burke are all entering their first year on varsity. “We have seven seniors, but Staff Photos Coach Ben Spencer and Piedmont’s basketball team are back in action this week, hosting a season-opening game against Analy. Brit Burden is the leading returner from last year. Declan Linnane, fresh off a NCS title in water polo, is another returning starter. two of them, Brit and Declan, played big minutes last year. We have all the pieces to be good if not better than last year. I say that every year, but we might be deeper this year in terms of talent and being able to move the ball,” said Spencer. Piedmont will host its annual winter tournament under a new name. Working with prep-sports webpage WestCoastPreps.com, Piedmont will host the West Coast Preps Winter Classic on Thursday, November 30 through Saturday, December 2. Games at Binks Rawlings Gym will include St. Ignatius, Archie Williams, Redwood of Larkspur, Northgate, Windsor, Acalanes, and Hayward. “We’re super excited for it. We have a good relationship with WestCoastPreps and they asked about hosting a tournament. It’s always great to bring in the best teams possible. Redwood is going to challenge Branson in D2, St. Ignatius has been a top team in CCS, Windsor from the North Bay is really talented. It’s a really good lineup,” said Spencer.

The campus was amazing, and the coaches were super nice, I connected with them right away.” “Of course, having Trinity there was an extra bonus, so I committed on the spot,” she said.
