articles.text: Basketball player Luke Barrett, Class of 2020, is a senior on the St. Mary’s College team. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team gets its season started this week, so we are taking a look at three former basketball stars currently active at the collegiate level: Luke Barrett at St. Mary’s College, Luke Harris at Carleton College, and JoJo Murphy at Chico State. Luke Barrett St. Mary’s Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, is a senior on the St. Mary’s basketball team appeared in 20 games last season. He helped lead Piedmont to its 2020 D4 North Coast Section title and won the Post’s Athlete of the Year award as a senior. The Gaels of St. Mary’s are off to a 2-3 start. Barrett has five appearances and is averaging 16 minutes per game. He has 14 points with four field goals and one 3-pointer, to go along with four assists and three steals. He’s been active on the boards with 22 rebounds, including 11 offensive grabs. St. Mary’s finished last season as the No. 22 ranked team in the country after going 27-8. They received the No. 5 seed in the NCAA Tournament, defeating No. 12 VCU 63-51 in the first round before losing 70-55 to UConn, the alma mater of Piedmont coach Ben Spencer. As a sophomore, Barrett made an appearance in the Gaels’ 82- 53 win over Indiana in the first round of the NCAA Tournament. Luke Harris Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, is a junior at Carleton College in Minnesota and was also a member of Piedmont’s D4 NCS title in 2020. We named Harris the Post’s 2021 Athlete of the Year. The Knights won their first game of the season 57-50 over North Central Minnesota on November 15, led by Harris who tied a career-high with 26 points, to go along with three assists. As a sophomore, Harris helped lift Carleton to the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference championship with a 86-76 win over St. Johns on February 26. Harris scored 19 points. He was second on the team in scoring with 16.4 points per game achieved double-digit points in 20 of 24 games last season, including eight games with at least 20 points. He led Carleton with 92 assists, was second on the team in field goals with 159 made, and was third in rebounds with 132. Carleton finished with a 24-4 overall record and lost 81-77 to St. Norbert in the first round of the Division 3 NCAA tournament. Harris departed from Piedmont High as an all-time great, finishing with over 1,200 points scored. He was a three-year starter in successful years, going 21-11 as a sophomore, won the 2020 D4 NCS Championship that finished 24-6, while the team went 11-5 in the pandemic shortened 2021 season. JoJo Murphy Chico State JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, is a sophomore at Chico State and was another member of Piedmont’s NCS title-winning team when he earned a starting role as a sophomore. The Wildcats are off to a hot 3-0 start to its season. Murphy has started all three games, scoring 35 points with 10 field goals and seven 3-pointers, including five steals and one assist. As a freshman at Chico State, Murphy earned first-team AllCCAA honors and was selected as the conference’s Freshman of the Year. He finished last season as the team’s leading scorer with Luke Harris, Class of 2021, is a junior at Carleton College.

articles.text: Photo by Matthew Washburn Associate Chorus Master Fabrizio Corona and Chorus Director John Keene. The San Francisco Opera will present the acclaimed San Francisco Opera Chorus to conclude the fall season on Friday, December 8. Chorus Director John Keene conducts the opera chorus and Associate Chorus Master Fabrizio Corona will accompany on keyboard for an evening of a cappella and accompanying choral works. The evening’s program features selections from opera repertoires, with music by Clara Schumann, Fanny Mendelssohn Hensel, Lili Boulanger and Florence Price as well as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Gabriel Fauré and Stephen Paulus. Seating is general admission. For tickets, click on sfopera.com or contact the San Francisco Opera Box Office at 301 Van Ness Avenue, (415) 864-3330. Additional information is available at sfopera.com/chorusinconcert.

articles.text: The historic Treasure Island Museum will be filled with holiday music on Saturday, December 9, with a free organ concert by Jerry Nagano at 1 p.m. Nagano was named organist of the year in 2017 by the American Theatre Organ Society and was the resident organist at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium, playing their Moller Pipe organ. In this concert, he plays the classics for guests. Nagano lives in Northern California and is a member of the staff of the Stanford Theater. For 10 years he was the featured artist at the famed Ye Olde Pizza Joynt in the Bay Area, home of the “Wurlitzer in the Pizza Parlor” concept. This event is free but registration is required. Museum staff encourage all attendees to bring a new toy, unopened and unwrapped, for the Treasure Island Museum Holiday Toy Drive. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/ holiday-organ-concert-1 to register. Organist Jerry Nagano
articles.title: Free holiday organ concert at Treasure Island Museum Dec. 9

articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland is delighted to welcome the community to a rare performance of the Choir of Clare College Cambridge in their only Bay Area performance. The internationally acclaimed choir will perform a Christmas concert, Magnum Mysterium, at 8 p.m. on Wednesday, December 13. Tickets are $40 General Admission, and $30 Seniors & Students, and are available in advance at https:// tinyurl.com/3j742ctz. Join us for an evening of festive melodies and harmonies at this highly anticipated event. The world-renowned Choir of Clare College, Cambridge, led by Graham Ross will perform for one night only at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, 114 Montecito Avenue, across from Lake Merritt in Oakland. The choir’s holiday program includes the richness of Renaissance polyphony by Praetorius, Morales, and Mouton and masterpieces by Howells, Sally Beamish, Will Todd, along with favorites of the holiday season. The choir’s holiday program includes the richness of Renaissance music by Praetorius, Morales, and Mouton and masterpieces by Howells, Sally Beamish, Will Todd, along with favorites of the holiday season. Audiences will be thrilled by the virtuosity and rich sonorities of the group that British composer Giles Swayne refers to as “a whopping jewel in Clare’s musical crown.” Don’t miss the opportunity to experience the extraordinary talent of the Choir of Clare College in person in Oakland. Since its founding as a mixed voice choir in 1972, the Choir of Clare College has gained an international reputation as one of the world’s leading university choirs. In addition to its primary function of leading services three times a week in the College chapel, the Choir keeps an active schedule recording, broadcasting, and performing. For mer directors have included John Rutter and Timothy Brown. Under the direction of Graham Ross, Director of Music since 2010, it has been praised for its consistently ‘thrilling’ and ‘outstanding’ performances worldwide. Recent engagements include performances with the Orchestra of the Age of the Enlightenment, London Philharmonic Orchestra, Britten Sinfonia, Aalborg Symphony Orchestra on Denmark, Malaysian Philharmonic Orchestra in Kuala Lumpur, and Orquesta Sinfonia Nacional de Mexico. They have also performed in Barcelona’s Palau de Musica, El Escorial in Madrid, Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City, St John’s Smith Square London, and across the USA and Canada. For more information, see: www.clarecollegechoir.com/ Homestay housing needed Members of the Piedmont community are invited to host two British college student singers for two nights. December 12 & 13. Contact Victoria Larson at designoffices74@gmail.com, or e-mail music@stpaulsoakland. org.
articles.title: St, Paul’s Episcopal hosts rare concert by Choir of Clare College, Cambridge

articles.text: San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater will premiere its annual holiday season favorite, A Christmas Carol, on Wednesday, December 6. The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dickens’ novella has been recounted onstage and in film for ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo. Music is scored by Karl Lundenberg with choreography by Val Caniparoli. Once again the cast is led by James Carpenter as Ebenezer Scrooge. A Christmas Carol has been included in ACT’s repertory for decades, and Carpenter has resided in the role of Scrooge for 15 consecutive seasons. Performances will take place at the Toni Rembe Theater, 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. The production uses theatrical haze and lighting that may not be appropriate for photosensitive groups. The holiday classic will play onstage through December 24. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets, or call the box office at 415-749-2228. Photo by Kevin Berne James Carpenter as Ebenezer Scrooge in ACT’s A Christmas Carol.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Bulrusher, a play by Eisa Davis and directed by Nicole Watson, will be performed on stage through Sunday, December 3. The coming-of-age story follows protagonist and titular character Bulrusher, a multiracial girl found as an infant floating in a basket on the Navarro River in Mendocino County. The girl, now 18-year-old, is clairvoyant, and struggles with feeling she is an outsider in the predominately white town of Boonville. The lyrical comedy takes a turn when the teenager meets a young Black woman from Birmingham, Alabama, who helps her uncover her past. The play deals with adults topics including sexual assault, but is grounded in humor and empathy. “Even though there’s a lot of pain and longing we’re left with, there’s also so much hope,” Davis told the Hollywood Reporter. “So that’s something that has kind of been sustaining for me in Bulrusher and a big part of why I wrote it – the possibility for love and forgiveness and joy, even amongst all of this pain.” The cast includes Cyndii Johnson, Rob Kellogg, Jamie LaVerdiere, Shyla Lefner, Jordan Tyson and Jeorge Bennett Watson. Bulrusher is directed by Nicole Watson. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/bulrusher/. articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside throughout November and December to see the 16-acre estate illuminated for holidays. The non-profit historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 7. Meet and take photos with Santa any weekend in December through December 23, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Afterwards, view an array of decorated Christmas trees inside the estate. Filoli’s decorating team has installed 22 decorated trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, with 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate home for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host The ballroom chandelier glistens from below. The ballroom features a pair of Baccarat crystal Louis XVI style fifty-light chandeliers. Staff Photos Each tree at Filoli is uniquely decorated; no two are the same. The dining room features elegant and festive meal settings. concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday decorations that reflect the esthetics of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents in the 19th century. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, Attendees view one of the many festooned trees in the estate. including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are a special time, the lighting enhancements glow as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission provides access to the estate trail before sundown and allows visitors to admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To learn more about “Holidays at Filoli” and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/. Fairy light fixtures adorn all corners of the gardens. The outdoor stage is a perfect spot for a photo opportunity, or to cozy up with a warm cup of apple cider.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Paris Can Wait, directed by Eleanor Coppola, is easy on the eyes and the palate. Through a series of circumstances, Anne Lockwood (Diane Lane), wife of film producer Michael Lockwood (Alec Baldwin), decides, because of a slight ear infection, not to fly with him to Turkey and then on to Paris where they’ll spend some time vacationing. Michael’s French friend, Jaques (Arnaud Viard), insists that he will drive Anne across the South of France to Paris where she and Michael have an apartment waiting. And so what begins as a daylong road trip turns into a sightseeing buffet with countless stops at restaurants and a charming hotel. The scenery is gorgeous, the meals that she and Jaques share are amazing, and the table chit-chat is conversation lite. As Anne keeps suggesting/ insisting that Paris awaits, Jaques reminds her in countless ways that it’s not the destination but the journey. This trip is not only a life lesson for Anne but a metaphor. As it turns out, Paris does wait and Anne begins to relax. She carries a point and shoot camera and photographs not only the scenery but the stunning food that is served, meal after meal. This proves to be an interesting adjunct to the story, an affirmation of what is before her. Jaques is a raconteur, charming and light-hearted, and who at the drop of a broken fan belt will suggest a picnic before concerning himself with a repair. He is filled with a casual joie de vivre that slowly breaks down Anne’s defenses, though she is not so naïve to be taken in completely by his suave though sincere romantic banter. Diane Lane is, in my opinion, one of the best actors working today. Her face is a tableau of emotions; she easily inhabits any role she takes on. It is Lane who carries this film from their departure in Cannes in Jaques’ antique Peugeot to their arrival in Paris, eventually. As an aside, Eleanor Coppola is the wife of Francis Ford Coppola and this, at the age of 80, is her first feature. My sense is that it is subtly autobiographical. Paris Can Wait. Directed by Eleanor Coppola. Romantic comedy starring Diane Lane, Alec Baldwin, Amand Viard. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG. Released 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/MAX/ Apple tv. articles.text: Madina Nalwanga in Queen of Katwe Queen of Katwe is a remarkable movie – moving, inspirational and yet possesses a frayed edge of reality that enhances the film. It is an example of the fine directorial work of Indian-American director, Mira Nair. There are two leading characters that fill the screen with a series of evocative and extraordinary moments. There’s Phiona Mutesi (Madina Nalwanga), child of the Kampala slum known as Katwe (Kampala is the capital of Uganda). And there is the slum itself, portrayed in all of its unforgiving, stark reality. But first, Phiona. She lives in a tin-roofed shack with her widowed mother, Nakku Harriet (Lupita Nyong’o), and her siblings. She is illiterate, having left school as a youngster to sell corn on the streets of Katwe to help her family survive. It is a life for her and her family, for all of the inhabitants of this grindingly poor community that is lived on a precipice. Phiona’s life is the life of her entire community. To its credit (and that of Disney), the film does not back away nor give the film a fairytale patina. Another dimension to this wonderful story is what happens to Phiona, who at the outset of the film is only 9-years-old. “Queen” is a character study of an astonishingly resilient young girl. One day, while selling corn, Phiona looks through the crooked planks of a youth ministry, run by Robert Katende (David Oyelowo). She hesitantly enters and what she sees is astonishing. Children are bent over chessboards. They are concentrating on a strange game. Robert urges her to take a closer look. She sits down and one of the children, a young boy, explains the rules and says to her with pride, “In chess the small one can become the big one.” And he tips over the king. Phiona studies the pieces and the board and unexpectedly what she sees resonates at an unexpected level. Her innate intelligence almost immediately responds to the game’s complexities. Soon Phiona is not only playing, but she is winning, a reality that some of the boys resent, wondering how is this possible. And so, an illiterate girl selling corn and carrying plastic cans of water home for her mother and her family, finds she possesses a gift she never could have imagined. She is now playing in Ugandan tournaments and finally in an international tournament in Russia. Her world of Katwe is widened beyond comprehension, with cities, airplanes, and a level of affluence that is startling. But know that her gift brings her both joy and disharmony, for she initially begins to feel she cannot go home again. She has changed and no longer sees in the same way what was once so familiar. She has gone to private schools and universities to play. She has been exposed to the world. To the credit of director Mira Nair, she reminds the audience that for all of her life Phiona has been surrounded by her peers and her family, and by a community that embraces her talent as if it were their own. Queen of Katwei is a wonderful must-see film. This story is larger than life in so many ways and revelatory from the beginning to the final scene. It is also filled with superb performances, beginning with newcomer Madina Nalwanga as Phiona. Queen of Katwe. Directed by Mira Nair. Starring Madina Nalwanga, David Oyelowo, Lupita Nyong’o. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv.

articles.text: To quickly establish this extraordinary and moving film’s bona fides, Son of Saul won the Palm Grand Prix at Cannes, followed by a Golden Globe and Oscar for Best Foreign Language film. Its genre is the Holocaust, a source for countless stories that ponder the existential question of how such a profound failure of the human spirit and conscience could ever have occurred? It is assumed that we have seen the horrifying images of men and women, mere skeletons, covered in striped rags, pressed against a wire fence, their hollow eyes gazing out, vacant and beyond reach. For that moment, at least, they have survived an abyss that still remains all but indescribable; yet, we know now, fully, that it did occur and some of those who stood at the wire or lay crowded in wooden slatted bunks have born witness to a barbarity the description of which still eludes even those who lived it. In the course of our lives it may be that we have grown inured to those images: human beings stacked like cords of wood, awaiting their final journey into deep pits or ovens. But Hungarian writer and director Laszlo Nemes has created in Son of Saul a film that avoids the standard Holocaust tropes: the camera panning a concentration camp (in this case its Auschwitz-Birkenau), shots of Nazi guards patrolling the perimeters with snarling dogs, or barracks with smoke stacks in the background. Instead, he focuses on one man, Saul (Geza Rohrig), and using a shallow focus format and an almost square screen, he follows him closely, intently. So tight are these sustained shots, that what Saul sees is what we see, the rest remains slightly out of focus, melding into a horror of sounds, gun shots, images of dead bodies, fires from the ovens. Saul, as it is explained, is a member of what was called the Sonderkommando – prisoners who were forced to assist the Germans in their industrial task of extermination, and ordered to guide the recent transport arrivals into large rooms, help them undress, and move them into “the showers” where they were gassed. They would then remove the bodies and prepare the room for the next group. His face, devoid of emotions, his feelings long ago extinguished, is a study in controlled,

pages.text: Wednesday, November 22, 2023 19 MOVIE FOR ADULTS Paris Can Wait an enjoyable romantic comedy Review by Chris Honoré Paris Can Wait, directed by Eleanor Coppola, is easy on the eyes and the palate. Through a series of circumstances, Anne Lockwood (Diane Lane), wife of film producer Michael Lockwood (Alec Baldwin), decides, because of a slight ear infection, not to fly with him to Turkey and then on to Paris where they’ll spend some time vacationing. Michael’s French friend, Jaques (Arnaud Viard), insists that he will drive Anne across the South of France to Paris where she and Michael have an apartment waiting. And so what begins as a daylong road trip turns into a sightseeing buffet with countless stops at restaurants and a charming hotel. The scenery is gorgeous, the meals that she and Jaques share are amazing, and the table chit-chat is conversation lite. As Anne keeps suggesting/ insisting that Paris awaits, Jaques reminds her in countless ways that it’s not the destination but the journey. This trip is not only a life lesson for Anne but a metaphor. As it turns out, Paris does wait and Anne begins to relax. She carries a point and shoot camera and photographs not only the scenery but the stunning food that is served, meal after meal. This proves to be an interesting adjunct to the story, an affirmation of what is before her. Jaques is a raconteur, charming and light-hearted, and who at the drop of a broken fan belt will suggest a picnic before concerning himself with a repair. He is filled with a casual joie de vivre that slowly breaks down Anne’s defenses, though she is not so naïve to be taken in completely by his suave though sincere romantic banter. Diane Lane is, in my opinion, one of the best actors working today. Her face is a tableau of emotions; she easily inhabits any role she takes on. It is Lane who carries this film from their departure in Cannes in Jaques’ antique Peugeot to their arrival in Paris, eventually. As an aside, Eleanor Coppola is the wife of Francis Ford Coppola and this, at the age of 80, is her first feature. My sense is that it is subtly autobiographical. Paris Can Wait. Directed by Eleanor Coppola. Romantic comedy starring Diane Lane, Alec Baldwin, Amand Viard. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG. Released 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/MAX/ Apple tv. articles.text: Music jokes were popular a few years ago. Do you remember this one: what is the difference between a violin and a fiddle? The violin has strings, and the fiddle has strangs. (It is better when you use a southern drawl.) But how about the difference between a violin and a mandolin? The violin emerged fully developed in northern Italy around 1500. The mandolin developed in southern Italy in the 1700s when steel strings were invented. Both instruments use pretty much the same left-hand technique, but the violin uses a bow, making it much more difficult to play. Both instruments can play the same repertoire. There was a fine concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, November 5, featuring the San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra. As usual, their program was very interesting. Who wouldn’t be interested by the title, “Napoli and the Revolution”? A successful concert must unite many aspects of music. First of all the playing needs to be good. Second, a good conductor unites all of the players to form a cogent interpretation. Third, the program should be well balanced, and that’s what we got in this concert. Another important aspect is The orchestra is tight-knit and so is the tone quality and a general sensitivity to nuance. All of these things reflect the inspiration of the conductor. These days, conductors like to make long speeches. Bocus doesn’t speak very much and lets the music speak for itself. His program notes were very informative. What a brilliant writer he is to go along with his mandolin virtuosity, elegant conducting, and superb musical arrangements. I would suggest that many of our local orchestra conductors should attend a San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra concert. They would learn a lot. articles.text: Safeway opened a new store in Piedmont on Highland Avenue in 1940. The store has a mission tile roof, large plate glass windows in front and a faux chimney with a weathervane. The weathervane is faintly visible in the sign. To blend in with Piedmont’s residential nature, the store was designed in a Spanish Colonial style with a mission tile roof and a faux chimney with a weathervane. Like many Safeway stores designed at the time, the building had decorative pilasters (columns) on the parking lot side of the building. Fentons Creamery on Piedmont Avenue is a former Safeway and still has pilasters on the parking lot side. When the Highland Avenue store opened, Safeway sold prime rib roasts for 23 cents per pound, ground coffee for 18 cents for a 1-pound can, and Wheaties for 10 cents a box. The store thrived until 1970 when the company closed it as being too small. Safeway was building large, bright, modern supermarkets with large Another rare photo shows Safeway and the Flying A gas station on Highland Avenue. parking lots, and the store was too small to be remodeled. It lacked the space to carry the expanded line of groceries. The large plate glass windows in front, seen in the 1940 sketch and photo, have been filled in and replaced with an arched entry on Highland for the bank. Grand Avenue businesses Residents living near Grand Avenue had a series of grocery stores dating back to at least 1914. The former A Mon Chateau saloon at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company. By 1922, it was the Del Monte Market. In the 1930s, George and Jacob Leisz ran the grocery store. Piggly Wiggly, a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store on the block at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand Avenues in the 1930s. Grocery stores operated at this corner of Grand and Linda Avenues until 1935.

articles.text: When addressing the history of central Piedmont, I would be remiss if I did not mention Piedmont’s Safeway store and other services. Hamby’s Market was the only grocery store in central Piedmont from 1915 to 1940. In addition to Hamby’s, Springman’s Pharmacy, and the Sweet Shop in the commercial center, Standard Oil operated a gas and service station by 1930. The expansion of Piedmont’s commercial center came after a long struggle. In 1929, the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance to allow businesses on Grand Avenue, on the west side from the city line to Linda Avenue, and on the east side from the city line to Fairview. Seven months later, voters turned down another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district in Piedmont on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. See more about the stores on Grand Avenue later in this article. More Stores For many years, the Piedmont City Council did “everything in its power to prevent the enlargement of the business district here,” according to news archives. Following a California Supreme Court decision in 1938, the Council reluctantly agreed to permit additional commercial development at Highland and Vista Avenues. In 1939, the Tidewater Oil Company built a gas station at the corner of Highland and Vista Avenues where Bank of America is currently located. It operated as the Flying A station into the late 1960s, when it became a Phillips 66 station. In 1940, Safeway Stores opened a new, modern supermarket at 333 Highland Avenue, occupying the space where both CitiBank and Mulberry’s Market are located. Officials at Safeway wanted to meet the wishes of the residents on the architecture and invited Piedmonters to an open meeting at City Hall to review and comment on the plans for the architecture of the new store. This rare photo shows the Chevron station and Highland Way, originally the Key System streetcar right of way. The narrow alley served Hamby’s Market for deliveries. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors group showed its generosity by donating a wide variety of toys to the annual “Toys for Tots program. The Piedmont Seniors group once again has shown its community spirit by giving back to those less fortunate. Over the years they have continued to support two important community service projects: Toys for Tots and Socks for Seniors. The “Toys for Tots” program is sponsored by the Piedmont Fire Department. Piedmont Seniors have generously supported this worthy cause for 27 years. New, unwrapped toys for children of all ages were donated by the Piedmont Seniors recently, as the Fire Department welcomes more donations during this holiday season. The Socks for Seniors project has been supported by the Piedmont Seniors for 10 years through the Lutheran Ministry of Oakland. In that time, the Seniors have donated hundreds of colorful holiday socks for underserved members of the East Bay community. The group wraps the socks in holiday paper. Often, they are the only gifts senior residents receive all year. The ministry serves underprivileged local nursing homes such as Trinity Health in Oakland. For further information on this nationwide project, see www. socksforseniors.com. Rev. Ned O’Donnell, who coordinates the efforts, has stated that if it were not for the generosity of the Piedmont Seniors, most of these nursing home residents would not receive any holiday gifts this season. In conjunction with the Lutheran Ministry, the Piedmont Seniors have added a new donor program. They gave dozens of books to ensure that the nursing home residents have ample library books to check out and enjoy. Often times the library carts are wheeled to the individual rooms for those who are not ambulatory. This location was convenient for Havens, as it was near Piedmont Park which he was developing. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road, and wanted to build his “Wildwood” estate on this land. The Havens family moved to the Randall house at the corner of Highland and Hazel and from there he could supervise the construction of “Wildwood.” The walkers entered Wildwood Gardens and made their way to 101, Havens’ former mansion. On the way they saw one of the many deer that have taken up residence in the area. Standing in front of 101 Wildwood Gardens, Meghan Bennett told its story. In 1906 Havens hired famous architect Bernard Maybeck to design a home with an oriental design including teakwood and fine carvings from India, China and Japan. It took two years to build. Lila Havens, the wife of Frank Havens was a student of Eastern religions, and the Eastern motifs can be seen in the house. Havens died suddenly on February 9, 1918 at his home from ptomaine (food) poisoning. His ashes are interred at Chapel of the Chimes on Piedmont Avenue. Frank C. Havens Curiously, the mansion had an unfinished and unused room to be used as a tomb. The walkers were curious about the room and if it is still there. Havens was in debt when he died, and Lila had to sell off his land to pay what was owed. The grounds of his estate were sold as the Wildwood Gardens Tract, and the current neighborhood is the result. The group made their way through the rest of Wildwood Gardens to the seldom visited Wistaria Way loop, then on to Woodland Way, Lafayette, Crocker, Lincoln, Sheridan, and Highland Avenue on the way back to town center. articles.text: The Oakland Zoo’s annual Glowfari adventure has begun. Oakland Zoo has opened its gates to nighttime visitors for Glowfari, its wildly popular illuminated lantern festival. Glowfari features hundreds of new, largerthan-life animal lanterns that will enchant guests of all ages. The experience of walking through the rows of glowing lanterns gives off a feeling of Disneyland’s Main Street Electric Parade. Each lantern tells part of the journey of wildlife, the importance of every species on the planet, and Oakland Zoo’s commitment to conservation. This year’s display features themes of the forests of North America with native wildlife, notably mountain lions and wolves. Lanterns also help draw attention to the Arctic, the Deep Ocean and animals of the Bayou. Guests can finish their nocturnal visit by riding on the Zoo’s train through the great red island of Madagascar, a wondrous world full of lemurs and chameleons. The winter wonderland also includes a visit from Santa who will be stationed (weather permitting) in the Rides Area from Friday to Sunday in November and every night in December to the 23rd from 6:00-8:45 p.m. Glowfari will continue in January on select days from 5:00- 9:00 p.m. Oakland Zoo will be open this month from November 18-22, 24-26, and 29-30. Oakland Zoo is located at 9777 Golf Links Rd in Oakland. Call 632-9525 for more information, or click on Oaklandzoo.org. A guest a Glowfari inspects a life-size polar bear lantern. Signs in the zoo help teach guests about each species and animal conservation efforts. ®

articles.text: As the holiday season approaches, many of us look forward to festive gatherings, delicious meals, and sweet treats. However, the fear of the notorious 8-lb. holiday weight gain can often cast a shadow over the joyous celebrations. The good news is that you can enjoy the holidays to the fullest without sacrificing your health and fitness. Here’s how to strike the right balance and savor the season guilt-free. One of the keys to avoiding holiday weight gain is practicing mindful indulgence. Rather than restricting yourself, allow yourself to enjoy your favorite holiday treats in moderation. Eat slowly, savor each bite, and listen to your body’s signals of fullness. By being mindful of your eating habits, you can avoid overindulging while still relishing the festive Don’t let the holiday hustle and bustle disrupt your regular exercise routine. Whether it’s a brisk walk after a hearty meal, a quick home workout, or a festive dance party, staying active can help counteract the effects of indulgent holiday feasts. Aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days of the week to keep your metabolism active and your energy levels high. Be sure to include family or friends for a nice walk. 3. Hydrate, Hydrate, Hydrate Often overlooked during the holiday season, staying hydrated is crucial for overall well-being. Sometimes, our bodies confuse thirst with hunger, leading to unnecessary snacking. Ensure you drink plenty of water throughout the day to stay hydrated and minimize the chances of overeating. 4. Choose Healthier Alternatives Get creative in the kitchen by incorporating healthier alternatives into your holiday meals. Experiment with lighter versions of your favorite recipes, substitute ingredients with healthier options, and focus on nutrient-dense foods. You can still enjoy delicious meals without compromising on taste or your waistline. 5. Prioritize Sleep A well-rested body is better equipped to handle the demands of the holiday season. Aim for 7-9 hours of quality sleep each night to support your overall health. A good night’s sleep can also help regulate your appetite and reduce the likelihood of mindless snacking. Minimize alcohol consumption as it can disrupt REM sleep. 6. Socialize and Move Instead of solely focusing on food during holiday gatherings, prioritize socializing and engaging in activities with friends and family. Plan active outings, organize games, or take a post-meal stroll together. By incorporating movement into your celebrations, you’ll not only burn calories but also create lasting memories. 7. However, the fear of the notorious 8-lb. holiday weight gain can often cast a shadow over the joyous celebrations. The good news is that you can enjoy the holidays to the fullest without sacrificing your health and fitness. Here’s how to strike the right balance and savor the season guilt-free. 1. Mindful Indulgence One of the keys to avoiding holiday weight gain is practicing mindful indulgence. Rather than restricting yourself, allow yourself to enjoy your favorite holiday treats in moderation. Eat slowly, savor each bite, and listen to your body’s signals of fullness. By being mindful of your eating habits, you can avoid overindulging while still relishing the festive flavors. 2. Stay Active Don’t let the holiday hustle and bustle disrupt your regular exercise routine. Whether it’s a brisk walk after a hearty meal, a quick home workout, or a festive dance party, staying active can help counteract the effects of indulgent holiday feasts. Aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days of the week to Son of Saul Continued from page 19 buried pain. He carries him not to the ovens but to a doctor (also a Jew) and asks him to hide the boy so that he might give him a proper Jewish burial and recite the Kaddish, the prayer for the dead. Avoid the Holiday 8-pound gain Balancing festive cheer and healthy living keep your metabolism active and your energy levels high. Be sure to include family or friends for a nice walk. 3. Hydrate, Hydrate, Hydrate Often overlooked during the holiday season, staying hydrated is crucial for overall well-being. Sometimes, our bodies confuse thirst with hunger, leading to unnecessary snacking. Ensure you drink plenty of water throughout the day to stay hydrated and minimize the chances of overeating. 4. Choose Healthier Alternatives Get creative in the kitchen by incorporating healthier alternatives into your holiday meals. Experiment with lighter versions of your favorite recipes, substitute ingredients with healthier options, and focus on nutrient-dense foods. You can still enjoy delicious meals without compromising on taste or your waistline. 5. Prioritize Sleep A well-rested body is better equipped to handle the demands of the holiday season. Aim for 7-9 hours of quality sleep each night to support your overall health. A good night’s sleep can also help regulate your appetite and reduce the likelihood of mindless snacking. Minimize alcohol consumption as it can disrupt REM sleep. 6. Socialize and Move Instead of solely focusing on food during holiday gatherings, prioritize socializing and engaging in activities with friends and family. Plan active outings, organize games, or take a post-meal stroll together. By incorporating movement into your celebrations, you’ll not only burn calories but also create lasting memories. 7. Set Realistic Goals Rather than aiming for perfection, set realistic and achievable health goals for the holiday season. This could include maintaining your current weight, staying active, or trying a new fitness routine. Having clear, attainable goals will help you stay focused and motivated. In conclusion, it’s entirely possible to revel in the joy of the holiday season without succumbing to the feared 8lb weight gain. By adopting a balanced approach to eating, staying active, and prioritizing overall well-being, you can create a holiday season that is both indulgent and health conscious. So, go ahead, savor the festive moments, and embrace a healthier you in the New Year. Happy Holidays. Contact Joe Phillips at eCoachJoe.com. articles.text: Early Monday morning, November 13, a residential burglary occurred at a house under construction on the 200 block of Greenbank Avenue. The suspects gained access to the rear of the house and forced their way in through the backdoor. The homeowner returned to the residence that morning to find several large items missing, including a new Samsung kitchen range, new TOTObrand toilet, miscellaneous tools, a paintball gun with the victim’s name etched onto it, and a Huusk brand knife. The loss was valued at $5,500 and damage to the residence of $6,000. Surveillance video from a neighbor showed that suspects used a white 2018 Ford F150 without a license plate. By using the city’s Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR), PPD officers were able to find the car’s license plate, and a records check revealed the car was registered to an address on Harrison Street in Oakland. Piedmont police observed the Ford pickup in the driveway at the Harrison Street address. A Samsung kitchen range was in the truck bed. The officer waited until the truck’s owners returned and then conducted an investigative stop, identifying the driver and passenger as Jose Lopez Escobar and Christian Briseno respectively. A search of Briseno revealed narcotics and narcotics equipment. Both occupants of the vehicle were detained, and a search of the Ford revealed stolen property in addition to three replica firearms and burglary tools. Both suspects were placed under arrest for burglary and possession of stolen property. Lopez Escobar was booked into Santa Rita Jail for burglary, possession of stolen property, possession of burglary tools, and driving with a suspended license. Briseno was booked into Santa Rita Jail for burglary, possession of stolen property, possession of drug paraphernalia, possession of meth, and an outstanding warrant. Piedmont Police Capt. Chris Monahan said that this arrest would not have been possible without the department’s ALPR cameras. “We did not have the plate of the truck from the neighbor’s residential video. The suspect’s vehicle was located in the ALPR system, which did have the plate, which ultimately led to their arrest,” said Monahan. articles.text: Piedmont Police received an automated license plate reader notification at 4:16 a.m. on Wednesday, November 15, for a stolen black Kia Sedona entering the city on Somerset Road. The vehicle was reported as stolen three days earlier from Cambridge Way in Piedmont. Officers located the vehicle minutes later on Somerset, but the driver of the Kia intentionally struck two patrol cars in an attempt to escape. One unoccupied patrol vehicle was pushed down Somerset before becoming lodged on the side of the roadway. Officers responded on foot and took both occupants of the Kia into custody. A search of the driver, Oscar Garcia, 36 years old from San Leandro, and the vehicle revealed burglary tools, narcotics, and stolen credit cards. The driver was arrested, and booked into Santa Rita Jail for assault with a deadly weapon, resisting police, vandalism, evading, possession of a stolen car, possession of stolen property, burglary tools and narcotics. A records check of the passenger, Diana Martinez Valencia, 36, showed that she was on a pretrial release with a full search clause. A search found narcotics and she was booked into Santa Rita Jail for failing to follow a court order and narcotics possession. A stolen Kia Sedona rammed two Piedmont Police cars on Somerset Road on Wednesday, November 15. 25th, clocking a 20:52.9. articles.text: Anticipation is building, and the energy is palpable as the city prepares for the upcoming Piedmont Turkey Trot, the second largest event in the city after the 4th of July Parade. With just over a week left until the 5K race on Thanksgiving morning, community members have been keen to share their favorite memories and to describe what makes the Trot special for so many Piedmonters. Jessica Freeman’s favorite memory of the Turkey Trot was when she and her husband, Crosby, both won the race in 2019. Freeman is an avid runner and longtime participant in the Turkey Trot. “I’ve been running it for eight or so years, almost consecutively. I think I missed one year outside of 2020,” said Freeman. Originally not a competitive runner, Freeman said that she started taking the sport more seriously when she and her husband started dating, slowly developing a competitive spirit and enjoying running the Turkey Trot with him. “And then in the last few years, I started getting more competitive and realizing that maybe I could win it,” said Freeman. Jessica Freeman fondly remembers the time she and her husband Crosby were crowned winners of the 2019 Piedmont Turkey Trot. It was the first time in the race’s history that a married couple had won the race.
articles.title: Community gears up for Turkey Trot

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team and coaches called it from Day 1. Since the very first practice, one thing was on the mind of the Highlanders – winning the North Coast Section title. After winning the league championship (Western Alameda County Conference) in 2021 and 2022, the school’s Golden Age of water polo came to its peak on Saturday, November 11. By defeating league rival Alameda 10-8, the Highlanders brought home the school’s first Division 2 NCS banner in the program’s first-ever finals appearance. Entering as the No. 4 ranked team, Piedmont and No. 3 Alameda marked the first time a school within Alameda County won the section title. After receiving a first-round bye, PHS dispatched No. 5 Newark Memorial 12-9 in the quarterfinals before upsetting No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals. It was Piedmont’s third consecutive appearance in the NCS semifinals, but its history had been a version of “twice a bridesmaid, never a bride.” During the regular season. Piedmont pulled out a last-second 10-9 victory over Alameda, but the Hornets went on to win the league title by beating Berkeley. Even so, the Highlanders were confident that this was the year to make history at a higher level. Just getting to the North Coast Section Finals was a major
articles.title: Highlanders make history, win school’s first NCS water polo title

articles.text: On Thursday, November 9, from 3:00 to 8:00 p.m. a long table with 241 chairs sat in the parking lot of Piedmont Community Hall as sympathetic members of the public walked solemnly from seat to seat. On the tables were the familiar items of Shabbat dinner – Manischewitz wine, sparkling grape juice, fine silverware and dishes – alongside more personal effects, like reading glasses and stuffed animals. Taped to each chair was a flyer bearing the face of a person being held hostage by members of the Hamas militant group, reading “BRING HIM HOME NOW” and “BRING HER HOME NOW.” The empty Shabbat table exhibit in the Community Hall parking lot was organized by members of the Piedmont Jewish community to raise awareness of the active hostage situation in the Israel-Hamas conflict. Each seat at the table symbolically represented one hostage in Hamas captivity. articles.text: Piedmont students, parents, teachers and community members braved the threat of rain Tuesday morning at 7:45 a.m. to honor the legacy of civil rights icon Ruby Bridges. Hundreds of Piedmonters showed up at Piedmont Park for Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day to learn about Bridges’ efforts as a six-year-old in 1960 to help end segregation in her New Orleans school by simply walking to school. Nationwide participation in the event has increased steadily since 2018 when fifth graders in South San Francisco decided to emulate Ruby and spotlight her bravery by walking to school in unity. “The event was amazing, we had an immense turnout,” said Jean Takazawa, PHS Director of Diversity Equity and Inclusion (DEI). pages.text: Volume 26, No. 5 Piedmont, California November 15, 2023 91¢ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ALL CITY EDITION ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont Community gears up for Turkey Trot By Matt Simons Anticipation is building, and the energy is palpable as the city prepares for the upcoming Piedmont Turkey Trot, the second largest event in the city after the 4th of July Parade. With just over a week left until the 5K race on Thanksgiving morning, community members have been keen to share their favorite memories and to describe what makes the Trot special for so many Piedmonters. Jessica Freeman’s favorite memory of the Turkey Trot was when she and her husband, Crosby, both won the race in 2019. Freeman is an avid runner and longtime participant in the Turkey Trot. “I’ve been running it for eight or so years, almost consecutively. I think I missed one year outside of 2020,” said Freeman. Originally not a competitive runner, Freeman said that she started taking the sport more seriously when she and her husband started dating, slowly developing a competitive spirit and enjoying running the Turkey Trot with him. “And then in the last few years, I started getting more competitive and realizing that maybe I could win it,” said Freeman. See Turkey Trot on page 5 Jessica Freeman fondly remembers the time she and her husband Crosby were crowned winners of the 2019 Piedmont Turkey Trot. It was the first time in the race’s history that a married couple had won the race. Staff Photo Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team and coaches celebrate after winning the school’s first North Coast Section championship after beating league rival Alameda 10-8 on November 11. See more photos on page 15. Highlanders make history, win school’s first NCS water polo title By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team and coaches called it from Day 1. Since the very first practice, one thing was on the mind of the Highlanders – winning the North Coast Section title. After winning the league championship (Western Alameda County Conference) in 2021 and 2022, the school’s Golden Age of water polo came to its peak on Saturday, November 11. By defeating league rival Alameda 10-8, the Highlanders brought home the school’s first Division 2 NCS banner in the program’s first-ever finals appearance. Entering as the No. 4 ranked team, Piedmont and No. 3 Alameda marked the first time a school within Alameda County won the section title. After receiving a first-round bye, PHS dispatched No. 5 Newark Memorial 12-9 in the quarterfinals before upsetting No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals. It was Piedmont’s third consecutive appearance in the NCS semifinals, but its history had been a version of “twice a bridesmaid, never a bride.” During the regular season. Piedmont pulled out a last-second 10-9 victory over Alameda, but the Hornets went on to win the league title by beating Berkeley. Even so, the Highlanders were confident that this was the year to make history at a higher level. On the tables were the familiar items of Shabbat dinner – Manischewitz wine, sparkling grape juice, fine silverware and dishes – alongside more personal effects, like reading glasses and stuffed animals. Taped to each chair was a flyer bearing the face of a person being held hostage by members of the Hamas militant group, reading “BRING HIM HOME NOW” and “BRING HER HOME NOW.” The empty Shabbat table exhibit in the Community Hall parking lot was organized by members of the Piedmont Jewish community to raise awareness of the active hostage situation in the Israel-Hamas conflict. Each seat at the table symbolically represented one hostage in Hamas captivity. Hundreds of Piedmonters showed up at Piedmont Park for Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day to learn about Bridges’ efforts as a six-year-old in 1960 to help end segregation in her New Orleans school by simply walking to school. Nationwide participation in the event has increased steadily since 2018 when fifth graders in South San Francisco decided to emulate Ruby and spotlight her bravery by walking to school in unity. “The event was amazing, we had an immense turnout,” said Jean Takazawa, PHS Director of Diversity Equity and Inclusion (DEI). articles.text: Designer Walter Hood hosted an event at the Alan Harvey Theater on Tuesday, November 7, to announce the beginning of the design phase for the newly announced Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial in Piedmont. The memorial would be located in Triangle Park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues, near the home the Dearings owned in the 1920s. Mayor Cavenaugh briefly discussed the history of the project, including the City Council’s decision to create a memorial at Triangle Park, the Park Commission’s discussions with relatives of Sidney and Irene Dearing, and the City’s selection of Hood Design Studio to create a fitting memorial. Walter Hood took attendees on a virtual tour of projects he has designed, discussing the creative process that led to each design. A few of the projects he highlighted included 7th Street Dancing Lights in West Oakland, the San Bernadino “Curtain of Courage” memorializing victims of the December 2015 domestic terrorist acts, the John Robinson Jr. Town Square in Arlington, VA, and the African Ancestors Memorial Garden at the International African American Museum in Charleston, SC. After the talk, Hood joined guests at a reception in the lobby. “Based on the audience’s reactions, the lecture was very well received,” said Yao Liu, a member of Hood Design Studio. “People seem to be looking forward to working with us on this project.” Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that he was “definitely impressed” by the presentation. “It really demonstrates Photo by Echa Schneider Walter Hood, designer and chair of UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning, gives a presentation at Alan Harvey Theater on the newly announced Sidney Dearing memorial. the level of expertise that Hood Design Studio brings to the project and to the city. We’re looking forward to working with them on next steps.” Hood Design Studio is an award-winning social art and design practice located in Oakland, CA, helmed by Creative Director Walter Hood, who readers may recognize as the current Chair of UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning. Among other things accolades, Hood is a recipient of the 2017 Academy of Arts and Letters Architecture Award, 2019 Knight Public Spaces Fellowship, 2019 MacArthur Fellowship (the “Genius Grant”), 2019 Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, and the 2021 recipient of the Architectural Leagues’ President’s Medal. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Matt Simons Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Micah Temple (intern) Clea Villaluz (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Camille Parker was born Camille Jabbie (pronounced JayBee) on November 9, 1926 in Amite, Louisiana. She recently died at her home in Castro Valley. The last lines of the obituary written by her son read, “Camille and Warren (her husband) enjoyed their children, grand-children and great grand-children. She was called home on September 1, 2023 at 96 years old after a long life well lived.” At her burial I built her eulogy around three words. Smile, Sunshine and Supplication. Camille had a beautiful, light-up-theroom, brighten your day smile. When she smiled the world instantly became a better place. For many years Camille was the Sunshine Chairperson of her Sunday School Class. This meant she sent get well-cards, birthday cards and thinking-of-you cards. It meant she called those who were absent, listened to those who were down, and comforted those who were grieving. It was her ministry to be a ray of sunshine – and she shined brightly. Supplication is to offer prayers for the well-being of others. There are many who were greatly helped by the knowledge that Camille was praying on their behalf. Her supplication was diligent, consistent and heartfelt. When Camille said, “I will pray for you,” it was more than a nicety – it was a promise. articles.text: Photos by Anne Hauss Davies Piedmont Scouts in Troop 4 help load donated food onto a truck during the annual Scouting for Food Drive. Pictured are: (front) Rohan Seshan (left), Niko Wolff, Felix Kansal; (back) Jerry Yu, Scoutmaster Arvind Seshan, Naomi Treichler, Joelle Frechette, and Assistant Scoutmaster Dante Rodriguez. On Saturday, November 11 at 8:30 AM, a truck from the Alameda County Community Food Bank lumbered into the parking lot at Community Hall. A half hour later a very busy day began, as Piedmont Scouts went door to door throughout the city as part of their annual Scouting for Food drive. Just like every year, the Scouts tackled the herculean task through a mixture of meticulous planning and selfless teamwork. Last week Piedmont Cub Scouts placed door hanger reminders on houses throughout the city, and on Saturday the older Scouts picked up bags of donated food city-wide. “It was a big task,” said Anne Hauss Davies, a member of the Piedmont Council Executive Board and chair for Scouting for Food. “Some troops had difficulty recruiting enough Scouts given the holiday weekend but thankfully other troops pitched in and we finished up just after noon.” Hauss Davies said that the Food Bank’s truck driver estimated the Scouts collected about 8,000 pounds of food, far more than last year’s total of 7,000 pounds. In addition, the Scouting for Food virtual food drive has raised about $3,500 in donations so far. “1 in 5 people in Alameda County are food insecure, and Piedmont has a lot to offer the community. The Food Bank is a wonderful avenue for Piedmont to give because its great purchasing power means they will be able to buy food at prices unavailable to other organizations. Basically, our money will go a lot farther at the food bank.” Scouting for Food’s virtual food drive is open until Thursday, November 30. articles.text: Piedmonters gearing up for the Christmas season will be happy to know that the Piedmont Scout Council’s Christmas tree Lot will be opening on Saturday, November 25 in the parking lot of Coaches Field. Community members looking to add a festive touch to their homes this holiday season will be able to buy trees, wreaths, garlands, tree stands, and mistletoe from the lot for pick-up and delivery. The tree Lot is also accepting online pre-orders at www.scouttreelot.org. Delivery service will be available throughout Piedmont and select neighborhoods in Oakland beginning the weekend of November 25. “I think it’s just one of those holiday traditions that people support because we’re a good cause,” said Tom Smegal, head of the tree lot volunteer committee. This will be his fourth year running the tree lot, although Smegal has been volunteering there since he was a scout himself. “The folks that we’re supporting are the youth programs for our scouts, our Cub Scouts, our venturing clubs, the Piedmont Community Service Crew, and others. It’s a good cause.” Smegal also asserted that there is something special about buying your tree from a local lot like their own. “When you’re up there at the tree lot, picking out a tree and have a fourth grader in a Cub Scout uniform that’s helping you pick out that 10-foot tree, it’s a fun experience – almost reminiscent of when you were a child. It’s the kind of thing that brings together families and creates family memories,” said Smegal. The Scout Tree Lot sells three kinds of trees: Noble firs, which are their most popular, tend to have a lot of branch definition while maintaining a delightfully bushy shape; Silver tips, which are taller and thinner and great for hanging large amounts of ornaments; and Douglas firs, the easiest to care for. They have a sweet fragrance to their needles when crushed. The Scout Tree Lot has been highly successful in previous years. In 2022, sales were high, generating as much as $50,000 on its opening weekend with an additional $30,000 in online sales before opening day. The tree lot will be open until the third weekend in December or until the lot sells out its entire stock. “Whichever comes first,” said Smegal. “Although, we usually sell out in mid-December.” Staff Photo Piedmont Community Service Crew members are shown volunteering at last year’s Piedmont Scout Tree Lot: Dave Feinberg (left), Ashley Ronen, PCSC Advisor Ken Li, Samantha Ronen, Ishaia Goldberg-Berman, Bruno Banuelos, Kyra Dang, and Holland Feinberg. “When I was an executive,I used to carry my lunch in a fancy briefcase, too.”

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is currently taking donations through December 23 for its annual toy drive. Piedmont residents looking to help local families in need can contribute one or more new, unwrapped toys to donation bins at the Piedmont Fire Station to make sure everyone in the area has a gift to open this holiday season. Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County, and any toys donated before December 8 will be distributed through the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated on or after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Toy Donation bins will remain at the Fire Department at 120 Vista Avenue through December 23.
articles.title: Annual Toys for Tots drive continues at Fire Station

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is pleased to invite the community to its annual Holiday Luncheon on Friday, December 1 at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. The guest speaker is former Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf, whose talk begins at 11 a.m. followed by a lunch from Market Hall. As an inf luential mayor, Schaaf led initiatives to make the city more resilient and equitable, and broke records in housing production, violence prevention, and road repair. She founded the non-profit Oakland Promise in 2016. By 2023 it had a $15 million annual budget and $50 million endowment raised by Schaaf. These funds are a commitment to Oakland’s next generation of children toward higher educational funding for two= or four-year college degrees or vocational trade certificates. Schaaf holds a fellowship with Mayors for a Guaranteed Income and mow teaches at the Goldman School of Public Policy at UC Berkeley. Former Oakland mayor Libby Schaaf is the guest speaker at the annual Holiday Luncheon hosted by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Don’t miss this unique opportunity as Schaaf shares perspectives about her public service and her current passions, followed by a brief Q&A. Tickets are $45 for members and $50 for non-members for this fundraising event for the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Space is limited. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, November 15, 2023 Local Items Annual Toys for Tots drive continues at Fire Station By Matt Simons The Piedmont Fire Department is currently taking donations through December 23 for its annual toy drive. Piedmont residents looking to help local families in need can contribute one or more new, unwrapped toys to donation bins at the Piedmont Fire Station to make sure everyone in the area has a gift to open this holiday season. Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County, and any toys donated before December 8 will be distributed through the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated on or after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Toy Donation bins will remain at the Fire Department at 120 Vista Avenue through December 23. articles.text: Community members can expect a few changes to their parks in the near future. Piedmont’s Public Works Department has announced it will be replacing a footbridge at the base of Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park due to damage suffered during winter storms last year. Public Works is also adding an ADA-accessible ramp in Dracena Park. Construction is expected for both projects to begin in February 2024. “Both handrails have fallen off on both sides of the footbridge,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “The bridge is also experiencing significant rot. Nails have fallen off, and planks have rotted off. The storm was the final thing that brought it down, but it was already in poor shape.” Gonzales said that despite the shape of the bridge, it does not pose an active danger to walkers in the park. “However, the time to fix it completely is now in order to avoid closure in the future,” said Gonzales. Gonzales also addressed the need for an ADA-compliant access pathway in Dracena Park. “The pathway would be a ramp leading from what we call Lower Dracena into Upper Dracena. There’s no accessible pathway that leads there right now. This would be the only ADA-compliant access point we’d have in Dracena Park,” said Gonzales. Staff Photo The footbridge in Piedmont Park sustained significant damage during a storm last winter.
articles.title: New footbridge for Piedmont Park, ADA ramp coming to Dracena Park

articles.text: The Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT), the teachers union, is hosting an informational Community Forum tonight, November 15, on Zoom to explain what it means for teachers to be at an impasse with the district. APT President Dr. Elise Marks will also discuss the financial issues and topics still open in contract negotiations, and answer questions. Community members who want to participate in the forum must first register for the event by scanning the QR code or visiting Zoom.us/meeting/register/tZIkdeGurTkjHNVRb7cL3VHMHnySKNMYOfFg#/registration The Forum will last an hour, from 6:30-7:30 p.m. APT will start with a presentation with charts and data to explain their position on salary and benefits, and then explain what happens during an impasse. “We’ll be collecting questions from community members and answering as many as we can live. After the presentation, To participate in tonight’s Zoom meeting register by opening your camera app, pointing it at the QR code and then clicking the link to register. we’ll be making the slide deck available on our website and will also publish an FAQ based on the questions from the forum,” explained Marks. After negotiations with new school Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and PUSD stalled, APT filled a “Request for Impasse Determination/Appointment of Mediator” form with the Public Employment Relations Board (PERB). From there, a state mediator may be assigned to assist in resolving matters between the district and the teachers’ union. If a mediator is unable to help both parties reach an agreement, either party may request a three-person fact-finding panel to analyze the situation. Piedmont teachers have been wearing their red union APT t-shirts every Tuesday to school make their plight visible. They have even taken their message to the street, by holding up signs in front of their schools when students arrive in the morning. Piedmont teachers are asking for a 8.22% salary increase for the current school year to keep up with the state’s Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA). The district’s initial counter-offer was for a 2% increase next year, then a 4% increase in 2024-25 and a 3% raise in 2025-26.

articles.text: More than meets the rye Bread – in all its forms – is a common food in many households. There are several methods to make bread but a common one involves the use of yeast. The process of making bread with yeast is a cool way to examine and experience science at home – not to mention that it’s delicious. What you knead to know Bread is a type of food that has existed throughout human history. Across different cultures bread appears in many different shapes and names. For example, flatbread is one of the oldest forms of bread. Versions of flatbread have existed in the Middle East, Africa, Europe, and beyond for thousands of years. Like most types of bread, flatbread is made with simple ingredients such as flour, milk or water, and salt. However, other kinds of bread use ingredients such as yeast to create bread that is fluffier and softer than flatbread. A feast for yeast So, what exactly is yeast and what is its function in the process of making bread? Yeast is defined as a single-cell, fungal microorganism, which basically means it is a very small form of life – like moss or mold. There are different types of yeast that exist around us, but the yeast that is added to bread is known simply as baker’s yeast. Bread is an example of how science is all around us Baker’s yeast often comes in a dried form and is added to dough to make it rise and create bread with an airy texture. In order to make bread rise, dried yeast first needs two important things: warmth and sugar. Yeast needs warmth in order for it to do its job in bread. Warm water is often used with dried yeast to raise it to a temperature where it can work well. Also, just like all living things, yeast needs food in order to function – specifically sugar. In bread dough, there are lots of sugars for the yeast to eat – in the flour and any other added sugars. As it eats the sugar, yeast creates a chemical called carbon dioxide which creates many small air bubbles in bread dough and causes it to rise. This process is called fermentation. Once the fermentation process is completed, the dough can go into the oven to bake. The yeast that was used in the dough creates an airy and light texture in the baked bread – a tasty result thanks to science. Last but not yeast! You may have thought that there isn’t much science in bread, but without chemical or biological reactions the loaf of bread on your dinner table would look a lot different. Bread is just another small example of how science is all around us – even in places we would least expect it. Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement, located in the Oakland hills. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Science is all around us, especially on the holidays

A lot of people dream of doing such work, but at later points in their life,” said sophomore Meher Bachher, an Affinity Mentor at Piedmont High. Beach Principal Anna Valva also held assemblies on November 13 to explain to each Beach student the importance of Ruby’s efforts and how to honor them. “On November 14, we gathered [on the playground] for coffee and donuts and to learn more about Ruby Bridges,” explained Beach parent Tam Bui. “When the school bell rang, the entire school commemorated Ruby Bridges Day by walking around the blacktop before entering class.” Piedmont schools joined thousands of other schools across the country to honor the desegregation that Ruby sparked 63 years ago. articles.text: Foreign language classes at Piedmont High School displayed their talents in the amphitheater on Monday, November 13, for the World Language Singing Competition. Each foreign language class performed a song they learned in their target language, and engaged in friendly competition with other French, Mandarin and Spanish language students. Period 7 Honors Spanish 4 students ended their performance by tossing roses and flower petals in the air. Staff Photos Eleventh grader Clare Weiss, a member of the All-State Jazz Choir, led her class, Honors Spanish 4, with a remarkable solo. Students and faculty members enjoyed the warm mid-November weather on November 13 for outdoor singing. Period 7 Mandarin class students strike poses at the end of their song and dance. Period 6, AP Chinese punctuated notes in their song with the snapping sound of opening red fans. Period 6 AP Spanish’s song and dance narrowly beat out AP Chinese to win the period. Each song and dance began with an introduction of the class to a large crowd on hand. Many students were allowed out of class to see the performances, which included choreography, matching outfits, and instrumental music. The competition’s origin can be traced back to 2017 when PHS French teacher Christele David, brought her French classes to other foreign language classrooms to serenade them with French carols. Since then, the grassroots activity has expanded into an all-day singing competition, with roughly three foreign language classes competing with one another every hour.

articles.text: On the first weekend in November, 15 Scouts and parents from Piedmont’s Troop 1 embarked on an overnight kayaking trip on Tomales Bay. Carrying all of their tents and camping supplies in two-person kayaks, the Scouts set off on a five-mile journey, paddling along the western side of Tomales Bay to their campsite. On the journey the Scouts saw multiple stingrays, many seals, a few otters, and hundreds of jellyfish – some of which even ended up in the kayaks. The weather was wet and damp, but the Scouts enjoyed a campfire and storytelling as night fell. A few Scouts and adults kayaked late at night to see bioluminescence – a phenomenon visible on Tomales Bay only on moonless nights in the late summer and early fall. It is a time when microorganisms give off light if they are physically disturbed. The Scouts formed eerie, glowing white clouds by agitating the water with a paddle. Rain the next morning didn’t dampen their spirits as they packed their supplies and prepared for the trip home. The Scouts powered through and, wet and tired, they were greeted by a rainbow upon arriving at the kayak rental facility. Overall, Troop 1 enjoyed their kayaking adventure and, despite some challenges, finished with their Scout spirit shining through. Theodore Cost is a member of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 1. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football season came to an end on Friday, November 10, after falling to No. 4 Alhambra 49-14 in the first round of the Division 5 North Coast Section playoffs. Despite the loss, this year marked the rebirth of the school’s storied 100-year football program at PHS. With a roster of only 17 players, the team finished with a 7-4 overall record, and won its first Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline title since 2015, and first NCS appearance Some predicted the team would not be able to complete its 10-game season with so few play- “Playoffs with football is always something where experience becomes a factor, Alhambra had 18 seniors and we had one senior on the field. But we had opportunities. No one picked us to be in the playoffs, let alone win a league title. We feel [that we’re] ahead of schedule. It’s terrible to lose, but this helps us grow, and we can be great with another year of experience,” reflected coach Jordan Seiden. With just three seniors on the roster – Derek Schleuning, Brayden Hong, and Emmett Maxwell – Piedmont fielded a young and talented group. When Hong and Maxwell went down with season-ending injuries, the team had to dig even deeper to perform well. On top of that, Piedmont was unable to play or practice on its field, due to the school district scheduling the returfing and replacement of the irrigation system at Witter Field during the summer and fall, and now into early 2024. Practices were held on the school’s baseball diamond. “Not having a field was kind of a blessing in disguise. It brought us all closer together and made us a strong team,’ said Schleuning. “Four years ago when we went undefeated, and we didn’t have a JV, I was pulled up to varsity and Sam Shelby runs into the end zone for a touchdown reception against Staff Photos Piedmont’s football season ended with a loss to Alhambra in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs. didn’t play at all. Then the next year, I got injured for most of the season. Then as a junior, our varsity year got cut short, so this season really meant a lot to me to watch this program grow. Now that we’re winning, we’re seeing more people come out and participate, it’s great for the program.” “No one really thought we’d be in this position and we continued to prove people wrong. We were projected to go 0-10 by some media. But we knew what we had; we pushed through and relied on each other,” said junior quarterback Markos Lagios. The team was aided by breakthrough performances. Junior Sam Shelby emerged as a game-breaking receiver and return specialist. Fullback Tommy Ashton is a bruising running back and linebacker, junior Jordan Alemania is a talented edge and interior rusher, and there’s a quality receiving core in Shelby, Brandon Dicke, and Albert Bellingrath. Meanwhile, Shelby, Miguel Long, and Vince Arbit make a solid defensive backfield. “Everyone in this group knew how important it was to improve. We knew what we were capable of. articles.text: Piedmont High’s No. 3 seeded girls’ tennis team saw its season come to an end on Saturday, November 11 with a 5-2 loss to eventual champions University at Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. On the road to the semifinals, they defeated No. 11 College Prep 6-1 on Thursday, November 9 at home, and defeated No. 14 Marin Catholic 7-0 in the first round two days earlier. The team compiled a 13-8 record this fall. They will lose No. 1 singles Tanya Knonova, doubles starter Cecilia DeFazio, and singles player Ellie Broscow to graduation next spring, but have a strong cast of returners with Emma Eisemon, Kate Jumper, Arianna Kortum, Carolina Romanczuk, Samantha Huyhn, and Maddie Tran. “During the offseason, Maddie (Tran) and I trained really hard to get a spot on varsity. It felt like the hard work paid off. I’m proud to be on varsity as a sophomore, and I’m surprised how much success Maddie and I had as a pair this season,” said Huyhn. 5-2 to University The Red Devils went on to win the NCS title by defeating O’Dowd, giving University its second consecutive Div. 2 NCS title. Piedmont won two of four singles matches but lost all three doubles matches. In singles, Kononova defeated Avery Fringer in straight sets at the top spot, 6-4, 6-2. Also winning was Kortum at No. 4 in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4. Kate Jumper lost to Allison Conner at Piedmont’s clinching fourth victory was at No. 2 doubles with Huyhn and Tran, defeating Makeda Faxio and Daphne Green in three sets 6-3, 6-7 (8-6), 6-4. “The adrenaline was flowing in the last game, especially at match point. We had an exciting match point with a lot of volleys and exchanges,” said Huyhn. “It was really back and forth. It was a tough match, but we just tried our best and tried to have fun,” added Tran. DeFazio and Eisemon won 6-2, 7-5 over College Prep’s top pair of Adele Beamer and Leah Luchansky. Kononova finished the night with a 7-5, 6-0 win over Angela Wang.
