articles.text: From first-time racket holders to remarkable wins, Piedmont’s JV Tennis Team has had an extraordinary season, culminating with the 9th annual Western Alameda County Conference Junior Varsity Jamboree on Saturday, October 28 at Castro Valley High School. The Highlanders finished second of eight schools in team competition with a 22-12 overall record in the tournament. Piedmont had the best record in performances by its single matches, winning 15 of 20 matches. Faith Chin won the singles bracket, defeating Bishop O’Dowd’s Sonja Abid in a hard-earned, 7-6 (7-5) tiebreaker victory. Hallie Burden came away with a decisive third-place win over O’Dowd’s Penny Wong, 6-2. The JV tennis team’s journey this season was more than just wins and losses; it was about building lasting friendships, pushing boundaries, and nurturing a love for the game. The young athletes displayed unwavering dedication, sportsmanship, and teamwork. Piedmont placed second at the WACC JV Jamboree on October 28. Pictured are: (front) Emma Chan (left), Jordan Kim, Nuala Price, Sparrow Lieu, Andrea Boothby, Sarayah Lewis; (back) Coach Sarah Spruch, Faith Chin, Katia Davis, Amelia Addington, Simran Titan, Kaysa Benson, Lily Colbert, Amelia Oldrin, Coach David McCaig. Not pictured: Elliana Neel, Hallie Burden.

articles.text: Olympic rower Scott Gault is inducted into the Olympic Club Hall of Fame in San Francisco. On October 12, Piedmont High alum Scott Gault was inducted into the Olympic Club Hall of Fame in San Francisco. At Piedmont High he played football, basketball and golf, but his world changed when he began rowing with the Oakland Stokes in his senior year. It led him to the University of Washington, where he spent four years in one of the nation’s premier rowing programs, while earning a degree in Industrial Engineering. After college, he joined the U.S. national team and helped bring home the gold medal in the men’s quadruple sculls at the 2008 Rowing World Cup in Lucerne, Switzerland. In 2008 he finished 5th in the Beijing Olympic Games. Gault eventually switched events to the men’s coxless four and qualified for the 2012 Olympic team. In the 2012 Olympics in London, he and his teammates had never competed together internationally, but they won the Bronze Medal, missing the gold by 3.5 seconds. Gault now spends his time on his other passions. He has played for more than a decade in the Olympic Club basketball league. He is also a pilot, cyclist and skier. He is raising his family in Marin County and currently a Senior Vice President at Newfront Insurance specializing in aviation insurance. Scott Gault with niece Henley Azad, who was named in his honor when she was born on opening night of the London Olympics.

articles.text: accomplishment for Piedmont. The school’s water polo team had never reached the finals according to records dating back to 1995. After advancing to the semifinals the past two years, any onlooker could tell this year’s team was made of championship quality, demonstrated last weekend by Piedmont’s upset of No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals, and 10-8 against No. 3 Alameda in the title game. As the clock struck zero against the Alameda Hornets, Finn Burke dragged coach Rik Krumins into the pool, while members of the PHS student rooting section jumped in the water to celebrate with their classmates. “It means everything. It’s such an accomplishment for this senior class, this program overall, all the guys that played before us, and even the girls’ team just from the excitement around the pool. This is really what we needed; I think the win over Marin Academy was that obstacle we were aching to get by,” said coach Krumins. “I mentioned at the beginning of the season that this was our goal, so for it to come true is such an accomplishment. I’m so proud of them,” he added. And they did it all without a pool to call home. The last team to play its games in a Piedmont pool was four years ago, 2019, when Patrick Conn and Henry Saunders made history as the school’s all-time leading scorer and assister. They led PHS to the North Coast Section semifinals in 2018, and since then Piedmont won the Western Alameda County Conference title in 2021 and 2022. And now the ultimate objective – the NCS championship. “It comes down to the boys; their willingness to do offseason training, play club water polo, and then commit to what John Savage and I ask as coaches. From having Patrick, Henry, Max Wagener, and all those players, we’re always looking for a little more and for what’s next. We’re hoping this helps build the next 10 years of this program, there’s a lot of excitement,” said Krumins. Longtime head coach John Savage, a science teacher at Piedmont High, stepped down from the lead job last year, enabling Krumins to take over. Savage attended and played for PHS from 2002-2005 before returning as a coach in 2012, becoming the leader of water polo’s ascent in the process. “We went 6-13 in my first year and our only goal was to make the North Coast [post-season] playoffs. Then our goal became to win league, then our goals became to go further and further. The team has done everything we have asked. They deserve all the credit,” said Savage. It was another big-game performance by senior Declan Linnane, who led with six goals. He had three goals in their semifinals win over Marin Academy and two goals in the quarterfinals over No. 5 Newark Memorial. “It’s special, especially to have two Alameda County teams here in the finals. As the clock struck zero against the Alameda Hornets, Finn Burke dragged coach Rik Krumins into the pool, while members of the PHS student rooting section jumped in the water to celebrate with their classmates. “It means everything. It’s such an accomplishment for this senior class, this program overall, all the guys that played before us, and even the girls’ team just from the excitement around the pool. This is really what we needed; I think the win over Marin Academy was that obstacle we were aching to get by,” said coach Krumins. “I mentioned at the beginning of the season that this was our goal, so for it to come true is such an accomplishment. I’m so proud of them,” he added. And they did it all without a pool to call home. articles.text: A new exhibit at San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora featuring work by local artist Salimatu Amabebe is on view now through December 10. The exhibition, entitled SON, is Amabebe’s first solo museum exhibit and is co-curated by the artist and Key Jo Lee, Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs at MoAD. A mabebe is a Niger ian-American chef and multimedia artist based in Oakland. He is the founder and director of “Black Feast,” a culinary event that celebrates Black artists and writers through food. His work primarily focuses on the intersection of food and art, drawing from family memories, Nigerian recipes and Black culinary history. In SON, the artist explores the relationship between home, memory, and metamorphosis by transforming an area of the museum with haunting red hues. Amabebe’s solo exhibition is the third of MoAD’s Emerging Artists Program series. Visit https://www.moadsf. org/exhibitions/salimatu-amabebe-grass to learn more. The works of artist Salimatu Amabebe are now on view at the Museum of African Diaspora.
articles.title: Salimatu Amabebe exhibit at MoAD on view through Dec. 10

articles.text: December tickets for San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Infinite Love, the highly anticipated and widely popular exhibition by artist Yayoi Kusama, are on sale now. The vibrant and immersive exhibition opened in October and tickets sold fast, but the museum is now offering tickets to visit in December. January tickets will be released December 5 for members and December 7 to the general public. Yayoi Kusama is one of the most iconic and globally celebrated artists working today, known for her use of mirrors and bright colors. The artist’s first solo presentation in Northern California encompasses two infinity mirror rooms in the museum, including her newest room, Dreaming of Earth’s Sphericity, I Would Offer My Love (2023), a kaleidoscope color and light. Love is Calling (2013) is the second room in the presentation and one of Kusama’s largest and most immersive works. The exhibition features a darkened environment lit up by vividly colored inflatable forms that extend from the floor and ceiling, accompanied by the sound of the artist reciting a poem about love. All tickets for Kusama exhibitions are timed. Visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ yayoi-kusama-infinite-love/ to learn more.
articles.title: Yayoi Kusama exhibit now on view at SF MOMA

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) curators and staff will host a gallery chat this Saturday, November 18, between 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. The event is designed to mimic a guided tour but with an opportunity to chat with and ask questions of the museum’s curators. The museum is encouraging meaningful conversations and fresh interpretations to connect with the artwork, artifacts, and stories in our galleries. Visitors may view and discuss with staff the museum’s newest exhibition, Por el Pueblo: The Legacy and Influence of Malaquías Montoya, which opened last month in the museum’s Great Hall. Montoya often uses political imagery in his work and has produced substantial art centered around the issue of immigration. His posters, graphic prints, and murals often highlighted political and social justice issues, and have helped define the Chicano identity and culture for nearly fifty years. Curators will be onsite on Saturday afternoon to answer questions about this important body of work. Gallery chats will take place every Saturday from 1 to 3 p.m. and are included with Museum and Special Exhibition admission. No reservation necessary. Visit https://museumca.org/ event/gallery-chats-at-omcanov-18/ to learn more about this new OMCA feature. Oakland Museum curators and staff will be onsite every Saturday between 1 and 3 p.m.
articles.title: Oakland Museum curators to host gallery chat on Sat.

articles.text: Shotguns Players’ newest Tony Award-winning production Hedwig and the Angry Inch is playing onstage at the Ashby Theatre in Berkeley now through December 17. Written by John Cameron Mitchell and directed by Richard Mosqueda, the play is adapted from the off-Broadway theater hit of the same name, later made into a movie in 2001. Hedwig and the Angry Inch follows German emigrant Hedwig, who is the victim of a botched sex-change operation. The current adaptation takes place in a seedy dive bar in Berkeley. Hedwig is an international song stylist and East German rock ‘n’ roll goddess. This outrageous play is performed by Pangaea Colter in the form of a rock gig and stand-up comedy routine backed by a hard-rocking band. Mosqueda said the inspiration came from their first viewing of the film back in a high school English class. “A crudely drawn animation played on the screen detailing a story about the origin of humans, Pangaea Colter plays the role of Hedwig in the Shotgun Players production of Hedwig and the Angry Inch. originally three genders, who were once attached and then separated, now looking for the other half. An androgynous blonde bombshell appeared on the screen wailing to the heavens. I was glued to the television. And as a deeply closeted queer kid, I felt seen, if only for a moment,” Mosqueda said. Lyrics and music are by Stephen Trask. To view showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/Online/default. asp.
articles.title: Hedwig and the Angry Inch onstage at Shotgun Players

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts marks the 11th year of its Berkeley Symphony and Friends chamber music series with a concert on Sunday, November 19 at 4 p.m. Titled California Connections, the concert is part of the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, and will weave the music of Berkeley composers with those they have mentored and influenced in their work. The performance will embrace the healing sounds of Andean folk music through Gabriela Lena Frank’s Kanto Kechua No. 2 and uncover the majestic beauty of the Eastern Sierra Mountains in Ben Shirley’s High Sierra Sonata. Berkeley High School Alum Anaís Azul’s Cascades and Canyons will transport audiences through the serenity and challenges of nature, while Gabriella Smith’s Carrot Revolution inspires new perspectives through historical references. Also being performed are selections from John Adams’s rhythmic Book of Alleged Dances. Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510.841.2800. The concert will be performed by Julia Churchill, violin; Sarah Elert, violin; Alexandra Simpson, viola; Michael Graham, cello; Michel Taddei, double bass; Stacey Pelinka, flute; Roman Fukshansky, clarinet; and Britton Day, piano. The concert is part of over 100 performances in California through the Festival of New Music from November 3 to 19.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Music concert at PCA on Nov. 19

articles.text: Legacy of Love, a 2-part series of Retro and Mid-Century Jewelry from the collections of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor (1935-1960s) will be held at Piedmont Center for the Arts starting on December 8. Jewelry from the 1930s-1960s is bold, colorful and extravagant. The Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor each amassed what are considered today to be the best collections of jewelry from the 20th century. They both had amazing taste and a passion for important gemstones and innovative and avant-garde design. As the majority of their collections were gifts from their husbands, these collections are truly legacies of love. Both women led extraordinary lives that were very public. They were often vilified, criticized and at certain points in their lives portrayed as “the most hated women in the world” by the press. Prince of Wales Brooch, 1935 Wallis Simpson and Elizabeth Taylor The lectures by Piedmont resident and gemologist Sacha Grippando will examine these two exceptional ladies, their fascinating and scandalous lives, and of course their fabulous jewelry. The first of two parts, on Friday, December 8, will explore in depth the jewelry collection of Wallis Simpson, Duchess of Windsor. The second part is scheduled for Thursday evening, February 1, 2024. Both lectures will begin at 6 p.m. and will last a little more than one hour, to be followed by light refreshments. Donations are encouraged, and both events are open to all.
articles.title: Sacha Grippando presents A Legacy of Love at PCA

articles.text: and he begins peeling the onion and so the film builds with a quiet, dark intensity. Just a word about the cast: it’s remarkable. Pierce Brosnan delivers a top-drawer performance, as does Olivia Williams as his wife. Tom Wilkinson, always superb, portrays an Ivy League professor with a hidden past. And there is the inestimable Eli Wallach in a cameo role as a hermit living on the Vineyard. Roman Polanski, 76, now resides in Switzerland under house arrest while a request by the U.S. for his extradition works its way through the courts. He is accused of molesting a 13-year-old girl in Los Angeles some thirty years ago and has been living as a fugitive in Europe ever since. There is something of his ordeal in the character of the P.M.: besieged, accused, and deserted by old friends. Perhaps for Polanski, “The Ghost Writer” is more personal than any before, with the exception, perhaps, of The Pianist It was extraordinary. The Ghost Writer. Directed by Roman Polanski. articles.text: Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, likely the best-known Spanish filmmaker of the last three decades. His most memorable film, at least in the U.S., was Volver (Return), and starred, as does Broken Embraces, Penelope Cruz, often referred to as Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and even prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the complex characters. Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. Gradually she is pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity and the film takes on a noirish tone as it moves from 2008 to 1994 in revealing flashbacks. The film is also completely taken with the transformative face of Elena/Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like a Vogue layout, so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached. as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance. It is perhaps because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from the fact that there is a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices and the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the filmgoer is not interested in knowing anything about the interior motivations of the characters. It is a missed opportunity by Almodovar to build intimacy with the audience; little is revealed. Even when the film is briefly set on two islands, Ibiza and Lanzarotte, Almodovar seems inclined only to use the lush scenery as a mere backdrop for Elena and her lover, Harry Cain (Luis Homar) and not as an extension of the heat of their relationship. If you love movies and have followed the career of Pedro Almodovar then Broken Embraces is a film not to be missed. Or if you simply love movies and are tempted to see a film by an artist like Almodovar who consistently conveys the elusiveness inherent in exploring the human condition. Broken Embraces. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. Starring Penelope Cruz, Luis Homar, Lola Duenas, Blanca Portillo and Angela Molina. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated R. Released 2009. articles.text: house on Martha’s Vineyard – the month is January, it’s cold, the sky and ocean a mix of wintry slate and teal, rain falling constantly. Everything feels ominous and unsettling; exactly why is, at first, unclear. Sitting in front of floor to ceiling windows, looking out at the sand dunes, the wind blowing unrelentingly, the Ghost watches a gardener sweeping leaves on a long wooden walkway, the wind blowing away his best efforts, a metaphor for what he is about to experience as he looks at 600 some pages of banal manuscript (the first draft has already been written; however, the first Ghost, drunk, fell of a ferry and drowned). This may be Polanski’s best film since Chinatown, and, as some critics have opined, it may be the last of a type, meaning films that are deliberate, wonderfully constructed, where the movement is essentially conveyed through elliptical conversations that take place in different rooms or during long walks on coldwind beaches. Eventually, the writer begins to sense that the initially charming P.M. is more than he seems and the anecdotes from his childhood and youth in the first chapters of the book are fictionalized. There is much to question here 86 Cañada Road Woodside, CA 94062 650.364.8300 filoli.org

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, November 15, 2023 MOVIE FOR ADULTS The Ghost Writer Ewan McGregor in The Ghost Writer By Chris Honoré I’m reluctant to say that The Ghost Writer is the antidote to those fast-paced, intense thrillers that are ever ubiquitous. Recent examples would be The Hurt Locker, The Green Zone, as well as the Bourne trilogy, all shot with the revolutionary handheld steadicam and the digital Red, creating a grainy, documentary style, jerky and intense, a gestalt of visual experience. Antidote is too strong a word, even a bit disparaging of a genre that is superbly entertaining. The Ghost Writer, directed by Roman Polanski, does possess all of the intensity of a thriller; however the narrative is conveyed not by action and physical confrontation, but through dialogue. This is a film of language, well written, with engaging set pieces wherein the characters reveal themselves and the plot – which is at first intriguing and then ever more complex. Told from the point of view of a thirty-something writer (Ewan McGregor) for hire (his name is never given; he’s referred to only as “Ghost” or “man”) who reluctantly agrees to edit the memoirs of Adam Lang (Pierce Brosnan), England’s recently resigned Prime Minister. Lang is now living in a stark, contemporary house on Martha’s Vineyard – the month is January, it’s cold, the sky and ocean a mix of wintry slate and teal, rain falling constantly. Everything feels ominous and unsettling; exactly why is, at first, unclear. Sitting in front of floor to ceiling windows, looking out at the sand dunes, the wind blowing unrelentingly, the Ghost watches a gardener sweeping leaves on a long wooden walkway, the wind blowing away his best efforts, a metaphor for what he is about to experience as he looks at 600 some pages of banal manuscript (the first draft has already been written; however, the first Ghost, drunk, fell of a ferry and drowned). This may be Polanski’s best film since Chinatown, and, as some critics have opined, it may be the last of a type, meaning films that are deliberate, wonderfully constructed, where the movement is essentially conveyed through elliptical conversations that take place in different rooms or during long walks on coldwind beaches. Eventually, the writer begins to sense that the initially charming P.M. is more than he seems and the anecdotes from his childhood and youth in the first chapters of the book are fictionalized. There is much to question here and he begins peeling the onion and so the film builds with a quiet, dark intensity. Just a word about the cast: it’s remarkable. Pierce Brosnan delivers a top-drawer performance, as does Olivia Williams as his wife. Tom Wilkinson, always superb, portrays an Ivy League professor with a hidden past. And there is the inestimable Eli Wallach in a cameo role as a hermit living on the Vineyard. Roman Polanski, 76, now resides in Switzerland under house arrest while a request by the U.S. for his extradition works its way through the courts. He is accused of molesting a 13-year-old girl in Los Angeles some thirty years ago and has been living as a fugitive in Europe ever since. There is something of his ordeal in the character of the P.M.: besieged, accused, and deserted by old friends. Perhaps for Polanski, “The Ghost Writer” is more personal than any before, with the exception, perhaps, of The Pianist It was extraordinary. The Ghost Writer. Directed by Roman Polanski. Starring Ewan McGregor, Pierce Brosnan, Olivia Williams and Kim Cattral. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Broken Embraces a gem from Pedro Almodovar By Chris Honoré Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, likely the best-known Spanish filmmaker of the last three decades. His most memorable film, at least in the U.S., was Volver (Return), and starred, as does Broken Embraces, Penelope Cruz, often referred to as Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and even prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the complex characters. Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. Gradually she is pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity and the film takes on a noirish tone as it moves from 2008 to 1994 in revealing flashbacks. The film is also completely taken with the transformative face of Elena/Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like a Vogue layout, so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached. as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance. It is perhaps because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from the fact that there is a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices and the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the filmgoer is not interested in knowing anything about the interior motivations of the characters. It is a missed opportunity by Almodovar to build intimacy with the audience; little is revealed. Even when the film is briefly set on two islands, Ibiza and Lanzarotte, Almodovar seems inclined only to use the lush scenery as a mere backdrop for Elena and her lover, Harry Cain (Luis Homar) and not as an extension of the heat of their relationship. If you love movies and have followed the career of Pedro Almodovar then Broken Embraces is a film not to be missed. Or if you simply love movies and are tempted to see a film by an artist like Almodovar who consistently conveys the elusiveness inherent in exploring the human condition. Broken Embraces. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. Starring Penelope Cruz, Luis Homar, Lola Duenas, Blanca Portillo and Angela Molina. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated R. Released 2009. Barry lives in a colorful, well-organized, hexagonal hive that buzzes with constant activity. articles.text: Part 5 in a series Because movies are so deeply embedded in our culture, we have included their titles and stories as familiar referents. Some are animated, others are portrayals of real life, both filled with a kind of magic. More than a few have become iconic. We are not as familiar with the countless behind-the-scenes individuals who write the narratives, create the characters, and oversee the productions. Watch the credits at the end of any film and you get a sense of the extraordinary number of people involved. Revealing who those people are and the depth of their talent has been the purpose of this series. In the Post’s search for community filmmakers, we discovered Katherine Sarafian. She grew up in San Leandro in an Armenian-American family. She attended San Leandro High School, and then enrolled at the University of California, Los Angeles, where she earned a Bachelor’s degree in communication studies followed by a Master’s degree in film and television critical studies. Aspired to be involved in the entertainment industry, Katherine joined Pixar Animation Studios in 1994, and began what continues to be a long and remarkable career. She was initially hired as an artist, but moved from the art department to marketing and soon became a film producer. In an article titled Adventures at Pixar Animation Studios, she describes the work of the producer: “From the outside the actor, director, screenwriter, and even the craft service person, all have obvious roles to play in the making of a movie, while the producer remains the behind-thescenes mastermind whose importance to the process few will ever Filmmaker Katherine Sarafian realize.” Regarding that process, for more than 20 years Katherine has been a part of almost every production at Pixar. Over the course of her career she has contributed to a panoply of the company’s much-acclaimed films, including the Oscar-winning animated feature Brave (2012), directed by Piedmont’s Mark Andrews, for which she was nominated for The Producer’s Guild Award for Outstanding Producer of an Animated Theatrical Motion Picture. Regarding her lengthy and fulfilling career at Pixar she commented, “I am still struck by how closely the company’s values are aligned with my own values and ethics. Every person here has such a profound commitment to telling truly great stories.” Katherine is married to Meher Gourjian, a visual special effects specialist, and she is the mother of two sons in Piedmont schools. articles.text: A scene from Avatar with Sam Worthington and Zoe Saldana Avatar is breathtakingly beautiful, a science fiction/ fantasy hybrid that is unparalleled in its use of state-of-the-art technology – motion capture and CGI. It creates an alternative world that stirs a sense of wonder and awe from the first frame. James Cameron, the writer and director, lived with the nascent idea of Avatar for decades, waiting for cameras to be invented that could convey his vision. For the last four years, and employing some 2,000 people, he has worked relentlessly to bring to the screen what was once only a dream. As a visual spectacle, the film is glorious. As a story, it’s a gumbo of themes, stitched together in a narrative that takes more than two and half hours to develop. Essentially, the film is set on the distant moon of Pandora, inhabited by the Na’Vi – ten feet tall, with cat-like features and blue humanoid bodies. They are an aboriginal people with nothing more than bows and arrows; yet, they possess a profound connection to their natural world, a place of floating mountains, lush, luminescent forests filled with exotic animals and Paleolithic flying birds that they fearlessly ride. Their lives are filled with the sacred, and a natural wisdom that transcends the technology of those from earth who have arrived to mine a much-needed mineral called unobtanium. Earth, it seems, has finally been all but depleted of its resources (the year is 2154). The conundrum is that the Na’Vi live on the richest deposit of unobtanium on Pandora and must either be relocated peacefully or driven into the forest by force. A warrior and ex-Marine, Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), is melded with a Na’Vi body, created from their DNA, and sent to collect intel on the clan (hence the title Avatar). Initially, he hopes he can negotiate with them, learn their ways; however, his sympathies gradually begin to change. Neytiri (Zoe Saldana), an impressive female and the daughter of the chief of the tribe, introduces him to Na’Vi and to the harmony with which the clan approaches all living things. The dialogue is serviceable and the narrative instantly recognizable. For all of its richness, Avatar is an old-fashioned adventure story. There’s the quintessential bad guys – led by a mercenary Col., Mike Quaritch (Stephen Lang), who hates the locals and loves the smell of napalm in the morning. articles.text: New Orleans is one of the most unique cities on the planet. What is the best way to see this unique city and how many days do you need? First, let’s talk about what makes New Orleans so special. Society there is an easy-going friendship with all races, and Southern hospitality is truly exemplified. You need to know that Creole and Cajun are not synonymous. What is surprising is that, despite wide differences, there is a true meeting of the minds. The original inhabitants of the area were the indigenous tribes. French Canadians moved down the Mississippi and founded the city of New Orleans as a small community on the only high ground available. The original part of New Orleans known as the French Quarter is really tiny. Soon after, the Spanish arrived. The two groups sort of got along. With the arrival of the Americans, things got a little bit more difficult. And then in quick succession were the arrivals of Africans and people from every part of the Caribbean. The interesting thing is that, even though there was friction, the people found a way to work together which helped New Orleans develop in a unique way. The cuisine is completely unique. It is important to remember that there is a huge difference between Creole and Cajun. People who are Creole are people of mixed European and black descent, principally in the Caribbean. Cajuns are descendants of the early French-Canadian settlers. The gourmet in me was happy to enjoy both cuisines and I encourage you to do the same. Cajun and Creole restaurants abound. articles.text: A group of 18 individuals met on November 6 for the monthly gathering of the First Mondays Reading Group. It had rained earlier in the day, but the afternoon was pleasant. The readers moved chairs from inside the Community Center to the patio. The group’s usual discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long were away, so Hilary Honore, who had suggested The Trees for this month’s discussion, led the conversation. The book is a 2021 novel by American author Percival Everett and was shortlisted for the 2022 Booker Prize. The story is set mostly in the small town of Money, Mississippi, and follows a series of murders that have an identical pattern. A white man named Junior Junior is found dead with the body of an unknown Black man beside him. When the bodies are taken to the morgue it is discovered that the Black man’s body has disappeared. However, the same body is found again in the home of Junior Junior’s cousin, Wheat, who has also been murdered, and the body of the Black man soon disappears again, too. Two Black detectives from the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, Ed Morgan and Jim Davis, are sent to Money to investigate the murders. They go to a bar frequented by members of the Black community and discover that both Junior and Wheat were relatives of Carolyn Bryant, a white woman who accused the teenage Emmett Till of making sexual advances towards her leading to his brutal 1955 murder. Ed and Jim believe the disappearing body resembles that of the battered Emmett Till. More bodies begin to appear around the country. Each is a white man who has been castrated and has the body of a Black or Asian man beside him. The detectives identify the Black man’s body found at the original crime scene, and they trace it to a company that sells bodies for research. They also suspect that Gertrude Penstock, a mixed-race person who passes for being white, and her 105-year-old great-grandmother, Mama Z, are involved in the murders. Gertrude and a group of like-minded Black people are suspected of having murdered Wheat and Junior Junior as retaliation for their father’s part in murdering Emmett Till. But the detectives are baffled by the other murders. There now are reports of other murders around the country by large groups of Black and Asian men. Bullets have no effect on them, and they are duplicating the murders orchestrated by Mama Z and Gertrude. The Trees was another great selection by the reading group; some readers loved it, while others couldn’t stand it. Those on the positive side said the book made them think about our nation’s history. There were over 800 counties in the U.S. where lynching occurred and where racial violence continues today. Percival Everett wants us to understand that not much has changed. Everett’s storytelling is often humorous and sometimes over the top, but this is a serious subject. Some felt guilty when laughing at the sad events in the book. Others felt this serious, tragic situation was handled too frivolously. The idea of how terrible each murder was didn’t come across for them. Some readers enjoyed the creativity and humor in the first part of the book, but the enjoyment fell off for them later. The presentation of most of the white characters as being backward, stupid, and bad didn’t seem realistic or balanced. Some readers found the ending with large groups of zombies unsatisfying and the many murders became repetitious. Perhaps that’s how Percival Everett and Black people feel about what they experience in their lives. The readers questioned how it feels to be threatened all the time. There was a lot to discuss and agree or disagree about. The readers did agree they would not have read The Trees if not for the First Mondays Reading Group, and they were pleased to be a part of it. The group had previously selected The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman for December, and Station Eleven by Canadian writer Emily St. John Mandel for their January read. For February the group picked The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson. The group’s next discussion will be on December 4 at 1:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee, Registration is required at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4.

articles.text: It’s hard to imagine a comedy based on the Holocaust, but the brilliant Italian comic Roberto Begnini not only imagined one, he wrote it, directed it, and starred in it. It went on to win the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival and picked up three 1997 Academy Awards as well, including Best Foreign Film and Best Actor. It’s called Life Is Beautiful (La vita é bella), and last week the audience at Piedmont’s Second Thursday Film Fest got to check it out. It’s set in the 1940s, when fascism had taken firm hold in Italy and the nation had formed an alliance with both Mussolini and Hitler. Italy also began persecuting Jews big time, establishing internment camps of its own. As the movie begins, the crisis point, when Northern Italy was occupied by the Germans, has not yet been reached, so the first half of the tale delights us with a charming rom-com set in Arezzo, in which Guido Orefice, a clever young Jewish restaurant worker, uses his smarts to win a pretty Gentile girl named Dora away from her fiancé (he steals her from her engagement party on a horse). They marry, have a child, a boy, Giosué, and open a bookstore. And then the bad guys march in, and the family winds up on a train to an internment camp. There, Dora is separated from her husband and son, so the sole parent, Guido, uses all his wiles to keep his son from understanding and suffering from their plight. We’re amused by Guido’s tricks and hairsbreadth escapes, but the movie can’t hold the truth of the situation and its consequences at bay. Despite its honors and awards, Life Is Beautiful had its critics. Entertainment Weekly called it “the first feel-good Holocaust weepie,” and, surprisingly, Mel Brooks, who wrote The Producers, panned it. But the worldwide audience vote was overwhelmingly positive, and, enlightened by Darby Gragg’s excellent introduction, the Piedmont audience liked it, too. The next Film Fest showing, on December 14th, is the international comedy, Dirty Rotten Scoundrels from 1988, starring Michael Caine and Steve Martin. The Film Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the Recreation Department PRD is recommended at https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Guests are welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays wanted to see some streets they hadn’t gone to this year, so they headed for Rose and Kingston Avenues. They are some of Piedmont’s earliest streets with some beautiful Victorians, including some built prior to 1900. A turnout of 40 walkers and three K-9 arrived for the walk. The group crossed Grand Avenue and climbed Greenbank up to Rose Avenue where they enjoyed seeing Rose’s many old homes that were built the early 1900s, especially three Victorians. It was noted that the homes on the south side of Kingston are in Piedmont and those on the north side are in Oakland. The walkers went down to Linda Avenue and crossed it to go up Kingston. 780 was the former home of walker Meghan Bennett. Research by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombard provided its story and also that of the house next door at 778. These two homes were built in 1892 by William Vickery and his sister, Elizabeth Vickery Hadden at costs of $4,300 and $3,300. They were the first homes on this street that was then called Summit Avenue. The houses were built in the fashionable shingle style of the 1890s. The backyard of the house at 778 is one of the deepest lots in Piedmont going back 150 feet, The entire lot is 220 feet deep. Google Maps shows the backyard of the home at 784 is even deeper. Neighborhood lore says the houses at 778 and 784 once shared a kitchen and the two families ate their meals together. Nancy DeRoche urged the group to go a little further up Kingston to see a historic brick home. It was designed by Albert Farr and built in 1908. An iron gate blocks the driveway entrance with the house further back. As the group was peeking through the gate, the owner, Chad Olcott, happened to be coming out and saw the group. Chad, who owns Mulberry’s Market in Piedmont, invited the walkers to come in for a tour of the house. The group noticed that there is also a chicken coop with live chickens just inside the gate. Chad said he once had ducks too. Showing great hospitality, he took the walkers through the house, and shared the stories of buying the house, rebuilding part of it, and remodeling much of it. The home is lovely and has a wonderful historical feel. The front of the house was also a great spot for a group photo with Chad, who later shared an early photo of the house. It was time for the group to make a direct return to the Exedra. They went back on Kingston to Linda, past Beach School, and on to Grand, Wildwood, and Magnolia Avenues, and finally to the Exedra. It was an almost four-mile walk on a beautiful, fall morning with an unexpected treat from Chad Olcott that was enjoyed and appreciated by all. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. The Walking on Wednesday group paid a visit to the home of Chad Olcott last week. articles.text: Carl West Anderson died peacefully on November 4, 2023 in Reno, Nevada after complications from a fall. A man of strong passion, devotion, and honor, he tackled life with enthusiasm, hard work, and love. Carl was born on September 11, 1935, in Monterey Park, California and grew up in Albany. He attended Cal, and after graduating in 1957, he completed six months of active duty as a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army Reserve. He returned to academia at UC Berkeley to attend Boalt Hall School of Law. Upon graduation, he was awarded a one-year fellowship to study with a German judge. Fortuitously, on the way to his internship in Germany, he visited Amsterdam where he met Margo at the Rijksmuseum. He returned home to serve as a deputy district attorney for Alameda County, was assigned to the Berkeley office, and married Margo. During his nine years as deputy district attorney, he was sent to Sacramento to lobby for the California District Attorneys Association, the California Peace Officers Association, and the California State Sheriffs Association. Governor Reagan appointed him to the Alameda County Superior Court on the last day of his term. The appointment was Carl Anderson in his back yard with his dog Lola. Retired First District California Court of Appeal Administrative Presiding Justice Carl Anderson died on November 4 at age 87. challenged by the new governor, but was subsequently confirmed. After nine years on the California Superior Court, Governor George Deukmejian appointed him a justice of the First District California Court of Appeal in San Francisco where he eventually became Administrative Presiding Justice. During his tenure, his court became a pilot court for the American Bar Association’s (ABA) project on appellate court delay reduction. Over the course of seven years, the court completely eliminated what had been a historical two-to-five-year backlog of appeals. During this period, Judge Anderson was active with the ABA and the Council of Chief Judges of the Courts of Appeal, encouraging all intermediate federal and U.S. state appellate courts to adopt time standards for processing their appeals. After retiring from the court in 1997, he worked for 23 years as a neutral arbitrator and mediator, affiliated with the American Arbitration Association. Carl’s passion for his community was demonstrated by his long involvement with the Piedmont Scout Council. He is credited with leading the effort to prevent the Piedmont Scout Council from being absorbed into larger councils and to retain its independence as one of the smallest councils in the U.S. Judge Anderson was also involved with the Rotary Club of Oakland, the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Volunteers of America of the Bay Area, Piedmont Educational Foundation, Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont Community Church, and his neighborhood utility undergrounding project. The family suggests that memorial donations in lieu of flowers may be made to any of those organizations or to the charity of your choice. A memorial service will be held at 10:30 a.m. on Friday, November 17 at Piedmont Community Church, with a reception immediately following. An avid gardener, he served on the UC Botanical Gardens Board of Directors and cultivated a beautiful native Sierra garden. He is predeceased by Margo Hart, his loving wife of 53 years. He is survived by his son, Thomas, his daughter-in-law Susan, granddaughter Samantha, daughter Marnie, and son-in-law Will. Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

Staff photos “host” a Shabbat table. Volunteer families were assigned the names of eight hostages in captivity and were encouraged to learn about the hostages’ lives and gather items that represented them. Those items were brought to Piedmont Community Hall and placed on seats to represent the 241 Israeli hostages being held by Hamas. “One person brought a music score because their person was a musician,” said Friedman Meir. “Another brought an army jacket to hang on the back of their chair.” “The message here is there are 241 people who are children, parents, grandparents who are being held as pawns in a war. As the hostage crisis enters its second month, this exhibit marks the fifth Shabbat our family, friends, and loved ones are missing. Kim Hunter (right) and son Hunter Fasteau walk from seat to seat at the exhibit. Tonight, these 241 seats will still sit painfully empty at what is usually a joyous weekly celebration,” Catherine Rogers (left) and Meghan O’Leary examine the empty Shabbat table. said Friedman Meir. Shabbat dinner is a tradition observed by Jewish families all over the world. Traditionally, Shabbat is a day of rest, and is meant to honor the day on which God rested after creating the Earth. It is often a time for Jewish families to come together and relax at the end of their week. The exhibit also featured a powerful candlelit memorial table honoring all innocent lives that have been lost in the conflict. Organizers of the event urged attendees to call or email their elected state and federal representatives on a daily basis and to demand the immediate return of the hostages. Resources are available through www.bringthemhome.com and www.oneminaday.com. Israeli flags fly in the Community Hall parking lot in a show of support for hostages in the Hamas-Israeli conflict. articles.text: Piedmont Police were dispatched to a report of a 2001 Dodge Ram that crashed onto private property on Park Lane on Wednesday, November 8, at 6:26 p.m. The driver and sole occupant, Robert Hickman, 61 years old from Berkeley, admitted to losing control of the truck which was pulling a trailer with a forklift attached. The truck and trailer ended up between two houses; no one was injured. The suspect denied drinking alcoholic beverages, but admitted to being addicted to heroin in the past. Officers stated he showed symptoms of being under the influence of a narcotic and arrested him for driving while under the influence of drugs and driving while addicted. A search of his truck revealed a small amount of suspected black tar heroin, drug paraphernalia, and Narcan. The suspect was transported to the hospital, where he consented to a blood draw. Hickman was booked into Santa Rita Jail without incident, and his truck and trailer were towed. A driver lost control of his truck and trailer, which careened onto private property in between two houses on Park Lane. Piedmont Real Estate Update November 2023 Seasonality in the Bay Area Real Estate Market As we’ve seen over the past few years, the real estate market in our area is a dynamic and ever-changing landscape. While you might not think certain seasons weigh on the amount you’re paying or asking for your home — they do! There can be a difference as high as 10% in some cases. [Source: National Association of Realtors.] Understanding the ebb and flow throughout the year is crucial for buyers and sellers. In this month’s newsletter, we’ll explore how different seasons affect the real estate market and what you can do to position yourself strategically. The Spring Market in the Bay Area — New Listings and High Demand It’s well known that certain times of the year can be more active than others, filled with either benefits or challenges, depending on your place in the process. Spring is typically a popular time to look for a new home because buyers have been waiting out the slow winter months for new inventory, and sellers have been priming for the best conditions to showcase their home — think sunshine and pretty gardens. These two factors mean it all starts with a bang in early spring and peaks in late spring/early summer. As a seller, spring can be an excellent opportunity for bustling buyer activity and the potential for multiple offers. But from a buyer’s perspective, you’re part of a bigger pool of buyers, which can translate into increased competition, multiple offers, and higher prices. Our strong market continues through June and July, usually showing some slowing in August. The fall season, once school is back in session, can be an excellent time to sell. Especially here in the Bay Area with our lovely Indian Summer weather. It’s a little less frenzied than spring and offers the opportunity to complete the sale before the holidays. For the buyers who have the drive and interest to keep looking through the winter season, it just might pay off. Sellers can’t always follow the market’s seasonality, and you might find a great opportunity with little competition. articles.text: Piedmont’s teachers union will host a community forum online on November 15 to describe details of the financial impasse between the teachers and the school district. The Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) filed with the California Public Employment Relations Board on October 20 to continue negotiations with the help of a state mediator. The forum will take place on Zoom and start at 6:30 p.m. Wednesday, November 15. Register for the meeting at Zoom.us/meeting/register/tZIkdeGurTkjHNVRb7cL3VHMHnySKNMYOfFg#/registration “We will discuss the topics still open in negotiations, take a look at the financial issues, answer your questions, and explain what it means to be at impasse,” said APT President Elise Marks. Piedmont teachers were in front of school sites at drop off Tuesday morning to promote the upcoming meeting and continue campaigning for an 8.22% salary increase to keep up with the state’s cost of living adjustment (COLA). Open your camera app, point it at the QR code and then click the link to register.
articles.title: Teachers Union to host online community forum Nov. 15 with details of impasse with school district

articles.text: After 17 years in business, Piedmont Auto Care, the Shell station at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenue, is closing its doors. Earlier this week, owner Jeff Hansen sold the station and the property to Shell Recharge, a division of the Shell corporation that specializes in EV charging stations. It would potentially be the first of its kind in the U.S. The Shell station has been in Piedmont for 95 years. Hansen said the decision was motivated by the cost of upcoming and necessary renovations to the property as well as his predictions of the future of the auto industry. “We have three 10,000 gallon gas tanks under our pumps that need to be replaced by 2025,” Hansen said. “That’s expensive, but not out of the question as far as maintenance goes.” The installation of new gas tanks under the property would have allowed the station to continue pumping fuel for decades. “But I don’t see people pumping more and more gas in the future,” he explained. Hansen has been watching electric vehicle sales climb steadily since 2010. He believes that in the near future electric vehicles will become far more common. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense to replace those tanks if that’s the situation. I’ve always been looking at trends, and this generation’s trend is electric vehicles.” Hansen will physically vacate the premises by the end of November, but all auto service has ceased and his mechanics will be working at other nearby stations. articles.text: Thanksgiving is approaching quickly and with it comes the time-honored tradition of the Piedmont Turkey Trot. On Thanksgiving morning, Thursday, November 23, at 8:30 a.m. an estimated 2,400 runners will hit the streets with running shoes, bibs, and water bottles to deliver a pre-emptive strike against those Thanksgiving calories. The Turkey Trot is a 5K course (3.1 miles) on city streets intended for all runners, joggers and dog walkers, young and old, casual and experienced. “The Piedmont Turkey Trot is a much-loved community event that raises funds for the high school cross-country and track and field team, as well as the Boosters,” said Race Director Sydney Proctor. The Trot is a USA track and field certified 5K race. Runners can sign up for the event through November 22 at piedmontturkeytrot.com. Registration currently costs $50 ($35 for youth 12 and younger) at regular pricing until November 14, when the price will increase to $55 ($40 for youth 12 and Staff photos Last year, Highland Avenue was elbow-to-elbow with runners participating in the annual 5K Turkey Trot. More than 2,300 runners participated in the 21st annual race.
articles.title: Turkey Trot returns on Thanksgiving for 22nd year

articles.text: November is finally here, which means it’s time for Piedmont Scouting’s 39th Annual Scouting for Food event. This Saturday morning, November 11, residents are asked to leave donations of non-perishable food by their front door. Piedmont Scouts will go door-to-door, street-tostreet, picking up donations for the Alameda County Food Bank starting at 9 a.m. Community members may also donate funds directly to the food bank through a QR code on this year’s door hanger, or they can donate with a check to the Piedmont Scout office. Door hangers were placed on doors throughout the city by Cub Scouts last weekend. “We ask for cereals, canned foods, bread mixes, pasta, instant soup, rice, items that will last a long time,” said Eris Turner, Program Manager for the Piedmont Council. The Piedmont Shell Station has closed after 95 years in business. Piedmont Shell station closes By Matt Simons After 17 years in business, Piedmont Auto Care, the Shell station at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenue, is closing its doors. Earlier this week, owner Jeff Hansen sold the station and the property to Shell Recharge, a division of the Shell corporation that specializes in EV charging stations. It would potentially be the first of its kind in the U.S. The Shell station has been in Piedmont for 95 years. Hansen said the decision was motivated by the cost of upcoming and necessary renovations to the property as well as his predictions of the future of the auto industry. “We have three 10,000 gallon gas tanks under our pumps that need to be replaced by 2025,” Hansen said. “That’s expensive, but not out of the question as far as maintenance goes.” The installation of new gas tanks under the property would have allowed the station to continue pumping fuel for decades. “But I don’t see people pumping more and more gas in the future,” he explained. Hansen has been watching electric vehicle sales climb steadily since 2010. He believes that in the near future electric vehicles will become far more common. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense to replace those tanks if that’s the situation. I’ve always been looking at trends, and this generation’s trend is electric vehicles.” Hansen will physically vacate the premises by the end of November, but all auto service has ceased and his mechanics will be working at other nearby stations. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has published a Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) for the implementation of the City’s 6th Cycle Housing Element for public review and comment. Community members may submit written comments on the Draft EIR to Planning Director Kevin Jackson through December 18 at 5 p.m. The Draft EIR studies the impacts of Housing Element implementation as a whole – looking at the overall impacts to Piedmont once each of the 77 programs included in the Housing Element are realized. For each impact identified, the Draft EIR assesses how significant it would be and lists steps the City would take to mitigate that impact, where possible. Community members may view the Draft EIR in person at Piedmont City Hall or online at piedmontishome.org. After December 18, staff will respond to comments received. The Planning Commission and City Council will then consider the EIR at public hearings, likely in early 2024.

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation invites community members to a discussion on Monday, November 13, with New York Times best-selling author Dashka Slater, to discuss her book Accountable, which has local implications. The event is sponsored by the Ed. Foundation, Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. Her talk in the Alan Harvey Theater will begin at 6:30 p.m. The book’s full title is Accountable: The True Story of a Racist Social Media Account and the Teenagers Whose Lives It Changed. It’s the story of a high school student who starts a social media account that divides the community. It’s something that could happen in Piedmont. The book is based upon an incident that happened in Albany, less than 10 miles away. How it unfolded is the basis of Slater’s new young adult book, based on five years of reporting and hundreds of hours of interviews chronicling how one problematic Instagram account resulted in broken friendships, community protests and a lawsuit that eventually was heard by the U.S. Supreme Court. Slater is also the author of The 57 Bus, a New York Times best-selling non-fiction book that takes place in Oakland. The 57 Bus also received the Stonewall Book Award. Her fiction includes The Book of Fatal Errors; the picture book Escargot, which won the Wanda Gag Book Award; Baby Shoes; and The Antlered Ship, which was a Junior Library Guild Selection. As a journalist Slater has written for Newsweek, Salon, Mother Jones, and The New York Times Magazine, which published her story about the Albany incident. Light refreshments and a book signing will follow the event. RSVP is encouraged at: Piedmontstore.org/products/accountable-dashka-slater.
articles.title: NY Times best-selling author Dashka Slater in Piedmont Nov. 13

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is currently receiving donations of new, unwrapped toys through December 23 for its annual Toys for Tots drive. NY Times best-selling author Dashka Slater in Piedmont Nov. 13 Piedmont Education Foundation invites community members to a discussion on Monday, November 13, with New York Times best-selling author Dashka Slater, to discuss her book Accountable, which has local implications. The event is sponsored by the Ed. Foundation, Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. Her talk in the Alan Harvey Theater will begin at 6:30 p.m. The book’s full title is Accountable: The True Story of a Racist Social Media Account and the Teenagers Whose Lives It Changed. It’s the story of a high school student who starts a social media account that divides the community. It’s something that could happen in Piedmont. The book is based upon an incident that happened in Albany, less than 10 miles away. How it unfolded is the basis of Slater’s new young adult book, based on five years of reporting and hundreds of hours of interviews chronicling how one problematic Instagram account resulted in broken friendships, community protests and a lawsuit that eventually was heard by the U.S. Supreme Court. Slater is also the author of The 57 Bus, a New York Times best-selling non-fiction book that takes place in Oakland. The 57 Bus also received the Stonewall Book Award. Her fiction includes The Book of Fatal Errors; the picture book Escargot, which won the Wanda Gag Book Award; Baby Shoes; and The Antlered Ship, which was a Junior Library Guild Selection. As a journalist Slater has written for Newsweek, Salon, Mother Jones, and The New York Times Magazine, which published her story about the Albany incident. articles.text: Last year Piedmont elementary school students took part in Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day, a nationwide event, for the first time. On Tuesday, November 14, the event will be expanded city-wide, inciting all students and community members to honor Ruby Bridges and her courageous message of kindness, inclusion and activism. In 1960, the courage of a sixyear-old student in New Orleans was on display every day as Ruby Bridges was the first Black student to attend an all-white school in New Orleans. She broke the segregation barrier every day, walking past a screaming mob under guard of federal marshals. In 2018, fifth graders in South San Francisco took inspiration from Ruby’s courage and advocated to make November 14, Ruby Bridges Day. San Mateo County Office of Education later made their dream a reality, and ever since schools nationwide have been following suit. In September 2021, the California State Senate passed a resolution proclaiming November 14 as Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day. Last year over 90,000 kids in 36 states, including California, participated. “Even though it can feel like Piedmont exists in a bubble, untouched from the issues Ruby Bridges was fighting for (desegregation, racial equity), that is simply not the case,” said PHS sophomore Meher Bachher, “Ruby Bridges’ actions and her teachings prove to us in our own community that no matter our age, we can accomplish incredible feats if we have the dedication.” 7:45 a.m.: Pathways of Kindness. Piedmont High School Affinity Mentors at Piedmont Park will create “Pathways of Kindness” with chalk in the city center. Create a bouquet of diversity, talk bubbles with important messages, rainbows of all colors, and other artistic expressions of “everyone is welcome and belongs.” 8:05 a.m.: The Ruby Bridges Pledge Piedmont Affinity Mentors speak about Ruby Bridges and her message. Take the Ruby Bridges Pledge together. 8:10 a.m.: Prepare to walk to school Learn the history, grab some cool Ruby Bridges swag and walk to school in unity on November 14.

articles.text: Curiosity drives human progress, yet modern life often stifles our innate sense of wonder. As Albert Einstein once said, “I have no special talent. I am only passionately curious.” Children are bursting with curiosity, eagerly investigating the world around them. But busy schedules, screens and standardized education can dampen inquisitive young minds. The good news is that parents can take steps to keep their child’s curiosity alive. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Allow unstructured free time for open-ended play and exploration. Don’t overschedule activities. a. Set aside 30-60 minutes per day for unscheduled, non-screen play. b. Allow taking healthy risks outdoors; get into open wilderness and see what happens. c. Go on a “wonder walk” with no set destination. Examine small things up close, like insects and plant buds. Notice patterns and details in nature, architecture, shadows. Provide access to new experiences through travel, museums, nature walks. Exposure sparks questions. a. Visit zoos, aquariums, children’s museums. b. Hike a new trail, swim in a lake, climb a hill. c. Travel whether near or far - explore diverse neighborhoods. Supply games, toys and books that encourage inquiry over predetermined outcomes. a. Use toys like Lego without a kit or instructions b. Find a “loose parts” playground c. Choose books on how things work Model curiosity by sharing your own wonderings and asking imaginative questions. a. Wonder aloud - “Hmm, I wonder how that tradition started?” b. Ask open questions like “What do you think AI will be able to do in two years?” c. Discuss what interests you and what you find fascinating. Embrace mistakes as learning opportunities rather than failures. Praise efforts. a. Emphasize effort over outcomes. Praise trying new things. b. Say “Let’s figure out what went wrong” versus “That’s not right.” c. Share your own mistakes and what you learned. Children love stories. :-) 6. Limit access to devices/information that satisfies all their questions immediately. a. b. c. Set boundaries for recreational screen time. Encourage reading books over quick online searches (experience more long-form inquiry). Withhold constant facts; let them sit with questions. Ask riddles, and work on them for days, or weeks. 7. Ask open-ended questions without easy factual answers. a. What would happen if...? b. c. Do you think there could ever be a rainbow at night? How might you build a car that would keep that person safe? 8. Introduce philosophy by discussing imaginative big questions. a. Do dogs have feelings? b. Is there life on other planets? c. What happens after we die? 9. Help make connections between different fields and ideas. a. Link art, music, math, and science through interdisciplinary projects. b. Compare diverse cultures, time periods, and perspectives. c. Show how seemingly unrelated concepts are connected. 10. Let children sit sometimes with uncertainty instead of answering all questions. a. Tell them it’s okay not to know; model being comfortable with the unknown. b. Admit you don’t have all the answers either. c. Let them research answers when developmentally appropriate. What beauty, understanding and progress lie ahead when curiosity takes flight? The only way to find out is to set it free. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, and family camps can be found at www. campaugusta.org. A Camp Augusta camper rides the camp’s gravity zip line.

Some of whom are reading this (perhaps with children of their own) and fondly reflecting back on the experiences they had that day on the Oakland Estuary,” said Wisniewski. After the tutorial, students paired up and were assigned to kayaks just south of Scott’s Seafood and Grill. After paddling about a mile the group played a version of water “tag” called sharks and minnows. They learned how to safely get out of a kayak and onto a dock at Estuary Park. There, the WizKids retrieved their lunches from drybags, stretched their legs, and reflected on a different kind of school day. After refueling, the WizKids challenged each other to races to test their kayaking skills. Then the group crossed the estuary to Alameda to meet former PE teacher Linda Jarvis, who retired in 2020. Jarvis awaited them on the yacht “Impatient” which she and her husband own. They had decorated it with signs reading “Ahoy,” and “Welcome WizKids.” Jarvis delighted in saying hi to Wisniewski, her teaching colleague of 20 years, and tossing candy for the student kayakers. “Kayaking provides an opportunity for everyone, regardless of experience/ athletic ability to enjoy exercise and reap the benefits of the many resources that the Bay Area has for us,” said Wisniewski. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: With most players 16 or under, Chad Ironside’s Barca soccer team clinched the Under 19 league title with an emphatic 5-2 win over long-time rivals EBU Warrior-Wolves in Alameda on Sunday, November 5. The victory capped an unbeaten run to hold off the Montclair Stingers, the Panthers, the Falcons and the Phoenix. Training in near darkness at Alameda Point, the 22-strong squad built a cohesive work ethic and inclusive spirit that proved too much for their older opponents. Barca started brightly. A rampaging run by Harry McNulty set up Miles Kim for the opening goal, followed later in the first half by Elias Reed-Miguel finding the top corner of the net with a sweet strike from the top of the box. Always dangerous, the Wolves made it 2-1 after a goalmouth scramble. Barca struck back when Peter Murdock threaded a pass to Lucas Ironside for a 3-1 lead at the break. The game’s outcome seemed in the balance when the Wolves made it 3-2 just after the restart, but Piedmont found its rhythm and took control. Peter Murdock found the net on a breakaway and iced the game with an assist to Thomas Ero in the dying minutes, setting off jubilation on the Piedmont bench. Players and coaches of the Under-19 soccer league champions Barca. Pictured are: Coach Chad Ironside (left), Eli Hildebrand, William Steele, Bodie Ironside, Coach Aaron Murdock, Dean Olliphant, Sean McKee, Miles Kim, Elias Reed-Miguel, Ryan Wendel, Peter Murdock, Thomas Ero, Dorian Poole, Shane McNulty, Harry McNulty, Lucas Ironside, Kasper Jansson, Declan Murphy, Kian Ghaderi, Jacob Ingle, Rocco Doubrava (Bishop O’Dowd), Coach Neil McKee. Not pictured: Finian Caulfield, Cary Ward, Owen Udkow.

The common Coccinellidae beetle is annually called to the fence posts and plants along the Stream Trail for mating season. “Here in Redwood, Ladybugs wait out the winter, often along the creeks. They are likely attracted to the area by chemicals in the air, or from pheromones, or scent markers, left behind in their footprints,” wrote East Bay Regional Parks on their informative panel describing the phenomenon. About 1.7 miles down the Stream Trail from the Canyon Meadows Staging Area are bushels of ladybugs. Scientists determined that their behavior is a mechanism for the species to reproduce and cope with a limited food supply during the winter months by laying eggs on the underside of leaves. The Stream Trail is mostly flat, so it’s a great location for children Here’s a peek at the ladybug swarm in 2022. The coccinellidae beetle is called to Redwood Regional for its mating season every year. The collection of boulders at Redwood Peak has names, initials, and dates from several generations etched into their surface. One of the oldest dates found on the Redwood Peak boulders. From now through February, Redwood Regional Park’s famous ladybug swarm is underway. and senior walkers. To reach the trail there are a few options. For an easy walk, start at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road and take the Stream Trail which starts at the end of the parking lot. At 1.5 miles you’ll reach a bridge and intersection with the Mill Trail. Take the bridge to continue down the Stream Trail and .2 of a mile later you will encounter the swarms of ladybugs. Turning around from this point will end your day at slightly over three miles of hiking. To experience more of Redwood Regional and add a workout to your visit, park at the Redwood Bowl Staging Area off of Skyline Boulevard. Take the West Ridge Trail until it intersects with the Madrone Trail, traveling left. You’ll walk slightly less than a half-mile until reaching the Starflower Trail, which you will take all the way until reaching the Stream Trail about 0.8 mile away. From there, you’ll walk about a half-mile to reach the ladybug swarm. Returning to the Starflower Trail and hiking back to your car will take about 1.6 miles and top out your day around 850 feet in elevation gain. Another option is taking the Redwood Peak Trail and walking uphill to Redwood Peak—taking 1.2 miles from the ladybugs. Redwood Peak is possibly the best hidden treasure of the park, where you can find a collection of boulders with initials, names, and dates etched into their surface. It is a great location to relax and hydrate while you scour the boulders to find the oldest date. The oldest year I was able to find was 1918. The Stream Trail is one of the most popular trails at Redwood Regional Park due to the ladybug swarm and the general ease of the trail. Staff Photos Millions of ladybugs gather on the Stream Trail annually from November to February. A closer look at the ladybugs on the Stream Trail. On a Sunday around 11:00 a.m., we passed approximately 122 people on the Stream Trail as we made our way to the Tres Sendas Trail. On the Tres Sendas and Starflower Trails, we passed just 20 people on the way to Redwood Peak and passed another 41 people while on the West Ridge Trail. On the Chown Trail, one of the most secluded and perhaps the most underrated, we passed just six people in the mile descent. Back on the Stream Trail, we passed another 51 people while making our way back to the car. 171 of the total head count of 249 people were on the Stream Trail. articles.text: An exhibition featuring over 20 pieces by local artist Bernice “Bingo” Bing (1936-1998) is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. Born in San Francisco’s Chinatown, Bing was a young artist among the city’s Beat Era art scene, creating works from the 1950’s on. Although she grew up in an orphanage and bounced between foster homes as a child, she was able to earn her B.F.A. and M.F.A. at the California School of Fine Arts (San Francisco Art Institute), where she studied alongside painter Elmer Bischoff and other greats. Her paintings and illustrations explore abstract expressionism and figuration as well as Zen calligraphy and Western abstraction. Bing only recently became recognized for her artworks, but was a fixture in the San Francisco art scene until her death in 1998. Into View: Bernice Bing is the first in an ongoing series of collection exhibitions at Asian Art Museum that highlight the work of under-recognized modern artists. articles.text: Opera review by Paul Hertelendy The latest sensation in opera is the unorthodox Omar, written by the polymath folksinger Rhiannon Giddens, winner of a Pulitzer, MacArthur “genius” award, and a Grammy. With co-composer Michael Abels, she turned out the multicultural drama, now staged at the San Francisco Opera. It is based on the true story of Omar ibn Sayyid, a 19th century African-Arab Islamic savant and author who had been forced into slavery and shipped off to bleak servitude in the cotton fields of America. The work is unique in opera annals, combining multiple cultures, languages and faiths. After a dark first act of capture and captivity, the work comes brilliantly to life in the second when Omar’s talents emerge as author and imam of divine inspiration. The music produces many threads, variously Afro-Arabian, NewWorld slave dance, jazz/blues and early Americana bordering on spiritual—what you can achieve with an unorthodox two-composer lineup, a new feature for the well-deserved operatic Pulitzer Prize. Above all, Omar dramatizes one of the little-known heroic tales of emerging America, known mostly for his voluminous writings (religious and otherwise) in the archives. In the end, the opera emphasizes the variety of cultures that made America great while dramatizing the times of slavery, both evil and cruel. The cast is almost entirely black, echoing Gershwin’s Porgy and Bess. For much of the show, the spark was slow in ignition, with voices more theatrical than truly operatic. But these too opened up to lustrous life in the triumphant finale that so many of us found moving, with Omar leading the the farthest corners. In a recurrent posthumous part, Omar’s mother Fatima was played tautly by mezzo Taylor Raven. Stage Director Kaneza Schaal held together this quasi-historical account sprawled over 10 scenes. Unforgettable was the stage design by Christopher Myers and Amy Rubin, with immense trees draped in white cloths, and countless bolts of stage-embracing fabric from above. Conducting the challenging score was John Kennedy. This is a multifaceted opera whose time is now, destined to continue playing on many stages in the U.S. and abroad. MUSIC NOTES Giddens, 47, is a 1995 alumna of the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics. She went on to graduate from the Oberlin Conservatory at Oberlin College. Like Omar, she is North Carolinian…This season, more adventurous than ever, the SF Opera has co-commissioned an unprecedented array of new works by Mason Bates, the Giddens-Abels duo, and the late Kaija Saariaho. In addition, 2023 brought on the Mexican-American saga of Frida Kahlo, Gabriela Frank’s bio-op The Last Dream of Frida and Diego. Three of the four involve women composers…. The Sunday matinee opener of Omar enjoyed a full house, with plaudits running close to double the four minutes penciled in by management….No protesters were seen inside or out, despite the current Middle-East warfare.
