articles.text: San Francisco Opera is premiering the opera Omar, with performances at the War Memorial Opera House through November 21. Written by Rhiannon Giddens and Michael Abels, it won the Pulitzer Prize in music this year. Omar is inspired by the true story of Islamic scholar Omar ibn Said, who was taken from his home in West Africa in 1807 and sold into slavery in South Carolina. While enslaved for his entire life, he wrote a series of Arabic-language works on history and theology. Said eventually chronicled his life into an autobiography, which Giddens and Abels drew heavily from to create the opera. Giddens’ libretto includes West African kora, bluegrass, spirituals, folk music and jazz. The opera is sung in English and Arabic with English supertitles. Tenor Jamez McCorkle sings the title role, with Taylor Raven as Fatima, Daniel Okulitch as Johnson, Brittany Renee as Julie, and Norman Garr as Abdul, Omar’s Pulitzer prize-winning composer Rhiannon Giddens. brother. The opera premiered at the Spoleto Festival in Italy in 2022. The creative team behind Omar is choreographer Kiara Benn, set designer Amy Rubin, costume designers April M. Hickman and Micheline Russell-Brown, lighting designer Pablo Santiago and projection designer Joshua Higgason. One hour before every performance music scholar Michael Mohammed will present an overview of the opera. Following select performances of Omar on November 11, 15, 17 and 21, audience members are invited to stay for a post-show conversation with the singers and the creative team. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com
articles.title: SF Opera presents Omar now through Nov. 21

articles.text: Cal Performances presents the award-winning Brad Mehldau Trio at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus this Saturday, November 11. The trio consists of Mehldau on piano, Larry Grenadier on bass, and Jeff Ballard on drums. Mehldau’s trio has been praised for its musical chemistry and wide range of stylistic and emotional terrain. Mehldau is an iconic jazz soloist in his own right. The New Yorker called him “arguably the greatest working jazz pianist,” with the touch of Bill Evans and the range of Keith Jarrett. He is also well-known for his jazz renditions of rock music, including hits by the Beatles and Neil Young. He has won a Grammy award for best contemporary instrumental album and was nominated for 13 other Grammies over his three-decade career. The 8 p.m. concert will include an evening of original compositions as well as reimagined jazz standards. Tickets are available at www. calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday through Friday, 12 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. and weekends from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. Pianist Brad Mehldau
articles.title: Brad Mehldau Trio at Zellerbach this Saturday

articles.text: Tickets to San Francisco Ballet’s annual performances of Nutcracker are on sale now, with performances December 13-30. San Francisco Ballet was the first company in the United States to present an annual holiday Nutcracker. The holiday favorite includes more than 150 dancers accompanied by the Ballet Orchestra performing Tchaikovsky’s classic score. Ar tistic Director Helgi Tomasson’s Nutcracker originally premiered the ballet in 2004 and it follows the same basic formula nearly 20 years later. The story begins on a foggy Christmas Eve in 1915, with Drosselmeyer putting the finishing touches on a magical nutcracker doll. It’s his gift for the Stahlbaum family, who have invited him to join their holiday festivities. Customers drop by his shop for last-minute Christmas gifts and Drosselmeyer shows them toys and clocks. Later, outside the Stahlbaum house, as people hurry home to their Christmas revelries, Drosselmeyer arrives with his beautifully wrapped present. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan, costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz, lighting design is by James F. Ingalls and projection design is by Wendall K. Harrington. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/nutcracker/ to learn more and to purchase tickets. San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker begins on December 13.
articles.title: Tickets to SF Ballet’s Nutcracker now on sale

articles.text: Artist Michael Stehr, a Piedmont native, has unveiled his recent paintings in an exhibit, titled “Going the Distance – Depicting Space on a Two-Dimensional Plane”. The show is on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through November 19. About Michael Stehr Michael received his degree in Art History from Stanford in 1991, where the focus of his study was on Michelangelo and the Italian Baroque period. Since then his love of art history has affected almost every facet of his professional life. He started his own business, Sistine Chapel Art and Art History, in 1992. This enterprise has him delivering lectures, guiding annual art history tours to Rome and Paris, offering an annual exhibition of his traditional oil paintings, and executing custom residential interior paint finishes, including murals, gold leafing, and colored plasters. In 2014, Michael had an international showing of his art with 14 paintings on display in Rome that celebrated his love for the Eternal City. Borghese Gardens with White Flowers, oil on canvas by Michael Stehr. Piedmont artist Michael Stehr Michael lives in Oakland with his wife Maryanne, his daughter Emily, and son Jack. Thirty-five new paintings are included among the 80 total paintings being shown. The show opened last weekend, November 4. To preview the exhibit online, go to www.bit.ly/3ZO1Urc.
articles.title: Michael Stehr art exhibit on view at Center for the Arts

articles.text: Let’s get in our time machine and go back more than 170 years. It all began in the 1850s. Just a few years later, it was the most popular resort in the Los Angeles area. During the 1890s it was the port of Los Angeles. The Southern Pacific Railroad maintained a wooden pier that extended almost one mile into the Santa Monica Bay. During the roaring 20s when silent movies flourished, the Keystone Cops filmed their antics just up the hill. Prohibition brought a few speakeasies, and Hollywood stars liked to go there because nobody annoyed them. Santa Monica Canyon was just about the coolest place there was. The interesting thing is that it retains its allure, and many of the original buildings remain in place. The entire business district of Pacific Palisades is exactly one block in circumference. As you walk, you will find anything to please your taste. Not so long ago there were two mom and pop motels. My parents had one. Prices started at $3.50 per room. These small motels are gone now; however, there is a bed-and-breakfast place just up the street. Prices are considerably higher than they were in my childhood, no surprise. If you go there, you can check out the Channel Road Inn or find something in Santa Monica, which is just a few minutes away. Santa Monica Canyon is located between Santa Monica and Pacific Palisades. In the old days, there were some really interesting local characters. Sam “the Greek“ operated a small restaurant at the corner of Pacific Coast Highway and W. Channel Rd. He had the best clam chowder ever. My father told me that there used to be meetings with some prominent California politicians and Sam. The dealings were not exactly on the up and up. There was another restaurant in the middle of the block, operated by Louie “the Frenchman” and his wife. This location became one of the most famous restaurants in the entire Los Angeles area, Sam’s By the Beach. Sam got an offer he couldn’t refuse and retired at an early age. Another restaurant will open in its place. It will be the Museum Restaurant. I will write a review after it opens in March next year. At the opposite end of the block is a classic American steakhouse, the Golden Bull. Across the street is a delightfully picturesque food truck, Rustic Coffee. The coffee is superb as are the entrées, and the owner makes fantastic scones. A few stores down the street is one of the finest Italian restaurants in the U.S., Cafe Delfini. My son and I ate there twice and were delighted with the cuisine, and the prices are moderate. The restaurant is jampacked almost every night, but don’t worry – the maître d’ will find a place for you. Alex, the owner who is from Rome, drops by every table during the evening to chat a little bit. For lunch, you’ll want to go to Patrick’s Café. It’s a funky-looking place, but the food is excellent American cuisine. If you want some exercise, there is a well-appointed gym about a one-minute walk from the beach. At the beach you can play volleyball or go roller skating or do some jogging. The ocean is excellent for swimming because the waves are gentle. If you want to go surfing, you’ll need to go to Malibu. I hate to mention it, but that former speakeasy is now a super loud Rock and Roll bar. There really is something for everybody. Next Week: Dateline New Orleans. Stay tuned for comments on cuisine and jazz. The Rustic Coffee truck has great breakfasts. It is on W. Channel Road, one block from the Pacific Ocean. ®
articles.title: A magical experience

The interesting thing is that it retains its allure, and many of the original buildings remain in place. The entire business district of Pacific Palisades is exactly one block in circumference. As you walk, you will find anything to please your taste. Not so long ago there were two mom and pop motels. My parents had one. Prices started at $3.50 per room. These small motels are gone now; however, there is a bed-and-breakfast place just up the street. Prices are considerably higher than they were in my childhood, no surprise. If you go there, you can check out the Channel Road Inn or find something in Santa Monica, which is just a few minutes away. Santa Monica Canyon is located between Santa Monica and Pacific Palisades. In the old days, there were some really interesting local characters. Sam “the Greek“ operated a small restaurant at the corner of Pacific Coast Highway and W. Channel Rd. He had the best clam chowder ever. My father told me that there used to be meetings with some prominent California politicians and Sam. The dealings were not exactly on the up and up. There was another restaurant in the middle of the block, operated by Louie “the Frenchman” and his wife. This location became one of the most famous restaurants in the entire Los Angeles area, Sam’s By the Beach. Sam got an offer he couldn’t refuse and retired at an early age. Another restaurant will open in its place. It will be the Museum Restaurant. I will write a review after it opens in March next year. At the opposite end of the block is a classic American steakhouse, the Golden Bull. Across the street is a delightfully picturesque food truck, Rustic Coffee. The coffee is superb as are the entrées, and the owner makes fantastic scones. A few stores down the street is one of the finest Italian restaurants in the U.S., Cafe Delfini. My son and I ate there twice and were delighted with the cuisine, and the prices are moderate. The restaurant is jampacked almost every night, but don’t worry – the maître d’ will find a place for you. Alex, the owner who is from Rome, drops by every table during the evening to chat a little bit. For lunch, you’ll want to go to Patrick’s Café. It’s a funky-looking place, but the food is excellent American cuisine. If you want some exercise, there is a well-appointed gym about a one-minute walk from the beach. At the beach you can play volleyball or go roller skating or do some jogging. The ocean is excellent for swimming because the waves are gentle. If you want to go surfing, you’ll need to go to Malibu. I hate to mention it, but that former speakeasy is now a super loud Rock and Roll bar. There really is something for everybody. Next Week: Dateline New Orleans. Stay tuned for comments on cuisine and jazz. Borghese Gardens with White Flowers, oil on canvas by Michael Stehr. The show opened last weekend, November 4. To preview the exhibit online, go to www.bit.ly/3ZO1Urc. The Rustic Coffee truck has great breakfasts. It is on W. articles.text: Achille Bocus, Musical Director of the San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, will be the featured soloist this Saturday, November 11 at 5 pm. in the rarely performed Concerto for Mandolin in B flat by Neapolitan composer Giuseppe Giuliano (1720-1776) at Piedmont Center for the Arts. According to Bocus, “Giuliano was composing in the mid 1700s in Naples, featuring a relatively new classical string instrument at the time – the mandolin. We’re delighted to bring this work to our audiences, as it’s a fantastic example of the kind of classical period piece that followed the baroque period and foreshadowed to the later more complex work of Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, and others.” Raised in Milan, Italy, Bocus studied mandolin, double bass, electric bass, composition and conducting. Following his studies he went on to play double bass with some of the finest symphonic, operatic and chamber music orchestras in Italy, performing throughout Europe. From 2005-2008 he was conductor of the Orchestra a Plettro Citta di Milano. He moved to the San Francisco Bay Area in 2009 and began teaching mandolin to students throughout the Bay Area with his “Il Tremolo” method, He created SF Mandolin Orchestra at that time. The Piedmont concert on November 11 will feature music from the late baroque and classical periods on a theme of “Napoli and the Revolution.” In addition to the Giuliano Concerto, the orchestra will perform: • Selections from Johann Sebastian Bach’s Art of the Fugue • Selections from Wolfgang Mozart’s London Notebook • Giovanni Battista Sammartini’s Sinfonia in G Major for String Orchestra The family-friendly concert will begin at 5:00 p.m. on Saturday, November 11. Admission is $20 general, $15 student/senior, and free for children 12 and under. Tickets may be purchased at the door, or at the Orchestra’s ticketing site: sfmandolin.square.site. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: Shailene Woodley in Adrift Before you watch Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is, in retrospect, two stories. The first – and I’m imposing something that doesn’t exist in the film – is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), both in their twenties. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Clafin),. He has just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, all awash in color and easy-does-it people. Their world is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together and their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them far off the grid. Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45-foote from Tahiti to San Diego. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class plane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave their boat in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film. This is a compellingly entertaining film, especially wellacted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Know that you don’t ever need to have stepped topside on a teak deck to become lost in Adrift. It’s an amazing film. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on VUDU/hulu/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: One Day relies on a familiar Hollywood trope: two attractive young people meet, have a strong mutual attraction, one often denied or ignored. Their lives ebb and flow and occasionally intersect. They may spend quality time together, best buds of a sort. And yet, they are unwilling to speak truthfully to one another about feelings and chemistry that are evident to the audience but only hinted at by them. It’s a sturdy template, recent examples being Definitely, Maybe; Made of Honor; Love and Other Drugs; and Friends With Benefits. And not to forget the brilliant 1989 rom-com When Harry Met Sally. In the compelling One Day, on the eve of their 1988 graduation from Glasgow University, Emma Morley (Anne Hathaway) and Dexter Mayhew (Jim Sturgess), fueled by celebratory alcohol, fall into bed. They are, however, suddenly overwhelmed by their mutual awkwardness and so they scuttle the plan to consummate what is a budding acquaintance and agree to be friends – but friends without benefits. And so the film becomes episodic, capturing one day each year when they reconnect, always on July 15. Over two decades, through stop and start jobs and careers, they meet, sometimes with good cheer, sometimes in despair. But they manage to meet. This is the source of the film’s charm; however, it’s also the source of its greatest weakness. Because their relationship has no real narrative arc – they only share 20 days together in a span of 20 years – there is no strong sense of a growing intimacy, ad distinctly no sense of urgency. Their conversations are, because of the constraints of time, often truncated, elliptical, but always rich with possibilities. As individuals, Emma and Dexter are ever appealing. But as a couple, their relationship seems a bridge too far. And the moment of honesty in which they declare what they feel for each other, never quite seems to arrive. Or if it does, it is too brief. It’s what the audience has been waiting for: that singular July 15th day, however fragile, when they overcome their hesitations and insecurities and grab onto one another as if their lives depended on it. Instead the movie begins to feel like two decades of speed dating – in first gear. It is, of course, those wonderful, disjointed vignettes that lead to a final act that holds the promise of being a culmination. What occurs is stunning and unexpected and it will be up to the audience to decide whether it is manipulative and heavy handed or a compelling transition to a long denouement. One Day. Directed by Lorie Scherfig. Starring Anne Hathaway, Jim Sturgess, Patricia Clarkson. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Furious 7 It’s hard to believe but this behemoth of a franchise, Furious, parts 1-7, started some 14 year ago. That was well before sequels morphed into franchises, which have become a staple of most Hollywood studios. Producers and writers in the last decade have counted on audiences viewing one installment and almost instantly beginning to wait for the next. It’s the equivalent of those old Republic Studios Saturday afternoon matinees that treated young audiences to Indiana Jones-type adventures, always careful to interrupt the action just as the hero was in serious jeopardy (driving off a cliff while duking it out with the bad guys in the rear seat of a very large black Packard), The screen suddenly filled with the promise: “To Be Continued!” Fast and Furious 1 found a recipe that worked (who knew?) and kept right on going. Dominic Toretto (Vin Diesel) was the quintessential heavy. His sister, Mia Toretto (Jordana Brewster), the attractive love interest for the charismatic Brian O’Connor (Paul Walker), who began the Furious journey as an undercover cop, but soon became part of what Dom refers to repeatedly as his “family.” Brian and Dominic are both serious gearheads. In truth, some of the most attractive characters in the franchise are cars – often vintage muscle cars, impeccably restored, their massive engines all tricked out with blowers, carbs and nitro injection. Some are heavily modified Japanese factory cars in jellybean colors with spoilers and power to spare. In other words, each film is all about frenetic speed, saturated with brio. Most fans would be hard pressed to recall the narratives of the last seven films. What remains unforgettable, however, are the countless set pieces that not only involve gorgeous cars going very, very fast, but lots of gravity defying stunts that take your breath away. Reactions are: Did they really just do that? Cars parachuting out of a perfectly good airplane? No worries. Driving under semi-tractors at high speeds? Yep. Tell me they didn’t just wreck that incredible black/oxblood red vintage Charger? Indeed. And as CGI has improved over the last decade – one could argue that techies have dominated one very large corner of Hollywood movies, to include anything made from the comics or SciFi/fantasy – the action scenes have only gotten better. Outrageously better. Sure, you have to suspend your disbelief when watching Furious, but where’s the fun if you don’t? There is embedded in Furious 7 an inherent sadness that makes the film all the more poignant. Brian is now a family man married to Mia with one son and another on the way. Mia worries that Brian “misses the bullets” – the adrenalin rush of hanging out with Dom while barely slipping out of some very tight spots. After the death of lead actor Paul Walker, it was only with the help of the techies and body doubles that “7” was seamlessly completed. Will there be an 8? Absolutely. Until we run out of high-octane fuel. Will the stories matter? Not in the least. These movies are not about tightly structured narratives. Ultimately, it’s all about the ride. Furious 7. Starring Vin Diesel, Paul Walker, Jason Statham and Michelle Rodriquez. Directed by James Wan. 2 hrs., 20 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: If there was life left in this long-running franchise, which came perilously close to jumping the shark, it had to reside with X-Men, the early years, long before the mutant heroes were galvanized into a world-saving, shape-shifting crew. First Class, based on the iconic Marvel comic books created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, has arrived and proves to be good entertainment. It’s always interesting to ask why mutants, aka Superheroes, have such generational appeal, seeming to resonate decade after decade, going back to the 1930s. It was 1963 when Lee and Kirby revealed a series of contemporary mutants: Spider-Man, the Hulk, Iron Man, the Fantastic Four, and, of course, the X-Men, all following their antecedents: DC’s Superman (why is it hard to think of Superman as a mutant?) and Batman (a man with lots of suspend your disbelief gadgets and a great costume), to name just two. Actually, the list of those with extraordinary powers is huge, creating a comic book genre that has had countless incarnations. X-Men: First Class includes all the usual suspects. Only younger. Think of this as X-Men: The Backstory. And, of course, there is the resident villain, pre-Magneto, played nicely by Kevin Bacon. The film opens in a Nazi concentration camp in 1944 and stretches to the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 when the U.S. and Russia played a serious game of chicken. The X-Men fans – and their numbers are considerable – should find this film solidly entertaining, Consider it a yearbook of their heroes. It has a globe-totting plot, beginning in Germany and then Russia, Miami, Argentina, London and Las Vegas. Of course, these films increasingly take advantage of stateof-the art special effects. Filmmakers doing comic books and graphic novels must worship at the shrine of CGI. Or at least genuflect. There is nothing that the writers from DC and Marvel can put on paper that the special effects folks can’t put on the screen with stunning realism, creating stories that teens and pre-teens will enjoy with jaw-dropping enthrallment. Tangentially, it’s hard not to think of these films as being a bit camp, bordering on kitsch. Mutants? Really? But then it’s unlikely a tween/teen out there can’t identify with these characters in some way. It’s not easy growing up, convinced you’re different and out of sorts among your peer group. There are times when mutant superpowers would come in handy, say, walking down the middle school hall while mind reading. Is it a stretch then to think of Harry Potter, magician extraordinaire, and all the residents of Hogwarts as mutants? X-Men: First Class. Directed by Matthew Vaughn. Starring James McAvoy, Michael Fassbinder, January Jones, Rose Byrne, Kevin Bacon and Jennifer Lawrence. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated: PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. It was 1963 when Lee and Kirby revealed a series of contemporary mutants: Spider-Man, the Hulk, Iron Man, the Fantastic Four, and, of course, the X-Men, all following their antecedents: DC’s Superman (why is it hard to think of Superman as a mutant?) and Batman (a man with lots of suspend your disbelief gadgets and a great costume), to name just two. Actually, the list of those with extraordinary powers is huge, creating a comic book genre that has had countless incarnations. X-Men: First Class includes all the usual suspects. Only younger. Think of this as X-Men: The Backstory. And, of course, there is the resident villain, pre-Magneto, played nicely by Kevin Bacon. The film opens in a Nazi concentration camp in 1944 and stretches to the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 when the U.S. and Russia played a serious game of chicken. The X-Men fans – and their numbers are considerable – should find this film solidly entertaining, Consider it a yearbook of their heroes. It has a globe-totting plot, beginning in Germany and then Russia, Miami, Argentina, London and Las Vegas. Of course, these films increasingly take advantage of stateof-the art special effects. Filmmakers doing comic books and graphic novels must worship at the shrine of CGI. Or at least genuflect. There is nothing that the writers from DC and Marvel can put on paper that the special effects folks can’t put on the screen with stunning realism, creating stories that teens and pre-teens will enjoy with jaw-dropping enthrallment. Tangentially, it’s hard not to think of these films as being a bit camp, bordering on kitsch. Mutants? Really? But then it’s unlikely a tween/teen out there can’t identify with these characters in some way. It’s not easy growing up, convinced you’re different and out of sorts among your peer group. There are times when mutant superpowers would come in handy, say, walking down the middle school hall while mind reading. Is it a stretch then to think of Harry Potter, magician extraordinaire, and all the residents of Hogwarts as mutants? X-Men: First Class. Directed by Matthew Vaughn. Starring James McAvoy, Michael Fassbinder, January Jones, Rose Byrne, Kevin Bacon and Jennifer Lawrence. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated: PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Furious 7 – the film franchise keeps going and going Michael Fassbender as Magneto in X-Men: First Class A scene from Furious 7 By Chris Honoré It’s hard to believe but this behemoth of a franchise, Furious, parts 1-7, started some 14 year ago. That was well before sequels morphed into franchises, which have become a staple of most Hollywood studios. Producers and writers in the last decade have counted on audiences viewing one installment and almost instantly beginning to wait for the next. It’s the equivalent of those old Republic Studios Saturday afternoon matinees that treated young audiences to Indiana Jones-type adventures, always careful to interrupt the action just as the hero was in serious jeopardy (driving off a cliff while duking it out with the bad guys in the rear seat of a very large black Packard), The screen suddenly filled with the promise: “To Be Continued!” Fast and Furious 1 found a recipe that worked (who knew?) and kept right on going. Dominic Toretto (Vin Diesel) was the quintessential heavy. His sister, Mia Toretto (Jordana Brewster), the attractive love interest for the charismatic Brian O’Connor (Paul Walker), who began the Furious journey as an undercover cop, but soon became part of what Dom refers to repeatedly as his “family.” Brian and Dominic are both serious gearheads. In truth, some of the most attractive characters in the franchise are cars – often vintage muscle cars, impeccably restored, their massive engines all tricked out with blowers, carbs and nitro injection. Some are heavily modified Japanese factory cars in jellybean colors with spoilers and power to spare. In other words, each film is all about frenetic speed, saturated with brio. Most fans would be hard pressed to recall the narratives of the last seven films. What remains unforgettable, however, are the countless set pieces that not only involve gorgeous cars going very, very fast, but lots of gravity defying stunts that take your breath away. Reactions are: Did they really just do that? Cars parachuting out of a perfectly good airplane? No worries. Driving under semi-tractors at high speeds? Yep. Tell me they didn’t just wreck that incredible black/oxblood red vintage Charger? Indeed. And as CGI has improved over the last decade – one could argue that techies have dominated one very large corner of Hollywood movies, to include anything made from the comics or SciFi/fantasy – the action scenes have only gotten better. Outrageously better. Sure, you have to suspend your disbelief when watching Furious, but where’s the fun if you don’t? There is embedded in Furious 7 an inherent sadness that makes the film all the more poignant. Brian is now a family man married to Mia with one son and another on the way. Mia worries that Brian “misses the bullets” – the adrenalin rush of hanging out with Dom while barely slipping out of some very tight spots. After the death of lead actor Paul Walker, it was only with the help of the techies and body doubles that “7” was seamlessly completed. Will there be an 8? Absolutely. Until we run out of high-octane fuel. Will the stories matter? Not in the least. These movies are not about tightly structured narratives. Ultimately, it’s all about the ride. Furious 7. Starring Vin Diesel, Paul Walker, Jason Statham and Michelle Rodriquez. Directed by James Wan. 2 hrs., 20 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Part 4 in a series In the Post’s ongoing search for filmmakers in Piedmont or with Piedmont roots, we discovered Piedmont resident Jessie Deeter, a highly accomplished documentary film producer. Her academic background includes a Masters in Journalism from U.C. Berkeley, and a separate Masters from Berkeley in International Studies with a Middle East focus. She has been producing, reporting, and shooting documentaries for more than two decades. Jessie got her start in documentary filmmaking as an associate producer working on different projects for Frontline and Frontline/World, the acclaimed PNS programs, and has also produced stories for Al Jazeera As a Fulbright scholar in Oman, Morocco, she began working on the documentary A Revolution in Four Seasons, about the Tunisian revolution during the Arab Spring. It is told from the perspective of two Tunisians with very different perspectives. It premiered at Hot Docs in 2016 and has since been screened worldwide. Deeter’s nominated and award-winning filmography is rich and varied. For example, working with Oscar-winning director, Alex Gibney, she produced the Emmy-nominated HBO documentary Out for Blood in Silicon Valley that told the story of Elizabeth Holmes, her meteoric rise and the scandalous fall of her company Theranos. The film premiered at Sundance in 2019. She co-directed and produced the chilling documentary Keep Quiet And Forgive, which tells the story of Amish survivors of sexual abuse. It was the recipient of ITVS’ Open Call funding in 2021 and is still in development. Deeter also produced the prescient Do You Trust This Computer? Released by Elon Musk, it explores the now timely issue of Artificial Intelligence. and can be viewed on Vimeo. Working with director Chris Paine, she produced two environmentally relevant documentaries, Who Killed the Electric Car? and the subsequent Revenge of the Electric Car. Both films examined the initial demise of the budding technology involved in the radical design changes required to transition vehicles from gasoline to rechargeable batteries, and its later unanticipated resurrection. Revenge debuted at the Tribeca Film Festival on New York and was aired by the PBS’ show Independent Lens in 2018. Relying on the zeitgeist of documentary filmmaking, Jessie produced the extraordinary Spark: A Burning Man Story that does a deep dive behind the scenes of the annual Burning Man Festival in the desert in Northern Nevada. It debuted at the SouthXSouthwest Film Festival in 2013 and later aired on Showtime. Deeter also produced the penetrating documentary Death By Fire that asks the question of whether the state of Texas executed an innocent man. Cameron Todd Willingham was convicted of deadly arson based on questionable investigative expertise and testimony. The film debuted on PBS’ 2010 Frontline season and has been aired several times since. Deeter is currently working on three documentaries: one on Bitcoin; a run-up to the Tokyo Olympics that will feature the equine horse sport of Eventing; and a documentary on Elon Musk. Peter Sohn, Pixar Also in our search for Piedmont filmmakers the name of the remarkable Peter Sohn rose to the top. He is an award-winning Pixar filmmaker, animator, and voice actor. He graduated from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts), and briefly worked for Walt Disney and Warner Bros. Studios where he worked with director Brad Bird on the animated feature The Iron Giant. In 2000, Sohn joined Pixar Animation Studios, where he has contributed to a panoply of acclaimed film projects. Early on Sohn was involved Animator and voice actor Peter Sohn Documentarian Jessie Deeter in creating the much-praised animated features Finding Nemo, The Incredibles and WALL-E, and directed the short film Partly Cloudy that was included in the Animation Show of Shorts. He went on to voice the character Emile in the animated feature Ratatouille, as well as voicing Squishy in Monsters University and Sox in Lightyear. He also directed the films The Good Dinosaur and the recently released Elemental, which debuted at the Cannes Film Festival. It is clear that his filmography is extensive and varied. For example, he co-directed the English-language version of Ponyo with John Lasseter and Brad Lewis and contributed to the highly regarded animated features Inside Out, Finding Dory, Onward, Soul, Cars 3, Toy Story 4, Soul, Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, and the anticipated Inside Out 2 and Elio. He was born in Brooklyn, N.Y. and is married to Anna Chambers whom he met at CalArts. They have two children. Why film? All of the above is testimony to the strong appeal of film and filmmaking, hence it is not by chance that the Piedmont Post includes weekly coverage of a spectrum of movies. For more than a century, the ever morphing technology of filmmaking – from grainy, flickering black and white silent images, to the extraordinary CGI-driven large screen representations in crisp colors and enhanced by Dolby surround sound – has found worldwide appeal. It’s a compelling, dynamic medium. And coming soon to a sofa near you is streaming. And not to forget A.I. Let’s face it, as a species we love to be told a story, both real and surreal. It’s it’s not a stretch to imagine our antecedents gathered around a warming fire listening to an elder tell a captivating, harrowing, or wonderfully embellished tale. And thus was born, with a cascade of stars filling an ancient sky, the promise of film.

articles.text: With the price of French Champagne and some American sparkling wines going through the roof, the world is in serious need of good sparkling wine that does not break the bank, especially when you are having a party that will require multiple bottles of wine. When it comes to good value in table wines, Argentina has always been a good place to look, especially for red wines. And now we find the Argentines working their price to quality magic on sparkling wines. Domaine Bousquet was founded by Jean Bousquet whose family had made wine in the Languedoc region of France for four generations. After taking a vacation in Argentina in 1990, he decided to start a winery in the Mendoza region, specifically the Tupungato district of the Uco Valley. With altitudes up to 5200 feet, the climate is chilly but has lots of sunlight. Today Domaine Bousquet produces 4 million liters of wine a year and exports 95% of its volume to more than 50 countries. All wines are made with certified organic grapes. Domaine Bousquet Brut, $18 Made in the Methode Traditionnelle, the Brut is scented of baked apples and caramel with creamy, flinty touches. The palate is soft and creamy, with a deep core of apple fruit that balances the expansive, savory accents, and it finishes long and flinty. Perfect for drinking over the next 5 years. Domaine Bousquet Rose, $18 Medium salmon-pink in color the Rose is scented strawberries mushrooms and brioche with nutty tones. The palate balances bright berry fruits and. Savory tones, supported by creamy mousse, bright freshness and flinty tones on the long finish.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 8, 2023 23 Features Turning 65? Know your Medicare options If you will soon be 65 and you don’t have health insurance through your employer or your spouse’s plan, you’ll need to start looking into Medicare – so you should know your options. And your first big choice will likely be whether to go with original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Which is right for you? For starters, there’s no one “correct” answer for everyone. Your choice will depend on a variety of factors, including your own health care needs, financial situation, preference for a particular provider, and so on. In any case, you’ll need to know the basics of the two programs to even begin evaluating your options. Here’s a quick overview: Original Medicare Original Medicare includes Part A (hospital insurance) and Part B (medical insurance for doctor’s visits and covered preventive services). You pay about $165 per month for Part B (or possibly more, depending on your income level). You can then choose to add Part D, which covers prescription drugs, for about $40 per month and Medigap, which may cost between $150 - $250 per month to cover gaps in Parts A and B. You may also want to pay for private coverage for dental and vision care. Medicare Advantage Medicare Advantage, also known as Part C, is offered by private plans and essentially replaces Medicare Parts A, B and Medigap. Because you must stay enrolled in Medicare Part B with Medicare Advantage, you pay the same $165 per month as you would in Medicare (again, subject to additional charges for higher incomes). Some Medicare Advantage plans have no premiums, while others may charge up to about $60 per month. Most Medicare Advantage plans include prescription coverage and many also include dental and vision. It’s not always possible to make an apples-to-apples comparison of Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage. Generally speaking, if you have Original Medicare with Part D and Medigap, you could expect less restrictive networks, making it easier to see the doctors of your choice, and less restrictive coverage – that is, you might be less likely to need pre-authorization for certain services as you might with Medicare Advantage. Furthermore, unlike Medigap plans, Medicare Advantage plans are not standardized – there’s a great deal of variation in provider networks, drug coverage, premiums, deductibles, copays/coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximums. And some plans have reputations for denying claims. When you’re shopping around for Medicare Advantage plans, you may want to talk to your friends and relatives who have them. You might also ask your doctors about their office’s experience with different Advantage plans regarding coverage of treatments and prompt payment of claims. And you might want to visit www. medicare.gov/plan-compare for help in finding plans. (For other Medicare-related questions, you could contact your state’s State Health Insurance Assistance Program at www.shiphelp.org.) One last point to keep in mind: Each year, during the open enrollment period, which, in 2023, runs from October 15 through December 7, you can switch from Original Medicare and Medigap to Medicare Advantage, or vice versa. However, if you switch to Medicare Advantage, you may face limits and restrictions on returning to your Medigap plan, should you ever desire to do so. As you can see, choosing the right type of Medicare coverage will take some research and comparisons – so leave yourself enough time to make the selection that best fits your needs. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a Financial Advisor in the Piedmont office of Edward Jones at 370 Highland. Avenue, Suite 201. Tel. 547-4589. E-mail: TJ.Stevko@edwardjones.com. articles.text: Nancy Lee Martz, a resident of Piedmont for 58 years, passed away peacefully at her home on Thursday, October 26, 2023. She was 88 years young. Nancy lived a full and colorful life surrounded by lifelong friends — contributing her time to different interests and hobbies, being an extraordinary wife, a fiercely loyal friend to all, and arguably the absolute greatest mom ever. Born on December 7, 1934, in Sacramento, she was the daughter of John and Dorothy Bagdanoff. An only child with a penchant for books and exploration, Nancy quickly realized that Sacramento was a jumping-off point to something bigger. After attending Sacramento State for two years, she transferred to the University of California at Berkeley in 1954 and soon thereafter became a proud member of the Sigma Kappa sorority. After graduating from Cal in 1956, Nancy moved to San Francisco and began working at the J. Walter Thompson advertising agency. Nancy’s roommate in San Francisco, Barbara Fox Roach, also of Piedmont and a lifelong friend, would play a pivotal role in Nancy’s life, introducing Nancy to her future husband, Charles Thomas Martz, Sr. of Westfield, New Jersey. Nancy and Tom became engaged less than a year after meeting and were married in Sacramento on November 12, 1960. After living in San Francisco and Los Angeles, the couple finally settled in Piedmont in 1965, where they would live for the remainder of their lives. Nancy and Tom became members at Claremont Country Club in 1971, where Nancy honed her tennis game and eventually, much to the surprise of Tom, became quite an accomplished golfer. In her golf career she had three holein-ones After making her first hole-in-one, she lost the ball on the next hole. Tom, ever the sportsman, explained to Nancy the significance of putting the hole-in-one ball on display in a case. The next time she made a hole in one, she merely handed him the ball without mentioning why. When asked, “What’s this?” Nancy replied with a smile, “I made sure not to lose the ball this time!” Nancy served as Captain of the Claremont Women Golfers, successfully played for Claremont Country Club’s East Bay Team Play team, and partnered with Tom to win four Mixed-4-Ball titles, to name just a few of her accomplishments. She loved golf and the incredible friendships she Nancy Martz died at home in Piedmont on October 26. She was 88. made through playing the game. Off the sports field, Nancy was an incredible cook. Her love of cooking and her ability to create thoughtful culinary presentations was the impetus to launch a successful catering business with her two partners, Diane Anderson and Linda Arellano. The business lasted over a decade. Her prized recipe collection is filled with very technical descriptions and precise instructions such as “a pinch of,” a “squoosh of,” and the ever-present “just a dash to taste.” One commitment close to Nancy’s heart was her volunteer work with the Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale. Nancy served on the Public Relations and Media Committee for several years and devoted hundreds of hours over decades to this highly successful annual event. Nancy also cherished being involved in various other clubs and groups, including the Hoe and Hope Garden Club, her book club, different bridge groups, the San Francisco Ballet, and the San Francisco Symphony. Nancy is survived by her son Kyle and daughter Jane. She will now be enjoying a family reunion in Heaven with her son Tom Jr. and her husband of 54 years, Tom Sr. The family expresses its deepest thanks to Nancy’s caregiver, Kalesita Leslie Tupou, who watched over her and loved her wholeheartedly. Leslie and her husband Petui Mailau also cared for Tom Sr. in his last months and should be regarded as earthly angels for their devotion to others, including the Martz family. A Celebration of Life will be held at a later date, with details to follow. In place of flowers, the family suggests making a memorial donation in her name to a charity of choice, and make a point of telling those close to you how much you love them.

articles.text: In previous columns, I have written about Wallace Alexander, Piedmont’s benefactor. In 1913, he gathered several successful Piedmont businessmen to purchase land opposite Piedmont Park, and hired Albert Farr to design the Piedmont Commercial Center, the first stores in Piedmont. Alexander also saved Piedmont Park from development in 1921 by purchasing the land (when the city had no funds) and selling it back to the city the following year. After the 1906 earthquake and fire, many San Franciscan residents fled to Oakland and the Piedmont hills and built new homes. By the 1910s, Piedmont’s population was expanding rapidly. Just as these residents needed a grocery store, they were also outgrowing Mowbray Hall, the 1908 Sunday School, and needed a church. When Wallace Alexander led a group of residents to purchase land for the commercial center, he also purchased an adjacent 1-1/2 acres and offered that land for a church. Alexander then hired Albert Farr to design it and construction began in 1916. Piedmont residents who contributed to the construction of the facility came from all faiths, and interdenominational services would be held in the new church. Albert Farr called his design “Mission” or “Spanish Colonial” and credited Junipero Serra and Jose Churriguera as his inspirations. He designed the church around a courtyard with a central fountain and an outdoor pulpit (now gone). Farr claimed the tiered fountain was an exact replica of an old Spanish fountain at the Santa Barbara Mission. The courtyard was to be planted with shrubs and was designed to be a resting place for all during the week. Farr designed the sanctuary with a domed ceiling, seating for 300, antique lamps, decorative screens to conceal the mechanisms of the organ, and elaborately carved Churrigueresque doors. He designed the south side The Piedmont Interdenominational Church sanctuary in 1918 with its dome, beamed ceiling and antique lamps. Gain and Loss of New France Explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in Newfoundland and the St. Lawrence River in 1534 to look again for a Northwest Passage. Cartier is credited with starting a few settlements, as well as originating the claims of New France and The Country of Canada. Several settlements were built at modern day Quebec City, but didn’t coalesce until a few outposts took root along the St. Lawrence River Valley. French farming was limited in scale with greater attention to establishing outposts for fur trading and attracting native Americans who were trappers. The native tribes allied readily with the French who, unlike the Brits, were not fencing off hunting grounds. At its peak in the early 1700s, New France had amassed territory from Newfoundland to the Rocky Mountains, and from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico, to include the Great Lakes. Several major French settlements are alive today, including Quebec; La Baye des Puants (Green Bay); Ville-Marie (Montreal); Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit (Detroit); La Nouvelle Orléans (New Orleans); and Baton Rouge. But France lagged far behind England’s colonization of America and was hindered by the paucity of settlements across such a large territory. In the span of 230 years (1534 to 1763) on the North American continent, France did not dominate. Throughout history the French reign as a premiere European nation, or its leader. In colonizing the New World, France had largely claimed Canada and the Great Lakes, while Britain held the 13 colonies. But frontier tenThe French Era in the New World from the date that Jacques Cartier declared New France to the end of the French and Indian War, 1634-1763. sion over control in the Upper Ohio River Valley boiled over in the mid-1700s between Britain, France, and the native American tribes. The Battle of Fort Duquesne in 1758 ignited the French and Indian War, a seven-year conflict ending in France’s loss of its eastern American territories. Initially, the French and tribal native Americans at Fort Duquesne (near Pittsburgh) were regularly defeating the British troops. After years of skirmishes, a full-fledged war broke out and the French were eventually ousted from the eastern U.S. territories. Known also as the Seven Year War, the French were warring against England (and Spain) in the New World colonies, which coincided with warring in Europe against Prussia, while aligned with Austria, Russia, and Sweden. Britain strategically decided to aid Prussia to weaken France in the American arena. While the multiple battlefronts dragged into a long, complicated war ending in defeat for France, the French still retained New Orleans and the Mississippi River Valley. Fifty years later, France presented a purchase opportunity to the fledgling United States of America, the Louisiana Purchase, the most significant territory expansion in the nation’s history. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, November 8, 2023 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth The United States is not typically thought of as a French country; but centuries ago, when Europe began exploring America, France claimed the Great Lakes and most of the west as New France (Nouvelle-France). However, frequent skirmishes with the British, war on five continents, and draining coffers eventually discouraged France’s sweeping claims over America and Canada. France joined the competition for New World discovery in 1524, when King Francis I dispatched Giovanni da Verrazzano to explore the region between Florida and Newfoundland, map the coastline, and find a sea passage across North America to Asia. A violent storm disrupted the journey disabling three of the four-ships in the flotilla. The one surviving ship returned to port, resupplied, and with 50 men, again set sail and made land in two months at present-day Cape Fear, North Carolina. The ship then entered Pamlico Sound, a large lagoon off the coast of North Carolina near the Outer Banks; and in seeking large open water, by the notations in the Captain’s log, the crew believed they had found it and celebrated reaching the South China Sea. Exploration nearly 500 years ago was riddled with miscalculations. Thirty years earlier, Christopher Columbus calculated the size of North America at about one third its size; and never in his lifetime did he believe he had not reached India, which is why he referred to American natives as Indians. Verrazzanno sailed to New York Bay, Long Island Sound, and explored Rhode Island before sailing up the coast to Maine and Newfoundland, where the ship was resupplied before sailing France in the New World home. French explorers after Verrazzano were chartered with the same mission: locate a sea passage across North America. None of them ever did. The Northwest Passage The famed Northwest Passage is a sea route across the continent through what now is known as the Arctic Archipelago. It comprises a string of barely populated islands entirely in the Arctic circle, and from Canada’s Baffin Island to the Beaufort Sea north of Alaska, the route is 900 miles. A 15th century search for the sea passage was never realized. Treacherous conditions of thousands of 300-foot icebergs on the water’s surface could lock a ship into the ice for months or years; and true tales of the men who died from the elements are written. articles.text: Claudius Ptolemy, geographer-astronomer-mathematician conceived of a Northwest Passage, a sea route from Europe to Asia, an idea represented on the world maps he drew in the second century A.D. Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen navigated the sea passage successfully in 1906. Climate change has now thinned the ice, and in 2007 the route for marine shipping is open for passage and requires no ice-breaking equipment. Recently, the luxury cruise industry began offering specialty tours aboard ships built for narrow passage. The U.S. considers this northern seaway to be international waters, although Canada disagrees, citing that some portions are entirely Canadian. Trading for luxury goods The powerful maritime nations – Portugal, Spain, England, the Dutch – and now France ventured forth to ally with wealthy merchants and banks in the search for valuable raw materials. Portugal during the Medieval Ages dominated the eastern sea routes to China and closely followed the west African coastline around Cape of Good Hope into the Indian Ocean. The Dutch mastered their own Eastern routes. Their supremacy was cartography, keeping maps detailed with classified State secrets benefitting only their own maritime industry. Spain was exploring and exploiting South America for gold and silver and the Caribbean for the slave trade. France was not as much interested in exploiting North America and its indigenous people as they were in seeking sea passage to Asia. They hoped to be able to cross the American continent to the Pacific Ocean and reach India and the Pacific Rim. Medieval Europe craved the riches of the Orient, and for thousands of years dating to the Roman Empire depended on the Silk Roads for luxury goods. Not only silk from China, but gems, pearls, metals, dried florals for perfume-making; opium; and spices, which were a world currency for two millenniums. As the Roman Empire declined, trade along the overland Silk Roads diminished for centuries until the Mongols conquered and then controlled Central Asia about 1200 A.D. But the Mongols lost territory and power, and to their west, the Ottomans seized North Africa, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe, including Greece, Turkey, Romania, Egypt, Hungary, and Syria. The Ottomans held power for 600 years

articles.text: On Wednesday, November 1, at approximately 3:25 p.m. two Piedmont residents were victims of an armed robbery at the corner of Monticello Avenue and Park Way. The victims were traveling home by car and upon arriving at their residence, they were confronted by two men armed with handguns. The men brandished their weapons and demanded the victims’ wallets, phones, watches, and keys. The victims immediately complied and the suspects fled on Park Way toward Highland Avenue. The vehicle was later identified as a stolen 2016 Nissan Maxima. No one was injured and the suspect vehicle has not been recovered. Piedmont Police Department is working with neighboring agencies to collect more information and apprehend the suspects. “On a local level, we continue to bring in extra officers to provide an increased presence of police officers in our community,” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “Our public safety cameras will be coming online soon to augment the ALPR cameras already in place. We continue to ask our community to report possible crime or suspicious activity and share any videos they have with us. Videos do help us with leads,” he confirmed. In the meantime, Monahan has reiterated his offer to make house calls in the area to discuss crime prevention. “Being located in a major metropolitan area, Piedmont continues to be a very safe place to live but is not immune to crime. Our CORE 4 crime prevention program continues to be full of good crime prevention techniques. In addition, if residents would like an officer to come to their home to discuss further crime prevention and reduction ideas, we are happy to make house calls.” Requests can be made to Capt. Monahan at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov, or by calling 510-420-3012. Police are still searching for a stolen 2016 Nissan Maxima used in an armed robbery on November 1.

City Hall CRIME REPORT Armed robbery at Monticello & Park Way By Matt Simons On Wednesday, November 1, at approximately 3:25 p.m. two Piedmont residents were victims of an armed robbery at the corner of Monticello Avenue and Park Way. The victims were traveling home by car and upon arriving at their residence, they were confronted by two men armed with handguns. The men brandished their weapons and demanded the victims’ wallets, phones, watches, and keys. The victims immediately complied and the suspects fled on Park Way toward Highland Avenue. The vehicle was later identified as a stolen 2016 Nissan Maxima. No one was injured and the suspect vehicle has not been recovered. Piedmont Police Department is working with neighboring agencies to collect more information and apprehend the suspects. “On a local level, we continue to bring in extra officers to provide an increased presence of police officers in our community,” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “Our public safety cameras will be coming online soon to augment the ALPR cameras already in place. We continue to ask our community to report possible crime or suspicious activity and share any videos they have with us. Videos do help us with leads,” he confirmed. In the meantime, Monahan has reiterated his offer to make house calls in the area to discuss crime prevention. “Being located in a major metropolitan area, Piedmont continues to be a very safe place to live but is not immune to crime. Our CORE 4 crime prevention program continues to be full of good crime prevention techniques. In addition, if residents would like an officer to come to their home to discuss further crime prevention and reduction ideas, we are happy to make house calls.” Requests can be made to Capt. Monahan at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov, or by calling 510-420-3012. Police are still searching for a stolen 2016 Nissan Maxima used in an armed robbery on November 1. Where in the World Are We? articles.text: The sun shone brightly on Mountain View Cemetery’s 15th Annual Pumpkin Festival on Saturday, October 28. The weather was perfect for the hundreds of kids wearing costumes. After four years of COVID-related hiatus, it felt as if the world was welcoming the festival back from an extended vacation. “It’s a great time here, it’s a beautiful day, it’s a perfect day to bring the kids and bring the family together for something really fun for everyone,” said Carol Lee, a parent at the pumpkin patch. Her husband, Chen Yan, agreed. “I love seeing all the kids in their costumes,” he said. Commenting on the festival’s return, he added. “I’m really happy because after several years of just not being able to do this, everyone’s out and having a good time again.” The greatest attraction at this year’s pumpkin festival was its Staff photo Elisha Mantione, 5, crawls through a tunnel at the festival’s pumpkin patch.

articles.text: Havens Elementary School celebrated Halloween with its traditional costume parade starting at 8:45 a.m. on Tuesday, October 31. Kids in imaginative costumes were only outdone by the bravado and creativity of their Havens teachers. Ghastly ghouls wandered the streets searching for an early morning candy snack, while parents snapped photos. Classes will be let out early all week for parent conferences, allowing the kids to rest up after the parade for trickor-treating fun at night. Havens students had a costume parade on Oakland and Highland Avenues.
articles.title: Ghouls seek safe haven at Havens Halloween parade

articles.text: A group of seven Piedmont residents have filed a lawsuit against the City of Piedmont over the dedication and restriping of the Linda Beach tennis courts as full-time pickleball courts. An attorney representing the group, Richard Drury, said that the city has unlawfully violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and that the plaintiffs are seeking an injunction to stop work on the courts as fulltime pickleball courts. “Their position is that the city has approved a project that’s going to have very significant noise impacts on nearby residents,” said Drury. He claimed that at the very least the city had a duty to conduct CEQA review before approving the project. Under CEQA, when a public agency like the city undertakes a project, it must also review the project’s impacts, disclose them to the public, impose all feasible mitigation measures, and analyze all feasible alternative locations, as well as select the environmentally superior alternative location for the project. “Instead, the city did what’s called a CEQA exemption, which means they exempted it entirely from any and all CEQA reviews,” Drury explained. “They didn’t do any environmental analysis[...] even though several experts, including the city’s own expert, suggested that there were a bunch of mitigation measures that the city should consider, like noise barriers or possibly putting [the courts] inside a noise enclosure.” Drury said his clients are currently seeking an injunction to stop the development of the Linda Beach courts until the city conducts a proper CEQA review of the project. articles.text: A Wildwood 2nd grader, Aya Crandall, correctly guessed the weight of the Wildwood Dads Club’s Giant Jack pumpkin and won free delivery of the 1036- pound pumpkin to her family’s Piedmont home. Crandall beat out 319 other guesses at this year’s Pumpkin Patch, which had a record year of more than 4,300 pumpkins sold and nearly $40,000 in sales to benefit the school. The pumpkin arrived at the Crandall residence early Tuesday morning, and quickly established itself as the grandest Halloween decoration in the neighborhood. “We don’t have any special plans for it. We are probably just going to leave it in front of the house and hopefully the squirrels don’t get to it,” said Crandall. The Crandalls are no strangers to the Wildwood Pumpkin Patch, Aya’s father Brian was president of Wildwood Dads Club when the pandemic started. “The one thing we knew were the previous numbers [weights], Aya Crandall dressed as a cheerleader on October 29 with her Halloween prize, a 1036-pound pumpkin named Giant Jack.

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief October is a busy month for those of us in emergency management. Wildfire season is at its peak, Loma Prieta’s anniversary is October 17, and the third Thursday is our annual Great ShakeOut exercise. It was in this setting that a surprise shook up my thinking...a real alert for an earthquake most of us didn’t feel. During this time of year, I tend to focus on wildfire season and preparing Piedmont for evacuations. Then last Wednesday, like most of you, I got an alert that an earthquake was imminent. At first, I thought it was a premature training alert for the Great ShakeOut. However, it was real and knocked me off my wildfire plans for the day as I and my colleagues around the region quickly got shaking with our earthquake procedures. Fortunately, this temblor was relatively minor. But it was a stark reminder for me that you never know what California is going to throw at you. We could wake up tomorrow and be in the middle of a firestorm or an earthquake or a flood. Does it feel overwhelming? I get it. It is overwhelming. Every year I stare at my earthquake food and think “I should really go through and update that.” I’ve always found that the best way – maybe the only way – to tackle an overwhelming task is to take it one step at a time. So over the next year or so, I’m going to help you break down getting prepared into simple, manageable steps. If you want to take on more, great! We have lots of resources for you at piedmont. ca.gov/disaster. For the rest of us, Dave Brannigan, Piedmont Fire Chief doing just one thing today is a step in the right direction. What I’d really like you to do today is sign up for AC Alert. Unlike the automated notifications we got last week, AC Alerts are geotargeted local messages sent by Piedmont and Alameda County safety officials in response to specific events and delivered over phone, email, or text. This is how we let you know that you need to start preparing to evacuate when wildfire threatens, where to go when the time comes, or what to do in the immediate aftermath of an earthquake. Sign up on ACAlert.org to receive these messages. After you’ve taken this one critical step, think about where else you might want to get alerts from. AC Alert is used throughout Alameda County, but other parts of the region have their own systems. If you send your kids to school in San Francisco, have relatives in the Contra Costa County, or work in the South Bay, it’s a good idea to get those alerts too. You can find a map with sign-up links for all the alerting systems in the region at AlertTheBay.org. Don’t wait for another earthquake to shake up YOUR thinking. articles.text: The first Revised Common Lectionary reading for the first Sunday of November is Joshua 3:7-17. We need to be careful in reading Joshua, for it is a violent book. It describes violence. It countenances violence. It depicts God commanding violence. Further, Joshua describes one group of people taking the land of another. Even though God is given credit for this conquest we need to be careful. We need to interpret wisely. In human history, including the history that is unfolding even now, such narratives have given rise to tragedies of epic proportion. I would assert that rather than reading Joshua as literal history, we read it as metaphor, as an examination of the challenges we face as we move into the unknown, as we face challenges to our dreams, as we face threats to the common good. As the book of Joshua begins, the great leader Moses has died. Joshua is named as his successor with these stirring words from on High, “Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.” Joshua’s chief work will be to lead the people into the promised land, their intended destination when they left Egypt 40 years earlier. It is the spring of the year and the river is at flood stage. There are no boats, there are no bridges. As so often is true in life, high hopes and great expectations are met with significant difficulty. God instructs Joshua to prepare the leaders and organize the people. The priests, carrying the Ark of the Covenant will lead the people across the raging river. Plans and preparations are made. Prayers are offered. Rites of purification are completed. The time to move forward arrives. The priests step foot into the river and then, and only then, the river waters stop their flow. They are dammed up. They are completely stopped. The people cross the riverbed on dry ground. There are likely many lessons in this account. The one I would like to make is that while faith involves planning, preparing, purifying and praying, sooner or later it involves taking action. articles.text: Scouts race their model boats at the Raingutter Regatta on the final day of Twilight Camp. It was nearly dark when Program Director Eris Turner raised the scout sign before a crowd of energetic, laughing Cub Scouts near Piedmont Community Hall. Recognizing the universal scouting gesture signaling that it’s time to listen to the adult leader, the scouts settled into their seats next to their parents. From there, Turner separated the fledgling Scouts into groups and sent them off to their respective stations, where they would make arts and crafts, eat snacks, and build boats in preparation for the annual Raingutter Regatta. Twilight Camp is an event for Cub Scouts in the Piedmont Council where they enjoy three evenings of fun activities. Held from Tuesday through Thursday evening, October 24-26, the camp is an introduction to scouting for kids who are thinking about joining. “It’s all about engaging them at this age,” said Turner, a lifelong Piedmont native and veteran Scout. articles.text: After months of deliberation, the City of Piedmont has taken the next step toward creating a memorial of Sidney and Irene Dearing, Piedmont’s first black residents. The city council voted to hire the prestigious design firm, Hood Design Studios in Oakland. The memorial would be located in the triangle park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues, near the house where the Dearings lived in the 1920s. The Sidney and Irene Dearing memorial is the city’s response to a dark chapter in Piedmont’s history. The Dearings purchased a house in the city in 1924 but were later driven out of the city by a mob of white Piedmont residents. The Piedmont Police Department did little to help at the time, faced with a mob of an estimated 500 people. In the same year the City Council offered to purchase the home from the Dearing family but offered less than the original price. The city wanted to purchase the property to build a street connecting Wildwood and Fairview Avenues. Eventually, the Dearings succumbed to the offer and moved away. The road was never constructed. Discussions about creating a memorial began in May 2022, when City Council considered naming the triangle as “Dearing Family Memorial Park.” The city adopted a resolution directing the Park Commission to explore opportunities to memorialize the Dearing family. Hood Design Studio caught the City’s attention for their extensive body of work on landscape projects reflecting the African American experience. Over the summer of 2023, the City reached out to Hood Design Studio about potential involvement in the project. In August, members of Hood Design Studio met with city staff at Triangle Park to discuss the project and an agreement was reached to move forward with the project. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore handled the contract Photo by Dearing Family. Sidney and Irene Dearing were the first black homeowners in Piedmont in 1924. and is the City’s primary point of contact with Hood Design Studio. Hood Design Studio is an award-winning social art and design practice located in Oakland, CA, helmed by Creative Director Walter Hood, who readers may recognize as the current Chair of UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning. Among other things accolades, Hood is a recipient of the 2017 Academy of Arts and Letters Architecture Award, 2019 Knight Public Spaces Fellowship, 2019 MacArthur Fellowship (the “Genius Grant”), 2019 Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, and the 2021 recipient of the Architectural League’s President’s Medal award. Hood Design Studio will develop conceptual designs for the memorial. Their team has been in close contact with the city and with the Dearing family to ensure the memorial respects the wishes of the Dearing family. Walter Hood, principal of the firm, is hosting a project kick-off event on Tuesday, November 7 at 5:30 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Avenue. At the event, the designer will discuss his approach to design as a cultural practice, weaving together history, landscape, and memory to express stories through the built environment. Members of the public are encouraged to attend. “If you’re bored in retirement, you could go back to your youth and think about algebra.”

articles.text: Starting today, the Piedmont Fire Department will begin taking donations for its annual toy drive. Piedmont residents looking to help local families in need can contribute new unwrapped toys to make sure everyone in the area has a gift for the holidays. Donation bins will be in the Fire Department, and also at City Hall, the Police Department, and Recreation Department. Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County. Toys donated before December 8 will be distributed through the US Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. City Council members will lead the way by making individual donations at the November 6 City Council meeting. Bins will remain available for donations through December 23. Lic. articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church invites the community to a presentation of a Requiem Mass for All Souls tonight, Wednesday, November 1 at 6:30 p.m. Ben Bachmann, Director of Music, will lead an orchestra and St. Paul’s Choir in a performance of the majestic Requiem in D minor, Op. 48, by Gabriel Fauré. Everyone is invited to remember and celebrate the lives of all the beloved departed. Fauré said of his Requiem, “Everything I managed to entertain by way of religious illusion I put into my Requiem, which moreover is dominated from beginning to end by a very human feeling of faith in eternal rest.” Fauré saw death as a “happy deliverance – an aspiration towards happiness above.” The church will be illuminated with candles, and votive candles will be available for individuals to light. You are invited to submit the names of loved ones to be held in remembrance and listed in the service sheet. articles.text: Haunted forests, lawn games, spooky stories, and candy drew costumed children to Piedmont Park on Sunday, October 29, for a Halloween Spooktacular event in place of the city’s long tradition of an elaborate Haunted House at the Recreation Department building on Hillside Avenue. The event began with a cosFirefighter Robb Hendry hands out candy to kids during the costume parade. Lara Gallagher plays a variation of bean bag toss, one of the carnivalstyle games at the Red. Department Halloween Spooktacular. Juliet Tucker smiles as she receives a black widow on her arm at the spooky face-painting table. Staff Photos Preschool Director Fallon Spencer reads to a group of kids at Spooky Storytime. tume parade of children walking from the Exedra to Community Hall. Costume participation was high at the event, with wizards and Jedi walking alongside lions, tigers, princesses, and different Pixar characters. Children and parents at the event were more often in costume than not. On-duty members of the Piedmont Fire Department handed out candy. Fire Capt. Mike Carlisle said that the most popular treats he handed out that day were tootsie rolls, pretzels, and Twizzlers. The Community Hall and plaza were covered with skeletons and ghouls. Kids had a variety of lawn games and carnival-style games to play, as well as arts and crafts booths, stations for crafting sugar skulls, and spooky face painting tables. A Spooky Woods area was created on the path next to the Japanese Tea House, with spider webs, ghost sheets, warning signs, and other Halloween decorations. Along the walk, there were small carnival game booths for kids to enjoy and several tables with a glass jar full of Halloween treats with signs reading: “Guess how many pieces inside to win this candy jar!” At the end of the Spooky Woods, a lifelike, animatronic witch statue waited for the young trick-or-treaters. At the Japanese Tea House Fallon Spencer hosted Spooky Storytime with readings of Halloween-themed stories. “I signed up for it because it’s a passion of mine. I love to read to kids,” Spencer said.
articles.title: Rec. Dept. Halloween Spooktacular draws kids to Piedmont Park
