articles.text: On September 24 Troop 11 recognized Arun Brahma’s advancement to Eagle Scout. the highest rank that Scouting offers. He is the Troop’s 137th Eagle Scout. It is a task started by many but accomplished by few. All Eagles have earned the ranks of Scout, Tenderfoot, Second Class, First Class, Star, Life to becoming an Eagle. Each has gone on numerous campouts and adventures, earned at least 21 merit badges, served in troop leadership roles for 16 months or more, and planned and executed an Eagle Service Project. Each Eagle has completed approximately 325 different requirements. On the journey to Eagle, Arun also earned a Gold and Bronze Palm for completing 11 merit badges beyond the required number. For his Eagle Service Project, Arun assembled 40 Welcome Kits for Afghan Refugees in the Bay Area. In 2021, the U.S. abruptly pulled its military forces out of Afghanistan, leaving behind thousands of Afghan residents who had supported the US-backed Afghan government and collaborated with American troops as translators, guides, and contract suppliers, as well as religious and political dissidents. A small number of these Afghani refugees resettled in the Bay Area, which already had a vibrant Afghan community. They are currently rebuilding their lives as they wait for asylum. As a grandchild of immigrants, Arun understood that even under more normal circumstances, coming to a new country is a daunting challenge that takes immense courage. Arun’s project helped these families settle in their new home. Troop 11’s newest Eagle Scout, Arun Brahma. Arun spent several months collecting supplies by reaching out to the local community and businesses for donations. With the assistance of Troop 11 Scouts and leadership, he was able to fill 40 baskets with household items to help Afghani families with basic day-to-day needs. Arun worked with The Afghan Coalition in Fremont to identify the most useful items to include in the kits. The Afghan Coalition is a non-profit community organization that helps Afghan refugees thrive as newcomers. The kits were delivered on April 30, 2023. “This project was especially meaningful to me,” said Arun. “I believe it is very important for minority groups to support each other and especially for US citizens to honor those who have given service to our country, particularly when it is not their own. I hope that these kits will help these families get settled and feel less burdened as they acclimate in their new communities.”
articles.title: Arun Brahma achieves rank of Eagle Scout

articles.text: With Thanksgiving just around the corner many of us are beginning to fill our dreams with visions of turkey, stuffing, pumpkin pie, mashed potatoes, gravy, and cranberry sauce. For parents of picky eaters, however, those dreams can quickly turn into nightmares. Although the holidays are typically filled with joy, delicious meals, and quality time with loved ones, this time of year can also be a particularly challenging time for picky eaters (and their parents.) What are you supposed to do if your child refuses to eat any of your family’s traditional dishes? What if your child refuses to sit at the holiday table? Here are some tips for surviving the holidays with a picky eater. Maintain a schedule We all know how difficult it is to maintain a consistent routine during the holidays. With that being said, maintaining regular mealtime routines is essential for picky eaters. Children are conditioned to eat certain amounts of food, at specific times of day. Maintenance of this schedule will keep their appetite steady and stable. by reviewing the expectations. Explaining the event, what foods will be there, and your expectations around mealtime behavior (how much to eat, manners) will help your child accept these changes and expectations. Feed your picky eater before the main meal High levels of excitement, adult pressure, and changes in routine are known to suppress appetite. A picky eater who is not necessarily hungry will have a hard time sitting down to eat several unfamiliar foods (many of which are only served during holidays) with large groups of people. In order to make your holiday meal run as smoothly as possible, and keep your child from getting “hangry,” feed your picky eater their preferred meal separately first. Additionally, making sure you include something on the holiday table that they will comfortably eat will make it more likely that they will sit at the table and engage socially with the larger group. Paige Bailey is a pediatric speech language pathologist and feeding therapist, and owner of Speech By The Bay (https://www. speechbythebay.org). Limit things that might be overstimulating Between background conversations, the parade/ game on TV, Aunt Betty’s perfume, and cousins running around the house, the holidays are typically quite overstimulating. Paired with the general increased level of excitement, this stimulation can be extremely disorganizing to a child’s nervous system, which may negatively affect their appetite. Providing quiet spaces and sensory breaks will help limit disruptions to your child’s appetite and eating/sleeping schedule. Preview expectations When you are going to change a child’s typical routine, it is beneficial to prepare them in advance
articles.title: How to survive the holidays with a picky eater

I hope that these kits will help these families get settled and feel less burdened as they acclimate in their new communities.” How to survive the holidays with a picky eater By Paige Bailey, M.A., CCC-SLP With Thanksgiving just around the corner many of us are beginning to fill our dreams with visions of turkey, stuffing, pumpkin pie, mashed potatoes, gravy, and cranberry sauce. For parents of picky eaters, however, those dreams can quickly turn into nightmares. Although the holidays are typically filled with joy, delicious meals, and quality time with loved ones, this time of year can also be a particularly challenging time for picky eaters (and their parents.) What are you supposed to do if your child refuses to eat any of your family’s traditional dishes? What if your child refuses to sit at the holiday table? Here are some tips for surviving the holidays with a picky eater. Maintain a schedule We all know how difficult it is to maintain a consistent routine during the holidays. With that being said, maintaining regular mealtime routines is essential for picky eaters. Children are conditioned to eat certain amounts of food, at specific times of day. Maintenance of this schedule will keep their appetite steady and stable. by reviewing the expectations. Explaining the event, what foods will be there, and your expectations around mealtime behavior (how much to eat, manners) will help your child accept these changes and expectations. Feed your picky eater before the main meal High levels of excitement, adult pressure, and changes in routine are known to suppress appetite. A picky eater who is not necessarily hungry will have a hard time sitting down to eat several unfamiliar foods (many of which are only served during holidays) with large groups of people. In order to make your holiday meal run as smoothly as possible, and keep your child from getting “hangry,” feed your picky eater their preferred meal separately first. Additionally, making sure you include something on the holiday table that they will comfortably eat will make it more likely that they will sit at the table and engage socially with the larger group. Paige Bailey is a pediatric speech language pathologist and feeding therapist, and owner of Speech By The Bay (https://www. speechbythebay.org). Limit things that might be overstimulating Between background conversations, the parade/ game on TV, Aunt Betty’s perfume, and cousins running around the house, the holidays are typically quite overstimulating. Paired with the general increased level of excitement, this stimulation can be extremely disorganizing to a child’s nervous system, which may negatively affect their appetite. Providing quiet spaces and sensory breaks will help limit disruptions to your child’s appetite and eating/sleeping schedule. articles.text: It was a brisk Halloween morning on Tuesday, October 31, for parents gathered on the Beach playfield for the school’s annual Halloween costume parade. Spirits were high and the parade route was packed. Students poured down the pathway at 8:45 a.m. from the school campus to the field in costumes of splendor and allure for the flashbulbs of the awaiting crowd. The parade was led by Claire Stephens and her Transitional Kindergarten class. Exquisite costumery put the imagination of Beach School students on display. A corn on the cob with a mustache recited corny jokes, a Rubik’s cube dodged minecraft characters, and inflatable costumes prompted frequent flashbulb action. The Beach teachers coordinated their costumes by dressing up at dominoes. Principal Anne Valva was number one, smiling for parents and leading her school’s students on a parade showcasing creativity. A sprinting gorilla leads the Beach School Halloween Costume parade. PE teacher Heidi Sawicki (left) and Principal Anne Valva were dressed as domino tiles. Cheerleaders, even gory cheerleaders, were popular costumes this year. A Beach student in a harvest-inspired costume with another dressed as a nobleman with a white wig Claire Stephens with students from her Transitional kindergarten class Photos by Ben Spohn, Roger Tsai, Kyle Killion The Highlanders 2023 Boys Purple (U11) team dressed as Kens from the Barbie movie. The Havens Halloween parade had costumes ranging from Pokemon to soccer players.

articles.text: The annual Halloween Carnival at Piedmont Middle School extended the lunchtime period for students on Tuesday, October 31, for costumed fun and games. Students elected to the Associated Student Body organized carnival games for their creatively costumed classmates to enjoy. Cowgirls, superheros and evil villains took to the carnival games with fervor. A bowling game awarded prizes for pins knocked over, while a shell game challenged the concentration of the students spending the day in disguise as an alter ego. A costume contest solicited many entries on the day, but with the level of costumed talent so high, results are hotly contested. Sugary treats fueled the fun all day long, with revelry continuing into the night for Halloween trick-or-treating throughout town. Eliza Hupp (left), Evie Luskin, and Amelie Wang decided to be beanie babies in a group costume this year. Carly Kemp-Malone (left), Quinn Wagener, Sofia Meyer, Kyla Williams, Maika Ting, and Allyson Huynh were cowgirls for Halloween this year. Staff Photos Middle school teachers dressed as characters from the Marvel and Barbie universes. Front row: Tim Wisniewski (left), and Keith Barlow. Nicole Straley (back left), Kate Waldron, Caroline Woods, Nikkola Yuen, Jamie Van Kleeck, Alex Escobar, Karen Bloom, Sam Wilde, and Colin Chang. Connor Khouri was prepared for the hunt this year, dressed as Poseidon with a trident that shot water out of its tip. The Bern courts at Piedmont Middle School were teeming with games and conversation during the school’s lunchtime Halloween activities. Gabi Stein poses in his Gloom Hands costume, a tribute to the popular enemy character in Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. Kaiya Lopez created an original Halloween costume with a handmade mask.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class presented four rousing performances of The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong from October 19-21 in the Alan Harvey Theater. The student actors, directed by Kimberly Taylor, proudly showcased a production which had been in the works since the second day of school. As this reporter sat in the audience on Friday night, things began to “go wrong.” Three stage hands gathered around the set’s mantlepiece as it barely hung to its place on the wall. With a thud, the audience quieted for a moment, as the sound technician of the play, performed by PHS junior Sophie Hess, buried her face in her hands. In the midst of the chaos creative director Chris Bean, played by Jake Hanke, made his way to audience members with an additional playbill titled The Murder at Haversham Manor, while apologizing for the mistaken The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong playbill. The award-winning play by Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, and Henry Shields is a play-within-a-play. In The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong, the cast is the Polytechnic Drama Society whose members are trying to produce The Murder at Haversham Manor: however, the low-budget production is constantly disrupted by poor actors, mishaps, and set difficulties. Throughout the night, laughter filled the theater in response to characters reciting lines from the palm of their hands, and actors being dragged off stage; all the while the set slowly deteriorates. “It was a really weird rehearsal process, and was the most chaotic Photos by Sophie Hess Ben Sachs as Charles Haversham informs everyone of how and why he knew the Inspector would try to kill him. Xander Schulte-Sasse (left) as Cecil Haversham, with Jake Hanke as Inspector Carter Sadie Shoop (left) as the butler Perkins, holds a broken stretcher with Charlotte Macola, that Xander SchulteSasse is falling out of, as Jake Hanke observes. Thomas Colleymoore as Charlotte Macola (left) and Ella Puckett as Annie Twilloli Xander Schulte-Sasse (left) rejects another whisky from Charlotte Macola as Eve Tellegen sits with Ben Sachs as the “dead” body of Charles Haversham.

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School presents Disney’s The Little Mermaid Jr this weekend, November 3-5. A total of 80 students have collaborated as cast and crew members to bring the joyful Disney musical to life. Favorite songs by composer Alan Menken and lyricists Howard Ashman and Glen Slater include “Under the Sea”, “Kiss the Girl”, and “Part of Your World”. With a book by Doug Wright, this show presents an enchanting look at the sacrifices we all make for love and acceptance and will bring joy to the entire family. The show will be directed by Amy Moorhead.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team finished third in the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament after defeating Castro Valley 15-8 on Saturday, October 28 at Encinal, but losing two days earlier in a heated 10-9 overtime match with Berkeley. “Winning league is nice, but our goal is to win NCS (North Coast Section). That’s still in front of us. We played really tough and knew our league had some quality opponents this year. We’re going into NCS feeling confident, I want to see how we respond,” said first year head coach Rik Krumins. The loss to Berkeley finished with controversy. Finn Burke drew a foul a few feet in front of net with four seconds left. However, the scorer’s desk never stopped the clock when the foul was committed and the referees did not have their eyes on the clock. Before Piedmont could set up for a final play time on the clock had expired. Head coach Rik Krumins and assistant coach John Savage instantly made their way to the scorer’s desk to voice their grievance, but to no avail. “They (the officials) have a really tough job and this was a great game. with two really evenly matched teams,” said Krumins. Piedmont’s defeat means their run of three consecutive league titles is over. The goal for a Division 2 North Coast Section championship is still in front of them. PHS enters the NCS postseason with the No. 4 seed and a firstround bye. 15-8 over Castro Valley Piedmont ended the first quarter with a 3-2 lead before getting out to a 9-5 advantage by halftime. Leo Hurwitz scored two goals and had two assists against Berkeley. Peter Krumins then scored two straight goals to go up 3-1 with 1:33 left, while CV scored on its next possession. In the second period, Linnane scored four straight goals to put PHS up 7-2 before conceding the Trojans’ next goal. Linnane added one more to make it 8-3 with 1:23 to go, while George Stein scored at the very last second to make it 9-5 going into halftime. Burke scored 20 seconds into the third, 10-5, but CV scored two to draw closer 10-7 with 2:43 on the clock. Leo Hurwitz scored for Piedmont to make it 11-7 with 37 seconds left in the third. But PHS opened the fourth quarter with three straight goals by Burke, Elles Kreickhaus, and Stein to lead 14-7 with 4:17 to go. CV scored its last goal with 38 seconds left, while Elles Kreickhaus put the exclamation point on the game by scoring with nine seconds left. Final stats: Linnane scored six goals, two assists, and steals. Stein scored two goals, two assists, one steal. Burke scored three goals, one steal. Kreickhaus had two goals and two steals. Luke McAuliffe had four saves, Gus von Metszch had two saves and three steals. 10-9 overtime loss to Berkeley The semifinal first quarter ended in a 1-1 deadlock after Burke scored the game’s initial goal 45 seconds in. Piedmont got out to a 3-1 lead in the second quarter with goals from Burke and Hurwitz, but the Yellowjackets eventually battled back to tie 3-3 with 3:27 left in the first half. McAuliffe had a big save with 1:05 left to keep it tied, while Hurwitz had a shot trail narrowly high with 48 seconds. In the third, Berkeley gained the lead after 30 seconds but Daniel Banin scored on a breakaway to tie 4-4 with 5:29 on the clock. Berkeley then scored in close distance at 3:36 but Linnane scored on an assist from Hurwitz 20 seconds later, 5-5. In the first of two three-minute overtime periods, both sides went scoreless through the first three minutes with both sides having multiple shots miss the target. McAuliffe recorded two saves through the period. In the second, Berkeley scored after 25 seconds to gain the 10-9 lead, and then sat defensively. articles.text: Photos by Steve Long Tommy Ashton led the way with 172 rushing yards and two touchdowns. With a football program revived after three years of questions about its survival, Piedmont is on the verge of capturing the Western Alameda County Conference’s Shoreline Division title. mont 52-30 on Saturday, October 28, Piedmont Is 4-1 in league. A victory in its game this week with Newark Memorial would mark its first league title since winning the Shoreline Division in 2015. Piedmont ended last week in a three-way tie for first place with Kennedy of Fremont and Newark Memorial. Newark, however, lost to Arroyo to push them down to fourth. Kennedy is also 4-1 in league, but PHS controls the tiebreaker after its win over the Titans on October 20. Kennedy will play lowly San Lorenzo, meaning the Highlanders need a win over Newark and the Shoreline is theirs. It was a big offensive day for both Piedmont and the winless American Eagles with 82 total points. Piedmont led 25-0 before American’s first points, as running back Tommy Ashton totaled 172 yards on 10 carries for two touchdowns. Game Recap After forcing American to punt, Piedmont scored in just four plays. On 3rd-and-10 from their own 37, Markos Lagios landed a 44-yard bomb to Shelby, followed by Shelby taking a 19-yard run of tackle into the end zone—making it 6-0 after a missed extra point. PHS then forced another punt, where Shelby received at the right hash mark of Piedmont’s 39, cutting to the left sideline to take it 61 yards to the house – 12-0 after a missed extra point. Piedmont forced another punt near the end of the first, leading to Tommy Ashton punching one across at the start of the second at the end of a 50-yard drive—18-0. PHS then forced a fumble recovered on American’s next drive, leading to a seven-play series capped off with a 13-yard touchdown run by Lagios – making it 25-0 with an extra point. American scored its first points on a 28-yard run on their next drive, while Shelby scored on a screen for 32-6, then Piedmont recovered a fumble on American’s kickoff return at the Eagles’ 38. After two plays, Piedmont scored on a 25-yard screen and run by Brandon Dicke, who switched the field on his reception on the right side, taking it across the field for the score – 39-6. Ashton scored on the first play of the second half on a 55-yard run and a 46-6 lead. American then scored on a 34-yard pass and got the 2-point conversion, following up with a recovered onside kick, eventually scoring on a short-pass – 46-20. Cash Elmquist scored on the following drive on a screen for a Sam Shelby had 3 touchdowns – receiving, rushing, and a punt return.

articles.text: Staff Photos Quarterback Mia Leggett prepares to launch a pass against San Leandro. Piedmont’s flag football team, in its first season of scheduled games, fought to the end, but finished fourth in the Western Alameda County Conference Tournament in Hayward on Saturday, October 28. PHS opened with a nail-biting 13-12 loss to topseeded Berkeley, but fell 22-6 to the No. 3 seed, San Leandro, in the battle for third place. “From the beginning of the season to the end, the girls had fun and enjoyed it. This season was a win because of what we created, It was a win because we got better with every game,” said PHS coach Beth Black. Despite the score with the Pirates, it was a tight battle in both games. PHS had a touchdown controversially wiped out at the end of the first half. In the previous round against Berkeley, the Highlanders rallied from a 13-0 deficit to make it 13-12 with 36 seconds left but fell short on its 1-point conversion. Piedmont’s last drive started after Dahlia Osman nabbed an interception for a takeaway in PHS’ own end zone, leading to a 22-yard touchdown pass from Mia Leggett to Erinn Gardere down the sideline, recording an incredible contested catch in oneon-one coverage. “The girls love to fight. We got so close in the end and wish we could’ve turned it around all the way,” said Black. PHS wraps up its first season of flag football as a varsity sport with a 4-6 overall record. They had the largest roster within the league by a considerable margin, showing how popular the sports can be even in a small-enrollment school. The team was coached by Black, head of the high school English Department, defensive coordinator Hayley Adams, and Athletic Director Bradley Smet as offensive coordinator. Alameda, the No. 2 seed, won the league title, beating Berkeley, 20-6. Semifinals vs. Berkeley The first league semifinals were played on a 40-yard field and a clock wasn’t available. Berkeley scored on a 4th-and-5 situation on a successful hook-and-ladder, where Jaima Harrison ran underneath the initial receiver on a short-pass—taking a pitch to the house for a 25-yard score. On the ensuing drive, Piedmont drove to the Berkeley 9-yard line, but a pass targeting Dorothy Nemeth was intercepted in the end zone. After the two sides traded possessions again, Berkeley scored on another hook-and-ladder, for a 13-0 lead. In the second half, PHS’s Lizzy Long recorded an intercepted on the Yellow Jackets first possession. The Highlanders scored on an eight-play series, featuring Nemeth converting a 4th-and-5 with a nine-yard reception, while Leggett landed a pass in traffic to Gardere. A failed 1-point conversion made it 13-6. After back-and-forth possessions, Berkeley drove to Piedmont’s 9-yard line, but Osman snatched an interception away from the Jackets’ receiver in the back of the end zone, setting up a critical final drive for PHS with one minute to play. The series started with passes to Nemeth, setting up 3rd-and-2 at the 22-yard line. That’s Leggett threw a bomb down the sideline to Gardere, who leaped to reach out with one hand to trap it between her and the defender. She corralled the pass as she crossed the goal line making it 13-12 in the waning seconds. Erinn Gardere (middle) celebrates a critical touchdown against Berkeley alongside Mia Leggett (left), Dorothy Nemeth (#32), and Miya Fujimoto. A photo of Miya Fujimoto’s reception in the end zone against San Leandro. After initially making the grab with her left foot down, referees ruled that her right foot came down out of bounds.

articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team completed its regular season last week, defeating Berkeley 5-2 on the road at Berkeley Tennis Club on Wednesday, October 25, but for the second time losing to rival Bishop O’Dowd 4-3 to O’Dowd at home the following day. The Highlanders celebrated its three seniors on the roster: Tanya Kononova, Cecelia DeFazio, and Ellie Broscow. Kononova came to the school in the summer of 2022 as a refugee from Ukraine and instantly stepped into the No. 1 singles role. “I’m going to miss the team a lot. When I moved, it was the first thing that I really did. It’s going to be a really good memory for me,” said Knonova. “I’m going to be missing these guys, because they are the best,” DeFazio is a three-year starter and was paired with junior Emma Eisemon to become the team’s No. 1 doubles squad. They’ve continued to improve every year on the courts and will likely step into the WACC tournament among the top seeds. “It’s a weird milestone, because I remember my first year on varsity and senior night for those girls. Now it’s my senior night and I feel almost out of place, I don’t want the season to be over. I’m not ready for this to be the last game,” said DeFazio. Staff Photos Tanya Kononova split her last two matches, playing the final regular season match of her high school career in Piedmont. “We just have great chemistry on the court,” added Eisemon. “We talk to each other after every point. If we give up a point we try to figure out what went wrong so we can improve.” 5-2 win vs. Berkeley Carolina Romanczuk started the day with a 6-2, 6-2 win at No. 3 singles, and Arianna Kortum finished a clean 6-1, 6-2 win at No. 4 singles. No. 3 doubles team of Inara Mehta and Abigail Call made it 3-0 for Piedmont with a Cecelia DeFazio (left) and Emma Eisemon are stepping into their final matches as Piedmont’s top doubles pair. articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is riding and having fun. They are introducing biking skills and good trail etiquette to new riders with Fun Rides. The co-ed Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is currently recruiting new riders. The team has fun riding the fantastic local trails and races in the Spring against other East Bay high school teams in the Norcal League (www.norcalmtb.org). Their motto is “Have fun, stay safe” and their season runs from December 1 to the end of May. The team is open to all abilities from beginner to advanced. No experience is necessary. Loaner bikes are available. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is partnering with Piedmont DEVO and Oakland DEVO with a GRiT (Girls Riding Together) Ride on December 2nd from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Elephant Barn in Joaquin Miller Park. This ride is open to all female identifying and non-binary teens. Ride with 6th through 12th grade kids and the amazing coaches. Sign up on www.piedmontdevo.com. Fun Rides are planned for November 5 and November 12. These rides are open to anyone, and there are no registration requirements until the season starts on Dec 1. For more information about the high school team and their Fun Rides, go to www.piedmontmtb.com or email piedmontbiking@gmail.com. Mountain bike riders enjoying the view of Lake Chabot

articles.text: Happy Halloween! What better time to awaken some spooky history of around the area, including your very own town? Here’s a look into a batch of locations with a spooky past. Tyson Lake, Piedmont Tyson Lake is a small reservoir located between private residences between La Salle and Sotelo Avenues, tucked quietly behind the Hampton Field. The location is not public property, but is the only body of water in Piedmont a few locals are known to reel out some carp. On July 20, 1951, the Oakland Tribune published that the Alameda County coroner’s jury today recommended that Tyson Lake, an unused reservoir here, be either drained or properly fenced to prevent further accidents following the drowning of 17-year old James Richards four days earlier. But near a year to the day of the first accident, a second victim on July 10 drowned in Tyson; 19-year old Donald Stracner after swimming with two other companions. World War 2 Navy diver John Haubner, who was a former Piedmont Police Officer, was called on to retrieve Stacner’s body. “As search for the body continued, Police Chief William Pflaum said he will “definitely recommend that some action be taken to alleviate this menace to life.” He said that in view of the fact there have been two drownings in the lake within a year, “something must be done’,” wrote the Oakland Tribune, via HistoryofPiedmont.com. Later on August 8 of 1952, the City of Piedmont sought out to determine the owner of Tyson Lake following the drowning of Stracner. City Council urged the 20 home owners surrounding the lake to erect a fence Tyson Lake now sits quant and quietly behind the lush homes of Sotelo and La Salle. Photo courtesy of HistoryofPiedmont.com A clipping of a 1952 Oakland Tribune article of Piedmont PD’s search for Donald Stracner. Photos courtesy of Thoughtsicle.com Tyson Lake is the only surface body of water in Piedmont. It is estimated to have 3 million gallons of water, and is the site of drowning victims in 1951 and 1952. Hayward Plunge, Hayward Allegedly, a swimming instructor back in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps pitter pattering, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in Staff Photo A spillway along Ward Creek on the Hayward Plunge Trail, which is a notoriously haunted park in the East Bay. legend says a nanny, named Mary, was executed after being accused of witchcraft when all of the children under her watch died of illnesses. Niles Canyon, Fremont The Niles Canyon ghost is an urban legend about young woman who died in a horse carriage accident over 100 years ago, said to have occurred specifically on February 28 when horses were spooked by two oncoming automobiles—throwing her from the carried. Legend has it a vanishing hitchhiker walks the road on that day every year, looking to hitch a ride to San Francisco See Hiking with Jon on page 28 Photo courtesy of East Bay Regional Parks The Black Diamond Mines of Antioch is supposedly haunted by a presence known as the White Witch and Wailing Witch. all-white garb from head-to-toe during the day as a teenager. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to continue the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in the process through the hills of Green Belt Park. Black Diamond Mines, Antioch The Black Diamond Mines is a location of the White Witch or Wailing Witch, per urban legend. The story goes that a nanny was expelled from town in the 1870s for practicing witchcraft, only to turn up dead in the mines under suspicious circumstances. Other Niles Canyon in Fremont is home of a 100-plus year old urban legend of a vanishing hitchhiker on her way to San Francisco.

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) retrospective of Filipina artist Pacita Abad is on view now through January 28. Born in 1946 and from Basco, Philippines, Abad enjoyed a 32-year artistic career and created a vast number of artworks that traverse a diversity of subjects, from colorful masks to underwater scenes to abstract compositions. The artist died in Singapore in 2004, but her colorful artwork uses a variety of mediums and reveals visual, material, and conceptual concerns that still resonate today. “When curator Nancy Lim and I learned that this exhibition was being planned, we knew that it had to come to San Francisco, the city that inspired Pacita Abad to commit her life to artistic expression,” said Eungie Joo, curator and head of contemporary art at SFMOMA. “While some of the works gathered here were shown locally during Abad’s lifetime, this is the first exhibition to reveal the profundity of her prolific practice.” The SF MOMA exhibition features more than 40 pieces, including Abad’s signature trapunto paintings, which are stuffed, quilted canvases adorned with other raw, found materials. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pacita-abad/ for tickets and to learn more. Pacita Abad exhibit at SF MOMA

articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek is hosting a wreath-making workshop on November 11, just in time for the holidays. True to the nature of Ruth Bancroft’s fauna and foliage, the wreaths will be created using drought-resistant succulents, a signature plant in the garden. An added benefit of succulent wreaths is that they are long-lasting and will be intact long after the holidays. Jennifer Ahlstrand will help guests create these modern takes on the classic ornament. Most of the succulents in the class are locally grown in Ahlstrand’s nursery, WestWind Succulents. Her love of succulent propagation melded into her fine art background. A Walnut Creek native, she has been a frequent guest of the Ruth Bancroft Gardens since the 1990’s. To reserve your spot, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org /event /workshop -succulent-wreaths/. Succulent wreaths are a modern twist on a holiday classic. articles.text: Byrd, Bull and Bach – Tonality and Color, a solo concert featuring the award-winning harpsichordist Liilian Gordis, will be held this Saturday, November 4 at 5 p.m. at St. Alban’s Episcopal Church. 1501 Washington Avenue in Albany. Born in into a family of scholars and mathematicians in Berkeley, Gordis fell in love with the harpsichord at age 9 and never looked back. Five years later, Pierre Hantaï discovered her during a tour to the United States. He encouraged her to move to France for further studies, and at age 16 she moved to Paris where she was mentored by Hantaï and Bertrand Cuiller. Lillian regularly performs as a soloist in festivals across Europe and the U.S. and plays frequently in a duo with Jérôme Hantaï. Her most recent album, a double-disc dedicated to Bach, was awarded a Diapason d’Or and has received praise in the press worldwide Her first solo recording, Zones, was dedicated to the sonatas of Domenico Scarlatti. In the spring this year she debuted at the Maison Française at New York University during a 6-city U.S. tour with J. Hantaï. She also performed with the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra. Lillian holds dual nationality with the U.S. and France and resides in Paris. This academic year she is serving as Visiting Assistant Professor of Harpsichord at Oberlin Conservatory in Oberlin, Ohio. About MusicSources MusicSources is a non-profit organization devoted to the historically informed performance of music from the Middle Ages through the Romantic Era (1500 to 1850). It serves as a local, national, and international base for professionals and promising students. Founded in 1985 by Laurette Goldberg, it is now led by JungHae Kim as Artistic Director. Tickets may be purchased at MusicSources.org or at the door using Venmo, credit card, or cash.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra under the baton of David Ramadanoff will present its Fall Concert on November 4 at First Church Berkeley. Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation, will present its Fall Concert this Saturday, November 4 at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The orchestra will perform Roman Carnival Overture by Berlioz (1843), Rhapsody On A Windy Night by Cavaterra (2022), and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4 in F minor Op. 36 (1877). Tickets are $20 General admission, and free for students who register at (http://data.ypsomusic.org/tickets). Call (510) 849- 9776 for additional information. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is celebrating its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director and Conductor. The orchestra has 99 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from throughout the greater Bay Area. YPSO will perform four concerts this year, will be a participant in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, and perform at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, before embarking on a 9-day tour to Japan in June 2024, which includes three concerts. The Fall Concert is the kickoff for YPSO’s 87th season. About California Festival YPSO is one of 95 organizations participating in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, (cafestival.org) presenting some of the most innovative and compelling music from around the world for two weeks, November 3-19, 2023, in venues throughout the state. Announced in January 2023 and conceived by Los Angeles Philharmonic Artistic Director Gustavo Dudamel, San Diego Symphony Music Director Rafael Payare and San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the California Festival invites musical organizations of all kinds to incorporate works written within the past five years into their broader season programs. About YPSO YPSO’s Music Director, David Ramadanoff, has always been thoughtful about selecting music programs that are able to showcase the diversity of talent in the entire orchestra, and he continues this tradition here. YPSO students engage in a wide range of orchestral music works spanning multiple musical eras and with composers from various backgrounds. Starting this season, YPSO will offer free admission to youth 13 and under accompanied by an adult, and high school and college students with valid ID. YPSO asks that all concert goers, including students, to please register on their ticket site, even if some tickets are free, in order to maintain appropriate seating capacity counts. New musicians invited YPSO is still auditioning for limited sections: trumpet, tuba, French horn, bassoon, and oboe. Piedmont students currently in the band and orchestra are encouraged to audition now to join YPSO for the second half of the season. Call (510) 849-9776 or click on ypso. org for additional information. 86 Cañada Road Woodside, CA 94062 650.364.8300 filoli.org 12-MONTH FINANCING *some restrictions apply CL#788850

articles.text: Cal Performances presents the Brad Mehldau Trio at Zellerbach Hall on Saturday, November 11. The award-winning jazz trio consists of pianist Mehldau, bassist Larry Grenadier, and drummer Jeff Ballard. Mehldau and his longtime bandmates have been praised for their musical chemistry and wide range of stylistic and emotional terrain. Mehldau is an iconic jazz soloist in his own right. The New Yorker called him “arguably the greatest working jazz pianist,” with the touch of Bill Evans and the range of Keith Jarrett. He is well-known for his jazz renditions of rock music, including hits by the Beatles and Neil Young. He is the winner of a Grammy award for best contemporary instrumental album, and has been nominated for 13 other Grammies in his career of more than three decades. The trio will perform an evening of original compositions as well as reimagined jazz standards on November 11. The performance begins at 8 p.m. Tickets are available at www. calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Photo by David Bazemore Pianist Brad Mehldau will perform a concert at Zellerbach Hall on November 11. ®

pages.text: Wednesday, November 1, 2023 17 Young People’s Symphony Orchestra under the baton of David Ramadanoff will present its Fall Concert on November 4 at First Church Berkeley. YPSO Fall Concert on Saturday night Young People’s Symphony Orchestra under the baton of David Ramadanoff will present its Fall Concert on November 4 at First Church Berkeley. Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation, will present its Fall Concert this Saturday, November 4 at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The orchestra will perform Roman Carnival Overture by Berlioz (1843), Rhapsody On A Windy Night by Cavaterra (2022), and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4 in F minor Op. 36 (1877). Tickets are $20 General admission, and free for students who register at (http://data.ypsomusic.org/tickets). Call (510) 849- 9776 for additional information. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is celebrating its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director and Conductor. The orchestra has 99 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from throughout the greater Bay Area. YPSO will perform four concerts this year, will be a participant in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, and perform at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, before embarking on a 9-day tour to Japan in June 2024, which includes three concerts. The Fall Concert is the kickoff for YPSO’s 87th season. About California Festival YPSO is one of 95 organizations participating in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, (cafestival.org) presenting some of the most innovative and compelling music from around the world for two weeks, November 3-19, 2023, in venues throughout the state. Announced in January 2023 and conceived by Los Angeles Philharmonic Artistic Director Gustavo Dudamel, San Diego Symphony Music Director Rafael Payare and San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the California Festival invites musical organizations of all kinds to incorporate works written within the past five years into their broader season programs. About YPSO YPSO’s Music Director, David Ramadanoff, has always been thoughtful about selecting music programs that are able to showcase the diversity of talent in the entire orchestra, and he continues this tradition here. YPSO students engage in a wide range of orchestral music works spanning multiple musical eras and with composers from various backgrounds. Starting this season, YPSO will offer free admission to youth 13 and under accompanied by an adult, and high school and college students with valid ID. YPSO asks that all concert goers, including students, to please register on their ticket site, even if some tickets are free, in order to maintain appropriate seating capacity counts. New musicians invited YPSO is still auditioning for limited sections: trumpet, tuba, French horn, bassoon, and oboe. Piedmont students currently in the band and orchestra are encouraged to audition now to join YPSO for the second half of the season. Berkeley Harpsichord concert in Albany this Saturday Byrd, Bull and Bach – Tonality and Color, a solo concert featuring the award-winning harpsichordist Liilian Gordis, will be held this Saturday, November 4 at 5 p.m. at St. Alban’s Episcopal Church. 1501 Washington Avenue in Albany. Born in into a family of scholars and mathematicians in Berkeley, Gordis fell in love with the harpsichord at age 9 and never looked back. Five years later, Pierre Hantaï discovered her during a tour to the United States. He encouraged her to move to France for further studies, and at age 16 she moved to Paris where she was mentored by Hantaï and Bertrand Cuiller. Lillian regularly performs as a soloist in festivals across Europe and the U.S. and plays frequently in a duo with Jérôme Hantaï. Her most recent album, a double-disc dedicated to Bach, was awarded a Diapason d’Or and has received praise in the press worldwide Her first solo recording, Zones, was dedicated to the sonatas of Domenico Scarlatti. In the spring this year she debuted at the Maison Française at New York University during a 6-city U.S. tour with J. Hantaï. She also performed with the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra. Lillian holds dual nationality with the U.S. and France and resides in Paris. This academic year she is serving as Visiting Assistant Professor of Harpsichord at Oberlin Conservatory in Oberlin, Ohio. About MusicSources MusicSources is a non-profit organization devoted to the historically informed performance of music from the Middle Ages through the Romantic Era (1500 to 1850). It serves as a local, national, and international base for professionals and promising students. Founded in 1985 by Laurette Goldberg, it is now led by JungHae Kim as Artistic Director. Tickets may be purchased at MusicSources.org or at the door using Venmo, credit card, or cash. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse will premiere Cinderella Enchanted on Friday, November 3. Based on the 1997 movie of the same name, the classic tale of Cinderella is reborn with a Bay Area twist. Cinderella, played by Kennedy Joy Fullard, is a free-spirited Berkeley artist and Prince Christopher, played by Vinh G. Nguyen, is a wealthy Silicon Valley romantic. Prince Christopher hosts an extravagant ball where he meets Cinderella, only for her to leave the festivities before he can express his true feelings for her. Cinderella leaves behind nothing but a glass slipper which prompts the prince to embark on a mission to find the dainty shoe’s owner. Cinderella Enchanted is directed and choreographed by Khalia Davis with music conducted by Jessica Igarashi. The director explained the significance of the mid-90’s film, and how it influenced Cinderella on stage. “[The 1997 movie] was really iconic and it set the bar for what is possible when you do musicals that are magical in that way,” Davis said. “[It was important that] audiences who are very familiar with that particular version see that reflected on the stage.” The Berkeley Playhouse production offers even more unique twists, she added. “I’m really excited about the fact that we get to honor and celebrate being able to see Prince Christopher’s life as well as Cinderella’s and that parallel life Photo by Ben Krantz Kennedy Joy Fullard and Vinh G. Nguyen in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Cinderella Enchanted. they are living. Cinderella is this aspiring writer who is fascinated by the world and Christopher is equally fascinated by the world but wants to know what he can do to make a positive impact that is outside of being married or born into royalty,” Davis said. Supporting cast members include Jennifer Marie Frazier as Fairy Godmother, Erika Coyne as Stepmother, Stephen Kanaski as Lionel as The Steward, Nicole Stanley as Queen Constantini and Kyle Herrera as King Maximillian. Cinderella Enchanted is performing November 3 to December 22. To purchase tickets see: https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse. org/Online/default.asp.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse premieres Cinderella Enchanted this weekend

articles.text: Tickets are still available to Oakland Ballet’s “Luna Mexicana,” performed this Friday and Saturday at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. “Luna Mexicana” is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for the holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food, orchestrated as a celebration of family and loved ones. The performance features the return of Viva la Vida, a ballet inspired by the life and spirit of Frida Kahlo. “Luna Mexicana” is co-choreographed by Martín Romero of Ballet Folklórico México Danza and Oakland Ballet’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig. Ballet Folklórico México Danza will present traditional Mexican Folkloric dance, and Mariachi Mexicanisimo will perform folk mariachi music. The Friday, November 3, performance begins at 7:30 p.m., followed by a 2:30 p.m. matinee on Saturday, November 4. Visit www.oaklandballet.org to purchase tickets or call the box office at (510) 893-3132. “Luna Mexicana” celebrates Dia de los Muertos (Day of the Dead).
articles.title: Tickets still available to Oakland Ballet’s Luna Mexicana this weekend

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Bulrusher, a play by Eisa Davis and directed by Nicole Watson, premiered last week and will be performed through December 3. The coming-of-age story follows protagonist and titular character Bulrusher, a multiracial girl found as an infant floating in a basket on the Navarro River in Mendocino County. The 18-yearold Bulrusher is clairvoyant and struggles with feeling like an outsider in the predominately white town of Boonville. The lyrical comedy takes a turn when the teenager meets a young Black woman from Birmingham who helps her uncover her past. The play deals with difficult topics but is grounded in humor and empathy. “Even though there’s a lot of pain and longing we’re left with, there’s also so much hope,” Davis told the Hollywood Reporter. “So that’s something that has sustaining for me in Bulrusher and a big part of why I wrote it – the possibility for love and forgiveness and joy, even amongst all of this pain.” The cast includes Cyndii Johnson, Rob Kellogg, Jamie LaVerdiere, Shyla Lefner, Jordan Tyson and Jeorge Bennett Watson. Bulrusher is directed by Nicole Watson. Post-show discussions with the cast take place on November 10, 16 and 21. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/bulrusher/. Photo by T Charles Erickson Cyndii Johnson (Vera), Jeorge Bennett Watson (Logger), and Jordan Tyson (Bulrusher) in Berkley Rep’s current production of Bulrusher
articles.title: Bulrusher now in production at Berkeley Rep

articles.text: Spokane River, oil on canvas by Michael Stehr. Artist Michael Stehr, a Piedmont native, will unveil his most recent paintings at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, November 3. The exhibit, titled “Going the Distance – Depicting Space on a Two-Dimensional Plane”, will explore the devices Michael uses to communicate a sense of space and atmosphere in a composition. Ultimately to create an envelope of space in which a viewer can enter a picture is one of the great challenges for a painter, he explains. When successful, this elevates a painting from a mere collection of colors and shapes and heightens it to an invitation to explore and escape. Thirty-five new paintings will be included in the display which totals 80 art works. The show will be open until November 19. Gallery Hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through Sunday, November 19. To preview the exhibit online, go to www.bit.ly/3ZO1Urc. The artist will host a reception to open the exhibit at the Center for the Arts at 6:30 p.m. on Friday, November 3. He will offer remarks about the exhibit at 7:15. RSVP at mstehrart@gmail.com by October 25 to attend the reception.
articles.title: Michael Stehr art exhibit opens Friday at PCA

This season’s theme is “Napoli and the Revolution,” and features works by Bach, Mozart, Giuliano, and Sammartini. Musical Director Achille Bocus will conduct and will be soloist in the Giuliano Mandolin Concerto in B flat. For more information and tickets (General $20, Seniors/Students $15) visit https:// sfmandolin.org. Sunday, November 12, 5:30 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a concert paying tribute to Duke Ellington, known as the greatest jazz composer and bandleader of his time. One of the originators of big-band jazz, he led his band for more than 50 years, composing thousands of scores. The concert is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing its magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets $25 at the door, or $23 at https://bpt.me/5691334. Seating limited to the first 70. Thursday, November 16, 6 p.m. Sacha Grippando Retro Jewelry Lecture Piedmont resident and certified gemologist Sacha Grippando returns to continue her lecture series focused on the development of the jewelry arts, with an illustrated lecture exploring the spectacular jewelry collections of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor. Come learn more about this fabulous period and its jewelry! Doors open at 5:45 p.m.; donations will be gratefully accepted at the door and refreshments will be provided following the talk. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up to date vaccinations.

articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra makes a return engagement with a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 11. The Orchestra’s season theme this year is “Napoli and the Revolution.” “We chose this theme because the 18th century was a time of revolutionary thought.,” explained Achille Bocus, musical director of SFMO. “Across Europe and America enlightened ideas of freedom, order, rationality, and happiness influenced politics, art, and music. The music of the time reflected this, with the end of the Baroque and emergence of the Classical Period, and the birth of mandolin as a popular instrument in Naples. “It’s the music that Jefferson, Franklin, Paine and other revolutionaries would have heard.” The Orchestra will perform music from the late baroque and classical periods, including: • Johann Sebastian Bach: Selections from Art of the Fugue • Giuseppe Giuliano: Concerto for Mandolin in B flat (Achille Bocus, soloist) • Wolfgang Mozart: Selections from London Notebook • Giovanni Battista Sammartini: Sinfonia in G Major for String Orchestra The family-friendly concert will begin at 5:00 p.m. on November 11. Admission is $20 general, $15 student/senior, and free for children 12 and under. Tickets may be purchased at the door, or at the Orchestra’s ticketing site: sfmandolin.square.site. Achille Bocus, musical director of San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, will be the soloist in the Giuliano Concerto for Mandolin in B flat at Piedmont Center for the Arts on November 11.
articles.title: SF Mandolin Orchestra at Center for the Arts on Nov. 11

articles.text: Part 3 in a series Piedmont, CA, population 11, 270, is a place apart, its quiet streets canopied by mature trees that frame vintage homes both large and small. Think of it as an island unto itself, possessing its own schools, parks, a small police department, and a classic city hall. Think of it as a small town, surrounded by the deeply urban and commercial Oakland, population 433,800. But taking a closer look at the denizens of this small, family friendly community, one discovers it has a diverse and unique populace. Many of of its residents are unobtrusively successful, some possessing a degree of under-the-radar fame derived from their extraordinary accomplishments. For the purposes of this series of articles we are exploring the creative endeavor of filmmaking. The filmmakers who have been covered in parts one and two are just the tip of the creative iceberg. Dana Murray, as example, the sister of Kiel Murray who was covered earlier, grew up in Placerville and now resides in Piedmont stage and an Oscar at the 93rd Academy Awards ceremony with Pete Docter, director, and co-producer of the extraordinary feature Soul that won Best Animated Feature Film in 2020. It was also the recipient of a Golden Globe award, the Producers Guild of America Award, and the Annie Award for Best Animated Feature. Dana was introduced to Pixar by her sister Kiel, who was then working at the studio as a screenwriter. Dana recalls that it was Kiel who wandered from their home in Placerville with a camcorder and recruited her sister to appear in ongoing film projects. Dana points out that she loves living in the same small town as Kiel and her brother, Seth (who also did a stint at Pixar as a product designer). She refers to their cohort of children who often play together as “the posse,” pointing out that Piedmont is a place where kids can be out and about, walking, or riding their bikes. Why film? The above is testimony to the strong appeal of film and filmmaking, hence it is not by custom or chance that the Piedmont Piedmont filmmaker Dana Murray with her family. She has worked at Pixar Animation Studios since 2003 where, as a producer, she has partnered with directors and creatives, making decisions that best serve the film. In that role Dana oversees budgets, staffing, crews, to include casts, composers, and screenwriters. As a producer she has garnered a number of nominations and wins for her contributions to acclaimed films, including Finding Nemo, Ratatouille, Up, Brave, Lou and Inside Out. articles.text: Ben Affleck and Anna Kendrick in The Accountant If you enjoy pulp-genre entertainment, then don’t hesitate to spend two hours viewing The Accountant. It’s an unusual thriller that has as its central character a high-functioning, autistic numbers guy, Christian Wolff (Ben Affleck). His clients range from farm families to drug cartels, arms dealers and money launderers. His resume also includes skill sets that allow him to work as a forensic accountant and uncook books that have sprung a leak. When it comes to spreadsheets, he is a savant who can examine a corporation’s profit/ loss statement and sort out where the profits have been going. The film has a number of flashbacks to Wolff’s childhood, which explain how he came to be wearing not only a narrow tie, plastic shirt pocket protector, but is also a black belt in karate. In other words, he is a highly unusual character who is profoundly uncomfortable in social settings. The film opens with Wolff at age 10 or 11 being given a puzzle. While his parents are interviewing a psychologist who runs a group home, the boy assembles a 1,000-piece puzzle upside down. He does this in the time it takes his parents to decide that the home is not for their son. That scene becomes a metaphor, and indeed this film is a puzzle: the challenge is to sort out Wolff’s many idiosyncrasies. Flash forward to the present day. Wolff now operates out of a nondescript office called ZZZ Accounting. He lives in a sparsely furnished apartment and keeps a Streamline trailer in a storage locker, filled with weaponry and incredibly valuable paintings. He is hired by a company called Living Robotics which specializes in high-tech prosthetics. They have a problem, however. Millions in profits are missing from the books and they can’t

articles.text: The term B-movie has long been used to refer to second-tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 40s and 50s. In fact, to make sure audiences felt like they received sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel a cartoon and two feature films. The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, smaller budgets, and were the equivalent of dime magazines widely popular during the same time known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subject matter often gritty detective mysteries, or wildly imagined tales of science fiction or melodramatic westerns. This is all to say that instead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B-movie, it might be more accurate to simply call it pulp cinema. That’s not to imply that such films are not entertaining. Indeed, lacking all pretense, with stripped down plot and dialogue, pulpy movies can entertain and then some. Edge of Darkness uses the familiar and satisfying trope of revenge to move the plot along at an intense clip. Boston Detective Mel Gibson and Shawn Roberts in Edge of Darkness
articles.title: Edge of Darkness a cool pulp film with Mel Gibson

articles.text: To write comedy well may be the most difficult endeavor undertaken by Hollywood screenwriters. More often than not, comedies made today too often miss their mark. Date Night falls into the category of what might be called a “screwball comedy,” meaning it is filled with surprising and improbable situations, to include a touch of parody blended with moments of scatological humor and more than a dash of farce. Given the set up, the film should have been a winner. Phil and Claire Foster (Steve Carrell and Tina Fey), a successful and reserved New Jersey couple, parents to three young children, decide to go to Manhattan for a special date night, hoping to add some much needed spice to their marriage. Both Carrell and Fey are gifted comedic actors who can do not only physical comedy, they are masters at the tight reaction shot. Both can stare off into the distance or at one another with aplomb and convey a hundred words. The premise of the film does work: The Fosters decide to go to an edgy and very expensive restaurant called ‘Claw,” but find that without reservations there is no hope of getting a table. Phil, an accountant, intent on making this night special, is suddenly all about high risk – high gain. So, when a party’s name is called out (“party of two, the Tripplehorns”), and they don’t answer, he steps forward and tells the hostess that he and Clare are that couple. Voila! A nice table at the Claw. All is going well, until two rough trade guys show up and ask them to get up from the table. Quietly. Phil and Claire think they’ve been busted and that the Tripplehorns have arrived. Instead, the hard cases take them out to the alley and explain that Phil and Calire have something their boss wants (turns out to be a flash drive) and they better give it up (guns come out, the Fosters insist that they’re not the Tripplehorns, mistaken identity, stolen reservation, and the muscle is not buying it). This all happens within 20 minutes of the beginning and it has real potential. Had the filmmakers let Fey and Carrell run with it (with a rewrite or two), Steve Carell and Tina Fey in Date Night

articles.text: Emma Thompson as Nanny McPhee in a scene from Nanny McPhee Nanny McPhee was last seen arriving to set right a dysfunctional family needing more than an intervention. They needed the McPhee magic, delivered by a snaggletooth, starched, ominous and mysterious nanny who arrives with magic at her fingertips and a cane to put things right. McPhee is a wonderful character, played perfectly by the gifted In the recent incarnation, Nanny McPhee Returns, written by Thompson, McPhee arrives at a bucolic farm in northern England. It’s the middle of WWII and children from London, which is subjected to Germany’s blitzkrieg bombing, are sent across England to wait out the war, most in the safety of the English countryside. And so, we are introduced to the Green children and their mother, Isabel Green (Maggie Gyllenhaal). The family is hanging on by a thread, financially and emotionally, while waiting for the father to return from the war in Europe. What is a normal state of chaos on the farm turns chronic when cousins Cyril (Eros Vlahos) and Cella (Rosie Taylor-Ritson), arrive from upper crust London in a chauffer-driven limousine. Dressed to the nines, they refuse to step out of the car, holding their noses, insisting they’ve arrived at a “poo and mud” museum. Everything is icky, they want to go home, and dig in their snobbish custom-made heels, refusing to help out. Things are dire. Isabel’s brother-in-law (Rhys Ifans), a weasel, is trying to sell the farm to pay off his gambling debts, the barley needs to be harvested, and a new batch of piglets must be sold to keep the family afloat financially. What to do? Enter Nanny McPhee – and just in time – ready to teach the kids five life lessons that will transform them and the farm, to the delight of all. The film is enhanced by CGI, showing that pigs can and do fly and even synchronize swim. At its center is a wonderful cast of characters that is charming and engaging. Kids and adults will enjoy without reservation this entertaining film that delivers a heart-tugging ending in which Nanny McPhee does indeed put everything right. Nanny McPhee Returns. Directed by Susanna White. Starring Emma Thompson, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Rhys Ifans and Maggie Smith. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released 2010. Now streaming on VUDU/Netflix/Prime/ Apple tv.

articles.text: Heartier side dishes and salads fill the bill these days. This grain and squash salad sees a few variations at our table. This version was made with staples from the pantry plus a seasonal delicata squash from the farmer’s market. Wild rice is not technically a true rice but is a cousin. It is the seed of a grass native to the upper Midwest in North America. Any hearty grain can be substituted – farro, wheat berries, barley – as well as other fall squashes such as butternut or kabocha. I prefer delicata squash as it cooks quickly, and the skin is edible. Adding a generous handful of pomegranate arils is delicious, bringing both tartness and texture. We enjoy this salad still warm or at room temperature. If prepared in advance, refrigerating allows the flavors to develop more fully. Wild Rice and Delicata Squash Salad Makes about 5 cups INGREDIENTS • 1 cup wild rice, raw • 1 large bay leaf • 1 medium delicata squash, yielding about 10 – 12 ounces of cut wedges • 1/2 cup pomegranate arils, optional • 1/2 cup walnut pieces, toasted • 1/2 cup fresh flat leaf parsley, rough chopped • 1/4 cup fresh shallots, 1/4” diced • 1 orange, for 1 teaspoon of zest + 2 tablespoons of juice • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra virgin, plus 1 tablespoon for roasting the squash • 1 tablespoon sherry or apple cider vinegar • 1 teaspoon Dijon-style mustard • 1 teaspoon Mexican oregano, dried leaves lightly crushed • 1 teaspoon ancho chile, ground • 1 teaspoon cumin, ground • 1/2 teaspoon coriander, ground • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground Photo by Deborah Quok • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste INSTRUCTIONS Prepare the wild rice according to package directions, adding the bay leaf to the water and salt. Combine the dry spices, pepper, and salt in a small bowl. Prepare the delicata squash. Place an oven rack on the lower third position and preheat the oven to 400°F. Cut the squash lengthwise in half and use a spoon to remove the seeds and membrane. Cut lengthwise again into quartered wedges. Slice these wedges crosswise into 1/ 2-inch pieces. Transfer to a small baking sheet and toss with the one tablespoon of olive oil. Sprinkle two teaspoons of the spice mix over the squash. Roast at 400°F for 15-20 minutes until tender and just beginning to brown on the edges. Remove from the oven and set aside as the wild rice cooks. Make the dressing. Finely zest the orange into a large bowl. Then slice the orange in half across the equator and express 2 tablespoons of juice. Add it to the bowl. Add the vinegar, Dijon mustard, 2 teaspoons of the dried spice mix and mix well. Slowly stream in the olive oil, whisking constantly to develop an emulsified dressing. Add the chopped shallots and let them marinate whilst the wild rice cooks and the squash is roasting. When the wild rice is ready (tender, puffed grains), make sure there is no water remaining in the bottom of the pot. If there is any, transfer the rice to a fine sieve to drain any remaining water. Add the hot wild rice to the dressing and stir to distribute the dressing throughout. Add the roasted squash pieces, pomegranate arils, and chopped parsley. Combine well, taste and add any remaining spice mix as desired. Add toasted walnut pieces just before serving to preserve their crunch. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: Photo by Steve Goodall Kendi was born on Thursday, October 19, at the Oakland Zoo. Oakland Zoo is celebrating the newest addition to the giraffe herd and the start of a new generation and family. After a long pregnancy giraffes have a gestation period of 14-16 months, the zoo’s Kijiji gave birth to her first calf, a female named Kendi, on October 19. At birth, Kendi measured 150 pounds and six and a half feet tall. The new mom, Kijiji, exhibited her protective nature by guiding Kendi into the giraffe barn. A separate area has been set up by the keepers in the barn for the calf and mother giraffe to bond peacefully. The baby Kendi is already standing and walking around the barn and has successfully nursed from her mother. Kendi stayed behind the scenes with mom for the first two weeks to develop their relationship, but is now available to be seen at the Zoo in the mornings. A recent photo of Kijiji and Kendi, mother and daughter. Oakland Zoo’s newest baby, Kendi, is a six and half foot tall giraffe.

articles.text: Rainy season is almost here! Is your home ready for heavy rain and high wind? Neglect can lead to costly and inconvenient issues. Here are five tips all homeowners should know about before inclement weather arrives. 1. Maintain your sump pump. This essential piece of equipment pumps water out and keeps your lower levels dry. Make sure it works before rain starts to pour! Ensure it’s free of damage and debris, check the wiring, and run a test to make sure it’s in full working order. 2. Inspect/seal weather strips on doors and windows. Drafts and leaks lead to increased risk of mold growth and inefficient energy usage. Keep cozy and dry during the rainy season by sealing these openings. 3. Gutters, gutters, gutters! Clean your downspouts and install a gutter guard. Clogs prevent gutters from doing their job effectively, resulting in potential water damage. Maintaining clean, efficient gutters to protect your home from foundation damage, cracks, and shifting during the rainy season. 4. Check your roof. Inspect your roof for damaged or missing shingles ahead of severe storms and wind. It’s critical to replace or repair any damaged shingles to prevent any water from entering your home. 5. Prepare an emergency kit. Heavy rain and strong winds can result in a loss of power, water, and heating. Make sure you have easy access to essential items that help you stay safe and comfortable during (and after) a heavy rain event - water, non-perishable food, a flashlight, first aid kit, rain gear, and extra warm clothing. articles.text: Fred Karren, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away peacefully in his sleep on October 4, 2023. He was 86. Fred possessed an unparalleled capacity to be interested in people and for friendship. He cared deeply for people, and he positively affected countless lives and organizations. His interests were wide ranging, particularly travel, and the visual and performing arts. He will be greatly missed by his family and his countless friends. Born Fred Lewis Karren on October 17, 1936, in San Antonio, Texas, he was the son of Joe and Mildred Karren. When he was two months old, he moved to Oakland with his family and graduated from Oakland High School in 1954. He attended UC Berkeley where he was a member of Zeta Beta Tau Fraternity. He earned a BS in Business in 1958 and a BS in Architecture in 1968. In 1963, he was introduced to the love of his life, Beth Davis Karren. They were married in 1964 in Toledo, Ohio, and enjoyed 53 wonderful years of marriage until Beth passed away in 2017. Their daughter, Leslie Karren, the apple of Fred’s eye, was born in 1967. In addition to a wonderful father-daughter relationship they enjoyed working side by side in the family real estate business. Fred, Beth, and Leslie, enjoyed many family trips throughout the world, and spending time in their vacation homes in Napa and Palm Desert. He had a career of more than 50 years as an architect. Fred designed or remodeled many homes and retail stores throughout the Bay Area. He served on the Piedmont Planning CommisArchitect Fred Karren died at home in Piedmont on October 4. He was 86. sion for many years and chaired it twice. His architectural expertise was called upon when realtors had a home to sell, and they would seek Fred’s advice on how the home could be remodeled to benefit the new owners. Fred kept active until the very end. On his last night, Fred went to the Opera, had a nightcap with his daughter at her home, kissed her goodnight and said, “See you in the morning, and we will go for coffee.” He enjoyed weekly bridge and dominos games with his friends. He was a big supporter of the arts. He had season tickets and supported the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Playhouse, Berkeley Repertory Theater, and many other institutions. He loved animals. He adopted his dog Bentley, an adorable terrier-chihuahua mix, in 2018. He encouraged his friends to do the same because so many dogs, especially senior dogs, need a good home. Over the years he was involved with many clubs and organizations. He was a member of The Pacific Union Club, The Family Club, Claremont Country Club, El Dorado Country Club, Marrakesh Country Club and Temple Sinai in Oakland. He served on the boards of Sinai Memorial Chapel, Jewish Community Federation of the East Bay, Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony, Goodwill Industries and the 100 Club. In addition to being survived by his daughter, Fred is survived by his sister Ann Karren Gitlis, his brother-in-law Sam Davis and his wife Joanne Cuthbertson, his nieces Sara Gitlis Schneider (Michael Schneider), Hadley Davis Reierson (Lee Reierson), Carrie Davis (Michael Lebovich), step-niece Jennifer Thomas (Michael), step-nephew Alex Cuthbertson (Elizabeth Meriwether), and five grand nephews, two grand nieces, three step-grand nephews, and one step-grandniece. He is also survived by many extended family members and friends. He was a loyal and great family member and friend. A celebration of life will be held at Claremont Country Club, 5295 Broadway Terrace in Oakland at 1:00 pm on Tuesday, November 7. In lieu of flowers, the family requests donations be made to Temple Sinai, 2808 Summit Street, Oakland, CA 94609; San Francisco Playhouse, 450 Post Street, San Francisco CA 94102; or a charity of choice. A private burial was previously held.
articles.title: Noted architect Fred Karren dies on October 4

articles.text: A record turnout of 71 walkers and four K-9 best friends were on hand on Wednesday, October 25, for the Walking on Wednesday group’s annual pre-Halloween tour of Mountain View Cemetery led by long time docent Jane Leroe. A retired, ground-breaking trial attorney, Jane, has developed an extensive knowledge of Mountain View Cemetery and loves sharing it. Her theme for the recent tour was “Rogues, Rascals, and Scandals.” In the early 1860s, a group of 12 local businessmen led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and also the 13th mayor of Oakland from 1867 to 1869, decided the area needed a private cemetery. Two public cemeteries existed, but they were not well maintained, and the group wanted something better for their own final resting places. They bought 200 acres of fields far from the center of Oakland at a cost of $13,000, and the Mountain View Cemetery was established in 1863. Twenty-six acres were added later. About 170,000 people are buried at Mountain View, and there is room for an additional 170,000. Jane took the group through the main mausoleum and up a hill to the grave of Clara Bedell, a wellknown madame in San Francisco in the latter part of the 19th century. Her “house of ill-repute” was located at the current location of the Prada store near Union Square on Post Street in San Francisco. In 1891, at the age of 37, she died of a mixture of opium and wine. Three years after her death she was named the beneficiary of a $10,000 life insurance policy from a local judge. Then it was time to see some Victorian family vaults. One belonged to Dr. Orran Warren. It has been stripped of the family name at the family’s request after a robbery in 1988 when a graduate of Skyline High School and a friend broke into the vault, opened two coffins and removed the skulls of two women. The young men reportedly had a “thing for science fiction and monsters and goblins.” Jane had more stories to share with the group. Frank Norris, who wrote the novel The Octopus, was a member of the Phi Gamma Delta fraternity at Cal in the late 19th Century. The fraternity has custody of his grave, where liquor bottles commonly take the place of flowers. Jane Sather made a gift of Sather Gate to UC Berkeley as a memorial to her husband, but marble panels on it had naked women and men, and an inscription “Erected by Jane K Sather 1909.” She had the panels removed. Jane Leroe also took the walkers up to one of the cemetery’s main attractions, “Millionaires’ Row.” This is where the most grand, elaborate crypts stand, housing some of the cemetery’s most wealthy residents. One is Charles Crocker, one of the “Big Four” who helped bankroll the construction of the transcontinental railroad. Crocker built a mansion on Nob Hill, and also a 30-foot-high fence around three sides of the home of a neighbor who wouldn’t sell him his property. The most enjoyable aspect of the tour was Jane herself and her skill at storytelling. Her opinions and humor gave life to these long dead people. At the morning’s end the walkers expressed their thanks to her for a most enjoyable pre-Halloween tour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A large group of 71 walkers took part in a tour of Mountain View Cemetery led by docent Jane Leroe on October 25. READ IT IN THE POST

Parks constitute the main and obvious category of open space, in fact “parks” and “open space” are often used interchangeably. One of the best parts of walking through Piedmont is to come upon our well used and well-maintained parks. They are clearly an invaluable and essential part of any city.
