The universal appreciation of open space is of course due to the many benefits. Recreational uses immediately come to mind – from more active uses like sports that require large fields of lawn or paved courts, to more passive uses like hiking and picnics. Protecting and enhancing natural resources is another benefit: ecological issues like air quality and animal, bird and insect habitat are inevitable beneficiaries of green open spaces. Open space can provide a wonderful aesthetic amenity for all of us, and even a partial view of a park’s vegetation can improve property values in a neighborhood. Like any successful public space, open spaces also foster community, bringing peoSee Walking Piedmont on page 31 Photos by Will Adams There are a number of public streets in Piedmont that are a pleasure for strolling, with mature street trees, plus beautiful bosques and planting in people’s yards. This is not technically considered “open space”, but it has almost all the qualities of open space (except access to people’s private property). I call this common valuable amenity “borrowed open space”. The 15-acre Piedmont Park is the city’s only “Community Park”. It is an incredibly beautiful and functional amenity, located in the geographical heart of the city and would be a wonderful and appropriate park for even a much larger city. Crocker Park is a delightful place with a large lawn area, mature pine trees and understory beds of rhododendrons, camellias, azaleas, and ferns. Punctuated with a granite sculpture of a mother bear and cubs by the noted sculptor Benny Bufano – the City’s best known public art – it is considered a mini-park (less than 1acre). Considered a Neighborhood Park, popular Dracena is the city’s third largest at 7.8 acres. It includes a number of swings and play structures in addition to large grass areas and a dog run. Here on the climbing wall, Piedmont free soloists work on their technique. The redwood bosque at Wildwood and Magnolia is a beautiful example of open space that has been created in a typically neglected area. It is one of a number of landscaped traffic islands and medians scattered throughout the city that have been put to good use.

articles.text: Tommy Craven (Mel Gibson) and his only child, daughter Emma Craven (Bojana Novakovic), are leaving his home when a shotgun blast kills Emma. Initially Tommy thinks the shot was aimed at him and wonders who from his past (an ex-con seeking his long contemplated revenge) might have tried to kill him. As he looks for the killers (there are two), he begins to discover pieces to the puzzle that are at first perplexing but soon point not to him as the target but to Emma. It turns out that she worked for a major defense contractor, Northmoor, located in Northhampton, and that she was flirting with the idea of becoming a whistleblower. Since this is pulp cinema there has to be pulp dialogue (here spoken with a Boston accent) in which the Chief of Detectives says to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous,” and Tommy says, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” What that means is a bit unclear, but no matter, the pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hard-edged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s perwonderfully portrayed by Mila Kumis and James Franco; and more. He meets, awkwardly, Dana Cummings, an accountant for the company, who discovered the irregularity. She sets up Wolff in a room with glass on three sides, glass that he uses to write down his algorithms and numbers as he closes in on the leak. It’s a stunning piece of work by Wolff, but one that is not what the CEO hoped for. Suddenly Dana and Wolff are in danger; what they know about the company puts them in harm’s way. But despite Wolff’s rigidity Edge of Darkness Continued from page 20 Tommy Craven (Mel Gibson) and his only child, daughter Emma Craven (Bojana Novakovic), are leaving his home when a shotgun blast kills Emma. Initially Tommy thinks the shot was aimed at him and wonders who from his past (an ex-con seeking his long contemplated revenge) might have tried to kill him. As he looks for the killers (there are two), he begins to discover pieces to the puzzle that are at first perplexing but soon point not to him as the target but to Emma. It turns out that she worked for a major defense contractor, Northmoor, located in Northhampton, and that she was flirting with the idea of becoming Date Night Continued from page 21 the movie would have been, if not hilarious, at least laugh-out-loud funny. Meanwhile, a Treasury Department agent (J.K. Simmons), close to retirement, wants to do one last thing before he walks out the door. He wants to find out who Wolff is and why he keeps appearing in photos with some very bad actors around the world. The hunt is on, also a forensic exercise, making the film still more interesting. Children (and later adults), who fall somewhere on the autism spectrum, often struggle to find a place in society. Many suffer, as do their families. My impression is that the writers of The Accountant do not regard this reality superficially. I did find the flashbacks to Wolff’s childhood credible and heartfelt. Since this is pulp cinema there has to be pulp dialogue (here spoken with a Boston accent) in which the Chief of Detectives says to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous,” and Tommy says, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” What that means is a bit unclear, but no matter, the pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hard-edged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s persona throughout the film. Is Edge of Darkness violent? Definitely. In the Craven world you can have conversations, brief and to the point, and then the moment is quickly reached when the best response is simply to hit or shoot the bad guy. articles.text: ple together for both interaction and simple people watching. Maybe the most important advantage of open space is the most abstract and difficult to define. I’ll call it the spiritual advantage. In our world of extensive development, our ability to interact with a bit of the natural world (the opposite of the built environment I am always referencing) can raise our spirits, give us a chance to slow down and reflect, to experience our connection to nature—just a little of what the naturalist Henry Thoreau wrote about at Walden Pond in the 1800’s. I suspect the activity of simply strolling through or sitting and resting to enjoy trees, lawns, plants and benches is the most common, and important, use of our open space. There are a number of other sites within Piedmont that contribute to the open space total. These include various EBMUD properties, landscaped medians and traffic islands, various wooded hillsides and ravines, part of the Rose Garden, and even part of the Mountain View Cemetery. Schools, with their large green playfields, seem to be burdened with the inconsistent open space definition mentioned earlier. In Piedmont however, the ongoing joint use of City and School District facilities realistically puts them in the open space category. In addition, because of our proximity and easy access to various nearby regional amenities such as Redwood Park, Temescal Recreational Area, or Joaquin Miller Park, these too can be considered as a part of Piedmont’s useable open space. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 27, 2021 This is the most undisturbed, natural part of our Piedmont Park. The many beautiful redwood trees located here consume more CO2 and release more oxygen than any other tree on earth.

Cemetery Groundskeeper Carlos Fierro helped transport this year’s pumpkins and estimates that well over 300 pumpkins were displayed in the pumpkin patch. But this year, it was the festival’s Live Animal Show that stole the hearts of festival-goers. Furs, Scales, & Tails, an entertainment company owned and operated by Tracy Hill, dazzled children when he brought out Nana, his cornstalk-colored Burmese Python, and lining up ten volunteers to help hold her. In terms of kids’ entertainment, his act has been sharpened into a latter-day vaudeville masterpiece. He talked rapidly to the audience like only the best auctioneers can and quickly established a rapport with children and parents through his calland-response banter. “Alright, now my friend Treasure’s going to come out. Everyone say, ‘Hi Treasure!’” “Hi, Treasure!” responded the audience, as Hill brought out his next animal, a black-furred bunny rabbit. Kids also enjoyed jumping in the festival’s bounce houses, then going to a different area in the meadow to decorate Halloween masks at arts & crafts tables. Meanwhile, parents were treated to the live music of local band Sweet City Blues, who displayed a wide-ranging repertoire that day by playing everything from “Spooky,” by Dusty Springfield, to “Little Wing” by Jimi Hendrix. Even after spending four years out-of-commission, the Pumpkin Festival certainly wasn’t rusty. Even after a four-year absence, the pumpkin patch at Mountain View Cemetery remained the highlight of the Halloween Festival for children and parents alike. Miguel Casas-Sanchez, Sophia Chen, and their child, Arthur Casas-Chen, pose for a photo at the pumpkin patch.

They might actually approve them somewhere else. But wherever they put them, the CEQA will require the city to impose all feasible mitigation measures to reduce the noise impacts,” confirmed Drury. However the filing of the suit doesn’t mean the matter needs to go to trial. The CEQA has a mandatory early settlement provision, Drury explained. “CEQA requires the parties to sit down and try to settle the case in the first 45 days. So, we’re trying to schedule that meeting with the city now.” In recent years pickleball has become a hot-button issue for some Piedmont residents. Since 2018, the sport’s popularity has grown and efforts have increased to accommodate the current number of players. From February 27 to July 31, 2023, the Piedmont Recreation Commission held a trial period of pickleball at the Linda Beach courts. During this time, multiple voices of support in addition to complaints were received from members of the surrounding neighborhood, including letters to City Council and calls to the Piedmont Police Department for noise complaints. On September 5, citizens supporting and opposing Linda Beach courts as dedicated courts for pickleball appeared at a city council meeting to give offer their views. That evening, the City Council voted unanimously to dedicate and restripe the Linda Beach courts for pickleball only. “The ball is in the city’s court now,” commented Drury. Staff photo Pickleball is known for a distinctive popping sound made when a player hits the ball. According to a new lawsuit, this noise significantly impacts the lives of residents in neighboring homes. Piedmont School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn notified members of the school community on Friday, October 20 via email that the APT is taking the action. articles.text: Piedmont School District Finance Officer Ruth Alahydoian provided an update on the school’s $51,000,000 budget at the October 11 school board meeting. Her report showed a continued decrease in enrollment and addressed the financial impacts from current and future population projections. articles.text: On Monday, October 16, George Sanen, Project Executive for the community pool project, delivered a report to the city council about the progress of construction on the community pool. Joined by President of Griffin Structures John Hughes and ELS Architect Clarence Mamuyac, Sanen reported that because of “unforeseen conditions,” the community pool is now delayed well past its original target of June 2024. Additionally the most recent completion date of September 2024 has been pushed back even farther and no estimated date of completion has been offered. Reasons for the pool’s altered timetable are several: delays with PG&E regarding power installation; discovery of old fuel tanks under the construction site; and difficulties posed by the pool’s all-electric design. “I wish I had right now the final date of when you are all going to go swimming, but unfortunately I don’t have it,” said Sanen. “There are still a lot of items that we need to refine and resolve amongst them in the schedule.” Photo by Staff Photos. Pool architect and Piedmont resident Clarence Mamuyac

articles.text: I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues. It was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. In the biblical narrative, grief and gratitude frequently travel together. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. The

articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church invites the community to a presentation of a Requiem Mass for All Souls on Wednesday, November 1, at 6:30 p.m. Ben Bachmann, Director of Music, will lead an orchestra and St. Paul’s Choir in a performance of the majestic Requiem in D minor, Op. 48, by Gabriel Fauré. Everyone is invited to remember and celebrate the lives of all the beloved departed. Fauré said of his Requiem, “Everything I managed to entertain by way of religious illusion I put into my Requiem, which moreover is dominated from beginning to end by a very human feeling of faith in eternal rest.” Fauré saw death as a “happy deliverance – an aspiration towards happiness above.” The church will be illuminated with candles, and votive candles will be available for individuals to light. You are invited to submit the names of loved ones to be held in remembrance and listed in the service sheet. Please submit names by October 30 via email admin@ stpaulsoakland.org or by phone at 510-834-4314, x501. St. Paul’s is located at 114 Montecito Avenue at Lake Merritt in Oakland. For more information, see stpaulsoakland.org.

articles.text: Piedmont students earned high scores on the California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) tests for 2022-23. As a district, Piedmont was third statewide in the ranking for both Math and English Language Arts. The annual standardized test is administered to students in California public schools. The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language and Literacy, Math, and Science. The CAASPP replaced the paper-based Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program in 2014. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and grade 11 (high school juniors) participated in the CAASPP. Students in grades 5, 8, 11 and 12, participated in the Science test “CAST”. The California Department of Education’s results, released on October 18, are shown below. Overall, over 86% of Piedmont students met or exceeded state standards in English Language Arts – a one percent drop from 2022. In Mathematics, over 82% of students met or exceeded state standards, improving on last year’s result. In Science, over 68% of Piedmont’s 5th, 8th and 11th and 12th grade students met or exceeded the rigorous state standards. This is double the state of California average of 30.2% and earned PUSD a rank of 5th in the state. “Piedmont Unified School District has a strong history of academic achievement, and this year’s CAASPP results reinforce the academic rigor of our instructional programs,” said PUSD Superintendent, Jennifer Hawn. “We are incredibly grateful to our teachers and staff for their high-quality instruction and support, along with our families who nurture and encourage our students’ overall achievement,” she added. articles.text: Amid discussions about negotiations between the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) and the Piedmont Association of Teachers, members of the PUSD School Board have a message. “To our educators - we hear you and we see you. We want the best for our educators, our students and our community. We have had countless hours of discussions about how we can fairly compensate our educators and we all agree that that is critical. We’ve discussed how to increase revenues. We’ve discussed cuts, we are reading your emails and we are working toward compensation,” said school board member Lindsay Thommason at the October 11 School Board meeting. Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign is one way to increase revenues, and the Giving Campaign team is urging the community to donate to help support teachers. “This year $2.3 million of PEF’s $3 million grant to PUSD, about 77%, is earmarked for instructional salaries,” confirmed Giving Campaign Co-Chair Kim Hunter, “The more money we raise, the more we can give.” The Giving Campaign raises money to fund teachers, intervention specialists, paraeducators, wellness, professional development, technology, and other activities that lead to PUSD student success. “When our budget is so extremely tight and we face really tough decisions, we’re looking for creative solutions. The Giving Campaign has a huge goal of $3.5 million but that doesn’t mean we can’t raise more than that. I would love to see our participation go up, especially as a sign of support for our amazing teachers. Every family should give to this important cause because we do have an amazing group of teachers. Please do your part by giving to the Giving Campaign.” said school board member Hilary Cooper The Piedmont Giving Campaign has raised over $1.5 million so far this year. The campaign’s goal is to raise another $2 million. “As part of the Superintendent’s Advisory Committee, I have been working on enrollment and looking at our peer schools, both public and private, at what the cost is of some of the private schools,” added Thomasson. For high school in particular it ranges from 45 to 60 thousand dollars per year. So, what the Giving Campaign is asking is less than one month’s tuition at a private school. It’s less than one month’s tuition at a lot of preschools. When you put it in that perspective it’s really a bargain.” Please support our community schools and amazing teachers by donating today at https:// www.piedmontedfoundation.org/ donate/.
articles.title: Giving Campaign urges support of teachers

articles.text: More than 150 robotics students converged upon the John Morrison Gym at Piedmont Middle School on Sunday, October 15 for a robotics scrimmage. All 25 Piedmont FIRST LEGO League Challenge teams were on hand with more than 50 parent coaches. The scrimmage format allowed younger students to prepare for official regional competitions during the year. This season’s “Masterpiece” theme has robotics students programming LEGO Spike robots to autonomously solve LEGO missions in timed runs of 2-1/2 minutes. articles.text: Gayl Hirschfeld is a person who reads a lot. “Mostly fiction or historical fiction,” she admits. Hirschfeld is also retired, so she has more time for reading these days than when she was working. However, she doesn’t often read aloud to other people. But on Thursday morning, October 19, Hirschfeld drove to Beach Elementary School to do just that – to read for others. Reading to 15 kids ages five and six from a copy of “Pete the Cat and the Missing Cupcakes,” Hirschfeld participated in a new program, Storytime Club, through the Recreation Department, showing storybook pictures to her audience. For each story, she asked them what they thought about the story and used a different voice for each character. “You’ve got to change your voice to represent who is on the page. That variety is what kids tune into. The more you can do to change things up, the better,” she said. Storytime Club is aimed at connecting children with seniors in the community. Senior adults are matched with classrooms at Beach and Wildwood Schools and then tasked with reading a storybook to a class of young students. “The hope is that the senior will form a relationship with the students or the program and be available to volunteer regularly at their chosen site,” explained Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen. pages.text: Wednesday, October 25, 2023 7 Seniors read to children in new program By Matt Simons Gayl Hirschfeld is a person who reads a lot. “Mostly fiction or historical fiction,” she admits. Hirschfeld is also retired, so she has more time for reading these days than when she was working. However, she doesn’t often read aloud to other people. But on Thursday morning, October 19, Hirschfeld drove to Beach Elementary School to do just that – to read for others. Reading to 15 kids ages five and six from a copy of “Pete the Cat and the Missing Cupcakes,” Hirschfeld participated in a new program, Storytime Club, through the Recreation Department, showing storybook pictures to her audience. For each story, she asked them what they thought about the story and used a different voice for each character. “You’ve got to change your voice to represent who is on the page. That variety is what kids tune into. The more you can do to change things up, the better,” she said. Storytime Club is aimed at connecting children with seniors in the community. Senior adults are matched with classrooms at Beach and Wildwood Schools and then tasked with reading a storybook to a class of young students. “The hope is that the senior will form a relationship with the students or the program and be available to volunteer regularly at their chosen site,” explained Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen. As beneficial as the programs are to the students, they are also beneficial to the seniors reading to them. “I like kids, and when I see happy little kids, or when I’m entertaining kids, it makes me happy,” said Hirschfeld. Research shows these reading sessions make a substantial difference in children’s learning, especially during early childhood. articles.text: I have made a habit of asking people that I meet in my day-today life whether or not they have a gratitude practice. Let’s just say it seems like a lot of people have heard of gratitude but most aren’t really sure how to try it in their daily lives. It seems to have joined mindfulness as a buzzword in wellness, but people might not know how to actually implement it. I am a Focus Coach located in Piedmont. I work with people (especially people with ADHD) to help them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week, I am writing about implementing a gratitude practice to make life easier and experience more joy. What are people actually saying when they are talking about gratitude? Gratitude reminds us that being happy is a state of mind rather than a finish line we’re all racing to. Genuine happiness comes from noticing the good in the present moment and trusting that there will be more good in the next one. A gratitude practice is simply the idea of intentionally noticing and appreciating the present moment because that does not come naturally to most of us at first. A common example of a gratitude practice is writing down three good things you noticed about your day either in the morning or at night before you go to sleep. Another example is creating a group text with some friends and everyone texts a few things they are grateful for from the day. A third example could be making a point to mindfully thank someone in your life (the barista at your coffee spot, a co-worker who helps you out, or a band you follow on Twitter). However you choose to practice gratitude, you’ll find over time that the more you practice noticing and appreciating the good things in your life, the more you’ll notice and appreciate the good things that already exist in your life and over time this will lead to a greater sense of wellbeing. Please don’t hesitate to reach out to me if you need help developing a gratitude practice or figuring out other Positive Psychology interventions that will work for your specific goals. articles.text: Libraries aren’t just book-holding archives. They are central pillars within our communities. This week, with free book tables at the Halloween parade, sugar skull making, and events for young children, the Piedmont Ave. Branch Library is sure to have a little bit of something for everyone in the community this Halloween season. The library will host several events related to the Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade on Saturday, October 28. Before the parade, visitors can join Storytime with Shani at 10 a.m. at Key Route Plaza, 41st and Piedmont Ave. Friends of Piedmont Ave. Library will staff a table there with free books and button-making. After the parade kids are invited to the library at 2 p.m. to make sugar skulls with their friends and library staff. Sugar skulls have their roots in Mexican cultural traditions and are typically used to decorate altars honoring ancestors during Día de los Muertos. Although the skulls are usually made out of cane sugar, library staff will be creating the skulls with modeling clay and then decorating them with glitter and other materials. In addition to participating in parade activities, the library will also have other programs throughout the month. Their Fall Stay & Play program is held every Tuesday at 10:15 a.m. For one hour each Tuesday, the library will provide a selection of toys and games for play. This program is aimed at children ages 18 months to 3 years, but kids of all ages are welcome. Meet the Manager The Piedmont Avenue Branch Library recently welcomed a new branch manager, Sabah Abdulla. A long-time resident of the neighborhood, she knows the library well. After missing two years of school as a teenager when her family had to return to Yemen, she had fallen behind in her studies. So, Sabah went to the Piedmont Avenue Branch Library every day to study and catch up. She always felt safe and welcome there. During college, Sabah worked part-time at several branches and she was encouraged by the amazing library staff to get her library degree. Sabah earned her MLS at San Jose State and immediately began working as a Teen Librarian at the Asian Branch Library. At the Piedmont Avenue Branch, Sabah is working to build back its programs: chess club, Baby Café, bringing books to seniors, among several. In the future, she plans to connect with neighborhood organizations to share the wonderful resources at the library. Piedmont Avenue Branch Library is located at 80 Echo Avenue, Oakland directly behind Piedmont Avenue Elementary School. For more information call (510) 597-5011, or send an e-mail to eanswers@oaklandlibrary.org. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. Reflecting upon her time with the choirs, Bohlin mused, “I became aware of the extraordinary gift of life guidance through music education that PEBCC and their staff were providing for chorus members. Rehearsals, performances, camps, tours, and festivals have profound impacts. Making music is a transformative process that trains us to relate to one another on a soulful and respectful level. articles.text: Piedmont’s rejuvenated football team pulled off a big 35-29 victory over Kennedy HS in Fremont on Friday, October 20. With Alameda losing to Newark Memorial on Friday – its second loss, Piedmont catapulted itself to the top of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division. There’s still work to do. Now with a 3-1 league record, there is a three-way tie for first-place between Piedmont, Newark Memorial, and Kennedy. Tiebreakers for the league title go by head-to-head, giving PHS the edge over Kennedy. With PHS playing a winless American HS team this Saturday and Newark facing Arroyo, it sets up an epic season-finale for the Shoreline crown on November 3 between the Highlanders and Newark Memorial. “Coming from where we were last year to first-place and controlling our own destiny over the next two weeks means a lot,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “To come from where we’ve been, having no home field, it’s been a heck of a ride. It’s the most memorable season of my coaching career thus far, no doubt,” The win against Kennedy proved to be another monumental performance by receiver Sam Photos by Steve Long Piedmont’s 35-29 win over Kennedy of Fremont moves them to the top of the WACC’s Shoreline Division. Shelby, who scored four touchdowns and had had 338 all-purpose yards. Shelby finished with seven receptions for 164 yards and 154 yards rushing, with two touchdowns each. He also converted all five extra point attempts, giving him 29 total points on the day. It marks one of the highest combinations of receiving and rushing yards since Gabe Watson in 2014. Tommy Ashton only had 10 yards, while quarterback Markos Lagios had 30 yards on nine carries and one score. articles.text: Piedmont’s cross country team returned to Oyster Bay Regional Park in San Leandro for its second league meet of the season on Wednesday, October 18. Xander Schulte-Sasse won the race with a best-ever time, and the girls’’ team placed third overall in a field of 10 teams. The PHS boys were fourth on a hot 90-degree day. Despite the heat, Schulte-Sasse posted a time of 15:22.89 for the victory. “The boys and girls all ran very well despite the heat with Xander Schulte-Sasse coming in first place overall with a terrific race. He was in complete control the entire time,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach, A four-year varsity runner, Schulte-Sasse has been in a hallmark year, improving his best time by five seconds on the 3-milec course. “In our last league meet, I felt like I was just cruising and had a lot left in me when I crossed the finish line. To feel like I could step it up one more notch made me even more excited,” said Schulte-Sasse. The girls’ team was without senior Jamie Schwarz, who was preparing for today’s Mid-Season Mania 3200M Invitational at Campolindo. “Jamie was getting some much-needed rest in preparation for the end of the season races. Our varsity runners will be competing at Campolindo High School this Wednesday on the track in a 3,200 meter race,” explained Zirkelbach. Sophomore Skylar Best led the way for the girls’ team with a time of 19:31.25, placing fourth in a field of 72 runners. Behind Best Staff Photos Xander Schulte-Sasse won Piedmont’s league meet at Oyster Bay with a PR time on the three-mile course.

articles.text: In an emotional end to Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball season, the Highlanders lost 3-2 to Berkeley on Wednesday, October 18 after opening the match with a 2-0 lead, The Highlanders needed a win to qualify for the post-season North Coast Section playoffs and nearly upset this year’s League (Western Alameda County Conference) champions in dramatic fashion. In a match before a Piedmont home crowd, it all came down to a final 15-point fifth set tiebreaker. Piedmont held match point at 14-13 before Berkeley scored the game’s final three points to win the match and eliminated the Highlanders from post-season play. “I’ve had this group since they were freshmen, so watching them for four years has been a blessing… I think we got a little fatigued, some of us aren’t used to playing in this kind of environment. They did a really good job. It was such a hard loss because of how hard they tried. It’s been a really good season regardless of the outcome,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. Piedmont entered the match with a 5-6 league record and needing the win to finish at .500 for an automatic bid to the NCS playoffs. The match marked an end to Sadie Town’s illustrious volleyball career at PHS. A three-year starter, Her total number of kills is likely the most by a player in the last decade. Her 28 kills against Bishop O’Dowd was the most by a Piedmont player since Samantha Fanger’s 24 in 2017. The team graduates a handful of players to graduation next spring: Bauer and Beck Peterson, Elena Stevens, Maddy Mullin, Molly Wagener, Maddy Hill, Izzy Grimmer and Town. Game Recap Piedmont came out hot in the first set, jumping out to a big 9-4 lead before extending to 12-6. articles.text: Piedmont’s flag football team took a tough 26-6 loss to San Leandro on the road at Burrell Field on Thursday, October 19. Piedmont trailed 12-6 with less than five minutes left in the game. “We were just a couple of yards away from scoring on a couple of occasions, it’s now happened to us several times,” explained PHS coach Beth Black. “We’re so close in connecting all the dots. We had a really physical game. The score may not reflect that we’re jumping to new levels.” The result brings Piedmont’s record to 3-4 entering its final week of the season. PHS will host Hayward for the regular season finale tomorrow, October 26, before competing in the first Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament at Hayward High on Saturday, October 28. In Piedmont’s losses to Alameda, Berkeley, and San Leandro, the Highlanders were in scoring position multiple times and the defense showed it could thwart each of their opponents’ attacks. A strong performance by San Leandro quarterback Jade Orta was the difference. She is a competitive player outside of school at the club level. She was a game-changer for the Pirates, using her speed and agility to weave around defenders for long runs, while also having a cannon of an arm. “She was amazing. She was so evasive, you put a rush on her and she can evade, leaving an opening. It took her a long time to find her passing options and that seemed to frustrate her. But when she could run, she took advantage of it, and she was fast,” said Black. Game Recap After both teams traded possession through the first dour drives of the game, San Leandro retained the ball with 9:30 left in the half after forcing a turnover on downs at its own 35-yard line. On 3rd-and-5, the Pirates completed an 18-yard pass to the 17 before Orta ran in a touchdown. A failed two-point conversion made it 6-0 with 5:30 remaining in the half. However, San Leandro nabbed an interception on a long pass down the sideline and returned it to Piedmont’s 31. Orta then ran the ball to the PHS 5 before tossing in a touchdown, 12-0 with Piedmont retaining possession with 1:51 on the clock. On the Highlanders’ 2-minute drive, they converted a 4th-and-2 when Mia Leggett found tall receiver Dorothy Nemeth for a 10-yard gain to the San Leandro 32. Leggett then hit Nemeth again on 3rd-and-10 for a 15 yard gain to the 17. With the seconds ticking away, Leggett found Miya Fujimoto for a 15-yard catch and run to the two-yard line, but without a timeout, the clock hit zero before Piedmont could get the play off. The two teams traded possessions to open the second half, while Piedmont had another opportunity to score on its next drive. Starting at San Leandro’s 36, Leggett hit Lucy Wheeler for a 17-yard gain to the 19 to make it 1st-and-Goal. Leggett then connected with Fujimoto for a 14-yard gain at the 5. But Staff Photos Receiver Dorothy Nemeth had a touchdown reception against San Leandro. Quarterback Mia Leggett takes a snap from Malia Hartford with Lucy Wheeler in at running back. Miya Fujimoto runs around a San Leandro defender. on 3rd-and-Goal, the Pirates grabbed an interception on a pass targeting Lucy Wheeler in the end zone. The PHS defense forced a punt with 10:30 on the clock, scoring after 10 plays to make it 12-6 with 4:30 left. During the series, Leggett and Nemeth converted a 3rd-and-10 situation on a 14-yard reception to SL 36-yard line. On 3rd-and-9 at the 21, Leggett found Malia Hartford for a 12-yard gain to the 9. After a four-yard gain by Fujimoto, Leggett hit her tall receiver, Nemeth, on a high pass at the goal line. However, San Leandro’s offense couldn’t be stopped on its next drive with Orta hitting her receiver for a 25-yard gain, followed by a 17-yard scamper by the QB. The Pirates scored on 2nd-and-Goal with a 14-yard pass making it 20-6 with 1:30 left. San Leandro got another interception on PHS’ next drive, which led to a long touchdown pass with eight seconds left—26-6. phries Diamond tomorrow, October 26 at 4:30 p.m. They will compete in the inaugural WACC Championship Tournament at Hayward High on Saturday, October 28. articles.title: HIKING WITH JON

articles.text: Happy Halloween! It’s the spooky season, so what better time to delve into haunted urban legends? Growing up around Hayward, the gruesome legend of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park is a well-known story, providing an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool in the 1960s led his entire class of child-aged students up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting as a teenager of children in all-white garb from head-to-toe. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be entirely covered by thickets of California Bays, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the inner East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep downhill declines. It is considered a very technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding out of the ground. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to continue the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in the process through the hills of Green Belt Park. You’ll top out above the tree-line, you have the option to do a 180 and head back down, or turn right and walk straight down Durham Way to continue the loop onto the Greenbelt Hiking and Riding trail—which reunites you with Ward Creek until reaching Campus Drive. In the six miles of hiking, we only passed 29 people around noon on a Sunday, so less than five people per mile on a popular day for hikers. The trail is a great spot for a lower leg workout with over 1,100 feet in elevation gain. No ghost sightings were made, but perhaps my own paranoia brought out the feeling that eyes were always following me. Punch in “Hayward Plunge” or “Memorial Park Hayward” into your GPS device to access this trail’s parking lot. To cut off the first 1.3 miles, park on Campus Drive. This article was originally printed in the Piedmont Post in October 2020. You’ll pass over numerous bridges on your hike. The view of the Greenbelt trail next to Ward Creek connects with the Hayward Plunge Trail. The trail is wide, giving ample space for hikers and bikers.
articles.title: More than 6 miles of hiking along Hayward Plunge Trail

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Nollywood Dreams, a new comedy by Jocelyn Bioh, is playing onstage now through November 11. Set in Lagos, Nigeria in the 1990’s, the play follows Ayamma Okafor, played by Angel Adedokun, who dreams of stardom. She has her heart set on the bright lights of Nollywood, the burgeoning Nigerian film industry akin to California’s Hollywood an Calcutta’s Bollywood. She and her sister Dede, played by Brittany Nicole Sims, toil in their parents’ travel agency and unexpectedly audition with Nigeria’s best-known director as the story begins to unfold. The playwright hoped to capture a moment in time in Nigeria, one that most Western audiences don’t see, and blend it with comedic elements. “That’s an important goal for me,” Bioh told the San Francisco Chronicle. “I really am trying to diversify and break open people’s singular narrative of Africa and African stories. We learn about these people who inhabit the continent, and it allows us to have a more humanizing perspective on them.” The play is premiered October 4 at San Francisco Playhouse and is directed by Margo Hall. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/upcoming-plays/ to see showtimes and to purchase tickets. Ayamma (Angel Adedokun) works at her parents’ travel agency in the SF Playhouse production of Nollywood Dreams.

articles.text: Oakland Ballet celebrates Dia de Los Muertos (Day of the Dead) with performances of “Luna Mexicana”on October 28 in San Jose and November 3 and 4 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for the Dia de Los Muertos holiday, which is celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food, and is a gathering for families and loved ones. The performance features the return of Viva la Vida, a ballet inspired by the life and spirit of Frida Kahlo. Luna Mexicana is co-choreographed by Martín Romero of Ballet Folklórico México Danza and Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig. Ballet Folklórico México Danza will present traditional Mexican Folkloric dance, and Mariachi Mexicanisimo will perform folk mariachi music. Performances at the Paramount Theater in Oakland will Oakland Ballet celebrates Dia de los Muertos October 28 to November 4. take place on Friday, November 3, at 7:30 p.m., and on Saturday, November 4, at Paramount Theater in Oakland. An earlier performance will be held at 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, October 28, at Hammer Theatre in San Jose. Visit www.oaklandballet.org to purchase tickets or call the box office at (510) 893-3132.

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, October 25, 2023 Arts & Entertainment SF Playhouse’s Nollywood Dreams performed through Nov. 11 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Nollywood Dreams, a new comedy by Jocelyn Bioh, is playing onstage now through November 11. Set in Lagos, Nigeria in the 1990’s, the play follows Ayamma Okafor, played by Angel Adedokun, who dreams of stardom. She has her heart set on the bright lights of Nollywood, the burgeoning Nigerian film industry akin to California’s Hollywood an Calcutta’s Bollywood. She and her sister Dede, played by Brittany Nicole Sims, toil in their parents’ travel agency and unexpectedly audition with Nigeria’s best-known director as the story begins to unfold. The playwright hoped to capture a moment in time in Nigeria, one that most Western audiences don’t see, and blend it with comedic elements. “That’s an important goal for me,” Bioh told the San Francisco Chronicle. “I really am trying to diversify and break open people’s singular narrative of Africa and African stories. We learn about these people who inhabit the continent, and it allows us to have a more humanizing perspective on them.” The play is premiered October 4 at San Francisco Playhouse and is directed by Margo Hall. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/upcoming-plays/ to see showtimes and to purchase tickets. articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra (SFMO) makes a return engagement with a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 11, its sixth concert at the Center in as many years. The Orchestra’s season theme this year is “Napoli and the Revolution.” “We chose this theme because the 18th century was a time of revolutionary thought,” explained Achille Bocus, musical director of SFMO “Across Europe and America enlightened ideas of freedom, order, rationality, and happiness influenced politics, art, and music. The music of the time reflected this, with the end of the Baroque and emergence of the Classical Period, and the birth of mandolin as a popular instrument in Naples. “It’s the music that Jefferson, Franklin, Paine and other revolutionaries would have heard.” The Orchestra will perform music from the late baroque and classical periods, including: • Johann Sebastian Bach: Selections from Art of the Fugue • Giuseppe Giuliano: Concerto for Mandolin in B flat (Achille Bocus, soloist) • Wolfgang Mozart: Selections from London Notebook Achille Bocus, musical director of San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, will be the soloist in the Giuliano Concerto for Mandolin in B flat at concert on November 11 at Piedmont Center for the Arts. • Giovanni Battista Sammartini: Sinfonia in G Major for String Orchestra The family-friendly concert will begin at 5:00 p.m. on November 11. Admission is $20 general, $15 student/senior, and free for children 12 and under. Tickets may be purchased at the door, or at the Orchestra’s ticketing site: sfmandolin.square.site.
articles.title: SF Mandolin Orchestra returns to Piedmont for Nov. 11 concert

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation, will present its Fall Concert on Saturday, November 4 at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The orchestra will perform Roman Carnival Overture by Berlioz (1843). Rhapsody On A Windy Night by Cavaterra (2022), and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4 in F minor Op. 36 (1877). Tickets are $20 General admission, and free for students who register at (http://data.ypsomusic.org/tickets). Call (510) 849- 9776 for additional information. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is celebrating its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director and Conductor. The orchestra has 99 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from throughout the greater Bay Area. YPSO will perform four concerts this year, will be a participant in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, and perform at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, before embarking on a 9-day tour to Japan in June 2024, which includes three concerts. The Fall Concert is the kickoff for YPSO’s 87th season. About California Festival YPSO is one of 95 organizations participating in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, (cafestival.org) presenting some of the most innovative and compelling music from around the world for two weeks, November 3-19, 2023, in venues throughout the state. Announced in January 2023 and conceived by Los Angeles Philharmonic Artistic Director Gustavo Dudamel, San Diego Symphony Music Director Rafael Payare and San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the California Festival invites musical organizations of all kinds to incorporate works written within the past five years into their broader season programs. About YPSO YPSO’s Music Director, David Ramadanoff, has always been thoughtful about selecting music programs that are able to showcase the diversity of talent in the entire orchestra, and he continues this tradition here. YPSO students engage in a wide range of orchestral music works spanning multiple musical eras and with composers from various backgrounds. Starting this season, YPSO will offer free admission to youth 13 and under accompanied by an adult, and high school and college students with valid ID. YPSO asks that all concert goers, including students, to please register on their ticket site, even if some tickets are free, in order to maintain appropriate seating capacity counts. New musicians invited YPSO is still auditioning for limited sections: trumpet, tuba, French horn, bassoon, and oboe. Piedmont students currently in the band and orchestra are encouraged to audition now to join YPSO for the second half of the season. Call (510) 849-9776 or click on ypso.org for additional information. 86 Cañada Road Woodside, CA 94062 650.364.8300 filoli.org 12-MONTH FINANCING *some restrictions apply CL#788850
articles.title: YPSO Fall Concert in Berkeley on November 4

articles.text: Cal Performances presents the Brad Mehldau Trio at Zellerbach Hall on Saturday, November 11. The award-winning jazz trio consists of pianist Mehldau, bassist Larry Grenadier, and drummer Jeff Ballard. Mehldau and his longtime bandmates have been praised for their musical chemistry and wide range of stylistic and emotional terrain. Mehldau is an iconic jazz soloist in his own right. The New Yorker called him “arguably the greatest working jazz pianist,” with the touch of Bill Evans and the range of Keith Jarrett. He is well-known for his jazz renditions of rock music, including hits by the Beatles and Neil Young. He is the winner of a Grammy award for best contemporary instrumental album and has been nominated for 13 other Grammies in his career of more than three decades. The trio will perform an evening of original compositions as well as reimagined jazz standards on November 11. The performance begins at 8 p.m. Tickets are available at www. calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Photo by David Bazemore Pianist Brad Mehldau will perform a concert at Zellerbach Hall on November 11.

articles.text: Narrowly defined, a dilemma is a predicament in which two possibilities present themselves, both equally undesirable. The Dilemma certainly meets that criterion. Ronny (Vince Vaughn), in partnership with his best friend, Nick (Kevin James), is scouting for an appropriate place to propose to his girlfriend, Beth (Jennifer Connelly), when he spots Nick’s wife, Geneva (Winona Ryder), hungrily kissing another man. His problem is what to do with this information. What is his moral duty to Nick? And how will it impact their business? They are close to signing a contract with Dodge for a green engine that has the power and the amplification of a 66 Ford GT-350 or the iconic Dodge Hemi: in other words, it’s a muscle car with batteries. It’s a guy car we’re told by Ronny, not a lame, quiet, hybrid. Telling Nick about Geneva at this delicate moment could unhinge the deal by distracting Nick, the engineering genius behind the engine, and already stressed to the max by deadlines. Ergo: Ronny’s dilemma. The scene of observed infidelity takes place at the end of act one, an act that establishes that Ronny and Nick are involved in a long-term bromance. They’re straight, the movie emphasizes, but they’re also best buds: they go clubbing, play hockey, and share a love of cars. As act two begins, it would seem natural that Ronny would go home to Beth – she’s bright, a successful chef, caring, and eager to be included in whatever speed bumps Ronny might encounter. In fact, she was there for him as he overcame a gambling problem some years back. This is a woman who can be leaned on. Instead of sharing his dilemma with her, however, Ronny begins a long period of deception, dissembling, and even stalking. He faults Geneva for her lack of honesty, yet rejects honesty as perhaps the best modus operandi, at least with Beth. And thus the film Vince Vaughn and Kevin James in The Dilemma

articles.text: Simply do the math. As a nation we spent the better part of two centuries failing to recognize the talent and humanity of a people, their gifts, their intellect, their potential. It was called racism. The loss has been incalculable. Hidden Figures is the exhilarating true story, based on the book by Margot Lee Shetterly, about three black women who worked at NASA’s Langley facility, in Hampton, VA. during the late 50s and early 60s. The race into space had been joined. Russia had gotten America’s attention and we scrambled to catch up. These women – all profoundly talented – were, in the eyes of NASA, all but invisible. They worked for the agency during a time when it was segregated and sexist. There were separate bathrooms, dining rooms and work areas for “colored only” and for “whites only.” The barriers Katherine G. Johnson (Taraji P. Henson), Dorothy Vaughn (Octavia Spencer) and Mary Jackson (Janelle Monae’) faced were appalling and, in retrospect, all but impossible to comprehend. What is remarkable about the film is that it is unflinching in its depiction of the bigotry, both overt and covert, that greeted them each day at NASA. Until, finally it didn’t. At the center of the film is Katherine G. Johnson, a gifted mathematician, who is brilliant at geometric calculations. Gradually, her genius takes her to the center of the mission to launch astronauts into orbit. NASA clearly had the hardware. What it didn’t have were the calculations to not only reach space, but to bring the likes of John Glenn, who orbits earth, safely back. It’s at that intersection that Katherine Johnson steps forward. She can do the math that is absolutely essential. It’s deeply satisfying watching her overcome the prejudice and discrimination, What is surprising is that the men of NASA are incredibly well schooled engineers, and yet they are blind to their own bigotry. They don’t see Katherine or her precocious gift. They see only color. But against all odds, the trio – Johnson, Vaughn and Jackson – persevere: they push back, they bend rules until finally NASA begins to see them not as black women but as individuals who have a great deal to offer. What is also wonderful about Hidden Figures is that the narrative includes moments when the women are at home, at picnics, at church, surrounded by children and husbands, who all view what they do as groundbreaking, and filled with pride and satisfaction. The film opens in a delightful way: the three women are stopped on a Virginia highway on the way to work after their car breaks down, with Katherine Johnson lying underneath the car to check the starter motor. Unexpectedly a local police officer pulls up and asks to see some I.D. They each show him their NASA badges and he looks at them with obvious disbelief and then says, with a shake of his head, “I didn’t know that NASA hired… women.” Indeed it did. And that decision was how we managed to get John Glenn home safely. Hidden Figures. Directed by Theodore Melfi. Starring Tara R. Henson, Octavia Spencer, Janelle Monae. 2 hrs., 7 min. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv

articles.text: A scene from Transformers: Dark of the Moon In most big tent blockbuster films – CGI driven, saturated with action – there is always a tension between spectacle and story. Generally, in movies of this ilk, plot and dialogue are given short shrift and spectacle prevails. If this trend persists, Michael Bay, director of T3, will dismiss the screenwriter and offer his films as experiences, absent any exposition at all. But no worries, action scenes that fill the screen to bursting with overwhelming energy and sound are Michael Bay’s specialty, and T3 is all about extraordinary moments that are can’tlook-away engaging. There may be no better vehicle for Bay’s particular brand of movie than one in which the characters are machines. Seriously. That doesn’t mean he doesn’t want his audience to identify with these giant Hasbro created Bots which were all the rage in the 80s. He does. Hence, they are nicely anthropomorphized, with individual personalities, well spoken. The good Bots (Autobots) and the bad Bots (Decepticons) have movie star blue eyes and satanic red eyes respectively. They also possess other humanoid qualities – interesting facial features, massive arms, tree trunk legs, hands (prehensile? probably not), all wonderfully and magically articulated – which makes them as interesting as the humans. In fact, Optimus Prime and Bumblebee have more heart than many of the humans. Regarding humanizing animals and Bots, it’s something that resonates, requiring little suspension of disbelief, and is essential to creating a relationship between the Bots and the audience. Disney divined this at the outset, creating grainy cartoons starring Mickey and Donald and later the memorable Bambi. If you’re a Transformer aficionado, you’re well versed in the backstory of Sam Witwicky (Shia LaBeouf) and the Bots, all explained in the first Transformers movie. It was the best of the three; far more interesting, long on character development, and fresh in its dialogue and premise and opening set up. In T3, not so much. Sam does have a new hottie, Carly (ex-model Rosie Huntington-Whiteley), whose derriere is introduced before she is, and who needs saving. A lot of saving. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Something Borrowed is all about triangulation. But then triangles are a staple of romantic comedies; in fact, they’re a staple of the human experience. Triangulation is familiar behavior involving three people, two are on the inside of a situation or issue or complaint and one is on the outside, essentially unaware. Triangles can be wicked. And they can be a source of endless comedic situations, which is why Hollywood writers return so often to this particular well. They have tapped that well in Something Borrowed. Darcy (Kate Hudson) and Rachel (Gennifer Goodwin) are best friends forever. They are also opposites. Darcy is a bit shallow and self-absorbed, as well as spontaneous and glowing. Rachel’s other BBF is Ethan See Something Borrowed on page 29 Transformers: Dark of the Moon is a long part 3 Kate Hudson and Colin Egglesfield in Something Borrowed A scene from Transformers: Dark of the Moon By Chris Honoré In most big tent blockbuster films – CGI driven, saturated with action – there is always a tension between spectacle and story. Generally, in movies of this ilk, plot and dialogue are given short shrift and spectacle prevails. If this trend persists, Michael Bay, director of T3, will dismiss the screenwriter and offer his films as experiences, absent any exposition at all. But no worries, action scenes that fill the screen to bursting with overwhelming energy and sound are Michael Bay’s specialty, and T3 is all about extraordinary moments that are can’tlook-away engaging. There may be no better vehicle for Bay’s particular brand of movie than one in which the characters are machines. Seriously. That doesn’t mean he doesn’t want his audience to identify with these giant Hasbro created Bots which were all the rage in the 80s. He does. Hence, they are nicely anthropomorphized, with individual personalities, well spoken. The good Bots (Autobots) and the bad Bots (Decepticons) have movie star blue eyes and satanic red eyes respectively. They also possess other humanoid qualities – interesting facial features, massive arms, tree trunk legs, hands (prehensile? probably not), all wonderfully and magically articulated – which makes them as interesting as the humans. In fact, Optimus Prime and Bumblebee have more heart than many of the humans. Regarding humanizing animals and Bots, it’s something that resonates, requiring little suspension of disbelief, and is essential to creating a relationship between the Bots and the audience. Disney divined this at the outset, creating grainy cartoons starring Mickey and Donald and later the memorable Bambi. If you’re a Transformer aficionado, you’re well versed in the backstory of Sam Witwicky (Shia LaBeouf) and the Bots, all explained in the first Transformers movie. It was the best of the three; far more interesting, long on character development, and fresh in its dialogue and premise and opening set up. In T3, not so much. Sam does have a new hottie, Carly (ex-model Rosie Huntington-Whiteley), whose derriere is introduced before she is, and who needs saving. A lot of saving. articles.text: It was a night all will recall, dripping with nostalgia and sentiment as the semi-retired MTT returned to conduct Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony. With the elderly, ailing podium laureate back, the tributes by the full house were never more pronounced. Yes, a love-in, by any measure. And with not one but two wars raging on the far side of Earth, never were Beethoven’s choral messages of hope, “All men will be brothers,” with the following “Be embraced, ye millions,” more needed. The messages struck home to the heart. No mere concert, this was a night to remember, with the imposing SFS Chorus’ 110-plus members outdoing themselves in the exuberant finale to cap the 75-minute performance. Shuffling on and off the stage with halting steps, Michael Tilson Thomas appeared to be the most beloved music director here since World War Two. Who else would have been honored with an eight-minute (!) standing ovation at the end, silenced only when the maestro withdrew to the wings for the last time, solicitously led by the singers. Else the sell-out crowd at Davies might still be clapping. His conducting was not lax, but rather relaxed – soulful and low-key, with a personalized that unprecedented choral finale. And that finale was glorious, doing something I hadn’t heard at the SFSC in three decades: pronouncing the consonants, so that the printed German texts could be followed. Credit the new SFSC director Jenny Wong for the warmly welcomed improvement as she too was celebrated by MTT at the conclusion. The finale had a robust launching by baritone Dashon Burton, who set the rafters ringing, followed by a consistent set of soloists: tenor Ben Bliss, soprano Angel Blue and mezzo Tamara Mumford. MUSIC NOTES The shorter companion piece scheduled, Shango Memory by the late Berkeley black composer and professor Olly Wilson, was dropped without explanation… MTT, 78, was diagnosed with aggressive brain cancer during the pandemic. He had retired as music director in 2020, after 25 years at the helm…The choral texts came from poetry by Friedrich Schiller (1759-1805), who, like the SFS, must have had a crystal ball to foresee how timely his texts would be at this very moment in history. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, also contributes reviews of the Bay Area classical concert scene on the web site www. artsSF.com. Michael Tilson Thomas, retired Music Director of San Francisco Symphony baton beat that only these veteran SFS players could read and respond to. Their affection, too. was palpable, as with the ensemble’s amiable chuckles when violist Jonathan Vinocour had to leap up to help him with his printed score, to the maestro’s gratitude. And again, during the plaudits, when his players donned bluerimmed glasses out of nowhere, matching his own. If the trumpets and timpani were unflinchingly zealous October 19, no one could miss the delicacy of the Scherzo, the silky strings in the Adagio with the eloquent woodwind ensemble, or the superior cellos leading into Violinist and composer Niccolo Paganini. playing while in prison. Others said that he had sold his soul to the devil. Most of the stories were ridiculous, but the public loved it. They were happy to pay inflated prices, and Nick reaped a fortune. The wonder of it all was that he was amazingly generous. He helped countless musicians gain important careers. He was generous in his praise and never badmouthed anyone. The funny thing is that he was accused of extreme avarice, similar to the radio & TV comedian Jack Benny. It is true that Nick was very careful with his money. But he was also very generous. Nick inspired generations of composers. As a composer himself, he was one of the greatest melodists of all time… ranking up there with Mozart and Schubert. Nick’s birthday is coming up pretty soon on October 27. If you go to Italy, you can attend music festivals in his honor. Let’s take Muhammad Ali at his word. He was “the greatest.” But the true “most sensational entertainer of all time” will always be violinist Niccolo Paganini.

articles.text: “I am the greatest” was Muhammad Ali’s mantra. Perhaps he was. But the title of the most sensational entertainer rests with another. There were no mantras… no shouting matches. None of that was ever needed. Over the years there have been many contenders. There were a couple of guys named Francis, separated by 100 years. The first Francis is considered the greatest pianist of all time. These were the 1830s and 1840s. We know him better as Franz Liszt. The second Francis of the 1940s through 1970s is better known as Frank Sinatra, the singer. And then came Elvis and the Beatles and Jimi Hendrix and Madonna. “The Boss” should be included and most recently Taylor Swift and her Swifties. But they all pale by comparison. In fact, if not for the original “most sensational”, none of these contenders would even know how to get publicity. Let’s go back in history and consider the life and legacy of a kid named Nick. He was born in Italy and was a sickly child from the start. It was a miracle that he even lived into maturity. His parents thought he was dead, and he was placed in a coffin. During the funeral services, someone noticed that he seemed to be breathing – he wasn’t dead after all. Then began his violin lessons. His brutal father beat him mercilessly. He left home as soon as he could and got a job with Napoleon’s sister. His first composition created a sensation. His career grew and grew. He remained in Italy until 1828 when he decided to go to Vienna to meet Beethoven, but alas. Beethoven died in 1827. Nick got publicity without even trying. Not only was he the most popular musician in Europe, he was even more famous than Napoleon. Nick continued on his concert tours and met the most famous musicians of all time. He was a regular guest in Mendelssohn’s home. Schumann was overwhelmed, as was Chopin, Liszt and Berlioz. It was the same story everywhere. Nick brought the violin to international prominence and, while doing so, classical music became the most popular form of music. Along the way he invented virtually every technique known to violinists. This enabled composers to move light years ahead. It wasn’t enough that he was simply the greatest violinist of all time. There were stories that he had murdered his wife and developed his sensational violin

articles.text: Artist Michael Stehr, a Piedmont native, will unveil his most recent paintings at Piedmont Center for the Arts on November 3. The exhibit, titled “Going the Distance – Depicting Space on a Two-Dimensional Plane”, will explore the devices Michael uses to communicate a sense of space and atmosphere in a composition. Ultimately to create an envelope of space in which a viewer can enter a picture is one of the great challenges for a painter, he explains. When successful, this elevates a painting from a mere collection of colors and shapes and heightens it to an invitation to explore and escape. Thirty-five new paintings will be included in the display which totals 80 art works. The show will be open until November 19. Gallery Hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through Sunday, November 19. To preview the exhibit online, go to www.bit.ly/3ZO1Urc. The artist will host a reception to open the exhibit at the Center for the Arts at 6:30 p.m. on Friday, November 3. He will offer remarks about the exhibit at 7:15. RSVP at mstehrart@gmail. com by October 25 to attend the reception. articles.text: Visit the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco to see its newest exhibition on view, Takashi Murakami: Unfamiliar People – Swelling of Monsterized Human Ego, on display now through February. Murakami: Monsterized is the first solo exhibition in San Francisco by Japanese artist Murakami, born in 1962. He is an internationally recognized contemporary artist and major figure in global pop culture, whose influences draw from the aesthetic characteristics of the Japanese artistic tradition and the nature of postwar Japanese culture. Murakami’s influence in the contemporary art world makes his works highly sought-after in art trades, and his vibrant prints maintain a consistently high value. In this exhibition, the artist’s larger-than-life paintings and sculptures use monsters, a common theme in his pieces, as a central motif. Senior Curator of Japanese Art Laura Allen said, “The visual DNA of Murakami’s characters has origins in centuries-old styles in Japanese art, such as depicting Buddhist arhats and Daoist immortals as wizened beings with strange features, bulging eyes, and bared teeth.” Murakami has added “technicolor palette, goofy expressions, and eclectic mixture of motifs” that quickly became his trademark, Allen added. Murakami: Monsterized is open an extra hour until 6 p.m. Friday through Monday and until 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Visit https:// asianart.org/ to learn more.

articles.text: One of the first French wine regions I fell in love with was Cahors. About 30 years ago I did a home exchange in the Dordogne Valley of France just a little north of the town of Cahors and was introduced to some of the magnificent wines of the region. Last month I made a return visit to southwest France and went back to visit some of the same wineries I had liked 30 years ago. For my money the Dordogne and Lot River valleys are the most spectacularly beautiful parts of France. The land is green with tons of chestnut, walnut and oak trees interspersed with fields of vibrant sunflowers and meticulously tended farmland. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, October 25, 2023 Features The Wine Corner The wines of Cahors and Bergerac By Pierre DuMont One of the first French wine regions I fell in love with was Cahors. About 30 years ago I did a home exchange in the Dordogne Valley of France just a little north of the town of Cahors and was introduced to some of the magnificent wines of the region. Last month I made a return visit to southwest France and went back to visit some of the same wineries I had liked 30 years ago. For my money the Dordogne and Lot River valleys are the most spectacularly beautiful parts of France. The land is green with tons of chestnut, walnut and oak trees interspersed with fields of vibrant sunflowers and meticulously tended farmland. The land is dotted with black and white and brown cows who not only look clean but are remarkably contented. No wonder their cheese is so good. The Cahors wine region is on the Lot River about 50 miles east of Bordeaux. It is the birthplace of the Malbec grape, and all the wines have to contain at least 80% Malbec. It is ironic that in today’s world when one hears the word Malbec the first thing that springs to mind is…..Argentina. Chateau Lagrezette is a 15th century castle. Malbec has become the national grape of Argentina and the country exports tons of it. To my mind the country has done the grape a disservice as most of the Malbecs from Argentina I have had are simplistic and boring monochromatic wines. The wines of Cahors will not remind you of Argentina but instead of Bordeaux. Cahors is influenced by the Mediterranean as well as by the Atlantic, and although winters are colder than in Bordeaux, the wines tend to be more concentrated. They were appreciated as suitable blending material with the lighter wines of Bordeaux, and in the early 19th century were famous as the “black wine of Cahors.” Vines for Cahors may be planted either on the notably thin topsoil of the arid limestone plaPascal Verhaeghe is director of Chateau du Cedre winery. The old house and cedar tree at Chateau du Cedre winery in Cahors, France The “Le Cedre” from Chateau du Cedre is one of Cahors’ finest wines. The tasting room at Chateau Lagrezette teau, the causses, or on the sand and gravel terraces between the plateau and the river. Wines from the plateau tend to be bigger and longer-lived than wines from the terraces. Chateau du Cedre I remember visiting Chateau du Cedre 30 years ago with my father. A young Pascal Verhaeghe who had recently taken over winemaking responsibility from his father greeted us and led the tasting. I have been a big fan of their wines ever since. This time as I drove up to the old farmhouse with the cedar tree out front, I was also met by the now gray Pascal who is in the process of turning operation over to his two sons. Du Cedre began the transition to organic farming in the 1990’s and they were certified fully organic in 2021. In the cellar they use only natural yeasts with a minimum of winemaker interference and minimal sulfites. Today they make 15,000 cases of wine per year of which 80% is exported. (Their U.S. exporter is Martine’s Wines in Novato, CA). • Favorite wine – 2021 Chateau du Cedre “Le Cedre” This is the middle range of their wines and my favorite. It is made from 30- to 50-year-old vines grown on the high terraces above the river and is 100% Malbec. The wine mingles aromas of dark berries and cassis with hints of bitter chocolate, sweet spices, tobacco and a hint of oak. It is medium to full-bodied, layered and concentrated with tangy acids and a deep, firm mid-palate framed by rich tannins. It concludes with a long, penetrating finish. The only missing ingredient is time. Chateau Lagrezette You drive around the corner of the narrow country road and suddenly you face a grand 15th century fortified castle perched on its imposing hill. Welcome to Chateau Lagrezette. The castle was purchased in 1980 by Alain Dominique Perrin, former CEO of the Cartier luxury group.
