Chateau Clos de Gamot The drive from Chateau Lagrezette to Clos de Gamot is only about 15 minutes but the two estates are worlds apart. While Lagrazette is clearly a well-funded, modern corporate winery, Gamot is a very small, old-school family run operation. They have the reputation of being the most ‘traditional” producer in Cahors. The owners, the JoufClos de Gamot Cuvee des Vignes Centenaries comes from 120-yearold vines. freau family, traces their roots in the village of Prayssac to the year 1290. In 1450 they planted the first vines for Clos Gamot and in 1510 they built a house that is still where the family lives. Their regular cuvee of Clos de Gamot is medium bodied and fresh and a great value at $14. The most interesting was the Cuvee Vignes Centainieres which comes from a section of the vineyard that has vines that are over 120 years old. • Favorite Wine – 2020 Clos de Gamot Cuvee des Vignes Centenaries The wine delivers notes of warm cassis, blackberry jam and cherries with nuances of leather, tobacco, and bay leaves. Medium to full-bodied, the palate is filled with generous blueberry preThe winery owners of Clos de Gamot still live in this 16th century family home. The Tour des Gendres Winery in Bergerac in the Dordogne River Valley of France Clos de Gamot is a traditional old-school producer of wines. serves, sparked by herbal and earthy hints supported with a firm, grainy texture, and finishing with gorgeous freshness. This wine is built to last for decades in the cellar. Chateau Tour des Gendres I visited this winery 30 years ago when Luc Conti oversaw the place. It is not in Cahors but farther north in Bergerac in the Dordogne River valley. The Conti family originally settled in the area in the 1920s, began planting vines in 1984 and making wine in 1986. On my return visit this year I was greeted by Luc’s daughter Margaux and Gilles Conti owners of Tour des Gendres Margaux and her brother Gilles who are now the winemaker and estate manager. I was drawn to the place on my first visit because I loved a wine they produced from Semillon and Sauvignon Blanc that was aged in new oak barrels that gave it a powerful oaky vanilla nose. The wine philosophy has changed dramatically as I heard disparaging comments about both new oak and the Semillon grape. Things have not gone downhill as the new wines that were poured were full of character and delicious. They started with Cantalouette rouge and blanc that were refreshing quaffers that they served slightly chilled. Both were clean, savory and satisfying and at $11 a bottle are a great bang for the buck. They went on to pour a nice 100% Merlot called Les Gendres and a 100% Cabernet Franc called Les Anciens Francs, both excellent representatives of the varietals. Tour des Gendres is imported by Martine’s Wines of Novato. • Favorite Wine – 2021 Tour des Gendres “Le Vif” Finding this wine was a delightful surprise as it is made from the Savagnin grape which is not usually found outside its native region of The Jura in France. It had a charming nose of honeysuckle and peaches, great body of melon, apricot fruit and minerals with layers of complexity. It reminded me of a first class Savennieres from the Loire Valley. While delicious now, this wine has the potential to improve in the cellar for a decade. Tour des Gendres VIF is made from the Savagnin grape.

articles.text: Race down the stretch at East Bay Agency for Children’s 24th annual Gala on November 4th at the Turf Club atop Golden Gate Fields in Berkeley. Guests at The EBAC Classic will take a victory lap for East Bay children and families as they enjoy specialty cocktails and an epicurean dinner paired with Keenan wines, raise their paddles to bid on world-class getaways in the live auction, stock their cellars with cases of premier vintages from the wine raffle, and “get down” with the Git With It Band. New this year will be the broadcast of the “Inf latable Derby”, a race previously filmed on the Golden Gate Fields track with six intrepid EBAC supporters wearing inflatable animal costumes. Gala guests will root for their favorite contestant in what promises to be a hilarious highlight of the evening. This year’s racing venue and theme encourages guests to wear derby styles such as fancy hats and ascots or equestrian attire including jockey colors or riding breeches. For the 24th year, volunteers from the EBAC Auxiliary are planning another epic party. The EBAC Auxiliary began in Piedmont with founders Diane Goetz and Claire Faughnan still involved today. Funds raised support EBAC, a local non-profit who has been meeting the mental health needs of east bay children since 1952. EBAC’s mission is to improve the well-being of children, youth and families by reducing the impact of trauma and social inequities. Gala chair Amanda Lacau Noguera said, “With the future of Golden Gate Fields and the gorgeous Turf Club uncertain, we are thrilled to give our gala guests perhaps one final opportunity to enjoy a night to remember at this landmark venue while raising money to address the current childhood mental health crisis.” For tickets and sponsorship details, see EBAC.org/Gala.

The group was pleased to welcome Don Fones who was walking with the group for the first time. There was a good turnout of 37 walkers and one K-9 best friend for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays gathering on October 18. The group had scheduled its annual pre-Halloween walking tour of Mountain View Cemetery for the following week and wanted to get into the Halloween spirit by looking for Halloween house decorations around the city. The group went to the lesswalked, block-long Sierra Avenue, and right away on the corner was their first Halloween sighting. In front of a house was a strange looking scarecrow with a metallic wrap exterior that looked a little like Big Bird. It was explained that this was one of the scarecrows that Piedmont elementary school students made for the Piedmont Harvest Festival. Each class creates a scarecrow out of recycled materials, and they are auctioned off as a fundraiser for the schools. After Sierra they went on Sheridan Avenue to Lakeview Avenue and climbed to the top at Sea View Avenue where they saw a larger-than-life sized ghost in front of a house. Further down Sea View, the front yard of one beautiful home had been taken over by a set of even scarier Halloween characters. The worst/ best of them was a smiling, Joker-style clown popping out of a Jack-in-the-box. He was surrounded by skeletons and ghouls emerging from the ground. They were quite a sight at 11 in the morning. The group made their way down Sea View to Hampton Road and the towards Glen Alpine Road, where they saw a wonderful historic mansion, Hampton House, designed by noted architect Albert Farr in 1926. In front, it had a set of life-size, playful, inflatable Halloween characters. There were dragons, ghost dogs, an octopus, a skeleton riding on a motorcycle, and several others. The walkers stopped briefly for a group photo. It was noted that the home is currently for sale for $14,850,000. It has eight bedrooms, nine baths, and is 11,870 square feet with a tennis court, a rose garden, mature hedges and trees, and a separate guest unit. The temperature was starting to rise, so the group thought it would be smart to start back before it got too hot. On their way back to the center of town, they passed Hampton Field, went down La Salle Avenue and onto Indian Road, where they passed more Halloween decorations. This Halloween house sightseeing was a fun way for the walkers to start their countdown to the always enjoyable tour of Mountain View Cemetery one week later – and also to get ready for all the wonderful, little trick or treaters at the end of the month. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Sunday, October 29 will be the last chance to visit the Wildwood Dads Club’s Pumpkin Patch at Coaches Field to purchase pumpkins and gourds for Halloween. Be sure to guess the weight of Giant Jack, the enormous pumpkin on view this week. Last weekend, the patch sold 735 pumpkins, of which 266 were carving pumpkins. The Wee-B-Little has emerged as a favorite as well, with 122 miniature pumpkins sold. As of Tuesday, the patch received 238 guesses for Giant Jack’s weight, with one enthusiDozens of student drawings have been turned into the Wildwood Das Pumpkin Patch in exchange for a free Wee-B-Little pumpkin. Wildwood 5th graders Eva Piniella (left) and Sophie Shartsis helping out at the Wildwood Dads Pumpkin Patch last week. astic prognosticator placing 50 one-dollar guesses. The deadline for guesses is 6:00 p.m. Saturday, October 28, for a chance to win free delivery (and later removal) of the prized pumpkin. “With the help of 65 volunteer dads, we are expected to exceed our goal of raising over $30,000 to help fund projects at Wildwood,” said first year Patch Papa Matt Derrigo. Standard operating hours continue, Monday-Friday, 4:00-6:00 p.m., and this Saturday from 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. On Sunday the dads will start at 10 a.m., launch a “blow-out sale” at 2:00 p.m., and begin dismantling the patch starting at 4:00 p.m. Discounts are available on the sale of the hay bales and corn stalks. “Historically this last week tends to be a big push on carvers so we’ll be stocked full,” said Derrigo. “We still have some beautiful Fairytales, Knuckleheads and several other varieties to spruce up your front door.” All members of the Kwok family took home a pumpkin friend from the Wildwood Dad’s Club Pumpkin Patch.
articles.title: Last chance for pumpkins at Coaches Field

Food truck vendors will also be on-site to sell tacos, empanadas, lumpia, burgers, fries, hot dogs, hot links, Italian ice, and more. “I am so excited that the Cemetery is hosting our annual Pumpkin Festival again this year,” said Kristie Ly, events manager at the Cemetery. “It is one of the Cemetery’s most popular community events alongside the Tulip Exhibition and Memorial Day event.” Despite the festival’s four-year hiatus, Ly said it wasn’t too hard to start things back up. “Getting back into planning the event was not too hard. Most of our vendors are familiar with the event, so they are happy to participate again. It will be a great Saturday full of events starting with the Piedmont Avenue Merchants Association (PAMA) parade on Piedmont Avenue,” said Ly. “We enjoy seeing all the families enjoying the festivities,” said Eliana Martinez of Mountain View Cemetery. “The costumes are always so creative and we look forward to seeing the animal show again. [Tracy Hill] does a fabulous job!” The 15th Annual Pumpkin Festival will take place following the Piedmont Avenue Halloween parade. Admission is free. Parents must accompany their children to this event. Mountain View Cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. The Pumpkin Festival will have large bouncy houses available for children of all ages.

Piedmont Real Estate Update October 2023 The Impact of Rising Interest Rates on Real Estate and the Economy The unprecedented surge in interest rates in 2022 and 2023 and the impact on the real estate market have ignited discussions in housing and financial circles. This month’s newsletter explores key elements of this conversation and how it affects the consumer. Interest Rates, Inflation, and the Jobs Report The September Jobs Report exceeded expectations by adding 336,000 new jobs, putting pressure on the Federal Reserve to consider another interest rate hike. As we have seen in real time over the past year, interest rates play a critical role in shaping the economy and housing market by influencing borrowing costs and investment decisions. While we don’t yet know if the Fed will go through with another increase, the real estate, building, and mortgage industries have been vocal about what another hike means for the ability to build, buy, or sell real estate. The Federal Reserve's historic efforts to combat inflation began with a series of interest rate hikes, which pushed mortgage rates above 7% and abruptly slowed down the booming pandemic-driven housing market. According to forecasts by researchers at the San Francisco Federal Reserve, we might be on the brink of experiencing the most significant decline in shelter inflation since the Global Financial Crisis of 2007 to 2009. (Source: CNN) Rolling Recession Rising interest rates can contribute to a recession by increasing borrowing costs, potentially reducing consumer spending, business investments, and housing demand. Gary Keller, co-founder of Keller Williams, has warned of a “rolling recession” that may affect different industries at different times in specific ways. Locally, residential real estate sales have slowed notably year over year, and prices are down 15-20% off of their highs in spring 2022. The complex relationship between Federal Reserve interest rate decisions and the economy affects various industries differently. The real estate sector, in particular, grapples with the impact of these rate hikes and their implications for housing market stability. It’s essential to stay informed as economic conditions evolve. Federal Reserve’s Interest Rate Hikes The Fed’s decision to raise interest rates has evoked mixed responses. While intended to curb inflation and ensure economic stability, critics fear it may slow down borrowing, investment, and spending, harming the real estate market and the overall economy. Comparing Interest Rates To put the interest rate changes in perspective, in 2022, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was around 3.0%, while in 2023, it rose to approximately 3.5%. For a million-dollar loan, this equates to an annual difference of $5,000 in interest payments. articles.text: On Monday, October 16, the Piedmont City Council appointed Anna M. Brown as Piedmont’s new City Clerk. Brown comes to Piedmont during a career in local government, most recently as City Clerk in Union City since 2014. Prior to that she served as Deputy City Clerk of South San Francisco for five years. Brown is a Certified Municipal Clerk, a Notary Public, with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Public Administration. On July 17, following the departure of John Tulloch as City Clerk, the council appointed Sheri Hartz as interim city clerk while the city searched for a permanent replacement. The recruiting firm Bob Murray & Associates was hired to initiate a professional search. Over the next six weeks, 25 applicants were considered and six were interviewed. A panel of current and former city clerks was convened to rank the candidates. The panel included Mark Numainville, Berkeley City Clerk, Joanne Robbins, Lafayette City Clerk, and former Piedmont City Clerk John Tulloch. Additional interviews were conducted by some members of the city government, including City Council members and City Administrator Roseanna Bayon Moore. “I am honored and excited to serve the city of Piedmont as its next city clerk,” said Brown. “It is my sincere hope that the work that I do here helps foster a greater sense of trust between the city’s residents and their city government.” The posted salary is $177,000 annually with an auto allowance and health benefits. Staff photo Anna Brown will be the new City Clerk for the City of Piedmont.

articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade will take place on Saturday, October 28, starting at 11:00 a.m. in front of Pet Food Express at the corner of Montel Avenue. Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson will be leading the parade as Grand Marshal in one of his many costumes. Merchants on the street founded the parade in 1986 as a way to celebrate Halloween safely. It has evolved into a highly anticipated community celebration that unites the neighborhood. The street will be closed to vehicles from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. from Yosemite Avenue to the Piedmont Theater at Linda Avenue. Kids can start stocking up on candy two days before Halloween by trick or treating along the Avenue at participating merchants’ shops. Live music, haunted houses, face painting, and skull craft will have everyone in high Halloween spirit. Free cartoons will be shown for children at the Piedmont Theater starting at 9:45 a.m., and Piedmont Avenue will be packed with kids and adults in costumes on Saturday, October 28, for the 36th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade.

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department encourages residents to stop what they’re doing this Thursday, October 19 at 10:19 AM and take a few minutes to practice what they would do during an earthquake as part of the annual Great California ShakeOut. Held annually on the third Thursday of October, International Shakeout Day challenges people across the globe to become better prepared to protect themselves in case of an earthquake. More than 9.6 million people in California have signed up to participate in this year’s ShakeOut. The Piedmont Fire Department offers the following advice: Anytime you feel shaking or get an earthquake alert, take these three steps immediately if you are able: 1. DROP to your hands and knees: This position protects you from being knocked down by shaking and reduces your chance of being hit by falling or flying objects. 2. Take COVER under a sturdy desk or table: Stay on your knees and bend over to protect vital organs while covering your head and neck with one arm. If there’s nothing available nearby to shelter under, crawl next to an interior wall. 3. HOLD ON until shaking stops: If you’re sheltering under furniture, hold onto it with one hand and be ready to move with your shelter if it shifts. Otherwise, hold onto your head and neck with both arms and hands. For those in a wheelchair or using a walker: For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. 1. LOCK the wheels of your device 2. COVER your head with your hands and arms 3. HOLD ON until the shaking stops. Living near the Hayward fault, earthquakes are a legitimate concern for millions of California residents. Analysts at the United States Geological Survey (USGS) predict that a major earthquake event of magnitude 6.7 or greater is likely to affect the San Francisco Bay Area before 2032. The Loma Prieta Earthquake of 1989 was measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale, lasted just 15 seconds and caused more than $5 billion in property damage. After practicing “drop, cover, and hold on,” the Fire Department recommends signing up for AC Alert emergency notifications, building or refreshing your disaster supply kit, and making a plan for how you will contact your loved ones after an emergency. The City of Piedmont encourages all citizens to join in this exercise.

One day maybe we’ll have a cure for it.” Fire Dept. urges residents to participate in Great California ShakeOut Annual event encourages earthquake safety, preparedness By Matt Simons Piedmont Fire Department encourages residents to stop what they’re doing this Thursday, October 19 at 10:19 AM and take a few minutes to practice what they would do during an earthquake as part of the annual Great California ShakeOut. Held annually on the third Thursday of October, International Shakeout Day challenges people across the globe to become better prepared to protect themselves in case of an earthquake. More than 9.6 million people in California have signed up to participate in this year’s ShakeOut. The Piedmont Fire Department offers the following advice: Anytime you feel shaking or get an earthquake alert, take these three steps immediately if you are able: 1. DROP to your hands and knees: This position protects you from being knocked down by shaking and reduces your chance of being hit by falling or flying objects. 2. Take COVER under a sturdy desk or table: Stay on your knees and bend over to protect vital organs while covering your head and neck with one arm. If there’s nothing available nearby to shelter under, crawl next to an interior wall. 3. HOLD ON until shaking stops: If you’re sheltering under furniture, hold onto it with one hand and be ready to move with your shelter if it shifts. Otherwise, hold onto your head and neck with both arms and hands. Analysts at the United States Geological Survey (USGS) predict that a major earthquake event of magnitude 6.7 or greater is likely to affect the San Francisco Bay Area before 2032. The Loma Prieta Earthquake of 1989 was measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale, lasted just 15 seconds and caused more than $5 billion in property damage. articles.text: The first Black family to live in Piedmont, the Dearing family, moved into their home at 67 Wildwood Avenue in early 1924. Within months, a mob of 500 people surrounded their house, demanding they leave because of the color of their skin. That history and more will be shared by Piedmont High School students on Monday, October 23 in a presentation supported by the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC). The event is open to the public and will include light refreshments after the program. History of Piedmont: Racism and Redlining will incorporate a conversation about the history of Piedmont, including the early origins of redlining in the Bay Area and how it affected the Dearing family in particular. Created by members of Piedmont High School’s Associated Student Body, the presentation also follows Piedmont’s complicated legacy in the hopes that it will inspire change and promote an inclusive environment. “The more we know about our past, the better we can aid the future of Piedmont,” said PHS senior Hailey Marshburn, one of the organizers. The presentation will be given to PHS sophomores and juniors in early November. The presentation will take place at 6:30 p.m. on Monday, October 23 in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Avenue, begin. We also invite you to stay after the program for light refreshments and conversation from 7:30 to 8:30 pm. “A few members of PADC had a chance to see this presentation last year. We were so inspired by it that we wanted everyone in our community to have an opportunity to experience it. The student presentation was well researched, powerful, and is moving.” said Ellen Lee, PADC President. For more information, contact Lee at hiellenlee@gmail.com.
articles.title: PHS students to present History of Piedmont: Racism and Redlining

articles.text: Taurid Meteor Shower as seen from Chabot Space and Science Center in the Oakland hills. When the night sky is stretched above us, there is so much to see – even in the dark. Sometimes the dark gives the perfect stage for a special show you would not be able to see clearly in the daytime. A few notso-small examples are the moon and the stars. However, in early November an even more exciting show is coming to the night sky: the Taurid meteor shower. What is a meteor shower? Meteor showers happen when the Earth passes through left over stuff like rocks from asteroids and comets. When these rocks enter the Earth’s atmosphere the air around them gets very hot. So, from Earth the rocks look like bright streaks of light across the sky. If you have ever seen a shooting star, then you know exactly what to look for. During the Taurid meteor shower, the Earth is passing through a comet named Encke. Encke is a small comet that takes 3.3 years to travel around the sun, the shortest travel time of any known comet in our solar system. Why is it called the Taurid Meteor Shower? Meteor showers get their names from the constellations that the meteors seem to be coming from. Constellations are a group of stars that sometimes look like the shapes of objects, animals, or people. For this shower, the meteors are coming from the direction of a constellation called Taurus, a group of stars that look like a bull, so it is called the Taurid meteor shower. When and where can I see it? The Taurid meteor shower is a meteor shower that happens in two parts: the Southern Taurids and the Northern Taurids. These showers begin mid-October and go on up to early December. pages.text: Wednesday, October 18, 2023 7 PHS students to present History of Piedmont: Racism and Redlining By Marja Germans Gard The first Black family to live in Piedmont, the Dearing family, moved into their home at 67 Wildwood Avenue in early 1924. Within months, a mob of 500 people surrounded their house, demanding they leave because of the color of their skin. That history and more will be shared by Piedmont High School students on Monday, October 23 in a presentation supported by the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC). The event is open to the public and will include light refreshments after the program. History of Piedmont: Racism and Redlining will incorporate a conversation about the history of Piedmont, including the early origins of redlining in the Bay Area and how it affected the Dearing family in particular. Created by members of Piedmont High School’s Associated Student Body, the presentation also follows Piedmont’s complicated legacy in the hopes that it will inspire change and promote an inclusive environment. “The more we know about our past, the better we can aid the future of Piedmont,” said PHS senior Hailey Marshburn, one of the organizers. The presentation will be given to PHS sophomores and juniors in early November. The presentation will take place at 6:30 p.m. on Monday, October 23 in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Avenue, begin. We also invite you to stay after the program for light refreshments and conversation from 7:30 to 8:30 pm. “A few members of PADC had a chance to see this presentation last year. We were so inspired by it that we wanted everyone in our community to have an opportunity to experience it. The student presentation was well researched, powerful, and is moving.” said Ellen Lee, PADC President. For more information, contact Lee at hiellenlee@gmail.com. Middle School to produce Disney’s The Little Mermaid Jr. Piedmont Middle School will present Disney’s The Little Mermaid Jr, on November 3-5, with 57 performers and 15 stage crew members. Favorite songs by composer Alan Menken and lyricists Howard Ashman and Glen Slater include “Under the Sea”, “Kiss the Girl”, and “Part of Your World”. With a book by Doug Wright, this show presents an enchanting look at the sacrifices we make for love and acceptance, Performances are at the Alan Harvey Theater on the following dates and times: Friday, November 3, 7 p.m. Saturday, November 4, 2 p.m. Saturday, November 4, 7 p.m. Sunday, November 5, 2 p.m. Performances will last approximately 1 hour and 20 minutes including intermission. Tickets are $12-$18 and may be purchased at the door or online at: https://www.showtix4u.com/ event-pmsmermaid For more information contact director Amy Moorhead at amoorhead@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Thinking Outside the Classroom Coming to a night sky near you – the Taurid meteor shower ADVERTISE IN THE POST Taurid Meteor Shower as seen from Chabot Space and Science Center in the Oakland hills. By Cameron Schneider When the night sky is stretched above us, there is so much to see – even in the dark. Sometimes the dark gives the perfect stage for a special show you would not be able to see clearly in the daytime. A few notso-small examples are the moon and the stars. However, in early November an even more exciting show is coming to the night sky: the Taurid meteor shower. What is a meteor shower? Meteor showers happen when the Earth passes through left over stuff like rocks from asteroids and comets. When these rocks enter the Earth’s atmosphere the air around them gets very hot. So, from Earth the rocks look like bright streaks of light across the sky. If you have ever seen a shooting star, then you know exactly what to look for. During the Taurid meteor shower, the Earth is passing through a comet named Encke. Encke is a small comet that takes 3.3 years to travel around the sun, the shortest travel time of any known comet in our solar system. Why is it called the Taurid Meteor Shower? Meteor showers get their names from the constellations that the meteors seem to be coming from. Constellations are a group of stars that sometimes look like the shapes of objects, animals, or people. For this shower, the meteors are coming from the direction of a constellation called Taurus, a group of stars that look like a bull, so it is called the Taurid meteor shower. When and where can I see it? The Taurid meteor shower is a meteor shower that happens in two parts: the Southern Taurids and the Northern Taurids. These showers begin mid-October and go on up to early December. It is believed that you will be able to see the Northern Taurid stream best between November 12 and 13 and the Southern Taurid stream around November 6. Just like a movie is best to watch in a dark theater, you want to make sure you are in the darkest possible place outside to see this meteor shower. This means you will want to be away from places like cities where all the lights make it more difficult to see the night sky entirely. A one-of-a-kind show There are so many interesting things in the night sky to see and learn about. The Taurid meteor shower is just one of the many examples of why sometimes the best show of all is right above our heads. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: At Piedmont High’s Homecoming Rally on Friday, October 13, school pride bubbled and boiled over inside Binks Rawlings Gym. The inventiveness of students was on display as each grade battled in fun competitions, with students and staff decked out in Piedmont purple. The ASB school-wide event was hosted by student government leaders Phoenix Nwodeki, Jane Hempeck, and Sadie Town. The games and antics that played out on the basketball court included the likes of decathlon competition with the air of a cirque-du-soleil improv variety show. Peter Stokes was named Homecoming King and Beck Peterson as Homecoming Queen. The Junior Princesses on the Homecoming Court were Alina Shahid, and Ellie Bleharski. Millennium High homecoming court royalty included seniors Amiyah Denard and Lana Ivovich and 11th graders Shay Ottavino, and Keda King-Polk. Piedmont Police’s Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz was invited to attend by Millenniumm High Principal Irma Nunez-Peters. It was the first school rally he has attended. “It’s really loud in here,“ Diaz said, “I’ve been to a bunch of football games, and this is louder,” he said. Piedmont students competed in innovative games, like sibling teams playing life-sized Hungry Hungry Hippos, with cardboard boxes for a mouth, a floor skate and colorful balloons. Student teams would push the other by their feet, like a wheelbarrow, while the “hippo” would try to “munch” the balloons. Students showed off their lung power, athletic prowess and creativity with an assortment of games on Friday afternoon. One class competition involved trash can targets, volleyballs and Connect Four. A well-rehearsed skit by memSiblings Charli (left) and Cash Panico in a new game called Hungry Hungry Hippos. Cash is trying to grab the balloons with the box. The second leg in a relay race had students dragged quickly across the court to the delight of the senior section. The Homecoming Court included Amiyah Denard (left), Shay Ottavino, Keda King-Polk, and Lana Ivovich of Millennium High, and Homecoming King Peter Stokes, PHS Junior Princesses Alina Shahid and Ellie Bleharski, and Homecoming Queen Beck Peterson. Piedmont students choreographed their skits and performances.

articles.text: Hollywood couldn’t write a better script. With just four seconds left in a 9-9 deadlocked Western Alameda County Conference battle between the Piedmont and Alameda boys’ water polo teams at Laney College on Thursday, October 12, the Highlanders called a timeout shortly after forcing a miss by the Hornets. From mid-pool, sophomore goalie Luke McAuliffe sent a high arching pass to Declan Linnane just a few feet in front of the Hornets’ goal. Reaching the ball at its peak, Linnane used his height and length to perfectly swat the ball into goal for a thrilling 10-9 victory. “At first I thought we might throw it up top and try to get a shot from the perimeter, but they were pressing us. Coach Rik told me to drive down and they will throw it over the top. Luke is one of the most accurate passers I’ve seen, so I knew it was coming. We only had a few seconds, so I had to go for the tap in,” said Linnane of the play. “Coach called a timeout Staff Photos Declan Linnane scored a dramatic tap-in shot at the last second of a 10-9 win over Alameda. and he said, ‘Luke, let it fly to Declan.’ I knew in my head Declan was going to make it. I was really nervous, but we did it. I was just thinking, loft it and make sure it’s above him,” mentioned McAuliffe. The play was called, “Storm The Castle.” It’s something they’ve only practiced on a limited scale. “We tried to get Declan in front of the cage and try to get a tip-ball. That was basically the play, when we saw the defender Coach Rik Krumins celebrates with Evan Dickason (left) and Gus von Metszch. Luke McAuliffe reaches for a save. He had the game-winning assist to Declan Linnane. come out and give Declan a path, I thought this might work,” said coach Rik Krumins. Linnane, also a basketball player, resembled Lakers’ Hall of Famer Kareem Abdul-Jabbar landing a skyhook as he held off a defender. articles.text: Homecoming Night for Piedmont’s volleyball team was a smashing success for a second year, With no football game at home, students packed the Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, October 13, cheering on the Highlanders to a 3-0 shutout of Alameda, 25-21, 25-23, 26-24. “To play in front of a crowd is amazing. It I were to think of what some of those Div. 1 colleges look like in a small increment, it really gives me fuel to keep going and cook up different things we can do to win. The girls were great out there,” said PHS coach Marias Cardeñas. The intensity of the gym with a packed house helped show how a loud, enthusiastic crowd can impact games. Piedmont trailed 22-16 in the second set and 23-18 in the third set before turning things around both times. “It’s definitely crazy and the most people I’ve seen at one of my games ever,” exclaimed veteran outside hitter Sadie Town. “You try to block it out and get tunnel vision on the court. We had so many friends in the stands and it was so fun. The atmosphere was electric.” “It was amazing to play in front of an atmosphere like that,” added middle hitter Jules DeYoung. “The crowd really hyped us up. The intensity makes you play so much better. I feel like the crowd made everyone play better.” Game Recap In the first set, Piedmont opened to a 5-0 lead in the first set, but Alameda cut the deficit to 5-4. The two teams traded points throughout the set, but the Hornets never took the lead. With the match at 22-19, DeYoung slammed a kill to make it 23-19, Alameda then scored two straight on errors, 23-21, but Piedmont got the final two points with a kill by Elena Stevens and an ace by Kalindi Kim. In the second set, Alameda was storming with a commanding 15-6 lead, but with the score 17-9, PHS rallied to close the score to 19-16. Alameda scored three straight, 22-16. That’s when the Highlanders scored eight straight points to go ahead 24-22. Town smashed down the winning kill to make it 25-23. Alameda opened the third set with a 5-1 lead, and the Hornets carried a multi-goal lead until 20-15. Town smacked down two kills, followed by one from Stevens to make it 21-18 Alameda. Sadie Town glides through the air for one of her 20 kills. Jules DeYoung with a spike, one of eight kills in the game.

articles.text: In spite of the score line, Piedmont’s 48-20 demolition of San Lorenzo last Saturday was not looking great. The Highlanders trailed 6-0 at the end of the first quarter. Apparently, coach Jordan Seiden chose to have a traditional halftime pep talk with his players well before halftime. The Highlanders went on to score 34 unanswered points before SLZ’s next touchdown which came near the end of the third quarter. PHS added 12 more points in the fourth. The win keeps Piedmont in contention for the WACC’s Shoreline Division title after Alameda lost to Arroyo. “It was a much-needed win, coming off a tough loss against Alameda. Seeing them lose to Arroyo gives us some life. We weren’t tackling well in the first quarter and weren’t blocking well. Once we got rolling and saw we could make some plays, we didn’t have any doubt,” said coach Seiden. It was another big day for receiver Sam Shelby, who had 11 pass receptions for 158 yards and two receiving touchdowns. He also had 68 rushing yards on three carries – two for touchdowns. His 55-yard touchdown run on an end-around boosted Piedmont’s lead to 34-6 with 4:17 left in the third quarter. “As a team, we played solid. We had a slow start but we started applying our offense as the game went on and ran things the way we needed to,” said Shelby. Shelby has been a catalyst in Piedmont’s breakout varsity season. He emerged as the team’s top receiver as a sophomore. He shows an innate ability to create deception e on the field by faking runs to the interior, only to break to the edge for long runs. It’s been a move Shelby has executed to perfection in several games. “It’s a credit to track. It’s really where I built up speed. I’m used on offense as a ‘sweep’ player, so I do my best to look for the outside,” said Shelby. Piedmont was without starting defensive end and left tackle Jordan Alemania, but filling in was senior Ben Breber. Appearing in only his third varsity football game, he impressed coach Seiden with his impact as a blocker and edge rusher. “Emmett Maxwell really encouraged me to come out and play. It’s my senior year so I thought I may as well play some Sam Shelby scored four touchdowns against San Lorenzo. Staff Photos football.” said Breber, a four-year tennis singles player. Game Recap Although Piedmont’s defense forced punts on San Lorenzo’s opening two possessions, the Highlanders committed turnovers and fumbles on their first two drives. The Grizzlies scored the game’s opening touchdown on a 51-yard broken play. With 1:35 left in the first period, Piedmont nearly scored on a 67-yard touchdown carry by Shelby on an end-around. The play was called back due to an illegal formation (no, not the A-11). Shelby then recorded three straight receptions before capping it off with a 25-yard reception into the end zone. Shelby kicked the extra point to make it 7-6 with 11:14 left in the second quarter. Piedmont forced a fumble on SLZ’s next possession where Brandon Dicke recovered at Piedmont’s 15-yard-line with 7:25 to go. From there, Piedmont drove 85 yards for a touchdown, sparked by a 30-yard touchdown by Albert Bellingrath, who shrugged off a tackle after catching a screen pass, making it 14-6 with 3:11 left. San Lorenzo’s next pass was intercepted by Miguel Long and returned to the 25-yard line with 1:44 remaining. PHS scored on four plays, including a seven-yard touchdown run by Shelby on another end-around with 36 seconds left for a 20-6 lead at halftime. Piedmont retained possession to start the third, and scored on a nineplay, 67-yard drive that featured a 25-yard touchdown catch by Shelby for a 27-6 lead with 7:57 left. Derek Schleuning forced a fumble on SLZ’s next drive, and the ball was recovered by recovered by Vince Arbit. On the next play, Shelby scored his 55-yard touchdown with 4:17 left in the third. Piedmont was rolling with a comfortable 34-6 lead. San Lorenzo got one back on its next drive, 34-12 after three minutes. Piedmont’s next score came from Cash Elmquist on a play-action pass for 23 yards in a 3rd-and-5 situation to boost its lead to 41-12. San Lorenzo scored with 4:46 left, 41-20, but Shelby responded with a 30-yard return to the Grizzlies’ 43, followed by a 20-yard run by quarterback Markos Lagios with 2:04 left. Final stats: Lagios completed 16-20 passes for 247 yards and four touchdowns, to go along with 48 rushing yards and a score. Shelby recorded 11 receptions for 158 yards and two receiving touchdowns, to go along with 68 rushing yards on three attempts for two rushing scores. Bellingrath had three receptions for 51 yards and a touchdown. Tommy Ashton had 45 yards on nine carries. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-3 overall, 2-1 league) heads to Kennedy High in Fremont on Friday, October 20 for a 7:00 p.m. game. Lineman Ben Breber made a big impact on offense and defense. articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team split its last two matches, defeating Lick-Wilmerding at home 6-1 on Thursday, October 12m but losing a key match 6-2 to Bishop O’Dowd at Mills College on October 10. “We split the singles with Tanya [Kononova] and Kate [Jumper] losing to very strong opponents in straight sets and Carolina [Romanczuk] and Arianna [Kortum] winning in straights,” explained coach Jim Landes. “Carolina and Arianna continued their strong play. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, October 18, 2023 Highlanders dominate Grizzlies, 48-20 By Jonathan Comeaux In spite of the score line, Piedmont’s 48-20 demolition of San Lorenzo last Saturday was not looking great. The Highlanders trailed 6-0 at the end of the first quarter. Apparently, coach Jordan Seiden chose to have a traditional halftime pep talk with his players well before halftime. The Highlanders went on to score 34 unanswered points before SLZ’s next touchdown which came near the end of the third quarter. PHS added 12 more points in the fourth. The win keeps Piedmont in contention for the WACC’s Shoreline Division title after Alameda lost to Arroyo. “It was a much-needed win, coming off a tough loss against Alameda. Seeing them lose to Arroyo gives us some life. We weren’t tackling well in the first quarter and weren’t blocking well. Once we got rolling and saw we could make some plays, we didn’t have any doubt,” said coach Seiden. It was another big day for receiver Sam Shelby, who had 11 pass receptions for 158 yards and two receiving touchdowns. He also had 68 rushing yards on three carries – two for touchdowns. His 55-yard touchdown run on an end-around boosted Piedmont’s lead to 34-6 with 4:17 left in the third quarter. “As a team, we played solid. We had a slow start but we started applying our offense as the game went on and ran things the way we needed to,” said Shelby. Shelby has been a catalyst in Piedmont’s breakout varsity season. He emerged as the team’s top receiver as a sophomore. He shows an innate ability to create deception e on the field by faking runs to the interior, only to break to the edge for long runs. It’s been a move Shelby has executed to perfection in several games. “It’s a credit to track. It’s really where I built up speed. I’m used on offense as a ‘sweep’ player, so I do my best to look for the outside,” said Shelby. Piedmont was without starting defensive end and left tackle Jordan Alemania, but filling in was senior Ben Breber. Appearing in only his third varsity football game, he impressed coach Seiden with his impact as a blocker and edge rusher. “Emmett Maxwell really encouraged me to come out and play. It’s my senior year so I thought I may as well play some Sam Shelby scored four touchdowns against San Lorenzo. Staff Photos football.” said Breber, a four-year tennis singles player. Game Recap Although Piedmont’s defense forced punts on San Lorenzo’s opening two possessions, the Highlanders committed turnovers and fumbles on their first two drives. The Grizzlies scored the game’s opening touchdown on a 51-yard broken play. With 1:35 left in the first period, Piedmont nearly scored on a 67-yard touchdown carry by Shelby on an end-around. The play was called back due to an illegal formation (no, not the A-11). Shelby then recorded three straight receptions before capping it off with a 25-yard reception into the end zone. Shelby kicked the extra point to make it 7-6 with 11:14 left in the second quarter. Piedmont forced a fumble on SLZ’s next possession where Brandon Dicke recovered at Piedmont’s 15-yard-line with 7:25 to go. From there, Piedmont drove 85 yards for a touchdown, sparked by a 30-yard touchdown by Albert Bellingrath, who shrugged off a tackle after catching a screen pass, making it 14-6 with 3:11 left. San Lorenzo’s next pass was intercepted by Miguel Long and returned to the 25-yard line with 1:44 remaining. PHS scored on four plays, including a seven-yard touchdown run by Shelby on another end-around with 36 seconds left for a 20-6 lead at halftime. Piedmont retained possession to start the third, and scored on a nineplay, 67-yard drive that featured a 25-yard touchdown catch by Shelby for a 27-6 lead with 7:57 left. Derek Schleuning forced a fumble on SLZ’s next drive, and the ball was recovered by recovered by Vince Arbit. On the next play, Shelby scored his 55-yard touchdown with 4:17 left in the third. Piedmont was rolling with a comfortable 34-6 lead. San Lorenzo got one back on its next drive, 34-12 after three minutes. Piedmont’s next score came from Cash Elmquist on a play-action pass for 23 yards in a 3rd-and-5 situation to boost its lead to 41-12. San Lorenzo scored with 4:46 left, 41-20, but Shelby responded with a 30-yard return to the Grizzlies’ 43, followed by a 20-yard run by quarterback Markos Lagios with 2:04 left. Final stats: Lagios completed 16-20 passes for 247 yards and four touchdowns, to go along with 48 rushing yards and a score. Shelby recorded 11 receptions for 158 yards and two receiving touchdowns, to go along with 68 rushing yards on three attempts for two rushing scores. Bellingrath had three receptions for 51 yards and a touchdown. Tommy Ashton had 45 yards on nine carries. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo team suffered a pair of losses against Western Alameda County Conference opponents last week, losing to Alameda 24-5 on Thursday, October 12, and 14-9 to American HS in Fremont the following day. In the first quarter, American opened to a 3-0 advantage until Abigail Jacoby got PHS on the board with 3:32 on the clock. After an Eagles goal, Anne Reardon made it 4-2 with 56 seconds left. American extended the gap with a player advantage at 4:40, then Esme Krumins scored after 36 seconds. The Eagles scored on its next possession, but Reardon scored again, 6-4. Piedmont rallied for a 9-7 lead in the third quarter with goals by Sage Gilbert, Jacoby, and two by Melian with three minutes left. However, it marked the last time the Highlanders got on the scoreboard. American scored with a player-advantage before tying the game at 9-9 with 24 seconds left in the third quarter. In the fourth period, American took the lead after 30 seconds, then made it 11-9 after another minute. They added three more goals for the 14-9 victory. articles.text: Piedmont High runners toed the line in a pair of meets over the past week, traveling to Woodward Park in Fresno for the Roughrider Invitational on Saturday, October 14. They earlier competed in a Western Alameda County Conference meet at Hayward High on Wednesday, October 11. At the Roughrider Invitational, Piedmont’s girls’ team placed fifth in a field of 23 schools. The boys’ team was sixth among 31 teams. For the league meet, Piedmont’s girls were fourth of eight and the boys placed fifth of 10. “We took them to Fresno for the Roughrider Invitational, giving the team a chance to get a taste of what it was like to run on the course where the state meet is held,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The tenacity of the girls and their ability to run together as a group and not lose contact is one of the main reasons why they were able to do so well. The boys continue to run well, and Xander continues to shine as our top runner.” It was an impressive pair of races for senior Schulte-Sasse, a senior. He placed fifth of 277 at the Roughrider Invitational with a time of 16:22.84 on the State course. He was fourth out of 86 runners at the league meet in Hayward, site of the North Coast Section championship. He finished with an impressive time of 15:45.97. A four-year varsity runner, Schulte-Sasse has been on teams with some highly successful runners, notably Jack Stein (Class of 2022), Parker Terrill (Class of 2022), and Parker Long (Class of 2023). “Jack Stein was a really inclusive leader. I think he did a great job at keeping a level head, staySebastian Swain (right) and Julien Lee (left) sprint go the finish line. Xander Schulte-Sasse placed fifth at the Roughrider Invitational Meet at Woodward Park in Fresno. ing relaxed, and not stressing, but at the same time, he was ready to give his all when he needed. We’ve had some tremendous runners, I just want to remember the feeling of seeing them and how cool would it be to help build our runners like they did,” said Schulte-Sasse. On the girls’ team, sophomore Skylar Best and senior Jamie Schwarz have been leading the way. At the Roughrider Invitational, Schwarz was 15th of 202 in 20:27.60 and Best was two spots behind her in 17th at 20:36.48. In the WACC meet, Best was seventh of 64 with a time of 19:49.62 while Schwarz was 10th in 20:05.02. “I remember my freshman and sophomore year where we had a really small girls team. It’s really great to have new runners each year, everyone is super passionate and we have a tight-knit team,” said Schwarz. “Everyone has improved so much and it’s really great to see. Everyone is putting in a lot of work every day, so it’s really motivating to be on the team,” added Best. Roughrider Invitational Following Schwarz and Best, sophomore Cora Chun finished 49th of 212 with a time of 22:04.75. After her was freshman Leighton Mand in 53rd, clocking a 22:12.73. Freshman Gladwin Horsley rounded out PHS’ best five with a time of 22:37.01, finishing 63rd. On the boys’ team, freshman Sebastian Swain followed Schulte-Sasse in 11th place in a field of 277 runners with a time of 17:06.51. Senior Julien Lee was one second behind in 12th place in a time of 17:07.03. Sophomore Noah Sohn was 62nd in 18:19.37, and junior Oliver Horsley had a time of 18:49.53. WACC Meet For the boys, after Schulte-Sasse was Lee placing 12th of 86 in 16:32.12. Swain was 25th with a time of 17:21.15. Sohn was 37th in 17:49.48, while Horsley rounded out the best five in 43rd, 17:59.23. For the girls, sophomore Mara Kemp-Malone followed Best and Schwarz in 16th place in a time of 20:44.40. Mand was 32nd in 21:40.75, and Chun rounded out Piedmont’s top five with a time of 21:49.79, finishing 34th. NEXT UP Piedmont has another league today, October 18, at Oyster Bay Regional Park in San Leandro at 3:30 p.m. They will compete at the Wilder Cross Country Invitational on October 21 at Hayward High, with races starting at 8:00 a.m.

articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas, former conductor of the San Francisco Symphony, returns to lead the orchestra this Thursday, October 19, and Saturday and Sunday, October 21 and 22. The program includes Olly Wilson’s Shango Memory and Beethoven’s majestic Symphony No. 9. Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125, is a choral symphony, composed and completed between 1822 and 1824 and was first performed in Vienna on May 7, 1824. Many critics and musicologists regard it as a masterpiece of Western classical music and is one best-known symphonic works and is the most frequently performed symphony in the world. Vocal soloists in Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony will be soprano Angel Blue, mezzo-soprano Tamara Mumford, tenor Ben Bliss and bass Dashon Burton. Wilson’s Shango Memory, a Retired San Francisco Symphony Music Director Michael Tilson Thomas will conduct the orchestra on Thursday, Saturday and Sunday this week, October 19, 21 and 22. modern piece that serves as a tribute to a Nigerian deity and the cultural contributions of the African diaspora. Performances on October 19 and 21 begin at 7:30 p.m. with a 2 p.m. matinee performance on Sunday, October 22. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse will premiere the musical Cinderella Enchanted, based on the 1997 movie of the same name, with performances shows opening November 3. The classic tale of Cinderella is reborn in this play with a Bay Area twist. Cinderella, played by Kennedy Joy Fullard, is a free-spirited Berkeley artist and Prince Christopher, played by Vinh G. Nguyen, is a wealthy Silicon Valley romantic. Prince Christopher hosts an extravagant ball where he meets Cinderella, only for her to leave the festivities before he can express his true feelings for her. Cinderella leaves behind nothing but a glass slipper which prompts the prince to embark on a mission to find the dainty shoe’s owner. Cinderella Enchanted is directed and choreographed by Khalia Davis. The director explained the significance of the mid-90’s film, and how it influenced Cinderella on stage. “[The 1997 movie] was really iconic and it set the bar for what is possible when you do musicals that are magical in that way,” Davis said. “[It was important that] audiences who are very familiar with that particular version see that reflected on the stage.” The Berkeley Playhouse production offers even more unique twists, she added. “I’m really excited that we get to honor and celebrate being able to see Prince Christopher’s life as well as Cinderella’s and the parallel life they are living. Cinderella is an aspiring writer who is fascinated by the world and Christopher is equally fascinated by the world but wants to know what he can do to make a positive impact outside of being born into royalty,” Davis said. Supporting cast members include Jennifer Marie Frazier as Fairy Godmother, Erika Coyne as Stepmother, Stephen Kanaski as Lionel as The Steward, Nicole Stanley as Queen Constantini and Kyle Herrera as King Maximillian. Cinderella Enchanted will be performed November 3 to December 22. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets. Photo by Ben Krantz Kennedy Joy Fullard and Vinh G. Nguyen in Cinderella Enchanted
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse premieres Cinderella Enchanted Nov. 3

articles.text: Treasure Island Museum presents Inspiring Escapism: The Golden Gate International Exposition Interiors of Frances Elkins, a historian-led discussion, on Saturday, November 4. Visit the museum to hear historian Scott Powell discuss the career of interior designer Frances Adler Elkins, who worked primarily in California, Illinois and New York. Elkins is widely regarded as one of the most prominent and influential designers of the 20th century. She settled in Monterey and her first commissions were for residential designs for friends and social acquaintances. She later did important commercial work including hotels and retail stores. Elkins was known for her innovative style that drew from elements of both traditional and contemporary design. Her work continues to influence designers today. She worked alongside her brother, notable Chicago architect David Adler, on more than a dozen large homes throughout California, and in Chicago and New York. The presentation will show examples of Elkins’ work overall, Frances Elkins but will place particular emphasis on three buildings she decorated at the 1939-1940 Golden Gate Exposition on Yerba Buena Island – the Clubhouse, the San Francisco Building, and Hostess House. The exhibition includes rare images that will bring these interiors to life. The lecture begins at 10:30 a.m. The Treasure Island Museum is located on Treasure Island, at 1 Avenue of the Palms, #111. Visit https://www.eventbrite. c o m / e / i n s p i r i n g - e s c a p - ism-the-ggie-interiors-of-frances-elkins-tickets-735707991407 to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum to host lecture about interior designer Frances Elkins

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s first retrospective of Filipina artist Pacita Abad opens on October 21, and will be on view through January 28. Born in 1946 and raised in Basco, Philippines, she had a 32-year artistic career, creating a vast number of artworks that traverse a diversity of subjects, from colorful masks to underwater scenes to abstract compositions. The artist died in Singapore in 2004, but her colorful artwork uses a variety of mediums and reveals visual, material, and conceptual concerns that still resonate today. The SF MOMA exhibition features more than 40 pieces, including Abad’s signature trapunto paintings, which are stuffed, quilted canvases adorned with other raw, found Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pacita-abad/ to learn more. An exhibit of the art of Pacita Abad will open at San Francisco’s Museum of Modern Art on October 21.
articles.title: SF MOMA opens Pacita Abad exhibit on October 21

articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Gardens and tour the Gentleman’s Orchard, where you can enjoy fruit-picking and tasting, live music, and spiced cider made from the Filoli apple trees. The 6.8 acre Gentleman’s Orchard at Filoli preserves more than 600 apple, pear, plum, apricot, walnut, fig, and quince trees. While the estate Filoli is world-renowned for its flower beds, flora and fauna, the orchard has only been open to the public since 2021. “This orchard is about preserving this landscape feature of this estate. But through that we’re also trying to preserve some of the more rare heirloom varieties of fruit trees,” said lead horticulturist Jim Salyards. Much of the bounty will be gone by the end of autumn, but guests can pick and taste fruit off the trees and enjoy table grapes from the harvest. Other apples, pears, plums and apricots will be churned into butters or liquified into ciders, which guests can enjoy under the shade of Filoli’s walnut grove while younger guests build scarecrows. Admission includes access to the 54,000 square-foot Georgian mansion, and 16 acres of English Renaissance gardens. Orchard Days take place on Saturdays and Sundays through October 29. Filoli is located at 86 Cañada Road in Woodside, and is open every day from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. See https://filoli.org/ for tickets. Filoli Historic House & Gardens welcomes visitors this Autumn.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 18, 2023 17 Treasure Island Museum to host lecture about interior designer Frances Elkins By Allyson Aleksey Treasure Island Museum presents Inspiring Escapism: The Golden Gate International Exposition Interiors of Frances Elkins, a historian-led discussion, on Saturday, November 4. Visit the museum to hear historian Scott Powell discuss the career of interior designer Frances Adler Elkins, who worked primarily in California, Illinois and New York. Elkins is widely regarded as one of the most prominent and influential designers of the 20th century. She settled in Monterey and her first commissions were for residential designs for friends and social acquaintances. She later did important commercial work including hotels and retail stores. Elkins was known for her innovative style that drew from elements of both traditional and contemporary design. Her work continues to influence designers today. She worked alongside her brother, notable Chicago architect David Adler, on more than a dozen large homes throughout California, and in Chicago and New York. The presentation will show examples of Elkins’ work overall, SF MOMA opens Pacita Abad exhibit on October 21 By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s first retrospective of Filipina artist Pacita Abad opens on October 21, and will be on view through January 28. Born in 1946 and raised in Basco, Philippines, she had a 32-year artistic career, creating a vast number of artworks that traverse a diversity of subjects, from colorful masks to underwater scenes to abstract compositions. The artist died in Singapore in 2004, but her colorful artwork uses a variety of mediums and reveals visual, material, and conceptual concerns that still resonate today. articles.text: A scene from Everest At 29,035 feet, Mt. Everest is not only the tallest mountain on earth, it is an iconic spire of snow and ice and rock that has beckoned climbers for more than a century. But, it wasn’t until May 29, 1953 that it was summited by Sir Edmund Hillary and his Nepalese Sherpa, Tenzig Norgay, a stunning accomplishment that would define both of them for the rest of their lives. Since that initial climb, the summit of Everest has been reached many times. However, it was the 1996 expedition that captured worldwide attention, a journey chronicled by Jon Krakauer in his book Into Thin Air and now the subject of the film, Everest. had gone commercial with organizations like Adventure Consultants, owned and operated by New Zealander Jon Hall. As well, in competition for clients was Scott Fischer’s Mountain Madness. For exorbitant prices, a mix of experienced and novice climbers were guided (some pushed and cajoled and assisted) toward Everest’s peak. Call it extreme tourism. Call it high risk/high gain adventure. Or call it a form of insanity accompanied by bragging rights if and when the expedition was completed (it was not uncommon for climbers to be turned around by their guides due to harsh and threatening weather). In the film, which is filled with a sense of foreboding, Jon Hall, portrayed by Jason Clarke, gathers his group of eight clients in a base camp tent and explains that the height of Everest – 29,025 feet – is the cruising altitude of a 747. the san francisco mandolin orchestra presents Piedmont Center for the Arts featuring music by Achille Bocus, mandolin & conductor John Pursey, concertmaster More information and advance tickets at sfmandolin.org General admission $20, students & seniors $15, 12 & under free PIEDMONT CENTER FOR THE ARTS STRONGLY ENCOURAGES PROPER MASKING INSIDE THE MAIN HALL AND HIGHLY RECOMMENDS THAT ATTENDEES HAVE ALL AVAILABLE UP TO DATE VACCINATIONS

articles.text: Given what is unfolding in Israel and Gaza, Lemon Tree is an extraordinary must-see film. The question that Lemon Tree begs is, “can art, no matter how beautifully rendered, bridge a chasm of suspicion and enmity between two peoples who are locked in a kind of ritualistic Kabuki dance of violence devolved over decades?” Israeli director Eran Riklis has created a powerful metaphor in a lovely lemon grove that sits on the Palestinian side of the Green Line that separates Israel from the West Bank and the occupied territories. The grove – deeply green and dimpled by yellow lemons – is a startling contrast to the desiccated land that surrounds it. It is owned by Salma Zidane (Hiam Abbass), a Palestinian widow. The grove has been passed down from generation to generation. Always lovingly tended, it provides her with a meager income. Israeli defense minister, Israel Navon (Doron Tavory) and his lovely wife, Mira (Rona Lipaz-Michael), take up residence in a new home on the other side of the wire fence, in plain view of Salma as she waters the grove and picks the ripe lemons. Navon’s security forces conclude that the grove is a security threat, a possible sanctuary for terrorists wishing to launch attacks against the minister. They send Salma a letter informing her that the grove must be removed. Having the letter translated (she doesn’t read Hebrew), she makes a stunning decision: she will hire an attorney, Ziad Daud (Ali Suliman), and go to court to fight the decree. In a patriarchal culture, this is Tarik Kopty, Hiam Abbass, and Ali Suliman in Lemon Tree

articles.text: Super 8 is a great movie. What makes it great is the story, a solid coming of age tale of four boys and a girl, all on the cusp of adolescence, all set free from school, eager to begin their summer project: the shooting of a super 8 monster movie. On a balmy night, having sneaked out of their respective houses at midnight, they drive (don’t ask) to the local railroad station, and under a canopy of stars, the camera on a tripod, begin shooting their film. That is until they hear a train in the distance. Charley (Riley Griffith), the kid directing their movie, director, tells his crew to wait. He wants the train for background. And so the kids wait, the light of the train growing larger, the noise of the locomotive reaching them. And it’s at that moment something happens that sends the narrative in a profoundly different direction. It’s a huge shift, delivered with a riveting crash. The movie quote that comes to mind is from Jaws, when Roy Scheider, small town sheriff, standing on the stern of a trawler, sees the great white shark for the first time. Eyes wide, backing toward the wheelhouse, he says, “I think we’re going to need a bigger boat.” Super 8 is set in 1979 in a small Ohio town. At the center of the kids’ adventure is Joe Lamb (Joel Courtney), 12 years old. He has recently lost his mother in an accident at the steel mill. His father, town deputy Jack Lamb Gabriel Basso, Ryan Lee, Joel Courtney, and Riley Griffiths in Super 8 (Kyle Chandler), is remote and, like Joe, still grieving. Joe finds solace with his friends. The prospect of spending the summer making a zombie movie offers a way to escape the wrenching loss he has experienced. It also helps that Charley has asked Alice Dainard (Elle Fanning) to be in the film, Alice being a girl that Joe has admired from afar but never dared speak to. For Super 8 to work, Abrams has to get the story and the kids just right. And he does, which is no small thing. The tale is compelling and the kids are wonderful, each delivering an excellent performance, led by Fanning and newcomer Courtney. The young filmmakers soon learn that they are caught up in circumstances they never could have foreseen. They soon realize that they must rely on one another to survive. Their fear and sense of urgency has an essential and overwhelming sense of verisimilitude, conveyed nicely to the audience. If this all sounds a bit vague, well, Super 8 is a movie that must be seen fresh, with as little information as possible. Of course, reviews and comments, even the trailer, will conspire to be too informative. But resist. As an aside: the second half of the film proves to be the most difficult, for it’s in act III that Abrams must decide how to reveal what is behind the phenomenon that is impacting everyone in town. Super 8. Directed by J.J. Abrams. Starring Kyle Chandler, Elle Fanning, Joel Courtney. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Paramont+/Apple tv.

articles.text: Ashley Boettcher in a scene from Aliens in the Attic Let’s assume that when the producers and director of Aliens in the Attic read the script and listened to the pitch, it was immediately clear that the audience would be tweens and very early teens. Who else would embrace the concept of four small gremlins, ETs, arriving on earth and setting up shop in the fourth floor attic of a large Victorian house in Michigan? A house slated to be the summer rental for two families of kids, mom and dad, and uncle. So, everyone arrives, rooms are selected, and even sister Bethany’s (Ashley Tisdale) older boyfriend arrives for a visit. Meanwhile, high schooler Tom (Carter Jenkins) is struggling with the high school reality that he’s a science nerd and not popular. He’d rather be cool than be smart. There are aliens to worry about, meaning aliens in the attic, the air ducts, and the basement (there are only four but they get around). It’s the kids who discover the ETs and realize that they’re not here to make friends but as scouts for millions more who are on their way and want to take over the planet. Let the games begin. The battle is joined with the kids pulling out all the stops: paintball guns, potato shooting guns, and fireworks. And the gremlins are no pushover. They have a stun gun that creates some interesting moments. This is an average B movie, the acting is satisfactory, as are the special effects. Nothing really is gripping and there is not one truly scary moment. The tweenteen crowd generally appreciates a bit more tension. Keep in mind, this is the Harry Potter generation. Anyway, if time is weighing heavily on those youngsters wandering around the house this Fall, round them up and sit down and watch Aliens in the Attic. It can’t hurt. Aliens in the Attic. Directed by John Schultz. Starring Tom Pearson, Ashley Tisdale, Ashley Boettcher, and Austin Butler. 1 hr., 26 min. Rated PG. Released 2009. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/MAX/Apple tv.
articles.title: Aliens in the Attic an easy family-friendly film

articles.text: It’s kind of fun to review your own concert. As an honest music critic, I must paint an honest picThe Piedmont Center for the Arts is our city’s gem. It can accommodate virtually any art media, drama and other plays, radio shows, dance, and even beer festivals… and this is just scratching the surface. Then, Sunday afternoon featured the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra. As I have said in the past, an orchestra legitimizes a community. That’s what the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra does. Let it be known that the orchestra is successful. It has been a conConductor Martha Stoddard serves as music Director. She has a busy career; the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is just one of her many orchestras. Stuart Gronningen serves as orchestra manager as well as playing first French horn. In addition to these tasks, he is also the personnel manager and chief of the set-up crew. The members of the orchestra are mainly amateurs. Among them are teachers, doctors, scientists, lawyers – just plain people who love to play music. There are a few professionals in the ranks. One member of the orchestra had a wide-ranging international solo career. If I remember correctly, Stuart Gronningen was an English teacher, in addition to playing horn in both the Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony. His daughter, Ellen, flies in all the way from New York to play with our orchestra. It would be good to have more students in the orchestra. Hint hint. The program on Sunday afternoon was a short one. Despite its brevity, the concert showed what the orchestra can really do. As a participant, I noticed that the orchestra rose to the occasion and played in inspired fashion. The program began with Johann Christian Bach’s Symphony in B-flat major conducted by young guest conductor Andrew O’Donnell. That got things rolling. RSVP to mstehrart@gmail.com for the opening reception on Friday, Nov. 3, You may preview this exhibit online at: https://bit.ly/3ZO1Urc. Jeanette Tietze will perform piano pieces by Schumann, Haydn, Bartók and Kohs. Ildikó Salgado will lead singers in newly published English translations of Lajos Bárdos arrangements made by the foundation’s late colleague, Gail Needleman, followed by work with the Clayton Valley Charter High School Women’s Choir. For more information about these amazing musicians, please explore their website at www.breshearsquartet. com, and for advance tickets, see www.bpt.me/6146513. Saturday, November 11, 5 p.m. San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra The SF Mandolin Orchestra will perform in Piedmont for the sixth time. This season’s theme is “Napoli and the Revolution,” and features works by Bach, Mozart, Giuliano, and Sammartini. Musical Director Achille Bocus will conduct, and also be the soloist in the Giuliano Mandolin Concerto in B flat. For more information and tickets (General $20, Seniors/Students $15) visit https://sfmandolin.org. Sunday, November 12, 5:30 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a musical tribute to Duke Ellington, who his band for more than 50 years and composed hundreds of scores. The concert showcases the Center for the Arts’ magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets $25 at the door, or $23 at https://bpt.me/5691334. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up to date vaccinations.

As an honest music critic, I must paint an honest picture. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is our city’s gem. It can accommodate virtually any art media, drama and other plays, radio shows, dance, and even beer festivals… and this is just scratching the surface. Then, there is the music. Sunday afternoon featured the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra. As I have said in the past, an orchestra legitimizes a community. That’s what the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra does. Let it be known that the orchestra is successful. It has been a concerted effort. Conductor Martha Stoddard serves as music Director. She has a busy career; the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is just one of her many orchestras. Stuart Gronningen serves as orchestra manager as well as playing first French horn. In addition to these tasks, he is also the personnel manager and chief of the set-up crew. The members of the orchestra are mainly amateurs. Among them are teachers, doctors, scientists, lawyers – just plain people who love to play music. There are a few professionals in the ranks. One member of the orchestra had a wide-ranging international solo career. If I remember correctly, Stuart Gronningen was an English teacher, in addition to playing horn in both the Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony. His daughter, Ellen, flies in all the way from New York to play with our orchestra. It would be good to have more students in the orchestra. Hint hint. The program on Sunday afternoon was a short one. Despite its brevity, the concert showed what the orchestra can really do. As a participant, I noticed that the orchestra rose to the occasion and played in inspired fashion. The program began with Johann Christian Bach’s Symphony in B-flat major conducted by young guest conductor Andrew O’Donnell. That got things rolling. Music Director, Martha Stoddard, then took the podium to Piedmont Center for the Arts Come and enjoy the performances and exhibits this Fall. Ongoing Horn player Stuart Gronningen is the primary organizer and manager of the Piedmont Community Orchestra. direct Danzi’s Concerto for clarinet and bassoon. Clarinet soloist Marcelo Meira and bassoon soloist Jeff Robinson played with consummate artistry. Both soloists have extensive international experience and their playing showed it. Brahms’ Serenade No. 2 concluded the program and the large audience responded enthusiastically. After the concert, everyone enjoyed beautiful refreshments. articles.text: Part 2 in a series The list of Piedmont residents who have been employed at Pixar Studios includes Kiel Murray, who joined the studio in 2000 as a producer, screenwriter and Development Executive responsible for assisting directors in shaping stories. Partnering with her husband Phil Lorin, whom she met as undergraduate students at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, she scripted the first two Cars animated features for Pixar, and then working alone, she wrote Cars 3. She and Lorin went on to write and shoot two short films that were widely screened at festivals. While at Pixar, Murray also contributed to the story development and writing of acclaimed features such as Finding Nemo, Inside Out, Ratatouille, Brave, Raya and the Last Dragon, and Up. In 2019, Murray moved from Pixar to John Lasseter’s new venture, where she wrote the animated feature film Luck that began streaming on Apple tv in 2023. She is currently working on another project in development at Skydance Animation, the release date still to be determined. Murray grew up in Placerville and unlike most professional aniPiedmont filmmaker Kiel Murray maters and filmmakers, attended St. Mary’s College on a volleyball scholarship. The studied Communications and Theater, but it was in a fiction writing class where she discovered what would become a lifelong interest in writing for films and filmmaking. Looking beyond Pixar, it is impossible not to acknowledge Piedmont High School graduate Colin Trevorrow, a director, screenwriter, and filmmaker, best known for the compelling Jurassic franchise films. He graduated from New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts in 1999. As a teenager he won filmmaking awards from the Mill Valley Festival and the Sam Francisco Youth Film Festival. His first theatrical release was a 2004 documentary titled Reality Show. He went on to team up with NYU classmate Derek Connolly and co-wrote and directed the buddy cop feature called Cocked and Loaded. In 2012 he directed Safety Not Guaranteed. The film was nominated for the Independent Spirit Award for Best Feature Film, and was also nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Festival. Based on the film’s accolades, Trevorrow and Connolly were hired by Walt Disney Studio to write a script for the film, Flight of the Navigator. While busy writing directing and producing the Jurassic sequels, Trevorrow directed The Book of Henry, released in 2017, based on a story written by Greg Hurwitz. Reviews were mixed but it may be his best film, one that captures in a deeply moving way the essence of one family’s love and profound connection. In 2018, it was announced that Trevorrow would return to the Jurassic franchise and direct Jurassic World: World Dominion. This year he is slated to direct and produce the film Atlantis. He currently lives in the United Kingdom with his wife, Isabelle, and their two children. All of the above is testimony to the strong appeal of film and filmmaking.
