Walkers take a peek at 1907 home on El Cerrito PBy Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group went two blocks downhill from the Exedra to see a house at the corner of Magnolia and El Cerrito Avenue. The house was built in 1907 by Dr. Carl Schmidt, a bachelor doctor, as a wedding gift for his bride. It is a one and half story Craftsman style home with wide eaves and exposed rafter ends that were typical of this style. The Schmidts were married in 1908 and lived in the house until the 1940s. The walkers then went down El Cerrito to Witter Field to see the work being done. Drainage trenches and pipes were being laid, and there were large mounds of dirt in the center of the field. According to a story in last week’s Piedmont Post, completion of the project has been delayed until January primarily because of work to be done by EBMUD. The Witter Field site has its own history. Land developer Frank C. Havens created Piedmont Park in 1898 as a way to draw visitors and future residents to Piedmont. The main entrance to the park was at the current bus stop across from the Wells Fargo bank on Highland Avenue. Visitors could also enter the park on a path from Grand Avenue on what is now Palm Drive. Havens also creates a large circular maze of hedges as an attraction in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. Havens lined the lane to the “Maze” with palm trees. Some of them still survive on Palm Drive. These majestic palms are over 125 years old and are the last remaining ones. One block later on Park View Avenue they saw a home with very large black spiders all over its exterior and a long line of crows along its roof line ready for Halloween. Then it was down the length of Palm Drive to Wildwood Avenue Along the way they couldn’t resist climbing a newly discovered alley road to Warfield Avenue, and then to Winsor and Wildwood Avenues. On Wildwood, neighbors Nadine Guffanti and Sarah Johnson told the group the history of the house between theirs. A woman built the house in 1927 and lived in it for 30 years. Later her daughter and granddaughter lived there. After the granddaughter died, it was vacant for many years until some squatters took up residence with the intent of living in it long enough to claim it. They were discovered and removed. The walkers made their way back to the Exedra via Piedmont Park. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: A 1906 scandal that riveted America resulted in two classic works of art: Theodore Dreiser’s 1925 novel, An American Tragedy, based on the lurid 1906 events, and 1951’s Hollywood version of the book, A Place in the Sun. A lucky Piedmont audience had a chance to check out the 1951 movie at last Thursday’s 10th iteration of the Second Thursday Film Fest. Audience members were treated to intense drama and romance. The film is an example of old-style filmmaking at its best, featuring taut storytelling, meticulous visual design, stunning black-and-white cinematography, and glamorous stars in the persons of Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift, with Shelley Winters making the third in a doomed love triangle. The central character is poor but eager young George Eastman (Clift), who arrives in town hoping to take advantage of a promise his wealthy industrialist uncle made to help him out. His reward is, at first, a low-level job in the Eastman swim suit factory, where he begins to romance a naive factory girl named Alice Tripp (Winters). When the wealthy Eastmans begin to notice George and set in motion plans to move him up in the business hierarchy, things begin to go wrong rather than right. He’s invited to an elegant social event, at which he meets beautiful and wealthy Angela Vickers (Taylor). They fall in love, but what’s George to do about Alice Tripp? She’s pregnant, it turns out, and she demands that he marry her. One thing he does, knowing she can’t swim, is row her out to the middle of a lonely lake. Charlie Chaplin called A Place in the Sun the best movie about America ever made. Directed by George Stevens, it was nominated for 9 Academy Awards and won six. The Piedmont film group’s post-showing discussion produced enthusiastic thumbs-up reactions, with praise for the actors, the suspense, and the drama. The Piedmont Film Fest’s next offering, on November 9, is the Italian comedy/drama, Life Is Beautiful, made in 1997 and starring Roberto Begnini, who earned a best actor Academy Award for his role. Successfully shown world-wide, it won the 1998 Cannes Grand Prix. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the Film Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. You’re welcome to bring snacks or lunch.
articles.title: Piedmont Film Fest features Elizabeth Taylor, Montgomery Clift in a classic

The film is an example of old-style filmmaking at its best, featuring taut storytelling, meticulous visual design, stunning black-and-white cinematography, and glamorous stars in the persons of Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift, with Shelley Winters making the third in a doomed love triangle. The central character is poor but eager young George Eastman (Clift), who arrives in town hoping to take advantage of a promise his wealthy industrialist uncle made to help him out. His reward is, at first, a low-level job in the Eastman swim suit factory, where he begins to romance a naive factory girl named Alice Tripp (Winters). When the wealthy Eastmans begin to notice George and set in motion plans to move him up in the business hierarchy, things begin to go wrong rather than right. He’s invited to an elegant social event, at which he meets beautiful and wealthy Angela Vickers (Taylor). They fall in love, but what’s George to do about Alice Tripp? She’s pregnant, it turns out, and she demands that he marry her. One thing he does, knowing she can’t swim, is row her out to the middle of a lonely lake. Charlie Chaplin called A Place in the Sun the best movie about America ever made. Directed by George Stevens, it was nominated for 9 Academy Awards and won six. The Piedmont film group’s post-showing discussion produced enthusiastic thumbs-up reactions, with praise for the actors, the suspense, and the drama. The Piedmont Film Fest’s next offering, on November 9, is the Italian comedy/drama, Life Is Beautiful, made in 1997 and starring Roberto Begnini, who earned a best actor Academy Award for his role. Successfully shown world-wide, it won the 1998 Cannes Grand Prix. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the Film Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. You’re welcome to bring snacks or lunch. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: Caroline Hutchnecker Peters, born to Holocaust Survivors on May 20, 1949, touched the lives of many with her boundless love, joyful spirit, and her unmistakable curly hair that could brighten even the cloudiest of days. She passed away September 7, 2023, leaving behind a legacy of laughter, love, and cherished memories. In the early days in Piedmont, Caroline was a vibrant force on the tennis courts. Piedmont Pool held a special place in her heart, where she later exercised, spending countless hours swimming laps and sharing smiles and laughter with friends and family. But perhaps what her friends will remember the most is her infectious giggles that could fill a room with happiness. Her laughter was a testament to her zest for life and her ability to find joy in the simplest of moments. Caroline is survived by her beloved family – her devoted husband Ronny Peters, her daughters Rebecca Triki and husband Cherif Triki, and Michelle McGilloway and husband Shane McGilloway. She is also survived by her son Jeff Peters and his wife Bailey Peters. Caroline was not only a loving mother and wife, but also a cherished grandmother (Bubba) to her five wonderful grandchildren, Adam, Logan, Liam, Tahlia and Brody. Caroline’s love and warmth extended to her family, and her legacy will continue through the bonds she created and the values she instilled in her children and grandchildren. May Caroline’s memory continue to shine brightly through the lives of her husband, children, and grandchildren. articles.text: Jason Darling of El Sobrante passed away unexpectedly at home in the early morning of Saturday, September 30, 2023, at the age of 50. Born Jason Allen Darling on November 13, 1972 in Oakland, Jason was the son of Diane Cameron Mockel and the late Kenneth Allen Darling. He was raised by his grandparents, Marilyn and Bud Miller, and then by his mother Diane and stepfather Kenneth Mockel of Piedmont. He attended Beach Elementary School and graduated from Piedmont High in 1991. Always full of life and boundless energy, Jason started doing voices and celebrity impersonations at a young age, constantly fooling his grandparents with prank phone calls. More than anything Jason loved to make people laugh. Jason became a big brother at age 10, when Diane and Ken’s second son, Jamieson “Jamie” Mockel, was born. Jason and Jamie became incredibly close over the years, In 2009, while living in Pinole, Jason met the love of his life, Kristen Hamlett, who was drawn to Jason’s irreverent sense of humor and ceaseless jokes. They were married on May 17, 2012. Jason was a loving husband and a devoted father. Jason was a lifelong technophile. At age 11 his uncle, Dennis Mockel, built him a high-powered i486 PC. Jason’s love of computers and cutSudoku Solution SUDOKU SOLUTION Jason Darling died on September 30, 2023 at age 50. ting-edge technology, aided by Dennis’ persistent support, led Jason to a career in information technology, including jobs at Meyer Corporation, Mondo Media, and Diversified Personnel, before starting his own IT firm, NeoExec, with his business partner, Nicholas Torres. Around 2014, following urging by his uncle Ron Mockel of the Piedmont Adult School, Jason returned to Piedmont School District as District IT Specialist II. Jason’s years of experience were instrumental in PUSD’s launch of the Connected Learning Chromebook 1:1 program and the technology infrastructure in the STEAM and Theater buildings. He loved his work and encouraged his brother Jamie to come work for PUSD as an English teacher and the two loved working together at their alma mater. Jason’s co-workers recall his boundless positivity and willingness to go the extra mile to help with any project, approaching every task with kindness and patience, even when dealing with the challenging nature of IT issues. Jason’s love of Piedmont also ran deep. After graduating from Piedmont High he became a paraeducator at the middle school and high school. He worked at Piedmont Adult School, along with his grandmother Peggy Mockel. He was also an intrepid world traveler, taking countless cruises over the years with his family, especially his uncle and constant companion, Ron. His travels included Central and South America, the Caribbean, Canada, and Alaska, and he loved to entertain fellow passengers at comedy open mics and with his karaoke skills. Jason is survived by his wife Kristen, son Jayden, daughter Jasmine, and three dogs, Dexter, Dorie, and Fonzie. He is also survived by his mother and father, Diane and Ken, brother Jamie, sibling-in-law Cassidy Williams, and the entire Darling, Mockel, and Hamlett families. Information about a memorial service is pending. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group will make its annual visit to Mountain View Cemetery in advance of Halloween. Come join friends and neighbors on Wednesday morning, October 25 in front of the main mausoleum. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue, with ample parking available. A special tour of the historic cemetery will be conducted by docent Jane Leroe, who will point out many of the cemetery’s historical sites, some of which date back to the Civil War. This year’s tour is titled “Rogues and Rascals.” Leroe is a long-time cemetery docent. Now retired, she was a ground-breaking trial attorney. She has developed an extensive knowledge of the Mountain View Cemetery and has a passion for sharing it. The tour will start at 10:30 a.m. and will last for about 1 hour and 45 minutes. For more information, contact Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net. WE PROVIDE: • Excellent in-home care • Quality caregiver training • Errands and transportation Start home care today. There are several categories of dog companions: service dogs, who assist their owners with various tasks; dogs for disabled owners who require more than simple tasks, such as opening doors; and dogs for veterans who have PTSD. Clients range in age from five years old to senior citizens, and they are eligible as long as they can properly handle the dog. Dear MacMama: I have very poor eyesight and am wondering if there is a way to make things easier to see on my Mac. Lynde, Oakland Dear Lynde: This is an excellent question! Many people don’t know that most computers, including Apple, have many ways to compensate for vision, hearing, and even touch. This is under the system preference pane, “Accessibility”. Here are some of the options that allow for help on your Mac if you have poor vision, hearing or difficulty with hand movements. There are separate settings for Vision, Hearing, Motor, and General. • Vision: Voice over, Zoom, Display, Spoken Content, Descriptions. Voice Over is a screen reader, and allows people with vision issues, and even blindness to navigate through voice prompts. For example, if you move through the dock, the voice will say “Mail, Safari, Pages” as you pass those with your cursor. You can also customize this and train this feature to recognize certain words and speed up or slow down the talk speed. Zoom, is just what it sounds like. It all allows you to zoom in full screen, or picture in picture and more through the use of modifier keys (like option or control). One feature in the zoom section is “Hover Text”. If you turn this on and hold down the command button, as you hover your cursor over text, it will show a larger version of that text. Display allows you to increase contrast, make the text bigger, changing size and color and size of the cursor, etc. Spoken Content allows you to customize the sound and speaking rate of the system voice, and determine what it tells you. Descriptions allows you to have audio descriptions for visual content in media. • Hearing: Audio, RTT, Captions. Audio does not have a lot of features, just allowing for the screen to flash if an alert comes in. RTT (real time text) allows for calls to deaf users that use a TDD device. Captions allow users to customize system wide captions. • Motor: Voice Control, Keyboard, Pointer Control

articles.text: Bathrooms can be a perilous place in the house, especially for people who are older or living with a chronic condition that can make falls more likely. Much like the kitchen, the bathroom is a risky space in the home with hazards such as slippery surfaces and sharp objects. One study found that the most common location for fall injuries in the home was the bathroom, including when people are hurrying to the bathroom. A National Institute on Aging statistic states that 80% of falls in the home happen in the bathroom. Yet, these injuries are not just the result of missing grab bars in the shower and not all of the risk involves a fall. Consider the following risk factors that could lead to your elderly loved one injuring themselves in the bathroom: 1) Bathmat in the tub or shower In theory, these mats are there to prevent a fall on the slick surface. In reality, they can become a tripping hazard as they bunch up or move when stepped on. The solution is to attach non-slip decals to the surface of the tub or shower. 2) Lack of adequate lighting It’s not uncommon for people aged 65 or older, or those living with certain conditions or taking specific medications, to need to use the restroom in the middle of the night. Unfortunately, being half awake is only going to increase the chances of tripping or slipping and possibly falling in the bathroom. The solution is to install a simple night light that can at the very least make it clear where the light switch is in the dark. 3) No handheld showerhead When someone needs to use a chair in the shower or tub, they will also need an easy-to-reach shower head that they can move around without too much twisting and turning. The solution to this potential bathroom hazard is to add an adjustable shower head that allows the individual to clean themselves while remaining safely seated. 4) Hot water As we age, our skin becomes thinner and more sensitive to exposure to high water temperatures. At the same time, there is a decreased ability to sense when water is so hot it can scald or burn the skin. Help prevent burn injuries to your elderly loved one by having a professional handyman set the water heater thermostat between 110 to 120 degrees, which is considered safe by experts. Learn more about helping the elderly stay healthy and safe at home by contacting our office or consulting with a Certified Senior Advisor (https://www.csa.us/). Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. and Switch Control. Voice Control allows users to control their Macs with just their voice. You can choose and customize commands for this feature. Keyboard has several features that allows users to configure the behavior of the keyboard. You can enable “sticky keys” for those that cannot hold keys down for shortcuts, customize the pointer (cursor). With Pointer users can enable the powerful “Alternate Control Methods”. With this feature, a user who does not have reliable use of their hands can use their head and even facial expressions to control the pointer. Switch Control allows users to operate their Macs with external buttons or “switches”, which Apple has for sale on their website. • General: Siri and Accessibility Shortcut. Siri allows users to use keyboards to type commands to Siri, which is useful for those who are deaf or have speech difficulty. Shortcut allows a user to get an Accessibility pop up menu using a keyboard shortcut (Option-Command-F5 is the default, but that also is customizable). Most of these features are also available on the iPhone, iPad and even Apple TV. Apple is committed to making sure that users of all physical, hearing, and visual capabilities can use their devices with ease. There are many more ways to customize all these features, from making the text larger on your system, to using voice over, to making your pointer larger with a customizable outline color. It’s comforting to know that if you can’t use your Mac, with the default settings, they can be customized to your comfort level. While the approach up Everest is stunningly beautiful, it is also profoundly dangerous. As Hall says, the mountain is a “beast.” Not only does it resist every attempt by men and women to reach its peak, it lies in wait, seemingly benign, allowing that rush of attainment to be suddenly and arbitrarily replaced by a lethal scenario of gale force wind and ice and plummeting temperatures that can turn momentary victory into tragic defeat, as is graphically demonstrated in Everest. While the climbers made their way toward the final ascent sault (20 groups gathered on the mountain on May 10-11, 1996), there were unexpected delays. They slowly crossed bottomless crevasses by walking across aluminum ladders precariously tied together. As the groups moved ever upward, some were struck by high altitude edema and were forced to turn back. Time was a critical factor, for to spend a night on the mountain at such altitudes, could spell death. The goal was to reach the summit by 2:00 PM at the latest and quickly turn around and begin the long, arduous trek down to base camp. As a result of an unexpected and relentless storm, seemingly demonic in its force, one that swept down on the mountain with little warning, eight climbers perished, three on the north face and five on the south face. articles.text: This year’s Pumpkin Festival at Mountain View Cemetery marks the return of the cemetery’s most popular After an absence of four years due to COVID and post-COVID, Mountain View Cemetery will host the 15th Annual Pumpkin Festival on Saturday, October 28, at noon. Community members and children are invited to Mountain View Cemetery’s pumpkin patch in the main meadow just inside the main gates for a fun-filled day of free Halloween events. There will be inflatable bounce houses, face painting, clown balloon artists, and a craft area where kids can decorate costumes, masks, treat bags, and pumpkins. Young children will be able to pick up one free pumpkin per child in person at the information booth while supplies last. The entertainment company Furs, Scales & Tails will also have a live animal show for kids at the festival. Former kindergarten teacher Tracy Hill has been performing shows in Northern California for 15 years. Hill’s shows have been known to include baby chicks, hamsters, guinea pigs, rabbits, turtles, snakes, ducks, tortoises, lizards, tarantulas, roosters, giant millipedes, frogs, chickens, and even hairless rats. Food truck vendors will also be on-site to sell tacos, empanadas, lumpia, burgers, fries, hot dogs, hot links, Italian ice, and more. The 15th Annual Pumpkin Festival will take place following the Piedmont Avenue Halloween parade. Admission is free. Parents must accompany their children to this event. Mountain View Cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. A live animal show for kids was part of Mountain View Cemetery’s 2019 Pumpkin Festival.
articles.title: Mountain View Cemetery Pumpkin Festival returns on Oct. 28

articles.text: Police Chief Jeremy Bowers attended the city’s Public Safety committee meeting on Thursday, October 5, to discuss the outcome of the city’s recent town hall meeting held on September 27. Bowers reasserted his commitment to a multipronged crimefighting approach, emphasizing the importance of a fully-staffed police department and harnessing current technology, including surveillance cameras and ALPRs (Automatic License Plate Readers) to reduce police response times. Reflecting on the town hall meeting, Bowers said that he understood the community’s concerns about crime and expressed gratitude for the support local residents have shown the police force. “I felt like I came away from it really having an understanding of the real concern that the community has, but also with the appreciation that our community is here to partner with us and to support the city. articles.text: Details of the Witter Field turf replacement and irrigation project were given to am estimated 15 neighbors who attended a 1-hour meeting held by the school district on Tuesday, September 26. Residents interested in the project could be roughly divided into two camps, those upset about parking restrictions and those worried about potential flooding. At the meeting, School District Facilities Manager Pete Palmer confirmed that the completion date has been delayed until January 8, 2024. Turf replacement in prior years had been done during the summer and completed by the start of school. Due to ongoing problems with drainage the current work includes a full replacement of the irrigation system, will take more than six months, and will cost more than $4 million. Piedmont School District has said that the delay is primarily due to work to be done by EBMUD, the water utility. That became a topic of discussion at the September 26 meeting. A key point of the in-person meeting was provided by the city’s Director of Public Works, Daniel Gonzalez. The school district was required to give the city an encroachment permit to allow the flow of water from Witter Field into the city’s drainage culvert which funnels water from Bushy Dell Creek under the field, and down Palm Drive towards Lake Merritt. “The Witter Field drainage system is under the State’s jurisdiction; however, the connection to the City storm sewer system is under the City’s jurisdiction,” explained Gonzalez. Witter Field completion delayed until January By Jay Russell Details of the Witter Field turf replacement and irrigation project were given to am estimated 15 neighbors who attended a 1-hour meeting held by the school district on Tuesday, September 26. Residents interested in the project could be roughly divided into two camps, those upset about parking restrictions and those worried about potential flooding. At the meeting, School District Facilities Manager Pete Palmer confirmed that the completion date has been delayed until January 8, 2024. Turf replacement in prior years had been done during the summer and completed by the start of school. Due to ongoing problems with drainage the current work includes a full replacement of the irrigation system, will take more than six months, and will cost more than $4 million. Piedmont School District has said that the delay is primarily due to work to be done by EBMUD, the water utility. That became a topic of discussion at the September 26 meeting. A key point of the in-person meeting was provided by the city’s Director of Public Works, Daniel Gonzalez. The school district was required to give the city an encroachment permit to allow the flow of water from Witter Field into the city’s drainage culvert which funnels water from Bushy Dell Creek under the field, and down Palm Drive towards Lake Merritt. “The Witter Field drainage system is under the State’s jurisdiction; however, the connection to the City storm sewer system is under the City’s jurisdiction,” explained Gonzalez. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has produced an online survey asking residents for input on housing plans for Moraga Canyon. This marks the beginning of public engagement with the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – an initiative that will study all City-owned land in Moraga Canyon with the goal of possible development in the future. “It’s a good opportunity to have Piedmont residents voice their concerns,” said Kevin Jackson, the city’s Planning Director. “We’re trying to move this project forward and engage with the community. It’ll be a stronger plan with greater community engagement.” A mandate by the state of California requires cities to plan additional housing units in their communities to help meet housing needs across the state. The City of Piedmont, though completely built out and with no additional land on which to build housing, was charged with creating plans to accommodate 587 units of new housing, including 257 affordable units by 2031. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan proposes to build 132 units of new housing (60 of which would be for low-income households). SURVEY QUESTIONS Among other things, the survey asks what community members the following: • When you visit Moraga Canyon, how do you and/or your family spend your time there? • What concerns do you have about new housing development in Moraga Canyon? • Would you be interested in living in multifamily housing in Moraga Canyon? Other questions ask citizens to rank the buildings they would like to see in Moraga Canyon based on architectural style with a scale from 1 to 5. The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/MoragaCanyonSurvey and will remain open through October 20th. articles.text: When Officer Jehan Liles joined the Piedmont Police Department, he noticed one thing immediately. “It’s a community where everybody waves,” he said. “I drive around with my windows down in the patrol car and I’m waving to everybody and almost everybody is waving right back.” It’s what he likes most about Piedmont. A Bay Area native, he grew up in Danville where he attended San Ramon Valley High School. “About half of my family is retired military or has served in the military, so for a long time I had an idea of serving others,” he explained. Liles remembers the exact moment that he wanted to become an officer. “The exact moment I would say… was when I was watching a lot of the footage in the George Floyd era, and a little bit pre-George Floyd, of police officers and their interactions with people.” Seeing those videos in the news marked a turning point for him. He felt there was a need for compassionate, community-based policing and that it was something he could do. “I thought, ‘I could probably help people in a law enforcement capacity and make a contribution to my community,’” he said. His decision to apply for a job in Piedmont came on the recommendation of a long-time friend. “[My friend] said, ‘You should New Piedmont police officer Jehan Liles said he enjoys the “small-town, family-oriented” feel of Piedmont. probably apply to this department... this would be a great fit for the type of policing that you would like to do.’” Shortly after, Liles called Police Captain Chris Monahan and put in his application. Liles believes that 21st-century police work is different from previous decades. To him, that means community policing is a must. “It’s really about being able to serve the community in all sorts of ways... basically, being part of the community even though I don’t live in Piedmont.” Liles said he prioritizes getting to know the members of the community and treating everyone he meets fairly. Liles also enjoys the amount of “like-minded” and “family-oriented” people he meets in Piedmont. Liles himself is married and has two daughters. “[My wife and I] graduated from high school together and started dating the summer we graduated,” he said. “Piedmont is a small town. A lot of people are walking. A lot of people are enjoying the parks. It feels very similar to the type of community that I live in. It feels like home for me.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission discussed on Wednesday, October 4 the replacement options for the recently removed sequoia tree on the corner of Bellevue and Mountain Avenue. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales was present to provide background information for commission members. “I’m not sure another sequoia is appropriate unfortunately, due to the shifting weather patterns that we have,” said Gonzales. “Greater heat, less fog – that may not be the type of replacement we would look at.” Gonzales added that the City wants to be sure any potential replacement tree would be appropriate for the climate and soil as well as drought tolerant and would have “low water usage.” Questions were also brought by the Park Commission as to the size and scope of the replacement trees the City is considering. “When we replace trees that are so stately, are we looking at trying to bring that scale of tree back into that site or is it just based on the water requirement?” asked Park Commission member Kimberly Moses. Gonzales said that the city was taking the tree’s “stately” elements into consideration while also striving for a “climate-efficient” replacement. The traffic circle that the sequoia was planted in received very little water which could cause problems for future replacements. When asked by Moses if there Photo courtesy of Oakland Public Library Piedmont’s sequoia gigantea was 133 years old at the time of removal this year. was any avenue for citizens to voice their input on the decision of a replacement tree, Gonzales said, “I don’t know that we have a formal process but it seems like a good idea. We usually welcome it.” “If it’s a stately space, we want a stately tree to be there,” affirmed Gonzales. Last month, the City decided to remove the historic sequoia tree from the corner of Bellevue and Mountain Avenue because its “significant lean” endangered local homes and property. This sequoia tree had been in Piedmont since 1890, making it 133 years old at the time of removal.
articles.title: City considers replacement for historic Sequoia

articles.text: During the weekend of September 15-17, 7th grade Girl Scout Troops from Wildwood and Beach reconnected on a camping trip to Caswell State Park along the Stanislaus River near the town of Ripon. The girls were a combined troop for part of elementary school and haven’t been together in six years. After a year in middle school, they were eager to get reacquainted as Girl Scouts. Beach Troop leader, Amera Rizk, planned the dinners and introduced another level of camping food to the Wildwood girls. On the first night, she prepared delicious turkey chile verde with cornbread. Everyone fell asleep with full bellies listening to the croaking frogs and buzzing bugs. Saturday morning revealed the lush campsite full of walnut trees, feral cats and mosquitoes. The rest of the camping party arrived shortly after lunch for a total of seven parents, seven cadette Girl Scouts, and three tagalongs. They spent the day on the Stanislaus River boating, swimming, and fending off the mosquitos. The girls shoved off from the beach at the campsite with a parent in tow. articles.text: Race down the stretch at East Bay Agency for Children’s 24th annual Gala on November 4th at the Turf Club atop Golden Gate Fields in Berkeley. Guests at The EBAC Classic will take a victory lap for East Bay children and families as they enjoy specialty cocktails and an epicurean dinner paired with Keenan wines, raise their paddles to bid on world-class getaways in the live auction, stock their cellars with cases of premier vintages from the wine raffle, and “get down” with the Git With It Band. New this year will be the broadcast of the “Inf latable Derby,” a race previously filmed on the Golden Gate Fields track with six intrepid EBAC supporters wearing inflatable animal costumes. Gala guests will root for their favorite contestant in what promises to be a hilarious highlight of the evening. This year’s racing venue and theme encourages guests to wear derby styles such as fancy hats and ascots or equestrian attire including jockey colors or riding breeches. For the 24th year, volunteers from the EBAC Auxiliary are planning another epic party. The EBAC Auxiliary began in Piedmont with founders Diane Goetz and Claire Faughnan still involved today. Funds raised support EBAC, a local non-profit who has been meeting the mental health needs of east bay children since 1952. EBAC’s mission is to improve the well-being of children, youth and families by reducing the impact of trauma and social inequities. Gala chair Amanda Lacau Noguera said, “With the future of Golden Gate Fields and the gorgeous Turf Club uncertain, we are thrilled to give our gala guests perhaps one final opportunity to enjoy a night to remember at this landmark venue while raising money to address the current childhood mental health crisis.” For tickets and sponsorship details, see EBAC.org/Gala.

articles.text: Isabella Wire and Eve Tellegen rehearse in the Piedmont High School Advance Acting Class production of The (One Act) Play That Goes Wrong, opening October 19 at the Alan Harvey Theater. The Piedmont High School Advanced Acting class will perform the one act comedy The Play That Goes Wrong from Thursday to Saturday, October 19-21, with two shows on Saturday. The Tony Award-winning play by Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, and Henry Shields is a global masterpiece guaranteed to make everyone laugh until their stomachs hurt. The Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society is producing a classic murder mystery, The Murder at Haversham Manor, but nothing goes according to plan. Come watch the cast try against all odds to make it through to the final curtain call. “This play has been hilarious and fun to rehearse,” says senior Jake Hanke. “I can’t wait to present some of the most well-coordinated chaos I’ve ever been a part of,” added Ben Sachs. The cast on Thursday, October 19, and the 7 p.m. show on Saturday, October 21, includes: Jake Hanke, Sophie Hess, Charlotte Mascola, Ben Sachs, Clio Salzer, Mary Schickedanz, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Isabelle Wire. The cast on Friday, October 20, at 7 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. includes: Jake Hanke, Sophie Hess, Charlotte Mascola, Ella Puckett, Ben Sachs, Xander Schulte-Sasse, Sadie Shoop and Eve Tellegen. The Play That Goes Wrong has won 11 international awards, including an Olivier Award in the UK for Best New Comedy, a Tony Award for Best Set Design, and the Theater Fans Choice Award for Best Play. Initially created in 2012, the play has toured UK, the U.S. and Australia, and was featured on Broadway from 2017 to 2019. Since 2019 it has been playing New World Stages in New York City. The authors have also created The Goes Wrong Show, currently on Amazon Prime, and Peter Pan Goes Wrong, The Christmas Carol Goes Wrong, among other titles. All performances are in the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School, 800 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont. General admission tickets are $16 for adults and $6 for students and seniors. Purchase tickets at: https://www. phs-drama.com/. The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong is recommended for audiences age eight and older. For more information and questions, contact director Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: I recently was asked, “How can I improve creativity in my life if I’m not an artist?” I was delighted by this question because the reality is that most of the time when we are asked to employ our creative minds, it is not in the mode of creating traditional art. There are a few among us who make their livings doing art professionally and a decent number of folks who regularly engage in hobbies that involve art. But all of us solve problems, all of us have to think of new solutions, all of us have to invent new pathways to get to an endpoint. So, how do we strengthen that portion of our creative minds? There are a number of traits that are associated with creative personalities and we can choose to grow and strengthen these parts of ourselves and our children. A few of these traits are: Curiosity, Openness, and Playfulness. If you are looking to grow your curiosity, start with the people you see every day. Pretend you are a journalist and start asking questions. Learn about where they came from, what they enjoyed doing in their childhood, what their favorite movie is and why. See if you can get beneath the surface level questions quickly. We can all ask, “What do you do for a living?” but it takes a truly curious person to ask, “Which of your teachers in high school inspired you to be the person you are today?” Openness is a trait all about accepting that there are multiple options to any potential question or problem. The open person practices divergent thinking, rather than convergent thinking, assuming that the list of solutions is always longer than they can even imagine. To practice openness, think of one thing that you are convinced only has one answer and ask yourself how it is possible that there is a different answer. How is it possible that 1+1 does not in fact, equal 2? You were playful when you were a child. Almost every kid is because that’s how children learn about the world around them. So, if you want to get in touch with your playful one, take some time to really watch your own children, if you have kids under the age of 9. See how they play. Remember your own childhood and ask yourself how you played? Try bringing a tiny bit of play back into your life, even if it’s baby steps, like making a smiley face out of your pees at dinner. Find your play, to find your creative! The more you practice curiosity, openness and playfulness, the easier all three will start to feel and the more you are wiring your mind for creative thoughts. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Speaker, Consultant and Coach. https:// gocreate.zone/
articles.title: Cultivating creative traits

articles.text: Villagers in Mitmebo build enclosures for rabbits. Their sales are an important source of livelihood for local families. I’ve been traveling with my family for as long as I can remember. I love seeing new things, trying new foods, and learning about people and their cultures. This year I had an amazing opportunity to visit a refugee camp called Dzaleka in Lilongwe, Malawi. Together with a project manager of Vijana Africa, a non-profit organization, I spent four days in the refugee camp meeting new people, learning about their lives, and listening to them talk about the problems they face in the camp. On the last day I met with some of the refugee camp beneficiaries who live on the boundary of Dzaleka. While residents of Dzelaka are struggling with dire situations of their own including meeting basic needs and seeking asylum, they also must support their bordering villages who see the refugee camp as an unwelcome neighbor. Community beneficiaries expressed the problems they face with their rabbit and pig farms. Vijana Africa supports 25 widows who are pig and rabbit farmers. The rabbits and pigs provide critical protein for the participants’ families, and a small but important source of income. When a beneficiary sells rabbits, she is able to satisfy some of her family needs. Eighteen of the 25 beneficiaries have been successful in raising rabbits as a regular source of income; the other seven are continuing to improve their farming. While meeting with the beneficiaries I learned that one of their main problems is keeping the rabbits alive and safe. More than 50% of the rabbits are lost due to lack of enclosures. With my resources at home and my experience with Girl Scouts, I quickly realized that I could help Vijana reach their goals. This is when I decided that building rabbit and pig enclosures would be the perfect project for my Gold Award. Over the next nine months I worked remotely with a team of refugees on the ground. We were able to build three large rabbit and pig enclosures in three different villages. Ultimately, I returned to Dzelaka in July to complete the final construction and meet with the refugees and beneficiaries again. I will follow the progress of the project and help with future developments. Julia Montes is a junior at Piedmont High School. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch had to restock its inventory early Tuesday morning, and one new addition to the patch is turning heads. Giant Jack has arrived and will be the centerpiece of the patch for the remainder of the month. Everyone is invited to enter a contest to guess Jack’s weight. The winner gets to take it home (or have it delivered). The pumpkin patch, which Piedmont Dads in the Wildwood club have operated annually for an estimated 40 years, raises money to make improvements and repairs at the school. “Despite all the distractions, beautiful beach weather, the Blue Angels at Fleet Week, and many Piedmonters enjoying a four-day weekend out of town, we had a stellar weekend of sales. We beat our weekend total last year by $300,” said Wildwood Patch Papa Matt Derrigo. This past week the patch took in $5,000 and restocked it for the first time. The patch will continue to restock its supply weekly. The Giant Jack will be a popular backdrop for Halloween photos this year as kids marvel at its sheer enormity. Last year’s gourd was won by Piedmont 1st grader Timothy Cain whose guess of 1004 pounds was 2 pounds shy of This year’s jumbo pumpkin, known as Giant Jack, was delivered before sunrise on Tuesday morning. the actual weight. So far, the most popular pumpkins are the $2 Wee-B-Little pumpkins. Whether you are a chef looking for a pumpkin to bake into something sweet, or a trick-ortreater excited about carving sinister features into a jack-olantern, the Wildwood Patch has what you need. To buy merchandise or sign up as a volunteer, visit their website: Wildwooddadsclub.org Pumpkin varietals include the fairytale, peanut, jarrahdale, American tondo, and knucklehead pumpkins. Coaches’ Field, 898 Red Rock Road Monday to Friday, 4:00-6:00 p.m. Saturday & Sunday, 10:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m. The lot will be open through October 29. articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country team traveled to Half Moon Bay for the Artichoke Invitational on Saturday, October 7. The girls’ team had a good day and placed third out of 11 teams. The boys’ team was fifth in a field of 21teams. The races were designed for smaller enrollment schools at 2.3 miles. It was the first race since the season-opener on September 9 at the Ed Sias Invitational. Poor air quality canceled their league meet on September 20. “It had been a while since the team raced. The team was excited to test themselves again after several weeks of intense training,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. It was an impressive race for senior Xander Schulte Sasse with a fourth-place finish in a large field of 145 runners with a time of 12:35. “Xander did his best to go out with the leaders and give them a run for their money, holding on strong, finishing in 4th place overall. He led the male harriers to 5th place as a team,” said Zirkelbach. On the girls’ side, senior Jamie Schwarz led the way, placing eighth of 87 runners, with a time of 15:49. Sophomore Skylar Best was 15th in 16:15. Freshman Leighton Mand made her varsity debut, impressing with a 16:47 to place 25th as Piedmont’s third best runner. Rounding out Piedmont’s topSenior Jamie Schwarz placed eighth in a field of 87 runners to lead the girls’ team. five was sophomore Cora Chun clocking a 16:55 and placing 27th, while junior Carolina Taylor placed 33rd in 17:20. Mand is joined by classmates Gladwin Horsley and Amalia Gray on the varsity roster. “This team of girls is a very tight unit; they are very supportive of each other in practices and races, By staying so close to each other, they were able to achieve another podium finish,” said Zirkelbach. “All of our freshman girls have been training hard and showing up in races with impressive focus.” Boys’s results Behind Schulte-Sasse was freshman Sebastian Swain in Senior Xander Schulte-Sasse placed fourth of 145 runners at the Artichoke Invitational in Half Moon Bay. Freshman Leighton Mand (left) and sophomore Cora Chun compete in the Artichoke Invitational cross country meet.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team suffered a devastating 16-13 loss on the road to Alameda on Saturday evening, October 7 at Thompson Field. Though it was Piedmont’s Homecoming game, it was played in Alameda due to Piedmont’s Witter Field being unplayable due to construction. With Piedmont driving to the 1-yard line and the clock ticking down to the final seconds, on a 3rd-and-inches situation, the Highlanders called a dive play for running back Tommy Ashton. Although Ashton appeared to have stretched the ball several inches past the goal line, the referees called the Highlanders’ running back short and the game over. It marks the second straight game in which Piedmont was come out on the wrong end of an official’s decisions. In a game with Arroyo on September 23, receiver Sam Shelby was Photos by Steve Long Tommy Ashton ran for 134 yards on 20 carries against Alameda. He was stopped short of the goal line for the potential game-winning touchdown in a controversial decision by the officials. wrongly ejected in the second quarter by the same official who called Ashton short in Saturday’s game. It’s a situation that has left a sour taste for PHS coach Jordan Seiden. “The clock was going from to Sam Shelby (#2) had seven receptions for 114 yards and a touchdown, including an 80-yard scamper down the sideline. 2 to 1 and Markos handed the ball off to Tommy. You could see on film that Tommy’s body is halfway across the goal line and our entire offensive line is in the end zone with the ball. According to them, we came up an inch short. Heartbreaker,” said Seiden. It leaves a dark cloud over what was a great game under the lights. The game was considered the Western Alameda County Conference’s Shoreline Division championship game with Alameda undefeated at 5-0 and Piedmont was surging after three straight wins at 3-2. “It was the heart of heartbreakers. It was awful, that one really hurt. It felt like a league title game, that’s what the sentiment was. Never mind that they were undefeated, Alameda hadn’t played with a deficit all season. We definitely felt like it was a game, while incredibly competitive, that we had a great chance to win,” said Seiden. After the first quarter with both teams deadlocked at 0-0, Alameda struck late in the second quarter on a drive capped by a 25-yard touchdown carry by the Hornets’ running back. Alameda was driving once again at the end of the second quarter, but Ashton intercepted a pass at the Piedmont 13-yard line with 13 seconds left in the half. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ flag football team wrapped up a difficult week, losing 19-6 to Berkeley at home on Humphries Diamond on Thursday, October 5. Twp days earlier, October 3, they were shut out by St. Ignatius 24-0 in San Francisco. articles.text: Tanya Kononova powers a forehand against Berkeley. Piedmont’s tennis team achieved its first two Western Alameda County Conference wins of the season last week, defeating Berkeley 6-1 on Thursday, October 5 at home, and blanking Alameda 7-0 on the road two days earlier. “Everyone continued their good play with the only loss at No. 2 singles against Berkeley. Kate Jumper ran into a very good opponent. We also defeated Alameda 7-0, which is quite the result after beating them 4-3 last year,” said coach Jim Landes. Tanya Kononova continued her strong play at No. 1 singles, beating Berkeley’s Ariana Alharazy and Alameda’s Juliana Johnson in straight sets. Kononova also defeated Johnson in last year’s WACC championship match. “I feel like I’m playing with a lot more control over the ball. It makes me happy,” said Kononova. “I’m not as consistent as I’d like it to be. It’s also about staying mentally composed on the court. But I’ve been able to put more focus on the details and refining the smaller things,” she added. 6-1 over Berkeley Piedmont made quick work of Berkeley with No. 1 doubles team of Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon winning the first match after the Yellowjackets had to forfeit due to an injury while PHS led 3-2 in the first set. From there, Kononova won her match 6-2, 6-0 at No. 1 singles. Maddie Tran and Samantha Huynh then won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2 doubles, while Inara Mehta and Abigail Call won 6-2, 6-0 at No. 3 to claim Piedmont’s clinching fourth victory. After that, Carolina Romanczuk won in three sets at No. 3 singles, 3-6, 6-3, 6-1. Arianna Kortum then brought in a 6-1, 6-3 win at No. 4 singles. The only loss of the day was Kate Jumper at No. 2 singles, 7-5, 7-6 (7-2). Staff Photos Carolina Romanczuk won both her matches with Berkeley and Alameda as Piedmont’s No. 3 singles player. 7-0 over Alameda There was a time 20 r so years ago when Alameda tennis ruled. For Piedmont to win, let alone shut out the Hornets, was unthinkable. But for the past two decades Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team has been the gold standard. In its match at Alameda on October 3, Kononova rolled to a 6-1, 6-4 victory at No. 1 singles. Jumper, at No.2 singles, had to battle in a three-set match, but came away with a victory, 1-6, 6-1, 7-6 (7-3). At No. 3, Romanczuk won 6-4, 6-1, while Sophie LaForte won 7-6 (7-5), 1-6, 10-8. On doubles, DeFazio and Eisemon won at No. 1 in three sets, 6-4, 2-6, 6-3. Tran and Huynh won 7-5, 6-3 at No. 2, while Ellie Broscow and Mehta paired at No. 3, winning 7-5, 6-1. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-5 overall, 2-0 league) hosts Lick-Wilmerding on Thursday, October 12 at 3:30 p.m. Emma Eisemon sends a serve. She won both her matches with No. 1 doubles partner Cecilia DeFazio.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team traveled to Stevenson High School in Pebble Beach for the 2023 Peter Cutino Cup. Playing against strong teams on Friday and Saturday, October 6-7, the Highlanders won one of four games. PHS opened with a 15-8 win over Pacific Grove then lost as close match, 12-10, with Carmel on Friday. On Saturday they suffered a 20-10 loss to Northgate and 22-6 loss to Soquel. Final stats for the loss to Soquel were not provided. “It’s a difficult tournament but it’s a good opportunity for our guys to see more good competition. These games refine us for league and section playoffs,” said coach Rik Krumins. 15-8 win vs. Pacific Grove Piedmont led 5-3 at the end of the first quarter and 10-6 by halftime. They extended the lead by three goals in the third quarter, Declan Linnane had four goals against Pacific Grove. Peter Krumins returned to the lineup for the Cutino Cup after missing a few games. Photos by Lynn Wright George Stein had four goals in Piedmont’s 15-8 win over Pacific Grove. 13-7, while both teams added two goals in the final going. In the first quarter, Elles Kreickhaus scored the game’s first goal after 30 seconds but Pacific Grove tied on its next possession. PHS’ Kreickhaus and Stein scored two consecutive goals to lead 3-1 with 5:43 to go. Following a PG goal, Stein scored to make it 4-2 a minute later. Declan Linnane scored with a man-advantage with 40 seconds left, 5-3. In the second, PHS’ Linnane and Quincy Scherman made it 7-3 with 5:15 to go but Pacific Grove scored three consecutive to make it narrowly close at 7-6 Piedmont with 3:04 to go. But from there, PHS scored three consecutive times with two of the goals coming with a man-advantage including two goals by Stein and one by Peter Krumins with 19 seconds left, 10-6. PHS added two more goals to open the third to make it 12-6 after two minutes of action with goals by Daniel Banin and Linnane. Pacific scored with 3:24 to go, but Stein added another goal with 1:43 in the quarter. In the fourth, Pacific made it 13-8 slightly over a minute into the final going, but Linnane scored on PHS’ next possession with 5:37 to go, following by a goal by Yotem Kariv 37 seconds later. Pacific Grove scored the game’s final goal with 1:45 left. Final stats: Stein scored four goals, one assist, and one steal. Linnane scored four goals and one assist. Kreickhaus scored twice, had two assists, and two steals. Banin and Karvis both had a goal and steal. Scherman had a goal and two steals. 12-10 loss to Carmel Piedmont led 3-1 to end the first quarter with goals by Stein, Hurwitz, and Krumins. However, Carmel stormed to the front in the second quarter, leading 5-4 by halftime. Carmel added two goals to the deficit to make it 9-7 to start the fourth quarter, while tyey extended the lead to 12-9 before Piedmont’s final goal by Charlie Wright with 20 seconds left. Final stats: Stein recorded three goals, one steal, and five steals. Linnane and Banin had one goal, assist and steal. Krumins had a goal and assist. Wright, Scherman, and Hurwitz scored once. Northgate wins 20-10 Piedmont trailed 4-1 by the end of the first quarter and extended the lead to 12-5 at halftime. The Broncos made it 18-7 in the third quarter and 20-10 in the final going. Final stats: Burke scored three goals. Banin also had a hat trick and a steal. Linnane and Leo Hurwitz had a goal, assist, and steal. Kariv had a goal and a steal. Krumins had an assist and steal. Scherman scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (9-8 overall, 2-1 league) hosts Alameda at Laney College tomorrow, October 12, at 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: Tommy Ashton Staff Photos Now in October, each team is identifying leaders to help propel their programs towards playoffs are on the horizon. Here we take a look at four key players this fall: Tommy Ashton in football, Tanya Kononova in tennis, Declan Linnane in water polo, and Bauer Peterson in volleyball. Tommy Ashton, Football Tommy Ashton, a junior, has been a critical player for Piedmont on both sides of the ball – as a running back and linebacker. Offensively, Ashton leads the team with 502 rushing yards on 87 carries for 5.8 yards per carry and five touchdowns, He is a bruiser-style running back, lowering his shoulder to put the boom on defenders. Playing linebacker, he recorded his first interception of the season in Piedmont’s narrow 16-13 loss to Alameda. He had 83 yards and a touchdown against Arroyo, 74 yards and a score against Encinal, and scored twice against Mt. Eden. Ashton recorded 134 rushing yards in Piedmont’s recent 16-13 loss to the Hornets. articles.text: Living in the Oakland hills, it can be easy to forget about the shoreline of San Francisco Bay with its wildlife native to the area and dependent on the marshlands. The Hayward Regional Shoreline is among the last wetlands of the entire Bay and has five miles of trails along the shoreline. The Hayward Regional Shoreline has 1,841 acres of water in three different marshes: the Hayward Marsh, Cogswell Marsh, and Ora Loma Marsh. The levees in the area were originally built in Hayward and San Lorenzo for salt production in the 1850s, with various landing sites to move products to San Francisco. There are still remnants of timber from old landings and salt farms along the trail. Don’t let the murky and muddy water of the marshland fool you; beneath the pickleweed and cordgrass are ideal breeding grounds for small fish, invertebrates, clams, and mussels. Larger striped bass are known to enter the channels which can attract leopard sharks, making it a popular place for fishermen. A common sight it observing snowy egrets and great blue herons snatching up food, while northern harriers scan the area for rodents. A great blue heron is seen hunting for food. Don’t be fooled by the murky water. Below the pickleweed is a wealth of small fish, invertebrate, and shellfish. The Hayward Shoreline puts you on the shoreline of the Bay at the edge of the marshlands.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 11, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Exploring the Hayward Regional Shoreline By Jonathan Comeaux Living in the Oakland hills, it can be easy to forget about the shoreline of San Francisco Bay with its wildlife native to the area and dependent on the marshlands. The Hayward Regional Shoreline is among the last wetlands of the entire Bay and has five miles of trails along the shoreline. The Hayward Regional Shoreline has 1,841 acres of water in three different marshes: the Hayward Marsh, Cogswell Marsh, and Ora Loma Marsh. The levees in the area were originally built in Hayward and San Lorenzo for salt production in the 1850s, with various landing sites to move products to San Francisco. There are still remnants of timber from old landings and salt farms along the trail. Don’t let the murky and muddy water of the marshland fool you; beneath the pickleweed and cordgrass are ideal breeding grounds for small fish, invertebrates, clams, and mussels. Larger striped bass are known to enter the channels which can attract leopard sharks, making it a popular place for fishermen. A common sight it observing snowy egrets and great blue herons snatching up food, while northern harriers scan the area for rodents. A great blue heron is seen hunting for food. Don’t be fooled by the murky water. Below the pickleweed is a wealth of small fish, invertebrate, and shellfish. The Hayward Shoreline puts you on the shoreline of the Bay at the edge of the marshlands. Photos by Jonathan Comeux Starting on Breakwater Avenue in Hayward, the Hayward Shoreline Interpretive Center starts your trail. The area is known for the old salt farms from the 1850s. Remnants can still be found today, especially at low tide. The Cogswell Marsh was created in 1980 and sustains wildlife native to San Francisco Bay. The trail is entirely flat and gravel, making it a popular area for off-road bikers. We passed 98 people on the 10-mile round trip, so slightly less than 10 people per mile. When factoring that more than 60 of which were on bikes, interactions are minimal and solitude is optimal. The hike begins as you pass the Hayward Interpretive Center on Breakwater Avenue in Hayward. The Center was constructed in in 1985 and is surrounded by 145 acres of fresh and brackish waters. You’ll then reach the Cogswell Marsh, a 250-acre tidal marsh completed in 1980. It’s among the most thriving marshlands of Hayward. The largest is the Ora Loma Marsh, a 364-acre tidal marsh with seasonal wetlands and transitional uplands created in 1997. You can spot various types of birds at all three wetlands, including herons, egrets, sandpipers, common yellowthroats, and black-necked stilts. If wildflowers are more your calling, the marshlands are host to all types of species. East Bay Regional Parks provides a comprehensive list (https://www. ebparks.org/sites/default/files/ ebrpd_hayward_shoreline_wildflowers.pdf) of all the wildflowers at the Hayward Shoreline. Punch in “Hayward Interpretive Center” in your GPS device to access this park. There are also entrances at Winton Avenue in Hayward and Grant Avenue in San Lorenzo –but parking at the Hayward Interpretive Center enables you to experience the full stretch of marshlands. articles.text: Murakami: Monsterized, the first solo exhibition in San Francisco by Japanese artist Takashi Murakami, is now on view at the San Francisco Asian art Museum. The exhibit, formally titled Takashi Murakami: Unfamiliar People — Swelling of Monsterized Human Ego, will be on display through February 2024. Born in 1962. Murakami is an internationally recognized contemporary artist and major figure in global pop culture. His influences draw from the aesthetic characteristics of the Japanese artistic tradition and postwar Japanese culture. Murakami’s influence in the contemporary art world makes his works highly sought-after in art trades. His vibrant prints maintain a consistently high value. In this exhibition, the artist’s larger-than-life paintings and sculptures use monsters, a common theme in his pieces, as a central motif. Laura W. Allen, Senior Curator of Japanese Art at the Asian, said, “The visual DNA of Murakami’s characters has origins in centuries-old styles in Japanese art, such as depicting Buddhist arhats and Daoist immortals as wizened beings with strange features, bulging eyes, and bared teeth.” Murakami: Monsterized is open until 6 p.m. Friday through Monday and until 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Visit https://www.asianart.org/ to learn more.
articles.title: Takashi Murakami exhibit now at SF Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Angel Adedokun and Jordan Covington in the San Francisco Playhouse production of Nollywood Dreams. San Francisco Playhouse presents Nollywood Dreams, a new comedy by Jocelyn Bioh, playing onstage now through November 11. Set in Lagos, Nigeria in the 1990’s, the play follows Ayamma Okafor, played by Angel Adedokun, who dreams of stardom. She has her heart set for the bright lights of Nollywood, the burgeoning Nigerian film industry akin to California’s Hollywood. She and her sister Dede, played by Brittany Nicole Sims, toil with their parents’ travel agency and unexpectedly audition with Nigeria’s best-known director, where Nollywood Dreams begins to unfold. The playwright hoped to capture a moment in time in Nigeria, one that most Western audiences don’t get to see, and blend it with comedic elements. “That’s an important goal for me. I really am trying to break open people’s singular narrative of Africa and African stories,” Bioh told the San Francisco Chronicle. “We learn about these people who inhabit the continent, and it allows us to have a more humanizing perspective on them.” Directed by Margo Hall, the stage play premiered on October 4. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/upcoming-plays/ to see showtimes and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents Nollywood Dreams

articles.text: San Francisco Opera premieres Lohengrin onstage this Sunday, October 15. The opera, composed by Richard Wagner, follows the story of noblewoman Elsa who faces charges of murder in the disappearance of her brother Gottfried, heir to the duchy of Brabant. King Heinrich, in Brabant to raise an army, calls on Friedrich von Telramund to explain why the country is torn apart. Telramund claims that Elsa, daughter of the late Brabantian ruler, has murdered her brother. The climax comes when a mysterious knight appears to defend Elsa’s honor on the condition that she marry him without knowing his name. Music Director Eun Sun Kim brings Wagner’s opera to life, with a well-rounded cast including Simon O’Neill as Longhengrin, Julie Adams as Elsa, Kristinn Sigmundsson as the king, and Brian Mulligan as Friedrich von Telramund. The opera also stars Judit Kutasi and Thomas Lehman in their San Francisco Opera debuts. The production is directed by David Alden, with Paul Steinberg as set designer and Gideon Davey as costume designer. Performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House on October 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, and November 1. Visit an hour before performances for a 20-minute overview of the opera. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/operas/lohengrin/ to purchase tickets, or call the box office at (415) 864-3330. Julie Adams as Elsa in Wagner’s Lohengrin, now in performance at San

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet will join other leading dance companies to celebrate the 10th anniversary of World Ballet Day on November 1. It will be part of a group of dance companies, including The Royal Ballet and The Australian Ballet. More than 60 companies from across the globe will have a 24-hour celebration of ballet and dance. The event will be streamed on YouTube and Facebook. Over the course of the day audiences can tune in to see classes, rehearsals, and other exclusive footage of the world’s ballet stars and performers. “As the oldest professional ballet company in the United States, we’re honored to partner with The Royal Ballet and The Australian Ballet in this global celebration and the tenth anniversary of World Ballet Day,” said Tamara Rojo, San Francisco Ballet’s new Artistic Director. “We’re delighted to be able to give viewers glimpses of the creative processes in real time, and honor ballet as a living art and universal language.” Other featured ballet companies include the Korean National Ballet, Hong Kong Ballet, Cape Town City Ballet, Finnish National Ballet, Singapore Ballet, and San Francisco-based Smuin Ballet. Visit www.worldballetday.com for more information on where to watch, including a schedule of streaming events. articles.text: October is a beautiful month. The summer heat is abating and so are the tourists. Baseball season is reaching its exciting conclusion. If you want music, there is the Paganini Festival in Italy. October in Germany means Oktoberfest with oompah bands everywhere. The Germans like to drink their beer and Piedmont has its own version of celebrating beer. In the case of the Piedmont Center for the Arts it celebrates the art of beermaking each year on the first Friday of October. The emphasis in Piedmont is on how beer is actually made. Last Friday, Piedmont had its special version of Oktoberfest. To get us in a good mood, three students from Piedmont high school treated us to some excellent background music. It wasn’t exactly an oompah band, but that hardly mattered. Alden Meil, Will Kennedy and Ryan St. John positioned their trio at the entrance to the Center and played their hearts out. Numerous brewers were inside the building showcasing the greatest aspects of beer. Dinner was outside on the lawn. It was what you might expect, with excellent bratwurst and veal sausages, potato salad, and a sweet sauerkraut. As always, Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery provided all of the food. He deserves the honorary title of “Mr. Generosity”. Opera Season October is also the beginning of the opera season and concert season in general throughout the world. If you are interested, you can attend the most famous opera productions. I have a better idea. Investigate our local opera companies. One of the very best is the Livermore Valley Opera. Their current production is Of Mice and Men. Carlisle Floyd’s musical adaptation of one of John Steinbeck’s most famous novels. The story is great in every way. That resulted in an excellent movie adaptation. It was logical to create an opera of the same name, and Floyd did just that. The wonder of it all is that he did it so well. articles.text: Part One Piedmont, California, population 11, 270, is a place apart, its quiet streets canopied by mature trees that frame vintage homes both large and small. Think of it as an island unto itself, possessing its own schools, parks, a small police department, and a classic city hall. Think of it as a small town, surrounded by the deeply urban and commercial Oakland, population 433,800. But taking a closer look at the denizens of this small, family friendly community, we discover it has a diverse and unique populace. Many of its residents are unobtrusively successful, some possessing a degree of under-theradar fame derived from their extraordinary accomplishments in filmmaking. Consider Piedmont resident Pete Docter who, in 1990, having recently graduated from the Institute of the Arts in Southern California, joined the fledging Pixar Animation Studios based in Emeryville. He became an animator, writer, and producer. He soon discovered he had found a community of kindred spirits and over the years has made imaginative contributions to a myriad of seminal and critically acclaimed animated Pixar films such as Toy Story; Toy Story 2, 3, 4; A Bug’s Life; Monsters, Inc.; Inside Out; Turning Red; Up; Buzz Lightyear; and many more. His filmography is extensive. He has been nominated for eight Academy Awards and has won three for Best Animated Feature. Additionally, he has won numerous awards to include BAFTA, the British Academy Children’s Award, and the 66th International Golden Lion Award for his lifetime achievement in film. He is currently the Chief Creative Officer at Pixar. He lives in Piedmont with his wife and their two children. Piedmont resident Mark Andrews – an animator, story supervisor, and filmmaker – has been nominated for 14 awards for his work. He is best known for the feature length animated film Brave, winner of the acclaimed 2013 Oscar and Golden Globe. The film is a delightful kids and family tale about Merida, an impetuous, strong-willed daughPiedmont native Sara Dosa’s award-winning documentary Fire of Love was nominated for an Academy Award in 2022. ter of a Scottish king who has an unruly, massive amount of red hair. She’s a wonderful character. A graduate of the California Institute of the Arts, he is married and has one daughter. And the list of Piedmont residents employed at Pixar continues. Looking beyond Pixar Animation Studios, it is impossible not to recognize the remarkable work of former Piedmont resident Sara Dosa. She was the writer, director and producer of the award-winning documentary Fire of Love which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in 2022, and subsequently purchased by National Geographic for international distribution. It was among five films nominated for Best Documentary Feature at the 95th Academy Awards, Another Piedmont resident, Peter Nicks, is an award-winning writer, producer, director, and recipient of the 2015 United States Artist Fellowship. He is known for his courageous cinema véré style, best demonstrated in the Oscar short-listed documentary film, The Waiting Room (2014). It was filmed in Oakland’s Highland Hospital emergency waiting room, which serves some 250 patients each day, it is an often grim, but involving portrait of our healthcare system. People in need may have to wait up to 14 hours in the waiting room for care. His filmography of documentary films include Anthem, Homeroom, The Force, The Fence, and the recent Stephen Curry which premiered this year at the Sundance Film Festival. Nicks lives in Piedmont with his wife and two children.
articles.title: Piedmont – a surprising enclave for filmmakers

articles.text: There are some life experiences from which there is no recovery. No matter how often the word “closure” is offered as an outcome, in truth, closure is a myth when parents lose a child. The only question is how those who face such tragedy endure. That is the essence of Rabbit Hole. The film begins with Howie (Aaron Eckhart) and Becca (Nicole Kidman) Corbett clinging to their routines while they cope with a canyon of distance that exists between them. The tension is palpable. Only gradually is it revealed that the source of their pain – the spare conversations, the brittle quality to their relationship – is the loss of their 4-year-old son eight months prior. He chased their dog into the street and was hit by a car. The performances of both Kidman and Eckhart are brilliantly crafted. Each copes with a grief that seems insurmountable in a completely different way. They are barely able to function as individuals while navigating the emotional wreckage that has become their lives. Rabbit Hole is never maudlin and never attempts to be melodramatic. It is instead a window without distortion. Audiences may shy away from this film for that very reason, but know that the narrative is rich with fine performances. Diane Wiest as Becca’s mother, who has also lost a son, is exceptional. Sandra Oh’s portrayal of a woman who has found help in a support group but is afraid to leave, is subtle and inspired. The film is adapted from the 2006 Pulitzer Prize and Tony-winning play of the same name, written by David Lindsay-Abaire. Kidman was nominated for an Oscar for Best Actress in a Leading Role. Rabbit Hole. Directed by John Cameron Mitchell, Starring Nicole Kidman, Aaron Eckhart, Dianne Wiest, Tammy Blanchard and Sandra Oh. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. John Cameron Mitchell and Nicole Kidman in Rabbit Hole T TH HE E

articles.text: Juliette Binoche stars in Certified Copy. Filmgoers who love movies in all their esoteric forms will enjoy Certified Copy. It is intriguing, unpredictable and even surreal. It is also a film carried by conversation. To review the film is dicey. It must be experienced by the filmgoer fresh and without expectation. Certified Copy opens with Elle (Juliette Binoche), the owner of a small antique shop in Tuscany, attending a lecture and book signing by noted art authority James Miller. He discusses the importance of art and its facsimiles, dwelling on original art vs. that which is forged. Seemingly taken with the author, she invites him to take a drive to Lucignano, a lovely village outside of Tuscany where couples go to marry in a small chapel, believing it will assure them of happiness together. James implies that courtship and the years following marriage are false (a forgery?), a romantic illusion, and not representative of what their life will be like later, after years of living together. She disagrees and challenges him over coffee in a small café. While he takes a phone call, she discusses men and marriage with the owner, an older woman, who assumes James and Elle are married. As it turns out, Elle finds James imperious, cold, and surprisingly cerebral given the PIEDMONT CENTER FOR THE ARTS STRONGLY ENCOURAGES PROPER MASKING INSIDE THE MAIN HALL AND HIGHLY RECOMMENDS THAT ATTENDEES HAVE ALL AVAILABLE UP TO DATE VACCINATIONS
