articles.text: Reese Witherspoon and Paul Rudd in How Do You Know How Do You Know is another romantic comedy, the genre du jour. The difference is this comedy was written by James L. Brooks, a veteran Hollywood writer for television and film who is known for snappy dialogue and comedic plots. So, does How Do You Know measure up? The ensemble does a fine job and are easy to watch. First there’s Lisa (Reese Witherspoon), a young woman who has spent her life perfecting her athletic ability (she is a Team USA softball player) and then abruptly, at 31, she’s cut from the team and finds herself a bit lost and at loose ends. When she faces this existential moment, the movie showed real promise. Athletes spend their lives on the field of play, preparing to play a game well, to compete, to run or row or cycle. Because sports are unforgiving, age and the ability of the body to renew declines, and for most athletes time becomes the sword of Damocles. But because this is a comedy and not a serious personal exploration, Lisa hooks up with pro pitcher, Matty (Own Wilson) and finds a diversion in the relationship, ignoring (a sprinkling of denial) that she is living with a well-paid, albeit charming man-child. At one point, frustrated, she looks at Matty and says, “Grow up!” His rejoinder is, “No!” But then Lisa has little faith in marriage or long-term relationships, convinced that couples who have been together for years, have kids and lead a conventional life, are pretending if they seem happy. All of this is somewhat interesting, and then along comes George (Paul Rudd), a mid-level executive, working for his father, Charles (Jack Nicholson). George also happens to be the target of a securities fraud investigation. That’s the setup. Is it charming, even funny? Well, it’s pleasant, with fine performances. Does Brooks display his nicely honed wit? On occasion. He does manage to insert lines such as, “Figure out what you want in life and learn how to ask for it.” Or, “We’re just one small adjustment away from making our lives work.” While both admonitions sound profound in the context of the movie, they also seem nonsensical and mean little. Notice also that the title, How Do You Know, is not posed as a question. The interrogatory is thrown out there by Matty to a group of ballplayers who haven’t a clue and respond with an answer that detracts, for a moment, from what is otherwise a charming movie. How Do You Know. Written and directed by James L. Brooks. Starring Reese Witherspoon, Paul Rudd, Owen Wilson, Jack Nicholson and Kathryn Hahn. 2 hrs., 1 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2919. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Netflix/Apple tv. The challenge of the film is to be able to sustain a feeling that the narrative has come unhinged, while still remaining engaged and willing to contemplate the questions it poses regarding art and love and marriage. Julliet Binoche won Best Actress in 2010 at Caanes Film Festival for her performance in Certified Copy. And indeed she is lovely and subtle and able to emote very complex emotions with merely a look or the set of her mouth or the narrowing of her eyes. It’s a tour de force portrayal by this gifted actress in a seriously enigmatic movie, the first film that director Kiarostami has made outside of Iran. Certified Copy. articles.text: Making full disclosure, I admit to loving westerns. A durable favorite is Open Range with Kevin Costner and Robert Duvall. But, I acknowledge that I’m pretty promiscuous when it comes to this genre. Westerns are, in their own special way, mythic, even iconic, no matter that they are filtered through the imaginations of novelists and screenwriters and often scrubbed of their burrs and harsh realities. One of my archival favorites will always be The Searchers with John Wayne, Ward Bond, Jeffrey Hunter and Natalie Wood. It was quintessential Wayne who was so good in so many films. Wayne doing Wayne. If I squint a bit, I can even convince myself that The Quiet Man is maybe an Irish western with hearty brogues, hounds tooth jackets, and the lovely, lush Innisfree, Ward Bond as the village priest, and the lovely Maureen O’Hara in a white apron and a simmering temper. Truly wonderful. So, here come the Coen brothers who took a great book by Charles Portis and made it their own True Grit, asking Jeff Bridges to do the heavy lifting as Rooster Cogburn, a dissolute marshal hired by spitfire, Mattie Ross, played perfectly by newcomer Hallee Steinfeld. It’s a great western. A great story, filled with interesting characters, the look of it having a certain patina, which will always be the quirky, ominous signature of Ethan and Joel Coen. The film follows the book closely, hence the eccentric language and formalized sentence structure that is both interesting and at times sharply funny. The actual plot is really immaterial, at least for purposes of this review. Suffice it to say that it’s a kind of road trip with willful Mattie Ross – who actually possesses true grit (or, in the vernacular of the day, sand) – pushing Marshal Cogburn hard into the Indian Territory to track down Tom Chaney, the man who killed her father. Mattie is at the center of the film and in every way special. She’s 14-years-old, hair parted severely, long braids, a remarkable gift of gab, hails from Yell County, Ark., and arrives in Fort Smith alone to settle her father’s affairs. She’s someone to be reckoned with. There is a glorious scene wherein she bargains with a horse dealer, Col. Stonehill, played by character actor Dakin Mathews, that is a treat to watch. True Grit is exceptional, if you appreciate the genre. Do not expect a remake of the Coen’s No Country For Old Men with its cruel, hard edges. This is a completely different movie, better for it. True Grit. Starring Jeff Bridges, Hallee Steinfeld, Matt Damon, Josh Brolin and Barry Pepper. Directed by Ethan and Joel Coen. 1hr 50min. Rated PG-13. First there’s Lisa (Reese Witherspoon), a young woman who has spent her life perfecting her athletic ability (she is a Team USA softball player) and then abruptly, at 31, she’s cut from the team and finds herself a bit lost and at loose ends. When she faces this existential moment, the movie showed real promise. Athletes spend their lives on the field of play, preparing to play a game well, to compete, to run or row or cycle. Because sports are unforgiving, age and the ability of the body to renew declines, and for most athletes time becomes the sword of Damocles. But because this is a comedy and not a serious personal exploration, Lisa hooks up with pro pitcher, Matty (Own Wilson) and finds a diversion in the relationship, ignoring (a sprinkling of denial) that she is living with a well-paid, albeit charming man-child. At one point, frustrated, she looks at Matty and says, “Grow up!” His rejoinder is, “No!” But then Lisa has little faith in marriage or long-term relationships, convinced that couples who have been together for years, have kids and lead a conventional life, are pretending if they seem happy. All of this is somewhat interesting, and then along comes George (Paul Rudd), a mid-level executive, working for his father, Charles (Jack Nicholson). George also happens to be the target of a securities fraud investigation. That’s the setup. Is it charming, even funny? Well, it’s pleasant, with fine performances. Does Brooks display his nicely honed wit? On occasion. He does manage to insert lines such as, “Figure out what you want in life and learn how to ask for it.” Or, “We’re just one small adjustment away from making our lives work.” While both admonitions sound profound in the context of the movie, they also seem nonsensical and mean little. Notice also that the title, How Do You Know, is not posed as a question. The interrogatory is thrown out there by Matty to a group of ballplayers who haven’t a clue and respond with an answer that detracts, for a moment, from what is otherwise a charming movie. How Do You Know. Written and directed by James L. Brooks. Starring Reese Witherspoon, Paul Rudd, Owen Wilson, Jack Nicholson and Kathryn Hahn. 2 hrs., 1 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2919. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Netflix/Apple tv. True Grit – a gritty western By Chris Honoré Making full disclosure, I admit to loving westerns. A durable favorite is Open Range with Kevin Costner and Robert Duvall. But, I acknowledge that I’m pretty promiscuous when it comes to this genre. Westerns are, in their own special way, mythic, even iconic, no matter that they are filtered through the imaginations of novelists and screenwriters and often scrubbed of their burrs and harsh realities. One of my archival favorites will always be The Searchers with John Wayne, Ward Bond, Jeffrey Hunter and Natalie Wood. It was quintessential Wayne who was so good in so many films. Wayne doing Wayne. If I squint a bit, I can even convince myself that The Quiet Man is maybe an Irish western with hearty brogues, hounds tooth jackets, and the lovely, lush Innisfree, Ward Bond as the village priest, and the lovely Maureen O’Hara in a white apron and a simmering temper. Truly wonderful. So, here come the Coen brothers who took a great book by Charles Portis and made it their own True Grit, asking Jeff Bridges to do the heavy lifting as Rooster Cogburn, a dissolute marshal hired by spitfire, Mattie Ross, played perfectly by newcomer Hallee Steinfeld. It’s a great western. A great story, filled with interesting characters, the look of it having a certain patina, which will always be the quirky, ominous signature of Ethan and Joel Coen. The film follows the book closely, hence the eccentric language and formalized sentence structure that is both interesting and at times sharply funny. The actual plot is really immaterial, at least for purposes of this review. Suffice it to say that it’s a kind of road trip with willful Mattie Ross – who actually possesses true grit (or, in the vernacular of the day, sand) – pushing Marshal Cogburn hard into the Indian Territory to track down Tom Chaney, the man who killed her father. Mattie is at the center of the film and in every way special. She’s 14-years-old, hair parted severely, long braids, a remarkable gift of gab, hails from Yell County, Ark., and arrives in Fort Smith alone to settle her father’s affairs. She’s someone to be reckoned with. There is a glorious scene wherein she bargains with a horse dealer, Col. Stonehill, played by character actor Dakin Mathews, that is a treat to watch. True Grit is exceptional, if you appreciate the genre. Do not expect a remake of the Coen’s No Country For Old Men with its cruel, hard edges. This is a completely different movie, better for it. True Grit. Starring Jeff Bridges, Hallee Steinfeld, Matt Damon, Josh Brolin and Barry Pepper. Directed by Ethan and Joel Coen. 1hr 50min. Rated PG-13. Their conversations turn unexpectedly brittle, remarkable for two strangers who seem to share a similar interest in art, even the esoteric niche James explores in his book, Certified Copy. And so, what began as a pleasant afternoon, surrounded by the verdant beauty of the Tuscany as well as Lucignano, evolves into something completely unexpected. The challenge of the film is to be able to sustain a feeling that the narrative has come unhinged, while still remaining engaged and willing to contemplate the questions it poses regarding art and love and marriage. Julliet Binoche won Best Actress in 2010 at Caanes Film Festival for her performance in Certified Copy. And indeed she is lovely and subtle and able to emote very complex emotions with merely a look or the set of her mouth or the narrowing of her eyes. It’s a tour de force portrayal by this gifted actress in a seriously enigmatic movie, the first film that director Kiarostami has made outside of Iran. Certified Copy. articles.text: I always look forward to tasting the new releases from Ridge Vineyards. In the fall each year they release their wonderful Lytton Springs blend as well as their well-regarded Montebello Chardonnay in addition to a couple of surprises. Ridge Winery has two main facilities. One is a spectacular location on a high ridge (hence the name) overlooking Silicon Valley. You keep climbing this steep road and you never think you ae going to get there and suddenly there it is – with a magnificent view. It’s hard to believe what caused the early Italian pioneers who planted these vineyards so long ago to undertake the effort. This is the home of the Montebello Vineyard, the source of Ridge’s iconic Chardonnay and award-winning Cabernet Sauvignon. The Ridge Montebello Cabernet was in the original Paris tasting of 1976 that knocked the French off the world wine throne. To this day it is one of the world’s most highly rated Cabernets. Their other facility is located on Lytton Springs Rd. just east of Hwy. 101 in Sonoma County. The winery is surrounded by nearly hundred-year-old Zinfandel vines that look like gnarled bonsai trees. This is the home of the Lytton Springs and Geyserville blends as well as many small single vineyard Zinfandels. It is also home to the great former York Creek Petite Sirah (rest in peace) and the dynamic Lytton Estate Petite Sirah – one of the greatest values in California wine. If you are interested in Ridge wines, be sure to check out their website where they have over 100 wines for sale. The wine tasting area at Ridge Lytton Springs.

Wednesday, October 11, 2023 23 By Will Adams Another important visual element of our built environment is signage. It is in many ways a lot like lighting, discussed in the last column. Both tend to stand out when done poorly and unrelated to their context. When designed well, both lighting and signage seem to go unnoticed as they appear to fit right in, as if there were no other way they could have been designed. Besides providing necessary information to people on foot or in cars, appropriate signage can enhance and complement the Signage architecture of a building or landscape of which it is a part. Walking around Piedmont, it is clear that the sensitive and understated use of signs pretty much everywhere contributes to the charm of the city. Like lighting, signage has both a functional requirement and an aesthetic character. Function is of course the first consideration: what is the sign’s purpose? And to whom is it addressed? Clearly there is a huge difference in sign requirements for people walking around town versus those driving cars at various speeds. Unfortunately, often the size and use or purpose of signage is confused. What is appropriate and exciting for Las Vegas or Times Square for example is neither appropriate nor necessary for pretty much anyplace else of less density or of smaller scale. The common signage mistake of using large retail advertising methods when only subtle information is required is not a problem we have in Piedmont. Signage should be designed to fit with the surrounding architectural character, because both in fact work together to orient visitors and let them know where they Four examples of building signage (above): all different, simple, understated, and designed to complement the architecture of which they are a part. This kind of variety adds interest and texture to the city without distracting or overwhelming. These examples, especially the Piedmont Community Church portal and sign, also fall into the “urban design” category, with which readers of this column are familiar. are and where they are headed. When approaching City Hall, for example, unfamiliar visitors, seeing the size of the building cluster, the associated communication towers, and then the landscaping and fountain, have a good idea long before they are sure that this is indeed a civic building. At the final destination, the rather small sign is only a final confirmation that the supposition was correct. A great sign. It is the right size for easy reading of the information without being too big and distracting, and the perfect color for its placement in the parks. Although a regulatory sign, I find it friendly. Photos by Will Adams The specific purpose of a sign and the people to whom it is directed should determine the design: the location, size, shape, text, images, and colors. There are usually numerous good alternatives. Signage is often lighted. Internally illuminated signage has been done badly so often it is prohibited in many places because it is often coarse and annoying. Externally illuminated signage generally has a better opportunity for aesthetic success, provided that the signage is appropriate for the genre of architecture/site/ environs and it is not over lit. In some cities, very strict design review requirements for signs are problematic as they have resulted in a completely uniform, bland, lifeless array of signs, which are ironically hard to interpret or to decipher the required information. In my opinion, the best signs are those that are creative but restrained, and also reasonably varied. These seem to add life, interest, and texture to the street and neighborhood. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 13, 2021. The historical “informational” signs placed throughout the Piedmont Park area are perfect: unobtrusive yet easy to find and read, informative and well designed. They were created for the City’s Centennial in 2007, with support from Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont Garden Club, Piedmont Historical Society, and the Bechtel Foundation.

articles.text: Piedmont open water swimmer Josh Bernstein, braved the waters of San Francisco Bay on Saturday, September 30, in the annual Swim Across America event, a major fundraiser for pediatric cancer research at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital. Saturday’s swim of more than 200 swimmers started at Little Marina Green and finished 1-1/2 miles later at Aquatic Park. The swim, which started at 9:30 a.m., was the 18th annual iteration of the local leg of Swim Across America, a national Photo by Noah Berger Piedmont’s Josh Bernstein (left) at the Swim Across America event with swimming colleague Susan Helmrich, leader of Team Susan Survives. Photo by Miguel Melendez Swimmers dive into San Francisco Bay at Little Marina Green near Crissy Field at the start of the annual Swim Across America fundraising event on September 30. Team Susan Survives had 52 members for the 18th annual Swim Across America event. Photo by Miguel Melendez The air temperature was 60 degrees and the water was 63 at the start of Swim Across America on September 30. fundraising effort. Saturday’s event generated $400,000 for the hospital. Bernstein was one of 52 members of Team Susan Survives, led by swimming colleague Susan Helmrich, who has survived three life-threatening cancers; starting as far back as 46 years ago. “Susan is the former longtime director of Swim Across America SF, and she is a hard-core competitive swimmer,” said Bernstein. “She is nationally ranked today at age 67, and she’s fast.” She credits her survival to outstanding physicians, a vegetarian diet, and high intensity swim workouts. Her team alone raised $134,000, with Helmrich as the lead donor of $32,000. Currently, one out of two men and one out of three women will get cancer in their lifetime.
articles.title: Piedmont’s Josh Bernstein and 200 swimmers raise $400,000 in annual Swim Across America event

articles.text: Thomas Young Kincaid, a 5th generation Piedmonter passed away peacefully at his home in Sparks, Nevada on September 23, 2023 with his loved ones by his side. He was 69. Tom was born in Oakland in 1954 and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1972. During his younger days he was an active member of the Piedmont Boy Scouts and a member of the Sea Scouts and Oakland Police Explorers. Tom retired to Sparks after many years working as the Division HR Manager for Golden State Overnight as well as the Security Lead for Aramark Sports & Entertainment at the Oakland Coliseum. He also worked as a police officer for the Oakland Housing Authority and as a Reserve officer for the Piedmont Police Department. One of his first jobs was as a Regional Training Coordinator for Greyhound Lines in Oakland. Tom is predeceased by his parents Donald H Kincaid and Gaye Lenahan and his beloved dog Brownie. He is survived by his sister Peggy Kincaid of Whitefish, Montana. Tom Kincaid, a 5h generation Piedmont native, died on September 23 at his home in Sparks Nevada. He was 69.
articles.title: Tom Kincaid dies on September 23

articles.text: A record turnout of 22 readers of the First Mondays Reading Group came to the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on a beautiful, warm day in early fall on October 2. On hand were: Dick Carter, Bob Hall, Bella Almanzan, Ken Young, Darby Gragg, Gerry Gragg, Hillary Honore, Martin Levy, Mike Henn, Adrienne Hamlin, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, June Cohen, Lois Price, Rich Seigel, Dale Benveniste, Carol Warren, Carol Long, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The subject of discussion was The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid, the 2006 memoir by best-selling travel writer Bill Bryson. It was a fun, summertime kind of book and the memoir of the childhood of the author. The group had previously read and discussed Bryson’s The Body: A Guide for Occupants Bryson’s 2019 book of popular science. In The Life and Times he tells of his youth growing up during the 1950s in Des Moines, Iowa. The book’s title comes from an imaginary identity Bryson created for himself, who had the ability to vaporize problem people with his heat vision. Bryson recalls many things that he invented through his imagination: frozen dinners, atomic toilets, and television. His middle class American lifestyle is present throughout the book, Bryson tells amusing stories of his misadventures, and the trouble he and his friends got into, which was common for the Thunderbolt Kid. At the book’s end, Bryson tells readers that “life moves on,” and he wishes the world could be more like life in the 1950s and 1960s. Almost everyone in the group enjoyed the book. Parts of it are can’t-stop-laughing funny, and the stories brought back childhood memories and some nostalgia for the readers. The group talked about 19 cent loaves of bread, kids spending all their time outside, front doors that were never locked, and getting BB guns at age 12, How much the world has changed is staggering. The readers questioned what has been lost versus what has been gained over the last 70 years. The constraints on women’s opportunities and the discrimination experienced by minorities are less today. Life was certainly not as wonderful for everyone as it was for Bryson’s white, middle class family. However, it seems life was a happier and more carefree than it is today. This may be because Bryson is remembering life from a child’s perspective. The impact of the Depression was still in his parents’ minds, but Bryson’s 1950s were fun times. articles.text: If you have grandchildren, you probably enjoy spending time with them and watching them grow. And to help them achieve a bright future, you might like to make some financial gifts — but which ones? You have several options. Let’s look at three of them: 529 plans When you invest in a 529 education savings plan, any earnings growth is distributed federally tax free, as long as withdrawals are used for qualified education expenses. (Withdrawals used for expenses other than qualified education expenses may be subject to federal and state taxes, plus a 10% penalty.) And in-state residents who invest in their home state’s 529 plan may also receive state tax incentives. A 529 plan can be used for college, approved trade school programs, qualified student loan repayments and even some K-12 costs. And if the grandchild you’ve named as a beneficiary of a 529 plan decides to forego further education, you can generally switch beneficiaries to another immediate family member. You can contribute up to $17,000 in 2023, per grandchild, to a 529 plan without incurring gift taxes. Furthermore, as of the 2024–25 school year, grandparent-owned 529 plans won’t affect financial aid eligibility. However, tax issues for 529 plans can be complex, so consult with your tax advisor about your situation. Roth IRA Any earnings growth in a Roth IRA is distributed tax free, provided the owner is at least 59½ and has had the account at least five years. If your grandchildren earn money from babysitting or a part-time job, they can open a Roth IRA with the help of a parent or other adult. You could “match” your grandchildren’s contributions, possibly on a dollar-for-dollar basis, to provide them with an incentive for saving. In fact, you could fully fund the Roth IRA, up to the annual contribution limit, which is $6,500 or the amount of your grandchild’s taxable compensation, whichever is less. (The annual limit is $7,500 for those 50 or older.) And your grandchildren can withdraw the contributions — not the earnings — at any time to pay for college or anything else. Plus, there’s an initial tax benefit to custodial accounts: The first $1,250 of your grandchild’s investment income (dividends, interest, capital gains) is tax free, and the next $1,250 is taxed at the child’s rate. Anything above that amount is taxed at the parents’ marginal tax rate. He also worked as a police officer for the Oakland Housing Authority and as a Reserve officer for the Piedmont Police Department. One of his first jobs was as a Regional Training Coordinator for Greyhound Lines in Oakland. Tom is predeceased by his parents Donald H Kincaid and Gaye Lenahan and his beloved dog Brownie. He is survived by his sister Peggy Kincaid of Whitefish, Montana. Tom Kincaid, a 5h generation Piedmont native, died on September 23 at his home in Sparks Nevada. He was 69.

The group was pleased that Jennifer Peltzer brought Nancy Odette. Nanda Parte from India had come for a wedding and joined the walkers. Lisa Leonard and Kris Keller with K-9 best friends Lucky and Rascal were also part of the weekly walk. A strong turnout of 46 walkers and four K-9 best friends arrived at the Exedra for a walk on October 4 as part of the Walking on Wednesdays group. One street that the group hadn’t walked and an early Piedmont land developer they hadn’t talked about this year was Sharon Avenue and William Sharon. The long stretch of Wildwood Avenue between Highland and Crocker Avenues with the leaves turning red on both sides of the street provided a colorful walk. The walkers went to Lincoln Avenue and over to Sheridan Avenue. Going up Caperton Avenue to Mountain Avenue provided some uphill exercise. At Mountain, they went to Sharon Avenue where its history was shared. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi had told of William E. Sharon, his family, and estate in a past issue of the society’s publication. Sharon was born in 1852 and grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872, he went to San Francisco and then Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, who was a successful banker and silver mine owner. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt in 1876 and became successful in finance and mining too. He was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. The Sharons initially lived in Virginia City, but they wanted their children to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. Three years later they purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. They built a magnificent three-story house in the middle of their land and called it Casa Montana. With seven children, Lillian’s mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener they moved into it in 1898. However, in 1914 the City of Piedmont, then seven years old, imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. In 1915, the Sharons subdivided their land in a development they called Sharon Terrace. It had 20 lots with frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. Some family members built homes there, and the driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue. Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home. Lillian lived in it until 1934 when she moved into a residential Oakland hotel. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon Avenue and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon. Sadly, in 1936 Windsor demolished Casa Montana and replaced it with three homes – 27, 33, and 37 Sharon Avenue. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses remain from the Casa Montana property – 235 Mountain, 56 Sharon and 52 Sharon Avenue. The walkers continued down to Dormidera Avenue and went to where it intersects with Sharon Avenue. They took a side trip to Sharon Court, which was not part of the original development. For the return walk to the center of town, they had an opportunity to take a somewhat hidden path from Mountain to Sierra Avenue and get back to the city center before the temperature rose to 80 degrees. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. pages.text: Wednesday, October 11, 2023 29 By Jay Russell The Indie Next List for October 2023 has some spooky and spectacular reads. While every month’s list has something for everyone, many novels on this list come from lands with strange scientific footing or purely fantastical origins. As the leaves turn and the days get shorter, slow down with a good book on your lap and a warm pumpkin spiced drink in your hand. This list consists of only the newest releases with rave reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support small independent bookstores. October #1 Pick Death Valley, is the most profound book yet from the visionary author Melissa Broder – a darkly funny novel about grief that becomes a desert survival story. Death Valley By Melissa Broder, Scribner, Fiction “A hike becomes a metaphysical journey straight into the center of grief, featuring literature’s most memorable cactus. Broder delivers us directly to the site of the wound and somehow makes us want to linger. Beautiful, exciting, and profound.” —Kristen Iskandrian, Thank You Books, Birmingham, AL Land of Milk and Honey By C Pam Zhang, Riverhead Books, Fiction “Zhang’s gorgeous prose sets a stark contrast between a world destroyed and a seemingly pristine utopia. While darkness pervades this literary thrill ride, thoughtful questions about humanity save the reader from total madness.” —Page Berger, Barrett Bookstore, Darien, CT North Woods By Daniel Mason, Random House, Fiction “North Woods is a novel about a house, its inhabitants, and the land over four centuries set in the hills of western Massachusetts. A gorgeous, layered tapestry in which the house and the woods play into the lives of those who live there.” —Fran Keilty, Hickory Stick Bookshop, Washington Depot, CT Starling House By Alix E. Harrow, Tor Books, Fantasy “Starling House has all the excellent, wry writing of A Spindle Splintered and A Mirror Mended. Still, it’s not a fairy tale retelling, just a deeply unsettling story with a house that might conceal the very gates of hell. Leave the lights on.” —Christy Peterson, Vintage Books, Vancouver, WA Family Meal By Bryan Washington, Riverhead Books, Fiction “Family Meal is a heartbreaking story of love, loss, and grief. Cam returns to Houston after the love of his life, Kai, dies. He and his estranged best friend, TJ, try to work through their grief and past hurts. A painful, gorgeous read.” —Kristen Beverly, Half Price Books, Dallas, TX The Fragile Threads of Power By V. E. Schwab, Tor Books, Fantasy “Like all of Schwab’s books, this will draw you in and dazzle you with her worldbuilding and characters, and keep you on the edge of your seat. A spectacular addition to the world of the Shades of Magic series!” —Melissa Fox, Watermark Books & Café, Wichita, KS Wellness By Nathan Hill, Knopf, Fiction “Wellness will capture your heart from the very beginning. Heartbreaking, funny, thoughtful, endearing – readers will be Top Indie Books of October The Maniac By Benjamín Labatut, Penguin Press, Fiction “One of the most fascinating books of the year. Labatut delivers a terrifying, dispassionate, utterly compulsive amalgam of fact and fiction, raising profound moral questions on unchecked scientific advancement and the dawn of AI.” —Alex Brubaker, Midtown Scholar Bookstore, Harrisburg, PA entranced by Jack and Elizabeth’s story as they struggle for the elusive life of family, truth, and true love.” —Betsy Von Kerens, The Bookworm of Omaha, Omaha, NE Bright Young Women By Jessica Knoll, S&S/Marysue Rucci Books, Thriller “We all know the names of serial killers, but not the victims. Jessica Knoll tells their stories with compassion and respect. You’ll be shocked by the multiple miscarriages of justice that cut short the lives of so many bright young women.” —Susan Kehoe, Browseabout Books, Rehoboth Beach, DE Cleat Cute By Meryl Wilsner, St. Martin’s Griffin, Romance “Meryl Wilsner is a must-read author. Grace and Phoebe’s sexy sapphic love story centers around their training as members of the U.S. Women’s National soccer team. Spicy and sweet, you’ll fall in love so fast and be sad when the book is over.” —Andrea Richardson, Fountain Bookstore, Richmond, VA Godkiller By Hannah Kaner, Harper Voyager, Fantasy “In a world scarred by warring gods and brutal battles, a godkiller sets off on a quest with an unlikely crew. This is immersive, diverse, and full of rage against the world and those who ruined it. This book doesn’t relent. I want more!” —Anna Rose Carleton, The Well-Read Moose, Coeur d’Alene, ID Our Strangers By Lydia Davis, Bookshop Editions, Short Stories “Lydia Davis is in a rare arena of master short story writers. She celebrates language, never using an unnecessary word. Just perfect sentences, unexpected images, and stories that make you laugh and cry and stay with you forever.” —Gayle Shanks, Changing Hands, Tempe, AZ Chenneville of Murder, Loss, and Vengeance By Paulette Jiles, William Morrow, Historical Fiction “Paulette Jiles has done it again. John Chenneville’s travails through the post-Civil War U.S. are written in a way that is thoughtful, profound, and fluid like poetry. Even if you’re not familiar with Jiles, once you read it, you’ll want more.” —Vicki Honeyman, Literati Bookstore, Ann Arbor, MI Sword Catcher By Cassandra Clare, Del Rey, Fantasy “I grew up reading Cassandra Clare. Here I am as an adult, reading her adult debut, a masterwork of worldbuilding and beautiful respect for her own history woven in. Sword Catcher is the next unstoppable force in the world of adult fantasy.” —Caitlyn VanOrder, Bookmarks, Winston-Salem, NC Starter Villain By John Scalzi, Tor Books, Science Fiction “Scalzi makes the absurd feel completely normal. Charlie is a down on his luck guy who gets thrust into the world of super villains and genetically-engineered cats. Fans of the spy genre will love the subverted super villain clichés.” —Scott Patnesky, Tattered Cover Book Store, Denver, CO The Hive and the Honey: Stories By Paul Yoon, S&S/Marysue Rucci Books, Short Stories “Paul Yoon portrays 400 years of violence suffered by Korean people, dispersed by uncontrollable events with profound consequences on their lives. His concise, incisive stories bring all of these tales to life and probe universal truths.” —Bill Cusumano, Square Books, Oxford, MS Bright Lights, Big Christmas By Mary Kay Andrews, St. Martin’s Press, Fiction “Nothing gets you in the holiday spirit like a festive read. Mary Kay Andrews delivers in her latest holiday story. Centered in NYC, the most spirited holiday city, this is a perfect read to enjoy in front of a Christmas tree and a cozy fire.” —Angela Sides, Monkey and Dog Books, Fort Worth, TX Wildfire By Hannah Grace, Atria Books, Romance “A fantastic follow-up to Icebreaker. A one-night stand with emotions left on the table leave Russ and Aurora thinking of each other. When the two end up as camp counselors, sparks fly. If you love a good summer romance, this is it.” —Kyle Churman, Werner Books, Erie, PA How to Say Babylon By Safiya Sinclair, Simon & Schuster, Memoir “This extraordinary memoir explores self-actualization at the crossroads of womanhood and Black liberation. Sinclair’s poetic brilliance brought grace to even her most excruciating experiences. I am in awe of her compassion and transcendence.” —Evisa Gallman, Uncle Bobbie’s Coffee & Books, Philadelphia, PA The Hurricane Wars By Thea Guanzon, Harper Voyager, Fantasy “In this lush, romantic debut, two mortal enemies are forced into an arranged marriage to save their countries from each other and forces that threaten their world. I loved the intricate world, its politics, and the steamy romance!” —Haley Calvin, The Novel Neighbor, Webster Groves, MO The Premonition By Banana Yoshimoto, (Asa Yoneda Trans.), Counterpoint, Fiction “Have you ever felt haunted by something from your childhood? A vague memory on the edge of remembrance? Yoshimoto unravels hidden grief, loneliness, and family secrets in The Premonition. Originally published in the ‘80s, this is timeless.” —Jenny Gilroy, E. Shaver, Bookseller, Savannah, GA A Holly Jolly Ever After By Julie Murphy, Sierra Simone, Avon, Romance “A gloriously spicy holiday romance that is hilarious and heart wrenching. It celebrates holiday joy while tackling topics like religion and purity culture. Holly Jolly is a trademark balance of laughter, spice, and everything nice!” —Jenni Marchisotto, Mysterious Galaxy Books, San Diego, CA Company: Stories By Shannon Sanders, Graywolf Press, Fiction “Members of a big, multigenerational Black family – with branches both Bohemian and bourgeois – live vibrantly in this debut collection of fiction. Linked together in a glittering chain of language, their stories create a treasured heirloom.” —James Crossley, Madison Books, Seattle, WA Landscapes By Christine Lai, Two Dollar Radio, Fiction “A celebration of co-creation at its best. Christine Lai chronicles the days of the end in a subdued manner. She makes sure we know that we all have something at stake in the climate crisis, and we can continue to reach towards each other in the end.” —Tay Jones, White Whale Bookstore, Pittsburgh, PA The Free People’s Village By Sim Kern, Levine Querido, Science Fiction “The Free People’s Village goes so hard. Sim Kern’s masterpiece burns with righteous fury. This book doesn’t pull punches, and instead of hopelessness, it slices straight through frustration, fatalism, and ennui and made me want to fight back.” —Shana Hausman, All She Wrote Books, Somerville, MA

articles.text: More than 75 people attended the city’s town hall meeting on public safety on Wednesday, September 27, voicing concern about recent crimes in the city. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers moderated the event which began with a presentation on crime statistics and police strategies. Afterward, Bowers took questions from the audience. He reiterated the police department’s strategy for crime prevention, describing it as a “full-court press.” Bowers seeks to maintain full staffing for the police department and the PPD has started placing crime suppression cars at strategic points in the city. When asked what the community can do to support police, Bowers stressed the importance of consistent crime reporting. “I think one of the biggest things is don’t stop calling and reporting [crimes], regardless if you’re in Piedmont or if you’re elsewhere outside of Piedmont,” said Bowers. “If we don’t know the severity of the problem, how are we going to hold folks accountable?” Bowers was also asked about police procedure. One audience member asked what happens to suspects when they leave Piedmont and enter Oakland. “Do they just get to go free?” he asked. “Good question,” Bowers

articles.text: This year’s Art Walk brought out the best in the city’s artists. Swirls of colorful abstract art showed up to do battle with impressionist, modern, and figure paintings in a lovely melee of sensory delights. Artwork was on display at various locations across Piedmont, including Piedmont High School, Havens Elementary, the Center for the Arts, and many of the artists’ homes. Many artist were there to sell their pieces to the public. Others were more interested in interacting with their local art scene. But virtually all of them were excited to share their work with their neighbors and friends. Part of the Art Walk’s uniqueness is that it brings together artBrian Judd explains the texture of his painting to on-lookers. articles.text: There is no more admired person in human history than Jesus of Nazareth. His name is often invoked. Millions worship him regularly. His followers pray as he taught them to pray and are known to offer loving service, as well as go to war, in his name. Yet, fierce debates rage as to exact nature of his being, the true essence of his ministry, the most accurate definition of his theology. I would be remiss to suggest that my sermon this morning will resolve these. They are likely to continue for centuries to come. I would humbly suggest that regardless of our faith backgrounds, religious traditions or our theological positions, we can find unity in the simple affirmation that Jesus is inspiring. One of the earliest hymns about Jesus is quoted by Paul in chapter 2 of his letter to the followers of Jesus in Philippi, a major commercial center of the Roman Empire located in northern Greece. In this warm letter Paul quotes two verses of what scholars call the Kenotic Hymn, the Greek work kenosis (empty) being central to the theology he wants to lift up. Paul writes, “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited, but emptied himself” I hear him saying. Let Jesus shape you. articles.text: The City of Piedmont sent out an online survey on September 28 to community members asking for input on housing plans for Moraga Canyon. This marks the beginning of public engagement with the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – an initiative that will study all City-owned land in Moraga Canyon with the goal of creating detailed housing plans for possible development in the future. “It’s a good opportunity to have Piedmont community members respond and voice their concerns and responses,” said Kevin Jackson, the city’s Planning Director. “We’re trying to move this project forward and engage with the community. It’ll be a stronger plan with greater community engagement.” These efforts are part of a larger initiative by the City of Piedmont to add housing units to the community. A recent mandate by the state of California requires cities to plan additional housing units in their communities to help meet housing needs across the state. The City of Piedmont was charged with creating plans to accommodate 587 units of new housing, including 257 affordable units by 2031. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan proposes to build 132 units of new housing (60 of which would be for low-income households). SURVEY QUESTIONS Among other things, the survey asks what community members the following: • When you visit Moraga Canyon, how do you and/or your family spend your time there? • What concerns do you have about new housing development in Moraga Canyon? • Would you be interested in living in multifamily housing in Moraga Canyon? Other questions ask citizens to rank the buildings they would like to see in Moraga Canyon based on architectural style with a scale from 1 to 5. The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/MoragaCanyonSurvey and will remain open through October 20th. articles.text: You might see something new as you pass by the construction site for Piedmont’s new community pool being built. On Wednesday, September 27, construction workers sprayed concrete on the retaining walls. Concrete was added to the walls using “shotcrete,” a method of applying concrete to a surface with a high-pressure hose at high velocity. – George Sanen Construction Manager Piedmont Community Pool “You’re going to start seeing the outlines of buildings,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. He said that current work will help the community visualize the progress of construction. Staff photos Construction workers spray concrete onto the retaining walls at the community pool construction site. Members of various city departments were present for an on-site tour. On-site Construction Manager George Sanen led the group through the project site, stopping at several places to talk about the work being done. “This will be the second all-electric public swimming pool in the country,” Sanen told the group on the tour. “If everything Pool construction manager George Sanen leads a group of city officials through the project site. George Sanen speaks with Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. goes well, by this time next year, we’ll be swimming.” Sanen also commented on the necessary maintenance that the pool will need after construction is complete. “I use the reference of buying a Ferrari. The city is buying a Ferrari and so the city needs different experts with experience to properly operate and maintain [the pool].” The community pool has experienced minor construction delays in recent weeks. In July, the discovery of an underground 100-year-old fuel tank created complications for the City. Because the tank still contained gasoline, it was considered a toxic substance, and the city was required to submit an inspection and work plan to the County of Alameda for its removal. Since then, the fuel has been pumped out of the tank and the surrounding soil has been successfully checked to confirm no contamination exists. The tank was removed from site on Friday, September 29. Gonzales also said that workers have also been digging holes for gas, water, and Comcast lines for future facilities at the pool site. “Most of our timeline depends upon when PG&E can install the power source.” PG&E has not yet provided a date to come to the site. Construction is currently scheduled to finish in September 2024. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. For questions about the project, contact George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at (415) 858-8582. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Most beer festivals held in October are described as Oktoberfest events. However, the Piedmont Center for the Arts event, the 11th annual Artisanal Beer Festival, emphasizes the art of beermaking. To complement this year’s event a jazz trio of Piedmont High School seniors – Alden Meil, Will Kennedy and Ryan St. John – will provide music on the lawn while guests enjoy a German dinner before going inside for the beer tasting. Musician Backgrounds Kennedy has been playing the sax for seven years. What started as a way to escape middle school PE has taken him to the California Jazz Conservancy and a summer program at NYU. St. John’s passion for drumming began 10 years ago. Like many drummers he first had to convince his parents he was serious enough to get his own drum set. He now plays with a variety of local combos. Meil has played the guitar for six years and the bass for two years. He initially pursued the guitar out of his love for rock music but his path has broadened through his involvement in the California Jazz Conservatory.

articles.text: The annual Piedmont Artisanal Beer Festival, which takes place this Friday at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, will feature the concoctions of around a dozen local home brewers. One of them is Brian Black, a dad of two recent Piedmont graduates and husband of Piedmont High School English teacher Beth Black. Black’s academic discipline as a molecular biologist turned into work as a cardiovascular scientist at UCSF. It also furnished him with a scientific lens for his hobby as a beermaker. On Friday evening he will bring two ales to share, Shelterwood Ale, an American Pale Ale, and Monastic Whisper, a Belgian Dubbel. Black’s pathway to brewing from the field of medicine and biology helped him start higher on the brewing learning curve. “Brewing is kind of a mix of microbiology, chemistry, and engineering,” Black explained. His professional passion also led him to install equipment in his Oakland home conducive to science and brewing. Two large ovens in his kitchen help him sterilize all brewing equipment. “Anyone can make good beer if they can follow a recipe if – and it’s a big if – if they can keep stuff sterile or sanitized,” he said. “If you can get your equipment sterile, your homebrew will at least be decent, if not outstanding.” It was when making a Kölsch, a type of ale from Cologne, Germany, that his passion for brewing sparked. “The first time I tried a more challenging style, what really solidified my desire to be a hobbyist was when I made a Kölsch. It’s a narrow style, with a narrow alcohol range, color range, bitterness range, and a very specific type of yeast that has to be used.” Living just outside of Piedmont, Black’s hillside yard allows him to grow two kinds of hops, enough to make at least one SMaSH (Single Malt and Single Hop) every year. “Beer [brewing] is basically wort, which is a sweet and bitter soup, and then we keep it sterile. We put the yeast that we want in there, they eat the sugar, and they produce carbon dioxide and alcohol – and that’s beer making,” Black explained. Black will be at the beer festival with a dozen other homebrewers this Friday at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The beer festival includes a freshly prepared German dinner on the lawn in front of the Center. Brian Black on a brewery tour in Alaska.
articles.title: Beer Festival’s Brian Black explains the science of brewing

articles.text: The inaugural Week of Wellness raised over $60,000 to fund Wellness Center staffing. On Wednesday, September 27, close to 80 PUSD Wellness Center sponsors gathered to celebrate the Center’s 15th anniversary. Hosted by Cortney and Ben Allen at their home, the event was the capstone of the first-ever Week of Wellness (WOW). Throughout the week, fitness studios and instructors offered free classes and activities to community participants who donated to the Wellness Center. As a key component of the school support structure for middle and high school students, the Wellness Center provides counseling services to Piedmont Middle and High Schools and Millennium High School students. During the 2022-2023 school year, the Wellness Center provided over 2,000 counseling sessions to Piedmont students. Nicki Gilbert served as the M.C. for the evening, introducing various speakers. Retired Middle School counselor Brooke Zimmerman, who co-founded the Wellness Center 15 years ago with a group of parents, spoke about the needs she saw in the Piedmont student community then. articles.text: Happy Halloween! Many kids (and adults) love celebrating Halloween traditions with costumes, decorations, trick-or-treating and displaying a jack-o’-lantern on the front steps. Celebrating these traditions not only creates lifelong memories, but also allows opportunities for supporting speech and language development. Here are some of my favorite ways to integrate speech and language skills into your holiday traditions. 1. Pumpkin Carving & Painting Pumpkin carving/painting is a fantastic way to promote speech and language development. Whether you pick out your pumpkin from a patch or the grocery store, there is an abundance of variety in your pumpkin options. This allows your child to practice using descriptive vocabulary in the selection process. For example, your child can practice describing size (little, small, tiny, medium, big, large, huge, tall, giant, gigantic, enormous), shape (circle, round, oval), color (orange, yellow, white, green), texture (smooth, bumpy, dented, curve, lines, crack), and weight (heavy, light). This is also a great opportunity to model the use of comparatives (this is big, but this one is bigger, and that one is the biggest). After selecting the perfect pumpkin, it’s time to carve or paint. To work on developing sequencing and narrative language, you can talk about the steps to carving a pumpkin before (or after) you carve your pumpkin. Narrate the following steps for your child: • First cut off the top • Second scoop out the seeds • Then draw the eyes, nose, mouth Halloween can be a learning opportunity for young kids. • Next cut out the eyes, nose, mouth • Last, put a candle or light inside For children who benefit from visual support, take pictures along the way. 2. “Trick-or-Treating” Trick or treating is for everyone. Halloween is an amazing time to practice communication during a super motivating activity (free candy), but remember Halloween is about fun and not about explaining why your child isn’t communicating verbally. For children who have difficulty with communicating, trick-ortreating can be a difficult task and we must find different ways to include all children that would like to participate. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: After a feast of juice and cookies for this year’s Medieval Faire (formerly Medieval Banquet), seventh graders at Piedmont Middle School headed outside to the many activities on the sports courts below the school. Students had choices of 10 activities related to the history of Medieval times, such as stilt walking and sword fighting. Other activities included a marriage booth – possibly the most popular – where kids could hold a small faux ceremony, and a fortune teller’s booth where they received a slip of paper with their future on it. At the Diet of Worms booth, students ate a gummy worm candy covered in whipped cream, but they had to eat it without using their hands, similar to bobbing for donuts on a string – no hands allowed. Favorite activities also included Medieval Hopscotch and games of cornhole using bean bags. Finally, students participated in The Soak-a-Bloke by throwing wet sponges at teachers with only their face were exposed. Faculty members included Ted Scherman, Nicole Straley, Shannon Fierro, and Michael Bracamonte. Students try to take a bite from a donut on a string.
articles.title: Middle School 7th graders celebrate annual Medieval Faire

articles.text: This year’s Medieval Faire presented a lord and a lady for each class, seven pairs in total. The roles were appointed to the select few by drawing numbers out of a hat. Once selected, the seven pairs came together to find out who would be the king and queen of the entire 7th grade. This year’s king and queen were Dylan Jerez and Eva Tyler. Ms. Kelly’s class prepared beautiful thrones for the two rulers to enjoy during the Faire. There were many beautiful costumes at the Banquet, with peasants, lords, ladies, Popes, knights, and entertainers. Some of the wonderful performances included the traditional stick dance and sword fighting with wooden sticks. Even an evil prince was there. There were people dancing in their dresses, suits, and costumes, and jesters to entertain the students. The king and queen wore beautiful costumes that helped make them stand out. Peasants and commoners dance before the court of noble ladies and lords.

articles.text: At the lovely Medieval Banquet before students went outside to take part in the different activities, everyone sat in the Multi-Purpose Room to enjoy a feast of juice and cookies. They did this while watching the different forms of entertainment that the core classes created. Before going to the MPR, people from all grades watched the Maypole dance on the main patio in front of the school. Ms. Brenemann’s class showed everyone their hard work. All the students in her class either held the pole, tossed flowers around, or weaved all the ribbons into an intricate design. The next entertainment was when the king and queen were presented. Two rows of students from Ms. Keenan’s class stood parallel to a red paper carpet as music played. The kids on the sides danced while the king and queen walked down the “carpet.” The king and queen then took their place and sat down wearing their thrones. Before everyone could eat, Mr. Scherman’s class presented a skit called “Don’t Put Your Whole Hand in the Pot.” It showed the seven rules about eating in Medieval times using seven groups and eight narrators. The rules included: clean your nails before eating, don’t pick your nose and then eat, and don’t pick or clean your teeth with a knife. Some other rules were: don’t be the first to reach into the pot, use a napkin or the tablecloth to wipe your hands, don’t put your used bones back in the pot, and take the first piece of food that you touch. The second of the three dances was the circle dance performed by another one of Ms. Brenemann’s classes. The students all started in rows, then formed into groups of four and danced in a circle formation. As the dance went on, this class formed circles of many different sizes and danced in many different ways. The final form of entertainment was the Stick Dance performed by Ms. Kelly’s core class. It was very well practiced and was interesting. The students started in two rows and banged silver sticks on the ground like drums. They rose and fell in unison, and the sounds as well as the visual represented how amazing the dance was. The dance also included scenes of sword fighting with each person changing partners several times.

articles.text: Photos by Rob Peterson Piedmont players celebrate after defeating Bishop O’Dowd for the first time in 30 years. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team accomplished something they haven’t achieved in nearly three decades. On Tuesday, September 26, they beat Bishop O’Dowd 3-2 in a five-set donnybrook played before a home court crowd at Binks Rawlings Gym. The final scores reflect how close the match was: 25-23, 25-21, 23-25, 18-25, 19-17. It was the first time a Piedmont volleyball team has beaten the Dragons in the Western Alameda County Conference’s 12-year history, and most likely was the first victory in 30 years/ “We’ve been working on staying consistent and starting fast. We came out and won the first two sets but it was a complete reset dropping the third and fourth, so it was 0-0. We try to compartmentalize and take games in five-point stretches,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. It was a record game for outside hitter Sadie Town, recording 28 kills – a huge number. It marks the most spikes in single game for a Piedmont player since Samantha Fanger recorded 24 against San Leandro in 2017. The performance puts Town among the school’s best players in the last decade. It was also an impressive performance by Bauer Peterson, a setter, but among the team’s most consistent servers. She finished with four against the Dragons and Elena Stevens had a critical block in the fifth set to enable Piedmont’s win over O’Dowd. kept O’Dowd’s back row off balance throughout the match. This season marks a down year for Bishop O’Dowd, which is currently 8-14 overall and 2-4 in league. This will be the Dragon’s first year to not win the WACC title since joining the league 12 years ago. They went 30-7 last season and were undefeated at 12-0 to win the league title. The Highlanders jumped out to a strong 9-4 lead before expanding to 14-7. Bishop O’Dowd eventually powered its way back to the lead late in the set, but the two teams traded points until tied at 23-23. Town put down a thunderous kill to win the first set, 25-23. The Dragons came out strong in the second set and led 10-5 before Piedmont worked their way back into the game, taking the lead at 20-19. With the match at 22-21 Piedmont, Town launched three straight spikes to the floor for the 25-21 win. After conceding the third and fourth sets by scores of 25-23 and 25-18, the two sides entered a 15-point fifth-set tiebreaker. In the fifth set, both teams traded points with multiple lead changes all the way until 15-15, with both teams exchanging points to make it 17-17. That’s when Elena Stevens recorded a monumental block to make it 18-17, followed by Town making the game-winning point on a huge spike. Piedmont’s players rushed the court to celebrate. Final stats: Town had 28 kills and two aces. Mira Sachs had five kills, Peterson had five kills and four aces, Stevens had four kills, Stella Wilks and Jules DeYoung both had two kills, while Maddy Mullin had one.
articles.title: Many heroes in Highlanders historic win over O’Dowd

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ flag football team kept up its wining ways, improving its record to 2-1 with an 18-6 win against the Encinal Jets in Alameda on Thursday, September 28. The jitters and excitement of being a new sport is starting to wear off for the Highlanders, who played with poise and purpose. They expect to be contenders for the inaugural Western Alameda County Conference banner. “We set a goal where we wanted to start strong both offensively and defensively,” said coach Beth Black. “The more we see, the better they are doing. Their eyes are opening and we’re recognizing that it’s not just girls playing football now and it has nothing to do with girls or guys; now they know the game, now we are nuancing things. We’re going for wins,” Piedmont led 12-0 at the half before putting the game away with a touchdown by Melea Hartford with 2:20 left in the game. The game’s first touchdown was scored on a recently installed play, where usual defensive back Dahlia Osman entered as a quarterback, taking the snap for a 55-yard quarterback keeper to the house. “It was a recent switch where I played QB. I saw the open lane and I took it. I saw there were fewer defenders on the right side and decided that’s where I was going before the snap,” explained Osman. It was a big day for the Highlander defense, scoring its first interception and touchdown when Maisy Richardson jumped on a sloppy fourth-down pass deep in Encinal’s half. “The short passes are easier to Staff Photos Piedmont celebrates an interception and touchdown by Maisy Richardson (#4). Also pictured is Ruby Guzdar (#3) and Lana Ivovich (#5). read. I think we could have gotten more pick-sixes on short passes in previous games, so we’ve been practicing on jumping those routes a lot. We’re just trying to be aggressive and get our hands up. That really helped today,” said Richardson. Piedmont’s defense has been solid through three games, showing consistent hand-eye coordination to swiftly grab flags without allowing extra yards. Their ability to make tackles on the first attempt makes a vital difference in preventing first-downs. “Defense gets the flag pulls, we practice it a lot. It’s all about keeping your eyes on the hips. The hips don’t lie!” said Osman with a laugh. “A lot of it has to do with us growing as a team. We’ve been getting a lot closer and that makes each other more comfortable on the field. As a defense, we’ve been meeting up outside of practice and that makes us even closer,” added Richardson. Piedmont looks ahead to its first home game at Humphries Diamond against league foes Berkeley tomorrow, Thursday, October 5 at 4:30 p.m. Game Recap Piedmont scored on its opening possession when Osman broke her 55-yard touchdown run in a 3rd-and-15 situation, springing down the right side all the way to the end zone. She gave Piedmont a 6-0 lead after a failed two-point conversion after less than three minutes on the opening quarter. After forcing a turnover on downs, Piedmont drove down to Encinal’s 12-yard-line before throwing an interception at the Jets’ 1-yard-line. After three incompletions, Encinal daringly went for the conversion at 4th-and-19 despite being backed against their own goal line. That’s when Richardson jumped on the Jets’ pass to walk it into the end zone for a 12-0 lead with 2:30 left in the half. In the second half, Encinal scored on its opening possession with a seven-yard pass. After back-and-forth possessions, PiedDahlia Osman raced 55 yards for a touchdown after entering the game as quarterback in a 3rd-and-15 situation. Malea Hartford scored Piedmont’s final touchdown.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team suffered a pair of surprising one-goal losses to Berkeley and Novato last week. It was a rough week for Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team, losing two games by one-goal each on the road. They lost to Western Alameda County Conference rivals Berkeley 12-11 on Tuesday, September 26. and lost to North Coast Section opponent Novato 7-6 on Monday, October 2. The good news came on September 27 with a 13-9 league win over Newark Memorial. Piedmont held leads in both games with Berkeley and Novato but couldn’t hang on for the wins. Piedmont could see them again at the end-of-season tournaments. articles.text: Now in October, each team is identifying leaders to help propel their programs towards playoffs. Here we take a look at four key athletes this fall: Sam Shelby, football; Sadie Town, volleyball; George Stein, water polo; and Dahlia Osman, flag football. Sam Shelby, Football Sam Shelby, a junior, is putting together quite the season on the gridiron, showing his speed as a track sprinter and soccer winger. He’s totaled 20 receptions for 400 yards and five touchdowns, to go along with nine rushing attempts for 137 yards and two touchdowns. He dominated in Piedmont’s 41-3 win over Encinal on September 15 with five receptions for 139 yards and two touchdowns. He also put up seven catches for 154 yards and two touchdowns in their 46-7 win over Mt. Eden. In the season-opening 33-21 loss to Pierce on August 25, he had with seven receptions for 102 yards and a touchdown. Shelby is set to play against Alameda on Saturday, October 7 after incorrectly being suspended against Arroyo. PHS successfully appealed the ruling with video evidence of no “violent conduct” by Shelby. Sadie Town, Volleyball Sadie Town, a senior, was identified as a leader at the end of last season as the school’s leading outside hitter. She’s taken on the same role this fall, helping lead Piedmont to a 7-9 record thus far, with improvement shown each week. Her recent 28-kill performance against Bishop O’Dowd led Piedmont to one of its only wins over the Dragons in school history. Her achievement was the highest number of spikes in a single game since Samantha Fanger recorded 24 in 2017. It goes down as one of the best offensive performances in team history. Town also had 18 kills against Berkeley, 14 against Head-Royce, and 13 against San Leandro. George Stein, Water Polo George Stein, another senior, is a leader on the water polo team and a three-year starter. He’s emerged as a leading scorer on this year’s team after putting in five goals in a recent 13-9 win over Newark on September 27. He also scored four goals in a 10-9 win over Newark at the Labor Day Bash on September 2. He scored a 3-goal hat trick in a 14-6 loss to Terra Linda and four goals in a 10-2 win over Mission San Jose at the Labor Day Bash. Staff Photos Sam Shelby is a huge part of Piedmont’s football team as a receiver, defensive back, and return specialist. He’s already scored seven touchdowns. Sadie Town may be the most dominant outside hitter Piedmont has had in the last decade. George Stein is emerging as a leading scorer on the water polo team.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team split their four matches at the Battle of the Bay tournament hosted by San Leandro and Encinal the weekend of Friday and Saturday, September 29-30. Piedmont opened with a 14-5 win over Pinole Valley but lost 16-2 to Marin Academy later on Friday. The next day, PHS lost narrowly 11-10 to Livermore and closed with a 12-6 win over El Cerrito. It was an impressive tournament for Kat Melian and Abigail Jacoby who combined for 21 goals in four games. 14-5 over Pinole Valley Piedmont jumped out to a 5-1 lead in the first quarter with goals by Melian, two by Sydney Olson, and two by Anne Reardon. In the second quarter, Reardon got her hat trick with a player-advantage at the 5:21 mark. After a Pinole Valley goal, 6-2, Sonja ten Grotenhuis scored with 3:53 remaining in the half. Esme Krumins made it 8-3 going into halftime for PHS. Piedmont then scored four unanswered goals in the third Kat Melian scored 13 goals in four games. quarter, including three straight by Jacoby and one by Krumins. PHS kept on the heat in the fourth with two more by ten Grotenhuis and Melian, while PV added two in the final minutes. Final stats: Jacoby and Reardon had hat tricks. Melian, Krumins, and Olson scored twice, while ten Grotenhuis and Sage Gilbert had individual scores. 16-2 loss to Marin Academy Marin Academy led 8-1 by the end of the first quarter and both teams went scoreless in the secAbigail Jacoby (2) had eight goals in the Battle of the Bay. Esme Krumins (11) looks for a pass. ond. The Wildcats made it 11-2 in the third quarter and added five goals in the final going. Final stats: Melian and Abigail Jacoby scored goals. Livermore pulls out 11-10 win Both teams ended the first quarter in a 2-2 tie and traded goals in the second quarter with Livermore leading 7-5 by halftime. Both teams scored twice in the third quarter to make it 9-7 Livermore starting the fourth, Melian had six of Piedmont’s goals at this point. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont trailed 10-7 after conceding a goal with 4:43 to go. From there, Reardon scored with 2:30 left. A big defensive stop led to Jacoby scoring to close the gap to 10-9. Both teams traded possessions until Livermore added an insurance goal with 1:02 remaining. Piedmont couldn’t get on the board again until Reardon sent one in with nine seconds left. Final stats: Melian had six goals, Reardon had two, Jacoby and Krumins had one. Big 12-6 win vs. El Cerrito Piedmont quickly jumped out to a 6-0 lead in the first quarter and extended to 9-1 by halftime. In the third quarter, PHS added three goals and conceded three, while El Cerrito scored twice in the fourth. Final stats: Melian scored four goals. Jacoby had three goals. Reardon and Vivian Burke scored twice. Gilbert scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-8 overall, 1-2 league) travel to Encinal on Wednesday, October 11 at 4:45 p.m. They also play the following day, October 12, hosting Alameda at Laney College at 5:00 p.m.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 4, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Fall colors at Mt. Tamalpais’ Dawn Falls Trail By Jonathan Comeaux Mt. Tamalpais has well over 100 miles of trails to hike; from the steep and strenuous, to the relaxed and nature focused. For this venture, we walk 1.5 miles on the Dawn Falls Trail to the Southern Marin Line Fire Road until reaching the Barbara Springs Trail and back to the car, making an easy but stunning 3.5- mile hike. The Dawn Falls Trail is a short and popular 1.4 mile walk with over 510 feet in elevation gain to Staff Photos A narrow corridor of redwood trees lines the Dawn Falls Trail on Mt. Tamalpais. The Dawn Falls Trail leads to the main attraction, Dawn Falls, which is active only after a heavy rain. its main attraction, Dawn Falls. Although the “Falls” is more of a trickle given that it is active only after a heavy rain, the walk shows you what makes Mt. Tam so magnificent. At times, you will pass through narrow corridors of redwood trees that appear to be out of a fairytale. Starting at the Dawn Falls Trailhead on Madrone Avenue in Larkspur, the trail along the inactive Larkspur Creek is a palette of vibrant fall colors from maple leaves; redwoods tower over in every direction, while lush green moss covers every tree, stone, and branch. It is worth mentioning that the Dawn Falls Trail is a mostly a slim passage, generally less than three feet wide. Patience is required when passing by hikers, runners, and large groups on weekends. Our 10 a.m. walk up to the falls passed a staggering 49 people in the 1.5 miles, passing another 34 people in the remaining two miles back to the car – making 83 people passed in total, so near 24 other patrons per mile. For those conscious of personal space, continue on the Southern Marin Line Fire Road; a dirt road which is wide enough to adequate two lanes of cars. Otherwise, you can continue up the Hoo Koo E Koo Trail and Blithedale Ridge trails, which will more than double your elevation gain to provide a workout of near 1,200 feet until re-intersecting with the fire road. You’ll get glimpses of Mt. Tam’s eastern peak from the fire road, a location we last visited over the summer. The 0.5 mile walk down the Barbara Springs Trail back to the car is a very steep 500- foot descent back with tree roots shooting out in every direction – so be wary. You’ll likely have to use your hands at various points. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on November 25, 2020. articles.text: Smuin Ballet’s Dance Series One will be performed in San Francisco on October 7. San Francisco-based dance company Smuin Ballet will close its Dance Series One at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco’s Fort Mason this Saturday, October 7. Tickets are still available for performances Thursday through Saturday. The program includes The Man in Black by James Kudelka, Tutto Eccetto il Lavandino (Everything but the Kitchen Sink) by Val Caniparoli, and the world premiere of Salsa ’til Dawn by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The performance opens with longtime Smuin collaborator Caniparoli’s Tutto Eccetto il Lavandino. It is a playful, energetic piece that premiered in 2014 and has been an audience favorite since. Kudelka’s The Man in Black is a ballad-style piece with choreography set to songs recorded by Johnny Cash, a country singer-songwriter whose music often contained themes of sorrow, moral tribulation and redemption. The dance celebrates working-class grit, and includes American country dance styles like line dancing, square, swing and step. The ballet premiered in 2010. The upcoming performance also features the world premiere of Moultrie’s Salsa ’til Dawn, with music by Charles Fox. Composer Fox collaborated with company founder Michael Smuin on two ballets, A Song for Dead Warriors, commissioned for the San Francisco Ballet, and Zorro!. His entire output of music is soon to be recognized at the Library of Congress. “Music is always the complete inspiration for me,” said Moultrie. “It’s been such an honor to work with an artistic giant like Charles [Fox} and bring his music to life by marrying it with the physicality of dance.” Visit https://www.smuinballet. org/events/dance-series-one-30/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Tickets available for Dance Series One October 5 - 7

articles.text: The Marcus Shelby Orchestra will perform for SF Jazz’s yearly tribute to Thelonious Monk on Tuesday, October 10. The special event is dubbed “San Francisco Holiday,” which references Monk’s classic 1960 composition. The evening’s program includes Monk compositions performed by Shelby, trumpeter and composer Erik Jekabson, and young trumpeter Skylar Tang, who recently became a member of the SF Jazz High School All-Stars. Bassist, composer, and arranger Shelby will be backed by his award-winning orchestra, which he modeled after the Duke Ellington Orchestra. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s POTUS: Or, Behind Every Great Dumbass are Seven Women Trying to Keep Him Alive is being performed on stage now through October 22. The comedic take on White House events is a feminist-focused satire, premiering in time for presidential primaries. When the president unknowingly spins a public relations nightmare into a global crisis, seven brilliant but beleaguered women must risk it all to keep the commander-in-chief out of trouble. The play features Harriet Deirdre Lovejoy as chief of staff, Kim Blanck as press secretary, Susan Lynskey as secretary, Stephanie Pope Lofgren as the first lady, Dominique Toney as a journalist, Stephanie Styles as the president’s dalliance and Allison Guinn as his sister. POTUS is written by Selina Fillinger and directed by Annie Tippe. Post-show discussions are held tomorrow, October 5, and on October 10, guided by members of Berkeley Rep’s artistic team. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/potus/. Photo by Kevin Berne Stephanie Pope Lofgren (Margaret) and Susan Lynskey (Stephanie) appear in Berkeley Rep’s production of POTUS.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s POTUS playing through Oct. 22

articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas, the longtime Music Director of San Francisco Symphony, returns from retirement to lead the symphony in performances of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 on Thursday, October 19, and Saturday and Sunday, October 21 and 22. The program includes Olly Wilson’s Shango Memory. Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125, is a choral symphony, completed between 1822 and 1824 and first performed in Vienna on May 7, 1824. Many critics and musicologists regard it as a masterpiece of Western classical music and is one of the best-known symphonic works in music. It is the most frequently performed symphonic work in the world. The concert will include Olly Wilson’s Shango Memory, a modern piece that serves as a tribute to a Nigerian deity and the cultural contributions of the African diaspora. Vocal soloists include soprano Angel Blue, mezzo-soprano Tamara Mumford, tenor Ben Bliss and bass Dashon Burton. Performances on October 19 and 21 begin at 7:30 p.m., with a 2 p.m. matinee on Sunday, October 22. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2023-24/MTT-Beethoven9 or call the box office at (415) 864-6000.
articles.title: MTT to conduct SF Symphony in Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony
