articles.text: Berkeley Symphony, led by Music Director Joseph Young, will open the 2023-24 Symphonic Series with American Kaleidoscope on Sunday, October 15 at 4 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall. The first of four Symphonic Series performances, American Kaleidoscope will showcase the Marcus Roberts Trio’s virtuosic style in a jazz-infused performance of James P. Johnson’s Yamekraw: A Negro Rhapsody, in addition to George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. Audiences will also experience the rare harmonies of Samuel Barber’s Essay for Orchestra No. 2 and Peter S. Shin’s introspective score Relapse. “We open this season with a celebration of the American sound, showcasing the intersection of different musical styles and the richness of our country’s culture,” said Music Director Joseph Young, “Samuel Barber’s powerful second essay is unapologetic and a tour-de-force piece that highlights the neoclassical American style, while Berkeley’s own Peter S. Shin brings a new contemporary work to our stage. I’m excited to welcome the Marcus Roberts Trio as we pair the music of two important American composers: George Gershwin, whose work is widely recognized, and James P. Johnson, a composer hardly heard in orchestral music. This program is an exciting way for Berkeley Symphony to begin its season, inviting audiences to gain a deeper understanding of American orchestral jazz.” The Marcus Roberts Trio is a long-term musical partnership between pianist Marcus Roberts, the phenomenal drummer Jason Marsalis, and gifted bassist Rodney Jordan. While most jazz trios feature piano, the Marcus Roberts Trio has an entirely new approach to jazz with all members equally shaping the direction of the music. Berkeley Symphony’s upcoming season of chamber music concerts at Piedmont Center for the Arts takes a closer look at the American sound, by zooming in on the Golden State. Taking place on Sunday, November 19 at 4 p.m., California Connections will feature Gabriela Lena Frank’s Kanto Kechua #2, Ben Shirley’s High Sierra Sonata, Anaís Azul’s Cascades and Canyons, Gabriella Smith’s Carrot Revolution, and selections from John Adams’ Book of Alleged Dances. The performance will highlight California and the Bay Area’s talented composers featuring Gabriela Lena Frank and John Adams as major influences. Subscriptions to Berkeley Symphony’s Symphonic Series and the Chamber Series are available now. Patrons can choose 3 or 4 concerts in Berkeley Symphony’s Symphonic Series and create a custom Pick 3 or Pick 4 Package, saving up to 25% off regular ticket prices. Single tickets are available now at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510.841.2800. Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus is the home of Berkeley Symphony.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony opens season on October 15

articles.text: (See additional photos on pages 16 & 17.) The. Piedmont Center for the Arts was abuzz with friendly voices during the Art Walk’s Artist Reception. On Friday, September 29, artists with work on display at the Art Walk were invited to spend an evening socializing with other artists and art fans while enjoying hors d’oeuvres and refreshments. “I think it is very friendly,” smiled Raffi Zaroukian. “People are very supportive here. Piedmont is a community where people really look out for each other. It’s an art gathering without the high-nose thing, but the quality is still there.” Zaroukian was also smiling because his painting, Cudillero Fishing Village, Spain, sold for $395 – two days before the actual Art Walk. Despite the feelings of familiarity and camaraderie, this was the first time the Art Walk has hosted an exhibit at the Center for the Arts. Larraine Seiden, a founder of the Piedmont Art Walk, says that when they Cudillero Fishing Village, Spain, by Raffi Zaroukian, digital hand painting, Giclee Print on Metal, 30” x 20” started, a reception like this just wasn’t possible. “I started the Art Walk with Jon in June 2020 and it had to be very dispersed [due to COVID],” said Seiden. “We worked with the Piedmont Police Department to make sure it was okay under the regulations at the time, but I think we always envisioned having an artist reception because the artists never got to meet each other.” she added. “It’s something that we always felt was lacking in the event.” In a final thought, Zaroukian added that he thinks it is important to socialize with other artists. “Otherwise we will be pigeonholed in our own world. We all have our own ideas, but it’s great to see other mediums, other thoughts, and other ways of doing things. It’s inspirational.” Regina O’Connor (left) speaks to artist Larraine Seiden at the artist reception at the Center for the Arts.
articles.title: A first of its kind exhibit, reception provides celebration of artists

articles.text: James Franco as Aaron Ralston in 127 Hours 127 Hours opens on an early April morning, 2003, well before sunlight. Aaron Ralston (James Franco), a 27-year-old engineer, packs light gear in a daypack intending to spend the day in the Blue John Canyon area, exploring some of Utah’s most breathtaking country. He drives to a trailhead, of sorts, and heads off on his mountain bike, pushing hard, exhilarated by the day and the breadth of the scenery and the cerulean sky overhead. Leaving the bike chained to a tree, he continues on foot, wearing only his pack containing a bottle of water, a little food, climbing rope, straps and carabiners. He meets two young women, Kristi (Kate Mara) and Megan (Amber Tamblyn). They spend time swimming in a stunningly beautiful, aqua blue underground pool before Aaron continues, again alone. He is experienced, familiar with the terrain, and fearless as he runs and jumps across open crevices and down cinnamon colored arroyos. While traversing a benignlooking crevice, he loses his footing and slides down a sheer wall with a sizable boulder behind him. He lands hard, as does the rock, which wedges his right arm tight against the side of the crevice. In a heartbeat, his circumstances change. What was a carefree, insouciant day is suddenly transformed into an existential crisis. He’s in real trouble. What happens next is chronicled in Ralston’s book, “The Rock and the Hard Place,” telling about his 127-hour ordeal, trapped with no good way to free himself. His only possible return to freedom is a passable multipurpose utility tool, his climbing gear, and one bottle of water. He had left the oranges and Gatorade in his car. It is an improbable story in a container movie in which a person is trapped in a confined space (an airplane, a deep cave, a panic room, etc.) and must find a way to survive. Hours pass and soon Ralston will run out of water and food and he will die, while hallucinating about family and his girlfriend, Rana (Clemence Poesy). He knows that he has cavalierly taken the day trip without telling anyone where he is going. His supplies are meager. No cell phone, no emergency equipment. He is completely alone and without hope. Danny Boyle (Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire, 28 Days), working with two cinematographers, Enrique Chediak and Anthony Dod Mantle, manages to create a compelling film, one that is intense and in its own way grimly surprising. As well, James Franco delivers a wonderful portrayal of Ralston as he struggles, courageously, to survive. The movie is gripping from first to last. 127 Hours. Directed by Danny Boyle. Starring James Franco, Amber Tamblyn, Kate Mara and Clemence Poesy. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released in 2011, Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Grab the youngsters and sit them down to see African Cats, a Disneynature production. The story, narrated by Samuel L. Jackson, is nicely told, and since this is Disney, the stars of the film are anthropomorphized, with names such as Sita, Layla, Fang and Mara. All are endowed with human characteristics, to include thought. In one scene a cub lion, Mara, looks at her father, Fang, and thinks, “He’s the best dad in the world.” But then Disney has been humanizing animals in animation, as well as documentaries, for decades. They know how to capture children’s attention while exposing them to greater themes. Set on an immense savanna in East Africa, the tale follows two families: a pride of lions and a single mother cheetah and her cubs. The lions are also raising cubs, a task that Fang, the alpha male, takes no part in. Just as he doesn’t hunt; he only shows up to dine, say, on the zebra du jour. What makes African Cats compelling, especially for young audiences, is the remarkable work of cinematographers Owen Newman and Sophie Darlington. Filmed in high definition, many of the tight shots – a lion’s paw, a mother licking and nurturing her cub, a male lion confronting an alligator – inherently pose the question: how was it done, so close and intimate? It’s astonishing footage. As well, the aerial shots of massive herds of wildebeests migrating across the savanna are breathtaking, these ungainly animals plunging up draws and across the river, driven by an instinct that is incomprehensible. There is also one scene when the clouds turn dark and cold, lightening splits the sky, and slanting rain falls. Sita and her cubs sit waiting, shivering from the wet, as do all of the animals of the savanna. This moment is contrasted with the magnificent sunrises and sunsets that fill the horizons of these plains. Yet all is framed by the reality that the animals of the savanna face a harsh existence, focused daily on survival. At no time does the documentary’s voice over become pedantic, drifting into explanations about the shrinking habitat of these animals. If the migration route of the wildebeest is altered or truncated, for example, the ripple effect for other animals, such as the big cats of Africa, is significant. For now, however, as the credits roll, all is good. African Cats. Disneynature documentary. Directed by Alastair Fothergill and Keith Scholey. Photographed by Owen Newman and Sophie Darlington. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. T TH HE E

articles.text: Alexander Valley is an area north of Napa Valley that that is not as well known as Napa but that also has an ideal climate for growing grapes and making wine. Soda Rock Winery is an historic property built in 1869 that was once the site of the Alexander Valley general store and post office and was the central hub of activity for the valley. The first winery on the site was bonded in 1880 and operated for many years before being abandoned. In 2000 Ken and Diane Wilson of Wilson Family Wines purchased the property and set about the arduous task of restoring the landmark property which had fallen into serious disrepair. The restoration was eventually completed and the winery was brought back to life. The location also serves as a popular event space for weddings and other social gatherings as the site regains its place as the hub of activity for the valley. In 2019 disaster struck and the Kincaid fire burned the winery to the ground. Once again, the Wilsons have set about restoring the property, with work still underway. Miraculously an old wooden structure next to the winery called “The Barn” survived the fire and now serves as the tasting room for Soda Rock Wines. They also have a tasting room in downtown Healdsburg. I recently had the opportunity to visit The Barn for a comprehensive tasting of the Soda Rock wines. I was hosted by the garrulous Jim Ferguson from Wilson Wines who has spent a lifetime in the wine industry and has an astoundingly comprehensive knowledge of California wines. Like the other Wilson wineries, I have visited and written about – Mazzoco, Pezzi King, Jaxon Keys, and Wilson – the wines from Soda Rock were uniformly well made and had a great quality/price ratio. The winemaker is the talented Antoine Favero who also makes wines at Mazocco and Jaxon Keys. Listed below are gems of Alexander Valley, with some amusing names. All are well worth searching out. Jim Ferguson, the grand ambassador of Wilson Wines Outdoor tasting at Soda Rock Winery

articles.text: If you have a loved one showing signs of Alzheimer’s or another form of dementia, you’ll obviously experience some strong emotions — and you’ll likely ask yourself this question: What can I do to help? While there are certainly many ways you could provide assistance over time, there’s one area that might require your immediate attention: finances. Alzheimer’s patients often exhibit a range of money-related problems. Here are some of the most common ones, according to the National Institute on Aging: • Trouble counting change or paying for a purchase • Difficulty in balancing a checkbook • Confusion over bank statements • Not paying — or even opening — bills • Making strange and unnecessary purchases with a credit card Of course, your awareness of these problems depends, to a great extent, on just how familiar you are with the daily life of your loved one with Alzheimer’s or similar dementia. But if you have noticed these issues, it may be time for you to act before things get worse — and they can get worse, because scam artists constantly target the elderly by making false promises, soliciting personal data, asking for money and even requesting changes in estate-planning documents. So, what steps can you take? You’ll need to clearly communicate your concerns to your afflicted loved one, and you’ll have to get their consent for the actions you wish to take on their behalf. This may not be easy, but it’s certainly worth the effort. Here are a few moves to consider: • Set up auto-pay. If your loved one has still been paying bills manually, now may be a good time to set up auto-pay for utilities, loans and other bills. • Open a joint checking account. account with your loved one, or perhaps adding your name to an existing account, you can help ensure all payments are accurate and appropriate. • Freeze credit reports. By freezing your loved one’s credit reports at the credit reporting bureaus — Equifax, TransUnion and Experian — you can prevent bogus credit lines from being opened in their name. • Create a durable power of

articles.text: • These cookies are super soft – mini cakes really. They’re like that tender, fluffy top of a cupcake that’s the best, first bite. If you’re a fan of soft cookies, try these for this pumpkin-spice season. This recipe comes together quickly. You mix everything by hand in just a few minutes and likely have most of the ingredients in your pantry. (If you don’t stock up on canned pumpkin, I highly recommend having a few on hand as they are hard to find in the off season.) I am partial to letting cookie dough rest in the ‘fridge overnight before baking. The flour has time to absorb the moist ingredients. In this case the overnight rest gives time for the spices to develop fuller flavor. It also firms up the dough, making for easier scooping. Note: This recipe uses one cup of canned pumpkin, leaving a bit more than one-half cup from the can. Do not discard it. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/ Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Help protect finances of loved one with Alzheimer’s If you have a loved one showing signs of Alzheimer’s or another form of dementia, you’ll obviously experience some strong emotions — and you’ll likely ask yourself this question: What can I do to help? While there are certainly many ways you could provide assistance over time, there’s one area that might require your immediate attention: finances. Alzheimer’s patients often exhibit a range of money-related problems. Here are some of the most common ones, according to the National Institute on Aging: • Trouble counting change or paying for a purchase • Difficulty in balancing a checkbook • Confusion over bank statements • Not paying — or even opening — bills • Making strange and unnecessary purchases with a credit card Of course, your awareness of these problems depends, to a great extent, on just how familiar you are with the daily life of your loved one with Alzheimer’s or similar dementia. But if you have noticed these issues, it may be time for you to act before things get worse — and they can get worse, because scam artists constantly target the elderly by making false promises, soliciting personal data, asking for money and even requesting changes in estate-planning documents. So, what steps can you take? You’ll need to clearly communicate your concerns to your afflicted loved one, and you’ll have to get their consent for the actions you wish to take on their behalf. This may not be easy, but it’s certainly worth the effort. Here are a few moves to consider: • Set up auto-pay. If your loved one has still been paying bills manually, now may be a good time to set up auto-pay for utilities, loans and other bills. • Open a joint checking account. By opening a joint checking account with your loved one, or perhaps adding your name to an existing account, you can help ensure all payments are accurate and appropriate. • Freeze credit reports. By freezing your loved one’s credit reports at the credit reporting bureaus — Equifax, TransUnion and Experian — you can prevent bogus credit lines from being opened in their name. • Create a durable power of attorney. In the early stages of Alzheimer’s or dementia, your loved one could create a durable power of attorney and name you, or another close family member, as the “agent” — which means you’d be empowered to make financial and other decisions when your loved one is no longer capable of doing so. (A durable power of attorney could also be created in cases of advanced Alzheimer’s, but it can be somewhat more challenging.) • Help establish a living trust. In addition to a durable power of attorney, a living trust can be valuable for families of Alzheimer’s patients. A living trust can hold a person’s financial assets and other property while the trustee manages the money and makes investment and spending decisions. A living trust can be complex, so before establishing one, you’ll need to consult with your legal and tax professionals. When you’re dealing with the financial issues associated with your loved one’s Alzheimer’s or dementia, it can feel like you’re on a long road. But diligently seeking out the appropriate financial moves can help make the journey less stressful — for everyone involved. articles.text: Hugh Smith, a lifelong Piedmont resident, passed away in the early hours of August 16, 2023 after a year-long battle with a heart condition. Born Hugh Langmuir Smith on December 10, 1953 in Oakland, he was raised by his parents in Piedmont. Growing up he became very involved in the Boy Scouts and earned the honor of Eagle Scout with Troop 11. One of Hugh’s more memorable experiences was traveling to Japan for the World Jamboree in 1971, where he weathered out a typhoon in a tent with his troopmates. It was in high school when he and his wife Victoria met and dated for the first time. After graduating from high school, Hugh took a three-month backpacking trip with friends through Europe, which sparked his lifelong love of travel. He went on to earn his Bachelor of Science in Business Administration from Cal State Hayward. Hugh’s business savvy led him into management at multiple Bay Area stores, as well as his own entrepreneurial ventures like the Left Hand Supply Company and a travel agency. He and his wife Victoria owned and operated AVB Travel for 25 years. Hugh came to specialize in cruises, and was affectionately known as the ‘Cruise Dude’ by many. He was proud to have visited all seven continents, stepping foot on the final one, Australia at the start of 2020. Hugh was married to his beloved Victoria for 40 years. In that time, the two returned to Piedmont, raised their two daughters, traveled the world, and often got the family together for holidays and barbecues. He was a kind and supportive father. articles.text: Pamela Wells Rafanelli, a resident of Piedmont for nearly 50 years, passed away peacefully on August 27 in Carnelian Bay, California. Born Pamela Wells on July 24, 1946 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Walter M. Wells, Jr. and Mary Louise Wells. She spent her youth in Corte Madera and Santa Rosa. She and her brother, Steve Wells, were very close and treasured their family camping and fishing adventures. Pam graduated from the University of California, Berkeley with a degree in History and French. Her passion for learning history and languages through books, museums, and travel continued her entire life. She began her life-long teaching career in Cupertino before moving to Piedmont in 1973. During the early years of teaching, she earned a Master’s degree in education, specializing in early childhood learning differences. She was a beloved teacher to generations of students who attended Havens or Beach School during the 39 years in which she taught in Piedmont School District, with a particular love for teaching second grade. In addition to being a dedicated teacher, Pam raised four daughters, participated in multiple book clubs, hiked and cycled across California, volunteered at the Oakland Museum of California, and traveled the world. This past May, Pam took Paris by storm as she participated in an art history trip, climbed to the top of the Arc de Triomphe, and walked miles each day to revisit some of her favorite museums and sites. One of Pam’s favorite places in the world was Lake Tahoe. Her lakeside home offered her a stunning view of the lake and mountains and allowed her to sip her morning mug of coffee from a kayak in the waters of Carnelian Bay. Pam was an incredible baker and cook. She made ravioli from scratch for family reunions, baked baguettes for family dinners, and created desserts for every get-together. She knew to bake twice as many holiday cookies as were needed, since half disappeared during the family decorating process. Pam’s greatest joy came from spending time with any (or all!) of her 13 grandchildren. She loved to be with family – whether for holidays, birthdays, school “grandparent day” events, or for no special occasion at all. Pam is predeceased by her parents, her brother, Steve, and her former spouse, Mark. Pam is survived by her daughters Stephanie and son-in-law Andrew Backer and their three children, Tucke, Oliver, and Emma; daughter Sarah and son-in-law Wyeth Goodenough and their three children, Sadie, Reese, and Ellis; daughter Gina and son-inlaw Jason Flynn and their four children, Scottie, Sofia, Mark, and Luke; and daughter Katie and son-in-law Colin Mistele and their three children, Olivia, Drew, and Grace. In keeping with Pam’s wishes, there will be no public memorial service. To celebrate Pam’s life and her passion for teaching and education, her daughters will make meaningful gifts to Beach Elementary School and the Oakland Museum of California in her name. Pam Rafanelli, who died on August 27, is shown with her four daughters, Stephanie (left), Katie, Gina, and Sarah.

articles.text: On a beautiful Fall day, a strong turnout of 50 walkers and two K-9 best friends showed up for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays on September 27. A recent article in the Post by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi on Wallace Alexander provided an inspiration for the day’s walk. The walkers were asked what historical figures they could think of who have Piedmont streets or buildings named after them. Frank C. Havens, Walter Blair, Hugh Craig, and even Isaac Requa came to mind; but Wallace Alexander was not named. Though he made many significant contributions to Piedmont, there is no public recognition of him. Drawing on Gail’s article, titled “Wallace M. Alexander - Piedmont’s Philanthropist,” the group learned about Alexander and his contributions. In 1912 he was instrumental in the construction of Piedmont’s first commercial center, today’s location of Wells Fargo Bank. In 1916 he arranged for the purchase of land for the Piedmont Interdenominational Church, now the Piedmont Community Church. Next, he organized the purchase in 1921 of land from the widow of Frank C. Havens for the construction of Piedmont High School. Additionally, Alexander helped establish and support the Piedmont Boy Scout Council in 1921. The walkers wanted to see some of Alexander’s legacy. They went past the former Piedmont commercial center, then across Highland Way to the Piedmont Scout Council office and the Community Church. They went up Mountain Avenue, but when they got to Bellevue, they were shocked to see that the giant sequoia at the traffic circle at Mountain and Bellevue Avenues was no longer there. For several years the City had the tree on a health watch list. It had gotten worse and arborists recommended removal before it fell over. The walkers followed Sea View to the northern edge of Alexander’s former estate, which ran from 87 Sea View to Hampton Road. More of Alexander’s history was shared. He was born in Maui in 1869, where his family was a leader in the Hawaiian sugar industry. They moved to the Bay Area so that Wallace could attend school in Oakland. He married his Oakland High School classmate, Mary Baker, in 1904, and they chose a large site on the corner of Sea View and Hampton, which was then called Union Street, for their home. The Alexanders built a threestory mansion that they named “Brown Gables” for its large, brown painted dormers. There was also a carriage house, which is now the home at 84 King Avenue. In 1911 Alexander’s mother built her own home at 92 Sea View across the street from Brown Gables, and his wife’s mother built a home further down the street at 236 Sea View. These homes are still there, but Brown Gables no longer exists. After Alexander died from a stroke in 1939, his wife followed his wish that the mansion be torn down, and the land subdivided into 13 lots so that more families could live in Piedmont. The walkers continued on to 92 Sea View, a 15,650-squarefoot home. An interesting reminder of the Alexanders is seen in inlays in the sidewalk that spell the word “Kailani.” the name of the Alexander family home in Hawaii. The walkers then crossed Hampton to see the home of Mary’s mother at 236 Sea View, which is now for sale. For $7,950,000 this 6,966-square-foot piece of history can be yours. The group then went on Farragut Avenue to King Avenue to see the Alexanders’ former carriage house at 84 King, currently being extensively remodeled. Across the street is Crocker Park, the land which Alexander donated to the City. The walkers continued up to Lincoln Avenue and back to the city center with a better understanding of Wallace Alexander’s service to Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Walkers learn more about Wallace Alexander By Dick Carter On a beautiful Fall day, a strong turnout of 50 walkers and two K-9 best friends showed up for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays on September 27. A recent article in the Post by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi on Wallace Alexander provided an inspiration for the day’s walk. The walkers were asked what historical figures they could think of who have Piedmont streets or buildings named after them. Frank C. Havens, Walter Blair, Hugh Craig, and even Isaac Requa came to mind; but Wallace Alexander was not named. Though he made many significant contributions to Piedmont, there is no public recognition of him. Drawing on Gail’s article, titled “Wallace M. Alexander - Piedmont’s Philanthropist,” the group learned about Alexander and his contributions. In 1912 he was instrumental in the construction of Piedmont’s first commercial center, today’s location of Wells Fargo Bank. In 1916 he arranged for the purchase of land for the Piedmont Interdenominational Church, now the Piedmont Community Church. Next, he organized the purchase in 1921 of land from the widow of Frank C. Havens for the construction of Piedmont High School. Additionally, Alexander helped establish and support the Piedmont Boy Scout Council in 1921. The walkers wanted to see some of Alexander’s legacy. They went past the former Piedmont commercial center, then across Highland Way to the Piedmont Scout Council office and the Community Church. They went up Mountain Avenue, but when they got to Bellevue, they were shocked to see that the giant sequoia at the traffic circle at Mountain and Bellevue Avenues was no longer there. For several years the City had the tree on a health watch list. It had gotten worse and arborists recommended removal before it fell over. The walkers followed Sea View to the northern edge of Alexander’s former estate, which ran from 87 Sea View to Hampton Road. More of Alexander’s history was shared. He was born in Maui in 1869, where his family was a leader in the Hawaiian sugar industry. They moved to the Bay Area so that Wallace could attend school in Oakland. He married his Oakland High School classmate, Mary Baker, in 1904, and they chose a large site on the corner of Sea View and Hampton, which was then called Union Street, for their home. The Alexanders built a threestory mansion that they named “Brown Gables” for its large, brown painted dormers. There was also a carriage house, which is now the home at 84 King Avenue. In 1911 Alexander’s mother built her own home at 92 Sea View across the street from Brown Gables, and his wife’s mother built a home further down the street at 236 Sea View. These homes are still there, but Brown Gables no longer exists. After Alexander died from a stroke in 1939, his wife followed his wish that the mansion be torn down, and the land subdivided into 13 lots so that more families could live in Piedmont. The walkers continued on to 92 Sea View, a 15,650-squarefoot home. An interesting reminder of the Alexanders is seen in inlays in the sidewalk that spell the word “Kailani.” the name of the Alexander family home in Hawaii. The walkers then crossed Hampton to see the home of Mary’s mother at 236 Sea View, which is now for sale. For $7,950,000 this 6,966-square-foot piece of history can be yours. The group then went on Farragut Avenue to King Avenue to see the Alexanders’ former carriage house at 84 King, currently being extensively remodeled. Across the street is Crocker Park, the land which Alexander donated to the City. The walkers continued up to Lincoln Avenue and back to the city center with a better understanding of Wallace Alexander’s service to Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: On Friday, September 22, Piedmont bid farewell to a historic sequoia tree at the corner of Bellevue and Mountain Avenues. The City of Piedmont made the decision to remove the tree upon the recommendation of arborists hired by the city. Originally planted in 1890, the arborists determined that the tree had a significant lean and posed a safety risk for nearby homes. “It’s always painful to remove a prominent tree,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “These trees have a history in the community.” The sequoia was the city’s official Christmas tree throughout the 1930s up until the beginning of World War II. Every year, the tree was decorated with lights and tinsel in anticipation of the holidays. The Public Works Department notified more than 80 of the homes closest to the tree to give residents time to say their goodbyes, but “there’s not a lot of time when arborists say they have to move on it quickly,” Gonzales said. “When the report came back this time, it said we should ‘look to remove it immediately.’ We don’t usually get that.” The sequoia has been in PiedStanding next to the sequoia tree in 1936 is Ah Foo who originally planted the tree. The sequoia tree had a significant lean which arborists determined was a risk to nearby homes. mont since 1890, making it 133 years old at the time of removal. The tree was planted by Ah Foo, an immigrant from China, who worked for a family on Bellevue and thought his employers’ orchard could use some beautification. The sapling he placed in that orchard grew into a large, healthy sequoia. When it came time to subdivide what was then the Bellevue district, the City thought that Foo’s tree was too beautiful to cut down. So, the City built around it and the tree settled into the position it would take for the next 100 years. Cameron Wolfe with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) shared Gonzales’ somber assessment of the situation but admits that the tree’s removal was inevitable. “It was only a matter of time before it was going to have to come down,” said Wolfe. “Thank goodness they got it before any damage was done. You could see from the way it was leaning that it could have fallen and done immense damage to some beautiful pieces of property.” Wolfe went on to say that sequoia gigantea — as the tree is scientifically known — more typically grow at elevations of 5,000 feet or higher as opposed to Piedmont’s 300 feet. The tree’s unique position in the middle of a rotunda at a street intersection meant very little water could get to it. In other words, the sequoia wasn’t thriving where it was planted. “The good news is that we got every ounce of enjoyment that tree could give us. It was such a long-living tree in such dire circumstances… So, it was a valiant tree, let’s put it that way,” explained Wolfe. “It’s going to be fun to see what comes in its place. I’m sure it will not be a sequoia because that would be inviting a repeat of a sad story. And I’m sure it won’t be a Cypress, but I think there’ll be a consensus and I’m actually excited to see what happens to that location.” A contractor begins removal of the historic sequoia tree at Bellevue & Mountain Avenues. After removal, the stump of the once-towering sequoia gigantea sits within its’ traffic circle.

When asked for his opinion on District Attorney Pamela Price’s effect on recent crime rates, Bowers said the matter was not the most important to the meeting’s discussion. “What I would say about the district attorney is a change could come tomorrow with the district attorney and not a whole lot would change right now. I think we need all components of the system to be working and there were several things that weren’t quite working before the current DA came into office.” “I’m not going to sit here and say that I agree with the district attorney’s policies,” Bowers continued. “But just focusing on that one problem is insufficient to deal with what we need to deal with.” Bowers cited high crime rates as a result of prolific, younger “crews” of criminals who are committing crimes for status among their peers instead of financial gain. articles.text: Photo by Jeff Hansen Police blocked off part of Grand Avenue after two people were arrested for attempted car theft. “Hey, someone’s breaking into your car,” whispered a coworker to Adele Pease. Tuesday, October 3 at around 2 p.m. marked the second time this month someone had broken into her car. It was even on the same street as last time. When she arrived at her car, her window was smashed in and the wires under her steering wheel were ripped out. Someone had tried to hotwire her car. That’s when she saw two figures sprinting in opposite directions on Boulevard Way near the corner of Grand Avenue. “At that point, a man came up [to me] and said that he had called 911,” said Pease. “That’s when all the police started coming,” added an eyewitness who has asked to remain anonymous. “Undercover police cars came out of nowhere chasing someone into Piedmont,” the witness added. “You wouldn’t have even known they were undercover [police] until their lights started flashing.” The suspects allegedly hid between houses in the area after Staff photo Piedmont and Oakland police officers on Grand Avenue gather to take statements after an attempted car theft. their theft attempt before running away. Piedmont and Oakland police arrived within minutes and both suspects were apprehended. Both suspects were juveniles wearing black hooded sweatshirts with camouflage bandanas covering the lower half of their faces. “We’re just grateful to have a good relationship with Oakland PD,” said Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. “One of our officers was at the right place at the right time, and with their assistance we were able to Staff photo An officer walks a detained suspect to the back of a police car. arrest the juvenile suspects in question. It’s all about collaboration and we’re grateful for the opportunity to collaborate with Oakland PD.” “The officer [I talked to] told me to buy a new car, and ‘maybe not invest in a KIA,’” said Pease. KIA model cars have been a frequent target of car thefts in recent months because of their lack of security measures. There are several methods that criminals can use to easily start the car without keys. There are also videos online detailing these methods step by step. The anonymous witness said that he doubted anything would happen to the two suspects because they were minors. “They’re being cooperative [with police officers], but they’re smiling like it’s nothing,” he said. Pease said that she believes that strong community ties are important for maintaining public safety in light of these events. “I think that making sure that you’re in contact with your neighbors and having a better community is what needs to happen. We just need to be watching each other’s back,” said Pease.
articles.title: Piedmont, Oakland police arrest 2 teens in attempted car theft

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, October 4, 2023 Piedmont, Oakland police arrest 2 teens in attempted car theft Photo by Jeff Hansen Police blocked off part of Grand Avenue after two people were arrested for attempted car theft. By Matt Simons “Hey, someone’s breaking into your car,” whispered a coworker to Adele Pease. Tuesday, October 3 at around 2 p.m. marked the second time this month someone had broken into her car. It was even on the same street as last time. When she arrived at her car, her window was smashed in and the wires under her steering wheel were ripped out. Someone had tried to hotwire her car. That’s when she saw two figures sprinting in opposite directions on Boulevard Way near the corner of Grand Avenue. “At that point, a man came up [to me] and said that he had called 911,” said Pease. “That’s when all the police started coming,” added an eyewitness who has asked to remain anonymous. “Undercover police cars came out of nowhere chasing someone into Piedmont,” the witness added. “You wouldn’t have even known they were undercover [police] until their lights started flashing.” The suspects allegedly hid between houses in the area after Staff photo Piedmont and Oakland police officers on Grand Avenue gather to take statements after an attempted car theft. their theft attempt before running away. Piedmont and Oakland police arrived within minutes and both suspects were apprehended. Both suspects were juveniles wearing black hooded sweatshirts with camouflage bandanas covering the lower half of their faces. “We’re just grateful to have a good relationship with Oakland PD,” said Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. “One of our officers was at the right place at the right time, and with their assistance we were able to Staff photo An officer walks a detained suspect to the back of a police car. arrest the juvenile suspects in question. It’s all about collaboration and we’re grateful for the opportunity to collaborate with Oakland PD.” “The officer [I talked to] told me to buy a new car, and ‘maybe not invest in a KIA,’” said Pease. KIA model cars have been a frequent target of car thefts in recent months because of their lack of security measures. There are several methods that criminals can use to easily start the car without keys. There are also videos online detailing these methods step by step. The anonymous witness said that he doubted anything would happen to the two suspects because they were minors. “They’re being cooperative [with police officers], but they’re smiling like it’s nothing,” he said. Pease said that she believes that strong community ties are important for maintaining public safety in light of these events. “I think that making sure that you’re in contact with your neighbors and having a better community is what needs to happen. We just need to be watching each other’s back,” said Pease. 2023 Calendar of Events October 5 - October 18 Meetings may be viewed on KCOM (Channel 27) and on the City’s website: piedmont.ca.gov.
